Trump Says US ‘Working Very Hard’ to End War in Ukraine Amid CIA Chief’s Visit to Moscow
“We believe it will not take place in the central cities,” Zelensky said. “But I don’t think they will be able to hide it very well.”
The European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) records Russia’s inactive mobilization reserve at approximately 25 million people, based on a 2022 claim by then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu. Russia’s active mobilization reserve officially consists of two million people, although researcher Igor Gretskiy said the actual figure may be below one million and that the number is a state secret.
The report does not present either figure as an estimate of how many reservists Russia could immediately train, equip and deploy.
Yet, Moscow denies all the reports regardless.
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, now known for his dubious social media commentary, said in March that there was no need for a new mobilization. In July, he called reports of an impending call-up “nonsense” and a “lying provocation” by Ukraine.
State Duma Defense Committee Chairman Andrei Kartapolov has likewise said there is “no need” for mobilization, while prominent state television figures have complained that rumors of another call-up are spreading across Russia.
On Aug. 21, Russia’s UN Ambassador Vasily Nebenzya said mass mobilization was “not planned or expected, as far as I know.”
He then added: “But let’s see what happens after the elections: who among us will be right and who won’t.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov followed on Aug. 25 by calling the reports “information canards” deliberately spread by Ukraine to destabilize Russia.
Echoes of 2022
The Kremlin has a habit of denying its obvious intentions.
On Sept. 13, 2022, Peskov said neither full nor partial mobilization was under consideration. Eight days later, Putin announced the mobilization of approximately 300,000 reservists.
By Oct. 28, 2022, Shoigu said 82,000 of the 300,000 mobilized personnel had been deployed to Ukraine and 218,000 were undergoing training. Mediazona calculated from marriage-registration data that approximately 492,000 men had been mobilized by mid-October, although the EUAA said it could not verify the methodology.
The call-up produced an immediate exodus and protests. OVD-Info said at least 200,000 people left Russia during the first week. It recorded 2,457 arrests at anti-mobilization protests between Sept. 21 and Oct. 10, including 976 in Moscow, 655 in St. Petersburg and 121 in Dagestan.
Women accounted for 56% of detainees in cases where gender was known. OVD-Info also documented military summonses being issued to detained protesters inside police stations in Moscow, Voronezh, Irkutsk and Ryazan.
In Dagestan, police clashed with anti-mobilization protesters and fired warning shots. At least 100 people were detained at a protest on Sept. 25, according to Reuters.
Russia subsequently declared that the call-up had been completed, but Putin never issued a decree formally terminating it.
According to Daniil Chebykin, a Yerevan-based Russian regional political activist and founder of the Omsk Civic Association, recruitment has quietly continued, with Russian authorities offering increasingly large payments to men who sign military contracts.
Why Russians don’t want to serve
Yet, the scheme effectively exhausted itself.
Chebykin told Kyiv Post that support for the war is substantially lower than official narratives suggest.
He is involved with Tvyordy Znak, a project that helps Russians avoid mobilization or leave the military after reaching the front. He said that when its anti-mobilization hotline began operating in 2022, most requests came from civilians trying to avoid being drafted.
By 2026, an increasing share of requests came from soldiers who had already reached the front and wanted to escape.
Even the relatively small Tvyordy Znak project receives more than 200 requests per day, Chebykin said. Other organizations, including Idite Lesom and Stoparmy, work with similar cases.
The men seeking help generally fall into two groups. Some were mobilized in 2022 and initially supported the war or accepted the Kremlin’s explanations but changed their views after experiencing military service and frontline conditions.
Others are younger conscripts caught in what Chebykin describes as a system of permanent mobilization. Electronic draft notices can trigger restrictions on travel and access to state services, while conscripts face pressure to sign contracts that allow the military to deploy them to Ukraine.
Higher salaries and signing bonuses are losing some of their appeal as inflation reduces their real value and information about Russia’s casualty rates becomes more difficult to ignore.
Chebykin said soldiers also become disillusioned by their treatment at the hands of commanders and by the difference between state propaganda and what they encounter in Ukraine.
“They increasingly understand that they are not fighting Nazis and that they are not defending Russia from NATO,” he said. “They see how they are treated by their own commanders and begin questioning why they are there at all.”
Russia still cannot take Donbas
Russia’s manpower problem is clearest when battlefield losses are compared with territorial results.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Russia controls approximately 79.9% of Donetsk region and 99.77% of Luhansk region.
That leaves roughly 5,300 square kilometers (2,046 square miles) of Donetsk region outside Russian control, including major elements of Ukraine’s fortified Slovyansk–Kramatorsk–Druzhkivka–Kostiantynivka belt.
The ISW has counted 15 separate deadlines set by Putin since 2022 for Russian forces to seize all of Donetsk region. Russia has missed every one.
The latest results are particularly damaging to Moscow’s claim that its forces are advancing everywhere.
Between Aug. 1 and Aug. 22, the ISW observed Russian forces seizing or infiltrating approximately 8.5 square kilometers (3.3 square miles) of Ukrainian territory. During the same period, Russia lost control of approximately 27 square kilometers (10.4 square miles).
Even counting infiltrated areas as gains, Russia lost more than three square kilometers for every square kilometer it entered. On those measurements, its net territorial position moved backward by approximately 18.6 square kilometers (7.2 square miles).
Ukraine’s General Staff reported approximately 29,120 Russian casualties between July 31 and Aug. 22 – around 1,270 killed or wounded per day. The casualty figure is a Ukrainian estimate and cannot be independently confirmed, but ISW used it to illustrate the increasingly negative relationship between Russian losses and territorial gains. (ISW)
Mobilization would deepen Russia’s economic problem
A new call-up would arrive as Russia’s fiscal room is narrowing.
The federal budget deficit reached approximately 6.46 trillion rubles – around $79 billion – during the first seven months of 2026.
Russia’s National Wealth Fund held 3.69 trillion rubles, or $46.2 billion, in liquid assets on Aug. 1. The accumulated seven-month deficit was therefore approximately 1.75 times larger than the fund’s remaining liquid portion.
Though Russia is not four months from insolvency – and Moscow can issue debt, raise taxes, cut civilian spending and sell assets – the liquid reserve created to absorb economic shocks is no longer large enough to cover the deficit already accumulated this year.
The state has also expanded its direct control over private property. Research cited by Reuters found that Russia confiscated approximately $50 billion in assets between 2022 and mid-2025. By March 2026, the head of Russia’s Federal Property Management Agency said around 805 companies had entered state ownership through court decisions.
The seizures illustrate the extent to which the Kremlin is concentrating economic resources as the war continues.
Mobilization would also remove more workers from an economy already facing severe skilled-labor shortages.
Russia’s Labor Ministry estimates that the country will require almost 140,000 additional welders and gas cutters and another 150,000 machinists, millers and CNC operators by 2032. Those occupations are essential for producing and repairing military equipment, industrial machinery, pipelines and damaged infrastructure.
The same workforce is being asked to expand military production, repair facilities damaged by Ukrainian strikes and provide recruits for the army.
Ukraine is adding to the repair burden
Repeated Ukrainian strikes have made that labor constraint more important.
Russian gasoline production covered only around 65% of seasonal demand by July 10 after attacks and unplanned refinery shutdowns disrupted production. Moscow responded by restricting fuel exports and arranging imports from Belarus, Kazakhstan, India and other suppliers.
By Aug. 24, AI-95 gasoline was reportedly available at only 22% of Russia’s operating filling stations, according to data from the Benzonavt monitoring service.
The pressure also reaches military production.
Ukraine struck the Kamensky Combine in Rostov Oblast on Aug. 16. Ukraine’s General Staff said two workshops producing explosives and propellants were destroyed and four others damaged.
The plant produces solid rocket propellant for Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems. Ukrainian forces struck it again eight days later, although the consequences of the second attack remain under assessment.
Each repeat strike forces Russia to devote additional workers, equipment and money to repairs while attempting to replace battlefield losses and expand weapons production.
Ratcliffe’s Moscow visit and the NATO warning
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Aug. 25 for talks with Russian intelligence officials.
The Kremlin said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin, although the Russian president was briefed on the discussions. Neither side disclosed the agenda.
Washington informed Kyiv that a senior delegation was traveling to Moscow and asked Ukraine to suspend strikes until it had left Russia, according to CBS News. Kyiv reportedly complied.
It was the first known visit to Moscow by a serving CIA director since William Burns traveled there in November 2021 to warn Russia against invading Ukraine.
The Wall Street Journal reported that US intelligence had identified early Russian preparations for a possible mobilization and separate plans to test NATO’s resolve.
A separate US intelligence assessment said Putin could use a limited assault on a NATO member within the next few years, with scenarios ranging from a cyberattack to a small-scale land incursion (The Wall Street Journal).
Euronews reported one theory being that Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn against further Russian escalation. The report linked the theory to US intelligence concerns that a new mobilization could be used not only for the war against Ukraine but also for provocations intended to test NATO. (Euronews)
There is no public evidence that Ratcliffe delivered such a warning or that mobilization was discussed.
Asked on Aug. 26 whether Ratcliffe had gone to warn the Kremlin against testing NATO or to discuss sanctions on Iran, Trump replied, “None of the above,” and called the trip “semi-routine.” He suggested that it could contribute to efforts to end the war.
Ratcliffe had, however, publicly described Russia’s battlefield problem just weeks earlier. In July, he said US intelligence was consistent with open-source estimates that a new Russian recruit entering frontline combat could be killed or wounded within 20 to 35 minutes because of Ukraine’s drones. He also said Russia had captured only around 1% of Ukraine during the previous 18 months
The Kremlin’s choice is becoming narrower
Mobilization would not solve Russia’s problems immediately. Hundreds of thousands of men would have to be processed, equipped and trained before they could support large-scale operations.
It would also risk another exodus, deepen labor shortages and force the Kremlin to explain why years of paid contract recruitment have failed to produce a decisive result.
Avoiding mobilization carries its own cost. Russia would have to continue paying larger bonuses, using more coercive recruitment methods and committing most new soldiers to replacing casualties rather than creating new offensive forces.
If Putin ultimately orders another mobilization, it will not be evidence that Russia’s existing strategy is succeeding. Rather, an admission that the strategy no longer supplies enough men to pursue the objectives he refuses to abandon.

Innovative virtual reality treadmill therapy offers relief for treatment-resistant PTSD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
20:00:06 UTC
05:00:06 KST

A study involving Canadian military veterans, public safety personnel, and healthcare workers showed that their PTSD, depression, and anxiety symptoms decreased after 10 to 14 weeks of 3MDR therapy. Their difficulties with life functioning were also reduced. The improvements were still present 12 months after the treatments ended. The paper was published in Brain and Behavior.
Multimodal Motion-Assisted Memory Desensitization and Reconsolidation (3MDR) is an innovative psychotherapy developed for people suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly those who have not responded sufficiently to conventional trauma-focused treatments. It combines established principles of exposure therapy (a psychological treatment that helps people safely confront traumatic memories) and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) with walking and an immersive virtual environment.
During treatment, patients walk on a treadmill toward personally selected images related to their traumatic experiences, while music and other cues are used to help evoke relevant memories and emotions. With the therapist’s guidance, patients describe the memories, thoughts, feelings, and bodily reactions that emerge rather than avoiding distressing traumatic material. An attention task involving eye movements is then used while the traumatic memory is active, with the aim of facilitating further processing and reducing its emotional intensity. The combination of movement, immersive stimulation, exposure, and memory-processing techniques is intended to make it easier for patients to approach memories that they might otherwise strongly avoid.
3MDR was initially developed for military personnel and veterans with combat-related and treatment-resistant PTSD (defined as having tried two or more previous therapies without success) but has subsequently been studied in other groups exposed to severe trauma. Overall, 3MDR represents a promising new approach for treating PTSD, especially in cases where avoidance or limited response to conventional therapy makes treatment particularly difficult.
Study co-first authors Matthew Robert Graham Brown and Phillip R. Sevigny, along with their colleagues, conducted a study in which they examined the effectiveness of 3MDR in Canadian military veterans. They also wanted to test it with public safety personnel (police, firefighters, paramedics, etc.) and frontline healthcare workers. Their general hypothesis was that 3MDR treatment would lead to improvements in mental health symptoms of participants and that the improvements would still be present a year after treatment.
Study participants were initially 56 Canadian military members and Veterans, public safety personnel, and healthcare workers. However, eight participants were excluded from the analysis for various reasons, making the total number of study participants 48. Twenty-four participants were women. Their average age was 45.4 years. Seventeen participants were Canadian military veterans or active members of the military, 21 were public safety personnel, and 21 were healthcare workers. All of them exhibited clinically relevant symptoms of PTSD. Twenty-two of them met criteria for treatment-resistant PTSD, and this included all 17 military members and Veterans.
Participants received 3MDR therapy at the Edmonton Operational Stress Injury Clinic (EOSIC), which partnered with the research team for this study, or at one of three clinical research sites: University of Alberta main campus in Edmonton, Alberta; Alberta Hospital Edmonton; or University of Alberta space rented at the University of Calgary’s downtown campus in Calgary, Alberta. The 3MDR treatment lasted 10 to 14 weeks.
At the start of the study and at the end of the treatment program, participants completed the CAPS-5 clinical interview (an assessment of PTSD symptoms). A smaller group of 30 participants who were available for the follow-up also completed it 3, 6, and 12 months after the end of the treatment. At the start of the study and after specific sessions during the treatment, participants also completed assessments of depression, anxiety, and difficulties with life functioning. Participants completed an assessment of resilience before the 3MDR treatment and after it was complete.
Results showed that participants’ PTSD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and difficulties with life functioning improved after the 3MDR treatment. These improvements were still present 12 months after the treatment ended. Resilience also showed improvement from before to after the treatment.
“These results support the growing body of literature illustrating 3MDR as an effective treatment for military-related PTSD as well as PTSD-related mental health conditions in public safety personnel and healthcare workers,” the study authors concluded.
The study sheds light on the effectiveness of 3MDR therapy as a treatment for PTSD. However, the study did not include a control group, although the study authors anticipated a natural waitlist control group to form due to expected scheduling delays, which ultimately did not occur. Because of this, it remains unclear how much of the reported improvements are a consequence of the treatment and how much can be attributed to natural reductions in symptoms over time or factors not related to the 3MDR treatment.
The paper, “3MDR Therapy Reduces Symptoms of PTSD and Related Conditions in Canadian Military Members and Veterans, Public Safety Personnel, and Clinical Personnel,” was authored by Matthew Robert Graham Brown, Phillip R. Sevigny, Katherine S. Bright, Helen Chau, Patricia Chai, Andrew J. Greenshaw, Lisa Burback, Olga Winkler, Chelsea Jones, and Suzette Brémault-Phillips.

Israeli entertainment continues to attract international attention, but the industry is facing challenges that could affect future productions, Jerusalem Post film critic Hannah Brown said on the latest episode of The Jerusalem Playlist.
This episode examines the current state of Israeli television, including the success of series such as Fauda, which will arrive on Netflix internationally on September 8. Brown explained that while Israeli television remains highly creative and continues to produce successful shows, producers are concerned about reduced budgets, uncertainty surrounding public broadcaster Kan, and a decline in international co-production funding. Because television projects can take years to develop, the impact of these issues may only become visible in several years.
Strength of Israeli television
Brown highlighted the long-standing strength of Israeli television, pointing to the success of In Treatment, a series built around conversations between a psychologist and patients that was later adapted internationally, including by HBO. She said the show demonstrated how Israeli creators have been able to develop original concepts that are both cost-effective and emotionally compelling.
The discussion also focused on Fauda season five and how the October 7 attacks reshaped the production. Brown said the creators scrapped their original plans and rewrote the season to reflect how the events would affect the show’s counterterrorism unit. The season includes flashback episodes depicting October 7, which were described as emotionally difficult for the cast and crew to film.
Brown also discussed Gal Gadot’s upcoming Amazon Prime Video thriller, in which she plays a London lawyer forced into a dangerous situation after her son is kidnapped. She praised Gadot’s strengths in action roles and noted the involvement of director Kevin Macdonald, who won an Oscar for One Day in September.
The episode concluded with a discussion about controversy surrounding the novel Upward Bound, attributed to autistic author Woody Brown. Brown examined questions raised over facilitated communication methods while emphasizing the importance of supporting genuine communication tools for people on the autism spectrum.

Col. (res.) "These images are a disgrace, and this is anarchy," Kahana said. "A member of Knesset, a person who did not serve in the IDF, is acting in such an anarchistic way. It harms the State of Israel, and it is shameful that such a party purports to represent the religious-Zionist public."
Kahana supports smashing memorials to terrorists
Kahana said he believed such memorials should be removed, but not in the manner Sukkot had done.
"These memorials to terrorists need to be smashed, no question about it. It only shows whom our enemies glorify, but we are a state: We have an army, police, and a government. If this were important to the right-wing government, it would order the IDF to destroy these memorials," the former minister said.
"It is amazing to see how something that was so firmly in the consensus has become controversial," he continued. "It is clear that Zvi Sukkot did this to get a video and attention, and he does not care that this is not how a properly functioning country is supposed to operate. Smotrich's party is showing that it does not care about the institutions of the state when a person like this endangers IDF troops and manipulates them."
Winter is in the Netanyahu bloc, Kahana says

Small parties should unite or withdraw

"Based on his latest statements, it is difficult to determine which bloc he belongs to and whether he intends to replace Netanyahu," Kahana said.
"Anyone who does not have six seats should either unite or withdraw," he added.

"Exactly what I said about Gantz applies to Chili, even though he is a good and worthy person," Kahana said.

Israeli arms, Iranian drones, Turkish oil: Azerbaijan’s high-stakes balancing act

“We cannot close our eyes and say there is no Iran, there is no Russia. There are.”
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Nargiz Mammadova, a research fellow in international relations at the CASPIA Center, was describing the reality Azerbaijan confronts whenever it looks at the map. Speaking with The Media Line in Jerusalem, she said decisions made in Moscow or Tehran cannot be dismissed as distant developments. Both countries border Azerbaijan, placing instability in either one directly inside Baku’s security calculations.
Mammadova was among 13 Muslim professionals from Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan brought to Israel by Sharaka, a nongovernmental organization founded after the 2020 Abraham Accords to promote people-to-people diplomacy between Israelis and communities across the Arab and Muslim worlds.
Holocaust remembrance and meetings about Israeli society were part of the visit, but regional security was never far from the discussion. For the Azerbaijani participants, Israel is one element of a crowded diplomatic picture that also includes Russia, Iran, Turkey, Armenia and the wider South Caucasus.
The result is a foreign policy built less around choosing sides than keeping several doors open. Azerbaijan buys Israeli weapons, regards Turkey as a vital ally, trades with Russia, shares a long border with Iran and is pursuing peace with Armenia after decades of conflict.
Azerbaijan is surrounded by countries at war
“If you look to the map in the South Caucasus, Azerbaijan has five neighbors, and two of them are into war situation, or kind of war situation,” Mammadova said.
She described the ability to work with competing powers as a defining characteristic of Azerbaijani diplomacy. Baku, she argued, cannot afford to organize its foreign policy around one dominant relationship.
Mammadova applied the same reasoning to Armenia, saying agreements between governments must be accompanied by “building bridges between people” and greater trust between the two societies.
Farid Shukurlu, an international law and security researcher and nonresident fellow at the Research Institute for European and American Studies, told The Media Line that his criticism was directed at the Iranian regime and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), not at Iranian society.
IRGC targeted Azerbaijan
“Even though Azerbaijan’s position was formally neutrality, the country was still targeted by the IRGC in the Nakhchivan enclave,” he said.
Nakhchivan is an Azerbaijani exclave separated from the rest of the country by Armenian territory. Azerbaijan said four drones arriving from Iran struck the region on March 5, injuring four people and damaging Nakhchivan International Airport and a school. Iran denied responsibility and promised an investigation.
The incident demonstrated, in Shukurlu’s view, that avoiding direct participation in a conflict does not necessarily protect Azerbaijan from pressure or military spillover from its southern neighbor.
Those concerns have contributed to stronger defense ties with Israel. Azerbaijan has purchased Israeli weapons for years and used Israeli-made systems during its conflicts with Armenian forces over Nagorno-Karabakh.
Shukurlu said “the military cooperation between Azerbaijan and Israel is at an all-time high,” but rejected suggestions that Baku would allow the relationship to turn Azerbaijani territory into a base for military action.
“It’s also in Azerbaijan’s national security concept not to get dragged into regional conflicts,” he said. “Azerbaijani territory will never be used against a third state.”
Balancing relations with Israel, Turkey
Baku faces a different balancing problem when relations deteriorate between Israel and Turkey. Ankara remains one of Azerbaijan’s closest political and security partners, while Israel has become an important supplier of military technology.
Shukurlu said Azerbaijani officials see no reason to sacrifice either relationship.
“Azerbaijan is not going to give up on Israel, Azerbaijan is not going to give up on Turkey, because these countries are equally important to our security, to our existence, and to our image in the international arena,” he said.
Energy makes the triangle even harder to separate.
Ibrahim Mammadov, head of the Turkic-Western Engagement Initiative and a visiting research fellow at the Danube Institute, pointed to the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, which carries crude oil from Azerbaijan through Georgia to Turkey’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan. Some of that oil is then loaded onto tankers bound for Israel.
“I do not believe that it will ever stop because, for Azerbaijan, it’s an extremely important pipeline,” he told The Media Line.
Closing the route would hurt Azerbaijan by restricting one of its principal export channels and Israel by reducing a major source of crude oil. Turkey receives transit and port benefits, while the state-owned Turkish Petroleum Corporation holds a stake in the pipeline consortium.
The same network that binds the three countries together economically also gives Baku a reason to prevent disputes between Israel and Turkey from becoming direct confrontations.
Azerbaijan has already hosted several rounds of talks between Israeli and Turkish officials seeking to prevent clashes in Syria, where both countries maintain competing security interests.
“We know that there have been formal and informal talks that were held in Baku,” Mammadov said.
He wants Azerbaijan to continue serving as a meeting place when its two partners cannot speak easily elsewhere.
“I hope they can be found in the middle ground.”

Al-Hijri has repeatedly thanked Israel for its position. His rhetoric has since evolved from calls for international protection and self-determination toward more explicit references to Israel as a potential player in determining Sweida's future.

Iran, Oman still negotiating Hormuz deal as Qatar joins mediation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:52:32 UTC
04:52:32 KST

Iran and Oman are still working out details of a possible agreement governing navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a senior Iranian source told Reuters on Wednesday, contradicting an earlier claim by an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson that the two countries had reached an agreement on shipping routes.
It was not immediately clear how advanced the negotiations were. Iranian officials said earlier this month that an agreement over the strategic waterway was close.
Qatar, meanwhile, is also holding talks with Tehran. Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said in an X post that Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani would travel to Tehran on Thursday for meetings with senior Iranian officials aimed at discussing ways to “de-escalate tensions & create the conditions conducive to dialogue.”
“The visit comes in line with the State of Qatar’s firm position that the diplomatic path is the best means of resolving differences & promoting security & stability in the region,” Al Ansari said. He said the talks would also address freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and “the need for it to return to the status quo prior to February 28.”
The strait, a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, is one of the world’s most important energy corridors.
Earlier Wednesday, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi blamed the United States for delaying negotiations and warned that Iran would keep the strait closed unless Washington accepted Tehran’s conditions.
“If the United States does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not open,” Mohebbi said.
“The Strait of Hormuz is under our control, and there are no enemy warships in the Gulf,” he said, claiming that all hostile warships were at least 400 kilometers, or about 250 miles, from the strait. “From a military and regional perspective, no vessel can cross this waterway without Iran’s permission and management.”
Mohebbi said political disagreements were natural but called for unity “in the face of the enemy.”
“If the United States stops creating obstacles and returns to the memorandum of understanding, we can open the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “The maritime corridor near Oman is under our full control. We have reached an agreement with Oman concerning our portion of the waters of Hormuz and the distribution of its revenues.”
The senior Iranian source who spoke to Reuters, however, said details of an agreement were still being worked out.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he was in no rush to return to negotiations with Tehran.
“I have no time schedule, none. I’m not in a hurry. I have no time schedule at all,” Trump said. “I have no time schedule; whatever it takes.”
Trump said the United States was “winning very big” as Iran suffered from inflation and an economy he described as collapsing. Trump has maintained that the Strait of Hormuz is open and safe for shipping and said Wednesday that the United States would achieve “a big victory in Iran very soon.”
Oil prices, meanwhile, fell more than 1.5% for a third consecutive day amid signs of renewed mediation efforts aimed at ending the war.
Iran declares Persian-language media ‘military targets’
Iran’s armed forces separately said several Persian-language media outlets operating outside the country, including BBC Persian, had been placed on what it called its list of “military targets,” accusing them of working for U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies.
Iranian armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said the list also included Iran International and Radio Farda.
Iran designated BBC Persian and Iran International as terrorist organizations in 2022.
“These hostile media outlets are soldiers of Zionism and the United States, and they are on our list of military targets,” Shekarchi said, accusing them of being “directly connected to Mossad, the CIA and enemy intelligence services.”
“Iran’s armed forces do not consider them media outlets,” he added.
Iranian authorities have repeatedly accused Persian-language news organizations based abroad of cooperating with Israel and Western governments. Access to many such outlets is restricted inside Iran, where viewers often use virtual private networks, or VPNs, to circumvent government controls.
The latest threat comes amid a broader crackdown on information since the war involving Iran, Israel and the United States began Feb. 28.
In mid-August, Iranian authorities seized control of a YouTube channel that had broadcast interviews with Iranian intellectuals and public figures discussing current political and social issues, accusing it of spreading “misinformation.”
The program’s founder and host, who lives in Iran, was also questioned by authorities and later released on bail.

For its latest special uniform celebrating the heritage of airpower, the U.S. Air Force Academy football team is looking to the future: the B-21 Raider.
The Academy unveiled the new outfit Aug. 25, replete with the B-21’s lambda wing silhouette and other visual details from the new sixth-generation bomber. The Falcons will wear the uniform Oct. 10 when they welcome Navy to Colorado Springs, Colo.
In keeping with the secrecy around the B-21 and its stealth nature, the new uniforms are minimalist and the Academy provided a relatively short list of details explaining the visual references.
“The uniform draws from the bomber’s distinctive shape, stealth, and advanced technology, with Air Force aviation details woven throughout the design,” Northrop Grumman said in a statement.
The uniform is mostly black, with lettering and numbers rendered in a metallic silver. The helmet has an oversized B-21 silhouette rendered in grey against a camouflage background, plus another silhouette across the back. The silhouette also appears as a shoulder patch, on the thigh of the pants, and on the players’ gloves.
The helmet has “B-21” on the front bumper just above the face mask, and “Northrop Grumman,” the B-21 manufacturer, across the back bumper.
Each of the uniforms features one of three patches on the collarbone: Air Force Materiel Command, Air Force Global Strike Command, and the 412th Test Wing. Those emblems are all on the test B-21s currently being flown out of Edwards Air Force Base, Calif.
Instead of the players’ names on the back, the jerseys will feature either the phrase “Strategic Deterrence” or “Power Projection,” reflecting the B-21’s nuclear and long-range strike missions. “B-21 Raider” will run vertically down both pant legs.
One detail sure to please aviation enthusiasts: red “Remove Before Flight” towels.
This is the 11th edition of the Academy’s Air Power Legacy Series of uniforms, always worn for a game against a rival service academy. Previous versions have touched on every era of Air Force history, from World War II (the Tuskegee Airmen and Doolittle Raiders) to Vietnam (Operation Linebacker II) to the present day (the F-35 and the Space Force).
Air Power Legacy Series
- 2025: F-16
- 2024: Air Force Special Operations Command
- 2023: Doolittle Raiders
- 2022: Space Force
- 2021: B-52 Stratofortress and Operation Linebacker II
- 2020: Tuskegee Airmen
- 2019: C-17 Globemaster III
- 2018: AC-130 Spooky
- 2017: F-35 Lightning II
- 2016: Tiger Shark Teeth nose art
Air Force enters the 2026 season seeking its 22nd Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy, awarded to the top service academy. It starts play Sept. 5 against Duquesne, faces Navy on Oct. 10, and takes on Army on Nov. 7.
The B-21, meanwhile, is progressing through testing and is expected to arrive at its first operational base, Ellsworth Air Force Base, S.D., in 2027.

E. coli, Salmonella, Cyclospora: Is the U.S. Seeing a Surge in Foodborne Illnesses?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:51:11 UTC
04:51:11 KST

This summer, it’s been hard for consumers to know what to put in their grocery cart. Recalls have affected hundreds of products, including lettuce, which was linked to a Cyclospora outbreak; eggs and jalapenos that were connected with salmonella; and blueberries that were potentially contaminated with E. coli.
These incidents have left shoppers across the United States wondering whether this summer has been a particularly bad one for foodborne illnesses.
Here’s what to know—and why consumers may be perceiving a greater number of outbreaks than usual, despite what the data shows.
The number of food recalls are about average, but a few have been unusually severe
According to federal data, the number of food recalls regulated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is relatively on par with an average year. So far, there have been 483 recalls in this fiscal year (Oct. 1, 2025 through Sept. 30, 2026), with a projected total of 551 by the end of October. In the past decade, the U.S. has seen a range of 400-800 annual recalls.
But what stands out in 2026 is the severity of some of the outbreaks caused by contaminated food this year.
“I don't know that I would necessarily say there are more outbreaks,” says Janet Hamilton, the executive director of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists. “However, what I would say is the scale and magnitude of outbreaks that we're facing right now are unprecedented. It's like we're being eclipsed by the scale and magnitude of these outbreaks with the staffing levels that we have.”
The summer’s Cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce alone sickened more than 10,000 people, caused over 400 hospitalizations, and led to at least two deaths, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Epidemiologists believe it could be among the largest documented foodborne illness events in U.S. history.
"We've never seen anything like that before,” Hamilton says.
The volume of food affected is higher than average
While the total number of recalls has been about average, USDA-regulated recalls affected more than 37 million pounds of food during the first half of 2026—the highest it has been in a decade.
At the same time, epidemiologist and former CDC adviser Katelyn Jetelina says that it’s very hard to tell just how bad this summer’s outbreaks have been—and our lack of federal data does not help.
“Our data is just not great in the United States,” she tells TIME. “We’re patching things together to try to figure out what is reality versus concern and public perception, and it's hard to know where the line is.”
“That’s what's most frustrating for me as an epidemiologist as well as a mom,” she adds.
There are seasonal factors, and surveillance has improved
It’s normal for foodborne illnesses to peak in the summer, since warmer temperatures help bacteria and other organisms multiply. That is why there have been more outbreak incidents in recent months. But this is a consistent seasonal threat, epidemiologists say, and not specific to 2026.
There has also been an increase in media attention around food safety, which can make it seem like the magnitude of any given event is higher than it actually is. This increased coverage is partially due to improved surveillance tools. Laboratories are better equipped than ever to detect foodborne illnesses, track how bacteria multiply, and find links between patients.
Because we have more information than ever on some of these bacteria, and we are able to process data faster than ever before, this means that the information can be quickly and easily shared with the population—which potentially makes it feel like the country is experiencing more outbreaks, when consumers are really just seeing more updates.
Federal staffing shortages may be weakening the safety net
Experts say that while we are able to more quickly detect and identify food safety issues in past decades, health departments at the federal and state levels have experienced significant decreases in funding and staffing—potentially weakening food safety oversight. It can be hard to tell how this is impacting outbreaks.
One potential outcome is having less ability to monitor and control an existing outbreak, Hamilton says.
“Health departments are mounting responses quickly, but when the outbreaks need additional sustained surge support, the system is quickly overwhelmed,” she says. “That leads to situations like what we have seen with Cyclospora. This would have been a complicated outbreak to begin with, and then when you don't have the staffing to keep pace with the level of detailed interviews that you need, the ability to rapidly control the outbreak diminishes.”
Hamilton and her colleagues at the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists conduct regular surveys to track staffing levels in state and territorial health departments, and their recent reports found that one-third of public health officials in state health departments have left their positions since the Trump Administration took control in 2025. On the federal level, some of the staffing cuts were led by the Department of Government Efficiency.
Federal cuts to the CDC and FDA also affect state and local health departments, since federal funds provide more than half of their total budgets, according to KFF.
Hamilton says that public health officials are like a “protective shield” around the complicated food systems in our country. Workers look at data “carefully and thoughtfully,” interview people impacted by foodborne illness, and “tease apart” what foods might be contaminated.
This work is harder with fewer staff members who are stretched increasingly thin. Even advanced tracking and surveillance technology may not be able to counter the loss of knowledgeable human engagement amid these outbreaks.
“Our food supply chains are complicated, and I don't know that people really appreciate the detailed work and the complexity that goes behind understanding where foods and ingredients come from and exactly how people are exposed,” she adds.
Jetelina adds that part of the role of public health officials is distinguishing “correlation from causation”—a consideration that applies directly to questions about whether and how staffing and funding cuts have affected responses to illness outbreaks this year. Reduced oversight may have allowed some contamination events to go undetected or unaddressed, while staffing shortages may have delayed the collection and dissemination of information that could have helped officials contain outbreaks and reduce the risk to consumers. But without further investigation, it is difficult to determine exactly how the cuts affected the number of recalls, the speed of outbreak responses, or other key measures in 2026.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said that cuts to the CDC and FDA have not hampered the investigation of Cyclospora.
“Those criticisms are invalid,” Kennedy said during a press briefing on July 21. “We had no cuts in the surveillance program. We did cuts in the FoodNet program, but they were for redundant surveillance.”
FoodNet, short for the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, was no longer required to actively report on six of eight pathogens, including Cyclospora, as of 2025. The CDC characterized the change in a statement to the Associated Press in August 2025 as a way to “prioritize core activities” and “steward resources effectively.”
TIME has reached out to the CDC and FDA for comment.
When it comes to consumer safety, it’s important to note that the vast majority of food moving through the system is free from contamination. Experts say consumers can stay safe from outbreaks by keeping up with food recalls, washing produce well, refrigerating produce properly, and monitoring symptoms linked to foodborne illnesses.

Russia’s fleet is set to get 150 uncrewed vessels in 2026, and possibly 230. Sanctions are holding the build back

04:48:21 KST

Russia is trying to build the weapon Ukraine used against it. The Russian fleet is set to receive more than 150 uncrewed surface vessels in 2026, with the state order possibly rising to 230 units, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence told Oboronka.
Ukraine's naval drones drove Russia's Black Sea Fleet out of its main base. Magura strike drones operated by Defense Intelligence sank or damaged more than a dozen Russian vessels and forced the fleet to relocate from Sevastopol to Novorossiysk, roughly 300 kilometers east.
Russia is now ordering the same class of weapon in volume, three years after Ukraine first attacked Sevastopol with drone boats in October 2022.
Intelligence lists Russia's priorities
Ukraine's Defense Intelligence has identified what Russia is prioritizing in its uncrewed surface vessel program. Those are building universal drones from Russian-made components, integrating protected communications and artificial intelligence, and increasing the vessels' operating range.
Sanctions slow the build
Russian production is held back by a shortage of electronic components caused by sanctions, according to the agency. Moscow is finding it harder to import and to develop communications resistant to electronic warfare, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence said.
Limits on Starlink access may also have shaped Russia's naval drone development, the agency added. Russian forces had actively used the terminals to control uncrewed systems.
The imitation runs behind the original
Ukraine unveiled the Magura V11, the largest boat in the family, at its Independence Day drone parade on 24 August.
Rather than ramming ships like the one-way craft that cleared the Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol, the V11 carries and launches other drones and stays at sea up to seven days.
UFORCE said the drone carries up to 2,200 kg (about 4,850 pounds) and can stay at sea for up to seven days. The company built it for reconnaissance, surveillance, support of landing operations, and resupplying fuel and equipment to other naval drones.

Tim Curry Dies at 80. Here Are the Movies and TV Shows That Made Him Unforgettable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:46:40 UTC
04:46:40 KST

Tim Curry, a multitalented star of the stage and screen, died Tuesday at his home at the age of 80. The three-time Tony Award-nominated icon was best known for his eccentric characters, his musical background, and his comedic chops, leading to a varied and successful career in cult classics and box office hits.
Curry “passed away peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles,” according to a statement from his longtime manager Marcia Hurwitz. The cause of death has not been made public, but Curry had suffered from several health issues since having a severe stroke in 2012.
Though he was best-known for donning fishnets and a corset as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in 1975’s “Rocky Horror Picture Show,” Curry had left his mark with a wide-ranging career spanning albums, voice work, and more.
Here are a few of the roles that allow his unmistakable artistry to live on.
The Rocky Horror Picture Show
Curry rose to cult status after taking on the role of Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the “sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania,” in the stage version of The Rocky Horror Show in London in 1973. His fan base crossed the Atlantic when he came to the United States to reprise the role in Los Angeles in 1974, before transferring to Broadway, paving the way to the now-famous screen adaptation from 1975, The Rocky Horror Picture Show.
Reviews from New York were mixed—the TIME review said of the initial Broadway run that it was “not easy to see why this campy trash was a long-running hit in London and a smash success in Los Angeles.” But by 1985, TIME’s film reviewer recognized the movie as a “cross-generational phenomenon.”
Chicago Sun-Times critic Roger Ebert said that Curry was “the best thing in the movie, maybe because he seems to be having the most fun.”
Now, Rocky Horror is an interactive midnight movie phenomenon, with fans showing up to screenings nationwide in costume, shouting lines back at the screen, and singing along. The stage version was revived on Broadway in 2026.
Curry’s breakout role in musical theater helped launch his music career in the 1970s and 1980s. He released three albums: Read My Lips, Fearless, and Simplicity.
Annie
In 1982, Curry starred in another stage adaptation—this time playing sleazy con artist Rooster Hannigan in the hit movie Annie.
Acting alongside legends like Carol Burnett and Bernadette Peters, Curry cemented himself as a scheming villain, the type of role he would continue to play in movies like Home Alone 2, Muppet Treasure Island, and The Three Musketeers.
In a 2020 interview with Forbes, Curry reminisced on the experience: “Rooster was a hustler, and people love that kind of character,” he said. “He was a lot of fun.”
Clue
In the 1985 board game adaptation Clue, Curry played the energetic butler Wadsworth, where he showcased his physical comedy. One of the most memorable moments comes at the film’s end, when Wadsworth runs about the mansion, trying to summarize the night’s events and explain the identity of the killer.
Since his death, tributes from his Clue co-stars have poured in.
“What an unbelievable joy to have shared a sound stage with him and to engage with such a master talent,” Lesley Ann Warren, who played Miss Scarlet in the murder mystery movie, wrote. “I adored him.”
It
In 1990, Curry took on a more straightforward villain in the miniseries adaptation of Stephen King’s It. He starred as an ancient cosmic evil that took the form of a child-killing clown called Pennywise in the town of Derry, Maine.
His portrayal of Pennywise horrified a generation of children—without relying heavily on special effects or prosthetics. In a 1990 interview, Curry said he was trying to get in touch with the “human element” of the horror genre.
“We had a much more prosthetic version of this makeup, which was very scary-looking and beautifully executed but did too much work by itself,” he said. “And I personally think that what is most horrifying is the moment of decision behind somebody’s eyes when they decide to kill somebody—rather than a pint of blood and a pound-and-a-half of latex.”
Other beloved roles
Beyond his most beloved roles, Curry had his fingerprints all over pop culture—in movies and television and on the stage.
His three Tony Award nominations came for his 1981 portrayal of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart in the play Amadeus, his portrayal of King Arthur in the musical Monty Python’s Spamalot which debuted on Broadway in 2005, and the lead role of troubled movie star Alan Swann in the musical My Favorite Year in 1992
On the screen, Curry was also beloved as the nosy concierge in 1992’s Home Alone 2, where he is outsmarted by the film’s young protagonist, as well as for his immersive work alongside a cast of Muppets as Long John Silver in 1996’s Muppet Treasure Island. Both his penchant for camp and his undeniable vocal talent were highlighted in 1986’s The Worst Witch, where he played the menacing Halloween harbinger, Grand Wizard Egbert Hellibore.
Curry’s distinct theatrical voice also made him a top choice for voiceover work, where his prolific career spanned hundreds of animated series, audiobooks, and video games. After voicing Captain Hook in Peter Pan & the Pirates, he won a Daytime Emmy Award in 1991.

Italian Football Federation withdraws support for FIFA head Infantino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:44:47 UTC
04:44:47 KST

Halis Sunnetci
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) announced Wednesday that it would no longer support FIFA President Gianni Infantino's potential bid for reelection next March.
The federation said the decision was intended to express its position clearly and transparently and cited Infantino’s recent controversial initiatives “concerning governance and the development of international competitions."
"We will continue to work alongside UEFA and the other European federations to promote a vision of soccer based on merit, solidarity, sustainability, and the centrality of fans," said Giovanni Malago, the FIGC president.
"We identify with a model of dialogue, listening, and shared responsibility that has, until now, allowed soccer to grow, innovate and at the same time defend its founding principles."
Infantino has faced growing pressure since launching this summer’s now-abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal, which involved selling stakes in a company controlling commercial rights to the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors.
The proposal was withdrawn following widespread opposition, but several national associations and continental governing bodies have continued to question Infantino's leadership.
UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and CONCACAF (for North, Central America, and Caribbean football) later issued a joint letter accusing Infantino of breaking trust "through deception" and called for a fully independent review of the abandoned proposal.
Several national federations, including those of England, Wales, and Ireland, have also withdrawn their support for his reelection.
Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is reportedly planning to seek reelection at the FIFA Congress in Morocco next March.

Mass of ice that fell one kilometer believed to be cause of Nepal flood &mdash — NYT

19:43:21 UTC
04:43:21 KST

NEW YORK, August 26. /TASS/. A snow-rock avalanche is believed to be the likely cause of the devastating flood in Nepal after a piece of a glacier chipped off and fell into a valley from a height of more than a kilometer, The New York Times quoted preliminary geological analysis as saying.
"It looks like a glacier in the area basically broke clean off, allowing it to fall just over a vertical kilometer to the valley bottom," said Daniel Shugar, a geologist at the University of Calgary in Canada who studied satellite imagery to analyze what happened.
"The bottom looks like a bomb exploded -- it’s just deposits from the broken-up glacier."
According to the geologist’s estimates, a chunk of ice with a width of about 2,000 feet snapped cleanly off the glacier sending a mixture of ice and water to the valley floor. By his assessment, the chunk of ice fell from an altitude of around 17,000 feet, dropping almost 4,000 feet.
But he said that it was too early to rule out other possible factors.
The flood hit the northern regions of Nepal on Wednesday morning. According to preliminary data, the flood wave was caused by a collapse of a snow·rock avalanche on the border between Nepal and China. According to the latest information, search and rescue teams found the bodies of 95 people. Hundreds were injured. Many houses and infrastructure were destroyed.
Earlier reports indicated that at least 384 travelers, including 291 foreign nationals, are missing in the flood zone. The rescue operation is ongoing.

Belarus builds railway near Ukraine capable of military transport, monitoring group says

Unknown Publisher

Belarus builds railway near Ukraine capable of military transport, monitoring group says
Belarus is building new railway infrastructure in the country's southern Gomel region that will be capable of receiving military trains carrying personnel and heavy equipment, the Belarusian Railway Workers' Community reported on Aug. 24.
The report comes amid a buildup of military infrastructure along the Belarus-Ukraine border, leading Kyiv to warn that Moscow may be planning to draw its closest ally deeper into the full-scale war.
Project documentation obtained by the independent Belarusian Railway Workers' Community shows that a separate railway siding is being constructed for a facility officially designated as "a training ground in Gomel Oblast" near the Yakimovka station. The station lies approximately 40 kilometers (25 miles) from the border with Ukraine.
The planned track will be able to accommodate up to 60 railcars, roughly comparable to a military train, and will include a high loading platform with ramps allowing wheeled and tracked vehicles to be unloaded directly inside the facility, according to the documents.
The project's customer is listed as Belarus' Institute Voenproekt, while earlier engineering documents named the Belarusian Armed Forces' capital construction administration, the monitoring group said. 
Once completed, the railway would allow military trains to move directly from Belarus' national rail network onto the training ground, where personnel, weapons, vehicles, fuel, ammunition, and other supplies could potentially be unloaded without remaining for long periods on publicly accessible station tracks, according to the Belarusian Railway Workers' Community. 
The group stressed that construction of the railway and training ground does not by itself indicate preparations for an offensive against Ukraine, but said the infrastructure would make it possible to rapidly reinforce a military grouping in the area if circumstances changed. 
read also
Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said it has not observed increased military activity in the immediate vicinity of the Belarusian border.
"Belarus continues to develop its military infrastructure," State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko told the Kyiv Independent, pointing to facilities for accommodating personnel, logistics infrastructure, and training grounds.
Demchenko noted that Belarus has repeatedly announced the creation of new military formations and regularly conducts exercises and combat-readiness checks, but cautioned that Minsk also frequently uses such activity to generate information pressure.
He added that Russia continues to view Belarusian territory as a potential direction from which it could expand its aggression against Ukraine, but said there are currently not enough Russian troops stationed in Belarus to form a significant strike grouping.
"Nevertheless, the border with Belarus, the direction from Belarusian territory, has remained a threat for Ukraine both before and now," Demchenko said.
For that reason, Ukraine continues strengthening defensive positions along its northern border, including engineering fortifications and mine barriers, he said.
Belarus allowed Russian forces to use its territory, airspace, and military infrastructure when Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russian troops advanced toward Kyiv from Belarusian territory during the opening phase of the invasion, and Moscow has since used Belarusian territory and airspace to launch strikes against Ukraine.

Ukrainians marched for a month to get Mykhailo Fedorov his job back as defense minister. Then he released a video calling for elections, and the crowds stopped coming.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:40:11 UTC
04:40:11 KST

Ukrainians marched for a month to get Mykhailo Fedorov his job back as defense minister. Then he released a video calling for elections, and the crowds stopped coming.
In mid-August, a video address by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov caused an uproar in Ukraine. In it, Fedorov argued that Ukraine needs to hold elections despite the war and spoke about corruption inside Volodymyr Zelensky’s team. Many Ukrainians, including Fedorov’s own supporters, have called the statements a misstep and criticized him sharply. Zelensky has already said that elections during the war would be a “tsunami that would split Ukraine apart.”
A source close to the Ukrainian President’s Office acknowledged to Meduza that Fedorov’s ratings have risen far enough that in an election he could be a strong rival to Zelensky and Valery Zaluzhny, the former commander in chief of Ukraine’s Armed Forces. Meduza explains what is known about Fedorov’s political intentions and how his ambitions are playing out in Ukrainian society and within the government.
Why everyone is suddenly talking about Mykhailo Fedorov
On August 18, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov posted a video to his YouTube channel that he called an “address to the people.” It went up the day before Yevhen Khmara was appointed to lead the defense ministry, and after more than a month of protests in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities by supporters demanding Fedorov’s reinstatement.
It was the first video on the channel, which Fedorov had created that same day.
In the address, the former defense minister took up a subject that is taboo in Ukraine: elections. Ukraine last voted in presidential and parliamentary elections in 2019; subsequent votes were canceled under the martial law imposed in 2022.
Fedorov said Russia had effectively acquired “the right to determine when Ukrainians will once again be able to choose their government”:
Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state. That is why we must find a legal, safe, and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to resume a fully functioning democratic process even amid a prolonged war.
Fedorov did not specify whether he meant presidential or parliamentary elections.
What do Ukrainians think about holding elections during the war?
There is broad consensus in Ukrainian society that presidential elections should be postponed until the war ends. According to the results of a March 2026 poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, only 12% of Ukrainians think elections should be held before the fighting stops.
Not even Volodymyr Zelensky’s political rivals raise the subject in public.
Valery Zaluzhny — the former commander in chief of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, now the country’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, and until recently described as the opposition’s unity candidate — has yet to say openly that he plans to run for president. He insists that talk of voting is premature until martial law is lifted.
Ukrainian election-law expert Olha Aivazovska, responding to Fedorov’s statement on Facebook, also came out against holding elections in a country at war without the necessary preparations for an electoral process:
I see hundreds of possible scenarios the Russians could use to delegitimize the electoral process or halt it altogether. It would be a complete collapse. I agree with Fedorov that the Russians shouldn’t be the ones deciding when we hold elections, because if they could, elections would have happened long ago. …
But I am firmly against holding elections to serve someone’s political interests, without regard for the real state of the infrastructure, an analysis of the risks, and proper preparation.
Fedorov also turned to corruption in government, which he said “takes on an entirely different meaning” in wartime. In peacetime, he said, stolen money means deteriorating roads, hospitals, and schools; in wartime it means the front goes short of drones, ammunition, and the military vehicles without which the wounded cannot be evacuated.
Fedorov also said Ukraine has a “systemic crisis of governance,” one in which the political system “too often lives by its own rules.” He did not name anyone he holds responsible for the corruption or the governance crisis, but as he spoke of the “old political system,” the video cut to portraits of former President’s Office head Andriy Yermak and David Arakhamia, who leads the Servant of the People faction in the Verkhovna Rada.
The day after the video went up, an unnamed source in Zelensky’s office told the British broadcaster BBC News: “It’s extremely strange to plan elections amid missile and drone attacks. This demonstrates a complete lack of realism.”
Why Fedorov chose to make his address now
Fedorov’s address was an attempt to “enter politics,” a source close to the President’s Office told Meduza: “In essence, he laid out a political program in three points: replacing Zelensky in order to fight the war more effectively, fighting corruption (which, as he sees it, requires removing Zelensky), and uniting”:
I think Misha sincerely wants to achieve these goals. He’s very goal-oriented. And he has a personal motive: his home village, Vasylivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, is under Russian occupation.
A Ukrainian politician called it “quite logical” that the address was released now: “Talks [with the President’s Office about returning as defense minister] didn’t work out, so he’s taken the fight into politics.” The problem, the source continued, was that the President’s Office had expected “something livelier” from Fedorov. “He could have announced his own political platform and called supporters out to a series of rallies,” the source in Kyiv said. “Instead he put out media content.”
Four days after the video appeared, Zelensky again addressed Fedorov’s dismissal in comments to Ukrainian journalists. The president repeated that a “very serious” conflict had arisen between Fedorov and Oleksandr Syrskyi, then the commander in chief, over the division of authority between the defense ministry and the military command. As a result, Zelensky said, the two men stopped speaking directly and discussed matters only at meetings in the president’s office.
The president stressed that after deciding to replace the defense ministry’s leadership, he had offered Fedorov different ways of working on the team four times, and that Fedorov had turned down every one. Fedorov had said he would return only as head of the ministry.
Bringing Fedorov back to his old post was impossible — the risks to the system would have been too high, a source close to the President’s Office told Meduza. “The ‘cardboard people’ won’t start liking us again, whether or not Fedorov got his job back,” the source said. Many Ukrainians associate government embezzlement with the president’s name, the source said, and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) is still pursuing its investigations.
“Cardboard people” is the dismissive term the source close to the President’s Office uses for the protesters supporting Fedorov.
So why are they "cardboard"?
Rallies in support of Fedorov began on July 16, the day after his dismissal. They became known as “cardboard” protests because his supporters turned up with slogans written on pieces of cardboard.
“The defense minister is being removed in the middle of effective (finally!) reforms and replaced by someone under whom you can forget about any reforms,” war veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi wrote on social media. In July 2025, Koziatynskyi had been one of the leaders of the “cardboard” protests in defense of the independence of NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO). He urged fellow protesters to gather at Franko Square in central Kyiv.
“Bring your cardboard signs, and remember this is a peaceful protest,” he said.
Protesters carried signs reading “Bring back Fedorov,” “The problem isn’t Fedorov,” “Fedorov is our hope for reform,” and “Don’t break what works.”
Rallies took place daily in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, with the largest turnout in late July. The Kyiv Independent and the news agency Reuters both counted “thousands” of participants in the “march for dialogue and reforms in defense” in Kyiv on July 31.
How Ukrainians reacted to Fedorov’s address
Fedorov’s speech left many of his supporters and Ukrainian journalists baffled. As soon as the video went online, his press service sent the link to its private chat with reporters, according to a Meduza source who belongs to that chat. The journalists, the source said, asked the press service to explain which elections Fedorov meant and what his point was in the first place.
Members of the chat found the video absurd; one wrote that “there will be a lot of memes.” Sure enough, “within a couple of hours the entire Ukrainian segment of social media was flooded with memes,” the Meduza source said with a chuckle. Many of the source’s colleagues recalled, in private conversations, an old video featuring the line “The wording’s kind of moronic,” which has since become a catchphrase. It shows the Kharkiv politicians Hennadiy Kernes and Mykhailo Dobkin recording an address to the city’s residents in 2007. Journalists who know Fedorov compared him to Dobkin and dubbed the former defense minister “Misha No. 2.”
A Ukrainian political commentator told Meduza the video address was “cringe”:
He’s sitting there at a desk looking grim, a lamp shining, the whole thing staged. In real life, he’s game for anything and improvises everything. But here it’s 10 iffy, canned minutes set to gloomy music, plenty of words about being for everything good and against everything bad.
He says we need to look for tools to hold elections. Well, yes, we do. How long have we been saying that … We need to guarantee democracy — well, sure. But it’s all generalities that are really hard to tie to any actual goal. What was the point of it?
The commentator also faulted Fedorov for “criticizing the old system”: “Never mind that you spent seven years in that system yourself? You only noticed all this once you stopped being part of it?”
He was also puzzled that Fedorov, “beginning his political story” and effectively announcing his readiness to move into opposition to Zelensky, “didn’t name him or even show him in the video,” limiting himself to photographs of Yermak and Arakhamia. The commentator suspects the former defense minister wants to “have it both ways.”
The commentator said Fedorov used the video, in effect, to accuse Arakhamia of corruption and of defending his own financial interests: “When he spoke about corruption and the harm to the country, it was Arakhamia who appeared on screen.” Some outlets, including Ukrainska Pravda, have described the head of the pro-presidential faction in the Verkhovna Rada as the principal organizer of the scheme to reshuffle the cabinet, under which Fedorov was to “disappear from the government,” the commentator said.
Fedorov draws support from some Ukrainian journalists and human rights advocates, as well as from young people and a “middle class that wants to see justice done” — groups that are sharply opposed to corruption, a source close to the President’s Office told Meduza.
“These ‘cardboard people’ are unhappy with how tightly power is centralized in the Ukrainian president’s hands, and they believe parliamentary elections would produce a new Verkhovna Rada, in which the existing single-party majority [of the Servant of the People party] would give way to a coalition,” he said. Zelensky would then have to negotiate with coalition partners, and the political process would become more democratic again. That, the source said, is the protesters’ logic.
Fedorov has worked with the political strategists Dmytro Tsarenko and Viktor Berezenko since his time at Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation, the source said. Ahead of the 2019 elections, the pair oversaw several Servant of the People lawmakers, and from early 2021 until July 2022 they even ran Zelensky’s social media accounts.
The strategists themselves confirmed in December 2024 that they were working with Fedorov. “It looks like [now] they decided the message about elections would land well with his audience. The idea that elections need to happen appeals to them. Misha took it [as the basis for his address]. But they screwed up a little here — in the end Misha turned a lot of people against himself and effectively narrowed his circle of supporters,” the Ukrainian politician said.
The political commentator believes “Fedorov’s team hit the post” — that is, they fell short of their audience’s expectations. “How could this be? Fedorov has an enormous following of young, progressive, creative people. How could they put out this shit? And why did nobody stop him at any point?” he lamented:
Even many of the people who had supported Fedorov until now are disappointed in him and stunned. As in: we came out for you, we backed you, and this is the shit you produced. After all, most of Ukrainian society believes elections during wartime are unacceptable.
Koziatynskyi, one of the main organizers of the pro-Fedorov protests, responded to the former defense minister’s video on Facebook. He thanked “everyone who came out to the protests” for helping secure the removal of Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander in chief and his replacement with Mykhailo Drapatyi.
Koziatynskyi said the main reason for the rallies, as he saw it, was the absence of communication between Ukrainian society and the authorities. For him, he said, “these protests were about dialogue and reforms, not about specific individuals.” On the idea of holding elections he was blunt:
I can’t imagine how you would technically make it possible for thousands of service members now on the front line to vote and to run for office. I’m also very worried about divisions in society during an electoral process, and about how that could affect the course of the war. In any case, street protest is definitely not the place for campaign discourse.
For his part, Oleksiy Sorokin, a political commentator at The Kyiv Independent, believes Fedorov put his political ambitions above the interests of the state.
“Zelensky himself is destroying the public support he’s had since 2022, because of self-centered decisions, corruption scandals, personnel policy, and the concentration of power. Should he lose the next election? Absolutely. But that doesn’t mean elections should be held now,” Sorokin said.
An independent Ukrainian political commentator who spoke with Meduza suggests Fedorov’s statement was meant to “stir up” the protests in his support. It didn’t work: only 100–150 people came to the Verkhovna Rada building on August 19, he said. (On July 31, Reuters correspondents had counted “thousands” of demonstrators in Kyiv.)
“After the deputies voted [to appoint Yevhen Khmara on August 19], the protesters said they’d gather outside the President’s Office that evening. Even fewer people came,” he continued. “The protests are winding down, and I think Fedorov’s statement sped up that process.”
More lawmakers voted to confirm Khmara that day than protesters gathered outside the Rada, a source close to the President’s Office said snidely.
How Fedorov’s team tried to explain what he meant in his video
In the days that followed, Fedorov made several more statements clarifying his position.
On August 21, Ukraine’s Channel 24 aired a long interview with the former defense minister, in which he clarified that he had not called for elections to be held urgently. The address, he said, was about carefully preparing electoral legislation with “the best experts in Ukraine and the world” — people he says he is “already in close touch with.”
He also said he meant parliamentary, presidential, and local elections alike. “What the sequence will be is a question for discussion with various experts,” Fedorov said.
Asked whether he would run for president, the former defense minister said he would know himself once the country was ready to hold elections.
A source close to the President’s Office believes Fedorov’s team “quickly understood that they had chosen the wrong message to begin with, and clarified that they meant not a blitzkrieg [that is, an immediate election] but a long, systemic fight” with Zelensky’s team.
In the same interview, Fedorov said he plans to set up a venture fund that will draw Western money into Ukrainian startups — for example, in producing inexpensive ballistic missiles and in the “robotization of the front line.” He also intends to create a think tank that will “generate ideas” about how to win the war and offer them to the government. And he wants to take on “civic work connected with preparing the country for the return of democracy.”
Fedorov told journalists he would soon travel to the United States for several meetings aimed at attracting investment in Ukrainian military technology projects, though he did not say whom he planned to meet.
Asked by Channel 24 whether he planned to line up the American president’s support before the elections, Fedorov said no. He stressed that discussing such questions is “Ukraine’s homework.”
Fedorov has continued making statements that appear designed to give Ukrainians a sense of his political program. On August 25, asked by Reuters journalists about Ukraine’s prospects in the war, he said: “I think there’s now a turning point that will determine our future trajectory [in the war], but it looks as though we’re gradually, slowly losing.”
What Zelensky’s team risks because of Fedorov’s public activity
Fedorov will decide which elections to contest as the situation develops, the source close to the President’s Office suggested. In the source’s view, it is still premature to talk about elections in Ukraine at all. An independent Ukrainian journalist agrees: “We really don’t know when there will be elections, and Fedorov could still flame out as a politician 150 times over.”
The 35-year-old former defense minister represents a new generation of opposition figures in Ukrainian politics, the Meduza source said. Unlike Valery Zaluzhny — who criticizes the authorities but is still officially part of the president’s team — Fedorov opposes Zelensky openly. Now, a Ukrainian official is convinced, Fedorov “will keep Zelensky’s team on edge”:
Fedorov still has a chance to fix this failure [with the video address] somehow. It will all depend on what he does next: whether he backs up his words with actions and highlights his strengths, or just goes on shooting little videos.
The journalist also points to what Fedorov’s actions have accomplished so far. Until recently, the Meduza source said, publicly calling for elections during the war came across as thoroughly fringe in Ukraine: “Mykhailo, criticized as he is, has still taken a step toward normalizing the subject — and may have pushed the people working on changes to electoral legislation [for elections under martial law] to get moving.”
Since Fedorov’s dismissal, the President’s Office has been tracking his electoral ratings alongside those of Zelensky’s other opponents, just in case, a source close to the office told Meduza. In mid-July, before Fedorov left the defense ministry, the top three presidential contenders were Zelensky, Zaluzhny, and President’s Office head Kyrylo Budanov, the source said. By mid-August, Fedorov’s rating had climbed from 2–3% to 12–15%. That pushed him abruptly into the top three and displaced Budanov, according to data from a private poll the source cited.
Fedorov now alternates between second and third place and runs roughly even with Zaluzhny, the source said. Either of them could reach a runoff against Zelensky.
The source told Meduza he is not sure Zelenskyy will run. “The election is still a long way off,” he said. The president’s disapproval rating exceeds 50%, according to the latest data, a level driven by Ukrainians’ fatigue with the war and government corruption. Such numbers usually hurt a candidate’s chances in a runoff.
