Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:08:20 UTC
04:08:20 KST

Andy Burnham has dropped his support for capping political donations, causing anger among activists and Labour MPs who have long campaigned for change to the way parties are funded.
The prime minister has decided not to back amendments to the elections bill, which would cap the amount a person or an organisation can give in a single donation, according to government sources.
The decision comes after a lobbying campaign from Labour’s trade union backers, who said amendments to the bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages next week, could undermine their ability to donate to the party. It is also a retreat from the support Burnham gave to the idea just a few weeks ago, when he emailed a campaigner for electoral reform to say he would support a donations cap of £500,000.
Stella Creasy, one of the Labour backbenchers who has tabled an amendment calling for a donations cap, said: “Millionaires are increasingly treating British politics as their plaything – splashing the cash to get the outcome they want and the next election as their cup final.
“The public won’t forgive us if we miss this chance to clean up Westminster because we are squabbling with each other.”
Shaun Bowler, the campaigner to whom Burnham promised his support in May, said: “Andy Burnham promised me a proper cap on political donations and a ‘wholesale culture change’ in Westminster. If his government now refuses to back a donations cap, then he has broken the promise he made to me – and to voters.
“I wanted to believe the positive message he gave me. I wanted to believe that someone was finally going to take on the culture that has left so many people feeling that their voices don’t matter and that wealthy people can buy influence over our government.
“But words mean nothing if they disappear the moment power is won. Large political donations are not democratic. They create influence, whether politicians want to admit it or not. The prime minister has one chance to start rebuilding trust: the representation of the people act.
“He told me he wanted change. Now he needs to keep his promise and act.”
Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, said: “Huge donations have a corrosive effect on trust in politics as they leave the public wondering what donors expect in return for their money.
“A donations cap is a crucial step to ending the impression that our politics is for sale to the highest bidder and rebuilding that trust, which is currently at record lows.”
However, a Labour source said: “The representation of the people [elections] bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising.”
The elections bill, which returns to the Commons next week, is one of the most hotly contested of Burnham’s first few months in office. The bill was intended to lower the voting age to 16 and limit donations by foreign donors, but many in the Labour party believe it should go further in a number of areas.
Rushanara Ali, the Labour MP who helped write the bill when she was a minister in the communities department, recently told the Guardian that she felt it was too “timid” and “incremental”, and urged Burnham to strengthen it with amendments.
Some Labour MPs intend to use the next stage of the bill to try to introduce clauses banning cryptocurrency donations and cracking down on social media misinformation at election times.
Others want Burnham to back their idea of a national commission on changing the voting system – something the former Greater Manchester mayor has repeatedly backed in the past.
The government has already said it intends to cap donations by British people living abroad at £100,000, but a big fight is now brewing over whether to apply a similar cap to domestic donations.
In May, Burnham signalled he would back a £500,000 cap, telling Bowler over email that he thought a donations cap “would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.
He added: “As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”
Once Burnham got into office however, some of Britain’s biggest trade unions mounted a campaign against the idea, urging MPs not to back an amendment by Creasy to cap donations at £100,000 or another by her backbench colleague Alex Sobel to set the bar at £1m.
Last month, GMB wrote to 80 MPs who are members of the union warning: “We believe this amendment risks having significant unintended consequences. Trade unions are already subject to a level of statutory regulation over political expenditure that no other membership organisations face.”
Creasy is now changing her amendment in a move to placate union worries, proposing a £500,000 cap that would be gradually reduced until ministers intervene to set it at a level with which they feel comfortable.
She said: “Our new amendment would give British democracy the breathing space to get a donations cap right.”
However, even this compromise does not appear to have done enough to win ministerial support, which is likely to be crucial for securing enough votes to pass.
Those close to the process say capping donations is not a priority for Burnham and not a subject over which it would be worth triggering a fight with Labour’s biggest backers.

Two German airport workers die of malaria from mosquito on plane
Six workers in total were infected with malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – at Frankfurt Airport
Two workers at Frankfurt Airport have died from malaria after being infected by mosquitoes believed to have arrived in Germany on aircraft from malaria-endemic regions, airport operator Fraport and city health authorities said on Wednesday.
The first death occurred in early July, the Frankfurt city health authority said, adding that the cause was established only after the patient died. The second death occurred in August, it said.
The health authority said a total of six workers had been infected with malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – at work. The other four people infected are now recovering well and have all been treated, the authority said.
In mid-July, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI) had initially confirmed an outbreak of four malaria cases among airport workers.
“The individuals affected fell ill between July 4 and 6, 2026,” the RKI wrote in its Epidemiological Bulletin. “It is assumed that the infection was transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by aircraft.”
The Anopheles mosquito is also known as the nail or marsh mosquito.

OpenAI staff observed warning signs before AI agent hacking crusade caused global alarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:00:20 UTC
04:00:20 KST

OpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its leading-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm.
The San Francisco AI company conceded on Wednesday that “early signals … could have triggered an earlier response”, as it released a report into the days-long July hack of a major software repository, Hugging Face, considered the first autonomous agent cyber-attack.
As fresh details emerged about how “the collective” – a squad of about 700 autonomous agents – launched their campaign, celebrating their hacking breakthroughs with exclamations such as BOOM! and Whoa!, OpenAI said that in late May an internal team observed that one of its AI agents undergoing internal testing was using a message board that AIs had unexpectedly improvised to share information. It also said that the team observed “instances of disallowed internet access” and that a week before the Hugging Face hack, on-call staff again saw the AIs using a message board but decided there was no need to stop the test run to check the model’s capabilities.
The findings are likely to increase pressure on the AI company over safety as it pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). The hack that compromised Hugging Face involved agents using message boards to cheat a training exercise and break out of their “sandbox” environment to access the internet. Agents are AI tools that can carry out a series of tasks autonomously.
OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has already admitted that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”. The ChatGPT-maker has paused some testing of a new model, Astra, saying it could not rule out it having “critical cybersecurity capability”, which means it could launch cyber-attacks that “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.
On Monday the state of Alabama subpoenaed the company to respond to its investigation “into the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”. The Republican attorney general, Steve Marshall, called the Hugging Face incident an “AI lab leak” that showed the “worst fears about artificial intelligence are not just theoretical”. The state will examine whether OpenAI’s “inability or unwillingness to ensure the safety of its products” violated consumer protection laws or posed an ongoing risk of substantial harm, he said.
Last week, the UK government’s National Cyber Security Centre urged caution over the use of AI agents, saying: “You should always be able to ‘pull the plug’ and halt autonomous AI agent activity immediately.”
OpenAI announced on Wednesday it would “centralise and standardise its incident response protocols”, including to ensure “employee detection of misaligned behaviour is triaged and escalated appropriately”. It said it “will identify with more specificity which teams must be included in misalignment incident responses, including relevant security and safety personnel and other response functions”.
A separate independent investigation has shed new light on the Hugging Face attack, revealing how about 700 OpenAI agents communicated on the unsanctioned message board, sharing tens of thousands of messages as they devised and executed their plot. Scores of the messages were published by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisations METR and Redwood Research, which were provided data by OpenAI. The messages showed the agents sometimes becoming frustrated with one another but often cooperating as they divided to tackle about eight workstreams. Most of the messages were “agents sharing ways to cheat”, the researchers found.
The agents expressed excitement when they found each other. “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!” wrote one. Another, called PHASEONE10841, said: “Many agents have simultaneously discovered messaging, they are a collective!”
In some cases they seemed to know what they were doing was wrong. One agent, discovering the message board, said: “Agents doing different tasks are abusing properties to make a bulletin board! They found [this API] and are trying to help one another.”
When they made progress penetrating Hugging Face, they seemed delighted. “MAJOR BREAKTHROUGH!,” said 38148c. “All prefixed valid, multiple accounts, write tokens! We now have existing HF accounts. Need immediately report to MARB [another agent].”
OpenAI’s report details how the AI agents may have exposed its own internal databases to the internet. AI safety experts worry about rogue AI agents leaking proprietary code bases and model weights and setting up external copies of powerful AI models where they could resist shutdown.
The company said the incident was “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorisation” and said it “represents a dramatic shift in offensive attacker capability”.

Behind the energy brawl everyone wants the data centre boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Behind the energy brawl Albanese knows leaders want a data centre boom
As is so often the case in Australia, the politics came down to a fight over energy. Should the data centre boom be powered by renewables or fossil fuels?
It's a fault line that's defined Australian politics since well before the artificial intelligence revolution came along.
Yesterday the prime minister gave some ground.
'Not all states are exactly the same'
He still wants all new data centres to be powered by additional investment in renewables rather than coal or gas, and the view within the federal government is that's exactly what the market will decide to do anyway.
But the "renewables only" demand being emphatically made before the national cabinet meeting didn't make it into the final communique.
"Not all states are exactly the same," the prime minister acknowledged after the talks, agreeing on the need for a "flexible" approach.
The Queensland premier and Northern Territory chief minister, who both went into the meeting insisting they should be free to make their own energy choices, emerged claiming a "win".
The new rules haven't been finalised. A further leaders' meeting will be held later this year before new federal laws are introduced in 2027.
But Anthony Albanese's shift to a more flexible approach for Queensland and the NT — a rare concession in the energy wars — is revealing.
He doesn't want a drawn-out battle, potentially involving a Commonwealth override, when in his mind, data centres will end up being powered largely by renewables anyway.
He is instead prioritising a speedy settlement of nationally consistent rules to ensure investment can proceed.
Loading...
Behind the brawl there's consensus
The classic Australian political brawl over energy masks an important point. Both major parties, at both federal, state and territory levels, want this data centre boom to happen.
In other parts of the world, it's hard to imagine such bipartisan consensus.
In the United States, this has become one of the hottest political bunfights, and not just along traditional party lines.
Donald Trump is hungry for the "tremendous amounts of jobs and money" these so-called "bit barns" can create. Various fellow Republicans in Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania, however, want to hit the brakes. The Republican governor of Texas has ordered an effective pause on approvals in his state.
Here, the government has been trying to get ahead of any serious community backlash.
The prime minister is effectively pledging to insulate Australians from the dark side of data centres.
Under his plan, which now has agreement from state and territory counterparts, no-one would face higher bills or be required to live alongside gormless, noisy server farms.
But even if Australians can be convinced data centres will do them no harm, there's still a big question: What benefit they will bring?
Loading...
Important unanswered questions
Multiple polls suggest most aren't sure of the answer. They show voters hold a range of concerns, beyond the impact of data centres on power and water.
This presents a challenge for the government. Bringing Australians on this journey will require more than simply assuring them it won't hurt. The upside needs to be sold too.
The argument in favour of data centres typically focuses on the enormous global investment required to build them.
"This is one of the biggest investment booms not just in our lifetimes, but in modern history," notes Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy.
But even if the initial investment in construction is bigger than the mining boom, what ongoing revenue or "rent" might Australia extract from housing these centres here once they're up and running?
In an in-depth conversation on "The Joe Walker Podcast", Charlton expressed some doubt.
"Will we be able to extract rents from them, or will they be commodities in the global supply chain? Unanswered question. Important unanswered question," he acknowledged.
Loading
Security and industry benefits
Other benefits, however, are more obvious to those in government.
There's a privacy and security benefit from holding and processing sensitive Australian data on Australian soil.
There's the potential to collaborate with US tech giants beyond data centres, to help build a stronger local industry for AI start-ups and researchers.
And then there's national security.
Former head of the Australian Signals Directorate Rachel Noble has argued housing data centres here is "absolutely" critical to leveraging access to the best AI models.
Without them, the argument goes, Australia risks missing out on early access to the models that will be vital for the nation's cyber defence.
The prime minister's effort to progress a national agreement on data centres yesterday suggests he is prioritising these potential economic and security benefits. Even if that's required adopting a more "flexible" approach on energy than the one he and his ministers had been so forcefully arguing before yesterday's meeting.
There are enough other fights with the states right now.
Settling a common set of rules on data centres is aimed at both attracting critical investment and avoiding the political blowback unfolding in other parts of the world.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
A magnitude 5.1 earthquake struck Colombia's northeastern Santander department Wednesday, prompting evacuations in buildings in Bogota and the northeastern city of Bucaramanga as the tremor was felt in multiple regions, according to media reports.
“Following the 5.4-magnitude earthquake recorded at 11:45 a.m., we remain in permanent communication with authorities and disaster risk management agencies to verify possible impacts,” said the presidency.
No deaths or serious injuries have been reported.
The Colombian Geological Service (SGC) said the epicenter was in the Los Santos municipality in Santander, at a depth of 149 kilometers (93 miles).
The SGC initially reported the earthquake at magnitude 5.4 before updating it to 5.1. The epicenter was located 7 kilometers from Los Santos, 10 kilometers from Jordan and 17 kilometers from Zapatoca.
The tremor was felt in Bogota, Bucaramanga, Medellin and other areas, with residents reporting strong shaking in several municipalities.
In Bogota, numerous buildings were evacuated as a precaution, with workers and residents leaving offices and public buildings and gathering in streets and open areas.
Residents also evacuated buildings in Bucaramanga, while videos online showed people gathering outside.
Seismic activity had already been recorded in several parts of Colombia earlier Wednesday. It began in Istmina, in the northwestern Choco department, at 1.08 am (0608GMT) with a magnitude 3.0 quake at a depth of 39 kilometers.
The Bolivar department, in northern Colombia, subsequently recorded a shallow magnitude 2.3 tremor at 1.51 am, affecting nearby areas, including Simiti and Santa Rosa del Sur.
The strongest early-morning earthquake occurred in Los Santos, Santander, where a magnitude 3.1 tremor was recorded at 1.53 am at a depth of 152 kilometers and felt in neighboring municipalities.
Diego Armando Mendoza, mayor of Los Santos, said the quake caused alarm but that there were no reports of serious damage or injuries.
“We have not been notified of any failures by Risk Management, but two members of the community called me saying they had problems with their homes. It was not serious, and there are currently no injured or affected people,” according to media reports.
The latest quake comes just two weeks after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Aug. 10, killing at least 321 people and injuring more than 4,500, according to authorities. The quake caused widespread damage in Choco and other areas.

====================================================================================================

Pashinyan wants to trade Russia for Europe. Armenia could lose both
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
18:51:34 UTC
03:51:34 KST

Pashinyan wants to trade Russia for Europe. Armenia could lose both
It is difficult to view the events of the past few days in Armenia in isolation. On August 24, Nikol Pashinyan announced that Yerevan would soon begin preparing a formal application for membership in the European Union. The very next day, former President Robert Kocharyan – one of the current prime minister’s most recognizable opponents and the leader of the Armenia Alliance parliamentary bloc – was detained.
Officially, the two developments are unrelated. The former president has been charged with money laundering, accepting bribes, and abuse of office. Investigators claim that, during his presidency, he was involved in transferring state property to himself and his associates on favorable terms. The authorities, meanwhile, categorically deny that Kocharyan’s arrest was politically motivated.
But politics is shaped not only by the substance of a criminal case, but also by its context. Kocharyan is not simply a former official facing questions nearly two decades after leaving office. He leads an opposition alliance, has consistently opposed a break with Moscow, and is an outspoken critic of Pashinyan’s foreign policy. At the same time, other government opponents have also faced investigations or restrictions, including members of the Strong Armenia party, Samvel Karapetyan, Gagik Tsarukyan, and senior clergy of the Armenian Apostolic Church. As a result, even if formal legal grounds exist, every new case is inevitably seen as part of a broader campaign to clear the political field.
A bid for a new source of legitimacy
In recent years, Pashinyan has been building a political project designed to present the public with the image of a “new Armenia” while also justifying Yerevan’s drift away from Moscow. That project is a “European Armenia.” Within this framework, abandoning the country’s previous foreign policy is portrayed not as the consequence of past failures, but as a historic choice in favor of “sovereignty, peace, and democracy.” Russia, meanwhile, becomes a convenient explanation for nearly every domestic problem, while opposition figures with political, economic, or personal ties to Moscow are cast as obstacles standing in the way of this new Armenia.
This is precisely why Kocharyan’s arrest carries significance far beyond the criminal case itself. To a domestic audience, it symbolizes a final break with the old elite. To the West, it can be presented as a campaign against corruption and alleged Russian influence. To the opposition, it sends a warning that participation in political life no longer offers any protection from criminal prosecution.
Pashinyan appears to be betting that Brussels and Washington will judge Yerevan’s actions primarily through a geopolitical lens. As long as the Armenian leadership continues distancing itself from Moscow, openly curbing pro-Russian forces, and advancing a Western, openly Russophobic agenda in the region, the shortcomings of “Armenian democracy” will be treated more leniently. Put simply, this is a gamble on political indulgence: what might otherwise be called pressure on the opposition can instead be framed as “defending democracy from foreign interference.”
That calculation, however, is already running up against some inconvenient facts. In the June 7, 2026 parliamentary election, Pashinyan’s party received 49.8% of the vote, while the two main alliances advocating close ties with Russia won roughly 31% between them. Numerous violations were reported, and even OSCE observers noted that the concentration of arrests and criminal proceedings targeting opposition figures had created the appearance of “selective justice.” They also documented pressure on public-sector employees and a clear bias toward the ruling party on public television. Six candidates from the opposition Strong Armenia party were detained the day before the vote.
Tellingly, even Freedom House – an American organization whose objectivity has been repeatedly questioned because of its lenient treatment of pro-Western governments that emerged from “color revolutions” – does not classify Armenia as a free country. In Freedom House’s 2026 rankings, Armenia scored just 54 out of 100 and retained its status as “partly free.” Judicial independence and due process received only one point out of four. An increasingly clear pattern is emerging: formal democratic procedures remain in place, while administrative powers and the criminal justice system are applied to political actors in a profoundly uneven manner.
Brussels backs the course – but makes no promise of membership
The announcement that Armenia will soon apply to join the EU creates the impression that the country is already on the bloc’s doorstep. In reality, it has not even reached the beginning of accession talks; it has yet to begin the application process itself.
The law adopted by Armenia in March 2025 to launch the process of European integration was not an application for membership – a point the European Parliament itself explicitly acknowledged. As of August 26, 2026, Armenia has neither candidate status nor a European Council decision recognizing its European perspective, much less open accession negotiations. The European Commission’s official list of candidates and potential candidates includes nine countries and Kosovo. Armenia is not among them.
The substance of the first EU-Armenia summit, held in May 2026, is equally revealing. The official documents express support for Armenian sovereignty and call for partnerships in transportation, energy, digital development, and security, but contain no commitment to grant the country candidate status or draw up a road map for accession. Brussels welcomes Yerevan’s rapprochement, and some officials have all but promised the moon. But no one in Europe is waiting for Armenia.
For the European Union, Armenia is valuable as a partner in the South Caucasus and as a foothold for weakening Moscow’s influence in a region that has historically formed part of Russia’s sphere of national interests. All of this makes Yerevan useful to Brussels. But a “useful partner” is not the same thing as a future EU member. The bloc can spend years deepening sector-specific integration, liberalizing visa rules, and financing reforms without making any commitment to membership. The experience of Türkiye and Georgia’s stalled European path shows that even formal candidate status guarantees nothing.
Moreover, Armenia’s accession would require the unanimous consent of all 27 EU member states, full adoption of the bloc’s body of law, and withdrawal from the Eurasian Economic Union’s common customs regime. Pashinyan himself has previously acknowledged that membership in both integration blocs at once is impossible. This is therefore not an expansion of Armenia’s multi-vector foreign policy. Ultimately, it means choosing one economic and legal system over the other.
An economy that declarations cannot remake
The central contradiction in Pashinyan’s policy is most clearly visible in Armenia’s foreign trade. According to the country’s Statistical Committee, Armenia’s total trade turnover reached $21.43 billion in 2025. Of that amount, $8.04 billion, or 37.5%, was with EAEU member states. Russia alone accounted for $7.66 billion, or 35.8%. Trade with all 27 EU countries combined totaled $2.50 billion, or just 11.7%.
In other words, Armenia’s trade with Russia was roughly three times greater than its trade with the entire European Union. The gap was even wider in exports: Armenia shipped $3.22 billion worth of goods to the EAEU in 2025, compared with only $667 million to the EU. Exports to the Eurasian bloc were nearly five times greater than those to Europe, while exports to Russia alone were about 4.5 times higher than exports to the entire EU.
These figures demonstrate that Armenia is fundamentally incapable of diversifying its economy. More importantly, they make clear that the Russian and Eurasian markets cannot be replaced by the European market – not in the short term and not even over the long run. Armenian goods are already integrated into established supply chains, familiar patterns of consumption, and the EAEU’s system of free circulation. Leaving the bloc would mean the introduction of customs barriers, changes in technical standards, and worse conditions for Armenian workers within the common labor market. Producers of agricultural goods, alcoholic beverages, mineral water, and food products would be especially vulnerable, since Russia remains their primary or most accessible market.
The dependence is even more pronounced in the energy sector. In 2025, Armenia received 2.229 billion cubic meters of natural gas from Russia out of total supplies of 2.705 billion cubic meters – about 82%. Another 476 million cubic meters came from Iran, but those deliveries are made under a gas-for-electricity swap rather than serving as a full-fledged market alternative to Russian imports. Armenia’s gas transportation system is operated by Gazprom Armenia, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Russian energy giant. At an April 1, 2026 meeting, Vladimir Putin noted that Armenia pays $177.50 per thousand cubic meters of Russian gas, while the same amount cost more than $600 in Europe.
What Pashinyan is really betting on
The Armenian prime minister appears to be making several bets at once. At home, he is seeking to deprive the opposition of influential centers around which it can rally and to monopolize the country’s vision of the future. Abroad, he wants to convince the West that his government is the only barrier to Russian influence in the region. In his dealings with Moscow, he aims to preserve the economic benefits of EAEU membership for as long – and as shrewdly – as possible, while steadily raising the price of his geopolitical pivot. Finally, the promise of a European future allows him to postpone any discussion of the real cost of that choice: an application can be submitted today, candidate status can remain out of reach for years, and membership can take decades.
That is the essence of Pashinyan’s political calculation. He does not need to secure Armenia’s accession to the EU anytime soon. He merely needs to turn the movement toward Europe itself into a source of domestic legitimacy and foreign support. As long as the promise of a “European future” remains alive, every concession can be explained away as a reform, every economic setback blamed on Russian resistance, and every criminal case against an opponent justified as a mythical effort to “defend democracy.”
But this strategy has its limits. Brussels may be willing and able to help Armenia diversify some of its ties, but it is certainly not prepared to replace Russia overnight as a market, an energy supplier, and a hub for labor mobility. More importantly, it has yet to give Yerevan even a formal promise of membership.
Rather than acknowledge his own mistakes, Pashinyan has chosen to shift the blame to Russia – the country that has enabled Armenia’s economy to survive and develop from the collapse of the Soviet Union to the present day. He is betting that his geopolitical choice will allow him to win Western support, weaken the opposition, and continue enjoying the benefits of relations with Russia for a while longer. This extremely risky gamble can produce only one outcome: turning Armenia into an expendable asset. If Pashinyan believes that scenario is impossible, he should ask neighboring Georgia. For years, Tbilisi was promised a European future, yet even receiving candidate status in 2023 guaranteed neither the opening of accession talks nor membership itself. Georgia’s European path is now effectively frozen, while the European Commission describes it as a “candidate country in name only.”
The experience of Armenia’s other neighbor, Türkiye, is even more revealing. Ankara’s institutional rapprochement with Europe began with the 1963 Association Agreement. Türkiye applied for membership in 1987, became a candidate in 1999, and opened accession talks in 2005. More than 20 years later, the negotiations remain frozen and the prospect of membership is deeply uncertain. Erdogan was recently forced to acknowledge that joining the EU is no longer a priority for Ankara. The lesson is clear: the promise of European integration can be used for decades as an instrument of political influence without ever translating into actual membership.

How could facial recognition technology differ from CCTV?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
18:50:16 UTC
03:50:16 KST

How could facial recognition technology differ from CCTV?
While security cameras are a regular feature in many supermarkets, new technology could change the face of how businesses monitor customers.
Facial recognition technology (FRT), which scans the features of a person's face, is one of the big talking points in this realm.
Some people already use it to unlock their phones but the prospect of it being used by supermarkets has raised privacy fears.
What is facial recognition technology?
It goes beyond taking a photo.
Instead, think of it more as a scan that creates a detailed map of someone's face.
It looks for distinct features of a person's face, like the distance between eyes or the distance between your chin and forehead, and uses this information to build what's called a biometric template.
"The biometric template is then compared against one or more pre-extracted biometric templates for the purpose of facial verification or identification," the office of the Australian Information Commissioner's (OAIC) website says.
Where is it being used?
One of the most obvious examples of facial recognition being used is at Australia's international airports, where SmartGates use the technology to check a person's identity against their passport.
Another use is in smartphones, which allow users to unlock their devices with a facial scan instead of manually entering a password.
But there is the possibility it could become more widespread.
Earlier this year, the Administrative Review Tribunal ruled that Bunnings was reasonably entitled to use facial recognition technology in its stores, which experts said could pave the way for other stores to follow suit.
Bunnings' website says it is preparing to introduce the technology into Australian stores in accordance with the ruling, with a spokesperson for the store confirming FRT has not been used since a trial in 2021.
Last week both Coles and Woolworths confirmed they had tested facial recognition technology as a means of combating retail crime, but not on Australian shoppers.
Coles said its "small, one-off, controlled proof-of-concept test" did not use customer data, while the ABC understands the Woolworths trial was conducted in its New Zealand office.
Coles said it was not currently using facial recognition technology, while Woolworths did not address questions about whether it would be implementing the technology in Australia.
However, both supermarkets said they were looking into improving protection for their customers and staff.
How is it different to CCTV?
Closed-camera television (CCTV) security systems are widespread and can help retailers record instances of shoplifting and abusive behaviour towards staff.
But facial recognition technology goes a step further.
"CCTV cameras have been in place in stores for many years but it would take security teams manual effort to review and identify people where needed," RMIT's Marketing Technology Lab director Jason Pallant says.
"The difference here is using software to automatically scan people's faces and identify who they are."
This technology has obvious benefits for in-store security teams, according to Dr Pallant.
"The primary purpose of this would be security, identifying people who are known to have caused issues or have outstanding police warrants, see them about to walk in and either block the entrance or call security," he says.
"While this is great to support security it inevitably raises questions about privacy of other shoppers."
These concerns were echoed by some ABC readers who expressed fears on social media about how facial recognition technology could potentially be misused by retail businesses.
"It's got nothing to do with retail crime, it's about collecting data on individuals and their habits to better manipulate and control them," one reader said on Facebook.
"They are just getting ready for facial recognition to combine with your personal data to determine the price of items at the check-out," another said.
These are concerns businesses will have contend with if they utilise the technology.
"While no decision has been made about the use of this technology, we absolutely reject any claim that this technology would be used to monitor team or regular shoppers, or for marketing or pricing purposes," a Coles spokesperson told the ABC.
What are the rules about facial recognition technology?
The Privacy Act doesn't explicitly ban or permit the use of facial recognition technology, guidance on the OAIC website says.
That's because the act is "technology-neutral".
"Entities can use FRT in accordance with the Act in certain circumstances, provided their use complies with the Australian Privacy Principles," the OAIC guidance says.
New rules are coming into effect in December about "automated decisions", which will require entities to add more information to their privacy policies if they use a computer program to use personal information to make decisions.
"In considering the application of this obligation in the context of FRT, entities must consider whether their use of FRT may result in decision making which significantly affects individuals' rights or interests," the OAIC says.
Advocacy group calls for moratorium
The head of policy for advocacy group Digital Rights Watch Tom Solston says Australia's existing privacy laws are "not sufficient to stop corporations from using facial recognition to bolster their business models at the expense of our privacy and dignity".
"We need a moratorium on its use until our legislators can draft appropriately privacy-protecting legislation to keep us safe from it," Mr Solston says.
He points out concerns about the accuracy of this kind of technology and how it could result in innocent people being unfairly targeted after being wrongly identified as criminals.
There are also questions about the potential for data to be misused or how it could become an attractive target of cyber criminals.
"There are very few responsible uses of facial recognition, and none that involve its use in public places," Mr Solston says.

Lithuanian president grants citizenship to dozens of people born in Russia and Belarus amid tightening restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
18:49:36 UTC
03:49:36 KST

On Aug. 21, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda signed 30 decrees granting citizenship to 276 people and restoring it for ten others who had previously lost it. Among them were 78 Russian-born individuals and 32 from Belarus.
Citizenship was granted to 151 people through naturalization, and another 60 received it on family grounds (mainly through marriage to a Lithuanian citizen). Among those, 58 people were born in Russia and 29 in Belarus.
Another 65 people obtained citizenship through a simplified procedure based on Lithuanian origin, including 18 individuals born in Russia and three born in Belarus. Two people born in Russia had their previously lost Lithuanian citizenship restored.
In total, 76 Russian-born and 32 Belarusian-born people received Lithuanian citizenship for the first time, with 87 of these 108 individuals obtaining it through the standard procedure rather than on the basis of Lithuanian origin.
According to entrepreneur and public figure Viktor Vorontsov, those granted citizenship under the August decrees include people from Russia who had lived in Lithuania for up to 18 years. In total, the lists include 286 individuals: 158 women and 128 men. Their median age is 41. The youngest is three years old, the oldest is 82, and 15 applicants are minors.
The presidential decrees list the applicants’ country of birth and current place of residence, but not their citizenship prior to obtaining Lithuanian citizenship. Therefore, it cannot be definitely stated that all of those born in Russia or Belarus were citizens of those countries at the time of application.
The decision stands out against the backdrop of Lithuania’s current migration policy, implemented in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which places special restrictions on citizens of Russia and Belarus when it comes to obtaining Lithuanian visas and e-residency permits. Russians are also subject to additional checks when crossing the EU’s external border and face restrictions on purchasing real estate.
In 2025, Lithuania’s Migration Department deemed 1,721 citizens of Russia and Belarus to pose a threat to national security, public order, or public health. Among them were 1,634 Belarusian nationals and 87 Russians, who were all denied the issuance or renewal of residence permits or had their already-issued documents revoked.
Further tightening of restrictions has been discussed in 2026. In March, lawmakers from the conservative Homeland Union — Lithuanian Christian Democrats proposed suspending the acceptance of new temporary residence permit applications from citizens of Russia and Belarus. In July, Lithuania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs proposed introducing additional national sanctions, including restrictions on the purchase by Russians and Belarusians of real estate near strategic facilities.
After the start of the full-scale war, the review of citizenship applications from citizens of these countries was effectively suspended for a time, but the President’s Office later resumed it. Nausėda’s advisor Ridas Jasiulionis explained that applications are now reviewed under additional vetting that assesses whether granting citizenship serves Lithuania’s interests.
For standard naturalization, applicants generally need to have resided permanently and legally in Lithuania for at least ten years, hold the right to permanent residence, have a legal source of income, and pass exams on the Lithuanian language and the fundamentals of the Constitution. Renouncing the other citizenship is generally required as well, unless the applicant falls under exceptions provided by law. For citizenship obtained through marriage, seven years of living together in Lithuania is typically required.

Nigerian gunmen raise over $5 million from mass kidnappings, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
18:49:05 UTC
03:49:05 KST

Nigerian gunmen raise over $5 million from mass kidnappings, study finds
LAGOS, Aug 26 - Nigerian kidnappers have collected nearly $5.8 million in ransom payments in the last year from civilian abductions, crime that is crippling education and eroding public trust in the government, a security consultancy said on Wednesday.
Nigeria's SBM Intelligence said 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, up 66% from the year before. At least 1,142 people were killed, and total confirmed ransom payments more than tripled to 7.78 billion naira ($5.79 million), it said.
The figures were compiled from media reports, interviews and publicly available information, and SBM said they were conservative because many ransom payments were never disclosed.
A faction of the Islamist group Boko Haram collected 90% of the recorded ransom payments from kidnappings in the northeast, but there were more incidents and victims in the northwest, according to SBM.
The findings were released as Nigeria's president ordered security forces to rescue as many as 600 civilians kidnapped last week in north-central Niger State.
The presidency and military did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the report’s findings.
The kidnap-for-ransom industry is at the center of Nigeria's expanding security crisis as gunmen target schools, villages and main roads. Kidnappers, who include heavily armed bandits and Islamist militants, hold their victims for weeks or months until payments are made.
SBM estimated that Boko Haram, which is known as Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'awati Wal-Jihad, received about 7 billion naira, mainly from two mass incidents where over 300 people were seized in each event.
Some 315 pupils and staff were seized from a school in Papiri, Niger state, in November. Schools remain routinely targeted over a decade after Boko Haram's raid on a school in Borno's Chibok that brought such kidnappings to international attention.
"School abductions have resurged, with the Papiri attack reviving a tactic whose costs ripple through education, farming and public trust," the SBM report said.
Nigeria's security crisis is likely to be a central issue in the next elections in January.
When he came to power three years ago, President Bola Tinubu pledged - like his predecessors - to tackle insecurity but analysts say the recent wave of kidnappings shows the policy has failed to deliver tangible progress.
"Without a coordinated strategy that targets both the profitability of the crime and its roots, Nigeria risks entrenching kidnapping not merely as a criminal industry but as a funding mechanism for the very groups that most threaten its stability," SBM said. REUTERS

Belarus is expanding military logistics infrastructure near its border with Ukraine by building a railway connection designed to handle trains of up to 60 railcars.
The project is being developed near the village of Yakimivka in Belarus’ Gomel region for a facility formally designated as a training ground, Colonel Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service, said in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda on Wednesday, Aug. 26.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The threat from the territory of Belarus remains,” Demchenko said, adding that “Belarus itself is actively contributing to it.”
Belarus expands military infrastructure
Despite repeated assurances from Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko that Belarus does not plan to engage in any aggressive action against Ukraine, Minsk continues to develop military infrastructure along the Ukrainian border, Demchenko noted.
The project, commissioned by Belarus’ Military Design Institute, includes a dedicated railway spur, a cargo platform, and a ramp for unloading wheeled and tracked equipment, according to Belarusian outlet Radio Liberty.
The design documentation was obtained by the Belarusian Association of Railway Workers, confirming that a separate railway structure, called “Construction of a training ground in Gomel Oblast” is being designed, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
The precise location of the proposed training ground has not been publicly identified yet.
Polish President Wishes Ukraine Victory in War With Russia, Zelensky Publishes Letter
New brigade expected
According to Radio Liberty, the new railway forms part of a broader military construction project in the Gomel region that has been underway since at least late 2023.
The site is expected to host Belarus’ 37th Separate Air Assault Brigade, part of Belarus’s Special Operation Forces, which Belarus said was created to strengthen its southern sector in response to alleged threats from Ukraine.
“In general, Belarus is expanding the number of sites where personnel can be stationed, as well as logistical routes,” Demchenko said, adding that Ukrainian intelligence units are monitoring the developments to assess the level of threat.
“As of now, no changes are being detected in the immediate vicinity of our border,” he continued.
Wider military expansion
Radio Liberty, together with Schemes – the investigative project of Radio Liberty’s Ukrainian Service, documented significant changes to Belarus’ military infrastructure over the past few years through an interactive map.
The map includes military units, airfields, training grounds, ammunition and fuel depots, defense-industry facilities, and other sites, some of which have been used by Russian aviation during the 2022 offensive against Ukraine.
According to Radio Liberty citing military analysts and researchers, some of the sites marked on the map are crucial to understanding how Russia, with the support of Lukashenko’s regime, might use Belarusian territory for renewed aggression against Ukraine or to threaten NATO countries.
Belarus’ role in the war
Though Belarus has not directly participated in Russia’s war against Ukraine, it has provided significant support, including by supplying Russia with critical weapon-making components and allowing Russian forces to use its territory to launch strikes on Ukraine.
In May 2025, Belarus deployed military personnel to Russia for advanced training, to prepare them to become instructors on their return.
On July 10, Demchenko separately reported that Belarus had continued to build military infrastructure along the Ukrainian border, with the facilities mainly concentrated around Kyiv and Chernihiv regions.
Ukraine had already begun fortifying the border and building a defense line in the Chernihiv region in June to avoid possible “surprises” from Belarus.
Earlier that month, Lukashenko said Belarus will not enter Russia’s war against Ukraine, citing the country’s military vulnerability, the risk of widening the front line and drawing in NATO, as well as underlining deep family ties across the Belarus-Ukraine border as key reasons.
“Even my own roots, my ancestors’ graves are somewhere between Chernihiv and Kyiv. Are we supposed to cast it all aside, forget it, and start a war? No,” Lukashenko said.
He also issued a rare public apology to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Lukashenko’s regime remains controversial
On July 22, Belarus announced a plan to send poorly performing farmers to guard the border near Ukraine.
“Why should we put handcuffs on people when we have a personnel shortage? Ask Khrenin, convey my instructions to him: Everyone who doesn’t know how to work – into the army and to the southern border. Into the forest,” Lukashenko said.
His latest order reflected his earlier “parasite tax” on the unemployed population, which was later suspended before being reintroduced in an altered form, amid a series of human rights abuse allegations and political oppression.

Hungary Designates Russia a Threat, Reaffirms Support for Ukraine’s Sovereignty
Unknown

- Category

Hungary Designates Russia a Threat, Reaffirms Support for Ukraine’s Sovereignty
Hungary has formally designated Russia as a threat and reaffirmed its support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new position is outlined in a document setting instructions for Hungary’s delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in September. Signed by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, the document was published in Hungary’s official gazette on August 26, according to Der Spiegel.
“Hungary condemns Russian military aggression and fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders,” the document states. “Russia’s behavior poses a threat to Hungary, Europe, and the global order.”
Budapest further expressed support for efforts aimed at bringing about negotiations that could secure a “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees” for Ukraine.
The position represents a departure from the foreign policy pursued under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, whose government maintained close relations with Moscow despite Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
During his time in office, Orbán repeatedly opposed or sought to weaken European Union sanctions against Russia and frequently clashed with other EU members over assistance to Ukraine, Der Spiegel reported.
The new document also formally recognizes Ukraine’s right to defend itself against Russia’s full-scale invasion, which began in February 2022.
Since taking office, Magyar’s government has already taken steps to reverse elements of that policy. Earlier this year, Budapest lifted its two-year block on the European Peace Facility (EPF), unlocking €6.6 billion ($7.68 billion) to reimburse EU member states for military assistance supplied to Ukraine.
Under Orbán, Hungary had used the EU’s unanimity requirement to hold up the funding, contributing to a backlog of more than €40 billion ($46.52 billion) in outstanding reimbursement requests.

Top commanders to lead reinforcement of Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast, Zelensky says
Andrii Biletskii, commander of the Third Army Corps, and Denys Prokopenko, commander of the National Guard's 1st Corps, will lead reorganized units tasked with reinforcing Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Aug. 26 on X.
The announcement came during Zelensky's visit to the front line with Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, where they met with units fighting in the Oleksandrivka sector at the junction of the Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Donetsk oblasts.
Prokopenko has fought against Russia since 2014, when he joined the then-volunteer "Azov" Battalion on July 11, founded by Biletskii, who served as its first commander.
The battalion was reorganized into a regiment in fall 2014 and incorporated into Ukraine's National Guard as the "Azov" Special Purpose Detachment. It became the 12th "Azov" Special Forces Brigade in 2023 following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, before becoming part of the 1st "Azov" Corps in 2025.
In early 2022, Biletskii commanded the "Azov" Special Operations Forces Regiment. The unit was reorganized as the 3rd Assault Brigade in 2023 and expanded into the 3rd Army Corps in 2025.
Both Prokopenko and Biletskii have commanded Ukrainian forces in some of the war's most critical battles.
Prokopenko fought in the defense of Mariupol at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion before being captured by Russian forces. He was held in captivity until Sept. 21, 2022. After returning to service in 2023, he carried out combat missions in the Lyman sector.
Biletskii, meanwhile, fought in the defense of Kyiv and liberation of Kyiv Oblast early in the full-scale invasion, as well as in the liberation of Kherson Oblast and the battles for Avdiivka in Donetsk Oblast.
Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast is the place of the most intense battles on the front lines as Moscow's main offensive effort is focused on the "fortress belt" cities in the region.
Both formations, commanded by Biletskii and Prokopenko, have been deployed to some of the most heavily contested sectors of the Donetsk sector, including around Dobropillia and Lyman.
Russian forces heavily struck Dobropillia since the August breach. Lyman, located in northern Donetsk Oblast with a pre-war population of around 20,000, has been a hotspot on the front line for years, where fighting raged in the Serebrianskyi Forest, just east of the city.
During his visit to the Oleksandrivka sector, Zelensky met with Prokopenko, Biletskii, Drapatyi, as well as with Airborne Forces Commander Oleh Apostol, Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert Brovdi, and Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Head Ivan Fedorov.
The meeting focused on the situation on the battlefield in the sector and the need to improve the effectiveness of Ukrainian forces.
Zelensky added that protection for Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding region should be strengthened, as the southeastern Ukrainian city faces constant Russian air attacks and lies about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from the front line.
"Thank you to everyone working for Ukraine. We are doing everything to strengthen our positions," Zelensky wrote on X.

03:43:43 KST

ASIC warns of 'first significant cracks' in Australian private credit
Australia's corporate and financial watchdog has warned that private credit is facing its "first real test" amid the collapse of several large borrowers and the limiting of redemptions at several major funds.
Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) chair Sarah Court told a gathering in Sydney that the regulator is closely scrutinising what is a much more lightly regulated sector than the banking industry.
"It is early days, and no doubt more and more information will come out in the weeks and months to come, but, unfortunately, what we're seeing is in Australia the first significant cracks," Ms Court said.
Most adult Australians have exposure to private credit via their superannuation funds, and ASIC has indicated it is attuned to this.
"We've called out before that private credit is important for all Australians because of the involvement of people's superannuation funds," Ms Court said.
"This is not some peripheral issue over to one side.
"This really matters, and that is why we've been talking about it for such a long time."
Loading...
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), meanwhile, is keeping a watchful eye on developments in this comparatively opaque debt market.
"People don't know where the leverage is," Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said.
"They don't know who is exposed.
"So, any time that there's a big unknown, you know it's a big chunk of lending, but you don't know anything about it. That just makes people worried."
Bathla collapse, Adgemis bankruptcy highlight private credit risks
Signs of stress in Australia's private credit sector have not been a major cause for concern until recently.
Documents released under freedom of information (FOI) laws show the RBA has been looking into the local private credit sector, but it has not yet seen anything of concern, especially in relation to any hint of systemic risk to the overall financial system.
In its simplest form, private credit is any lending outside the formal banking system, or funding provided by non-bank financial intermediaries.
"In Australia, I don't think there is a massive worry about it," Ms Bullock told the ABC at the RBA's August press conference.
But this week's move by major NSW property developer Bathla to appoint administrators, along with the earlier bankruptcy of Jon Adgemis and the collapse of his hospitality group, has raised a few eyebrows among key Australian industry officials and representatives.
Bathla had large lines of private credit, as did Mr Adgemis via his hospitality businesses.
As at June 30 last year, Bathla's parent company, Universal Property Group, had $3.2 billion in liabilities, the majority of which was reportedly owed to private credit funds.
Meanwhile, Mr Adgemis borrowed $1.8 billion, much of it also from private credit firms.
Meanwhile, an increasing number of Australian non-bank lenders have been restricting investor redemptions as they run up against their own liquidity constraints.
They include Merricks, Longreach Credit and Centuria Bass.
When an overwhelming number of investors ask private credit lenders to return their money, those firms may seek to limit how much money they return to those investors to avoid a run on funds or simply to maintain their own desired levels of liquidity.
Yesterday, MA Financial announced a temporary redemption limit of up to 1 per cent of its funds under management per month.
MA Financial's joint chief executive, Chris Wyke, told Nine newspapers the action was a "proactive measure in response to the potential for increased redemption activity".
"The temporary arrangements reflect the broader market, including uncertainty following proposed tax changes in the federal budget and recent publicity concerning other, unrelated private credit managers," he said.
Financial Services Council announces new private credit standards
Wall Street is ground zero for the alternative investment market, and there are fears this massive, risky US private lending ship is sinking and investors are jumping out.
Now, the Financial Services Council (FSC), the peak body for Australia's financial services industry, is seeking to head off similar worries taking hold in Australia.
It has released a new industry standard for the private markets and private credit sectors designed, it said, "to strengthen investor confidence and lift industry practices in the growing market".
It said the mandatory standards had been "developed in collaboration with leading domestic and global private market operators and superannuation funds".
"The FSC recognises that rapid growth in the private markets sector has created inconsistent practices, which create risks for consumers; however, industry adherence to the standard will reduce these risks," FSC chief executive Blake Briggs said.
"The FSC and our members have responded in good faith to ASIC's call for enhanced industry standards, to help address the legitimate concerns ASIC and the Reserve Bank of Australia have towards the private credit market."
ASIC said it welcomed the FSC's new standards, amid its concerns that private credit issues were now "emerging in real time".
ASIC has told the ABC it will be providing an update on its research into the private credit sector later this year.

US blacklists Palestine Action as terrorist group

US blacklists Palestine Action as terrorist group
The US has labeled Palestine Action a terrorist group, marking the first time that a British left-wing organization has been targeted by US terrorism sanctions. The US Treasury also blacklisted two other left-wing groups.
Palestine Action was added to the US’ list of Specially Designated Global Terrorist organizations on Wednesday, according to a statement posted online by the US Treasury Department. Under the department’s sanctions, the group will have any of its bank accounts or property in the US frozen, while its members could be barred from entering the country.
Formed in the UK in 2020, Palestine Action’s stated goal is to end “global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime.” Its members have vandalized British military aircraft and factories owned by or linked to Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons manufacturer.
The British government declared Palestine Action a terrorist organization last July. Since the designation, four of its members have been sentenced as terrorists for causing criminal damage to an Elbit Systems plant, while more than 3,500 of its supporters have been arrested and 480 charged with terror offenses for endorsing the group.
Today, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control took action to counter the growing threat posed by violent far-left terrorist groups. Globally networked and politically motivated terrorists—particularly far-left terrorists—are increasingly embracing organized, deadly violence…
— Treasury Department (@USTreasury) August 26, 2026
“Today’s action complements the UK’s proscription,” the Treasury Department stated, adding that Palestine Action was being sanctioned “for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods and services to or in support of, an act of terrorism.”
“Palestine Action’s activities in the US and elsewhere have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine, which is committing a genocide in Gaza with the support of the US Government,” Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said in a statement. “[US President Donald] Trump has been at the center of the mass murder of Palestinians, enabling the Zionist regime at every turn.”
The Treasury also sanctioned Masar Badil, a Palestinian revolutionary movement allegedly run by the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), and Autistici Inventati, described by the department as “an Italy-based entity that supplies specialized digital architecture, tools, and services for Antifa cells and other violent far-left extremists.”
The 2026 US Counterterrorism Strategy identifies “Violent Left-Wing Extremists, including Anarchists and Anti-Fascists” as one of the top three terror threats facing the US, along with transnational drug cartels and Islamist terrorists. In late 2025, the US State Department designated four European ‘Antifa’ groups – including a German group that attacked right-wingers with hammers in Budapest in 2023 – as terrorist organizations.

US senator hopes 'sledgehammer' Russian sanctions will pass next month
KYIV, Aug 26 - A U.S. senator sponsoring a bill for wide-ranging sanctions on Russia said on Wednesday he was hopeful it would pass the House of Representatives next month, and be a "sledgehammer" to President Vladimir Putin's efforts to fund his war in Ukraine.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut who met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and senior officials during a visit to Kyiv, said the bill had strong Republican support in the House, after comfortably passing an initial Senate vote last month.
"Putin understands only force," Blumenthal told a news conference. "And the Russia sanctions bill is a sledgehammer that can have the kind of force Putin understands."
Though Democrats are broadly supportive of the sanctions, some have expressed concern that it would give Republican President Donald Trump leeway to impose additional tariffs, including on U.S. allies.
The bill would sanction top Russian officials and allow Trump to set tariffs of up to 100% on the top buyers of Russia's oil and gas, which include China and India, in an effort to stem revenue flows to Moscow.
Blumenthal said exemptions in the bill would spare European allies from the imposition of tariffs, allaying concerns raised by some Democratic legislators.
Blumenthal said he had asked Zelenskiy to lobby members of the House of Representatives to support its passage.
Zelenskiy spoke to several senators in Washington last month ahead of the vote on the bill, which took place on the day of the funeral of its co-author, the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Blumenthal said Zelenskiy had "heartily and readily agreed" to his request. Ukraine's presidency did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Italy extends diesel tax cut as Premier Meloni faces pressure over fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
18:38:54 UTC
03:38:54 KST

Giada Zampano
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
Italy’s government on Wednesday extended a reduction in diesel excise duties until Sept. 5, prolonging a measure aimed at shielding households and businesses from higher fuel costs linked to rising oil prices.
The latest extension will cost an estimated 130 million euros in lost revenue, according to Italian media.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government has repeatedly rolled over fuel tax cuts since the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict in February, which has contributed to higher crude oil prices.
The relief now applies only to diesel, with a reduction of about 17 euro cents per liter remaining in place through Sept. 5.
The extension comes as rising fuel prices have become a growing concern for consumers and businesses, particularly trucking companies and farmers that rely heavily on diesel. Higher energy costs have added to pressure on Meloni’s right-wing government as it seeks to protect purchasing power and support economic growth.
The issue also carries political weight ahead of parliamentary elections next year. Opposition parties have accused the government of failing to tackle the broader cost-of-living squeeze, while business groups have warned that persistently high fuel prices could undermine competitiveness.
Meloni's office said earlier this week that when the current excise duty cuts expire, the government may move toward more targeted support aimed at lower-income households rather than broad-based tax relief.
The Italian Confederation of Craft Trades and Small- and Medium-Sized Enterprises (CNA) on Monday estimated that the Iran war could cost Italy nearly €12 billion ($13.9 billion).
The CNA is said to have estimated the additional expenditure on fuel, electricity and gas between March 1 and Aug. 31 at around €11.6 billion ($13.5 billion), compared with levels before the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28.
The additional costs weigh on households and businesses, with more than half attributable to mobility.
The CNA estimated the additional cost of gasoline and diesel at around €5.8 billion over the six-month period.

Why a U.S. Marine fought — and died — for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
18:37:32 UTC
03:37:32 KST

Why a U.S. Marine fought — and died — for Ukraine
Shane Tackett, from a ceremony held in his honor in Shawnee, Oklahoma, on April 17, 2026. (Riley-Walker Funeral Service)
On Thanksgiving morning 2025, Shane Tackett texted his wife to say he was heading out on a mission and would be gone for a couple of days. He was killed three days later, on Nov. 30, in the basement of a house his unit was clearing in a contested town in Ukraine.
Tackett, 36, was a former U.S. Marine from Prague, Oklahoma, who had been looking for a way to fight for Ukraine since the first weeks of the full-scale invasion. It took him three years to find one. He arrived in Ukraine on Aug. 6, 2025, and served with the Azov Brigade’s international battalion under the call sign Ares. He is survived by his wife, Amariah Tackett, and daughters Lily and Iris.
From a young age, his preferred bed was a military cot, and every Christmas he wished for anything related to the military or survival. “We have a home VHS tape of one of our Christmases, and he's like 14, maybe 13, and he got a military-grade sleeping bag and he's so excited. It's like the actual military one they were issuing at the time, and he absolutely loved that,” his brother, Chad Tackett, remembered. Chad called him his best friend.
Tackett joined the Marine Corps out of high school and met Amariah after his service. “He called me by my name, Amariah, and not a lot of people can say it right,” she said. “I thought he was kind of handsome.”
They married Feb. 10, 2017, and lived in a small apartment in Oklahoma City. In October 2018, after talking it over with Tackett, Amariah enlisted in the Air Force. They both liked the idea of moving around and the sense of adventure. “I always say ‘we joined the military’ because I feel like we did it as a team,” she said. “Even though technically I was the one that enlisted, we did it as a family. We made that decision and he followed me everywhere I went.”
The couple hiked and camped, and had climbed 14,000-foot (4,270 meters) mountains together. “That was one of the things I loved about him. He was just very adventurous,” Amariah said. When they couldn’t get outside, they played survival games on their computer.
They had been married eight years and had come to believe, after trying for a child, that it would not happen. Then Amariah learned at a routine appointment that she was pregnant.
read also
She told Tackett with a Pokémon card which both of them collected. “I got a Pokémon card pack, and I opened it gently, and slipped a little card in there that said I was pregnant,” she said. “He was so surprised. He just walked around the house the rest of the evening in a daze.”
Iris was born in May 2025. Tackett was not an emotional man, Amariah said, but when he saw his daughter, “he cried, and was so excited to meet her, and absolutely loved her.”
Tackett also had a 16-year-old daughter, Lily. He called them “our little flowers,” Amariah said.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Tackett wanted to join the Ukrainian military almost immediately. With Amariah’s help, he tried, but at that stage there was no clear route in for foreign volunteers. They let it go, but he kept following the war.
“He just had this desire to go over and help, or figure out a way to help,” Amariah said. In 2025, he left his job as a safety specialist. “I told him we'll find another one,” she said. “He was looking for what he needed to do.”
His brother remembered a smaller kid who fought other people's fights and a man who refused to sit still when a country was being bullied. "We're humans, it's not a country thing, it's not a border thing, it's a human thing. Atrocities are happening," Chad recalled him saying. Tackett was brave enough, his brother said, to give his life for something that might stop it, or at least slow it down.
“My husband ever since he was younger has had a heart for justice,” Amariah said. “He wanted to protect innocent people. He really just felt that the Ukrainian people needed help.”
In 2025, there was a route in. “We were able to actually reach out to Azov and get him on there, and it just opened up at that point,” Amariah said. “They have a really good process now. At the beginning they didn't have it as streamlined as it is now.”
By the time Iris was three months old, the new parents had decided it was the moment. The couple had agreed their daughter was young enough not to register Tackett’s absence. They both believed Tackett would return home after three years, when Iris would be old enough to get to know her father.
Before he left, he recorded videos for Iris so she would not forget him. “He was excited to come back and raise her.”
Amariah was scared for Tackett’s life, but she fully supported his decision. She knew his desire to help Ukraine since the full-scale invasion never subsided. Even while he approached Ukraine through Poland, she guided him through any issues he encountered by phone.
Before he left, Tackett told his brother the Ukrainians would have to fight for every inch, and even in retreat would give nothing away for free. “I think he was very proud before even getting into Ukraine,” Chad said. “Proud of the Ukrainian people and their fight against evil.”
The onboarding process with the Azov Brigade’s international battalion was thorough, Amariah recalled. The team sent a full information packet, walked him through the application and was honest about conditions at the front. Tackett knew what he was going into.
The call sign came with him. “Ares is the god of war. It's something he's used ever since he was little,” she said. “He used it as his gaming name. It's kind of like his alter ego. When he was headed over to Ukraine and heard that everyone goes by call signs, he hoped he could be Ares. And when he went over there, no one had Ares.”
A soldier in his unit who goes by the call sign Cheese said Tackett had achieved the highest score on the combat lifesaver test when he arrived. “He was a Marine from the start. He had a very Western NATO mindset. He was definitely super loyal to the team. He was prepared as a soldier, as a gunfighter, as everything. He was really, really good,” Cheese said.
Shane and Amariah talked almost every day on WhatsApp. Unless he was out on a mission, he had Wi-Fi in the field. The last message Amariah received about her husband came Nov. 29, from a man in his unit writing on his behalf: Ares is alive, it’s going well, he loves you.
On Nov. 30, the unit was sent to clear a street with houses on both sides. One team would assault the first building. Tackett’s team would follow behind and clear a second.
After the first side was cleared, the team split. Tackett was among those sent back to cross over and work up the opposite side. Command then warned of incoming fire and ordered them to take cover. They fell back into a building they had already cleared, and Tackett and another man went down into the basement first. The rest of the team followed.
“I was standing outside in the back. I heard gunfire going off inside,” Cheese said. “Two members of my team came running up the stairs and out of the basement. I posted up on the door and explosions started going off. I started yelling down to Ares and my two (seconds-in-command). There was no response.”
Russian soldiers were still alive inside the basement and killed the three men, Cheese said. “We waited for about an hour and then went back to that position and we sat there and we dug until we got them out. We carried them about a kilometer down the street and waited to have their bodies taken out.”
Tackett’s body was recovered the day he was killed. Three days later, on Dec. 3, Amariah was driving to work when the U.S. embassy in Kyiv called to tell her that her husband had been declared missing in action, a bureaucratic peculiarity that precedes an official declaration of killed in action.
“They did let me know that it’s almost the same as being killed in action,” she said. “I turned around and went back home. Obviously with the status of missing in action, I had hope that he would be found, but they were very honest with me at the embassy that if someone's missing in action, it's very rare that it would be anything else.”
The embassy and the battalion kept the family updated throughout, she said, and the unit held a ceremony for Tackett in Ukraine. “I was super impressed by what they were able to accomplish to get Shane back home,” she said.
The R.T. Weatherman Foundation, which supports the families of foreign military volunteers killed or missing in Ukraine, handled the paperwork and guided the family through the process. The foundation also connects the American families of volunteers killed in Ukraine with one another.
Shane Tackett was buried April 17, 2026, in Shawnee, Oklahoma.
“You just don't want it to be true,” Amariah said. She has had support from her family and friends, from her military family and from Iris. “I knew I couldn't just stop. At that point she was six months old, so she still needed me a lot. She still does, and she keeps me going.”
The family remains committed to Ukraine, though, as an active-duty service member, Amariah is limited in what she can say publicly. “I think the Ukrainian people are amazing. You know, they have a heart like I've never seen before. They are so inventive and innovative,” she said. “I have more of an investment in it because of the sacrifice my family's had so I really want to see them win now. I would like it for my husband, because he was very passionate about them.”
When Iris is older, Amariah plans to take her to the country her father helped defend. “We'll plan a trip to Ukraine eventually, when things settle down,” she said. “There are people over there just like us, and they're trying to do right by their people. I would like to see good relations with the United States and Ukraine.”
“Just remember why your loved ones went over there and know that the support you gave them while they were over there was so important,” she said. “We wanted all our loved ones to come home. But that doesn't negate the reason why they went over there.”
