Foreign minister heads to Palau for island meet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:52 UTC
01:47:52 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) is to attend an annual gathering of Pacific Island leaders in Palau next week, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday, after Taiwan and other non-members of the bloc were barred from the event last year.
Lin departs for Palau today to attend meetings coinciding with the 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) summit, to be held in Koror from Sunday to Sept. 4, the ministry said.
Events include the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue and the Pacific Prosperity Exhibit, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
The exhibit showcases Taiwan’s ongoing efforts to help its Pacific partners in areas such as digital resilience, renewable energy, smart medicine and healthcare, infrastructure and social empowerment, the ministry said.
Lin is leading a delegation with representatives from the energy, technology, food, construction and agricultural sectors, the ministry said.
The minister plans to visit Palauan President Surangel Whipps, Jr. and Vice President Raynold B. Oilouch, and inspect a Taiwan-funded project in Palau — the development of the Belau National Hospital’s artificial intelligence system — to see its progress and discuss future cooperation, the ministry said.
He is to meet with “Taiwan’s Pacific allies and other friendly nations to discuss deepening Taiwan’s partnerships with Pacific Island nations and jointly maintaining peace, stability and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific region,” it said.
Although not a member of the PIF, Taiwan has been a “development partner” in PIF mechanisms since 1993. It usually holds the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue and other side events alongside the PIF’s annual summit.
However, the Solomon Islands, the host of last year’s meeting, barred Taiwan from attending at the time.
This resulted in all external countries being disinvited, despite the island states’ reliance on foreign aid and investment, and the PIF Leaders’ Meeting was attended only by the bloc’s 18 member states.
China has poached several of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the Pacific as part of its efforts to expand its dominance in the region and isolate Taiwan from the international community.
PIF members Nauru, Kiribati and Solomon Islands have all switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to Beijing since 2019.
Reports suggested that the Solomon Islands sought to block Taiwan’s participation due to coercion from Beijing.
This year’s host, Palau, is among Taiwan’s 12 remaining diplomatic partners, along with Pacific nations Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands.
China’s test-firing last month of a missile into the Pacific alarmed regional powers, but failed to spur a unified response from Pacific Island governments, underscoring divisions over how to confront growing strategic competition in the region.
China has expanded its influence in the Pacific in the past few years through infrastructure financing, diplomatic outreach and security cooperation, which has prompted concern among traditional partners including Australia, New Zealand and the US.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lin’s visit to Palau.

A rare urban colony of Formosan flying foxes has been found in Hualien City, where century- old trees and abundant food sources planted under colonial- era urban planning have inadvertently created a favorable habitat for the endangered species, researchers said in Taipei Wednesday.
The findings were presented at a press conference held ahead of International Bat Night, an annual event promoting public awareness and bat conservation that will take place Aug. 29-30 this year.
A 2024 survey found 154 Formosan flying foxes, the largest bat species in Taiwan, living in and around Hualien City, making it one of the largest known populations of the endangered endemic bats in Taiwan and an unusual example of a colony thriving in an urban environment, according to the researchers.
Photo courtesy of the Hualien County Government Agricultural Department
Lin Ching-lung (林清隆), a doctoral researcher at National Taiwan Normal University, said the first known sighting in Hualien City was reported by a teacher at Hualien Girls’ Senior High School in 1992.
Researchers initially thought the animal was an isolated visitor, but later discovered an established colony living in the city, Lin said.
He said the colony’s presence may be linked to trees planted as part of Hualien’s colonial-era urban development, adding that many trees along the city’s streets and in its parks produce fruit eaten by flying foxes, including century-old sea mango trees.
The abundance of food and tall trees allows the flying foxes to feed and roost in the eastern Taiwan city during the day, Lin said.
The contrast with Taitung City is notable, he added. Although Taitung has similar coastal geography, it does not have a comparable urban flying fox population, possibly because Hualien has more green space and suitable trees.
However, climate change could threaten the colony. Lin said fruit production by one of the flying foxes’ major food sources, the large-leaved tree, was only about one-third of normal this year, raising concerns that the population could decline as food becomes scarcer.
Formosan flying foxes are fruit bats that play an important role in seed dispersal and pollination, researchers said, adding that they hope to work with local communities to preserve suitable urban habitats and encourage people to view the animals as an important part of the ecosystem rather than a threat.
The species was once mainly found on Green Island, but nearly disappeared due to overhunting. It is classified as an endangered protected wildlife species under Taiwan’s Wildlife Conservation Act.

US unites in mourning of country star Dolly Parton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:51 UTC
01:47:51 KST

Flags across the US yesterday flew at half-staff, as grieving fans gathered in the late country music star Dolly Parton’s hometown in Tennessee and the nation paid tribute to the beloved cultural icon.
Parton, who rose from grinding poverty to become a rhinestone-studded entertainment giant with hits like Jolene and 9 to 5, has died at 80, her family announced on Tuesday.
Parton was more than a singer — she wrote 3,000 songs, starred in major Hollywood films and donated millions to charities in her home state and beyond.
Photo: AFP
Parton died after a brief battle with cancer, her third cousin Brent Allen confirmed.
US President Donald Trump called Parton’s death a “true loss for millions of people.”
“There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump wrote on social media.
Photo: Reuters
He ordered flags lowered across the country, while New York’s Empire State Building was to be lit in pink at 9:25pm — a nod to Parton’s hit song and movie 9 to 5.
As the news of Parton’s death spread, hundreds gathered in Sevierville, Tennessee, to pay tribute.
Mourning fans laid flowers at a statue in the town which depicts Parton strumming an acoustic guitar.
Photo: AP
“We’ve always called her our patron saint of Tennessee,” fan Callie Konane Rickards said.
Parton’s death sparked a rare moment of unity in a country often bitterly at odds over Trump’s presidency, the war against Iran and cultural issues.
Former US president Joe Biden called Parton “an American original” who “treated everyone with kindness and respect.”
Former US president George W. Bush praised “her work to promote literacy, advance health, and strengthen communities.”
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani praised Parton as “an irreplaceable champion of the working class.”
“We are a better country because of her,” he said.
Singer Miley Cyrus took to X to mourn the passing of Parton, who was her godmother.
“So many evil people in this world and we had to lose a pure heart like Dolly Parton,” Cyrus wrote. “Devastating day for humanity.”
Across the world of entertainment there was a palpable sense of loss, but also one of gratefulness for a person whose life was filled with joy and compassion.
Actress Jane Fonda, who performed opposite Parton in 9 to 5, mourned Parton’s loss.
“Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever,” Fonda said on Instagram.
Beatle Paul McCartney posted on Instagram about meeting Parton early in her career, adding that “she was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed.”
Even rapper Eminem praised Parton, sharing a letter she had written him after he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
“She definitely didn’t have to take the time to do it. Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon. A superstar in every sense,” he wrote on X.

BOOK REVIEW: Does protest make a difference?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:50 UTC
01:47:50 KST

At 74, the comedian Alexei Sayle is approaching a dangerous phase for veteran British leftists: becoming a national treasure. Once described by special branch, in a surveillance file gleefully quoted in this memoir, as an “intellectual thug” who made “foul-mouthed comments about the royal family,” Sayle now appears regularly on Radio 4. His jolly, self-deprecating, man of the people side — one of his radio series is called Alexei Sayle’s Imaginary Sandwich Bar — has made him almost cosy.
But not quite. One fascination of his meandering career, which has included villainous Hollywood cameos, subversive podcasts and successful novelty pop songs, is the persistent fierceness of his politics — the underlying subject of this short, sharp book.
“My decision to become … a professional funny man,” he writes, “wasn’t a choice made simply out of monstrous vanity … I was also … taking part in [Antonio] Gramsci’s war of position: attempting to get examples of communist thought on to Top of the Pops, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade and Doctor Who.”
Alongside such sometimes well-paid efforts to apply the culture war strategies of the late Italian Marxist, Sayle has also been on a lot of marches. The contrasts and contradictions between these two forms of activism — one repetitive but comradely, the other more glamorous but often isolated — are pondered, mocked and mined for anecdotes in these busy, digressive pages. From marching against American imperialism with his communist parents in Liverpool in the 1960s to marching for the Palestinians in London last year, Sayle richly conveys the mix of enthusiasm and doubt which anyone who goes on demos will recognize: “believing in the cause but also skeptical that protesting about it would be sufficient.”
He confesses to other complicated feelings about street politics.
“I have always found it a sad thing to be alone on a demo, lonely in a crowd,” he writes.
Then he describes watching protesters fight the police: “I didn’t join in but nevertheless experienced a tremendous rush of exhilaration.”
With his bulging eyes and cannonball head, straining suits and air of menace, the Sayle who first became famous as a standup and a star of the boisterous sitcom The Young Ones in the early 1980s seemed like someone who could handle himself in a political pavement battle. But this book shows he is much less macho, constantly examining his own motives and often finding himself ridiculous, “a capering jester.”
In 1991, during one of his sporadic attempts at US success, he went to Hollywood with his wife for auditions. Beforehand, “we went out for a walk along Sunset Boulevard in the hot night,” he writes.
“The pavement was deserted except up ahead … was a single figure. ‘I bet they’re British,’ I said to Linda. When we reached this solitary pedestrian it turned out to be Billy Bragg.”
There is a beautiful absurdity and melancholy about these two mouthpieces of austere alternative Britain in the 1980s now wandering a seductively escapist part of California in a less politicized decade. Although, given the way the book flits cheekily between droll stories, polemic and fantasy, we can’t be completely sure this meeting actually happened.
There are other irreverent encounters with fellow radicals. The Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arabian Gulf once held their annual congress in a small, suburban London flat where Sayle lived in the 1970s. To him at least, “Their main activity seemed to be smoking, staying up all night and reading foreign newspapers in cafes.”
During the 1990s, he drifted away from activism, disillusioned by the left’s flagging momentum and distracted by his career’s proliferating demands. He is cutting about the left’s — and his own — frequent lack of focus and forward thinking. But then the 2003 Iraq war protests re-energized him: “There is something elemental, ancient and magical about … a huge crowd of one mind.”
Towards the book’s end, its tone becomes more consistent and serious.
“I have marched on every Palestine demonstration since Oct. 7,” writes Sayle, who is Jewish, and he has lost friends as a result.
Like a good political pamphlet, this slim volume is fiery and addictive. Yet unlike a pamphlet, it shows how politics relates to the rest of life.
When we recall the 1990s, we usually identify them as the time of great transitions, from authoritarianism to democracy, and the public’s shift to acknowledging a Taiwanese identity. But another transition occurred, one that we take for granted and hardly notice anymore. The 1980s opened with the massacre of members of the family of democracy activist Lin I-hsiung (林義雄). While Lin was in detention, on Feb. 28, 1980, persons still unknown broke into the Lin family home despite round-the-clock police surveillance. Lin’s mother and two of his three daughters were slain. His eldest daughter survived multiple stab wounds. The following year

Smartphone camera lens supplier Largan Precision Co (大立光) has made its fourth land purchase this year, announcing on Tuesday that it has bought land and a building in Taichung for NT$3.08 billion (US$96.8 million) to expand production.
While Largan did not disclose any further details on the purpose of the acquisition, analysts said it was likely aimed at supporting efforts to develop copackaged optics (CPO)-related products, such as fiber array units, a business the company recently added to its product portfolio.
The new plot covers about 20,800m2, and the building has a floor area of 23,319m2, the company’s filing with the Taiwan Stock Exchange said.
Photo: CNA
Largan, a supplier to Apple Inc, said the seller of the property was Ke Hung Industrial Co (科宏工業).
The linking of the purchase to the CPO product line came after Largan chairman Adam Lin (林恩平) told reporters that the company had secured its first fiber array unit orders, with trial production expected at the end of the third quarter.
Lin said at the time that Largan’s fiber array units are expected to begin generating revenue in the middle of next year at the earliest.
Largan shares attracted strong interest after the market opened yesterday on news of the property deal. The stock soared 10 percent, the maximum daily increase, to close at a new high of NT$6,290, outperforming the TAIEX, which rose 1.47 percent to 45,832.62 points.
Buying in Largan also spread to other CPO-related stocks, with EZconn Corp (光紅建聖) rising 0.31 percent to NT$1,610.

Interactive traffic safety park opens in Kaohsiung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:49 UTC
01:47:49 KST

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications yesterday opened southern Taiwan’s first interactive traffic safety education park in Kaohsiung, a NT$10 million (US$314,288) facility featuring simulated roads, vehicle demonstrations and interactive technology to promote road safety awareness.
There were more than 400,000 traffic incidents in Taiwan last year, claiming 2,858 lives, with motorcyclists and pedestrians among the groups at highest risk, ministry data showed.
Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Chiayi City have similar facilities, and one is under construction in Taichung, Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said.
Photo: CNA
“We hope to educate the public about the importance of road safety through such facilities, which would be available nationwide,” Chen said.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Lin Tai-hua (林岱樺) told the opening ceremony that elderly people and children in Kaohsiung should have priority access to the park to enhance their road safety awareness.
Kaohsiung Motor Vehicle Office Director Feng Ching-man (馮靜滿) said the park has a 1,320m2 outdoor traffic-safety simulation area and a 430m2 indoor interactive area.
Visitors can simulate crossing intersections with and without signals, learn about large vehicles’ blind spots and watch a live demonstration of vehicle off-tracking in the outdoor area, Feng said.
The hands-on exercises are designed to help visitors better judge right of way and recognize the dangers of being in a car’s blind spot, she said.
In the indoor area, visitors can learn about road safety in a fun and intuitive way through board games and augmented-reality experiences featuring bicycles and micro electric vehicles, she said.
The Kaohsiung Department of Social Affairs has added the park as a stop on its “Happy Shuttle for Seniors” route, allowing more elderly people to refresh their knowledge of traffic safety, she said, adding that the Kaohsiung Department of Education has shared information about the park with schools at all levels, helping instill traffic-safety awareness among students from a young age.
The Kaohsiung Motor Vehicles Office said the park is open for online group reservations, with each session accommodating 20 to 30 people and lasting about two hours.
Schools, government agencies and organizations are welcome to make reservations online through the Kaohsiung Motor Vehicles Office’s Web site or by phone to experience a different approach to traffic-safety education firsthand, it said.

Leadtek reports limited impact from Nvidia hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:48 UTC
01:47:48 KST

Leadtek Research Inc (麗臺科技), a distributor of graphics cards, artificial intelligence (AI) workstations and AI servers, expects limited impact from Nvidia Corp’s price hikes on certain products, a Leadtek source told the Taipei Times yesterday.
Leadtek is a long-term partner of Nvidia and an authorized reseller of the US chipmaker’s products.
Nvidia recently notified customers of another round of price increases, with high-end computing cards and RTX PRO-series graphics processing units (GPUs) rising 40 to 60 percent amid higher memory costs. Further increases remain possible by the end of this year, people familiar with the matter said last week.
Photo courtesy of Leadtek Research Inc
Leadtek’s inventories secured before the price increases could meet demand through October, the source said.
In the second quarter, the company’s revenue rose 59.68 percent sequentially and more than doubled year-on-year to NT$2.5 billion (US$78.6 million), driven by strong demand for Nvidia gaming graphics cards, AI workstations and high-end GPUs.
Net profit was NT$154.13 million, surging 42.99 percent quarter-on-quarter and growing by more than five times year-on-year. Earnings per share rebounded to NT$1.64 from NT$1.15 in the previous quarter and NT$0.27 a year earlier. Gross margin rose to 12.28 percent from 10.65 percent in the previous quarter.
The company expects revenue this quarter to exceed last quarter’s, with growth momentum mainly from high-end GPUs, particularly the RTX PRO 6000, the source said.
For the full year, revenue is expected to outperform and could even double from last year’s NT$4.44 billion if supply and demand for GPU products remain strong, the source added.
China remained the company’s biggest market in the first half, accounting for about 50 percent of its total revenue, the source said.
Leadtek sees stronger growth opportunities in South Korea this quarter, as government-led AI investment and local tenders for software, hardware and training are expected to boost sales of AI workstations, servers and high-end graphics cards, the source said.
The company also expects more shipments of GPUs used in AI image processing to Vietnam’s government security surveillance and image-recognition projects, the source added.

Sea warning for typhoon likely today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:48 UTC
01:47:48 KST

A sea warning for Typhoon Saudel, which shifted to a more northerly track as it approached Taiwan, is likely early today, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
As of 2pm yesterday, the center of typhoon was about 630km northeast of Taipei, moving west-northwest at 14kph with maximum wind gusts of up to 162kph, CWA data showed.
Saudel is a moderate typhoon and is expected to weaken as it nears Taiwan due to atmospheric and ocean conditions, CWA forecaster Lin Po-tung (林伯東) said.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
A sea warning indicates hazardous typhoon conditions in waters surrounding Taiwan within 24 hours, Lin said.
The storm is forecast to make its closest approach to Taiwan today and tomorrow, he said.
Saudel’s track is forecast to shift northward toward China’s Zhejiang Province, bringing it closer to Taiwan’s outlying Lienchiang County (Matsu), he said.
While the typhoon’s circulation is forecast to mainly affect waters north of the county, it could also brush its islands, meaning a land warning for Matsu is possible.

Heavy rain in the past week have caused widespread agricultural damage across Taiwan, with losses totaling about NT$108 million (US$3.39 million) as of 11am yesterday, the Ministry of Agriculture said, citing data from local governments.
Southern Taiwan has experienced days of torrential downpours due to strong southwest winds and a low-pressure system.
Chiayi County sustained the most damage, reporting losses of NT$41.77 million, the data showed.
Photo courtesy of the Tainan Agriculture Bureau
Crop damage accounted for the majority of the nationwide financial toll at about NT$90.84 million.
Among crops, papayas were the most severely affected, with 127 hectares damaged nationwide, it showed.
Losses for the fruit totaled NT$20.14 million, as 27 percent of papaya operations were affected, the data showed.
The other top losses among crops were guavas (NT$13.82 million), peanuts (NT$8.75 million), scallions (NT$8.50 million) and bamboo shoots (NT$7.24 million), the ministry said.
Livestock losses were about NT$2.08 million, primarily affecting chickens, the data showed.
Fishery losses were estimated at NT$12.31 million, with milkfish accounting for the greatest portion, followed by marble goby and tilapia, it showed.
To help resume operations, farmers in Chiayi city and county, Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung County are eligible for natural disaster cash relief and low-interest recovery loans, the ministry said.
All aquaculture ponds in Tainan and Kaohsiung are included in the relief program, it added.
The Agricultural Finance Agency said that a review of insurance policies showed that four weather-index policies covering aquaculture, papayas, wax apples and guavas met the threshold for payouts, with claims totaling NT$21 million.
Households affected by flooding of 30cm to 50cm can apply for NT$10,000 to NT$20,000 in relief, along with an additional NT$10,000 subsidy for damaged home appliances, President William Lai (賴清德) said.

Artificial intelligence threatens the democratic bargain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:47 UTC
01:47:47 KST

In a county in northern Virginia, a family’s electricity bill has doubled. A few miles away, a windowless building the size of a shopping mall hums through the night — yet another artificial intelligence (AI) data center, consuming more power than the town it was built beside. The dispute would be conducted in the language of rate structures, zoning variances and transmission corridors. However, a non-technical political question drives it: Are the people who live in the county still needed by the people who constructed the building?
The question is not just about AI. It concerns the bargain on which modern democracy rests.
Democracy was never the gift of elites who discovered justice. Constitutions and elections are the visible machinery of limited government, but why did those with power accept limits at all?
Rights were won by workers, women, soldiers, dissidents and movements that made exclusion politically dangerous, and material dependence helped make those victories durable. When modern states needed armies of ordinary men rather than a warrior caste, they needed recruits, taxes and sacrifice — and therefore some measure of consent. People asked to fight, pay and suffer for a state would eventually ask what place they have in it.
A similar dynamic was apparent in industrial cities, which discovered that disease ignores class boundaries. Sewers, clean water and quarantine laws reflected the recognition that a city’s poor breathe on its rich. Elites paid for the wellbeing of people they did not love because they could not be well without them.
Likewise, Henry Ford’s five-dollar day was not philanthropy. Mass production required mass consumption. Ford recognized the industrial order’s larger truth: wages, consumption and output held each other up.
Because the powerful could not prosper without the cooperation of ordinary people, they had reason to honor claims that they would rather have ignored. AI raises the possibility that this bargain is weakening.
It is not disappearing, at least not yet — and perhaps never in the crude form the futurists imagine. The technology might augment more workers than it replaces and create occupations no one has yet named. However, the political danger is not that every worker would be made redundant. To destroy the democratic bargain, AI does not have to make ordinary people useless. It has only to make elites less dependent on them.
The older dependencies have already thinned. Wars are increasingly fought by professionals, contractors and drones, and decades of automation have produced a narrow social stratum that is deemed intensely valuable, a larger group that is made insecure, and a great many citizens who are told, in effect, that their contribution is optional.
Suppose the technology delivers much of what its promoters promise, allowing firms to replace rather than merely assist large numbers of workers. An automated economy would not thereby lose its customers; it could sustain demand through exports, government purchases, credit or transfers to households.
However, a society in which most people receive a stipend drawn from wealth they neither own nor govern distributes political leverage very differently from one in which people earn wages, pay taxes, organize and bargain over production. The latter is full of conflict, inequality and exploitation — but it gives citizens bargaining power because they have something to withhold. A stipend-based society might be richer in goods, but poorer in standing. It could preserve consumption while hollowing out citizenship.
Data centers are not oil wells, but the political economy resembles the “resource curse” long associated with rentier states: When decisive wealth is generated from assets requiring little ongoing contribution from the population, a narrow group of rulers and owners has less reason to bargain broadly. The old slogan was “no taxation without representation.” Yet the darker converse is also true: When those who govern and those who own no longer depend on broad-based taxation, labor or consent, representation begins to look less like a right than a cost they would prefer not to pay.
That is why the local politics of data centers is so important. The industry cannot manufacture everything it needs. It needs land, water, electricity and local permission. Public resistance is already conspicuous.
In a Gallup survey conducted in March, 71 percent of Americans opposed constructing a data center in their own area, including 48 percent who strongly opposed it. People might be uncertain about AI in the abstract, but they understand a higher power bill, a threatened water supply and an industrial facility promising few permanent local jobs.
Local permission is more than obstruction. It is one of the last forms of leverage available to citizens in an economy organized around assets they do not own and systems they cannot inspect. It is also why the uneasy alliance between Silicon Valley and the populist right is splitting at the substation rather than on the talk shows.
However, local permission is leverage only so long as it must be asked for. A government sufficiently committed to the industry has other instruments — eminent domain, federal preemption of local siting authority, emergency authority over the grid — and US history is not reassuring about what befalls communities that hold land the powerful want and supply nothing the powerful need.
The answer is neither to halt the technology nor to romanticize the industrial order it might replace. That bargain was never fair enough, but if labor ceases to be the principal basis on which ordinary citizens claim a share of national wealth, citizenship would need another foundation — beginning with treating automated wealth as a public problem rather than a private achievement. That could mean public claims on the gains from automation, through taxation and through democratic control of the infrastructure on which AI depends.
The underlying arithmetic is simple. Every sanction that ordinary citizens have ever possessed — the ability to withhold labor, taxes, sons or votes — presupposes someone who needs what you can withhold. Where there is no need, there is no leverage. Rights that no longer have a price do not vanish; they become favors, held at the pleasure of those who grant them.
For now, the citizens of northern Virginia still possess one thing the industry cannot code into existence: their permission. The question is whether they would use that leverage merely to say no or to demand a new bargain. The owners of the machines might come to need fewer workers. Would they be allowed to need fewer citizens?
Stephen Holmes is a professor of law at New York University School of Law and the Richard Holbrooke Fellow at the American Academy in Berlin.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Nepal yesterday deployed helicopters after a massive flash flood swept away villages in the Himalayan nation, killing eight and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.
Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with some missing in neighboring Gyirong County after a mudslide hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, Xinhua news agency said.
The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous Rasuwa District, with a population of about 50,000, officials said, while flagging the risk of casualties.
Photo: AFP
“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” Rasuwa Chief District Officer Narendra Pariyar said. “But I cannot say for sure now.”
Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away.
“It all came suddenly,” the Onlinekhabar portal quoted a witness from the area as saying. “We heard a loud sound, like a volcano erupting. People started to scream and ran away.”
The cause of the inundation was not immediately clear, but a deadly flash flood on the same river last year was eventually traced to the draining of a glacier lake.
The mudslide on the Nepalese side hit China’s Port of Gyirong, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region near the border with Nepal, Xinhua said, without giving details.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) urged “all-out” search efforts for the missing as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.
The Nepalese Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said that 430 megawatts of electricity supplies were affected, mostly from hydroelectric projects, or more than 12 percent of total national hydropower capacity of 3.2 gigawatts, a Reuters calculation showed.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said police and military were joining rescue and relief teams.
“Instructions have been given ... to move the people living in the lower areas to safer places,” he said. “People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert.”
From its origins in Tibet, the Bhote Koshi empties into Nepal’s Trishuli River, which eventually flows into India as the Gandak river.

A record number of Japanese players are in the English Premier League this season, with clubs attracted by their proven quality, value for money and the “very little risk” involved in signing them.
Ten players from Japan were registered with top-tier English teams when the campaign started last weekend and more are potentially on the way before the transfer window closes.
Zion Suzuki was the highest-profile arrival with his switch to Aston Villa, with former Arsenal defender Takehiro Tomiyasu returning to London with Crystal Palace, midfielder Hidemasa Morita joining Hull City and Daizen Maeda swapping Celtic for Ipswich Town.
Photo: AFP
They join an established group of Japanese players already in the Premier League, including Brighton’s Kaoru Mitoma, Liverpool’s Wataru Endo and Palace’s Daichi Kamada.
FIFA-registered agent Joel Pannick of CAA Base said that English clubs have “increased confidence that signing a Japanese player is a good move to make.”
“There aren’t many examples of clubs signing Japanese players and having issues with their adaptation, with their personality, with their integration into the squad, with discipline,” said Pannick, who has about 60 Japanese players on his books.
“The risk element that teams previously feared, this fear of the unknown, has gone because with each example of a successful Japanese player it gives more confidence,” he added.
Also in the Premier League are Ao Tanaka (Leeds United), Kota Takai (Tottenham Hotspur) and Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry City).
Midfielder Tanaka, who has played 41 times for Japan, joined from German side Fortuna Dusseldorf for just ￡3.3 million (US$4.5 million at the current exchange rate) two years ago.
Japanese players in England have come a long way since Junichi Inamoto signed for Arsenal in 2001 and left for Fulham a year later without making a league appearance.
There have been successes along the way, with Shinji Kagawa, Shinji Okazaki, Takumi Minamino and Endo all picking up league winner’s medals.
Suzuki, 24, would become the first Japanese goalkeeper to play in the Premier League if he makes his debut after joining Villa from Italian side Parma last week.
Veteran Japanese soccer journalist Yoshiyuki Osumi said he is “10 or 20 years ahead of his time for a Japanese goalkeeper.”
“If he can play in the Premier League as a goalkeeper, I think that would have a big impact on Japanese football,” Osumi said.
Suzuki’s transition to the Premier League would be helped by that he can already communicate in English.
Not all of his compatriots have had that ability in the past, but more are realizing that being able to speak the language is crucial to succeeding in Europe.
Pannick said that his client Maya Yoshida started a culture change when he captained the Japan national team ahead of the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar.
Pannick said that Yoshida, who spent almost eight years at Southampton, would insist that any player who sat at his lunch table must communicate in English.
“To get this more worldly mentality is something that he was very keen to emphasize to the players,” Pannick said. “This current generation of starting national team players or squad players at the World Cup, almost all of them now will speak English to a pretty good degree.”
Most Japanese players would spend time in other European leagues like Belgium, the Netherlands or Portugal before making the step up to the Premier League.
The English Championship has become another popular staging post, and there are currently eight Japanese players in England’s second tier.
Post-Brexit changes to work permit rules have forced English clubs to look beyond Europe for signings.
Osumi said an overall improvement in the level of Japanese players has allowed them to thrive in the Premier League.
However, he said he believes a change in the nature of the league has also made it easier for them to adapt.
“The Premier League has become more tactical, and there are more teams that play as a coordinated unit,” he said. “That kind of football is something Japanese players find very easy to adapt to.”

Taiwan industries should follow electricity supply in AI era: Executive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:43 UTC
01:47:43 KST

Taiwan should reverse its traditional approach to industrial planning by locating artificial intelligence (AI) and other power-intensive industries where electricity and grid capacity are already available, an energy executive said yesterday.
“In the past, electricity followed industry, but in the future, industry should follow electricity,” Fabulous Power Co (結元能源) general manager Sam Hung (洪向民) said at the New Energy Forum in Taipei.
Hung said AI and high-tech industries should develop in areas where power plants, generation sources and grid resources have already been planned, rather than continuing the practice of establishing industrial parks first and then rushing to build power infrastructure nearby.
Photo: CNA
The proposal came as Hung and fellow panelist Kelsey Kuan (關婷怡) discussed the challenge of supplying stable, low-carbon electricity while Taiwan expands renewable generation and energy-intensive AI industries.
“Increasing installed capacity does not mean that the same amount of renewable electricity will be available. 24 hours a day, seven days a week,” Hung said during the panel discussion at the Business Today-organized forum.
Solar and wind power are intermittent, while geothermal energy can provide continuous generation with a capacity factor exceeding 90 percent, making it a potential complement to those sources, he said.
Despite that potential, geothermal development in Taiwan remains constrained by high exploration risks, drilling costs and the limited scale of the domestic industry, Hung said.
More comprehensive geological surveys by the government, combined with investment and participation from private companies and electricity users, will help reduce those risks and expand the sector, he added.
Speaking on the same panel, Kuan, general manager of Star Trade Co (星星電力), said the rise of AI data centers (AIDCs) will create additional challenges for Taiwan’s power system.
Many AIDC operators have RE100 commitments, while Taiwan’s green electricity supply remains tight, Kuan said.
RE100 is a global initiative under which companies pledge to source 100 percent of their electricity from renewable sources.
Storage, microgrids and more sophisticated power-management systems will therefore have to be developed before that demand materializes, Kuan said, noting that a storage project can take between 18 months and two years from securing land to completing procurement and construction.
Such facilities could store surplus renewable electricity and shift it to periods when companies need it, allowing businesses to use a larger share of the green power they purchase, she said.
Kuan also called for clear and consistent government policies and technical standards for energy projects.
“As long as policies and regulations are clear, businesses can respond quickly,” she said.

ALBAWABA- The death toll from devastating floods and landslides in Nepal’s northern Rasuwa district has risen to 100, with hundreds of people still missing, including dozens of foreign tourists and pilgrims, as rescue teams race to reach communities swept away by torrents of mud and water.
Terrifying scenes from the disaster showed powerful floodwaters engulfing settlements, destroying bridges and roads, and carrying away vehicles and buildings near the border with China. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port, a major China-Nepal crossing used for trade, tourism and pilgrimage routes toward Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar.
Security footage showed people fleeing as a torrent of mud and water swept through the border area, damaging buildings and vehicles and cutting roads, communications and power supplies. Chinese authorities said the roads leading to the port were severely damaged, while rescue teams faced thick sediment and difficult weather conditions.
China reported three deaths and 265 people missing in Gyirong County, according to state broadcaster CCTV, while authorities continued to verify the figures. President Xi Jinping ordered an “all-out” search and rescue operation, the evacuation of people at risk and stronger monitoring to prevent secondary disasters. More than 600 rescuers and emergency personnel were deployed, supported by vehicles, drones and other search equipment.
On the Nepalese side, the disaster was even more devastating. Nepalese authorities reported that at least 95 people had died, while hundreds of others remained missing. The Nepal Tourism Board reported 384 tourists and travelers unaccounted for, including more than 100 Indians and nationals from the United States, United Kingdom, South Korea, Malaysia, Australia, the Netherlands and other countries. Many were traveling through the region for tourism or pilgrimage.
The hardest-hit areas included Nepal’s Rasuwa district, particularly the settlements of Timure and Syapru Besi along the Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi river system. Entire settlements were swept away, while at least 19 bridges and about 40 kilometers of roads were damaged. Several hydropower projects were also affected, further disrupting infrastructure in the mountainous region.
The German Research Centre for Geosciences detected a magnitude 4.4 earthquake in the area shortly before the disaster, raising the possibility that seismic activity contributed to the landslide. Experts have also warned that an upstream blockage could trigger another flood.
Nepal deployed its army, police, helicopters and emergency teams to search for survivors, although difficult terrain, high water levels and continuing instability have hampered operations. China has likewise mobilized large rescue teams and equipment on its side of the border.

NTNU showcases its contributions to bat-related research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:41 UTC
01:47:41 KST

National Taiwan Normal University (NTNU) yesterday highlighted its contributions to bat research ahead of International Bat Night this weekend.
Speaking at a news conference, NTNU researchers said they discovered a unique biological mechanism that protects bats from frostbite and detected unsafe concentrations of heavy metals in guano, an ingredient often used in traditional Chinese medicine.
International Bat Night is an annual global event to raise awareness regarding bat research and conservation efforts.
Photo: Yang Mien-chieh, Taipei Times
When bats hibernate in the winter, their body temperature drops to nearly freezing as frost and ice cover them, yet they wake no worse for wear in the spring, life science professor Wu Chung-hsin (吳忠信) said.
The researchers found that bats in low temperatures suppress their reactive oxygen species levels to prevent cellular oxidative damage, he said.
The research suggests that bats might have synapses that are hardened against low temperatures, allowing their brains and organs to function in extreme cold, Wu said.
It also suggests that animals in the bat family can secrete chemicals that thicken the blood in cold temperatures, preventing harmful coagulation from taking place, he added.
These traits, which are extremely rare among mammals, give bats an important advantage for surviving cold environments, he said.
The study paves new ways for researchers to analyze mammalian hibernation, Wu added.
A separate study on the properties of guano found that bat dung contains small amounts of vitamin B, which explains its use in traditional Chinese medicine to improve eyesight and adjust an overly “hot” constitution, he said.
However, the research found that as bats eat thousands of insects daily, their bodies rapidly accrue heavy metals, pesticides and other environmental pollutants, Wu said.
The study suggests that people should take vitamin B tablets instead of guano, he said, adding that sampling bat dung could be a useful method to gauge the severity of pollution in a region.
Lead, mercury, arsenic, tungsten and imidacloprid-based insecticides can affect a bat’s voice, hearing and sense of direction, compromising their echolocation, and even causing them to lose their bearing entirely, he said.
That makes declining bat populations effective indicators of excessive pollution from industrial or agricultural sources, he added.

China urges citizens to evacuate Taiwan’s last friend in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:40 UTC
01:47:40 KST

China is urging its citizens to evacuate Eswatini and warning others not to visit the tiny African kingdom over what it said were safety concerns and scamming risks in Taiwan’s last remaining diplomatic partner on the continent.
In a post on WeChat, the Department of Consular Affairs of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs described Eswatini’s security situation as “complex,” with crimes involving online fraud and illegal gambling “rampant” and public-security and safety risk “extremely high.”
“Chinese citizens and institutions currently in the country are urged to evacuate or relocate to relatively safer areas — such as South Africa — as soon as possible,” according to the WeChat post. “Those who insist on traveling to or remaining in the country will face extremely high security risks, and the timeliness of receiving assistance may be compromised.”
Photo courtesy of the Presidential Office
Officials in Beijing made no connection to Taiwan in issuing the advisory. Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters on Wednesday that such notices were a common international practice, saying China “will take necessary measures” to safeguard the safety, rights and interests of its citizens overseas. The government issued its security advisory after what he called a “prudent assessment” of the situation in Eswatini, which has no official diplomatic ties with China.
A spokeswoman for the Eswatini government didn’t immediately answer a call and a text message seeking comment.?
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs denounced China’s action, describing it as a deliberate effort to undermine the island’s historical friendship with the African country. It called on the international community to recognize “the egregious nature of China’s authoritarian intimidation.”
Photo: AFP
Located in the southeast corner of Africa, Eswatini is about the size of New Jersey with just 1.2 million people. Two Chinese nationals were fined for running an illegal online gambling operation there and face the possibility of imprisonment if those charges aren’t paid, Times of Eswatini has reported. A similar case was reported by Chinese publication Caixin in March.?
While cyber crime has been on the rise, the kingdom is generally far safer than neighboring South Africa, which has one of the world’s worst murder rates. South Africa has the second-highest criminality score in Africa, according to rankings from the European Union-backed Enact. Eswatini, meanwhile, ranks 45th.
And although scams and cyber crime are widespread in Southeast Asia, Beijing rarely issues comparable travel advisories for nations in the region. Its most recent notice for any Southeast Asian country concerned the situation in the Philippines a year ago, when China’s Foreign Ministry said it was experiencing “a period of social unrest, with a surge in crimes targeting Chinese citizens.”
This isn’t the first time that Eswatini was accorded special treatment by Beijing. When it announced zero tariffs for African countries last year, it excluded Eswatini by limiting the policy to countries that have diplomatic ties with China.?
Africa has become a key front in China’s efforts to isolate Taipei’s presence on the world stage.
In August, Taiwan urged citizens to postpone travel to Uganda after a series of passport disputes in which Taiwanese business travelers and their family members arriving at Entebbe airport had their documents seized by immigration officials, who demanded Chinese passports instead. ?
Earlier this year, Beijing persuaded three African countries to close their airspace to Taiwan President Lai Ching-te’s plane in a bid to derail his trip to Eswatini, which is one of 12 countries worldwide to recognize Taiwan. Lai eventually visited Eswatini in May, though at the time Taiwan’s government didn’t disclose details of how he traveled to the country.
China’s Foreign Ministry later released a statement titled, “Lai Ching-te’s travel to Eswatini on its king’s private jet.”
Taiwan also suspended visa processing for Moroccan nationals in late July after Morocco imposed similar restrictions, while Taipei threatened retaliation after Kenya barred Taiwanese delegates from a global maritime conference and detained an academic from the island for 20 hours in June.
While Taiwanese business interests are widespread in the kingdom, mainland China’s are more limited. State-owned Power Construction Corp. of China in 2023 won a 2.6 billion-emalangeni ($165 million) contract to build a major dam in Eswatini.
Eswatini had 3,251 visitors from China in 2025, compared with 1,333 from Taiwan, according to official statistics.
The WeChat post was trending at No. 1 in China on Wednesday morning, generating more than 89 million reads, over 8,000 discussions, and 39,000 interactions as of noon.?
Some commenters said they weren’t aware of the country. “Didn’t even know where Eswatini was until I was reminded,” wrote one.?
Another user focused on the diplomatic dimension. “Take note: China and Eswatini have no diplomatic ties. Refusing to leave is dangerous, and it will be difficult to get help if you run into trouble.”

Would you pay for an algorithm to pick your friends?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:36 UTC
01:47:36 KST

Would you pay ￡20 (US$27) a month for the chance of making a friend, on the understanding that an algorithm — not you – gets to decide who you’ll meet?
Driven by the decline of “third spaces” such as youth centers and pubs, an increase in remote working and rising loneliness — 40 percent of adults aged 16 to 29 feel lonely “always, often or some of the time,” according to the Office for National Statistics — paid social events are now in vogue.
“There hasn’t been anything that feels authentic to helping people meet people,” says Nicola Gunby, a co-founder of Cliq, an online platform and app that aims “to bring people together through shared interests and real-world experiences.”
Photo: AP
The mechanics are fairly simple: platforms such as PLY (it stands for People Like You) and Agora match people using information such as their interests, lifestyle habits and profession. Then, typically, an algorithm decides which events a user should attend, as opposed to free alternatives, such as the Meetup platform, that leave that choice with members.
The ideal outcome for participants is showing up, making some new connections and leaving with plans to meet up again.
But as these clubs spread across UK cities — typically charging from nothing at all to £20 a month — the question for anyone considering joining, is the same as you would ask about any subscription: what are you actually paying for, and is it worth it?
At PLY, memberships tend to start at £19.99 a month, giving members access to exclusive events and discounts with other businesses, falling to about £9.99 a month for longer commitments.
“When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” says Karen Harris, the founder of PLY, of its membership model. “People need someone who’s committed, who’s looking to maintain friendships and taking it seriously.”
According to Harris, the majority of PLY’s customers sign up for longer-term memberships — a reflection of both the lower cost and of how long a friendship takes to build. On average, she says, it takes three events “to find your person.”
Other clubs offer a mix of pay-as-you-go and subscription options. This is Agora’s model as it makes things more accessible, argues its founder, Sahil Shirazee.
In the two years since its launch, the club has hosted more than 300 events and claims to have helped form hundreds of friendships.
For some of those looking to make new friends, flexibility is important.
“A membership fee would make me feel pressured into attending so many events every month,” says Charlotte Johnson, 29, from Hertfordshire, who is a Cliq user.
Paying per event “encourages me to go if I’ve paid for it” while leaving her free to not attend those that aren’t of interest to her.
Johnson says that “what really surprised me was I got more than expected.” She highlights a recent brunch event that included things such as a take-home goodie bag. She has since signed up for a pottery event.
“Everyone’s there for the same, if not similar, reasons,” she adds, “which takes a lot of the fear out of meeting strangers.”
If participants don’t click with anyone within a month of joining, some of the platforms, including PLY, offer a money-back guarantee.
Not everyone is convinced that paying for friendship is something to celebrate.
Shirazee admits he still gets asked why people should have to pay to meet each other at all. But, he says, if you want to solve problems such as loneliness, and create meaningful communities as quickly as possible, “you need to make sure the people who want to crack this issue are able to not only get compensated, but grow.”
Harris rejects the idea that people are “paying for access to strangers.”
“You’re paying for a system, for structure, that makes connections much better,” she says. Free socialization, she argues, usually relies on the presence of a host or facilitator, whereas at PLY events, “interaction is peer-to-peer, without a facilitator moving you forward.”
Free events haven’t disappeared, though — and continue to be the preferred option for some.
“I tend to choose free events most of the time because I can’t always afford to pay for social activities,” says Giovanna Giusi, a primary school teacher.
The 28-year-old says she appreciates having access to a mixture of free events, such as hikes or walks, and paid events. This allows her to “be part of a community even when money is tighter.”
She says the paid events “make it possible to offer experiences that couldn’t realistically happen for free, such as workshops with instructors, private classes or activities that need a venue.”
“People always say they want more community and more opportunities to meet others, but it’s easy to forget that organizing those communities still takes time, work and money,” Giusi says.
Whether paid socialization becomes the norm is, for now, an open question.
Despite it being the foundation of their business model, the organizers say they hope not.
“In the long run, I don’t want Agora to exist,” Shirazee says, because “meeting people is so natural” it shouldn’t rely on an algorithm. But in the meantime, after establishing a “proper base” in London, he is already planning to expand to different cities next year.

Kaohsiung airport new terminal to be done by 2040
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:36 UTC
01:47:36 KST

Kaohsiung International Airport’s new international terminal is scheduled to be completed by 2040, which would expand its service capacity from 10 million to 16.5 million passengers per year.
Civil Aviation Administration Director-General Ho Shu-ping (何淑萍) said 26 airlines operate flights from Kaohsiung to 35 destinations worldwide.
There are 415 weekly flights on the summer flight schedule, up from 368 before the COVID-19 pandemic, Ho said.
Photo courtesy of the Civil Aeronautics Administration
The number of weekly flights to Japan and South Korea has reached 200, she added.
The average load factor of international flights in Kaohsiung has topped 82 percent, up from 78 percent last year, Ho said.
The airport was accessed by 5.74 million international passengers last year and that number could exceed 7 million this year, she said, adding that it had already reached 3.68 million last month.
It can accommodate 10 million people per year, which is expected to rise to 16.5 million once the new terminal begins operations, Ho said.
“The Kaohsiung International Airport is an important gateway in southern Taiwan. We will continue to expand the flight work by encouraging more carriers to launch more international flights in Kaohsiung,” she said.
The airport’s curfew hours would remain from 12pm to 6:30am, Ho said.
The construction of the new terminal has two stages.
The first stage involves building a new multistory parking garage at the airport’s east side, moving Taxiway A north, building the east side of the new terminal and Concourse C, and revamping the existing parking lot and connecting it to the Kaohsiung MRT Line.
The parking garage is expected to be operational by July next year.
Domestic and international flights still operate at separate terminals at the first stage.
For the second stage, the new terminal’s west side would be built, while the current international terminal would be torn down, and international flight services would be offered from the new terminal’s east side instead.
Domestic flights would still depart from the domestic terminal.
Concourses A and B would also be revamped during the second stage.
When the new terminal is completed, it would accommodate domestic and international flights, with domestic flights departing from the east side of the terminal.
The entire project is estimated to cost about NT$88 billion (US$2.77 billion).
Regarding questions about building an airport that operates around the clock, Ho said there is limited space available on land for such a facility.
While there is discussion over building a 24-hour airport on the coast, there remain many technical issues, she said.
“According to International Civil Aviation Organization regulations, a runway can only be built after having collected wind speed and direction data for more than 10 years. Geological data are also needed if reclaiming land from the sea is necessary,” Ho said. “We will continue to identify and assess all possible issues, and take into account issues of sustainability and resilience.”

Two domestic cases of mpox clade Ib have been confirmed this month, marking the first locally acquired infections of the virus strain, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
The patients, both men in their 30s, are in stable condition and had not received an mpox vaccine before developing symptoms, the CDC said.
The first man developed a fever late last month, followed by a rash and pustules on the abdomen and groin, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
He was diagnosed with mpox after seeking medical care and undergoing testing, Lin said.
The other man developed a rash on the torso and legs early this month, followed by fever and muscle aches, and after rashes appeared on multiple parts of his body, he was tested, Lin said.
Genetic typing confirmed that they were infected with mpox clade Ib, he added.
Mpox is a viral infectious disease primarily spread through close contact, including sexual contact, hugging, kissing or direct skin-to-skin contact, the CDC said.
The clade Ib strain has symptoms similar to the more common clade II, including fever, swollen lymph nodes, rashes and blisters, but its rash might be more widespread and the virus might spread more easily within households, Lin said.
Young children, pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses are at higher risk of severe disease if infected, he said.
Mpox vaccines are effective against clade Ib, while the antiviral drug tecovirimat could be used to treat severe cases, he added.
As of Sunday, 28 new mpox cases had been recorded in Taiwan this year, including 19 locally acquired cases and nine imported cases, all involving men aged 20 to 50, the CDC said.
Since the first imported mpox clade Ib case was reported in May, nine clade Ib infections have been confirmed, including seven imported and two locally acquired cases, it said.
Since mpox was designated a Category 2 communicable disease in 2022, Taiwan has recorded 544 cases, including 500 locally acquired cases and 44 imported cases, CDC data showed.
Most people with confirmed mpox had a history of higher-risk sexual activity, and nearly 90 percent were unvaccinated against mpox, the centers said.
People who engage in higher-risk sexual activity, particularly those without a steady sexual partner, face a higher risk of infection, it said.
The risk to the general population remains low, it added.
Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent infection, Lin said, adding that as of last month, 79,216 people had completed the recommended two doses of the vaccine, while 31,755 people had received only one dose.
As two doses provide about 90 percent protection against mpox, compared with 40 to 80 percent protection after one dose, those who are considered at risk should complete the two-dose series as soon as possible, he said.
In Taiwan, 318 medical institutions offer government-funded mpox vaccines, the CDC said.
People who have engaged in higher-risk sexual activity within the past year, have previously had a sexually transmitted infection or have sexual partners with related risk factors are eligible for the government-funded vaccine, it said.
Mpox has an incubation period of up to 21 days, and some people might be infectious one to four days before symptoms appear, the centers said.
People who develop rashes, blisters or pustules along with symptoms such as fever, headaches, muscle aches or swollen lymph nodes should wear a mask and seek medical attention, and inform their doctor of any travel, exposure and contact history, it said.

Taipei Tech joins Taiwan-Germany semiconductor training program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:34 UTC
01:47:34 KST

National Taipei University of Technology (Taipei Tech) signed an agreement with Dresden University of Technology (TU Dresden) on Wednesday to join a Taiwan-Germany semiconductor talent development program.
The partnership will take effect this fall, making Taipei Tech the fourth Taiwanese university to participate in the Semiconductor Talent Incubation Program Taiwan (STIPT), Josef Goldberger, head of the Saxon Science Liaison Office Taiwan, told CNA.
As the program expands, the number of students from German universities coming to Taiwan each year is expected to rise from a previous maximum of around 70 to about 100, German Institute Taipei Director General Karsten Tietz said at the signing ceremony.
Photo: CNA
According to TU Dresden’s website, the six-month program combines semiconductor-related coursework at a Taiwanese university with practical training at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) in Taichung.
STIPT was established in conjunction with TSMC’s investment in Germany to cultivate the semiconductor talent needed in Dresden, Tietz said.
German students increasingly view semiconductors and artificial intelligence as promising career fields, while those in Dresden were among the first to recognize the opportunities created by the TSMC-led plant under construction there, he added.
“Taiwan is the world champion in this area,” Tietz said, noting that the opportunity to study on the island and train at TSMC made the program attractive to German engineering students.
TSMC’s investment has also raised awareness among German students of Taiwan’s strength in microelectronics and electrical engineering, according to Goldberger.
“If we want to catch up, if we want to be part of the industry, we have to come to Taiwan to learn from Taiwan,” he said.
Taipei Tech was selected because it offers English- language semiconductor courses at the master’s level, has strong ties with German academia and responded quickly to the proposed partnership, Goldberger told CNA.
Taipei Tech President Jen Yi-Jun (任貽均) said the university and its German counterparts shared a focus on hands-on engineering education and industry-oriented research, providing a strong basis for cooperation in training students to solve real-world industrial problems.
Taipei Tech joins National Taiwan University, National Taiwan University of Science and Technology and National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University in STIPT.
National Cheng Kung University is scheduled to join in spring 2027, bringing the number of Taiwanese partners to five, Goldberger said.
Beginning this year, Germany’s Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space and the Free State of Saxony will each fund half of the program’s participants, according to Goldberger.
Selected students have their tuition and program fees covered and receive a monthly grant of 700 euros (US $816.5) and a travel allowance of 1,500 euros, according to TU Dresden’s website

CEC warns of potential ballot disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:32 UTC
01:47:32 KST

Putting all proposed referendums on one ballot, as some opposition lawmakers have proposed, could severely affect the local elections in November, Central Election Commission (CEC) Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said yesterday.
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP)-controlled Legislative Yuan is expected to vote to pass the proposal tomorrow.
With fewer than 100 days remaining before the Nov. 28 elections, You told reporters at a news conference in Taipei that although he was reluctant to say that he hoped the legislature would withdraw the proposal, deep down he strongly hoped it would.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
KMT Legislator Lai Shyh-bao’s (賴士葆) argument that the US has long used consolidated ballots for referendums was based on a faulty premise, You said.
The US does not have a single nationwide practice for referendum ballots, and each state has its own referendum rules, ballot design and election procedures, which can vary substantially by locality.
Implementing the opposition’s proposal would require changing the entire election-administration system, with corresponding changes to equipment and operating procedures, You said.
Printing all proposed referendums on one ballot would not decrease the number of initiatives or the time needed to vote or count votes, because results still have to be tallied question by question, he said.
Changing Article 21 of the Referendum Act (公民投票法) without changing other laws would create a legal mandate that cannot be implemented, he said.
The cause of problems in the 2018 local elections was that voters had to consider 10 referendum questions, which led to long lines and delayed vote counts; it was not simply due to ballot collection, You said.
It is not clear what problem consolidated ballots are supposed to solve, he said.
He said that since Aug. 4 he had visited the legislature’s three party caucuses to warn them against the proposal.
The CEC outlined 11 problems raised by the proposal.
Among the issues, voting and vote-counting procedures in US states differ from those in Taiwan, making a direct comparison or adoption difficult, it said.
The proposal would not amend the regulations necessary to implement the changes, and a consolidated ballot would not reduce the amount of time voters need to mark their ballots and could increase invalid ballots due to ink transfer or overlapping marks, it said.
Changing the ballot design so close to the elections would not give the CEC enough time to adapt voting aids for people with visual impairments, and the vote-counting process could exceed the capacity of poll workers, who must call out and count the ballots one by one and decipher voters’ marks, it said.
In addition, the consolidated ballot bill in its present form would interfere with numerous essential electoral tasks, including determining valid and invalid votes, ballot sealing and recounts, it said.
The CEC does not have enough time to implement the lawmakers’ proposal in a manner that ensures fairness, it added.

Chip packaging service provider Powertech Technology Inc (力成科技) yesterday said that its advanced fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) production line has secured a 100 percent utilization rate through 2030 ahead of its scheduled volume production next year.
Powertech made the remarks during the first public unveiling of its FOPLP production capabilities. The company expressed strong confidence in its long-term order pipeline, saying that robust market traction has mitigated any client acquisition concerns.
“Our capacity has been fully booked by two major customers. Customers are not an issue through 2030,” Powertech chairman Tsai Du-kung (蔡篤恭) told reporters at the company’s plant in the Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科學園區).
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
The chairman said the investment was the largest strategic gamble of his career. Powertech plans to invest a total of NT$70 billion (US$2.2 billion) on ramping the FOPLP facility, which would have an installed capacity gradually increasing to 5,000 510x510mm panels per month in 2028 from 1,000 panels this year.
Powertech said that it is on track to roll out its initial shipments of artificial intelligence (AI) server central processing units from its Hsinchu facility, called P11, next year, using its advanced FOPLP technology.
The company is also building a FOPLP production line in Singapore through a joint venture with Broadcom Inc.
Advanced Micron Devices Inc and Broadcom are the major customers for the panel-level packaging services.
As AI chip sizes continue to expand, cost-effective panel-level packaging has emerged as an optimal solution compared with circular wafer-based packaging technology, Tsai said.
Powertech said its panel-level packaging technology has at least four-fold better throughput than wafer-based packaging technology.
The company is capable of packaging 45 AI chips using its FOPLP technology, surpassing eight to nine chips packaged using wafer-based packaging technology, it said.
The company said with technology advancement, it plans to integrate optic engines with AI accelerators or switches next year.
It said it is scheduled to ship the first optical engines made for a key customer by the end of this year.
With FOPLP volume production set to commence next year, Powertech expects the production line to reach a break-even point, Tsai said.
Heavy equipment depreciation costs significantly erode the company’s profitability by about NT$3 per share a year, he said.
Powertech was the nation’s first chip packager to invest in the development of FOPLP technology in 2016.
The company said it has been utilizing the technology to package power management chips for six years, overcoming most technological barriers.
As the technology becomes more sophisticated, the company is utilizing it in the production of higher-margin AI chips, it said.

Freedom for Indonesian fishers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:47:30 UTC
01:47:30 KST

What does Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy mean to the Indonesian migrant workers who help sustain its economy?
That question might sound detached from the policy’s language of trade, investment and technology. Yet it became very concrete on Sunday last week, when almost 100 Indonesian migrant fishers gathered at Donggang Fishing Harbor in Pingtung County to celebrate Indonesia’s 81st Independence Day and launch their “Freedom for Fishers Campaign.”
Their demands are fair wages and contracts, access to Wi-Fi, the right to organize, safe working conditions and a transparent mechanism for lodging complaints. For these workers, freedom means being able to work with dignity, speak without fear and seek protection when something goes wrong.
That makes the campaign more than a labor issue. It offers Taiwan a useful test of whether its New Southbound Policy is truly people-centered.
Taiwan’s relationship with Indonesia is usually measured through trade, investment, education, technology and labor. However, for thousands of Indonesians working in Taiwan’s fishing industry, that relationship is their workplace, income and daily life.
About 4,500 migrant fishers work aboard offshore and distant-water vessels based in the Donggang area. Their concerns range from basic facilities to whether they can exercise their rights without fear of retaliation.
The union reported a case in which a fisher who allegedly experienced violence aboard a vessel was dismissed and repatriated after the incident was reported. The allegation deserves due process, but the broader question is difficult to avoid: Can migrant workers safely speak up when their employment depends heavily on employers and brokers?
Even something as mundane as Internet access illustrates the issue. Fishers who spend months at sea need connectivity to contact their families, obtain information and, when necessary, seek assistance. A Wi-Fi connection can become a channel to rights and protection. It also shows where foreign policy meets everyday life.
The New Southbound Policy was designed to deepen Taiwan’s ties with Southeast Asia and South Asia. Much of the discussion around it has focused on investment, supply chains, education and technology. Personal relations are harder to build through agreements alone. They are built through everyday experiences.
As Taiwan confronts labor shortages, Indonesia is not simply a source of workers, but an increasingly important Southeast Asian partner. How Indonesians experience Taiwan can shape how Taiwan is perceived in Indonesia.
This is where migrant-worker protection becomes a question of soft power. Taiwan has limited diplomatic space and cannot rely on conventional influence alone. Its reputation as a democracy, open society and reliable partner is a strategic asset.
Soft power is not created only by what a country says about itself. It is created by what people experience. If Taiwan wants to present itself as a trustworthy partner to Southeast Asia, the treatment of Indonesian workers matters.
A worker who can report abuse without retaliation, communicate with family, join a union and access a fair grievance process experiences Taiwan differently from one who feels trapped by the system. It means that how Taiwan responds to problems matters as much as the values it promotes abroad.
The campaign brings accountability to the international seafood supply chain, where workers at sea are far removed from the companies and consumers benefiting from their labor.
Taiwan can treat the campaign as another labor dispute to be managed, or it can recognize it as an opportunity to demonstrate what a genuinely people-centered partnership with Southeast Asia looks like.
For an Indonesian worker, the New Southbound Policy is measured by whether he can work safely, speak freely and return home with dignity. For Taiwan, protecting Indonesian migrant workers is not only the right thing to do, it is smart diplomacy.
Najamuddin Khairur Rijal is an associate professor in the International Relations Department at the University of Muhammadiyah Malang in Indonesia.

Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack.
