UK Green members prepare 'Zionism is racism' motion ahead of party conference
Ahead of the UK Green Party conference in October, pro-Palestine members are preparing a motion to be heard that could officially declare the party as anti-Zionist.
The "Zionism is racism" motion seeks to define Zionism as a racist, settler‑colonial ideology and declare the party as against it.
Its key demands include supporting the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and enforcing embargoes like those used against South Africa during apartheid, releasing Palestinian prisoners, acknowledging the right to resistance under international law, and supporting a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights and the right of return.
"This is a historic motion that could change the face of British politics," Lubna Speitan, Palestinian activist and author of the motion, told The New Arab.
"We're not asking for something new, to acknowledge Palestinian rights to not just self-determination but to resistance by all available means, as per international law."
"This is something that's based on law, the Equality Act, international law, the Geneva Convention."
Despite facing accusations of antisemitism and being reported to anti-terrorism police, the motion received a record-breaking number of 745 co-proposers, double that of the last motion, which garnered 333.
It has also been endorsed by over fifty organisations and individuals, including Greta Thunberg and Mohammed El Kurd.
The motion is currently on the prioritisation ballot, where members can decide the order they want to see motions come forward in October.
While the motion was scheduled to be debated at the Spring Conference in March, it never reached the floor, but supporters hope it will not only be heard but also passed.
"I think that should this motion pass, it will have ripple effects in sort of British and international politics," Tariq Khawaja, member of the Green Party and one of the backers of the motion, told The New Arab. "[The motion] already has achieved what we set out to achieve."
"It has changed the conversation. There are people now who are talking and questioning about Zionism in a way that they weren't doing a year ago; there are signs that we're seeing on protests that weren't there a year ago."
Speitan and Khawaja highlight that the Green Party is the first UK political party to acknowledge that Israel is an apartheid state committing genocide.
"This is basic stuff. For a UK political party to be the first political party to call for equality amongst Palestinians in Palestine, and also to call for liberation of Palestinians, but also to call for justice and reparations," Khawaja said.
"We have a responsibility as the arbiters of empire and imperialism to be a voice for those that don't have one."
Khawaja also noted that they are in discussions with supporters worldwide in other political parties, hoping the motion will pass internationally as well.
Following the appointment of Zack Polanski as leader of the Greens, the party has seen a surge in support from voters concerned about Palestine, reflected in recent elections and polling.

Archaeologists unearth 15th-century hoard of 2,600 silver coins near Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

MOSCOW, August 26. /TASS/. Scientists conducting rescue excavations in Kolomna, a city about 100 kilometers southeast of Moscow, have uncovered a hoard of 2,600 silver coins dating to the 15th century, when Russia was ruled by Vasily I, the son of Dmitry Donskoy, and his grandson, Vasily II the Blind. According to the press service of the Institute of Archaeology of the Russian Academy of Sciences, the discovery is the first major find of its kind and offers an unprecedented glimpse into the monetary structure of a regional market in the Moscow Principality.
"It's crucial that the hoard has been preserved in its entirety. This is the largest coin collection of its time available to researchers and the first source that allows us to reconstruct the monetary structure of a single regional market in the Moscow Principality, down to the precise details of individual issues," the institute said.
Archaeologists from the Institute of Archaeology made the discovery during rescue excavations in Kolomna in the summer of 2026. The hoard consists of a jug filled with coins that had been buried in a shallow pit during the first third of the 15th century, possibly amid one of the plague epidemics that swept across the Russian lands at the time.
The principal currency of the period was the silver denga, also known as a "fish scale" because of its small, irregular shape. The newly discovered hoard contains 2,600 such coins, with a total estimated value of about 13 rubles. Experts say that sum could have been enough to purchase two houses in the city or an entire herd of horses, underscoring the considerable wealth of its owner.
The hoard is particularly significant because it contains coins bearing a previously unknown design featuring the image of a flying bird.
Researchers believe that similar coins were minted in Kolomna itself, which ranked as the Moscow Principality’s second city after Moscow. Comparable silver coins are exceptionally rare in hoards from other regions, and some varieties are absent even from the numismatic collections of the country’s largest museums, further enhancing the importance of the discovery.
"The rescue excavations conducted ahead of construction have yielded thousands of valuable artifacts that will allow us to add new details to this fascinating chapter of Kolomna’s history," Asya Yengovatova, head of the Institute of Archaeology of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Moscow Region expedition, said, according to the institute’s press service. "Once the research is complete, we hope that this treasure will be displayed in the museum of the city where it was discovered.".

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

Reported by
A court in Yerevan ordered the eldest son of former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan held in pretrial detention on Wednesday, expanding a sweeping corruption investigation that has ensnared the former leader and several high-ranking ex-officials.
The decision to hold Sedrak Kocharyan for two months followed his detention on Tuesday alongside his father. Investigators carried out coordinated raids on family-linked real estate and commercial holdings, escalating a long-running political battle between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and the country's former ruling elite.
Lawyers for the younger Kocharyan said they would appeal the ruling, with defense attorney Alexander Kochubayev describing the case as an "extralegal prosecution" driven by political motives.
Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Committee stated that the elder Kocharyan, who served as president from 1998 to 2008, used his office to acquire state property at artificially low prices and accept substantial bribes. Officials said several prime parcels of land were improperly funneled to the family and later developed into commercial ventures.
Investigators are scrutinizing financial wire transfers to Sedrak Kocharyan between 2001 and 2019 totaling approximately 144 billion drams (about $392 million), $309 million, 77 million euros, and 18 million rubles.
Authorities detained six people in connection with the probe. Tax officials simultaneously sealed the offices of Toyota Yerevan and Orange Fitness, two businesses linked to the family, as part of a parallel tax-evasion inquiry.
The Prosecutor General’s Office said criminal proceedings were initiated on Aug. 24 against the former president for abuse of power, bribery, and large-scale money laundering. Nine others were also named, including former President Serzh Sargsyan—who also previously served as defense minister—a former prime minister, a former mayor of Yerevan, and a prominent businessman.
Following his arrest, the former president’s office reported that his health had deteriorated at the Anti-Corruption Committee’s headquarters, requiring emergency medical attention following a recent medical procedure. His office characterized the arrests as "another assault by the authorities."
The legal actions came shortly after a fiery clash in parliament between Prime Minister Pashinyan and the former president’s younger son, Levon Kocharyan, an opposition lawmaker whose home was also searched.
In parliament, Levon Kocharyan accused the prime minister of exerting improper political pressure on the judiciary. Pashinyan countered by questioning the origins of the family's wealth, promising that assets acquired at public expense would be returned to the state "piece by piece."
Ex-President Kocharyan previously faced charges of "overthrowing the constitutional order" linked to a deadly crackdown on post-election protests in Yerevan in 2008. Armenia’s Constitutional Court ruled in 2021 that the legal provision used in that case could not be applied retroactively, leading to the dismissal of those charges.
Former President Serzh Sargsyan, who succeeded Kocharyan in 2008 and is also facing criminal prosecution in the same case, was summoned to the Anti-Corruption Committee headquarters in Yerevan on Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters outside the building, Sargsyan said he did not yet know the specific reason for the summons.
“When we receive the case materials, we will talk. I don’t understand anything,” he said.
Sargsyan was placed under a travel ban on Wednesday.

Nickolay Mladenov, President Donald Trump’s top official overseeing Gaza, warned Wednesday that continued Israeli strikes could jeopardize the ceasefire with Hamas and undermine efforts to disarm the terrorist group.
Speaking before the UN Security Council, Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, sharply criticized Israel’s recent operations in the territory.
“These strikes do not change the status quo that produced 7 October 2023,” Mladenov said. “They preserve it.”
His comments came a day after other Board of Peace officials criticized both Israel and Hamas for violating Trump’s 20-point agreement. Against the backdrop of a wave of incendiary kite launches from Gaza toward Israeli border communities, the officials said every violation was being addressed directly with the responsible party through a mechanism led by the U.S. military.
“Every violation is handled immediately with the side responsible,” the officials said. “We established a mechanism led by the U.S. military that deals with this quickly. The violating side understands there are serious consequences if the violations continue.”
Board officials said the goal was to return both sides to implementing the agreement as quickly as possible so the next stage, disarming Hamas of both heavy and light weapons, could begin.
“The sooner we implement the 20-point agreement, the sooner we can begin disarming Hamas,” the officials said. “Alternatively, if Hamas does not disarm, Israel will be able to act forcefully and with international diplomatic backing. It is a shame Israel is missing this enormous opportunity for a small number of tactical operations that will not really lead to Hamas’ disarmament.”
Officials on the Trump-established board also sharply criticized recent IDF operations in Gaza, arguing that they were producing limited security gains while causing significant strategic damage.
“The IDF’s actions in recent weeks have generated a lot of media attention, but they are tactical operations with no meaningful security value that cause significant strategic damage,” the officials said. “These actions perpetuate Hamas’ civilian and military rule and do not really eliminate Hamas. For every operative killed, Hamas recruits 100 new young people.”
Mladenov made a similar argument at the UN.
“Will another strike on a munitions depot stop Hamas from rearming or loosening its grip on Gaza?” he asked. “It will not.”
He said such attacks were delaying rather than advancing the demilitarization of Gaza, while also stressing that Hamas must fulfill its own commitments by fully halting military activity and dismantling its underground tunnel networks.
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, meanwhile, made clear that Israel would not ease its campaign against Hamas before Gaza is demilitarized.
During a tour of the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, Zamir said the military had changed its approach following the failures that preceded the October 7 attack.
“We are implementing lessons, we have changed the concept. The IDF will not return to October 6,” Zamir said.
He added that the military would not give up its overriding objective in Gaza: demilitarizing the territory and stripping Hamas of its weapons “by all necessary means.”
“We continue to act systematically to continuously damage Hamas and its leaders everywhere, including through an ongoing campaign to prevent its military buildup,” he said.
Despite Israeli operations, Hamas has continued rebuilding parts of both its military and civilian infrastructure in Gaza. In recent months, indications have accumulated that the group retains significant governing and military capabilities, continues paying employees, recruits new members and is positioning itself to re-enter the Palestinian political system.
Reuters reported during the war that Hamas recruited between 10,000 and 15,000 new members, including young men with little significant military training. Subsequent assessments said the organization sought to recruit around 30,000 young Palestinians into its military wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades.
Israeli assessments published in 2026 also said Hamas had added about 12,000 new recruits in an effort to replenish ranks depleted during the war.
The differing estimates cover different periods and categories and do not establish the current size of Hamas’ military force, but they indicate that its recruitment apparatus remains active.
Hamas has also continued operating civilian institutions in Gaza. Sources in the territory told ynet that the group is still paying salaries to tens of thousands of government employees, while its institutions continue policing, tax collection and regulation of economic activity in areas where it retains influence.
This month, it was reported that Hamas’ administration had collected as much as $100 million in taxes on goods entering Gaza since the ceasefire, including levies of up to 20% on declared goods and as much as 80% on undeclared goods that were seized. Hamas denies that the revenue is transferred to its military wing.
Mladenov warned that the growing gap between the terms of the ceasefire and events on the ground threatened the entire process.
“The distance between what has been signed and what is happening on the ground” poses a risk to both the ceasefire and the disarmament plan, he said.
While casualties in Gaza have “fallen sharply” since the ceasefire took effect, Mladenov said Israeli strikes were still killing people.
“A ceasefire under which civilians are still buried is not yet one the people of Gaza can feel,” he said.

Surge in families renting puts more children at risk of housing insecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:15:43 UTC
00:15:43 KST

More children are growing up in rental housing and moving every couple of years
In short:
A new report by researchers at Adelaide University shows children who grow up in rental housing move every 2.3 years, on average.
Around one-in-eight children who grow up in rentals have moved at least 10 times by age 14.
The proportion of Australian children growing up in private rental housing jumped by 20 per cent between 2001 and 2023.
More children are growing up in private rentals and facing housing insecurity, a new report finds, warning that it could have long-term implications for their development, physical health and mental wellbeing.
The study by four researchers at Adelaide University — Amy Clair, Emma Baker, Lynne Giles and Claire Morey — has been released by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute today.
By analysing a range of comprehensive and long-term datasets, such as the Household Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey and the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, the authors attempted to determine the effects of Australia's multi-decade housing affordability crisis on children.
The report found that as housing prices surged between 2001 and 2023, the proportion of households with children living in homes owned outright plunged 52 per cent.
Those in social rentals fell 46 per cent as the public housing sector stagnated, those who owned with a mortgage increased 27 per cent and those in private rentals rose 20 per cent.
Research lead and associate professor Amy Clair said the latter statistic was particularly concerning as children growing up in private rental properties moved every 2.3 years on average.
"By age 14, a child in a private rental had moved an average of six times. By comparison, those in households that owned their home had moved a little over twice on average, and children in social housing had moved just over four times," she said.
The data shows children growing up in households with a mortgage tend to have moved about three times by age 14, which is half as often as those in a family renting.
However, those averages also mask more extreme housing instability in many cases.
Around one in eight children growing up in private rentals had lived in 10 or more homes by age 14, compared to approximately one in 40 children living in a home owned with a mortgage, the research found.
"Results were concerning, as housing impacts mattered most during developmental transitions, such as starting school, when disruption can compound other disadvantages,"
It may not surprise you to learn that few households with children were renting by choice, with only 7 per cent reporting they did so because they preferred it and 8 per cent saying they appreciated its flexibility, while more than half said they did not have a housing deposit saved and around half said they could not afford to buy.
'Housing a critical determinant of physical and mental health'
The research also showed that children growing up in rental housing were more likely to live in a household suffering financial stress or poor living conditions.
Roughly 18 per cent of households with children in private rentals were late on a housing payment, compared to about 7 per cent of households with a mortgage, while around 10 per cent of children in private rentals experienced overcrowding, which was more than twice the rate of children living in owner-occupied homes.
Dr Clair said children's experiences were often ignored in the public discussion of housing affordability, partly through a lack of data about their housing status, and better information could help foster the housing conditions that allowed children to thrive.
"There is a growing evidence base positioning housing as a critical determinant of children's physical and mental health, behavioural outcomes, developmental vulnerability and educational attainment,"
"However, Australia's data is fragmented, creating blind spots that hinder early intervention, response targeting and accountable policy."
The report suggests that maternal and child health services, early childhood education, schools and primary care services could routinely collect indicators of affordability stress, overcrowding and dwelling problems, while population surveys could include indicators of thermal comfort, damp, mould, crowding, safety and amenity.
"Children's lives are being shaped by housing, but we need the data to see how this is happening, and for policymakers to use the insights to craft policy that will improve housing outcomes for children," Dr Clair said.
She said the resulting insights could support early warning systems, local service planning and targeted intervention.

Career criminal with 38 convictions: who is the suspect in crime boss Yanis Yushvaev's killing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:15:24 UTC
00:15:24 KST

The main suspect in the killing of reputed organized crime boss Yanis Yushvaev has spent nearly four decades cycling through the criminal justice system, accumulating 38 convictions for offenses ranging from violence and weapons violations to drugs, burglary and livestock theft, according to court records.
The suspect, a career criminal whose name is barred from publication under a court order, remained silent during questioning after his arrest Tuesday and was ordered held for an additional nine days at a court hearing Wednesday. Police have imposed a sweeping gag order on details of the investigation.
His attorney, Yaron Shomron, said the man denies any involvement in the killing and maintains that he had never met Yushvaev.
“As much as I can say, the suspect, my client, denies any involvement in the incident itself,” Shomron said after the hearing. “He did not know the deceased and there was no previous dispute.”
Shomron said he could not address additional details because of the gag order. He also criticized the circumstances of his client’s arrest, describing footage showing the suspect with a cloth covering his eyes as “very unusual.”
The arrest marked the first major publicly disclosed breakthrough in the investigation into Yushvaev’s killing, which triggered a two-day manhunt involving roadblocks, extensive searches and a police helicopter.
38 convictions spanning nearly four decades
The suspect is well known to law enforcement, with a criminal history dating to his adolescence and continuing throughout his adult life.
He has accumulated 38 convictions and served repeated prison sentences. His record includes property offenses and burglaries, drug crimes, threats and violence, weapons and knife offenses, obstruction of justice and violations of court orders.
Over the years, he was sentenced to both prison terms and suspended sentences, some of which were later activated after he committed further offenses.
As recently as April, he was arrested on suspicion of throwing a fragmentation grenade at a home in Beit She’an, a city in northeastern Israel.
One pattern stands out in his lengthy criminal history: repeated offenses involving agricultural theft, particularly horses and livestock.
He has been convicted in several cases involving the theft of cattle, sheep and other animals, sometimes after entering agricultural property and operating with accomplices. Those offenses also resulted in prison terms.
A recent criminal case followed the same pattern. Prosecutors accused him and another man of breaking into a stable at Kibbutz Moran in northern Israel, cutting through a fence and stealing a mare valued at about 15,000 shekels. According to the indictment, the two led the horse through the opening they had cut in the fence and fled with it toward agricultural land.
Elite police unit sent in over fears he was armed
Police arrested the suspect Tuesday in a storage room inside an apartment building in Hadera, a coastal city north of Tel Aviv.
Investigators had received intelligence pointing to his location about 24 hours earlier. The suspect, described as an older man, did not resist arrest, and officers found a utility knife in his possession.
Police had intelligence indicating that he might also have been carrying a handgun. Because commanders feared ordinary officers could come under fire while attempting the arrest, the operation was assigned to Yamam, the police's elite national counterterrorism unit.
Yamam officers prepared for a forced entry before reaching the building and surprising the suspect, taking him into custody without a confrontation. He was then transferred to the Coastal District’s Central Unit, which investigates serious and organized crime, for questioning.
Shomron said his client was stunned by the scale of the operation.
“My client denies any connection to the murder, has never met the deceased and does not know him, and there was no dispute between them,” Shomron said. “He is certain he will be released in the coming days.”
“He is in shock over the arrest,” the lawyer added. “Yamam forces stormed him as though he were a dangerous terrorist about to carry out an attack.”
Crime boss killed at point-blank range
Yushvaev, an Or Akiva resident in his 40s, was shot at point-blank range Sunday afternoon at a gas station near the Caesarea interchange in northern Israel. The killing was captured by security cameras.
Police said from the outset that the shooting appeared to be criminally motivated. Suspects were initially believed to have escaped in a vehicle, prompting a major search operation involving large numbers of officers, roadblocks and a helicopter. Police Commissioner Danny Levy and the Coastal District commander both traveled to the scene.
The Magen David Adom emergency service received the report at 3:51 p.m. Paramedics found Yushvaev unconscious, without a pulse and not breathing, with severe penetrating wounds. They performed CPR and treated his injuries before he was pronounced dead.
Yushvaev had been identified by police as the head of an organized crime organization associated with Israel’s Caucasus community and had for years been considered one of the Coastal District Central Unit’s most significant organized-crime targets.
Despite repeated arrests and his name being linked by police to investigations involving shootings, arson, threats and violent underworld disputes, many of those investigations did not produce significant indictments.
About a decade ago, Yushvaev was himself shot and wounded while visiting mourners in Hadera. He recovered and subsequently accumulated considerable influence in the Sharon region, north of Tel Aviv.
Police arrested him over the years on suspicion of involvement in several shootings, including gunfire directed at the home of a Hadera businessman and a shooting in Or Akiva in which a civilian was wounded. He was also arrested at Ben Gurion International Airport after returning from abroad following intelligence that he intended to harm rivals. Authorities at one point barred him from entering Or Akiva. Those cases ended without charges because of insufficient evidence.
In November 2025, during a hearing on a request to extend his detention on suspicion of conspiracy to commit a crime, a police representative described Yushvaev as the leader of a “criminal gang involved in blood feuds.”
Two years earlier, in 2023, he was arrested on suspicion of involvement in a wave of arson attacks in Or Akiva and Hadera in which dozens of vehicles were torched over about a month.
$1.1 million threat case
One investigation did result in an indictment.
In 2021, prosecutors charged Yushvaev with threatening a businessman from Be'er Sheva in southern Israel over a financial debt.
According to the indictment, Yushvaev contacted the businessman through a WhatsApp voice call and arranged to meet him at Soroka Medical Center in Be'er Sheva.
Prosecutors alleged that Yushvaev told the businessman he had taken responsibility for collecting the debt and demanded $1.1 million within less than a month.
“The handling of the debt has been transferred to me,” Yushvaev allegedly told him. “You have until Dec. 1 to transfer $1.1 million to me or we’ll eliminate you.”
When the businessman said he could not raise the money, prosecutors said Yushvaev instructed him to sell his home or take out a loan.
About three weeks later, prosecutors alleged, Yushvaev called again to ask whether he had obtained the money. When the businessman proposed another arrangement, Yushvaev insisted on payment.
After the businessman said he could not do it, Yushvaev allegedly replied: “You understand I’m not calling again. You know what will happen,” before ending the call.

Hundreds Feared Dead, Including Foreign Tourists, After Flash Floods in Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:14:01 UTC
00:14:01 KST

Over 150 people have been killed and hundreds more are missing after devastating flash floods swept through the Himalayan region along the Nepal-Tibet border, officials from both countries confirmed Wednesday.
Severe flooding was reported across the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, north of the Nepalese capital Kathmandu. The majority of the flooding has occurred along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi rivers in the north of the country.
Nepal’s Tourism Board said that 403 people were missing as a result of the flooding, including 341 foreign nationals and 62 Nepali citizens.
Of the missing, from figures compiled by several travel companies, 133 are confirmed to be Indian, 24 are Canadian, 33 are British, 19 Malaysian, 34 Austrlian, and 47 are from the U.S.
The U.S. embassy in Nepal issued a warning to U.S. citizens in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan, and Tanahun, urging them to “stay away from riverbanks and low-lying areas, seek higher ground, and follow local instructions.” The embassy added that it was working to account for Americans affected by the flooding.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah met with local Members of Parliament (MPs) earlier Wednesday to discuss issues including flood damage, condition of settlements in local areas, rescue and relief work, his office said.
“The government has intensified the search and rescue operations by deploying security forces in the flood affected areas,” Shah’s office added.
How Nepal is responding to the crisis
Nepal’s Minister for Foreign Affairs Shisir Khanal said that 79 security personnel remained unaccounted for, and that 13 helicopters from both the army and private sector were involved in rescue efforts.
Nepali Police published the details of 49 people hospitalized due to injuries from the flooding, most of whom are from the Nuwakot and Rasuwa regions. The list of injured included a 3-month-old who was in a stable condition.
Video shared by police showed the catastrophic flooding, with entire buildings swept away in the powerful currents. Other footage shared shows a bridge and multiple buildings on the banks of the Trishuli river destroyed in the flooding. Officials have since confirmed that nine bridges and nearly 40 kilometers of road were swept away.
Police also issued a warning that they expect the flooding to continue down the Bhotekoshi river into the regions of Dhading and Muglin in the center of the country.
One of Nepal's busiest roads, the Prithvi highway, that connects Kathmandu to the second largest city, Pokhara, passes through these regions along the Trishuli river. Police later confirmed that it would be closing this section of the highway.
The flooding has also resulted in widespread casualties at the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region. A mudslide occurred near the Gyirong checkpoint on the border, resulting in at least three deaths and 265 people missing in Gyirong County, according to Chinese state media.
Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered “all-out efforts” for search and rescue operations in response to the mudslide, as well as calling for the strengthening of “monitoring and early warning, ensure scientific rescue operations and guard against secondary disasters,” Chinese media reported.
Footage from the checkpoint shows water engulfing buildings as people flee the oncoming currents. TIME has been unable to independently verify the footage.

Reuters could not immediately locate contact details for Nanjing Xinjiuwei.

Experts who follow Chinese cyber activity say that private contractors routinely carry out high-profile intrusions on behalf of various Chinese government agencies.
“Over the last decade, the number of companies offering niche offensive services has exploded,” said Dakota Cary, a China analyst with cybersecurity company SentinelOne. REUTERS

Commander of the 79th Separate Tavriia Air Assault Brigade, Colonel Eduard Kolodii. Russian losses amount to at least 9,550 killed and more than 6,600 wounded. It was also possible to replenish Ukraine's prisoner-exchange fund.

26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
The US Treasury Department on Wednesday designated the British group Palestine Action as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT).
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the agency responsible for administering US economic sanctions, added the group to its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN).
The designation was made pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886. Originally signed in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, the legal authority targets US-designated terrorists and those providing financial, material or technological support to them. It allows for secondary sanctions against those providing support to the organization.
The US accused the group of supporting "numerous acts of terrorism since" its establishment.
Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori characterized the US decision as “beyond hypocritical.”
“As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist, is beyond hypocritical,” Ammori said on US social media copany X, adding that US President Donald Trump represents the "antithesis" of Palestine Action’s values.
The US Treasury Department also sanctioned Masar Badil, including two of its senior leaders, which it alleged operates as a front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which is designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization by US.
The moves came as a part of the Treasury Department’s "action against violent far-left terrorist networks," which also covered a sanction against Autistici Inventati, an Italy-based entity that the US said supplies services for Antifa.
“Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Founded in 2020, Palestine Action defines its mission as “ending global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime.”
The move follows a decision by the UK government in July 2025 to proscribe Palestine Action under the Terrorism Act. That ban came after activists entered a Royal Air Force base and spray-painted two aircraft. The group also targeted Elbit Systems, an international defense electronics company with ties to the Israeli military.

Study: Istanbul residents shun culture and arts with high ticket prices main barrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:10:53 UTC
00:10:53 KST

According to IPA’s Istanbul Barometer survey, 45.8% of Istanbul residents did not attend any cultural or arts event in the past year, with high ticket and entry prices cited as the main obstacle.
According to the July edition of the Istanbul Barometer survey conducted by the Istanbul Planning Agency (IPA), 45.8% of Istanbul residents did not attend any cultural or artistic event in the past year.
While the biggest obstacle to participation in cultural events was high ticket and admission prices, cited by 45%, economic conditions led people to cut back most on spending in social venues such as restaurants and cafés.
The July issue of Istanbul Barometer, the monthly data bulletin of IPA, which is affiliated with the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM), focused on the heading "Cultural and entertainment habits in Istanbul". The survey, conducted with 758 participants, examined Istanbul residents' level of engagement in cultural life, the barriers to participation, their culture and entertainment spending, and their digital entertainment habits.
Concerts are the most popular outing for Istanbul residents
Of those taking part in the survey, 45.8% said they had not attended any cultural or artistic event in the past year.
Among those who did attend events, concerts were the most popular choice with 33.9%. They were followed by theatre and stand-up shows at 21.8%, and visits to art galleries and museums at 21.2%.
The share of people attending book fairs or author events stood at 16.2%, street festivals and open-air events at 16.1%, and film festivals at 11.9%. Design, photography and fashion events were chosen by 6.2%, dance performances by 5.9%, and opera, ballet and classical music concerts by 5.7%.
The main reason making it difficult to attend cultural events was "high ticket and admission prices", cited by 45% of respondents. In second place, at 38.1%, was a lack of time due to work or school.
Economic conditions affect spending on culture and entertainment
Participants were also asked whether they had cut back on culture and entertainment spending over the past year because of economic conditions.
The category where people saved the most was spending in social venues such as restaurants and cafés, at 41.4%. Meanwhile, 39.8% of respondents said they had not reduced any of their spending categories.
The proportion of people cutting back on concert and theatre tickets was measured at 37.6%, and on cinema tickets at 37.2%. For museum visits the figure fell to 26%, to 25.9% for purchases of books, magazines and digital content, and to 25.2% for subscriptions to streaming platforms.
Digital content seen as more accessible and convenient
The study also showed that digitalisation is playing an increasingly prominent role in Istanbul residents' cultural and entertainment habits.
While 56.9% said they preferred attending in-person events, 28.5% opted for social media and digital content instead of cultural experiences.
Of those who favoured digital content over cultural experiences, 34.3% cited the fact that it is more practical when time is limited. The greater accessibility and lower cost of digital content ranked second, with 29.6%.
A further 18.1% pointed to their social circle also shifting towards digital, and 12.5% said reaching physical venues was difficult or tiring.
Istanbul residents consume more than three hours of digital entertainment a day
According to the survey, Istanbul residents spend an average of 3 hours and 8 minutes a day consuming digital entertainment content.
Their average daily free time, excluding work, sleep, meals and childcare, was calculated at 3 hours and 44 minutes. The fact that these two figures are very close indicates that Istanbul residents devote a large share of their spare time to digital content consumption.

South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:09:58 UTC
00:09:58 KST

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.
A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.
The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.
Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.
The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”
Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.
The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.
South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

Moscow opens its first dinosaur skeleton exhibition, where visitors can buy the exhibits
An exhibition of dinosaur skeletons, prehistoric animal skulls, and meteorite fragments — all offered for sale — opened in Moscow on August 25.
The exhibition “Relictum: Traces of Time” is being held at the Stargift gallery space on Bolshaya Yakimanka Street. Among its centerpieces is a complete psittacosaurus skeleton more than 125 million years old, measuring 168 centimeters (66 inches) and listed in the catalog at 12.5 million rubles.
Another highlight is a complete cave bear skeleton, more than 12,000 years old, which the catalog prices at 10 million rubles. The exhibition also features a pair of mammoth tusks weighing a combined 74 kilograms (163 pounds), along with fossils containing dinosaur eggs and other artifacts.
According to the exhibition’s organizers, this kind of sale is already familiar to the international clientele of Sotheby’s and Christie’s auctions. The tyrannosaurus skeleton “Gus,” for instance, sold at Sotheby’s for a record $50 million in July 2026.
Under Russian law, paleontological finds are treated as part of the subsoil, which belongs to the state. Handling them is governed by the subsoil law and requires state approval.

Israel launches organized pogroms against defenseless Palestinian towns

Israel launches organized pogroms against defenseless Palestinian towns
TEHRAN — The occupied West Bank is systematically being suffocated. Israeli forces and armed settler militias have fused into a single apparatus of terror, waging a relentless campaign of raids, land theft, and violence across Palestinian neighborhoods.
Backed by Washington, Tel Aviv is accelerating a coordinated project of ethnic cleansing.
Erasing institutions
The assault on Palestinian existence extends directly into international humanitarian facilities.
The Israeli military raided the Qalandiya Training Center in the Kafr Aqab neighborhood of East al-Quds (Jerusalem) on August 25.
This UNRWA facility provided educational services and vocational training to some 16,000 Palestinian refugees.
The troops forcibly expelled the staff, ordered them never to return, and initiated a complete takeover.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir arrived to celebrate the seizure. Broadcasting his triumph from inside the facility, he declared that the United Nations agency "has no place in Jerusalem."
The Israeli regime immediately announced plans to confiscate the site and replace it with a settlement complex.
The brazen takeover amounts to a direct assault on one of the few remaining institutional lifelines for vulnerable Palestinian refugees, while openly trampling the international legal protections and diplomatic immunities that are supposed to shield UN premises from precisely this kind of unlawful intrusion.
Organized pogroms
Outside al-Quds, the violence takes a more visceral form.
Settler attacks across the West Bank have surged by 63 percent in the first seven months of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented over 4,100 incidents of settler aggression.
These are regime-sanctioned pogroms. United Nations Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese has explicitly used the term to describe the organized violence against defenseless civilians.
The cruelty is calculated. In the village of Qusra, settlers and soldiers laid a brutal two-week siege on three families, cutting off their water and trapping them inside a single home while the military commandeered another property.
In Za'atara, armed settlers beat residents in their homes, leaving three Palestinians requiring hospitalization before stealing their livestock.
In Burin, attackers cut electricity poles feeding a Palestinian family home. In Duma, Israeli troops bulldozed agricultural land and demolished tin shelters.
The objective is clear: make everyday life so unbearable that Palestinians are eventually driven to leave.
Official vandalism and medical terror
The lawlessness is driven from the highest levels of the Israeli government.
In a vivid display of regime-sponsored hatred, extremist Knesset member Zvi Sukkot recently entered the village of Madama armed with a sledgehammer.
Flanked and protected by Israeli soldiers, the lawmaker physically smashed a monument commemorating Palestinian martyrs.
His staff joined in the vandalism. The military later claimed the demolition was unauthorized, yet the footage clearly shows that troops stood by and watched a politician destroy Palestinian property for an abhorrent propaganda video.
This sadism also permeates the Israeli prison system. Palestinian medical professionals are being aggressively targeted.
Dr. Dima Amin, a 55-year-old gynecologist abducted from Ramallah, suffered a massive heart attack in custody.
Interrogators refused to loosen the tight restraints that caused her condition to deteriorate.
Even after she was rushed to a hospital for emergency cardiac catheterization, Israeli authorities immediately threw her back into a harsh interrogation center without adequate medical follow-up.
Human rights organizations report that thousands of Palestinians face deliberate starvation, torture, and lethal medical neglect in these dungeons.
A shrinking horizon under American cover
Israel is weaponizing every aspect of Palestinian life.
Crippling fuel shortages engineered by the occupation regime have been paralyzing basic civic functions.
Meanwhile, authorities are aggressively pushing the E1 settlement expansion plan, a project designed to geographically sever the West Bank in two and isolate East al-Quds (Jerusalem) entirely.
None of this happens in a vacuum. The United States provides the diplomatic shield and military hardware required to sustain this violence.
From time to time, Washington may issue hollow warnings about settler aggression. However, it has been consistently funding the very military that arms those settlers.
Israel is actively attempting to crush the spirit of Palestinian resistance and erase Palestinian identity. Yet despite the sieges, the demolished homes, and the stolen land, the Palestinian people remain rooted to their soil.

If Iceland joins the EU, where does that leave Norway?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:03:34 UTC
00:03:34 KST

On Saturday, Icelanders will vote on whether to resume negotiations to join the European Union. A “Yes” could squeeze Norway’s position in the European Economic Area and put Oslo under pressure to reconsider its own relationship with Brussels — a question with a long and divisive history.
A “Yes” vote could leave the EU’s other Nordic neighbour in an awkward position, putting pressure on Norway to reconsider its relationship with Brussels.
Beyond Reykjavík and Brussels, one European capital is watching Saturday’s vote particularly closely: Oslo. Norway is arguably the non-EU country with the most at stake, especially if the “Yes” side wins.
“We must recognise that an Icelandic membership process will pose special challenges for Norway as an EEA country,” Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told parliament in May.
Norway’s government has so far maintained that the European Economic Area (EEA) should remain the basis of its relationship with Brussels. But the implications of an Icelandic “Yes” would be difficult to ignore.
A shrinking club
The EEA extends the EU single market to three non-EU countries: Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. If Iceland joins the Union, the EEA would be reduced to two members, one of them Liechtenstein, a country of just 40,000 people whose economy is closely tied to Switzerland.
In effect, the EEA would become a bilateral arrangement between the EU and Norway, leaving Norway as the only major country in the European single market without a seat at the decision-making table.
Iceland would not be the first country to move from EEA membership to full EU accession. When the agreement entered into force in 1994, it also included Austria, Finland and Sweden, all of which later joined the Union after positive referendums.
Technically, the EEA would remain in place if Iceland joined the EU. Politically, however, it would become harder to argue that the arrangement remains a meaningful alternative to full membership.
“If Iceland should become a member of the EU, the balance of power between the parties to the EEA Agreement – originally 12 countries to 7 – will become 28 to 2,” Eide said.
That imbalance explains why Norway’s government, while defending the EEA as the basis of its relationship with Brussels, cannot ignore the consequences of a “Yes” vote.
“Whatever path Iceland takes, we must work to strengthen our cooperation with the EU,” Eide added.
Iceland’s Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir struck a similar note after meeting her Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre, in February.
“We will keep the EEA Agreement active whatever happens,” she said. “Because if a yes comes out of this referendum on our side, there is still a decision to be taken on full membership. If a no comes out of it, we need to rely on the EEA Agreement being strong and active.”
A troubled history
The EEA was the product of Norway’s complicated relationship with the European project. Norwegians have twice rejected EU membership in referendums: in 1972 and 1994.
On both occasions, Norway was the only candidate country to vote against joining, with 53.5% and 52% respectively voting “No”.
That pattern remains. A poll published earlier this month by Norwegian daily ABC Nyheter found that 49% would vote against EU membership, compared with 37% in favour.
The underlying concerns – fisheries, farming and a reluctance to trade sovereignty for a limited say in a much larger bloc – have changed little since the 1990s.
Iceland shares many of those concerns. But Saturday’s referendum is not on EU membership itself. It asks whether the government should be given a mandate to resume accession negotiations, which were suspended in 2015.
A second referendum would then decide whether voters approve any eventual deal.
That means Iceland’s negotiations will be closely watched in Oslo and could potentially weaken the position of Norway’s EU sceptics.
Hallgrimur Oddsson, director of the think tank Evrópustraumar, told Euronews that Norwegians would “follow very closely” how the negotiations develop, particularly on issues such as fisheries.
He expects pro-EU parties to use any momentum to revive the membership debate, while noting that Norway has already held two referendums on the issue.
“Their history is also different,” he said.
Iceland’s vote could provide fresh momentum, but Norway would still need to find its own reasons for joining the bloc. That would require a major national debate, for which there has so far been little appetite.
Reopening old wounds
Norway’s concerns have changed little since EU membership was last debated, and neither have the positions of the main political parties.
There has been little serious discussion about reopening the membership question, partly because politicians and voters remain wary of the divisions left by previous referendum campaigns.
In the current geopolitical climate, there is also an argument that reopening such a sensitive issue – one that has divided the country and even families in the past – is the last thing Norway needs.
When the Icelandic government formally asked parliament to hold a referendum, Trygve Slagsvold Vedum, leader of the Eurosceptic Centre Party, warned that it could reinvigorate Norway’s own pro-EU movement.
“The EU forces in Norway will paint a frightening picture of Norway outside the EU. We will see an unprecedented black painting,” Vedum said, describing opposition to EU membership as the most important issue in Norwegian politics.
By contrast, Guri Melby, leader of the pro-EU Liberal Party, said Iceland’s referendum should give fresh impetus to a debate on Norwegian membership and urged Norway to learn from Iceland’s less divisive approach.
At a parliamentary hearing in March, Conservative MP Ine Eriksen Søreide argued that conditions in Europe and the wider world had fundamentally changed. As the EU deepens its integration, she said, it will become increasingly difficult for Norway to safeguard its interests from outside the bloc.
Whichever way Iceland votes on Saturday, Norway will feel the consequences. And if Reykjavík’s path towards EU membership becomes more likely, Norwegians may find themselves forced to revisit the thorny question of their own place in Europe.
Jorge Liboreiro contributed to the reporting.

The Siberian Ring Photon Source: Inside Russia’s latest megascience site (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:03:08 UTC
00:03:08 KST

The Siberian Ring Photon Source: Inside Russia’s latest megascience site (VIDEO)
Russia’s latest megascience undertaking lies not far from the river Ob, south of Novosibirsk in Siberia, some 3,000 km east of Moscow. The Siberian Ring Photon Source (SKIF) synchrotron complex is effectively an ultra-powerful X-ray microscope for research ranging from medicine and chemistry to metallurgy and geology.
RT has been granted access to SKIF, a state-of-the-art megascience project built to let scientists examine matter at the atomic scale.
SKIF was officially unveiled by Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this month. At the time, he said that the opening was postponed from 2024 because foreign suppliers failed to deliver certain equipment due to Western sanctions, forcing Russian teams to reproduce key components domestically. Now, the first research stations are expected to enter operation before year-end.
The construction of the nearly $600 million facility began in 2021, becoming one of Russia’s most expensive scientific projects. As for its principles, the device accelerates electrons to almost the speed of light and sends them around a 476-meter storage ring, where magnets bend their path and make them give off extremely bright radiation. Scientists can then select the part of that radiation they need, from infrared through hard X-rays, and aim it at a sample.
The scientists can then watch a chemical reaction as it happens, studying how metals behave under shock waves, examining proteins and medicines, or looking inside archaeological objects without cutting them open. The method is also expected to drastically reduce the development time for new materials, pharmaceuticals, and cancer drugs.
“The emission that the source creates is well suited to studying the atomic or molecular structure of a compound… It’s viruses, medicine, bone fractures, aircraft engine, turbines, chemical reactions, high-speed processes. Indeed, it’s useful to everyone,” SKIF Director Evgeny Levichev told RT.
One of the upcoming experiments will examine titanium-based catalysts used to produce ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene, while other planned work includes studying difficult-to-extract gold and searching lake sediments near the site of the 1908 Tunguska event for possible extraterrestrial particles.

UK firm to demo autonomous vessel tech at SMM 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:03:02 UTC
00:03:02 KST

- Cambridge Pixel will demonstrate USV and ASV radar and sensor processing software at SMM 2026 in Hamburg, September 1-4.
- The company's software is integrated with more than 80 radar systems and used by customers including the U.S. Navy and British Royal Navy.
Cambridge Pixel will show its software for uncrewed and autonomous surface vessels at SMM 2026, a maritime trade fair running September 1-4 in Hamburg, Germany.
The UK-based company will set up at Hall B1, Stand 321, where it plans to demonstrate radar, camera and sensor processing modules used for tracking, data fusion, display, control, recording and simulation on USVs and ASVs.
Cambridge Pixel has supplied software components to USV and ASV developers for more than a decade, working with manufacturers across the United States, Europe and Asia. The company says its software is integrated with more than 80 different radar systems, providing tracking, navigation and situational awareness without requiring additional hardware.
The company’s core product for this market is SPx Server V2, which handles radar video processing, proximity detection and tracking for collision avoidance and autonomous navigation. A Detection Server configuration within that software provides plot extraction and proximity detection, while a Tracking Server configuration adds multi-hypothesis target tracking. Cambridge Pixel says the software can output obstacle and target data to external autonomy or vessel-control systems using formats including ASTERIX, NMEA-0183, TAK and SAPIENT.
The company says its technology also supports navigation in GPS-denied environments, along with camera control and unlocking maritime radar systems for use with custom software.
Cambridge Pixel lists customers in 65 countries, including BAE Systems, the British Royal Navy, Echodyne, Furuno, Hanwha, Hensoldt, L3Harris, Lockheed Martin, OSI Maritime, QinetiQ, Raytheon, Saab, Thales and the U.S. Navy.
SMM 2026 is expected to draw more than 2,200 exhibitors and nearly 50,000 visitors from over 100 countries, according to the event organizers. This year’s edition will include a new Maritime Security and Defence Expo section, featuring exhibitors focused on unmanned systems, cyber solutions, maritime surveillance and critical infrastructure protection.

AI Is Lowering the Barriers to China’s Information Warfare Against Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

Japan’s Ministry of Defense recently released its 2026 Defense of Japan white paper, once again drawing attention to China’s rapid advances in artificial intelligence and their implications for the regional security environment. Yet the most immediate danger to Japan may not come from AI’s application to conventional military systems. Generative AI is also lowering the barriers for Chinese information operations targeting Japanese society.
In late 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae made comments in the Diet linking a Taiwan contingency to Japan’s own security. Since then, disinformation targeting Japanese political figures and domestic issues has grown – not only in volume but also in sophistication. Research by organizations including the Sasakawa Peace Foundation and OpenAI suggests that China-linked influence operators are increasingly using AI to adapt their activities to Japan’s online environment and improve the efficiency of their operations.
AI is beginning to erode what was once one of the most obvious weaknesses of Chinese information operations against Japan: the linguistic and cultural barrier. Content that once featured grammatical mistakes, awkward translations and unnatural expressions is becoming harder for ordinary users to identify at a glance.
If these capabilities are deployed to interfere with elections, discredit politicians or amplify social divisions, their effects could extend far beyond any single piece of false information.
A special report by Nikkei in February found that more than 400 China-linked social media accounts spread negative content about Takaichi during Japan’s House of Representatives election. Separately, the Yomiuri Shimbun, citing research by Japan Nexus Intelligence, reported that under a different set of criteria, thousands of coordinated accounts on X were involved in sharing and amplifying related content.
The narratives did not focus solely on attacking Takaichi personally. They also linked Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense capabilities with concerns over social welfare, seeking to promote the argument that military expansion was coming at the expense of ordinary people.
In the past, such accounts often left obvious clues. Some had been created only recently. Their Japanese reflected Chinese word order and linguistic habits, while others mixed simplified Chinese characters with Japanese usage. AI-generated images also frequently contained visual errors that made them relatively easy to identify.
Those weaknesses, however, are becoming less pronounced.
The Sankei Shimbun has continued to track PAPERWALL, a China-linked information network that includes 15 websites masquerading as Japanese news outlets. The continued operation of these sites, and the broader ecosystem surrounding them, points toward an increasingly localized approach to influence operations. Improvements in language, imagery, and the appearance of fake news sites are making it more difficult for ordinary readers to distinguish legitimate sources from fabricated ones.
A report released by OpenAI in February offered another important clue. The company found that China-linked actors had used ChatGPT to assist in planning an online influence campaign targeting Takaichi. Influence actors appear willing to incorporate different AI systems into their existing workflows whenever those tools make their operations more effective.
What matters is not the nationality of the model. What matters is that generative AI is reducing the cost of cross-language information operations. In the past, producing large volumes of content tailored to a Japanese audience required translators, graphic designers, social media operators and people familiar with Japanese political and cultural contexts.
Large language models can now help operators correct grammar, adjust tone, generate images, and produce multiple versions of the same narrative for different audiences within minutes. In other words, AI is making China’s information warfare more scalable, faster and more localized.
How, then, should Japan respond? Taiwan offers one useful point of reference.
Taiwan has faced Chinese information operations for years and shares a Chinese-language environment with the mainland. Beijing therefore does not face the same linguistic barrier when targeting Taiwanese society that it encounters in Japan. Precisely for that reason, Taiwan was forced to develop social mechanisms for dealing with large-scale disinformation campaigns and networks of suspicious accounts.
Taiwan’s experience does not rely solely on government agencies or third-party fact-checkers. Individual users also identify, report, and block suspicious accounts, while civil society organizations and researchers continuously monitor information networks and patterns of coordinated behavior.
Language and culture themselves can also serve as tools for identifying manipulation. Although Taiwan and China both use Chinese, there are clear differences in vocabulary, grammar, social experience, and political context. Chinese influence operators can use AI to reduce these differences, but they cannot easily reproduce the cultural background and lived experience accumulated within another society.
Japan retains the same kind of advantage. Japanese language and social culture are highly contextual. Even if Chinese operators use AI to improve translation and content generation, that does not mean they can fully understand the linguistic and political differences between generations, regions, and social groups in Japan.
Japan should therefore move beyond a defensive model that waits for false information to appear and then fact-checks it. The more important task is to strengthen society’s ability to recognize coordinated influence operations before they gain traction.
This is also why information-security cooperation between Japan and Taiwan should become more institutionalized. The two sides could deepen exchanges on identifying coordinated accounts, detecting deepfakes, analyzing foreign influence networks and monitoring information environments during major disasters, elections, or political crises.
AI is making Chinese information operations cheaper, faster and easier to deploy across language barriers. But it still cannot fully replicate the cultural knowledge and lived experience embedded in a society.
Japan therefore does not need to build a wall capable of blocking every piece of false information. It needs to build an information environment in which foreign influence operations are less likely to succeed. As Japan and Taiwan confront increasingly similar information-security threats, sharing their experience in identifying and countering Chinese influence operations could become an increasingly important part of regional security cooperation.

‘Pilot areas’ in southern Lebanon still being defined, US envoy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:02:49 UTC
00:02:49 KST

Wassim Seifeddine and Mohammad Sio
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
Progress has been made in defining co-called “pilot areas” in southern Lebanon where the Lebanese army is meant to deploy as part of a June framework agreement calling for Israel’s gradual withdrawal, US Ambassador to Lebanon Michael Issa said Wednesday.
Issa made the remarks after meeting Sheikh Abdul Latif Derian, Lebanon’s grand mufti, in Beirut, where they discussed the country’s future and ongoing talks between Lebanon and Israel, according to the Lebanese National News Agency.
Asked about continued Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon, Issa acknowledged that they “have not stopped” and were happening mainly “outside the designated pilot areas.”
He added that Washington had yet to reach an agreement with Israel to halt the attacks.
Reiterating his support for the Israeli position, Issa linked the continued attacks to what he described as Hezbollah’s “failure to honor the ceasefire.”
Defending Israel's continued aggression, he added: “Hezbollah has never said it is prepared to hand over its weapons. So how can you ask Israel to withdraw from Lebanon?”
Talks with Hezbollah ‘possible’
Asked whether Washington could negotiate with Hezbollah, Issa said, “We have never said we will negotiate with it,” but added that talks were “possible if the group is willing or has something to offer.”
He also dismissed what he described as “unproductive contacts,” saying negotiations must be more than merely “exchanging visits and drinking coffee.”
According to Issa, Lebanon-Israel negotiations remain underway in Rome.
He described the talks as “technical negotiations” that do not require fixed dates, adding that sovereignty-related issues were being handled separately and were scheduled in advance to avoid overlap.
‘Pilot areas’
So-called “pilot areas” are areas of southern Lebanon where initial arrangements are being made in line with the June 26 framework agreement, which calls for a gradual Israeli withdrawal and the deployment of the Lebanese army into vacated areas.
“Everything is first determined on paper, and it takes a long time to implement on the ground,” Issa said, adding that defining a pilot area requires field teams to identify every feature forming its boundaries.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued staging relentless attacks in several parts of southern Lebanon, which Beirut says are hindering the army’s planned deployments.
Since March 2, wide-ranging Israeli attacks have killed 4,348 people and injured more than 12,000 others, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.
Israeli forces remain present in several parts of southern Lebanon, some of which they have occupied for decades.
Others were occupied during a previous round of fighting in 2023 and 2024, when Israeli forces advanced more than 10 kilometers into sovereign Lebanese territory.

Genetic vulnerability appears to have amplified the pandemic’s toll on teen mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:54 UTC
00:00:54 KST

A recent study provides evidence that adolescent mental health declined markedly during the COVID-19 pandemic, with youth who carry a genetic predisposition for psychiatric conditions experiencing an even greater overall burden of symptoms. The findings indicate that the environmental stressors of the pandemic caused lasting emotional and behavioral difficulties, particularly for adolescent girls. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
The COVID-19 pandemic introduced widespread disruptions, including school closures, social isolation, and shifted daily routines. These rapid lifestyle changes took a heavy toll on young people worldwide. For example, a 2021 meta-analysis found that rates of clinically elevated depression and anxiety symptoms among children and teenagers roughly doubled across the globe during the first year of the pandemic. Researchers have been trying to understand why some adolescents adapted to these changes over time while others experienced worsening psychological health.
Psychiatric conditions are known to have a strong hereditary component, meaning genetic differences play a role in how adolescents handle environmental stress. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that a higher shared genetic risk across various psychiatric conditions was strongly associated with a persistent pattern of high depressive symptoms throughout adolescence. To measure this inherited risk, scientists often use polygenic risk scores. These scores combine the small effects of thousands of genetic variations into a single number to estimate an individual’s broad biological susceptibility to mental health conditions.
“We are particularly interested in the impact of social isolation on adolescents’ health,” said Chun Chieh Fan of the Center for Population Neuroscience and Genetics at the Laureate Institute for Brain Research. “While there were many studies reporting the crisis among youth, there was limited discussion on who is most susceptible.”
To identify these at-risk groups, Fan and co-lead author Lucy Shao of the University of California San Diego analyzed data from 10,374 adolescents. The participants were drawn from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, a large ongoing project tracking child development in the United States. The youth were between 10 and 14 years old in 2020.
The researchers tracked 20 different measures of mental health over five assessment waves. These visits covered the period before the pandemic, the early pandemic in 2020, and the late pandemic extending into early 2022.
The team calculated four distinct polygenic risk scores for each participant based on past genetic research in adults. These scores estimated the genetic likelihood of compulsive disorders, psychotic disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, and internalizing conditions like depression and anxiety. By comparing these scores with parent-reported and self-reported mental health surveys, the scientists could track how symptom levels changed over time in relation to each participant’s genetic profile.
The findings indicate that the pandemic was associated with broad increases in psychological distress. During the early pandemic, symptom scores across various mental health measures increased by 4% to 14% compared to pre-pandemic levels. Symptoms tended to remain elevated during the late pandemic period, ranging from 6% to 24% above early pandemic levels. Specifically, parent-reported withdrawn behavior, depression, and rule-breaking increased, as did self-reported internalizing problems.
Genetic predispositions also played a distinct role in symptom severity. For every one-unit increase in a participant’s neurodevelopmental or internalizing polygenic risk score, they experienced between a 3% and 21% increase in symptoms across most mental health categories.
“The COVID pandemic imposed a long-term impact on youth, especially when the disruptions lingered over years,” Fan told PsyPost. “The cumulative stress compounded upon those who are particularly vulnerable, emerging a wide range of behavioral issues among youth.”
The researchers noticed marked differences when separating the data by sex. Female adolescents exhibited a greater increase in mental health challenges during the early pandemic, including a 25% increase in parent-reported affective problems. In contrast, male adolescents showed a smaller initial bump in symptoms that tended to stabilize or even decrease during the later pandemic stages. Female participants with a high genetic risk for neurodevelopmental conditions also experienced a larger increase in conduct problems and aggressive behavior during the early pandemic.
These results are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that the global population-level burden of mental disorders surged among children and teens during the pandemic. That earlier study, which modeled broad disorder prevalence rather than tracking specific symptom scores in a cohort, similarly noted that female youth experienced the largest increases in anxiety and depression.
The study has some limitations to consider. The polygenic risk scores used by the researchers are broad statistical tools designed to measure traits across a large population. They are not diagnostic tests and cannot predict individual behavior or clinical outcomes for a specific child. The genetic data primarily relied on models derived from adults, which might not perfectly capture how mental health conditions develop during early adolescence.
The calendar-based periods used to define the pandemic phases do not isolate the specific causes of adolescent distress. Increased symptoms could be tied to school closures, financial strain at home, fear of infection, or physical health changes, but the data cannot separate these intertwined factors. The researchers also adjusted for age, but because adolescence is a period of rapid emotional change, normal developmental shifts might still overlap with pandemic-related trends.
Future studies could focus on identifying which specific pandemic disruptions had the strongest impact on adolescent well-being. Researchers might also examine protective factors in the home or community that help mitigate mental health risks. Expanding genetic research to include more diverse ancestral populations would help ensure that these scientific models accurately reflect the experiences of all youth.
The study, “Contributions of Genetic Liability and the COVID-19 Pandemic to Rising Psychopathology Among Youth in the United States,” was authored by Lucy Shao, Jonathan Ahern, Robert Loughnan, Bohan Xu, Holly E. Baker, Susan F. Tapert, Fiona C. Baker, Wesley K. Thompson, Orsolya Kiss, Eva M. Müller-Oehring, Marie Gombert-Labedens, and Chun Chieh Fan.

De Brigard and Robins Win 2026 Lebowitz Prize
The American Philosophical Association (APA) has announced the winners of its 2026 Dr. Martin R. Lebowitz and Eve Lewellis Lebowitz Prize.
They are:
Felipe De Brigard, Professor of Philosophy and Psychology & Neuroscience, a member of the Center for Cognitive Neuroscience at Duke University, and Principal Investigator of the Imagination and Modal Cognition Laboratory (IMC Lab) at the Duke Institute for Brain Science
and
Sarah Robins, Professor of Philosophy at Purdue University and founding co-director of Purdue’s Cognition, Agency, and Intelligence Center (CAIC).
The Lebowitz Prize is jointly awarded by the APA and the Phi Beta Kappa Society. Its winners must be two philosophers who hold contrasting views on a chosen topic of current interest in philosophy. They present their views and engage in a dialogue at an annual Lebowitz symposium, held during an APA divisional meeting. Each winner receives an honorarium of $25,000.
