What Spain’s response to Ukraine reveals about Its approach to immigration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:44 UTC
00:00:44 KST

Spain’s response to people displaced by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has offered a revealing look at how the country approaches immigration more broadly. Ukrainians received access to residence, employment, healthcare and education under temporary protection, while everyday integration still depends heavily on navigating Spain’s administrative system. For foreigners establishing economic, professional or personal ties with the country, that often includes obtaining a Spanish NIE number, one of the key identifiers used when dealing with public authorities and private institutions.
More than four years after the full-scale invasion began, Spain is now home to a substantial Ukrainian population. By June 2026, more than 353,000 Ukrainian nationals held valid residence or stay documentation in the country, according to Spain’s Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration. Temporary protection remains valid until March 4, 2027.
But Ukraine is only one part of a much larger immigration story.
Ukraine tested Spain’s capacity to turn emergency protection into integration
The European Union activated temporary protection for people fleeing Ukraine in 2022, creating an exceptional framework that allowed displaced Ukrainians to establish themselves quickly across member states.
In Spain, temporary protection grants both residence and work authorization. Beneficiaries can work as employees or self-employed workers, access healthcare and use the reception system, while minors are entitled to education under the same conditions as children from the host country. The framework can currently be requested until March 4, 2027.
These measures were designed as an emergency response, but four years is long enough for temporary arrangements to become ordinary life.
People find jobs. Children enter schools. Families build social networks. Businesses hire workers who originally arrived under an emergency mechanism. Housing contracts, bank relationships and interactions with public institutions gradually replace the initial questions of immediate safety and shelter.
That process offers a useful perspective on Spanish immigration policy because integration is ultimately measured less by what happens at the border than by what becomes possible afterward.
Spain’s approach to immigration extends well beyond Ukrainians
Spain’s willingness to bring foreign residents into formal administrative status did not end with the Ukrainian response.
In 2026, the country carried out an extraordinary regularization process for foreigners already living in Spain under qualifying circumstances. Between April 16 and June 30, authorities received 1,174,978 applications.
Nearly 80% were applications based on exceptional circumstances linked to established ties in Spain, while the remainder came from applicants for international protection. About 87% of applicants were of working age, and 59.4% were younger than 34.
The nationalities involved also show how much broader this phenomenon is than any single humanitarian crisis.
Colombians represented 25.9% of applications, followed by Moroccans, Venezuelans, Peruvians and Hondurans. Two-thirds of applicants came from Central or South America.
That matters because it places Spain’s treatment of Ukrainians within a wider policy environment.
The mechanisms are different. Temporary protection for Ukrainians and extraordinary regularization for other migrants should not be treated as equivalent immigration routes. But both demonstrate a willingness to create pathways through which foreigners already connected to Spain can move into recognized legal and administrative structures.
Openness does not mean the bureaucracy is simple
This is where Spain can appear contradictory from the outside.
The country can adopt relatively integration-oriented immigration policies while still requiring foreigners to navigate a highly procedural administrative system.
Residence status is only one part of that system.
Foreign residents, investors, property owners, entrepreneurs and others with interests in Spain frequently encounter identification requirements, appointments, registrations, tax procedures and digital interactions with government agencies.
The NIE, or Número de Identidad de Extranjero, is one of the most visible examples. It identifies foreigners who have economic, professional or social interests connected to Spain and appears in a wide range of administrative and private transactions.
But obtaining an identification number does not itself grant residency, just as holding residence status does not eliminate all the other administrative requirements that come with establishing a life or economic connection in the country.
This distinction can be especially important for people looking at Spain from abroad.
Someone can have a reason to interact with Spanish authorities without necessarily immigrating permanently. An investor may need Spanish identification. A property buyer may encounter local administrative requirements. An entrepreneur can develop business interests in Spain while remaining resident elsewhere.
The relevant bureaucracy depends on what the person is actually trying to do.
Spain is also increasingly digital; but that creates another layer to navigate
One notable feature of Spain’s administration is how much of it now takes place electronically.
The scale of the 2026 regularization illustrated this clearly: 83.2% of applications were submitted digitally. Among online applications, professionals handled a large share, while some applicants submitted their own cases using digital certificates.
Spain’s digital certificate system allows individuals to identify themselves securely online, sign official documents and interact with government bodies without completing every procedure in person.
For someone familiar with the system, this can make administration considerably easier.
For someone approaching Spanish bureaucracy for the first time, however, digitization does not necessarily make the process intuitive. It can simply move unfamiliar forms, identification requirements and institutional terminology onto a screen.
That gap has created demand for services focused specifically on administrative navigation.
Gestoraz is a Spanish administrative-services platform that helps foreign individuals, international investors and businesses manage bureaucracy in Spain, with services including NIE and NIF applications and digital certificates. Its model is particularly relevant to people who need to establish an administrative or economic connection with Spain, including those completing Spanish procedures from abroad rather than relocating permanently.
Gestoraz is also an authorized verification point for digital certificate applications and offers an online process that does not require applicants to be physically present in Spain.
This is an important distinction when assessing Spain as an international destination. The country’s immigration environment is not only about who can move there. It is also about how foreigners interact with the state once some form of connection has been established.
The Ukrainian experience shows what integration looks like after arrival
Spain’s Ukrainian population makes that distinction particularly visible.
By June 2026, Ukrainian nationals with valid residence or stay documentation exceeded 353,000. Women accounted for 58% of the population, and the Ministry noted that a Ukrainian community had already been established in Spain before the full-scale invasion.
Temporary protection gave newly displaced Ukrainians an immediate legal framework.
What followed was a much more ordinary process: employment, schooling, documentation, housing and long-term decisions about whether Spain would remain temporary or gradually become home.
The same distinction applies, in a very different context, to other foreigners considering Spain.
A country may be attractive because of employment, investment opportunities, climate, culture or family connections. But the lived experience of entering a country depends partly on whether its institutions create realistic ways for newcomers to become administratively integrated.
Spain’s recent record suggests that policymakers increasingly see migration not only as a question of entry but also as one of participation in the labour market and formal society.
The 2026 regularization provides one unusually large example. By June 30, the government reported nearly 160,000 additional Social Security contributors linked to the process, with hospitality, retail, administrative services and construction among the sectors recording the largest numbers of new registrations.
What Spain’s response tells people looking at the country from abroad
None of this means that moving to Spain is straightforward, that every foreigner qualifies for residence or that Spanish immigration policy is uniformly permissive.
It does suggest something more specific.
Spain has repeatedly used administrative mechanisms to integrate large foreign populations into legal residence, employment and public systems. Its response to Ukrainians made that particularly visible because it happened rapidly and at significant scale. The 2026 regularization showed that the broader policy direction was not confined to Ukrainians.
For people elsewhere considering Spain as somewhere to live, work, invest or build a longer-term economic connection, that distinction may matter.
Spain can be institutionally receptive while remaining bureaucratically demanding.
The Ukrainian experience demonstrates the first half of that equation particularly clearly. The paperwork encountered by anyone who subsequently tries to establish an ordinary life, investment or business connection with the country demonstrates the second.
Understanding both offers a more useful picture of Spain than either describing it as simply “open” to immigration or reducing the experience to its administrative hurdles.
The country’s recent record suggests that access and bureaucracy are not opposites in the Spanish system.
Very often, they arrive together.

US Air Force rescues five Navy crew after hard landing
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:00:17 BST
00:00:17 KST

Two HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopters were launched from Nellis Air Force Base to recover five US Navy personnel after an MH-60S Seahawk made a hard landing in mountainous terrain near China Lake.
US Air Force rescue crews have recovered five Navy personnel after their MH-60S Seahawk made a hard landing during a high-altitude training flight in mountainous terrain near Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake, California, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The incident occurred on 10 August, prompting the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center to notify the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron at approximately 11:30am. According to a US Air Force account of the rescue, the squadron immediately recalled personnel and coordinated with the Navy unit involved while the 355th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron prepared two HH-60W Jolly Green II combat rescue helicopters for the mission.
Despite the alert arriving on what had been scheduled as a training day, maintenance personnel generated both HH-60Ws in less than 30 minutes. The rapid preparation included troubleshooting an electrical problem on one of the helicopters after a circuit breaker issue threatened to prevent it from launching and no replacement component was immediately available.
Staff Sergeant Lucas Seney, an aerospace propulsion craftsman with the 355th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron, said, as quoted in the news update: “When production gave us the word for a real-world mission, I gathered the Airmen I had on the line and started directing traffic. The crew worked well together, and I was proud to see just how efficiently everyone was able to get the job done.”
Staff Sergeant Cody Adams, an avionics craftsman, helped identify the fault affecting one of the aircraft. He said: “We diagnosed the master caution warning press-to-reset button as what was causing the circuit breaker to pop and provided aircrew with a workaround to keep the system operational and allow on-time takeoff.”
The two HH-60Ws departed Nellis Air Force Base at 1pm. By 3pm, their crews had established two-way radio communications with the stranded Navy personnel and visually identified their position. Captain John Howe, a combat rescue officer with the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron, then led the pararescue element into the landing zone to assess the five survivors.
The team confirmed that none of the Navy personnel had been injured. After evaluating the terrain and the condition of the survivors, the rescuers elected to move the helicopters to a closer landing area rather than requiring the group to make a more demanding movement through mountainous terrain.
Lieutenant Colonel Kenneth “Buddy” Wilkins, commander of the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron and flight lead for the mission, said the crews had to carefully consider aircraft performance in the high-altitude environment. He said: “It was a good call by the team getting on the ground, making a good patient assessment, and then solid planning on the aircrew side of the house to determine what our ragged-edge power margins were that we needed to get into the zone and get out.”
The HH-60W is the US Air Force’s current-generation combat rescue helicopter and is designed for personnel recovery in demanding environments. High-altitude operations can be particularly challenging for helicopters because thinner air reduces rotor and engine performance, making aircraft weight, temperature and available power important considerations when selecting landing sites and extraction profiles.
All five sailors were aboard the rescue helicopters by 3:50pm. They were subsequently returned to their unit’s ramp at Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake before the Air Force helicopters flew back to Nellis.
Howe said preparation before an emergency was central to the speed of the response: “The preparation is what makes the execution smooth. It’s the combination of preestablished operating procedures, keeping equipment staged and ready for use, and hasty mission planning prior to departure, that makes this process effective, and expeditious.”
The Air Force said the operation drew directly on repeated training between the 88th Test and Evaluation Squadron and the 355th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron. Wilkins said: “This mission was a really good example of us taking the lessons learned from those previous events and executing as quickly and efficiently as possible. Within five minutes, I knew we had tails. Within 30 minutes, they were ready for us to go out.”

Stuck bundts? You need ‘cake goop’: Natalie Paull’s lime and yoghurt bundt – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:17 UTC
00:00:17 KST

When all the layer cakes are baked and iced, I will always love a slice of pretty patterned bundt. Especially one that is lightened with the perfect amount of baking powder (overly dense bundts are stodgy sadness) and brightened with limes and yoghurt.
Cake goop – a mix of flour, oil and butter – is a gift of guaranteed cake release that I found on the internet, and it means no more stuck bundts. Bless the baker who invented it! Goop has it all – release, plus enough sticking power to hold the batter as it rises and cools, without slumping. Additionally, mixing the flour with oil means you don’t get that fine, white, dusty crust on the outside of the cooked cake. Goop is 100% reliable with a 100% untarnished release record in my kitchen.
If you do have a small stuck piece of cake, shimmy it out of the tin with an offset spatula and patch it back on to the cake while warm. Pretty easy! If a whole ring of cake has stuck, cut it into workable sections, prise each out and place back on the cake. Drench the bundt with icing sugar after its soak to hide the Franken-bundt’s monster appearance.
The recipe calls for the eggs to be warmed before cracking. Warmer-than-room- temperature eggs emulsify into the creamed base better, and an emulsified mix means no “curdled” appearance. To do this, submerge the uncracked eggs in hot tap water for five minutes.
The cake will keep for three days, covered, at room temperature. And it freezes perfectly for up to three months.
Lime and yoghurt bundt cake – recipe
Makes 1 bundt or a 20cm round cake
 Takes 2-3 hours
For the cake goop
20g plain flour (10% protein)
20g vegetable oil
  20g unsalted butter, squidgy soft, at 22C
For the cake batter
  6 juicy limes
400g caster sugar
280g unsalted butter, soft, at 20C
5 eggs, warmed, but uncracked
375g soft plain flour (8-9% protein)
2 tsp baking powder
¼ tsp fine sea salt
240g plain yoghurt, at room temperature, or microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring in between, to de-chill
For the lime syrup
250g lime juice (from the limes used for the cake batter)
300g icing sugar mix
Preheat the oven to 170C/150C fan.
Make the cake goop by mixing the ingredients into a paste, then brush it into every nook and cranny of the bundt tin. Set the tin aside.
Make the batter. Zest the limes, then in a bowl rub the zest into the sugar with your fingers to release maximum fragrant oil. In the bowl of a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, cream the butter and lime sugar on medium speed for around six to eight minutes until the mix is pale and fluffy. Stop and scrape the side down once or twice during the creaming. In a separate bowl, crack the eggs, whisk and weigh 250g, then add to the mixer bowl in three batches, beating after each addition, then beat for another five minutes on medium speed.
Combine the flour, baking powder and salt together in a bowl.
Remove the bowl from the mixer and push the batter off the paddle. Sift half the flour mix over the top and fold it in with a sturdy plastic spatula. When it is almost fully mixed in, fold in half the yoghurt. Repeat with the remaining flour, then the remaining yoghurt. Make sure the final mix is very thorough so no flour or yoghurt streaks remain. Scrape the batter into the bundt tin and carefully smooth the top with a spoon.
Bake for 60 to 70 minutes until the cake has a fawn-coloured crust, the top has gently puffed and cracked, and a skewer inserted into the thickest part of the bundt comes out clean (internal temperature should be 95C).
Make the syrup while the cake bakes. Place the icing sugar in a wide bowl and hand-whisk half the juice in. Then whisk in the remaining juice. (By making a thick paste first, then thinning with the remaining juice, you can avoid sifting the icing sugar.)
Remove the cake from the oven. Using a metal skewer, poke lots of holes in the top of the cake, then slowly spoon half the syrup over the cake – it will attempt to run off the sides but concentrate most of the syrup on the open cracked ring of cake on the top. It’s quite mesmerising to watch it soak in. Leave for 10 minutes.
Invert the cake on to a serving plate. With a skewer, poke a few fine holes on the top and inner ring wall and brush more syrup over. I have given you a little extra syrup if you want a super-soaked cake, but I brush on two coats, then dab it again as it cools. Cool for 30 minutes before cutting the first slice.
- 
  This is an edited extract from Sweet Heart by Natalie Paull, with photography by Rochelle Eagle, available in Australia 1 September through Murdoch Books, $49.99

Andy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagree | Neal Lawson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:16 UTC
00:00:16 KST

A poll in the Mail on Sunday at the end of June was remarkable. It had not just Reform as low as 21%, but also Labour and the Tories. It was remarkable because it starkly demonstrated the fragmented landscape of the UK’s electoral terrain, as well as the electoral weakness of its main players.
Polls since have varied, not least with the Burnham bounce, but this week’s YouGov voting intention figures put Reform, Labour and the Tories on 23%, 22% and 20% respectively (although it almost no longer matters which exact figure applies to which party). Add in the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on 13% apiece, the SNP dominating Scotland and Plaid Cymru Wales, then Restore UK and independent candidates and you have an unprecedented variety of options laid out before the British electorate.
And all this despite the first past the post (FPTP) electoral system, which has for so long upheld two-party politics. It does so by punishing any party outside the duopoly by refusing to match votes to seats. If this unprecedented level of fragmentation exists in the face of a voting system that coerces people to back only their least bad option, then how diverse would this landscape be if people could vote with their heart and know that their vote really counted?
This now complete mismatch between what voters want and what they get is the root cause of the governing crisis destabilising British politics. Labour won two-thirds of the seats in the Commons in 2024 on just a third of the vote, and its leadership assumed that this result conferred it legitimacy in the eyes of the public. But governments increasingly find that a Commons majority upheld by an unrepresentative voting system is more vulnerable to voter backlash. In this context, support quickly melts away, as Keir Starmer and Morgan McSweeney found out.
If Britain continues under FPTP, then this governing chaos will deepen, and the only beneficiaries will be anti-democratic extremists.
But now there is a golden chance to change all this. Next Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament for its final stages. An amendment has been tabled to set up a national commission to look at which system of proportional representation (PR), which does match votes to seats, would best suit our country. It has huge backing in the Commons, in the Labour party and among the public. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is also a longstanding supporter of electoral reform. The political conditions have never been more favourable to begin making changes to the voting system. What could possibly go wrong?
This: a minority but powerful view within the upper reaches of the Labour party, the cabinet and the party bureaucracy is vehemently opposed to PR and the plural politics of cooperation it demands. According to this tribal view, only Labour, governing alone, can represent the interests of “their voters”. And so it is preferable to lose all power than to share it. Labour winning – however tiny its share of the vote – is more important than democracy working. At best, those with this view may calculate whether PR or FPTP delivers the most Labour MPs, equating self-interest with the national interest.
But all their paternalistic calculations miss the very big point: democracy should not be designed around what is best for Labour – or any party – but around what works best for the country.
Labour’s rearguard reactionaries will try to block the idea of a national commission, water it down or kick it bureaucratically into touch. They will say only the cost of living matters, and that no one brings up PR on the doorstep. But it is precisely our rotten voting system that denies the changes people want, because it prioritises the cautious views of a few swing voters in a few swing seats and impels Labour to pander to them.
The game is over for this old top-down, command-and-control politics. The myth of strong government from FPTP is dead. It is time for change, to do what Willy Brandt, the fabled leader of the German Social Democrats, implored the left to do in 1969, and “dare more democracy”. That means finally embracing multiparty government, and ensuring everyone’s vote is counted equally: it is the only way to end the cycle of chaos.
Radical Manchesterism beats in our prime minister’s heart. There, he made big changes happen by listening to voices beyond Labour and working cross-party to build a long-term consensus to transform a region. Next week, by backing himself and his best instincts on PR, he can transform the country.
- 
  Neal Lawson is director of the cross-party campaign organisation Compass

How valid are U.S. commitments under Trump?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:09 UTC
00:00:09 KST

How valid are U.S. commitments under Trump?
TEHRAN - Under Trump, America’s agreements increasingly appear conditional, reversible, and vulnerable to sudden policy shifts, raising fundamental questions about the credibility of U.S. commitments.
Chas Freeman, former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia and former assistant secretary of defense, said: “We’ve convinced the entire world that we don’t know what we’re doing, and we can’t be trusted, and we don’t keep our word, and we don’t even stay consistent from one day to the next. So how can you deal with us? That’s the question everybody has out there.”
American duplicity and betrayal intensified following the conclusion of the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed on June 17, 2026, by Trump at the Palace of Versailles.
Pakistan, with the assistance of several regional countries, mediated the agreement. It was described as an initial accord intended to pave the way toward a broader, final agreement. The memorandum contained 14 provisions setting out the terms for an immediate ceasefire and mechanisms for negotiating a lasting peace.
Trump quickly reneged on his commitment to the memorandum. John Mearsheimer, professor of political science at the University of Chicago, said in July 2026 that, from Iran’s perspective, the United States had failed to honor its commitments under the agreement.
“When we look at what is happening from the Iranian perspective… the Iranians [rightly] believe that the United States has failed to honor its commitments under the agreement,” he pointed out.
The Strait of Hormuz and oil-export waivers
Iran had several reasonable grounds for accusing Trump of failing to comply with the agreement. Provision 5 addressed what had replaced enriched uranium as a central focus of the illegal war: Iran’s position on shipping through the economically vital Strait of Hormuz.
The provision was understood to mean that Iran would lift its blockade while continuing to oversee and direct maritime traffic. When Iran took control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026, it replaced the pre-war shipping route, which ran through the middle of the strait, with another route directing vessels along its own coastline.
After the memorandum was signed, however, the Trump administration began directing ships onto a different route through Omani territorial waters. Following the ceasefire, there were three routes: one along the Omani coast, the central route used before the war, and one along the Iranian coast.
“We violated [the memorandum] by creating a southern corridor,” said retired U.S. Army Colonel Daniel Davis, host of the Deep Dive podcast, which focuses on geopolitical issues.
“There is nothing in the memorandum we signed that authorizes the creation of a southern corridor, or allows the United States to enter it and unilaterally determine how it should operate. It simply is not there in the memorandum.”
Davis, who returned from Afghanistan and exposed in 2012 how civilian and military officials had misled the public about the course of the war there, said the U.S. move in the Hormuz Strait was a deliberate provocation.
According to American writer Brian McGlinchey, author of the Stark Realities blog, whether intentional or not, it was indeed a provocation by the United States.
After issuing radio warnings to vessels attempting to use the southern route, Iran fired disabling projectiles at them. Trump then resumed his bombing campaign against Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate against U.S. forces and the countries hosting them. The Iranian armed forces subsequently began a prolonged cycle of retaliatory strikes.
Then there is Provision 10 of the memorandum, under which the Trump administration promised to issue sanctions waivers allowing Iranian oil and petroleum products to be exported without restrictions. Trump revoked the waivers on July 7, citing Iranian attacks on vessels that had failed to comply with its control over the Strait of Hormuz, a control that the United States had implicitly accepted under Provision 5.
Legitimizing Israeli occupation of Lebanon
Given its enormous importance to Iran, Provision 1 of the memorandum called for “the immediate and permanent cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon.” The provision did not specifically focus on Iran and the United States, but rather on their allies: Hezbollah, aligned with Iran, and Israel, America's staunchest ally in the world.
Nevertheless, the Zionist regime continued its aggression and the wholesale destruction of civilian infrastructure in southern Lebanon, on a scale comparable to what the regime's occupation forces had done in Gaza.
Some might argue that the United States was not in a position to impose the memorandum’s provisions on Israel. Even if that were true, Trump should not have signed a memorandum implicitly committing him to do so.
The Trump administration went a step further, taking measures to legitimize the Israeli regime's occupation of Lebanon.
“The memorandum stipulated that the Israelis had to leave Lebanon. We made no effort to achieve that. On the contrary, Marco Rubio mediated an agreement between the Lebanese government and Israel to jointly attack Hezbollah. What is that, then? At the very least, it was an unwise course of action,” Freeman pointed out.
More importantly, Trump’s conduct strengthens the credibility of the Iranian government and armed forces, who have long argued that Washington cannot be trusted and that negotiations should be backed up by military readiness.
The Saudi-U.S. nuclear deal
Trump’s repudiation of agreements has not been limited to adversaries of the United States who have been hit by his sudden reversals of terms he himself had accepted. Take Saudi Arabia for example.
On July 22, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, signed an agreement allowing the kingdom to build nuclear reactors and enrich uranium using American technology.
Both governments issued official statements, and the agreement was hailed as a victory for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The very next morning, Trump stunned, indeed, blindsided, the Saudis and his own officials with a social-media post adding a major condition retroactively: there would be no nuclear agreement unless Saudi Arabia joined the “Abraham Accords,” which entail recognizing the occupying regime's legitimacy and establishing formal diplomatic relations.
Trump’s demand that Saudi Arabia move closer to Israel comes at a time when Muslims in the kingdom and throughout the Islamic world are outraged by the regime's destruction of Gaza and southern Lebanon, making such a demand politically risky for the Saudi royal family.
Contrary to the agreement signed by his own energy secretary, Trump also suddenly announced that there would be no enrichment of nuclear material inside Saudi Arabia.
“Trump makes a deal, signs it, announces it, boasts about it, and within 24 hours radically changes its terms,” observed Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, on the Deep Dive podcast. “If this is what he will do to Saudi Arabia, a country with which the United States has extremely close relations… and with which the Trump family also has very close business ties, what will he do to Iran? How long is any U.S. commitment to Iran under Trump actually valid under any agreement?”
More recently, Ambassador Freeman told Colonel Davis: “We have convinced the entire world that we do not know what we are doing, that we cannot be trusted, that we do not keep our promises, and that we do not even maintain a consistent position from one day to the next. So how can anyone deal with us? That is the question everyone is asking.”
Alastair Crooke, a former British intelligence officer and diplomat, believes that American diplomacy may never return to what it was.
Summarizing the impact of Trump’s multi-front assault on confidence in the United States, Crooke said on Norwegian academic Glenn Diesen’s podcast: "I think the U.S. capacity to negotiate in the traditional diplomatic sense is over. I mean, we are in a new era!"

Early Leavers – Pension Rights Notice
A world class pension scheme for your military service
When a member of the armed forces reaches their retirement age, they receive one of the most generous pensions available in the UK. This fairly reflects the unique sacrifice they have provided their country throughout their career.
All members of the armed forces are automatically enrolled into the Armed Forces Pension Scheme. Unlike all other public schemes, members pay 0% in contributions each month. The scheme is unfunded and paid from the public purse.

Transfers in and out of the schemes
If you have built up pension benefits elsewhere before joining the armed forces you have the option to transfer in the value of your other benefits to receive a service credit in your Armed Forces Pension Scheme.
Before you apply to DBS Veterans UK for a transfer in, you need to obtain details of the amount of your transfer value from your previous pension scheme, and then an estimate from DBS Veterans UK of the additional pension that this will buy. If you decide to go ahead with the transfer, you should make your application to DBS Veterans UK in writing.
You must be serving in the armed forces to be eligible to transfer in and once you have committed yourself to a transfer from your previous pension scheme, you cannot change your mind and you will have given up forever your rights and those of your dependants under the previous schemes.
Transfers into AFPS 15 must be completed within one year of joining the scheme. For members who remain solely in AFPS 75 and AFPS 05 who may still make transfers in from a non-public service scheme. AFSP 75 the transfer in must be made before your 54 birthday and in AFPS 05 the transfer in must be made before the beginning of your final year of service before your pension is due.
If you leave without receiving immediate pension benefits (including leaving with an Early Departure Payment (EDP) under AFPS 15 or AFPS 05) you have the option to transfer the value of your deferred pension benefits to other defined benefit schemes. A pension in payment cannot be transferred.
However, the government has prevented transfers from unfunded public service defined benefit schemes (such as the AFPS to funded defined contribution schemes in UK or abroad. The Pension Schemes Act 2015 and the Taxation of Pensions Act 2014 made this rule. Application for pension transfers should be made to:
DBS Veterans UK Pensions Division
Mail Point 480
Kentigern House
65 Brown Street
Glasgow
G2 8EX
Resettlement Grant
Resettlement Grants assist those leaving the regular armed forces to resettle into civilian life after completing a substantial period of service. A Resettlement Grant is not a pension.
It is a tax-free lump sum paid to regular service personnel, who, at the time they leave the services, are not eligible for Early Departure Payment benefits, an Immediate Pension or ill health award (or any other immediate pension benefits) and they meet Resettlement Grant qualification criteria, which are:
- 
    AFPS 2015 and AFPS 2005: all personnel need to have 12 years’ relevant service (from date of entry)
- 
    AFPS 1975: Officers to have at least 2 years’ Commissioned service and have 9 relevant years of reckonable service from age 21
- 
    AFPS 1975: other ranks to have 12 relevant years of reckonable service from age 18.
The value of the Resettlement Grant at April 2025 is:
- AFPS 2005 and AFPS 2015: £14,059
- AFPS 1975: £20,397 (Officer) and £14,058 (Other Rank)
Please see the latest tri-service codes published each year on gov.uk.
The Resettlement Grant is increased each year at the same rate as armed forces pensionable pay.
Only 1 resettlement grant is awarded, for those who have service in more than one scheme. If personnel are re-employed after leaving they may have to re-pay some or all of the grant. See the re-employment booklet for more details.

Once upon a time, insects had 24 legs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Once upon a time, insects had 24 legs
This ancient oddball fills a major gap in the fossil record
Insects are famous for their six-legged body plan, but that wasn’t always the rule. A 324-million-year-old fossil dug up from a shale bed in West Texas had a markedly different setup, sporting a whopping 18 extra legs along its belly — a body plan unlike that of any living insect.
It is one of the oddest insects ever found, and possibly the most consequential, researchers report August 26 in Nature.
The discovery “straddles a big gap in the fossil record,” says paleoentomologist Erik Tihelka of the University of Cambridge. It offers a glimpse of the transition from many-legged, shrimplike ancestors to the six-legged insects of today. “It shows that there were these transitional forms along the way,” he says, before insects shed their extra legs and settled on six.
Tihelka and his team named the fossil Chosha praecursor. It is inspired by the Navajo creation myth, in which a primordial world was inhabited by insectlike people whose descendants went on to populate Earth, combining the Navajo word for “insect” (ch’osh) with the Latin for “predecessor.”
For decades, however, the fossil bore a different name. Collected from a rocky outcrop north of Big Bend National Park in 1985, the specimen was initially mistaken for a juvenile of a crustacean called Tesnusocaris goldichi, found in the same dark shale. Researchers saw little significance in the find, and it languished in a museum drawer in San Diego for years.
Then Tihelka spotted a line drawing of the fossil in a Russian paleontology textbook he had bought secondhand. He tracked down the original papers, but the specimen’s supposed identity as a crustacean didn’t sit right with him. He traveled to the San Diego Museum of Natural History to see it for himself.
At first glance, the unassuming fossil resembled little more than a “black smudge,” Tihelka recalls. But by peering at it through polarized light filters, which cut the glare and sharpened contrast, he could make out a series of anatomical details that all pointed toward insects: a three-segmented thorax; an extended abdomen with 11 sections; whiplike antennae; a long central tail flanked by two shorter ones; a stiff tube for laying eggs; and, of course, three pairs of walking legs.
There was just one, tiny hangup. The Chosha fossil had nine extra pairs of short, stubby legs on its abdomen, the rear ones ending in flattened, grooved paddles. These paddles may have helped the insects swim or scuttle through muddy shallow seas.
What struck Tihelka was that he had seen other fossils like it, including a 405-million-year-old specimen from Scotland and an undescribed pair of multi-legged, insectlike fossils from the Mazon Creek beds of Illinois.
Comparing the bodies of these ancient oddballs with known insects and crustaceans, both living and extinct, more closely, Tihelka could see that Chosha and the other fossils all landed same place. They all sat just outside the group containing every insect alive today, with crustaceans a distant branch away.
The picture that emerges, then, is of Chosha and its many-legged kin, with their extra limbs and paddlelike appendages, living semi-aquatic lifestyles. Somewhere along the way, one such protoinsect presumably made the leap onto land full-time, shedding the surplus legs until only six remained. That terrestrial ancestor then gave rise to the millions of insect species on Earth today.
“It’s a funny thing,” Tihelka says. “We call insects ‘hexapods,’ meaning six legs. But it turns out that the original ones had many more.”
For all its strangeness, though, Chosha may offer a surprisingly straightforward explanation for how insects made the leap from water to land. “This fossil is a major milestone in a puzzling period when everything was changing from mostly aquatic to terrestrial, and we had almost no fossil evidence from that time,” says Dany Azar, a paleoentomologist at Lebanese University in Fanar and the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology in China.
“It opens a lot of doors to the study of insect evolution,” says William Shear, a retired paleobiologist from Hampden-Sydney College in Virginia. “And one can only hope that more fossils of this particular organism will turn up upon further searching.”

Restricted postal voting, US-Canada trade war, and thoughts of a Nobel scientist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Restricted postal voting, US-Canada trade war, and thoughts of a Nobel scientist
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
On the day Dolly Parton was celebrating her 28th birthday – perhaps raising a glass to Jolene, which was shooting up the charts – across the Atlantic in London a future Swissinfo journalist was born. But beyond sharing a birthday, Dolly and I have very little in common. The musician, actor and philanthropist “rewrote the American dream”, said one Swiss newspaper on Tuesday, after her death aged 80. “She could unite the whole of America,” said another.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
The Supreme Court has ruled that US President Donald Trump can press ahead with his plans to restrict postal voting. “Fears of chaos are mounting,” according to one Swiss newspaper.
“In around two months, the mid-term elections for Congress will take place in the United States, and the country […] is arguing over the rules,” the Tages-Anzeiger wrote on Tuesday. “In March, Donald Trump issued new ones.” The Zurich paper explained that, by executive order, Trump had decreed that the Post Office may send out postal ballot papers only to people listed on the electoral register. These registers would be compiled by the federal authorities.
“Trump cited the desire to make the elections more secure as his reason,” the newspaper said. “Since his defeat by Joe Biden, he’s been talking about ‘electoral fraud’. He claims that, in the past, large numbers of foreign nationals took part in elections and distorted the result. This has only been proven in isolated cases. There is no evidence to suggest that ineligible voters have taken part in elections in large numbers.”
According to the Tages-Anzeiger, Trump’s opponents view his efforts to restrict postal voting and take control of elections in the states as an attempt to influence the result. “The Democratic base votes by post more frequently than the Republican base,” it said.
On Tuesday Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported that a coalition of 23 predominantly Democrat-governed states and the capital, Washington, D.C., had filed a lawsuit against this. “They argue that, under the Constitution, the states are responsible for the rules governing voter eligibility. A federal judge in Boston ruled in their favour in June. She concluded that Trump did not have the authority to alter the organisation of federal elections in this way,” it wrote. “The states also warned that changing the rules shortly before the elections could result in many people being unable to exercise their right to vote.”
On Monday the Supreme Court’s conservative majority didn’t decide the legality of Trump’s order – it ruled that states who sued did not have the legal right to challenge it.
The Tages-Anzeiger concluded by pointing out that civil rights organisations fear the government will station agents from the immigration agency ICE outside polling stations to intimidate US citizens of migrant background and deter them from voting. “Hardly anyone expects the elections to go off without a hitch – and certainly not that Trump will accept the result without complaint, whatever the outcome.”
“Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney isn’t crazy,” the Tages-Anzeiger diagnosed on Monday. “He’s doing the right thing” by standing up to Donald Trump in the escalating trade war, it said, adding that this could be a solution for other countries, too.
On Monday the Wall Street Journal reckoned Carney was “crazy as a loon if he thinks his country will prosper by distancing itself from the US”. The Tages-Anzeiger responded that Carney did indeed take a risk when he rejected the US’s terms for a deal and announced retaliatory tariffs in no uncertain terms. “The US can inflict more damage on Canada than vice versa. This applies to most countries and is the basis on which Donald Trump blackmails the world,” it said.
But the US President has been “particularly brazen” in his dealings with Canada, it said. “Since the start of his second term, he has been saying he wants to annex the country. Carney is doing something that not everyone in his position would do: he is standing up to the superpower.”
According to polls, two-thirds of Canadians support a tough stance towards the US, the Tages-Anzeiger continued. “Americans who have spent their summer holidays in Canada say they are impressed by how consistently and cheerfully US products are being boycotted there,” it said.
“Sometimes it’s not the stronger party that wins, but the more determined one. What’s more, Trump’s second term in office has so far shown that swallowing his terms is no guarantee of peace. So Carney is not crazy. He’s demonstrating to the world an alternative way of dealing with Trump.”
The Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ) believed Trump’s hardline approach had left Carney no choice: Canada would rather suffer than capitulate, it wrote on Monday, with Carney preferring no deal with Washington than a bad one. “In doing so, he is taking major economic risks. But as the leader of the resistance against Trump, he has no other political option,” it said.
The NZZ noted that Canada exports around 70% of its goods to the United States, whereas the US sends only about 15% of its exports to Canada. Carney said Canada had been prepared to abandon its retaliatory tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars if the US were to “substantially” reduce its import duties of up to 50% in these sectors. However, Canada was not prepared to compromise “its sovereignty” or “the protection of the French language”. According to Carney, Washington had demanded, among other things, that his government curtail state support for the French language in Quebec. Carney therefore instructed his negotiators to walk away from trade talks last week.
“Other countries, including Switzerland, are likely to be watching closely to see what happens next,” the Tages-Anzeiger concluded. “At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Carney said in a widely noted speech that the US was no longer a guarantor of stability. Middle powers would have to join forces in order to survive. Now would be a good time to do so.”
It’s likely that China will overtake the United States in certain fields of science, believes Swiss Nobel laureate Kurt Wüthrich in an interview with the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).
Wüthrich, 87, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002 for his groundbreaking work on determining the structure of proteins using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. For many years, he conducted his research in parallel in Zurich and at Scripps Research in California. Since 2013, he has also maintained his own research group at Shanghai Tech University in China.
“In biomedical research, China is closing the gap on the US and other countries,” Wüthrich told the NZZ on Sunday. “But they have also made quite astonishing progress in industry, for example in cancer treatment. There are new cancer drugs from China that are right up there with the best. The biggest problem at the moment is that Chinese companies are testing drugs on Chinese patient groups. The next step will be for them to also use test groups from non-Chinese populations for drug trials.”
The NZZ pointed out that, according to the Nature Index, a ranking compiled by scientific publisher Springer Nature, China is already a world leader in many specialist fields. Eight of the top ten universities in the ranking are Chinese. Has China already overtaken the US?
“I would put that into perspective, as this index only takes into account research published in the Nature journals,” Wüthrich replied. “Furthermore, these journals earn a great deal of money from advertising from China. But it is true that China is already on a par with the US in fields such as materials science. In chemistry, China is actually ahead of the US. And in biology and the life sciences, the country is catching up very quickly.”
The NZZ said that, according to an OECD report, in 2024 China spent more money on research and development than the US for the first time, when adjusted for purchasing power. Was China set to overtake the US as the leading scientific nation in the foreseeable future?
“I’m better suited to analysing historical facts than making predictions,” Wüthrich said. “But there’s now a new five-year plan in China for the years 2026 to 2030, and in this plan, funding for research and development has been dramatically increased. We’re talking about billions of dollars. However, the vast majority of these billions are being channelled into a handful of major projects. And it’s therefore likely that China will overtake the US in certain areas.”

Text description provided by the architects. Casa El Trébol stands on the highest point of the neighborhood of the same name in San Carlos de Bariloche, Río Negro, in Argentine Patagonia. Set within a dense native forest on a steep slope, the project does not stem from a pre-established form, but rather from the unavoidable experience of the site: an introspective ascent through a forest of coihues and pines that culminates in a flat area open to the landscape. The architecture translates this journey into a processional route seeking stillness at the summit. The house was conceived as a device that guides the gaze, capturing the best views of the forest and, ultimately, the open horizon of Laguna El Trébol.

Early trial of "common cold" vaccine candidate shows encouraging signs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:59:50 CST
23:59:50 KST

LONDON, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- A vaccine candidate designed to protect against rhinoviruses, which cause the great majority of common colds and exacerbate chronic respiratory illnesses, has shown encouraging early results in a Phase 1 clinical trial, Imperial College London said Wednesday.
Initial findings suggested that the candidate, known as APL-10456, was well tolerated in healthy volunteers and that a single dose generated immune responses against all three major rhinovirus species.
The vaccine was developed through a collaboration between Imperial and biopharmaceutical company Apollo Therapeutics, building on years of research led by Sebastian Johnston, a professor of respiratory medicine and allergy at Imperial's National Heart and Lung Institute.
Since 2017, Imperial researchers and Apollo have evaluated and refined different vaccine approaches. More than 20 preclinical studies conducted with contract research organization VirTus Respiratory Research Ltd helped identify the candidate and produced evidence supporting its progression to human testing.
Enrollment and dosing have been completed in the randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 1 trial involving 144 healthy participants, according to the university.
The first stage assessed the safety, tolerability and immune response of APL-10456 in healthy participants and evaluated three single-dose levels in adults aged between 18 and 54. The second stage is evaluating a two-dose regimen in adults aged 55 and above, with further data expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.
There are around 180 rhinovirus strains across three species -- A, B and C -- making them a difficult target for vaccine development. Although most infections cause a mild common cold, the viruses are a major cause of flare-ups in people with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. No targeted antiviral treatment or vaccine for rhinovirus infection has yet been approved.
"It is very encouraging to see this progress into clinical results, which follow years of research and development," Johnston said.
However, further clinical research is needed to determine whether APL-10456 can prevent rhinovirus infections or reduce illness in people with asthma, COPD and other respiratory conditions. A study involving COPD patients is anticipated to begin in the first half of 2027. ■

Why a Christian group is suing the Dutch government for West Bank trade ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:59:22 UTC
23:59:22 KST

Why a Christian group is suing the Dutch government for West Bank trade ban
The Israeli Product Centre says it has not been given enough time to sell off its stock of wine from illegal Israeli settlements.
Dutch group Christians for Israel is taking the government to court in the Netherlands over its plans to introduce a ban on importing goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and Golan Heights.
The ban, which was announced in July, is due to take effect on September 22 and will run for three years. It bars importing, buying and selling goods produced in Israeli settlements, as well as intermediary services and any attempt to circumvent the rules.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli forces raid UNRWA training centre in occupied East Jerusalem
- list 2 of 3How Israel’s Netanyahu weaponises religion in his war rhetoric
- list 3 of 3US lawmakers urge Trump team to free American student held by Israel
But the Israel Product Centre (IPC), part of Christians for Israel (CvI), a Dutch evangelical organisation which a recent study found has donated about $300,000 to illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, has responded by filing summary proceedings against the state, with the hearing due today.
Here’s what we know about this case.
What is the case about?
The IPC has issued summary proceedings against the Dutch state, seeking to block the July decree.
The IPC argues the measure is “one-sided” and that the window it now has to clear its existing stock – some 20,000 bottles of wine – is too short.
It is also arguing that a national ban conflicts with the European Union’s principle of free movement of goods.
A verdict is not expected for about two weeks.
How has this case come about?
EU rules have long required goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank to be labelled by their origin – Palestine – rather than as “product of Israel”, but the bloc has not placed an outright ban on trading with Israeli settlements. That remains up to individual countries.
In February 2020, the Dutch advocacy group DocP urged consumers to file complaints with the Dutch food safety authority, NVWA, if they found wine and Dead Sea cosmetics had been mislabelled.
Following complaints, the IPC changed its labelling to “product uit een Israelisch dorp in Judea & Samaria [product from an Israeli village in Judea and Samaria],” which it argued accurately reflected the exact geographical and administrative reality of the origins of the products without deceiving the buyer. Judea and Samaria is the biblical name used by the Israeli government to refer to the West Bank. DocP argued this fell short of the requirement to label products correctly, and continued its campaign.
In 2021, the NVWA agreed and fined the IPC 2,100 euros (about $2,500) for mislabelling goods.
Then, in July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued an advisory opinion that Israel’s presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful and must end “as rapidly as possible”.
This shifted the legal argument beyond mere consumer labelling, with the court saying countries should take steps to prevent trade or investment relations which help to maintain the unlawful presence of Israeli settlers in the Palestinian territories.
The lower house of the Dutch parliament acted on that in September 2025, proposing an import ban.
The national decree against importing goods from Israeli settlements was made in July this year.
Does Christians for Israel describe the West Bank as ‘Israel’?
CvI describes the West Bank as a “disputed territory” rather than accepting the international legal description of it as “occupied Palestinian territory”.
It says it believes that Israel has strong claims to sovereignty there and that Jews have a right to live there.
The vocabulary matters in a legal sense, as “disputed territory” is not the same as “annexed territory”, therefore, the legal apparatus which would make settlement trade unlawful doesn’t straightforwardly apply.
The group’s stated reasons for funding projects there, it says on its website, are rooted in the Bible; it cites Ezekiel 47:21-23: “Peace for the Jewish people and resident foreigners inheriting alongside the tribes of Israel.”
However, the ICJ’s July 2024 advisory opinion is clear that the Fourth Geneva Convention’s Article 49(6) and successive Security Council resolutions treat the territories as occupied and the settlements as unlawful.
How have other Christian organisations in the West responded to trade with settlements?
Western churches are split on the issue, with CvI sitting at one end of the spectrum.
Mainline Protestants, including the Presbyterian Church in the United States, have divested shareholdings in Caterpillar, HP and Motorola Solutions as early as 2014, and from Israeli bonds in 2024. The United Methodist Church has opposed Israeli settlements since 1996 and sold its Israeli bond holdings last August.
The World Council of Churches called for sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in 2025, divestment and an arms embargo.
The Vatican calls settlements an obstacle to peace but has avoided divestment so far.
Christian Zionist bodies, however, including Christians United for Israel (CUFI) and the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, send funding for settlements and fight against boycotts.
How significant is this ban?
It is significant considering that the Netherlands is one of only four EU countries currently imposing a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.
Trade from illegal settlements to the EU is estimated to be worth up to $400m per year.
The Netherlands is also a big market for the illegal settlements; a recent investigation by legal advocacy group Global Echo, which analysed thousands of shipments from Israeli settlements between 2017 and 2026, shows that within the EU, the Dutch market is the largest importer of goods from illegal settlements, with about 30 percent destined for or passing through the country.
Which European countries have banned products from West Bank settlements?
Spain has banned all imports of products from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, since September 2025. The decree also enforces an embargo on defence exports and dual-use technology to Israel, bans ships carrying military fuel for Israel from Spanish ports, and restricts advertising for services or goods linked to Israeli settlements.
Ireland’s parliament approved the text of its Israeli Settlements (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill in May and the bill was signed into law in July. It covers all goods produced in Israeli settlements, but excludes services.
Belgium’s federal government approved a draft royal decree in July introducing a specific regime for goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. The precise details of the new law will be determined by the government in due course.
Slovenia imposed restrictions on imports from Israeli settlements under its previous government, but the new conservative government reversed them in June 2026.
The EU as a bloc remains deadlocked over whether a ban counts as foreign policy requiring unanimity or trade policy needing only a qualified majority, with ministers not meeting again in a decision-making format until October.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar last year described the push by some European governments to implement the ICJ advisory opinion as “shameful”.
Which European countries still allow trade with West Bank settlements?
Nearly all of them.
Outside the three European Union states which still have bans in place, settlement goods can be sold legally everywhere, including in most of the EU.
At a July 2026 meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, which addressed trade from Israeli settlements in Palestinian territories, Germany, Austria, Czechia and Hungary were opposed to an EU-wide ban.
Beyond the EU, the United Kingdom does not forbid trade with illegal Israeli settlements, although new Prime Minister Andy Burnham is reportedly considering a ban. In a recent parliamentary briefing, Amnesty International called on the UK government to implement a ban.
It said: “The argument for a UK ban on trade with settlements is clear. The UK government itself accepts it should take stronger action in response to settlement expansion and annexation. The International Court of Justice has directed states not to trade with Israel in relation to the Occupied Palestinian Territory; and there is precedent in UK law and policy to not trade with illegally occupied lands, ie Crimea and other illegally occupied parts of Ukraine.”

Latvia lands $233 million explosives plant near Russia’s border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:59:02 UTC
23:59:02 KST

- Wolfram Europa plans a $233 million explosives and warhead complex near Jēkabpils, Latvia, close to Russia's border, with construction starting in 2027.
- At full capacity, the site aims to produce 200,000 warheads and 100,000 anti-tank mines a year to help close Europe's explosives supply gap.
A European company plans to build a $233 million explosives and warhead factory in Latvia, a NATO ally that sits just 175 miles (280 km) from Russia’s border, in a project aimed at closing a supply gap that has left Europe dependent on outside sources for the raw materials behind its weapons.
Wolfram Europa announced the €200 million ($233 million) project Wednesday at an event in Jēkabpils, a city in eastern Latvia. The company plans a 40-hectare (99-acre) site, secured under a long-term land agreement with Latvijas Valsts Meži, the Latvian state forestry company, with construction happening in three phases starting in 2027.
For American readers, the scale is easier to picture in terms of output. At full capacity, the plant is designed to make enough explosive material to fill 200,000 warheads and 100,000 anti-tank mines every year. It will also produce RDX and HMX, two explosive compounds used across NATO munitions, including artillery shells and missile warheads.
Wolfram Europa was registered in Latvia’s commercial register in January 2026 with initial capital of just $3,260, according to Latvian outlet Dzentlmenis.lv. The jump from a startup-sized registration to a $233 million industrial project happened in a matter of months.
The company describes itself as a European defense manufacturer building explosives, warheads and counter-mobility products, meaning items like anti-tank mines, without relying on long international supply chains. Once fully operational, the project is expected to create 200 jobs in the region.
Company officials say the plant is designed to meet NATO explosive safety standards and will be licensed under Latvian regulation. They describe it as a low-footprint, relocatable design meant to let production scale up or move if needed during a crisis.
The project has the backing of Latvia’s government. Latvian Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis, Minister of Smart Administration and Regional Development Edgars Tavars, Ministry of Defence State Secretary Airis Rikveilis, and Jēkabpils County Municipality Chairman Raivis Ragainis all attended the announcement alongside Wolfram Europa CEO Magnus-Valdemar Saar.
“Investments of this scale represent a significant step forward in the development of Latvia’s defence industry and, at the same time, demonstrate Latvia’s ability to attract strategically important industrial projects to its regions,” said Viktors Valainis, Minister of Economics.
For American readers less familiar with the issue, Europe’s explosives shortage has become a significant concern within NATO. Company officials point to a widening gap between Russia’s explosives output and Europe’s, arguing that European countries have spent billions on missiles, artillery shells and drones in recent years but have not scaled up the raw explosive material those weapons ultimately require.
“For the last 35 years, Europe has been scaling down its explosives and munitions industry, and technological development has stalled with it,” said Magnus-Valdemar Saar, CEO of Wolfram Europa. “Now Europe is rearming, but investment is still focused mainly on platforms and final assembly. That is the explosives gap: Europe is scaling its weapons faster than the explosives and warheads that make them effective.”
Saar said Latvia is meant to be the first of several sites Wolfram Europa builds across the continent.
“Jēkabpils will not serve Latvia alone. Latvia will host strategic production capacity for Europe. It will be our first major site, but not our last,” Saar said.
“The establishment of such a company strengthens the involvement of Latvia’s defence industry, promotes the development of technologies and expertise, and demonstrates Latvia’s ambition to become a significant regional hub for defence industry and technology development,” said Airis Rikveilis, State Secretary of the Ministry of Defence.
The Wolfram Europa project is one of several recent defense manufacturing investments in the Baltic region, an area U.S. policymakers watch closely given its proximity to Russia. Rheinmetall, the German defense contractor, signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Latvia’s government in March 2026 for an artillery shell factory, structured as a joint venture with Rheinmetall holding 51 percent and the Latvian State Defence Corporation holding 49 percent. That plant is expected to produce between 60,000 and 80,000 shells (155mm, or 6.1 inches, in caliber) a year once construction begins in spring 2027.
Rheinmetall has also signed a $350 million deal for a similar shell plant in neighboring Lithuania, which broke ground in November 2025 with a target of 100,000 shells a year by 2027.
“My task is to ensure that unnecessary bureaucracy does not stand in the way of this project and that the investment can flow into Jēkabpils,” said Edgars Tavars, Minister for Smart Administration and Regional Development.

More than 1 in 3 UK employers cut entry-level jobs amid rise in AI investment: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:58:59 UTC
23:58:59 KST

Burak Bir
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
More than one in three UK employers have reduced the number of entry-level jobs available to young people aged 16-24 over the past year, according to a new report released Wednesday.
An analysis of a Survation survey of 1,001 senior UK business leaders, commissioned by the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, found that 36% had reduced entry-level jobs for young people over the past 12 months.
Almost half of medium-sized (48%) and large employers (46%) reported cuts, compared with 24% of small employers, according to the study.
Meanwhile, nearly three-quarters (73%) said the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET) was a “national crisis,” while 76% said employers had a responsibility to do more to support young people into work.
“Just over two in five employers (43%) report having invested in AI or automation that has reduced the number of entry-level roles available, rising to 60% among large employers.”
Following the findings, researchers called on the government to press ahead with reforms aimed at making work more secure, create additional good-quality jobs and provide practical, local support to employers to help them hire, particularly smaller firms.
The survey also found that just over two in five employers (44%) had used AI or automated systems to screen applications, while 43% said investment in AI or automation had reduced the number of entry-level roles.
“Young people are entering one of the toughest labour markets in years, facing intense competition for a shrinking number of entry-level jobs and fewer opportunities to get a secure foothold in work,” said Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University.
Harrison warned that the challenge was not simply about providing young people with more employment support, but also about the decline in available opportunities, particularly for those living in weaker local labor markets where options are more limited.

Ireland keeps nuclear door open as data centre energy demand surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:57:05 UTC
23:57:05 KST

The power-hungry AI revolution is driving Dublin toward a historic decision on nuclear power after decades of opposition and a legal ban.
Ireland is keeping the door open to nuclear power as a potential answer to the growing energy demand from data centres, even as the government insists its immediate energy strategy will remain firmly focused on renewables, an Irish government official told Euronews.
"There is a need to consider all options (with decarbonising potential) in the long-term," a spokesperson for the Irish Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment said.
Political talks about the future of data centres are heating up in Dublin, the Silicon Valley of Europe. According to the country's Central Statistics Office, data centres consume roughly 21% to 22% of Ireland's total electricity, a figure projected to rise toward 31% by the early 2030s with the massive surge of artificial intelligence models.
Ireland has never produced nuclear power and officially banned domestic nuclear generation by law in 1999, citing an international record of nuclear accidents.
The government maintains that Ireland should prioritise technologies that can deliver quickly, including onshore wind, solar, battery storage and interconnectors, as well as the country’s first offshore wind projects.
But Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin hinted in May at a new "openness" on turning to nuclear, shortly before urging the Irish people to stop the "demonisation of data centres".
Data centres in the EU consumed an estimated 70TWh of electricity in 2024 and are projected to reach 115 TWh by 2030, enough to power roughly 32.9 million European homes for an entire year.
A long road ahead
Nonetheless, Dublin acknowledges that conventional nuclear power plants would take years to develop, and wouldn't be a quick fix for the growing demand from data centres expected in the future.
Moreover, investment in nuclear would require Ireland to build an entirely new regulatory system covering everything from construction and operation to decommissioning and radioactive waste.
According to the government official, "nuclear power could not practically be part of our electricity system until at least the 2040s". Nonetheless, Dublin is increasingly signalling that it does not want to rule it out beyond that point.
According to the government spokesperson, a technical study is examining 30 technologies capable of helping decarbonise the electricity system, including nuclear.
The assessment will compare technologies on cost, readiness, deployment times and public acceptance. The decision would also help Ireland lower electricity prices, currently the highest in the EU, followed by Cyprus.
Revoking the ban
However, the biggest immediate hurdle to unleashing nuclear power in Ireland is legal. But in May, Fianna Fáil legislator James O'Connor introduced a bill to legalise nuclear energy, inaugurating a new debate on the matter.
And on 2 June, the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism & Employment, Fine Gael's Peter Burke, presented an economic study showing that the data centre sector in Ireland generates €2.2 billion in economic activity annually and supports 19,500 jobs.
The Irish government coalition hailed the report as proof that the data centre sector plays a critical role in driving economic activity in Ireland.
“The report highlights that the continued development of data centre capacity must be aligned with Ireland’s economic, energy and climate objectives," Burke said. "Through our new Large Energy User Plan, all new data centres must provide their own energy generation onsite or nearby, 80% of which must be from renewable sources."
Tom Parlon, chair of the Irish Data Centre Supplier Alliance, welcomed the economic study, saying it provides "clear evidence" of the scale of economic activity the data centre sector can deliver in Ireland.
"We routinely hear claims that the data centre sector creates no jobs and provides little benefit to the Irish economy, yet this report shows these claims couldn’t be further from the truth," Parlon said.
Economic prosperity vs environmental degradation
But data centres aren't viewed so positively by the general public. Critics argue they use as much electricity as entire cities and require millions of litres of water a day just to stay cool. In many cases, water is pulled straight from local communities, often already hit hard by drought.
A new EU law that would force data centres to reveal their true energy costs and push them to clean up their emissions is being challenged by Big Tech lobbyists. If unchallenged, the new data centre rating scheme is expected to apply from 15 August 2027, with the first sustainability labels generated.
Worried about the environmental impact, green groups are urging Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen to stop data centres' rapid expansion ahead of a final decision between the EU co-legislators due by the end of the year.
Commenting on the growing debate about the possibility of building a nuclear power plant in Ireland, Oisín Coghlan, policy adviser to the Irish Environmental Network, derided the Irish premier's recent words on nuclear as "vice signalling".
"From his St Patrick’s day trips to the US he knows the Trump administration is very keen on AI," Coghlan told Euronews. "Taoiseach Micheál Martin is making it clear that his Government will do whatever it takes to power US tech data centres, not just with the ‘windmills’ that Trump hates, but with macho nuclear too. Even if it takes too long, costs too much and isn’t needed."
Scott Lane, founder and CEO of Speeki, an independent environmental, sustainability and governance assurance firm, said that despite the environmental risks, data centres are a "necessity" for the future of the world's economies despite their "massive impact" on the environment and the question of where they can be built fairly.
"Rather than fighting a foregone conclusion, the onus must now be on policymakers and ESG leaders to mitigate, and wherever possible turn positive, the environmental impact of these centres," Lane told Euronews.
"That might be through tougher due diligence on operators and third-party providers when it comes to how they interact with and impact local communities, or it might look like fast-tracking renewable energy solutions and responsible water-cooling systems. If data centre providers cannot evidence that they are making progress on these fronts, businesses and their Chief Sustainability Officers must walk away."

EU must agree on long-term budget by year-end to avoid funding disruption: Council president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:57:00 UTC
23:57:00 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
The EU must agree on its next long-term budget by the end of this year to prevent funding disruptions in 2028, European Council President Antonio Costa said Wednesday.
Speaking in Vilnius after meeting Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, Costa described negotiations on the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget as a “decisive challenge” for this autumn.
“To ensure that there is no interruption in the European Union funding for farmers, our businesses, our students, and other recipients in 2028, we need to reach an agreement by the end of this year,” he said.
Costa said the budget should place competitiveness, industrial transformation, defense, security and strategic resilience at its core while continuing to support cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy.
Balancing traditional priorities with emerging challenges will require a significantly different budget structure, he said, adding that new EU revenue streams will be essential to reaching an overall agreement.
Costa visited Lithuania on the second day of a four-week tour of EU capitals aimed at consulting national leaders ahead of European Council meetings and assessing their willingness to compromise on the budget.
The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, EU enlargement, threats on Europe’s eastern flank and Lithuania’s preparations to assume the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU in January 2027.
Costa praised Lithuania’s military support for Kyiv and said the EU would continue increasing pressure on Moscow until Russia entered negotiations “in good faith.”
He also called the accession processes of Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans “the best investment” Europe could make in the continent’s future peace, security and stability.

Basketball star Henri Drell to be 'man in the mask' in Hungary qualifier
National team basketball forward Henri Drell is having to don a mask during this week's FIBA World Cup qualifier away to Hungary, following an injury.
Estonia's basketball team arrived in Miskolc, Hungary, on Tuesday ahead of tomorrow's game.
Drell (Neptūnas Klaipėda) had an excellent game in a recent friendly against Lithuania, but then took a blow to the nose against Italy. He will be able to play, but will have to wear a mask. "Nothing else directly restricts him, his breathing is unobstructed and he can play. After the window, the relevant specialists can deal with it further," team doctor Kaido Stroom said. "It will certainly cause some discomfort, but Henri is very professional in that regard. It doesn't directly limit his playing minutes; that's up to [team coach] Heiko [Rannula] to decide."
Guard Martin Paasoja will however miss the game, as he is recovering from an upper respiratory tract infection, Stroom said.
Kasper Suurorg, another guard, fell awkwardly during training and knocked his elbow on his non-shooting hand, so will miss the Hungary game.
Beyond that, the team will take the traveling to and fro between Estonia and Hungary in their stride, Stroom added.
The national team reached the second phase of the qualifying campaign with a record of 3:3, the same as other group L teams Slovenia, Hungary and Sweden. After playing Hungary, Estonia faces Finland at the Unibet Arena on Sunday.
Both the Hungary and Finland games can be watched live via ERR's Sport portal.
