Is Toilet Paper Bad For You? Here’s What Experts Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:41:06 UTC
23:41:06 KST

Toilet paper has become a hot topic online. You don’t have to look hard to find videos of health-conscious influencers warning about supposedly harmful ingredients in toilet paper. But how concerned should you be?
Not very, most experts agree. But some also say that TP is worth examining more closely.
Concerning chemicals
Studies have found some concerning chemicals in toilet paper. A 2023 study looking for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in toilet paper found them in 21 brands from around the world. Also known as “forever chemicals,” PFAS exposure has been linked to reproductive issues in women, developmental delays in kids, an increased risk of some cancers, and more. A 2019 study in Ghana found “elevated levels” of phthalates, which are endocrine disruptors that may cause developmental and reproductive harm, in toilet paper. That research also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), which are associated with cancer, and semi-volatile chlorinated organic compounds, which have also been connected to cancer and reproductive harm, in toilet paper.
Some research cautions against toilet paper made from recycled paper because it could be made with discarded newspapers or recycled cash-register receipts, which can contaminate the product with BPA, a substance linked to reproductive issues, cardiovascular disease, and more.
There have also been concerns over toilet paper that is bleached, as bleaching can create dioxins, and concerns over toilet paper that includes formaldehyde, a carcinogen.
The ingredients in toilet paper, which manufacturers aren’t required to disclose, are potentially concerning because the skin on the genitalia and anus is thinner and more absorbent than other skin on the body, says Dr. Julia Saylors, an oncologist and integrative medicine physician based in Charleston, South Carolina.
While skin is known to absorb chemicals, including PFAS, genital and anal areas are made of mucosal surfaces, a type of thin, moist, and more sensitive skin that leads to the interior of the body. This skin is more absorbent than the surfaces on our arms and legs, says Saylors.
“It is well known that applying a medication to the vaginal mucosa results in a substantially higher absorption if the same medication is applied to the skin,” Saylors says. “Therefore, any potentially harmful chemical is best to avoid in that area.”
And while Saylors says that toilet paper probably isn’t a person’s highest exposure to toxins—food packaging, cleaning products, and textiles are more significant sources—she says that any changes we can make to reduce toxin exposure are potentially helpful.
Toilet paper does not pose a major risk
How toilet paper interacts with people’s skin in these areas and their overall health is not well studied. But the research that has been done suggests that toilet paper does not pose significant health risks, experts agree.
Dr. Amar Rewari, chief of radiation oncology at Luminis Health in Maryland, notes that PFAS and some other industrial chemicals are under study for possible long-term health effects, “but the levels typically found in consumer products like toilet paper are very small and not clearly linked to cancer.”
“Many of these chemicals, including PFAS, phthalates, BPA, and trace dioxins, can be found in small amounts throughout modern life,” he adds. “The highest exposures usually come from what we eat, drink, or breathe over time, not from brief skin contact with toilet paper.”
While BPA may be found in recycled paper, “the levels of BPA detected are generally low, and the clinical significance of these findings remains uncertain,” he says.
Bleaching, likewise, is not a huge concern, and modern processes don’t pose a significant cancer risk, he says.
“The concerns people sometimes hear about chlorine-bleached paper products largely stem from older manufacturing methods that used elemental chlorine. Today, most toilet paper is produced using elemental chlorine-free (ECF) bleaching, which relies on chlorine dioxide instead of chlorine gas. This process dramatically reduces the formation of dioxins and other potentially harmful byproducts and is widely accepted as the standard in modern paper manufacturing,” Rewari says. “The amount of residual chemicals in finished products is extremely low.”
Dr. Alok A. Khorana, professor of medicine in the department of hematology and medical oncology at Case Western Reserve University, agrees that toilet paper probably isn’t a major cause of exposure to toxins. “Exposure to environmental toxins through toilet paper is likely much smaller than those we’re exposed to in food and water, which has a more direct route into our system,” he says. Still, he says exposure to toxins through toilet paper is "worth investigating further.”
“There are several potentially harmful substances present, such as PFAS, and it's worth understanding whether exposure to these is carcinogenic in any way,” Khorana explains.
He adds that we don’t have many studies yet, likely because concerns over toilet paper are relatively new—plus, Khorana notes it may be difficult for researchers to find people in the U.S. who don’t use toilet paper to compare to those who do. “Studies become challenging to conduct when the candidate risk factor is as prevalent as toilet paper use,” he says.
“I don’t think people need to avoid conventional toilet paper altogether,” Rewari says. “Most people will use conventional toilet paper throughout their lives without any problems.”
Still, he advises patients to choose products with fewer unnecessary additives when possible. “Fragrances, lotions, and dyes don’t improve hygiene, and they may increase the risk of irritation in susceptible individuals. For most people, a simple, unscented, dye-free toilet paper is a reasonable choice.”
An unexpected issue with toilet tissue
Chemicals in toilet paper can present other issues, says Dr. Hannah Kopelman, a dermatologist based in New York City. She says the paper product comes up in her practice more often than one might expect.
“I’ve had patients come in with itching and irritation, which they thought was a yeast infection or eczema flare, only to discover that the culprit was their toilet paper,” Kopelman says. “Most people assume all toilet paper is the same, but the reality is that some formulations can cause problems.”
“When they switch to plain, unbleached, fragrance-free options, the irritation usually clears quickly,” she says.
Dr. Meagan W. Shepherd, an allergist and immunologist based in Barboursville, West Virginia, says people are often surprised to learn how commonly allergens are found in toilet paper, noting that both traditional paper and flushable wipes can cause irritation.
“Wet varieties such as flushable wipes often have preservatives like methylchloroisothiazolinone and methylisothiozolinone, which together account for about 10% of contact allergen sensitizations in North America,” says Shepherd. Dry varieties, on the other hand, are more likely to include added fragrances or dyes, which can act as irritants or allergic triggers, she says.
“I frequently see patients with severe vulvar rashes caused by hidden chemicals,” she adds.
Shepherd also says that if people are struggling to find toilet paper they can tolerate, she recommends skipping recycled paper. “It can be rougher than regular varieties, leading to irritation,” she says. “Plus, trace amounts of various allergens found in the original paper product sources could still be present and potentially cause a reaction in those who are sensitized.”
Shepherd also cautions against recycled toilet paper—as well as anything marketed as “ultra soft.” “While meant to soothe, these products may contain softening agents such as lanolin, as well as fragrances, dyes, preservatives, and adhesives,” she says. “These can be irritating for some people and can cause unpleasant symptoms like itching, redness, and contact dermatitis.”
Kopelman adds that looking for words including “unscented,” “dye-free,” or “chlorine-free” on the packaging is more important than the base material.
“On its own, toilet paper is unlikely to be a major source of chemical exposure,” says Kopelman. “But for those with sensitive skin, choosing products without unnecessary chemicals in toilet paper is a simple way to avoid skin irritation.”

Ukraine asks US orchestra to drop Russian-born violinist, citing ties to Kremlin-backed cultural initiatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:37:06 UTC
23:37:06 KST

The Embassy of Ukraine in the USA asked the Annapolis Symphony Orchestra (ASO) on 25 August to cancel Russian-born violinist Vadim Repin's participation in its Forces of Nature concerts on 6–7 November at Maryland Hall, citing his involvement in Russian state-sponsored and state-linked cultural initiatives.
Since 2022, Ukrainian diplomats have turned individual concert bookings into an object of foreign policy, arguing that a performer carrying Russian state honors and state money brings the state onto the stage with him. Western institutions have answered case by case rather than by policy, so every booking is renegotiated from scratch, and what one venue cancels, another can quietly restore.
The embassy said Repin performed with the State Kremlin Orchestra on 21 February 2024 at a concert the Kremlin Foundation staged for Defender of the Fatherland Day, a Russian military holiday, framed as a tribute to Russia's "great defenders." It said his Vadim Repin Foundation for the Development of the Arts has received substantial funding since the start of the full-scale invasion from Russia's Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives, a state-established institution supporting Russia's cultural policy.
The embassy's request comes four years after the Annapolis Symphony dropped Repin from a March 2022 program and staged a tribute to Ukraine in his place—a decision the orchestra said at the time reflected both the war and respect for Repin's apolitical stance and the safety of him and his family.
The orchestra has not addressed the reversal directly, but the program notes for the concert argue that Shostakovich wrote the concerto for Ukrainian-born David Oistrakh under Stalinist repression and that it "calls on listeners to reject the politics of revenge and hate while embracing the healing cycle of forgiveness." The embassy is asking ASO to reaffirm what it describes as the solidarity with Ukraine shown in 2022.
"We hope the Annapolis Symphony Orchestra will give these concerns careful consideration and reaffirm the solidarity with Ukraine it demonstrated in 2022, when it withdrew Mr. Repin from its program and replaced his performance with a musical tribute to Ukraine," the embassy said.
In March 2022, days after Russia's full-scale invasion began, ASO replaced Repin's planned appearance. The orchestra's then-executive director, Edgar Herrera, told WTOP that the decision was not only a response to the war but also "out of respect to Repin's apolitical stance and concerns for the safety of himself and his family."
The embassy noted that Germany's Mannheim Philharmonic, the Hungarian National Philharmonic, and Florida's Palm Beach Symphony have all reconsidered working with Repin this year, and that Palm Beach canceled his performance in March. Mannheim dropped a February concert after a request from Ukraine's embassy in Berlin, and the Hungarian orchestra replaced him at its Budapest season opening in June. A Change.org petition launched in June by Ukrainian Cultural Front DC had already called on ASO to cancel the November concerts.
Neither ASO nor Repin has commented publicly on the embassy's request.

Stubb: After war with Russia, Finland agreed to lose territory. But it’s not going to be like that for Ukraine
Alexander or Alex Stubb is one of those politicians whose importance to Ukraine goes far beyond his official position. The former prime minister, now president, of Finland has been a staunch supporter of our country and maintains close, trusting relations with the Ukrainian leadership. But most importantly, he is one of the few Europeans who has a good personal relationship with US President Donald Trump.
This has made Stubb a natural intermediary in discussions with the United States concerning Ukraine and ending the war.
Finland’s own experience of war with Russia makes his involvement all the more significant. Incidentally, Alex’s father, Göran Stubb, was born in Karelia, which was later occupied by the Soviet army.
We discussed these issues, as well as Ukraine’s European future, in Kyiv, which the president was visiting to attend celebrations marking Ukraine’s Independence Day.
"It's not going to be about dead soldiers. It's going to be about a threat to the regime"
Mr President, it’s good to see you here. How many times have you been to Kyiv? Five?
Well, quite a few times over the years, but since I became president, I think this is my fifth visit.
It was my first trip abroad when I became president in March 2024. I came here in April. I always find it important to come to Kyiv and talk to people, talk to the president, to the administration and to get a sense of what's going on.
Of course, things are looking much better now than they were two and a half years ago.
That’s good to hear, because now we are preparing for a harsh winter. At least, that’s the forecast we’ve been hearing. Does that coincide with your expectations?
Yes, certainly. It's always important to prepare for the worst in order to be able to be ready for it.
I think right now, if you look at the military side, the Ukrainian offensive has been very strong for about 8 to 9 months.
If we only look at the numbers, you’re basically eliminating 30,000 to 35,000 Russian troops per month, basically because you’re able to carry out long-range hits into the core of Russian society – I mean oil refineries in St Petersburg or Moscow, or Wildberries logistical centres, or Shahed factories.
All of these are indications that Ukraine is doing much better.
But that doesn't mean that winter is not coming. It will come, and that's one of the reasons why Finland is working a lot on energy supply to Ukraine, on electricity, on diesel generators, for instance, made by a Finnish company called Wärtsilä.
We have to prepare for the worst. That's just how it goes.
You referred to Russian losses. In my assessment, which is widely shared in Ukraine, Putin doesn’t count human lives. Yes, 35,000 Russians a month are being killed in action, but he doesn’t care.
I think you're right. If you look at reasons for Putin or for Russia to end this war, the economy will not be a reason. The Russian economy is doing badly, but that's not going to be a reason to end the war.
Dead or wounded soldiers are not going to be a reason either, because we’re already talking over a million, and it's not making a difference in Russia.
But the thing that might make a difference is people turning against the war.
And now we're seeing, with what I call legitimate opinion polls, about 65% of Russians wanting to end the war. And why is that? Because Ukraine is hitting the oil refineries, and therefore we’re seeing the rationing of petrol and diesel, we're seeing high prices, et cetera, et cetera.
And also, they've had to close the internet a couple of times [because of people’s public outrage – ed.].
So yes, I think you're right. It's not going to be about dead soldiers, it's going to be about a threat to the regime.
And of course the big question is: will Russia mobilise? Because if Russia mobilises 300,000 to 500,000 troops, that is going to have a direct impact on young men in St Petersburg and Moscow.
I believe they will mobilise. But do you think there could be some kind of revolt or uprising in Russia?
I'm a student of Russian history, but I don't pretend that I'll be able to predict the future.
The only thing I can say is that Ukraine is doing much better politically, militarily and financially than it was a year ago, let alone two or three years ago. And right now it's about numbers, and the numbers, in my mind, are on Ukraine’s side, as painful as it is at times.
I'm just fresh out of the commemoration of Ukraine’s independence and the decoration – posthumously – of soldiers who have lost their lives. It's a very moving moment.
We all understand that the cost of the war is extremely high for Ukraine and Ukrainian society. But at the same time, it's a question of preserving your independence and your sovereignty and your identity.
"There will be a team of negotiators to end the war"
Do you personally expect, having access to all the information and intelligence, that the war could end soon, or at least that a ceasefire could come soon?
It's impossible to give it a date. I think we need to work pretty much on three tracks.
Track number one is to continue to supply Ukraine with the necessary means for it to continue to conduct the war. That means financial and military support, and right now one of the key elements is air defence and especially Patriots.
The second element is to continue the policy of sanctions, especially sanctioning the companies in Russia which provide components for, say, drones or missiles, so for the war industry.
And then the third track is the negotiation track, where we see a lot of public negotiations, but there should be some negotiations happening in the background as well.
Are there any signs indicating that Putin is ready to start meaningful negotiations?
To give you a very blunt and direct answer, the answer is no.
It's a very sort of classic Russian tactic.
But eventually there will be a day when perhaps Russia understands that it has lost this war
or that it will not achieve its strategic aims, and that is the time to work on it. So we work a lot with the Americans and of course with our Ukrainian friends almost every day, and with the Europeans, to try to bring Russia to the negotiating table. But I can't give you a deadline for it.
And that's why we need to prepare for a harsh winter.
Once negotiations start, what would the role of Europe be?
I come from a small country, so I feel very strongly that I need to stay in the back office.
My job is to provide information from Ukraine to America, from America to Ukraine, and if there is a need for information to be provided to the Russians, I'm happy to do that as well.
But I do feel that the Americans are in the lead on the negotiations.
They provide the umbrella.
But of course, we cannot take decisions on Europe over Europe. So I try to work in the back office and engage with as many people as I can.
If you were offered the position of negotiator, would you agree?
First of all, it's a hypothetical question, so you can't answer in that sense.
Secondly, if that question were to be posed – of course! But I think it will be a team of negotiators.
I'm happy to do a lot of the background work – I don't need any of the exposure to it.
Do you know why we in Ukraine have such great respect for your experience?
Probably because it's so similar. In 1939, Russia attacked us, and we went through the Winter War in very harsh conditions. But that was only 105 days, whereas you've been at war now for over 1,600 days with four harsh winters.
And then of course Finland had the War of Continuation.
For us, it was a fight for independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. And as I've said before, Finland retained its independence, unlike our Baltic friends at the time. They lost it.
But we did lose a part of our sovereignty.
We weren't as free as Ukraine will be after this war.
So yes, there is an understanding of the history of Russian imperialism and therefore a very strong sympathy with Ukrainians.
"The war is not sustainable for Russia in the long run"
Do you think there are any recipes or lessons that Ukraine can learn from your experience of that time?
The only thing that comes to mind is a word in Finnish called sisu.
It’s basically resilience and grit and grinding it out.
And I see a lot of that in Ukrainian society today, when I talk to a lot of my Ukrainian friends. Or if I talk to foreign ambassadors here, they just say, "The Ukrainians are so cool. How are they able to sustain this?" That's about sisu and resilience.
But you cannot really compare war over 80 years ago to modern warfare.
One thing that is quite similar is that if you look at the ratio of Russians [killed in action] versus Ukrainians, and the ratio of Soviets versus Finns, the figures are quite similar at the end of the day.
But I think, in earnest, not only have you already won the war, but at the end of the day, you will win the war. And that is linked to the theory of warfare. If a big aggressor tries to deny the independence, sovereignty and full territorial integrity of a country, and that country survives it, then by definition it wins.
That's why we in Finland talked about a "defence victory" at the end of the day.
You mean that Finland won the war?
Yes, definitely. I mean, for us, we call it a defence victory, because we survived. We exist as a nation, as Finland.
Despite losing territory?
Yes. Wars are not an accounting exercise.
And I'm not by any means suggesting that Ukraine should lose territory.
There are so many different ways of dealing with this. But in our case, there was a peace agreement, and in that, we decided, okay, this is how the borders are going to be drawn.
But for Ukraine I don't think it is going to be like that, and it doesn't have to be like that.
I'll give you just one example.
Only this year, Russia has gained roughly 900 sq km of territory in Donetsk and the Eastern part, whereas Ukraine has regained or liberated 800 sq km.
We understand that this is now a war of attrition. And a war of attrition where – sorry to be morbid – the killing ratio is one Ukrainian for eight Russians.
So it's not sustainable for Russia in the long run. And they know that. It's just a question of when they come to admit it to themselves.
"Europe needs to have the mindset that Ukraine is helping us"
Are there any red lines that are unacceptable to Europe or to you personally? I understand that it’s for Ukraine to define what peace should look like.
Yeah. I mean, Ukraine decides its own red lines, and we follow. We support.
But don’t you also have your own red lines?
Of course Europe has red lines.
And Europe's red lines are that there's no conversation about European security without Europe. That is the absolute starting point. And I think all Ukrainians need to have the mindset that we are on the same team – Ukraine and Europe, or Ukraine and Finland.
And that's why I for instance think that eventually we should have Ukrainian EU membership and NATO membership. And I say this because I think the value base of Ukraine is in Europe.
Russia tried to make Ukraine Russian, but Ukraine showed that it wants to be European.
And not only that, it is in our interest, because you have the largest military in Europe, because you have experience in modern warfare.
If in the beginning it felt like "Europe must help Ukraine", now Europe needs to have the mindset that Ukraine is helping us and will help us in the long run as well, when it comes to security.
Does this mean that Ukraine’s membership of the EU – and also NATO, I hope – is also some kind of red line in future peace negotiations?
For me, definitely. No one else is going to decide about Ukraine's EU or NATO membership – no one except EU members and NATO members.
And Ukraine.
Of course. Ukraine decides on it. But for me, again, Ukraine is European.
Do you see us in the EU?
Yes, I do. I do.
I'm an EU nerd – I've been doing this EU stuff since the early 1990s. I was excited when Finland joined in 1995 when I was a young student. I was negotiating at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs at intergovernmental conferences on the Amsterdam Treaty, on the Nice Treaty, on the Lisbon Treaty, et cetera, et cetera.
The EU is my bread and butter.
But my point is, be patient, because the EU is always slow.
It's always going to be frustrating. You're going to be debating about which cluster is still open and which not. At the end of the day, Ukraine will be a member of the European Union, and that is going to be the greatest outcome, I think, of this war.
And sooner rather than later, because now we have to move fast, otherwise it won’t work. It will end up nowhere. The world is moving fast!
Yes, I think the window of opportunity is now.
Because my feeling is that when the world order settles to some kind of new form, then we'll start fighting over different kinds of things. I don't think the accession negotiations would have opened had it not been for the war. I don't think anyone would be talking about Ukraine's NATO membership in earnest had it not been for the war.
So the window of opportunity is now.
But all I'm trying to say is: be aware that there will be difficult moments in these negotiations. There are difficult moments for everyone. For Finland, it was about agriculture or the eastern part of Finland. But for Ukraine, it's going to be about different things. Just be patient.
The EU is not a utopia. It's not perfect. And when you join the EU, remember, life is not going to end. It's not going to be only green fields and flowers and peace signs and rainbows.
You know, it's a tough club.
And the last thing. I was at your meeting with President Zelenskyy in Ankara. You started by saying that currently you see NATO as "32 + Ukraine".
Yes, that's my take. Obviously, I'm a new member, like Sweden. We became the 31st and the 32nd members.
But to be honest, if we look at the whole idea of a more European NATO, meaning that we need all the possible military means in Europe, then you don't have to have a PhD in military strategy to understand that. You look around and say: "I want Ukraine in."
Do people in NATO understand that?
Most of us do. Most of us do.
Don't worry, you'll be a NATO member at the end of this.
Sergiy Sydorenko
Editor, European Pravda

Russian Guided Bomb Strike Seriously Damages Kherson’s Main Heating Plant
Russian forces struck the Kherson Combined Heat and Power Plant (CHP) with a guided aerial bomb on August 26, causing serious damage to the facility, Ukraine’s state-owned energy company Naftogaz reported.
According to Naftogaz, the Kherson CHP plant serves as the primary source of heating for the city and sustained significant damage in the attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The extent of the damage will be assessed as soon as the security situation allows. We are coordinating further actions with the local authorities,” said Serhii Fedorenko, acting chairman of the board of Naftogaz of Ukraine.
The company stressed that the Kherson CHP plant, which is part of the Naftogaz Group, is a civilian facility whose primary function is to provide heating to residents of the city.
The latest strike follows a series of attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure in Kherson in recent weeks. On August 10, Russian airstrikes hit critical infrastructure in the city, disrupting electricity and water supplies across several districts.
The attacks partially cut power to the Central, Dnipro, and Korabel districts, prompting emergency crews to assess the damage and carry out repairs needed to restore essential services.
Less than two weeks later, on August 23, a Russian drone strike sparked a fire at a Ukrainian Red Cross warehouse in Kherson, damaging or destroying humanitarian supplies valued at approximately $626,000.
The Ukrainian Red Cross said the warehouse contained supplies intended to help communities prepare for the upcoming autumn and winter season, as well as emergency materials used to assist residents following Russian attacks.

Flight attendant’s breast cancer was occupational disease, court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:36:19 UTC
23:36:19 KST

A flight attendant in France has succeeded in having her breast cancer recognised as an occupational disease, a first for the country’s aviation industry, her lawyer and a trade union said.
The ruling, which recognised that Sophie Lainault, a former flight attendant for Air France, had frequently worked at night and been exposed to passive smoking, could pave the way for similar claims, the lawyer and the CFDT union said.
Lainault, from Anglet in south-west France, told the news agency AFP that she hoped her legal victory could help other women.
“It is truly my dearest wish that this opens the way for other women who might not have dared until now,” the 59-year-old said.
Now in remission, Lainault said she worked for Air France, the country’s flagship carrier, between 1989 and 2019 as a flight attendant and later as a purser on long-haul flights, accumulating more than 12,600 flight hours, including more than 6,500 at night.
The ruling, seen by AFP, came from a court in the city of Bayonne in early July and recognised the occupational origin of Lainault’s cancer.
The court highlighted the role of night work, exposure to ionising radiation and passive smoking. Smoking was permitted on Air France flights until 2000.
Two regional committees responsible for recognising occupational diseases had previously concluded that no link had been established.
Breast cancer is not included in France’s official list of occupational diseases, meaning that obtaining recognition can be a lengthy and difficult ordeal for patients.
Lainault said that she had fought for two and a half years for the recognition, supported by CFDT activists. She said the ruling would allow her to take early retirement.
Lainault’s lawyer, Elisabeth Leroux, said the court decision set a legal precedent. The ruling was final and no appeal had been lodged, she added.
Some studies have suggested that women who regularly work night shifts may face a higher risk of developing cancer.
Air France said it “was not a party to the proceedings and has not been informed of the court’s reasoning”.
The airline said: “The health and safety of employees at work is an absolute priority.”
In 2023, a French nurse who had worked night shifts for 28 years and been exposed to radiation succeeded in having her breast cancer recognised as an occupational disease.
With nearly 13,000 deaths each year, breast cancer is the deadliest cancer among women in France.

African states push for greater control over mineral wealth – official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:35:45 UTC
23:35:45 KST

African states push for greater control over mineral wealth – official
African gold producers are pushing for greater resource sovereignty as governments seek to retain more of the economic value generated by their mineral wealth, Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) representative has said.
Speaking to RT, Prince Kwame Minkah, the agency’s media relations officer, stated that African countries are increasingly moving away from a model in which minerals are extracted domestically and much of the processing, certification, trading, and financing takes place abroad. He noted that the shift is part of a broader African drive toward resource sovereignty and local value addition.
“If we produce the mineral, why should we capture only the value extraction while other countries continue to capture the value processing and, for that matter, trading?” Minkah said.
Ghana is among several major African gold producers tightening control over its gold sector. From September 1, gold doré purchased by self-financing aggregators under arrangements with approved offtakers must be refined in Ghana before it can be exported.
Several other African nations have also moved to tighten control over their gold resources. Guinea has introduced mandatory domestic gold refining, while Mali has taken steps to expand local processing. Burkina Faso has expanded state purchases of artisanal gold through its National Precious Substances Company. Tanzania has also tightened state control over the gold trade and requires exporters to sell part of their output to the central bank.
The policy forms part of the Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama’s broader goal of ending raw mineral exports by 2030, according to Minkah. Ghana has already increased state involvement in the gold trade through the country’s artisanal gold marketing agency GoldBod, which was established in 2025 and given exclusive authority over the purchase and export of artisanal and small-scale gold.
According to the Ghana Chamber of Mines, the country is now the world’s sixth-largest gold producer, behind China, Russia, Australia, Canada, and Peru, after producing about 185 tons in 2025, marking a 23.41% increase from its 2024 production of 4.82 million ounces. It is the only African state in the global top ten and remains the continent’s largest producer.

Pubs, bars and hotels report ‘Burnham bounce’ in optimism but call for further tax relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:35:24 UTC
23:35:24 KST

Pubs, bars and hotels have reported a “Burnham bounce” in optimism as a result of the prime minister’s overtures to the sector, polling suggests, but they warn that the goodwill could evaporate without further tax relief.
Andy Burnham has positioned himself as a staunch ally of the UK’s hospitality industry both before and since his arrival at No 10, announcing last month a discount on business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
The result, according to a survey by multiple trade bodies, is that 37% of businesses in the sector now feel that his government will benefit hospitality and brewing, which are collectively worth about £100bn to the economy.
The degree of optimism is more than double the 18% recorded before the policy on business rates was announced, an increase described by the trade bodies as a “Burnham bounce”.
The government has signalled further changes to business rates to ease pressure on the sector. But with the details still uncertain, some venue owners have warned that the steps taken so far have done very little to reduce their groaning pile of rising costs.
The survey findings, shared with the Guardian, also show that the industry believes the tax burden, in particular VAT, is continuing to hold back the sector.
Three-quarters of respondents pointed to tax as the biggest barrier for businesses, with political instability (37%) cited as the second biggest.
The survey was compiled by the British Beer & Pubs Association, UK Hospitality, the British Institute of Innkeeping and Hospitality Ulster.
The trade bodies in a joint statement: “The new prime minister’s action to back hospitality has clearly driven a boost in the sector’s optimism, yet significant challenges remain. The support for pubs and live music venues on business rates was a great first step and now we need to see wider support and conditions to allow the entire hospitality sector to grow and create jobs.
“Our tax burden – amongst the highest in the economy – along with new regulatory costs is overwhelming us and the real victims are high streets, jobs and communities. A lower rate of VAT, wider permanent business rates reform and changes to employer NICs [national insurance contributions] would help deliver the prime minister’s bold ambitions for every postcode.”
More than 330,000 people have signed a petition calling on the government to cut VAT on hospitality from 20% to 10%, a sector-specific relief that would bring the sales tax on the sector in line with that in many European countries.
However, critics have said this would be an inefficient way to spur growth and would cost more than £10bn, much of which would benefit large, profitable, multinational chains.
A government spokesperson said: “The chancellor prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues – saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year. This is on top of providing a tax break on poured pints and capping corporation tax.”

Man who attacked Jerusalem nun acquitted due to mental illness, hospitalized for up to six years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:33:35 UTC
23:33:35 KST

The Jerusalem Magistrate’s Court acquitted Yona Simcha Schreiber on Wednesday over his attack on a Christian nun near King David’s Tomb on grounds of mental illness, ordered him to be hospitalized for up to six years.
Judge Ophir Tischler found that the evidence established that Schreiber did commit the acts described in the indictment, but he accepted the district psychiatrist’s conclusion that Schreiber was psychotic at the time and could neither understand the nature of his actions nor stop himself from carrying them out.
The ruling means that Shreiber cannot be held criminally responsible for the attack because of his mental condition at the time.
He had been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm motivated by hostility toward a religious group, as well as common assault. On April 28, he pushed a nun to the ground, then returned and kicked her, and finally assaulted a passerby who tried to intervene.
Acquitted by reason of insanity
The district psychiatrist diagnosed Schreiber with schizophrenia, finding that he had been psychotic for many years and lacked insight into his illness.
There was no conclusive evidence that specific psychotic thoughts directly caused the attack, the psychiatrist said. He nevertheless concluded that Schreiber’s illness directly influenced his actions and that, at the time, Schreiber could not understand what he was doing or refrain from doing it.
The psychiatrist recommended inpatient treatment, a position the prosecution ultimately accepted after requesting additional clarifications.
Under the court order, Schreiber’s hospitalization, dated from August 24, may continue for a maximum of six years, corresponding to the maximum penalty attached to the most serious offense in the case.
That period is a ceiling rather than a fixed sentence. A psychiatric committee may order his earlier release if it concludes that his medical condition permits. The committee has been instructed to notify both the prosecution and the defense of any such decision.
The court reached its final decision after several hearings over the psychiatric findings and the rights of the woman who was attacked.
At an August 16 hearing, the prosecution raised questions about the psychiatric opinion, prompting the court to ask the district psychiatrist for clarification. In a response filed the following day, the psychiatrist said he was convinced that Schreiber suffered from schizophrenia, had experienced psychosis for years, and was unable to understand or control his actions during the attack.
The prosecution initially agreed that the case should end with an acquittal and a hospitalization order. It then sought a short delay after an attorney representing the nun arrived at an August 24 hearing and said she had not been properly informed of the psychiatric findings.
Harassment and attacks against Christians in Jerusalem
The nun’s attorney, Zaki Sahlia, questioned the assessment and argued that the fact that Schreiber targeted the nun rather than other people nearby raised doubts about whether the attack resulted from his illness. He also placed the case in the context of recurring harassment and attacks against Christian clergy in Jerusalem.
Tischler rejected the argument that the law required a further delay before the court could act on the psychiatric opinion. The law provides victims with an opportunity to state their position before a plea bargain or another negotiated arrangement closes a case, he wrote, but this was not such an agreement.
The opinion came from the state’s own district psychiatrist and left the court required to address Schreiber’s continued detention, the judge added. He ordered that Schreiber be held in hospital conditions while the prosecution completed its consultations.
At Wednesday’s final hearing, the prosecution said it had fulfilled its obligations toward the nun, heard her position, and remained in favor of accepting the psychiatric opinion. The prosecution and defense then jointly asked the court to acquit Schreiber.
The nun’s attorney said she remained uncomfortable with the psychiatric findings but respected the court’s decision.
Schreiber’s public defender, Idan Gamlieli, said the district psychiatrist had determined that the “regrettable incident” resulted from Schreiber’s illness and that he required inpatient psychiatric treatment.
“We hope the medical treatment will help him return to optimal functioning,” Gamlieli said. “It is important to note that we understand the complainant’s difficult feelings and wish her recovery from the consequences of this regrettable incident.”
Nun's attack caught on video
The attack occurred at approximately 5:42 p.m. near King David’s Tomb in Jerusalem.
Schreiber, a resident of the West Bank settlement of Peduel, saw the nun wearing clothing that identified her as Christian, ran toward her, and pushed her forcefully to the ground.
She struck her head and became dizzy. Schreiber initially walked away but returned several seconds later and kicked her while she was still on the ground. When a passerby intervened, Schreiber attacked him with punches and kicks.
The nun suffered bruising to her face and leg. The assault, which was captured on video, prompted widespread condemnation from Christian representatives, academics, and Israeli officials.
Sahlia told The Jerusalem Post that an appeal was not likely, but that he was “still studying the decision” and that there were other avenues to pursue.

Iran says US must fully accept its terms before Strait of Hormuz can reopen under new agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:33:26 UTC
23:33:26 KST

Iran and Oman have reached an agreement regarding the Strait of Hormuz, according to an IRGC spokesman.
“The US is obstructing an agreement between Iran and Oman to secure a safe transit route through the Strait of Hormuz,” the spokesman said.
Oman has not issued a corresponding statement, however. A source familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post that suspected disagreements between the two countries remain.
“The Omanis say they will not agree to imposing fees on ships, while the Iranians continue to insist that, from their perspective, this is a condition for passage through the strait,” the source said.
The source added that, according to Oman, there is also no agreement on clearing mines from the Strait of Hormuz, contrary to the Iranian statement.
Iran and Oman have held on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strait, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February.
Trump says Hormuz is already open after Iran, Oman reportedly reach deal
Most shipping has since been shut down, driving global energy prices higher, as Tehran and Washington have tried to assert control over the channel, imposing separate blockades.
"The Strait of Hormuz belongs to Iran and the country of Oman... We have been in negotiations with Oman for about a month, and we have reached results that are acceptable to both sides," Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said in comments published by Iranian state media.
The IRGC accused the United States of seeking to obstruct the negotiations between Iran and Oman and said this had caused the agreement to be delayed.
Iran has denounced the US effort to isolate its economy as an act of "gross lawlessness," expressing confidence that many countries would not join the pressure campaign.
"If the United States stops obstructing and returns to the agreement, we can open the Strait of Hormuz within the framework of the agreement reached... If the United States does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened under any circumstances," Mohebbi said.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in a radio interview later on Wednesday morning, insisted that the strait was already open.
“We take a lot of ships through the strait now. We’re taking them in,” Trump told conservative radio host Glenn Beck.
“Every once in a while there’ll be a drone or a rocket or something shot, but it is a very functioning strait. A lot of oil is pouring out,” the president said.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi arrived in Tehran on Tuesday for talks on the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran and Oman issued a joint statement on Tuesday saying their foreign ministers had discussed a “proposed framework” to establish “a joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz,” as well as an agreement to implement “a joint project to clear the Strait of mines.”
Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani was expected to arrive in Iran on Wednesday to discuss freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
“The prime minister’s visit to Tehran underscores our position that diplomacy is the way to strengthen regional security,” Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Stubb: After war with Russia, Finland agreed to lose territory. But it’s not going to be like that for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
17:33:00 EEST
23:33:00 KST

Stubb: After war with Russia, Finland agreed to lose territory. But it’s not going to be like that for Ukraine
Alexander or Alex Stubb is one of those politicians whose importance to Ukraine goes far beyond his official position. The former prime minister, now president, of Finland has been a staunch supporter of our country and maintains close, trusting relations with the Ukrainian leadership. But most importantly, he is one of the few Europeans who has a good personal relationship with US President Donald Trump.
This has made Stubb a natural intermediary in discussions with the United States concerning Ukraine and ending the war.
Finland’s own experience of war with Russia makes his involvement all the more significant. Incidentally, Alex’s father, Göran Stubb, was born in Karelia, which was later occupied by the Soviet army.
We discussed these issues, as well as Ukraine’s European future, in Kyiv, which the president was visiting to attend celebrations marking Ukraine’s Independence Day.
"It's not going to be about dead soldiers. It's going to be about a threat to the regime"
Mr President, it’s good to see you here. How many times have you been to Kyiv? Five?
Well, quite a few times over the years, but since I became president, I think this is my fifth visit.
It was my first trip abroad when I became president in March 2024. I came here in April. I always find it important to come to Kyiv and talk to people, talk to the president, to the administration and to get a sense of what's going on.
Of course, things are looking much better now than they were two and a half years ago.
That’s good to hear, because now we are preparing for a harsh winter. At least, that’s the forecast we’ve been hearing. Does that coincide with your expectations?
Yes, certainly. It's always important to prepare for the worst in order to be able to be ready for it.
I think right now, if you look at the military side, the Ukrainian offensive has been very strong for about 8 to 9 months.
If we only look at the numbers, you’re basically eliminating 30,000 to 35,000 Russian troops per month, basically because you’re able to carry out long-range hits into the core of Russian society – I mean oil refineries in St Petersburg or Moscow, or Wildberries logistical centres, or Shahed factories.
All of these are indications that Ukraine is doing much better.
But that doesn't mean that winter is not coming. It will come, and that's one of the reasons why Finland is working a lot on energy supply to Ukraine, on electricity, on diesel generators, for instance, made by a Finnish company called Wärtsilä.
We have to prepare for the worst. That's just how it goes.
You referred to Russian losses. In my assessment, which is widely shared in Ukraine, Putin doesn’t count human lives. Yes, 35,000 Russians a month are being killed in action, but he doesn’t care.
I think you're right. If you look at reasons for Putin or for Russia to end this war, the economy will not be a reason. The Russian economy is doing badly, but that's not going to be a reason to end the war.
Dead or wounded soldiers are not going to be a reason either, because we’re already talking over a million, and it's not making a difference in Russia.
But the thing that might make a difference is people turning against the war.
And now we're seeing, with what I call legitimate opinion polls, about 65% of Russians wanting to end the war. And why is that? Because Ukraine is hitting the oil refineries, and therefore we’re seeing the rationing of petrol and diesel, we're seeing high prices, et cetera, et cetera.
And also, they've had to close the internet a couple of times [because of people’s public outrage – ed.].
So yes, I think you're right. It's not going to be about dead soldiers, it's going to be about a threat to the regime.
And of course the big question is: will Russia mobilise? Because if Russia mobilises 300,000 to 500,000 troops, that is going to have a direct impact on young men in St Petersburg and Moscow.
I believe they will mobilise. But do you think there could be some kind of revolt or uprising in Russia?
I'm a student of Russian history, but I don't pretend that I'll be able to predict the future.
The only thing I can say is that Ukraine is doing much better politically, militarily and financially than it was a year ago, let alone two or three years ago. And right now it's about numbers, and the numbers, in my mind, are on Ukraine’s side, as painful as it is at times.
I'm just fresh out of the commemoration of Ukraine’s independence and the decoration – posthumously – of soldiers who have lost their lives. It's a very moving moment.
We all understand that the cost of the war is extremely high for Ukraine and Ukrainian society. But at the same time, it's a question of preserving your independence and your sovereignty and your identity.
"There will be a team of negotiators to end the war"
Do you personally expect, having access to all the information and intelligence, that the war could end soon, or at least that a ceasefire could come soon?
It's impossible to give it a date. I think we need to work pretty much on three tracks.
Track number one is to continue to supply Ukraine with the necessary means for it to continue to conduct the war. That means financial and military support, and right now one of the key elements is air defence and especially Patriots.
The second element is to continue the policy of sanctions, especially sanctioning the companies in Russia which provide components for, say, drones or missiles, so for the war industry.
And then the third track is the negotiation track, where we see a lot of public negotiations, but there should be some negotiations happening in the background as well.
Are there any signs indicating that Putin is ready to start meaningful negotiations?
To give you a very blunt and direct answer, the answer is no.
It's a very sort of classic Russian tactic.
But eventually there will be a day when perhaps Russia understands that it has lost this war
or that it will not achieve its strategic aims, and that is the time to work on it. So we work a lot with the Americans and of course with our Ukrainian friends almost every day, and with the Europeans, to try to bring Russia to the negotiating table. But I can't give you a deadline for it.
And that's why we need to prepare for a harsh winter.
Once negotiations start, what would the role of Europe be?
I come from a small country, so I feel very strongly that I need to stay in the back office.
My job is to provide information from Ukraine to America, from America to Ukraine, and if there is a need for information to be provided to the Russians, I'm happy to do that as well.
But I do feel that the Americans are in the lead on the negotiations.
They provide the umbrella.
But of course, we cannot take decisions on Europe over Europe. So I try to work in the back office and engage with as many people as I can.
If you were offered the position of negotiator, would you agree?
First of all, it's a hypothetical question, so you can't answer in that sense.
Secondly, if that question were to be posed – of course! But I think it will be a team of negotiators.
I'm happy to do a lot of the background work – I don't need any of the exposure to it.
Do you know why we in Ukraine have such great respect for your experience?
Probably because it's so similar. In 1939, Russia attacked us, and we went through the Winter War in very harsh conditions. But that was only 105 days, whereas you've been at war now for over 1,600 days with four harsh winters.
And then of course Finland had the War of Continuation.
For us, it was a fight for independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. And as I've said before, Finland retained its independence, unlike our Baltic friends at the time. They lost it.
But we did lose a part of our sovereignty.
We weren't as free as Ukraine will be after this war.
So yes, there is an understanding of the history of Russian imperialism and therefore a very strong sympathy with Ukrainians.
"The war is not sustainable for Russia in the long run"
Do you think there are any recipes or lessons that Ukraine can learn from your experience of that time?
The only thing that comes to mind is a word in Finnish called sisu.
It’s basically resilience and grit and grinding it out.
And I see a lot of that in Ukrainian society today, when I talk to a lot of my Ukrainian friends. Or if I talk to foreign ambassadors here, they just say, "The Ukrainians are so cool. How are they able to sustain this?" That's about sisu and resilience.
But you cannot really compare war over 80 years ago to modern warfare.
One thing that is quite similar is that if you look at the ratio of Russians [killed in action] versus Ukrainians, and the ratio of Soviets versus Finns, the figures are quite similar at the end of the day.
But I think, in earnest, not only have you already won the war, but at the end of the day, you will win the war. And that is linked to the theory of warfare. If a big aggressor tries to deny the independence, sovereignty and full territorial integrity of a country, and that country survives it, then by definition it wins.
That's why we in Finland talked about a "defence victory" at the end of the day.
You mean that Finland won the war?
Yes, definitely. I mean, for us, we call it a defence victory, because we survived. We exist as a nation, as Finland.
Despite losing territory?
Yes. Wars are not an accounting exercise.
And I'm not by any means suggesting that Ukraine should lose territory.
There are so many different ways of dealing with this. But in our case, there was a peace agreement, and in that, we decided, okay, this is how the borders are going to be drawn.
But for Ukraine I don't think it is going to be like that, and it doesn't have to be like that.
I'll give you just one example.
Only this year, Russia has gained roughly 900 sq km of territory in Donetsk and the Eastern part, whereas Ukraine has regained or liberated 800 sq km.
We understand that this is now a war of attrition. And a war of attrition where – sorry to be morbid – the killing ratio is one Ukrainian for eight Russians.
So it's not sustainable for Russia in the long run. And they know that. It's just a question of when they come to admit it to themselves.
"Europe needs to have the mindset that Ukraine is helping us"
Are there any red lines that are unacceptable to Europe or to you personally? I understand that it’s for Ukraine to define what peace should look like.
Yeah. I mean, Ukraine decides its own red lines, and we follow. We support.
But don’t you also have your own red lines?
Of course Europe has red lines.
And Europe's red lines are that there's no conversation about European security without Europe. That is the absolute starting point. And I think all Ukrainians need to have the mindset that we are on the same team – Ukraine and Europe, or Ukraine and Finland.
And that's why I for instance think that eventually we should have Ukrainian EU membership and NATO membership. And I say this because I think the value base of Ukraine is in Europe.
Russia tried to make Ukraine Russian, but Ukraine showed that it wants to be European.
And not only that, it is in our interest, because you have the largest military in Europe, because you have experience in modern warfare.
If in the beginning it felt like "Europe must help Ukraine", now Europe needs to have the mindset that Ukraine is helping us and will help us in the long run as well, when it comes to security.
Does this mean that Ukraine’s membership of the EU – and also NATO, I hope – is also some kind of red line in future peace negotiations?
For me, definitely. No one else is going to decide about Ukraine's EU or NATO membership – no one except EU members and NATO members.
And Ukraine.
Of course. Ukraine decides on it. But for me, again, Ukraine is European.
Do you see us in the EU?
Yes, I do. I do.
I'm an EU nerd – I've been doing this EU stuff since the early 1990s. I was excited when Finland joined in 1995 when I was a young student. I was negotiating at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs at intergovernmental conferences on the Amsterdam Treaty, on the Nice Treaty, on the Lisbon Treaty, et cetera, et cetera.
The EU is my bread and butter.
But my point is, be patient, because the EU is always slow.
It's always going to be frustrating. You're going to be debating about which cluster is still open and which not. At the end of the day, Ukraine will be a member of the European Union, and that is going to be the greatest outcome, I think, of this war.
And sooner rather than later, because now we have to move fast, otherwise it won’t work. It will end up nowhere. The world is moving fast!
Yes, I think the window of opportunity is now.
Because my feeling is that when the world order settles to some kind of new form, then we'll start fighting over different kinds of things. I don't think the accession negotiations would have opened had it not been for the war. I don't think anyone would be talking about Ukraine's NATO membership in earnest had it not been for the war.
So the window of opportunity is now.
But all I'm trying to say is: be aware that there will be difficult moments in these negotiations. There are difficult moments for everyone. For Finland, it was about agriculture or the eastern part of Finland. But for Ukraine, it's going to be about different things. Just be patient.
The EU is not a utopia. It's not perfect. And when you join the EU, remember, life is not going to end. It's not going to be only green fields and flowers and peace signs and rainbows.
You know, it's a tough club.
And the last thing. I was at your meeting with President Zelenskyy in Ankara. You started by saying that currently you see NATO as "32 + Ukraine".
Yes, that's my take. Obviously, I'm a new member, like Sweden. We became the 31st and the 32nd members.
But to be honest, if we look at the whole idea of a more European NATO, meaning that we need all the possible military means in Europe, then you don't have to have a PhD in military strategy to understand that. You look around and say: "I want Ukraine in."
Do people in NATO understand that?
Most of us do. Most of us do.
Don't worry, you'll be a NATO member at the end of this.
Sergiy Sydorenko
Editor, European Pravda

A new Right? Winter’s ‘Amcha Yisrael’ could secure six seats, at expense of Smotrich's RZP - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:32:56 UTC
23:32:56 KST

A Walla poll published Wednesday showed Ofer Winter’s newly formed Amcha Yisrael Party potentially securing six seats in the Knesset, while the Religious Zionist Party leader and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s faction fell below the electoral threshold with 2.6% of the vote. The poll also showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc receiving only 43 seats, leaving it short of the majority needed to form a government even with Winter’s party joining the coalition.
The poll pointed to a significant shift within the national camp following Winter’s entry into politics. While his party received six seats, Smotrich’s party would fail to enter the Knesset, while National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit maintained significant support with eight seats. The Likud party led by Netanyahu received 21 seats.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar Party led the poll with 25 seats. It was followed by Likud with 21 seats; B'Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett, with 15; the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, with 10; Yisrael Beytenu, led by Avigdor Liberman, with nine; and Otzma Yehudit, led by Ben-Gvir, with eight.
Ra'am drops to the bottom of the list
United Torah Judaism and Shas each received seven seats. The United Arab List of Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad also received seven seats, while Winter’s new Amcha Yisrael Party received six. Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, received five seats and ranked at the bottom of the list.
The bloc breakdown highlighted the challenges facing Netanyahu’s camp. Netanyahu’s coalition stood at 43 seats, the opposition at 59, Winter’s party at six, and the Arab parties at 12. Even if Winter joined Netanyahu’s bloc after the election, it would have reached only 49 seats, well short of the majority needed to form a government.
Several other parties remained below the electoral threshold, but the most significant result was the Religious Zionist Party, led by Smotrich, which received only 2.6%. Zionist Home–The Reservists, led by Chili Tropper and Yoaz Hendel, received 2.1%; Blue and White; Israel First, led by Sharren Haskel; and Unity, led by Gilad Erdan, each received 1.2%, 0.9%, and 0.3%, respectively.
The poll's election breakdown was as follows:
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar: 25
Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud: 21
Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad: 15
Yair Golan’s The Democrats: 10
Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu: Nine
Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit: Eight
Arye Deri’s Shas: Seven
Yitzhak Goldknopf’s United Torah Judaism: Seven
Yousef Jabareen's Joint List, comprising of Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad: Seven
Ofir Winter’s Amcha Yisrael: Six
Mansour Abbas’ Ra’am: Five
Winter's party and Smotrich's party appeal to similar voter bases
Pollster Dr. Menachem Lazar, director of Lazar Research, said Winter’s entry into the race directly pushed Smotrich below the electoral threshold because the two parties appealed to a similar voter base.
“In my estimation, he took approximately one seat from the Religious Zionist Party,” Lazar said.
He added: “The poll also indicates a drastic decline in Gilad Erdan’s strength as a result of Winter’s candidacy. It appears that Otzma Yehudit and United Torah Judaism are also losing votes following the entry of the new player into the race,” he explained.
“Additional votes that Winter is gaining appear, as far as we can see, to come from voters from the Religious Zionist Party who had previously been undecided. Winter is currently perceived as part of the third bloc, and as a result he is managing to draw many seats from the potential voter pool of that bloc,” Lazar emphasized.
Lazar Research, headed by Dr. Menachem Lazar, conducted the poll for Walla in cooperation with the Panel4All online respondents panel.
The poll was conducted on August 26, 2026. A total of 3,189 people were asked to participate, of whom 500 responded, representing a sample of Israel’s adult population aged 18 and above, including both Jewish and Arab citizens. The poll’s maximum margin of error was 4.4%.

Meta reaches $17 billion settlement with US states over social media harm to teens

Meta reaches $17 billion settlement with US states over social media harm to teens
Meta Platforms on Wednesday agreed to pay $17 billion to settle claims, filed by 47 US states, that the company designed Facebook and Instagram to deliberately make teens addicted to their products while deceiving the public, according to state attorneys general. The company agreed to add child-safety measures as part of the settlement.
Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states, state attorneys general announced Wednesday.
California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deal cuts short the trial, which was expected to see CEO Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California.
The agreement is worth $353 million in Virginia alone and is one of the biggest in state consumer protection history, Attorney General Jay Jones said in a statement.
Read moreMeta sued by US states for hooking and exploiting kids in pursuit of profit
“For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health," Jones said. The settlement "will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm”.
Meta did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The $17 billion settlement is a fraction of the company's 2025 revenue of $201 billion.
The lawsuit accused Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hiding them from the public. It also argued that Meta violated federal laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent.
The trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, with US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers overseeing the proceedings. Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, began his testimony late Tuesday and defended Meta’s record and progress on child safety and privacy.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The cases in other states had been expected to go to trial later. In addition, nine attorneys general filed lawsuits in their respective states.
Under the proposed settlement, Meta agreed to adopt a series of safety features, including a “hard cap” on daily time limits and pauses for children using Instagram and Facebook.
It will eliminate push notifications during weekday school hours and bring in “robust” age-assurance measures and “age-appropriate” content controls to prevent bullying and harmful material about eating disorders and self-harm.
There will be stronger and more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social comparison features such as “like” counts.
The federal lawsuit was the result of an investigation led by a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general from California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Vermont. It followed newspaper reports, first by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, that found that the company knew about the harm Instagram can cause teenagers – especially teen girls – when it comes to mental health and body image issues.
Meta has since added a host of safety features to Instagram, including separate accounts for teenagers with stronger protections around messaging and privacy, along with content restrictions.
But child safety experts, along with some former Meta employees, have long contended that the features are little more than window dressing.
Read moreFacebook and Instagram must stop ‘addictive’ features like infinite scroll, EU tells Meta
Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director, said during his testimony last week that Meta consistently prioritised profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being.
“If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money,” he said.
While the four states in the Oakland trial did not officially say how much they had been seeking, Meta said in a court filing that financial penalties in the case could amount to as much as $1.4 trillion – a figure legal experts said was unlikely, if not impossible.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Sweden seeks to seize Russian-owned land by naval base
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:30:24 BST
23:30:24 KST

Sweden’s Armed Forces have asked the government to expropriate a strategically placed property at the entrance to Muskö Naval Base, arguing that its Russian ownership and location create an unacceptable national security risk.
The Swedish Armed Forces have asked the government to expropriate a Russian-owned property overlooking an approach to Muskö Naval Base, saying control of the site is necessary to strengthen protection of the installation against surveillance and drone threats, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The Swedish Fortifications Agency submitted the application on behalf of the Armed Forces on 25 August, seeking government permission to acquire the property through compulsory purchase. Swedish defence officials say the site occupies a unique position at one of the approaches to Muskö, south of Stockholm, and is the only property in the immediate area required for the base’s protection that is not already available to the military.
The property is owned by an individual holding Russian citizenship whom the Swedish Armed Forces say they assess to pose a security threat. Open-source discussion of the site has drawn particular attention to its position on the inlet leading towards the naval area, but the Armed Forces’ formal case rests on the combination of its location, current ownership and the changing threat from uncrewed systems.
Lieutenant General Carl-Johan Edström, Chief of the Defence Staff, said, as quoted in a Swedish Armed Forces news update: “Nothing is more important than Sweden’s security. We are facing the most serious security situation since the end of the Second World War, and the threat to Sweden and the Alliance is real.”
He added: “Against this backdrop, the Swedish Armed Forces have instructed the Swedish Fortifications Agency to apply to the Government for permission to expropriate the property in question.”
Swedish defence officials are placing particular emphasis on the rapid development of Russian drone warfare, arguing that military installations now need protection not only from conventional airborne surveillance and attack but also from small aerial and maritime uncrewed systems that can approach sensitive sites from directions which were previously less difficult to monitor.
The Armed Forces say the property at Muskö represents a gap in that defensive arrangement. Because the surrounding locations are already available to the military, acquiring this final site would allow protection measures around the entrance to the base to be planned as a continuous system rather than around privately controlled land.
Edström said: “A strong defence is essential to our freedom. Unmanned systems can be employed in many different ways—for surveillance and intelligence gathering, as well as for direct attacks. That threat is real and must be countered, not least by establishing robust systems capable of detecting and countering drones around our military bases.”
He continued: “The current security environment requires us to act and not accept the risks associated with the property’s current ownership. The present situation does not benefit Sweden or NATO—it benefits Russia.”
The language used by the Armed Forces is unusually direct, with the application explicitly linking the owner’s Russian citizenship and the military’s security assessment to the case for expropriation. The Swedish authorities have not merely argued that the land would be useful for expansion; they describe it as critical to the effective protection of Muskö Naval Base and say its present ownership creates a risk that can no longer be accepted.
The request also reflects Sweden’s wider adjustment to the security environment since joining NATO, with military infrastructure now considered not only in terms of national defence but also its role in protecting Alliance assets and operations. In its statement, the Armed Forces repeatedly referred to both Swedish and NATO security when setting out the need to bring the property under state control.
The Swedish Fortifications Agency has now submitted the application to the Government Offices of Sweden, which must now consider whether to authorise the compulsory acquisition and determine the next steps under Swedish law.

During a visit to the front lines, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded the Golden Star orders to Heroes of Ukraine Andriy Biletsky and Eduard Kolodiy and presented other state awards to soldiers participating in Oleksandrivka operation.

South Africa saved over 47,000 jobs – minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:25:57 UTC
23:25:57 KST

South Africa saved over 47,000 jobs – minister
South African Minister of Employment and Labor Nomakhosazana Meth has revealed that more than 47,000 jobs were saved over the past year through interventions by the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCMA).
The Minister revealed this in a written reply to Parliament after Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) MP Tebogo Mokwele asked what concrete measures the department had taken to address South Africa’s persistent unemployment. Mokwele also asked what measures had been put in place to hold corporations accountable for exploiting workers and denying them fair wages and benefits, as well as what strategies were being implemented to boost job creation in key sectors such as manufacturing and agriculture.
”The Department has implemented a number of measures to help curb the unemployment challenge. The Department has provided in the last financial year, counselling to more than 357,000 work seekers, more than 116,000 work seekers were placed in employment opportunities,” Meth said.
She added that more than 1.1 million work seekers were registered during the last financial year, while the CCMA’s interventions helped save more than 47,000 jobs. Meth said the subsidy funding allocated by the National Treasury also created 1,215 work opportunities for people with disabilities, while the Labour Activation Programme of the Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) supported more than 174,000 participants and created 93,730 jobs.
On measures to ensure that companies comply with labour laws and protect workers’ rights, Meth said the department’s Inspection Services had conducted more than 309,000 inspections.
”Working with the National Pathway Management Network (NPMN) and the Presidential Youth Employment Initiative (PYEI), the Department aims to create demand in key sectors, including manufacturing and agriculture, amongst others,” she added.
”The NPMN has created more than 96,418 employment opportunities during the last financial year. The Department has also introduced the National Labour Migration Policy and amendments to the Employment Services Act, that will create further employment opportunities for local South Africans”.

MOSCOW, August 26. /TASS/. Russian stocks narrowed losses to 1% during the main trading session on the Moscow Exchange, according to trading data.
The MOEX and RTS indices lost 1.2% to 2,091.83 and 780.19 points, respectively, as the main trading session started, according to trading data as of 10:00 a.m. Moscow time (07:00 a.m. GMT).
As of 3:50 p.m. Moscow time (12:50 p.m. GMT), the MOEX and RTS indices were down by 2.35% at 2,067.32 and 771.04 points, respectively. By 4:15 p.m. Moscow time (1:15 p.m. GMT), the indices had narrowed losses to 0.95% reaching 2,097.03 and 782.12 points, respectively.
The MOEX Index with additional IMOEX2 ticker fell by 0.67% as morning trading session started on the Moscow Exchange as of 7:00 a.m. Moscow time (4:00 a.m. GMT) to 2,103.07 points.

Russians strike business centre in Kharkiv Oblast twice: 10 injured, fire breaks out – photo
Russian forces attacked a business centre in a residential area of the town of Lozova in Kharkiv Oblast, causing a fire and injuring at least 10 people.
Source: Serhii Zelenskyi, Head of the Lozova hromada A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories , on Telegram
Quote: "In Lozova, the enemy struck a business centre in a densely populated residential area. The building caught fire, and nearby apartment buildings were damaged. After waiting for a while, the Russians launched a repeat strike… Ten people are currently known to have been injured, some of them seriously."
Details: According to Zelenskyi, this was a "deliberate attempt to cause the maximum number of casualties", as the Russians struck during working hours and targeted an area with shops, medical and social facilities.
All emergency services are currently working at the scene of the strike.
Zelenskyi urged residents not to ignore air-raid warnings and not to approach strike scenes to avoid exposing themselves to the risk of repeat attacks.
