Saxony-Anhalt a state dominated by the Chemical industry and a strong AfD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:24:00 UTC
23:24:00 KST

Saxony-Anhalt: an AfD stronghold in Germany's east
August 26, 2026
Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage: Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.
Saxony-Anhalt is home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still provides around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the River Elbe, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.
The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.
Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.
Nevertheless, in September 2026, international attention is likely to turn to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, holds a clear lead in all opinion polls.
The AfD is far ahead in the polls
Just before the election, the AfD is polling at more than 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since its re-establishment in 1990, trails far behind, with support ranging between 23% and 26%.
The state office for the protection of the constitution classifies the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters. The Left Party is polling at 13%, while support for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) stands at between 6% and 7%. It remains uncertain whether the Greens and the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP) will succeed in returning to the state parliament.
CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as State Premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said that he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."
The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.
Haseloff's successor, Sven Schulze, also of the CDU, must now take on the AfD. If he fails, the CDU's long dominance of state politics could come to an end in September. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the FDP.
1994 experiment: a minority government backed by the PDS
From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt once again found itself at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the late Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party (SED).
Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.
Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.
Dissatisfaction, demography and immigration
Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in Saxony-Anhalt feel with developments in Germany. In the years following reunification, large numbers of jobs disappeared, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.
Saxony-Anhalt faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.
Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the Statistical Office of Saxony-Anhalt, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.
A long history of far-right support
According to many observers, the DVU's success some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy programme.
Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded. "I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely." In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.
Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script."
One thing seems certain: on September 6, all eyes will be on this small state in the center of Germany.
This article was translated from German.

Meta agrees to pay $17bn in landmark US child-safety settlement deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:23:05 UTC
23:23:05 KST

The tech giant agreed one of the largest consumer protection settlements in US history, ending a trial that could have put Zuckerberg on the stand.
Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion (€14.6bn) and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states, state attorneys general announced on Wednesday.
California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deals have now cut the trial short.
Child safety advocates were hoping to see chief executive Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California.
The settlement is worth $353 million (€302m) in Virginia alone and is one of the biggest in the history of US state consumer protection, according to attorney general Jay Jones.
"For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health," Jones said in a statement.
The settlement "will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm".
The $17 billion (€14.6bn) settlement is a fraction of the company's 2025 revenue of $201 billion (€172bn).
Why was Meta on trial?
The lawsuit accused Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by deliberately designing features that make children addicted to its platforms and of hiding this knowledge from the public.
It also argued that Meta violated federal law by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without parental consent.
The trial began last week in Oakland, California, with US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers overseeing proceedings.
Cases in other states had been expected to go to trial later. Nine attorneys general also filed lawsuits in their respective states.
Under the proposed settlement, Meta has agreed to adopt a series of safety features, including a "hard cap" on daily time limits and pauses for children using Instagram and Facebook.
The company will eliminate push notifications during weekday school hours and introduce "robust" age-assurance measures and "age-appropriate" content controls to prevent bullying and harmful material relating to eating disorders and self-harm.
Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social comparison features, such as "like" counts, will also be introduced.
Instagram under fire
Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, began testifying late on Tuesday and defended Meta's record and progress on child safety and privacy..
Mosseri pushed back as prosecutors pointed to the low take-up of safety tools among young users, including Instagram’s Take a Break feature, which prompts users to step away after scrolling for a certain amount of time.
He said “most teens didn’t want it”, but that “we [Instagram] decided to push forward with it anyway”. An internal memo shared earlier in court that day showed that Meta and Instagram knew opt-in safety features such as Take a Break were not effective.
Mosseri appeared frustrated by the prosecution’s focus on the feature. He acknowledged that some of Instagram’s safety measures work while others do not, adding that there are “no silver bullets” when it comes to safety.
He also argued that “there are many features we launch over many aspects of safety and well-being” that the company seeks to improve over time, including ‘Quiet Mode’ and ‘Take a Break’.
States led the charge
The high-profile case was brought by a coalition of 29 state attorneys general, including those from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. They argue that the social media giant deliberately designed features to hook children, including infinite scrolling, push notifications and “like counts”, contributing to a youth mental health crisis.
The ‘Take a Break’ feature is an in-app tool launched in 2021 that reminds users to step away from scrolling after a set amount of time, with alerts after 10, 20 or 30 minutes of continuous use. It was initially optional before becoming a default setting for teenage accounts in September 2024.
Instagram’s ‘Quiet Mode’, launched in January 2023 and sometimes referred to as ‘Sleep Mode’, silences notifications and works in a similar way to a do-not-disturb setting. It also sends automatic replies when someone tries to contact a user while the feature is activated.
Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, has also been accused of covering up its own internal findings showing that its platforms are addictive and psychologically damaging to teenagers, as well as failing to warn parents and protect children.
Mosseri was also questioned about the so-called ‘Facebook Files’, documents shared by former Meta employee and whistleblower Frances Haugen with the Wall Street Journal in 2021.
The leaked documents revealed that Meta was aware of the platform’s impact on teenagers’ mental health and had done little to address criminal activity and the spread of misinformation.
Big Tech’s Big Tobacco moment
The latest trial follows two other lawsuits involving Meta this year, with the company facing thousands more legal claims.
In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google liable in a separate trial in which Mark Zuckerberg testified, awarding $6 million in damages to a 20-year-old woman referred to as 'KGM'. Meta was held responsible for 70% of the damages.
Her lawyers argued that her compulsive use of YouTube and Instagram since childhood had contributed to severe body dysmorphia, major depression and suicidal ideation."
In another case brought by the State of New Mexico, Meta was fined $375 million (€321 million) in March for allegedly misleading parents and minors about platform safety, and $567 million (€486 million) earlier this month for being a public nuisance.
The court also ordered structural reforms to the company, including measures relating to time restrictions and age controls.

How Sliman Mansour and his fellow artists built a Palestinian art movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:22:00 UTC
23:22:00 KST

Hardly four years after the 1967 Six-Day War, I was stunned by the sudden appearance of a new group of visually striking and contextually strong paintings. The works were by a young artist from the West Bank town of Birzeit. There he stood on the side of the exhibition hall, a handsome, tall, red-haired man, talking humbly about his work. Perhaps few had heard of Sliman Mansour in those days, when he held his first solo exhibition at the East Jerusalem YMCA. But it was my first encounter with Sliman, with whom I would go on to build a long-standing friendship. We worked together alongside other artists to create a Palestinian art movement.
The colorful, large oil canvases in that East Jerusalem exhibition portrayed large, built women in traditional embroidered Palestinian thobes. They stood defiantly in a frontal stance, their heavy feet solidly planted in the earth, their large working hands carrying the crops of the land. The figurative subjects gave Sliman’s works a certain edge, but his sensitive brushwork and vibrant color schemes revealed the high artistry he continued to develop, making him one of the most defining modernist Palestinian artists.
Almost half a century since that first exhibition, Sliman Mansour passed away on August 24, 2026, at the age of 79. In those decades, Sliman was at the vanguard of the art movement and one of its central pillars. In the mid-1970s, he and a few other young fellow artists, most of them fresh art graduates, established the League of Palestinian Artists, the first official art body in occupied Palestine. With Sliman helming the League, voluntarily serving as its president on several occasions alongside other members, the art movement in Palestine gained unequaled momentum.
Being one of a few women members in the League did not deter me from being active and outspoken, although I often felt bypassed when the male members — with Sliman, of course — spent late-night social gatherings together, smoking away and enjoying time of merriment and camaraderie.
In the absence of formal art colleges, academies, exhibition halls, and museums, we, as artists, took it upon ourselves to fill the institutional vacuum by organizing exhibitions in any available public space, usually schools or municipal halls. But the drive to use those spaces was also political: we aimed, through our art, to raise awareness of the national struggle for liberation and an end to the occupation. Through our work, we also wished to plant a love for the land, its culture, and its identity.
There was a thirst among viewers who thronged to those early exhibitions to see such artistic renditions of the national struggle. Sliman once described to me how some visitors stood so close to his paintings that they almost rubbed their noses into the varnish, as if to fully absorb the message the works held.
The exhibitions themselves became increasingly popular, traveling widely from the North of Palestine to the Gaza Strip in the South. Eventually, they crossed borders and appeared at international exhibitions. Solidarity groups also formed partnerships with the League, fostering alliances to promote Palestinian art.
But the art produced by the League wasn’t confined to exhibition halls. Committed to circulating our art as widely as possible, the League printed several artworks as posters for easier dissemination. One of them was Sliman’s iconic Jamal al-Mahamil, or “the Camel of Burdens,” a symbol of endurance and resistance that hangs in countless Palestinian homes to this day — in refugee camps, in villages, in the diaspora.
Sliman Mansour was a prolific painter, producing hundreds of artworks throughout his career, all of them dedicated to Palestine.
His paintings largely honored the endurance and hard work of Palestinian peasant farmers as they went about their seasonal activities, tilling the land, picking olives, harvesting wheat — the trappings of the “sumud,” or steadfastness, that has become synonymous with the Palestinian experience.
The landscape also had its own character in Sliman’s paintings, lovingly depicted in the scenes upon scenes of olive groves in the hill country and the orange groves on the coast. In one of his paintings, a woman hugs a tree whose two branches intertwine, one bearing oranges, the other olives, perhaps insinuating the unity of Palestine from the river to the sea.
Coinciding with the First Intifada, Sliman, with Nabil Anani, Tayseer Barakat, and myself, co-founded the New Visions Collective in 1987. Its primary aim was to find new ways of making art without using Israeli products, in response to the national movement’s call to boycott all products made or purchased in Israel.
We started to use new, unconventional materials for our artworks. Sliman chose to work with mud and straw, adding colorants from natural local herbs and spices. He perfected the production of cracked surfaces from this new amalgam, giving the semblance of parched earth and archeological sites, in a powerful reference to memory and history. As artists, the members of New Visions worked closely together, showcasing our new works at the Hakawati Theater in Jerusalem in 1989. The exhibition later traveled to Germany, Italy, and the United States.
In 1994, Sliman and the rest of us in the New Visions Collective founded the al-Wasiti Art Center in a renovated old home in Jerusalem. For many years, it served as a hub for showcasing Palestinian art and hosting workshops, lectures, and research. I remember the countless meetings and discussions we held to make al-Wasiti a specialized art and cultural venue for the public in Jerusalem and its environs. Its inaugural exhibition, “From Exile to Jerusalem,” featured the works of many important Palestinian artists living in exile and unable to return to Palestine, including Jabra Ibrahim Jabra, Samia Halaby, Kamal Boullata, Vladimir Tamari, Samir Salameh, Naser Soumi, and countless others.
But al-Wasiti was ultimately forced to scale back its activities when access to Jerusalem became off-limits to Palestinians living in the West Bank and Gaza after the Second Intifada, meaning that three of its founders — Nabil, Tayseer, and myself — were unable to reach it. Sliman was left by himself to try to steer the place.
Sliman worked relentlessly, never missing the opportunity to promote Palestinian art. He was also one of the founders of the International Academy of Art-Palestine in Ramallah. He was an inspirational teacher, generously sharing his expertise and artistry with young Palestinians. He traveled widely, becoming an internationally renowned artist and an eloquent ambassador of Palestinian art and culture. He appeared in both the media and local and international arenas, always speaking simply, but with convincing arguments grounded in extensive research.
With his health failing over the last year, I observed Sliman growing weaker and weaker, but never once did the spark in his expression fade. He tenaciously continued his involvement almost until the last day before his departure, holding fast to his sacred mission and love for Palestine.
I’d like to believe that Sliman has now joined other beloved and sorely missed artists and cultural activists who have departed before him: Mahmoud Darwish, Naji al-Ali, Muhammad al-Bakri, Laila Chahid, Hani Joharriyeh, Laila Shawwa, Joumana Huseini, Vladimir Tamari, Samir Salameh, Fathi al-Ghaben, Kamel al-Mughanni, and countless others. They probably will welcome Sliman, cheering him on as he joins them in his eternal abode.
Sliman, do I dare ask you to say hello to each of them? Undoubtedly, you will find a way to lead them into forming another Palestinian Artists’ League up in the heavens.
Your departure will be sorely missed; it will undoubtedly leave a huge physical vacuum in your family, among your art colleagues, and in the Palestinian cultural scene as a whole. But your brilliant art, your luminous personality, your humility, humanity, and your ever-smiling expression will remain with the thousands of people who knew, loved, and admired you.
Ma’ al-Salama, until we meet again.
Rest in Peace, dear Sliman.
Vera Tamari
Vera Tamari is a Palestinian visual artist, Islamic art historian, art educator, curator, and lecturer of Islamic Art and Architecture. She is the co-founder of the New Visions Collective, alongside Sliman Mansour, Nabil Anani, and Tayseer Barakat. Tamari is actively involved in promoting art and culture in Palestine as a member of the League of Palestinian Artists and the New Visions Collective. She founded and directed the Ethnographic and Art Museum at Birzeit University Museum and the Virtual Gallery at Birzeit between 2005 and 2010. She initiated and curated numerous exhibitions, namely the “Palestinian Cities Exhibitions series”, “Framed Unframed,” and “Unlike other Springs.” As an artist, Tamari specializes in ceramic sculpture and conceptual art, and has participated in scores of personal and collective exhibitions since 1974.

Meta agrees to settlement, platform changes in youth addiction case
Meta settles $16.68bn lawsuit over child addiction claims, agreeing to major changes in Facebook and Instagram features.
Meta Platforms has agreed to settle a lawsuit that accused the company of designing Facebook and Instagram in a way that addicted children, misled consumers about safety and collected personal data of children on the platform.
On Wednesday, the social media giant agreed to pay a maximum of $16.68bn as part of a settlement to resolve claims brought in the United States case, championed by a coalition of 29 US states. The case, which started on August 18, was expected to last six weeks.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran, Oman agree on new temporary route in Hormuz
- list 2 of 4Trump threatens Iran’s partners: How do secondary sanctions work?
- list 3 of 4Ukrainian strikes kill 12 in Russia and Donbas, target Wildberries

While 29 states brought the suit, 52 different attorneys general from both states and US territories signed on to the agreement.
US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers agreed to suspend the trial and is “inclined” to approve it but needs time to review it.
Meta has also agreed to make changes to Facebook and Instagram nationwide as part of the settlement.
“Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months. We are talking about time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters, and so much more,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement.
Among these are daily usage limits of two hours for those under the age of 18, which can only be removed by a parent, and nighttime blocks, among other features. Bonta said time restrictions will drop to one hour if other social media giants agree to similar terms. Meta echoed those calls.
“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” CJ Mahoney, chief legal officer at Meta, said in a release.
The platform will hide likes and reaction counts from users below 18 years and remove cosmetic procedure filters. It will also give teens the option to use a non-personalised feed that does not rely on algorithms to recommend content.
The California Attorney General’s Office said that the Mark Zuckerberg-led company would also identify and remove accounts belonging to children under the age of 13.
Advocacy groups praised the decision.
“Real accountability and real consequences are the only things that drive meaningful change and help prevent harm before it happens,” the parents’ advocacy group the National Parents Union said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.
Meta denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement, which still needs court approval. It had faced up to $1.4 trillion in fines in the case, but the coalition had been seeking a penalty closer to $200bn.
The company will pay the settlement over the course of 10 years and will cost the social media giant $10bn in legal fees alone.
The settlement comes after a loss in a comparable landmark case in New Mexico, where a jury ordered Meta to pay $375m in March and another $567m in August.
Meta’s stock tumbled in early trading on Wall Street but has since rebounded. It is up 2.2 percent for the day.

German forces end military mission in Iraq’s Kurdish region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:21:12 UTC

Sahin Demir
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
German forces have ended their military mission in Iraq’s Kurdish region after years of involvement in the international coalition against the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh), the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) Peshmerga Ministry said Wednesday.
A ceremony was held at Stephan Camp at Erbil International Airport to mark the end of the German military advisers’ mission, the ministry said in a statement carried by the Iraqi News Agency.
The ceremony was attended by senior officials from Iraq’s Kurdish region, representatives of coalition countries, and military commanders.
The ministry said the conclusion of the mission came after years of German military involvement in the fight against ISIS in Iraq and Iraq’s Kurdish region.
It praised the German military team’s role in supporting Peshmerga forces, particularly during operations against ISIS.
Germany also provided military and medical assistance as well as logistical and advisory support that helped develop the Peshmerga forces’ capabilities and military infrastructure, the ministry added.
Germany has supported Peshmerga forces in Iraq’s Kurdish Region since the fight against ISIS intensified in 2014, providing military equipment and deploying troops to Erbil to train local forces. The German parliament approved the training mission in January 2015.
The end of the German mission comes as Iraq moves toward completing the second and final phase of the drawdown of the US-led coalition.
Baghdad and Washington agreed in 2024 on a two-phase plan to end the coalition’s military mission, with the remaining coalition mission linked to operations against ISIS in Syria scheduled to conclude by the end of September.
Iraqi officials have repeatedly said the remaining foreign military presence under the coalition will end by Sept. 30.
They have described the deadline as final and said the withdrawal would mark a transition toward Iraqi forces assuming full responsibility for the country’s security, with future military cooperation with coalition countries conducted through bilateral arrangements.
Iraqi authorities have also held talks with German officials in recent days on completing the coalition withdrawal and developing future bilateral military and security cooperation.
The US-led coalition was formed in 2014 after ISIS seized large areas of Iraq and Syria. Iraq declared victory over the terrorist group in 2017, though its remnants continue to carry out sporadic attacks.

Nepal floods, mudslides kill dozens, leave hundreds missing near China border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:19:15 UTC
23:19:15 KST

At least 384 tourists and travellers, as well as soldiers and police, were reported missing in Nepal after flash floods and mudslides near the China border, while at least 157 deaths were confirmed, officials said.
The death toll from the flash flood that struck the Himalayan border region of Nepal and China's Tibet on Wednesday has risen to 157, police said.
Briefing parliament on the disaster, Nepalese foreign minister Sishir Khanal said officials, soldiers and police were among those missing after flash floods swept away their barracks.
The Nepal Tourism Board said separately that it recorded 384 missing people.
Authorities “are working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of the tourists and travellers who were in or travelling through the affected areas,” the board said.
Khanal said 29 police officers and 44 Nepalese army soldiers were also missing after the floods swept away their barracks in Rasuwa district.
According to government estimates, 19 bridges were swept away, and 40 kilometres (25 miles) of road were damaged, along with 13 hydropower projects.
About 200 trucks were also swept away.
Widespread destruction
Khanal said an earthquake struck the border area on Wednesday, triggering an avalanche that “eventually caused the collapse of glacial lakes in the Tibet region of China.”
Beijing identifies the region as the Xizang Autonomous Region.
“Due to the flood, a large number of hydropower projects, government offices and road facilities were erased,” Khanal said.
According to the US Geological Survey, a magnitude 4.4 earthquake struck Kodari village in Nepal, which borders Tibet in China, at 8.37 am local time (0252GMT).
Massive search and rescue operations were launched on both sides of the border.
Those reported missing include people from Nepal, India, the UK, South Africa, Australia and the Netherlands, while the nationalities of many others have yet to be confirmed.
Eight South Korean nationals were “unaccounted for,” while 10 others were stranded following the floods in Nepal, Seoul-based Yonhap News reported, citing South Korea’s foreign ministry.
Khanal said the floods caused widespread destruction in the Rasuwa, Dhading and Chitwan districts.
Mass search, rescue operations underway
“Equipped with helicopters, drones and rafting boards, rescuers from all state forces - Nepal Police, Armed Police and Nepal Army - were deployed to the flood-hit area,” Khanal said.
China’s state-run Xinhua News Agency reported that a mudslide struck near Gyirong Port, a major land port connecting the two countries, in southwest China’s Xizang Autonomous Region.
“The disaster has cut off roads leading to the port on the Chinese side, as well as communications and power supplies,” Xinhua reported, citing the emergency management bureau of Gyirong County in Xigaze City.
Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered “all-out efforts” to search for and rescue people.
Xi also called for efforts to “evacuate residents at risk and provide timely medical treatment to the injured to minimise casualties.”
“Authorities in Xizang have mobilised forces to carry out search and rescue operations. All relevant operations are underway,” Xinhua reported.
It remains unclear how many people were affected on the Chinese side of the border.
In Kathmandu, government-run hospitals and medical facilities operated by security agencies were cleared to accommodate people injured in the disaster.
Tourists travel to the Rasuwagadhi area to trek in the Langtang region, one of Nepal’s most popular trekking destinations.
Other travellers pass through Rasuwagadhi en route to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar in China.

MPs want to scrap far-right TV show over “Hitler was right” item
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:18:23 UTC
23:18:23 KST

MPs want to scrap far-right TV show over “Hitler was right” item
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
TV broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON!) is facing fresh calls to have its licence revoked in the wake of an online panel show that presented Nazi leader Adolf Hitler as an anti-globalist crusader.
The segment, Let’s Twist Again, featured a clip of Hitler delivering a tirade against a “rootless international clique”, prompting one person in the crowd to shout out: “Jews!”
Presenter Arlette Adriani then asked the two panellists, Joost Niemöller and Raisa Blommestijn, to comment on the statement: “The cosmopolitan elite is compelled to take an essentially hostile position towards the ordinary indigenous people”. Both said they agreed.
MPs from the coalition parties CDA and D66, as well as the left-wing opposition party Pro, tabled questions in parliament asking culture minister Rianne Letschert if ON! should be taken off the air.
The public broadcasting ombudsman Margo Smit said she had received around 20 complaints about the item since it was put online on July 31, most of them in the last week.
“This fragment is proof that this broadcaster is deliberately flouting basic standards,” Pro MP Mohammed Mohandis told RTL.
“Nazi propaganda”
Oufa Oualhadj, for D66, said: “This thinking is bound up with Nazi propaganda and the depiction of people such as Jews as the enemy by presenting them as a rootless international force that supposedly undermines national communities.”
ON!’s director-general Peter Vlemmix said Niemöller and Blommestijn had made it clear during the broadcast that they felt “nothing but disgust for Hitler’s regime and the barbaric consequences of it”.
But he admitted that the channel had “not paid enough attention to the sensitivities around this subject”. “We should have approached them more carefully in this video.”
ON! has faced repeated calls to have its licence withdrawn since it started broadcasting in 2022. It has been fined for broadcasting misleading information and was found to have used discriminatory language when it advertised the post of editor-in-chief with the words: “man or woman, no X”.
Blommestijn received a criminal conviction for discrimination for a social media post in which she used the term “negroid primates” to describe a group of black men who were filmed assaulting a white man.
“Complex” position
Last month a majority of MPs from all three coalition parties and Pro called on Letschert not to renew the broadcaster’s licence next year.
Erik van der Maas, of right-wing liberal party VVD, said: “There is no place in the public network for a broadcaster that is funded by taxpayers’ money but systematically breaks the rules and is not prepared to keep to them.”
But the minister said the legal position was “complex” because the public broadcasting service NPO had not asked her to withdraw ON!’s licence. “That does not take away the concerns about Omroep Nederland,” she said.
The channel’s future is due to form part of a debate in parliament on September 24.

United States President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera he has “no time schedule” for when he expects Iran to return to the negotiating table to end the conflict the US began months ago.
“I have no time schedule, none. I’m not in a hurry. I have no time schedule at all,” Trump told Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury on Wednesday, after he was asked how much time he was giving Iran to return to talks.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

“We are winning very big,” Trump said. “They’ve got massive inflation, their economy is falling apart, they’re treating their people very badly, they are killing many, many protesters. I have no time schedule; whatever it takes.”
Asked whether economic measures were more effective than military strikes, Trump told Al Jazeera, “I think they are both effective.”
This Friday marks six months since the US war on Iran began.
The comments depart from previous statements by the US president. After launching the war on February 28, Trump went on to repeatedly downplay how long the conflict would last, saying at one point it would be over in “four to six” weeks.
In June, the US and Iran signed a 60-day memorandum of understanding that was supposed to deal with issues like transit through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting sanctions on Iran and starting talks on how to deal with Tehran’s nuclear programme. That agreement expired earlier this month.
Enhanced sanctions to bring Iran back to talks
On Monday, the US announced enhanced sanctions on Iran and 60 entities in various countries doing business with the country, in what officials have called an “economic D-Day” and the administration has dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast“.

“No honorable state that values its sovereignty and national interests will accept the normalization of such gross lawlessness and systematic bullying,” it said.
The war with the US and sanctions have already made life difficult for ordinary Iranians, who have seen their currency fall at a staggering pace and the prices of essentials like food and medicine skyrocket. The Iranian rial has fallen to a new all-time low against the US dollar, dropping past 2 million rials to $1 on the free market. Before the war, 2 million rials could buy about four kilogrammes (nine pounds) of tomatoes, half a kilo (one pound) of chicken and a little less than a litre (34 ounces) of cooking oil. Today, the same amount buys about half as much, with the average price of tomatoes increasing by 71 percent, chicken by 74 percent and cooking oil by 177 percent.
Analysts have questioned whether the economic measures can force Iran to return to talks with the US. In particular, the US has not targeted major Chinese entities involved in trade with Iran. At least 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports end up in China, netting Tehran tens of billions of dollars in revenue.
When asked this week why the US did not immediately target those Chinese entities, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent responded by saying, “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”
Tehran has proven more resilient during this conflict than Washington expected, analysts say, and new sanctions will likely make things more difficult for Iranians, but are unlikely to force Iran to reach an agreement with the US. “I think they will likely be quite impactful and painful for the Iranian people,” Trita Parsi, the head of the Washington, DC-based Quincy Institute, told Al Jazeera. “But translating that pain into a shift in their policy is a completely different thing.”

2026-08-26

Finland's unemployment rate slumped to the bottom of the EU rankings around the turn of this year, and the level has remained stubbornly above 10 percent ever since.
There were a total of 289,000 unemployed people in Finland last month, with data showing a sharp increase in the number of women looking for work.
But amid all the doom and gloom, there have been some signs that Finland's economy, and the labour market, could be about to bounce back.
Last week, the number of new job vacancies being advertised by potential employers increased on a quarter-by-quarter basis for the first time in more than four years.
There have also been faint rumblings among Finnish economists that a recovery is on the cards.
Finland's employment ministry expects to see improvement in the long-term joblessness situation starting now, before the job market returns to more robust growth in 2027 and 2028.
After years of frustration, there may finally be some light at the end of the tunnel for Finland's jobseekers.

Meta reaches $21.2b settlement over social media harms to children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Meta reaches $21.2b settlement over social media harms to children
SAN FRANCISCO – Meta Platforms agreed to pay a maximum of US$16.68 billion (S$21.2 billion) and make major changes to Facebook and Instagram to resolve claims by states across the US that the company designed those platforms to addict children, misled consumers about their safety and improperly collected children’s personal data.
The settlement resolves claims brought by 29 US states, and will end a federal trial that had been one of the highest-profile tests yet of allegations that social media companies harmed young users.
Meta will impose daily usage limits and restrict night-time usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.
The Menlo Park, California-based company denied wrongdoing in agreeing to settle.
The settlement also resolves lawsuits by California, Illinois, New Mexico and Washington, DC, over privacy claims related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the consulting firm collected personal data of millions of Facebook users.
Those states will receive US$459.3 million to resolve those lawsuits. Shares of Meta rose 2.3 per cent in early trading.
The claims were part of a broader wave of litigation brought by states, local governments, school districts and individuals alleging that Meta and other social media companies fuelled a nationwide youth mental health crisis.
The trial in the Oakland, California, federal court covered claims from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that Meta violated their state laws protecting consumers. It also covered claims from 29 states that Meta violated the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting personal data from users it knew were children without parental notification or consent, and using the data to train machine learning and generative AI models.
Meta has long argued it could not have misled consumers about whether its services were addictive because “social media addiction” is not a recognised psychiatric condition. Before the trial began on Aug 18, Meta said California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were seeking up to US$1.4 trillion in penalties. The states suggested that the figure would be closer to US$200 billion.
A mental health crisis
Meta, Snapchat and its parent Snap, YouTube and its parent Alphabet, and TikTok and its parent ByteDance still face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims they knowingly designed their platforms to have features that addict children and teenagers, fuelling a mental health crisis. A trial in Nashville over claims brought by Tennessee against Meta began in July.
The federal cases were consolidated before US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, and include lawsuits brought by individuals, school districts and state governments.
Earlier in 2026, Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico. A jury in March ordered it to pay US$375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms.
On Aug 6, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional US$567 million and implement youth-safety measures.
Also in March, the first trial over an individual’s claims against Meta and Google ended with a verdict in the plaintiff’s favour. A Los Angeles jury found the companies liable for plaintiff Kaley G.M.’s depression and anxiety and ordered them to pay a combined US$6 million in damages.
The companies have said they will appeal those verdicts. REUTERS

Warsh's first Jackson Hole: Bond yields, a Treasury rescue and inflation that refuses to fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:13:11 UTC
23:13:11 KST

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole address on Friday with long-term borrowing costs elevated, inflation above target and the US Treasury already intervening in bond markets to do what monetary policy has not.
The most closely watched speech in central banking arrives at an awkward moment for the man giving it.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh takes the podium in Wyoming on Friday morning with government borrowing costs high, inflation stalled well above target and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent already stepping into the bond market to hold yields down.
The symposium itself explains why this matters. Hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City since 1978 and held at Jackson Lake Lodge in Grand Teton National Park since 1982, it gathers roughly 120 central bankers, academics and policymakers from more than 70 countries for three days of papers and panels.
This year's theme is "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy". Its significance is one of timing, as the event always falls between scheduled Fed meetings, making Warsh's Friday keynote one of the few moments when policy direction can be signalled outside a formal decision.
The Fed Chair has been unambiguous about the destination.
"There is no soft inflation target," he has said. "There's only a target, and it's 2%."
What he has not offered is a route as five internal task forces are currently reviewing how the Fed operates, including one on communications, and Warsh has so far avoided the forward guidance his predecessors used freely.
Wednesday's data gave him little cover.
The personal consumption expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, rose 0.2% in July against expectations of 0.1%, leaving the annual rate at 3.7% rather than easing to the 3.6% forecast.
Core prices rose 0.2% on the month and 3.3% over the year, both in line, but that keeps core inflation above the 2% target for a 65th consecutive month. Consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to July.
The Federal Open Market Committee held rates at 3.50% to 3.75% in July, but three regional Fed presidents dissented in favour of a quarter-point increase, the most dissents in one direction since September 2016.
Markets have since moved the other way.
CME's FedWatch tool puts the probability of a September hike at around 40%, down from roughly 55% a month ago. Investors are pricing less restriction than the committee's hawks are demanding, and that gap is what Friday's speech has to address.
The bond market is the real test
The pressure point is at the long end of the curve.
US national debt has passed $40 trillion, and yields on 10 and 30-year Treasuries have climbed sharply, pushing up borrowing costs across the economy.
That forced the US Treasury to act.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced plans to at least double buybacks of 10 to 30-year bonds, from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation, reducing the supply of long-dated paper to support prices and pull yields lower.
The market was unconvinced as yields subsequently rose back above where they stood before the announcement which prompted Bessent to immediately state publicly that the US Treasury is ready to intervene with much higher amounts, which he purposely left undefined.
That creates an unusual tension as the US Treasury is intervening to suppress long-term yields at precisely the moment the Fed chair appears content to let market forces do the tightening work.
The debasement trade
When investors suspect a government cannot manage its debts without allowing inflation to erode them, they buy assets that cannot be created at will. Markets call it the debasement trade, and it is having an exceptional run this month.
Gold has gained roughly 15% so far in August and, with only days of trading left, is on track for its strongest month since 1999. It traded near $4,713 an ounce on Tuesday, a three-month high.
Bitcoin is up over 25% this month, its best in around two years, pushing above $80,000.
The dollar has moved the other way, with the index measuring it against six major peers heading for a third consecutive monthly loss.
Hard assets rising, the currency falling and long-term borrowing costs stubbornly high point in the same direction. If Warsh reads market prices as information, as he has suggested he does, the message is that policy is too loose.
Europe's stake in Wyoming
The ECB will also be represented on the ground at Jackson Hole.
Executive board member Isabel Schnabel takes part in a panel discussion at the symposium on Friday at 17:55 CET, addressing the payments and financial innovation theme rather than the immediate policy outlook.
The transatlantic timing matters more than the panel.
The ECB publishes the account of its 22 to 23 July meeting on Thursday, and its next rate decision falls on 10 September, days before the Fed's own September meeting.
A hawkish signal from Warsh would strengthen the dollar and tighten global financial conditions, complicating the calculation in Frankfurt, where policymakers are already managing energy-driven inflation and now face food price pressure building into 2027.
Either way, Friday is no longer a routine central banking speech. It is a test of whether the Fed can persuade markets that 2% remains a genuine destination, and that it has a credible way of getting there.

Frankfurt Airport worker dies after malaria infection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:13:00 UTC
23:13:00 KST

Frankfurt Airport workers die after malaria infection
August 26, 2026
At least two Frankfurt Airport employees have died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by infected mosquitos brought into Germany on an aircraft, according to Frankfurt health officials and Fraport, which operates the airport.
Citing Frankfurt health officials, Germany's DPA news agency reported that the first death occurred in July and that the cause of death was not immediately clear at the time. The second fatality was in August.
The cases are part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria, with six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country.
The other four infected employees are recovering well, health authorities said.
What we know about the Frankfurt Airport malaria death
Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport confirmed the latest death on Wednesday. A spokesperson said the company had been informed by the responsible health authority and expressed "deepest sympathy" to the employee's relatives.
The first four infections became known in mid-July. Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI) for public health said those affected fell ill between July 4 and 6 and that the infections were believed to have been transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by aircraft.
What is airport malaria?
Malaria is a life-threatening disease transmitted by mosquitoes and causes hundreds of thousands of deaths per year, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa.
"Particularly in at-risk groups, the disease can lead to coma and death," Germany's Foreign Ministry wrote in a travel advisory. "Protection against mosquito bites and the taking of preventive medication can prevent the disease."
Treatments for malaria exist and are widely regarded as effective when caught early in the infection.
Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad.
Airport malaria, however, can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area.
The RKI describes such cases as very rare. The last documented case at Frankfurt Airport was in 2023.
Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual.
Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin.
"The mosquito is probably already dead," Peter Tinnemann, head of the Frankfurt health authority, told DPA. "There is no likelihood of person-to-person spread. The risk to the Frankfurt population is negligible."
Still, Fraport has informed employees at the airport and advised them to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms.
Edited by: Rana Taha

San Francisco startup claims two-week build for jet interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:10:46 UTC
23:10:46 KST

- IMPACT Drones says it built a SABLE interceptor prototype in two weeks, according to co-founder social media posts this week.
- The Y Combinator-backed startup launched its Air Defense as a Service offering on August 4 with the HUNTER and SABLE interceptors.
Y Combinator-backed startup IMPACT Drones says it built a working prototype of its high-speed interceptor drone, called SABLE, in two weeks, according to posts by the company’s two co-founders on social media.
Jasper Lortije, whom the company lists as CEO, and Alessandro Fiume, listed as founder, both posted about the prototype this week. IMPACT Drones incorporated nine weeks ago and is part of Y Combinator’s Summer 2026 batch, according to Fiume’s post.
SABLE is designed to reach 750 km/h (466 mph), Fiume said in the post. That figure differs from the 825 km/h (513 mph) design speed the company gave for SABLE at its public launch on August 4, when it first detailed the interceptor alongside a second system called HUNTER.
San Francisco-based IMPACT Drones unveiled its Air Defense as a Service offering at that August 4 launch. The company builds autonomous interceptor drones that ship inside sealed containers, which the company says can be placed at sites such as data centers, airports and power grids. When onboard sensors detect a hostile drone, an interceptor breaks through the container’s lid, launches and rams the target, guided by onboard visual navigation the company says continues to function when GPS is jammed.
HUNTER is described as a close-range, point-defense interceptor with a top speed of up to 300 km/h (186 mph), using electro-optical and long-wave infrared terminal guidance. The company has said HUNTER’s hardware lineage has been used against Shahed-136, Geran-2 and Gerbera-type drones in Ukraine.
SABLE is described as a longer-range pursuit interceptor built around a turbine engine and delta-wing airframe, intended to catch faster threats before they reach a protected site.
“SABLE and HUNTER are the cornerstones of our Air Defense as a Service offering, built to protect critical infrastructure,” Lortije wrote.
“Incoming drones keep getting cheaper and faster. Air defense has to catch up,” Fiume wrote.
“If you are responsible for protecting a data center, airport, or power grid, my inbox is open,” Fiume wrote.
IMPACT Drones is based in San Francisco and has two employees, according to its Y Combinator company profile. Lortije has an aerospace engineering background and previously worked on GNC systems, according to earlier reporting by Data Center Dynamics. Fiume previously co-founded Aerointel, a company building visual navigation and targeting software for autonomous interceptors, and lists $300,000 in revenue from European defense customers on his Y Combinator profile.
The company has said it holds more than $180 million in signed letters of intent, according to its Y Combinator listing. IMPACT Drones has targeted the third quarter of 2026 for pilot deployments of its interceptors, according to Data Center Dynamics.
The company has tied its launch to a string of drone and missile strikes on data centers this year. Data Center Dynamics reported that Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates were struck in March, with a further facility in Bahrain damaged in a nearby strike, and that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps later claimed a cruise missile strike on an AWS data center in Bahrain in late July.
IMPACT Drones has argued that existing air defense systems cost too much to use against low-cost drones. On its Y Combinator profile, the company says legacy effectors cost $1 million or more per shot against drones it values at around $30,000, and that its own interceptors are built to cost closer to the price of the threats they are meant to stop.

Meta agrees to pay US$17 billion to settle teen social media addiction case in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:09:56 UTC
23:09:56 KST

Meta agrees to pay US$17 billion to settle teen social media addiction case in US
Under the proposed deal, the company pledged to adopt a series of safety features for children using Instagram and Facebook
Meta Platforms has agreed to pay US$17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 US states, state attorneys general announced on Wednesday.
California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deal cuts short the trial, which was expected to see CEO Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California.
The agreement is worth US$353 million in Virginia alone and is one of the biggest in state consumer protection history, Attorney General Jay Jones said in a statement.
“For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health,” Jones said.
The settlement “will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm”.
Meta said in a blog post that it was “building on our long-standing efforts to empower parents and support teens”.

MOSCOW, August 26. /TASS/. The jubilee 30th St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF) will take place on June 16-19, 2027, the Roscongress Foundation reported.
"For 30 years, SPIEF has tackled the most pressing issues of the time - from questions of a secure and sustainable future and the challenges of globalization to economic sovereignty and dialogue focused on practical results. The SPIEF agenda has always reflected key changes in the world and the need for coordinated action. I am confident that the anniversary 30th St. Petersburg International Economic Forum will be a major milestone in the history of SPIEF and will create new opportunities for forming partnerships and implementing joint projects," Adviser to Russian President, Executive Secretary of the SPIEF Organizing Committee Anton Kobyakov was quoted as saying.
SPIEF is currently a force that unites the global community on the basis of trust and a commitment to development, he added. "The Forum creates conditions for interaction among all creative forces interested in equal and pragmatic cooperation," Kobyakov said.

Hungary declares Russia a ‘threat’, breaking with Orbán policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:09:21 UTC
23:09:21 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin meets with the Minister of Industry and Trade of Russia (unseen) in Moscow. | Pool photo by Mikhail Metzel/AFP via Getty Images
´Hungary’s government has formally condemned Russia’s military aggression and announced its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity, according to policy guidelines published late Tuesday — marking a sharp break with the Russia-friendly policies of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
“Russia’s conduct poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order,” the document says, adding that Moscow puts the Hungarian minority in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region “in serious danger.”
The guidelines, signed by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, set Budapest’s foreign policy priorities for next month’s U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Advertisement
“Hungary condemns Russian military aggression and fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders,” the document reads. It also recognizes Kyiv’s right to self-defense and backs negotiations toward “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees.”
Magyar has steadily shifted Budapest’s foreign policy since ousting Orbán this spring. He moved to repair ties with Brussels, secured a deal that unlocked €16.4 billion in frozen EU funds and lifted Hungary’s vetoes on reimbursing EU countries for weapons sent to Kyiv.
He also announced a review of Orbán’s landmark Paks II nuclear deal with Moscow earlier this month. Orbán signed the agreement with Russia’s Rosatom in 2014, backed by up to €10 billion in Russian financing.
However, Magyar's government still opposes fast-tracking Ukraine’s EU membership and has sought to slow down accession talks between Brussels and Kyiv.
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said that if negotiations are completed, a referendum would take place to decide whether Hungary agrees to accept Ukraine into the bloc.

Dartmoor firing times
Information on Dartmoor Training Area's firing times.

Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.

Girl, 13, among missing British citizens after flash flood in Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:08:43 UTC
23:08:43 KST

Thirty-three British citizens including a 13-year-old girl are among more than 400 travellers missing after a flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, according to Nepal’s tourism board.
The sudden flood happened on the Tibetan side of the Bhote Koshi River at about 8.30am local time on Wednesday. The 33 UK citizens are among at least 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for.
Earlier on Wednesday, the tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said a 13-year-old girl was among the missing British nationals, as well as two Irish citizens.
Among the missing British nationals are three men aged 65, 64 and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63 and 65, according to travel logs.
The firm, which offers guided tours and expeditions in Nepal, confirmed four of its Nepali tour guides – aged 38, 35, 45 and 29 – are missing as well.
Kumar Adhikari, the manager of Alpine Eco Trek, said on Wednesday: “I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next.
“We are in pain at the moment, deep pain.”
Adhikari said the tour group, who were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash, were crossing into Tibet from Nepal when they became trapped at the border as the flash floods struck.
He said he was in contact with his tour guides until 8.40am when their phones went offline, at which point the group would have been inside Tibet’s immigration office.
“We were hoping that inside it was safe,” he said. “But later the video came from China’s government which (showed) even Tibet’s side was hit by the flood.”
The tourist board said more than 100 of the missing people were yet to have a nationality confirmed.
Police in Nepal said 157 bodies had been recovered and more than 40 people were injured and receiving treatment in hospital.
A wall of mud and rock appeared to have collapsed into the river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and Tibet, triggering catastrophic flooding on the Nepali side, Reuters reported. It said verified videos showed dozens of people being swept away at the border.
Houses, roads and energy infrastructure were destroyed in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties”, with some people missing in the county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a border land crossing.
Initial reports suggested an earthquake had triggered an avalanche and caused the floods, Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister, told the country’s parliament.
Eight South Koreans working on a hydropower plant were missing and 10 others stranded, South Korea’s foreign ministry said.
Local authorities said tourists in the Rasuwa district of Nepal and other areas along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers should “exercise extreme caution”, remain in safe areas and move to higher ground if required.
Visitors were urged to stay in regular contact with hotels and travel agencies. People planning to travel to the affected areas in the coming days were warned to postpone their journeys.
The UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “I am deeply concerned to hear of the flash floods on the Nepal-China border. All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home.”
The British embassy in Kathmandu urged people in affected areas to follow local advice. A joint statement with the embassies of Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland said: “We are deeply saddened by the devastating flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts and surrounding areas. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time.
“We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.”

====================================================================================================

Meta Will Pay Up to $16.7 Billion to Settle Its Social Media Harms Case—and That’s Not All
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:08:37 UTC
23:08:37 KST

Well, that was quick. Not even a quarter of the way into an expected 19-day federal trial over Meta’s alleged failure to protect young users, the social media giant agreed to settle the case. The company has agreed to pay up to $16.7 billion to 51 US states and territories and make substantive product changes for how teens engage with its platforms.
Attorneys general representing some of the 29 US states that had taken Meta to trial announced the deal on Wednesday, shortly before Instagram head Adam Mosseri was set to return to the witness stand. In a separate announcement detailing the settlement, Meta urged YouTube and TikTok to adopt similar changes to their platforms.
The settlement is a stunning development; while other social media services, including YouTube, Snapchat, and TikTok, resolved similar lawsuits out of court, Meta has repeatedly chosen to go to trial. Earlier this year, it lost state trials in California and New Mexico, notching nearly $1 billion in penalties. The company’s first federal trial on the youth issues began last week and threatened to leave the company on the hook for what it estimated to be over $1 trillion in damages.
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” the company wrote in its announcement. “We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that’s why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard.”
“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” said California attorney general Rob Bonta in a statement.
The product changes that Meta has agreed to will apply to Instagram and Facebook and will focus on both features and time limits. Pending judicial approval, teens on Instagram and Facebook will have a two-hour time limit by default across both platforms; they’ll need parental approval to turn it off. Those limits don’t apply, however, to “longform content”—defined as audio or video at least 22 minutes long—or messaging, meaning teens can still DM for as long as they please.
The apps will also be blocked between midnight and 6 am for teens by default, and notifications will be muted between 8 am and 3 pm—from August 15 to June 15—to minimize distractions during school hours. Teens will also get prompts every 15 minutes of continuous screen time, with additional notifications when they hit 60 and 90 minutes of use.
Parents will also have more control over how teens interact with Instagram and Facebook. They can set the default experience to a chronological feed rather than algorithmic and can similarly turn off autoplay by default. Similarly, Meta won’t display the number of likes and reactions on posts by default for teen users. (Bonta described these steps as a “ban” for teens rather than a default setting; it appears that parents will need to approve any changes from the default settings either way.) The company will also disable “cosmetic surgery and extreme makeup filters” for teens.
The $16.7 billion payout comes with an interesting asterisk. While around $12.7 billion of that is guaranteed and will be paid out over 10 years in annual installments, the remainder is contingent on other “core industry members”—defined as Snap, TikTok, and YouTube—implementing similar safeguards. Meta says those changes include a one-hour daily limit, a comparable night mode, and age assurance measures. (If adopted, Meta’s own daily limit will also go down from two hours to one.) TikTok and YouTube would also have to make a combined payment that’s comparable to the amount that’s outstanding from Meta.
All 29 states argued that Meta violated federal child privacy laws by collecting data on users under 13 years old. Four of the states—California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey—alleged Meta deceived parents with misleading statements about protections for adolescent users and that it engaged in unconscionable practices in designing some features for Facebook and Instagram. Meta denied all of the accusations.
The states began presenting their case by calling on current and former Meta employees to describe an alleged culture of maintaining or growing engagement above all else, to the detriment of young users. An academic psychologist testified that adolescents, and especially girls, who spent more hours on social media were more likely to be depressed or unhappy, which contributed to increases in teen loneliness and self-harm over the past 15 years.
This week, the attorneys general coalition zeroed in on Instagram’s well-being team, which has been developing features to address some of the concerns about teen social media use since 2018. Testimony from a former Meta data scientist, current product design director, and veteran executive Mosseri started to show how the states hoped to convince Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, and the eight jurors advising her, that Meta engaged in unfair and deceptive business.
On Tuesday, the focus was largely on a feature called Take a Break, which reminds teen users to limit extended use of Instagram. According to testimony, less than 1 percent of Instagram’s weekly teen users had actually activated the feature months after its launch. Two years in, adoption still sat at only 1.8 percent. Uptake for another usage-limiting feature, called Quiet Mode, was barely any better, documents presented during the trial on Tuesday showed.
As part of the settlement, Meta has also agreed to enforcement measures, including an independent auditor who can relay any concerns to the attorneys general and the development and deployment of more robust tools for parental supervision. The company will also be prohibited from “making further false, misleading, or deceptive statements around its safety features.”

Xinhua Headlines: China's anti-desertification solutions contribute to a greener world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:08:22 CST
23:08:22 KST

ULAN BATOR, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- A giant panda sculpture welcomes visitors to the "China Pavilion" at the ongoing 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) in Ulan Bator, Mongolia's capital.
Inside, photographs, videos and exhibits tell a story that stretches far beyond the pavilion -- how China has been battling desertification at home and is now sharing that experience with countries facing similar challenges.
From restoring degraded grasslands to curbing desert expansion, China's experience is drawing growing international attention, while its technologies, expertise and approaches are finding applications across borders.
CHINA'S DESERTIFICATION BATTLE
One of the countries most severely affected by desertification, China has vast arid heartlands spanning the northwest, north, and northeast, leading Beijing to launch the "Three-North" Shelterbelt Forest Program in 1978 to curb the spread of deserts and restore degraded land.
Since the launch of the program, forest and grass coverage across project areas has reached 40.76 percent, and 67.82 percent of treatable sandy land has been brought under control.
Since 2021, China has restored over 15 million hectares of degraded grassland, and close to 81 million hectares of grassland have recovered through grazing bans and enclosure measures.
Moreover, China's desertification-control efforts in multiple regions have delivered both ecological benefits and tangible gains, including economic returns, for local people in recent years.
Since launching a critical-phase battle to advance the "Three-North" program in 2023, through work-for-relief programs, some 1.526 million farmers and herdsmen have secured jobs close to their homes. A total of 100 projects integrating ecological conservation and industrial development have been carried out. The total output value of forest and grass industries in project areas has exceeded 800 billion yuan (about 119.04 billion U.S. dollars).
Some 3,528 kilometers of desert-crossing highways have been built, bringing 6.8 million mu (about 453,333 hectares) of desert land under control and opening up roads for local farmers and herdsmen to pursue development and prosperity.
In just a few decades, China has evolved from a recipient of international green aid into a major global provider of land restoration expertise, becoming the world's first country to reverse land degradation and shrink its desert footprint.
"China is among the most successful nations in desertification control over the past four decades," said Mishal Al-Fawaz, director of the Environment Protection Directorate of Zarqa Governorate, Jordan, citing the "Three-North" Shelterbelt Forest Program.
Yasmine Fouad, the UNCCD executive secretary who visited China in July, said: "China has become one of the clearest large-scale examples of how land degradation can be reversed."
LESSONS FOR THE WORLD
Nasser Bouchiba, president of the Africa-China Cooperation Association for Development in Morocco, said China's achievements in desertification control reflect not only its technological innovation capacity, but also its governance philosophy of harmony between humanity and nature, balancing ecological protection with economic development.
"Our biggest source of confidence in desertification prevention and control comes from the people-centered philosophy. This approach constitutes our most fundamental advantage," said Jia Xiaoxia, deputy director of the desertification prevention and control department at China's National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
Jia said the advantage has three dimensions: sustained and stable funding to ensure uninterrupted restoration work, long-term holistic planning that enables consistent efforts across generations, and an integrated governance approach that takes into account mountains, rivers, forests, farmlands, lakes, grasslands and sand lands, rather than pursuing isolated, single-track measures.
"Jordan can draw lessons from China's experience in long-term planning, community participation, integrating environmental protection with economic development, leveraging technology and scientific research, and sustained government support," said Al-Fawaz.
"China's experience demonstrates that when restoration is integrated into broader development planning, environmental action becomes an investment in people and prosperity," Fouad said.
"As we move toward COP17, the priority is to translate practical experience like this into stronger cooperation, greater investment and faster implementation, because the scale of land degradation and drought today requires stronger and more coordinated action," she said ahead of the conference.
TAKING CHINA'S EXPERIENCE GLOBAL
Chinese expertise is empowering desertification-control work in many parts of the world. The country's international cooperation framework on desertification now covers policy and governance experience transfer, talent training and capacity-building, technical cooperation, scientific research innovation, and global governance, among others, said Jia.
In Mongolia, China has established ecological restoration demonstration zones, shared practical techniques for planting trees and controlling sand, provided support for saplings, monitored sand and dust, and exchanged knowledge to enhance Mongolia's land rehabilitation efforts.
Meanwhile, China runs international workshops to train desert-control professionals for other nations. It has set up cooperation platforms for China-Arab, China-Mongolia and China-Central Asia anti-desertification work, as well as the Northeast Asia network on desertification, land degradation and drought.
In July, the UNCCD launched the Business for Land China Hub with the China National Sand Control and Desert Industry Society in Beijing, which will help mobilize Chinese enterprises to engage in global land restoration efforts and share China's desertification-control experience.
Sheradil Baktygulov, director of the Institute of World Politics of Kyrgyzstan, noted that China's desertification-control assistance is no empty rhetoric but delivers tangible outcomes.
Chinese technologies, including drip irrigation, irrigation channel water storage and tree cultivation, are spreading across Central Asia and help curb desert spread, said Baktygulov.■

Study finds evolution favors paths that protect against future change
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
22:08:20 CST
23:08:20 KST

JERUSALEM, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Israeli researchers have found that evolution does not choose randomly when there are several equally good ways for organisms to survive, the Israel Institute of Technology (Technion) said in a statement on Wednesday.
In their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the researchers revealed that when different evolutionary routes provide equal advantages, evolution favors paths that make biological systems more resilient to future mutations and environmental changes.
Scientists often view evolution as a process where organisms adapt to better survive in their environment. However, the Technion researchers wanted to explore what happens when competing evolutionary paths yield identical levels of success.
Their findings showed that evolution tends to navigate toward "flatter" areas of the evolutionary landscape. These are regions where subsequent minor mutations are less likely to cause harm.
This means that when presented with equally beneficial options, evolution tends to favor the path that offers greater long-term stability.
The researchers noted that these insights could help explain the natural resilience of biological systems and deepen the understanding of evolutionary dynamics. ■
