Meta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram as it settles US trial over teen addiction for up to $18bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:37:15 UTC
22:37:15 KST

Meta agreed to significant changes to its Instagram and Facebook apps in a settlement that ended a landmark lawsuit on Wednesday. Dozens of US states had accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products.
The agreement curtails a major trial in California and will require the social media company to pay up to $18bn. Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and blocks on nighttime use nationwide in the US.
This is the first time in the US that Meta has been forced to change key features of the experience of everyday users.
The jury trial, which took place in federal court in Oakland, California, began with opening statements just last week. California and 28 other US states sued the $1.36tn (£1tn) company over allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claimed the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.
“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, said in a statement. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms – and will do it within months.”
Bonta said those changes included time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters and more.
The $18bn settlement will be divided between the states over a period of 10 years, subject to court approval. For example, California would receive between $1.5bn and $2.1bn and Colorado will get about $615m.
“The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order,” said Phil Weiser, the attorney general for Colorado, adding: “The focus of this case was to protect our kids.”
Throughout the proceedings, Meta denied all allegations saying states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. On Wednesday, the company’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the settlement reached with the states would only work if all social media companies changed their platform designs.
“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok, Snap, and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement. “As a parent, I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new groundbreaking agreement. But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta’s lead.”
Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap face thousands more similar US lawsuits brought by families, individuals, school districts and other attorneys general. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February, being ordered to pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits that were slated to go to trial this summer, one federal and one in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.
Meta lost a separate suit, brought by the attorney general of New Mexico, where it was ordered to pay nearly $1bn to the state of New Mexico for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms.
The trial in Oakland was expected to last for several weeks with dozens of witnesses taking the stand. Instead, there were only four days of proceedings.
Jurors first heard from the states’ star witness, Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower. He testified that the company had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms.
Béjar said that Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, was aware of the harms of Instagram and Facebook, but that the executive publicly touted the platforms’ safety.
“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.
Zuckerberg had been listed as a witness in the trial but did not testify before the settlement agreement was reached.
On Tuesday, questioning of Adam Mosseri, the Instagram CEO, began with the lawyer for the states accusing the company of touting safety features for teens, but not being forthcoming that young people don’t use them.
When the executive was faced with multiple questions about not disclosing those low user numbers, Mosseri brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”

Iran and Oman reach Hormuz deal, but reopening hinges on US compliance

Iran and Oman have reached agreement on their share of the Strait of Hormuz and its revenues, but the vital waterway will not be reopened if the US does not accept their conditions, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday.
Iran and Oman have held on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strait, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February.

“The Strait of Hormuz belongs to Iran and the country of Oman … We have been in negotiations with Oman for about a month, and we have reached results that are acceptable to both sides,” Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said in comments published by Iranian state media.
“In these negotiations, agreements have been reached regarding the share of each country in the waters of the strait and the share of Iran and Oman in its revenues,” Mohebbi added.
The IRGC accused the US of seeking to obstruct the negotiations between Iran and Oman and said this had caused the agreement to be delayed.
“If the United States stops obstructing and returns to the agreement, we can open the Strait of Hormuz within the framework of the agreement reached … If the United States does not accept our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened under any circumstances,” Mohebbi said.

The Nepal Tourism Board said those missing included 105 Indian citizens, 12 British nationals, three Americans and travellers from Malaysia, South Africa, Australia and the Netherlands. Eight South Koreans were also out of contact, according to South Korea’s foreign ministry.
Reuters reported that the floods struck settlements along the Bhote Koshi river near the Nepal-Tibet border before spreading downstream through Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.
Images and verified footage showed buildings collapsing into muddy water, vehicles being swept away and bridges disappearing under the force of the river.
Nepal’s army said it had mobilised 15 helicopters and rescued 88 people, according to the BBC. High water levels prevented aircraft from landing in some areas during the first stages of the operation.
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told parliament that early information suggested a magnitude 4.4 earthquake struck shortly before an avalanche, which then blocked or displaced water and triggered the flood. Authorities had not confirmed the sequence.
The German Research Centre for Geosciences recorded a magnitude 4.4 earthquake in the area around seven minutes before security footage showed the flood reaching the border crossing, Reuters reported.
Qianggong Zhang of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an ice and rock avalanche in the Lhende Khola river appeared to have triggered the surge. He warned that debris remained upstream, creating a risk of another flood.
The disaster also struck Tibet.
Chinese state media Xinhua reported casualties and missing people around the Gyirong border crossing, where mud and debris cut roads, communications and electricity. President Xi Jinping ordered search operations and stronger monitoring for further hazards. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said at least 574 rescuers had been deployed.
Nepal’s electricity authorities said about 430 megawatts of generation capacity had been affected, including hydropower facilities.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah ordered people living in lower areas to move to safer ground and urged residents along rivers to remain alert.
India also offered assistance. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Indian and Nepalese teams were coordinating rescue and relief work.
Yle reported that Finland’s Foreign Ministry had no information indicating whether Finnish citizens were among those missing. Around 30 travel notifications for Nepal had been filed with the ministry.

Not only Putin and Lukashenko: which world politicians are disliked in Ukraine - poll
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainians have the most favorable views of Macron, Merz, and Erdoğan. They have the most negative views of Putin, Lukashenko, and Trump. Ukrainians’ attitudes toward Russians and Belarusians have worsened since 2022.
Ukrainians have the most negative attitudes toward the Russian and Belarusian dictators, Vladimir Putin and Alexander Lukashenko, as well as toward US President Donald Trump. At the same time, they have the most positive attitudes toward French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. This is stated in the results of a survey by the Rating Group, conducted on August 4–9, 2026, reports UNN.
Details
Sociologists surveyed 2,000 respondents among Ukrainian citizens aged 18 and older in all regions except the occupied territories.
According to the survey, 79% of respondents have a positive attitude toward Macron, 64% toward Merz, and 61% toward Erdoğan. At the same time, 77% of respondents have a negative attitude toward Trump.
Ukrainians have the most negative attitudes toward Putin (97%) and Lukashenko (90%).
Among neighboring countries, Ukrainians expressed the warmest attitudes toward the residents of Moldova (55% warm, 39% neutral), Turkey (45% warm, 48% neutral), and Bulgaria (43% warm, 48% neutral).
Ukrainians most often have a warm (36%) or neutral (39%) attitude toward the residents of Poland. A notable share (24%) has a cold perception.
The coldest attitudes are toward the residents of Russia (91%) and Belarus (70%). Since 2022, attitudes toward them have only deteriorated.
According to respondents, the friendliest countries are the United Kingdom (80%, including 40% who describe their attitude as definitely friendly), Lithuania (77%), France (81%, including 27% who describe their attitude as definitely friendly), Germany (77%), and Moldova (68%).

At the same time, according to a survey by the Russian "Levada Center", Russians' trust in the authorities and President Putin is declining, especially among young people. Ban on trade with Iran could destabilize global economy — NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:35:36 UTC
22:35:36 KST

NEW YORK, August 26. /TASS/. Imposing a complete ban on trade with Iran could destabilize the global economy, The New York Times (NYT) reported.
Enforcing sanctions entails numerous problems, and in case of Iran, it risks confrontation with "allies and powerful rivals capable of retaliation, most notably China," according to the publication. A complete ban on trade would create even more difficulties, the report said. According to experts, the policy of sanctions against Iran is unlikely to succeed without cooperation from China and India, Tehran’s key trading partners. "I don’t think that’s going to happen," Alan Eyre, a former US diplomat and Iran expert, told the newspaper.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on August 24 that Washington planned to sharply tighten its unilateral sanctions regime against Iran, aiming to completely block Tehran’s revenue sources. The US would be prepared to impose secondary sanctions on any countries refusing to comply with new restrictive measures against Iran, Bessent said. He also threatened such nations with a loss of access to the dollar.
On Monday, the US administration added 48 legal entities, 24 individuals, and six oil tankers to its sanctions list against Iran. Citizens and companies from Azerbaijan, Greece, India, Iran, China, Malaysia, the Marshall Islands, the UAE, Singapore, Turkey, Ukraine, France, and Switzerland were blacklisted.

Israel expels Dutch team from Gaza observatory over sanctions
Unknown

2026-08-26
13:34:29 UTC

Breadcrumb
Netherlands doubles down on settlement sanctions as Israel expels Dutch from Gaza observatory
The Netherlands' foreign minister has doubled down on his country's sanctions against Israel after his Israeli counterpart announced the expulsion of Dutch personnel from a ceasefire monitoring centre for Gaza.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen told local media this week that Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar's announced expulsion of Dutch observers from the Kiryat Gat observatory was "unnecessary", and that his country would uphold its sanctions against Israel.
"We will (have to) respect this decision by Israel, but we will continue to commit ourselves to the best of our ability and in every way possible to the implementation of the 20-point plan and humanitarian aid for the people in Gaza," Berendsen said in comments relayed to The New Arab by the Foreign Ministry.
"This will not affect the decision of the Netherlands to ban products from illegal settlements," he said, adding that he viewed the decision in the context of Israel’s upcoming elections in October.
Sa'ar announced the decision to expel Dutch personnel from the US-backed International Support Centre for Gaza on Tuesday, citing "anti-Israel measures" pursued by the country, including the prohibition of trade with settlements in the illegally occupied West Bank, Golan Heights, and East Jerusalem.
The Dutch decision to ban trade with illegal settlements comes into force on 22 September, having been made in July. The Netherlands has also banned far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from entering the country.
The centre, which has observers from several countries, including the UK, the US, Egypt, Germany, and Jordan, among others, was set up in October 2025 to monitor a ceasefire in the enclave and facilitate the delivery of aid into Gaza.
Spanish personnel were similarly expelled in April from the centre, with Spain being one of the foremost critics of Israel's war on Gaza and policies in the occupied West Bank in Europe.
Alongside the announcement, Sa'ar added: "Those who act against Israel will have no foothold in the region. Israel will not allow measures to be taken against it without a response."
The spat between the two countries is the latest in a deterioration of Israel's diplomatic relations, particularly with Western states, prompting fears within Israel of it becoming a pariah state.
Ongoing settler terrorism against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has caught the attention of Western media outlets and politicians, alongside the expansion of Israeli settlements and the release of tenders for the E1 settlement east of occupied East Jerusalem.
The EU is actively considering a series of bloc-wide measures against Israeli settlements, while the UK is reportedly drawing up new sanctions ahead of the Labour Party conference in September, according to The Times.
This comes after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband warned the UK would "set out a comprehensive set of measures to respond to Israeli government policies".
A joint statement from 21 Western governments and the EU on Thursday also condemned Israel's plans for the E1 settlement, which would split the West Bank in two and has prompted fears it would kill a potential two-state solution.

Taiwan legislators to vote on military drone bill after negotiations fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:31:55 UTC
22:31:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Legislators will vote Thursday on a bill supporting drone and uncrewed vehicle industries after party negotiations failed to resolve disputes over oversight, funding, and spending.
CNA reported that Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) held cross-party talks Wednesday on 14 versions of the bill submitted by the Cabinet and political parties. Legislators also agreed to move Friday’s legislative session to Thursday because of the approaching Typhoon Saudel.
The main disputes involve which ministries should oversee the program, whether funding should come from regular annual budgets or a special budget, and how much money should be allocated. After nearly 30 minutes of private talks, Han focused the negotiations on those three issues.
TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said his party supports giving the defense ministry responsibility for defense procurement, research, technology imports, cybersecurity reviews, and testing. The party also favors annual budgets, with government agencies setting funding levels based on need, per UDN.
KMT Legislator Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said the party wants the bill to cover both defense procurement and industry development. She said the economics and defense ministries could each oversee areas under their responsibilities.
The KMT supports annual budgets and proposes NT$240 billion (US$7.5 billion) over six years, or NT$40 billion a year. Hsu said this approach would allow the legislature to review spending every year.
DPP caucus whip Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said the economics ministry should oversee industry development, supply chain upgrades, and domestic production. He said it could also be reasonable for both the economics and defense ministries to share responsibilities, per Economic Daily News.
However, Chuang said a special law and special budget would be more suitable for a long-term program requiring continued defense planning. Unlike regular annual budgets, a special budget could provide separate funding for the multiyear program.
Han ended the talks after the parties failed to reach an agreement and said the bill would be handled during Thursday’s legislative session. Legislators are expected to settle the remaining disputes through votes.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tickets for expanded high-speed rail service during the Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers’ Day holiday period will go on sale at midnight Thursday.
The six-day schedule runs from Sept. 24–29 and adds 176 trains — 70 southbound and 106 northbound — bringing the total to 1,150 services, according to Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation.
Passengers without reservations can check projected waits for nonreserved seating through the high-speed rail website, T-EX app, or Line Today before traveling. Station screens will identify the nonreserved cars on each train, which will be numbered between two and nine. Capacity north of Taichung will be increased at busier times, with additional staff deployed to direct passengers.
Thirteen services will reach their final stops after midnight, with the latest arrival scheduled for 12:59 a.m. Only Cars 11 and 12 will be available for nonreserved travel on these trains.
The affected services are southbound trains 1337 and 1297 on Sept. 24; northbound trains 1336, 1698, and 1296 on Sept. 27; and northbound trains 1336, 1338, 1698, 1296, 1340, 1712, 1588, and 1298 on Sept. 28.
TGo rewards and some group offers will be unavailable. Early-bird and student discounts and limited business-class upgrades remain, and booking is recommended for reserved seating.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Uber said Wednesday it has expanded its service to all 19 cities and counties on Taiwan’s main island in July, 13 years after launching in the market.
Uber Taiwan General Manager Cesar Molina Leguia said the company’s next priorities are “everywhere” and “everyone,” with no plans for another acquisition in the near term, per CNA. Following its acquisition of Crown Taxi, he said Uber will instead focus on integrating its resources and strengthening its services in Taiwan.
Uber said annual trips in cities outside Taiwan’s six special municipalities rose more than 30% over the past year, with Keelung and Miaoli recording growth of nearly 50% each. Overall, annual trips through Uber’s taxi service increased nearly 44% year-on-year.
The company said it has accumulated more than 2.6 billion kilometers in trips since launching in Taiwan, equivalent to about 600,000 round trips between Taipei and Tokyo, per Tai Sounds. Uber also said its Uber Courier parcel delivery service has seen trips rise to 2.8 times the level of the same period last year, while airport trips increased more than 30%.
Uber said it now offers ride-hailing across the main island along with services including Uber Courier and Uber Pet. It said a vehicle typically arrives about three minutes after a ride is requested.

LONDON, August 26. /TASS/. Up to 70 vessels are waiting near the Danube’s Sulina Canal to access Ukrainian ports and load grain for export, Reuters reported, citing sources.
After access to several Ukrainian Black Sea ports was restricted, a significant share of dry cargo vessels was rerouted to Danube ports, which have far lower capacity, the agency said.
As of August 25, more than 50 vessels were waiting to pass through the Sulina Canal, while only five to seven vessels per day were proceeding to Ukrainian Danube ports, agricultural consultancy ASAP Agri said. Each day of delay costs about $8,000, substantially increasing freight rates for companies.
Reuters added that the situation with Ukrainian grain exports could worsen in the coming days, as shipping agents at Danube river ports plan to close access to them for at least two days because of deteriorating weather conditions.

National Taiwan University Hospital responds after patient dies awaiting bed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:31:43 UTC
22:31:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) plans to establish a 20-bed transition ward and increase monitoring of long-stay emergency patients after a woman died while waiting 12 days for an inpatient bed.
Her condition worsened before a bed became available and she died of septic shock, TVBS reported. The hospital acknowledged that its emergency department had recently been overcrowded and some patients had waited more than 10 days for admission.
Patients kept under observation for more than 72 hours will receive more frequent and intensive monitoring and intervention, per TVBS. NTUH also intends to speed up discharges to improve bed turnover and strengthen transfer channels with Taipei City Hospital and other partners.
Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said NTUH was the only one of the Taipei area’s nine medical centers experiencing overcrowding. He plans to meet NTUH Superintendent Yu Chung-jen (余忠仁) and Taipei Department of Health Commissioner Huang Chien-hua (黃建華) to discuss how to manage hospital admissions as well as cooperation with other facilities, per CNA.
Asked about allegations that hospital wards “cherry-pick” less complicated patients while others remain in the ER, Shih said he could not rule out isolated cases, per UDN. Chief residents currently assess admissions for their respective departments, but the process should be standardized as much as possible, he said.
Shih urged patients to consider transfers when doctors determine they are medically appropriate. In response to a question, he noted that urgent care centers operating on Sundays and national holidays are among the many strategies used by the ministry to address ER overcrowding.

Mooncake orders spark fight over Taiwan president’s discretionary fund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:31:25 UTC
22:31:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Spokesperson Wu Cheng (吳崢) criticized opposition lawmakers Wednesday for encouraging purchases of mooncake gift boxes from sheltered workshops, saying the purchases could not make up for the impact of cuts to the State Affairs Fund.
KMT lawmaker Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲) proposed and secured approval for an NT$10 million (US$314,252) reduction and an NT$20 million freeze in the Presidential Office’s State Affairs Fund, per UDN. She said Sunday that the frozen funds would be released if President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) promulgated laws that Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) had refused to countersign.
Under Taiwan’s Constitution, the premier can ask the legislature to reconsider passed bills. If the legislature upholds a bill after reconsideration, the premier must accept it. If the Cabinet believes a bill may violate the Constitution, it can refer the legislation to the Constitutional Court for a ruling on its constitutionality.
Weng’s proposal drew criticism. Political commentator Huang Wei-han (黃暐瀚) noted that former President Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) had also used discretionary funds for charitable purposes with the backing of KMT lawmakers, per Liberty Times. Huang said Lai could not promulgate a bill into law if Cho refused to countersign it. He added that the president has the constitutional authority to appoint the premier.
The Parents’ Association for Persons with Intellectual Disability criticized the opposition’s budget cuts for their potential impact on sheltered workshops, per UDN. While acknowledging the need for government oversight, the association said vulnerable groups should not bear the political cost of disputes between political parties.
The association also called for greater integration of workers with disabilities into society. Rather than relying on seasonal orders, it said consistent year-round demand could allow workers to contribute more fully to the economy instead of depending on charitable support.
Opposition lawmakers and municipal officials have promoted additional purchases from charitable organizations and sheltered workshops. KMT Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) said the KMT makes such purchases every year and would be willing to contribute more, per FTNN.
Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) accused the Presidential Office of “maliciously” canceling the orders, per ETtoday. She said the Taichung City Government would step in to cover losses suffered by charitable organizations in the city.
DPP lawmaker Wang Shih-chien (王世堅) pushed back against Lu’s characterization, saying the government was forced to cancel the orders rather than doing so with malicious intent, per Newtalk. He called on both political camps not to tarnish charitable efforts with unfair political framing.
Wu said the opposition’s efforts to make up for the roughly 15,000 canceled orders from sheltered workshops showed that opposition lawmakers understood the consequences of their cuts, per Tai Sounds. He argued that the controversy ultimately stemmed from what he called unreasonable reductions to the government budget.
KMT lawmaker Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) rejected the DPP’s attempt to link the budget reduction directly to charitable purchases, per NOWNews. She said the government is already required to allocate a certain percentage of its procurement to charitable organizations or sheltered workshops, meaning the State Affairs Fund cuts should not necessarily have such a significant impact on sales.
Hsu nevertheless urged the opposition to be cautious about its cuts, noting that the loss of even a single order could harm organizations serving some of society’s most vulnerable people. If alternative funding is available to support sheltered workshops, she said, the issue should not be framed simply as whether the government can make purchases without using the State Affairs Fund.
Hsu said the central issue should instead be whether public budgets are being used properly and whether the government’s existing programs effectively support vulnerable groups.

Why US visa pause could have ‘real consequences’ for Asian applicants

Why US visa pause could have ‘real consequences’ for Asian applicants
Observers warn the pause ‘risks months of cascading delays’ for Asian countries with large numbers of pending applications
Asian workers and families already facing years-long waits for US visas could be pushed deeper into uncertainty by a global pause on immigrant visa appointments, as President Donald Trump’s administration tightens legal immigration through new screening and higher costs, experts warn.
The US State Department on Tuesday said it had launched a global training initiative for consular officers at all US embassies and consulates, and that immigrant visa appointments would be adjusted to accommodate it.
The department did not specify the scope or duration of the training, beyond saying it was intended to help officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits and ensure they were evaluated “comprehensively and consistently”.
Immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates have begun receiving notices that their appointments are being rescheduled, with new dates to follow, according to reports.
The disruption has left applicants uncertain not only about when they will be interviewed, but also whether documents tied to existing appointment dates – including police clearances, medical checks and financial records – will need updating.
For Asian applicants, experts say, the impact could be especially acute in countries with large visa pipelines and already crowded consular calendars.
“It’s not clear if this is being handled embassy by embassy or centrally. The Asian countries with the largest number of pending applications will likely be hit the hardest,” said Russell A. Stamets, a partner at the New Delhi-based law firm Circle of Counsels.

Army comms programme hit red rating after Morpheus pause
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:30:21 BST
22:30:21 KST

The Army’s wider tactical communications programme received a red delivery confidence rating in February 2025, while the paused Morpheus project had already cost around £766 million.
The British Army’s Land Environment Tactical Communication and Information Systems programme was given a red delivery confidence assessment in February 2025, prompting a strategic reset after Project Morpheus had already been paused with expenditure of around £766 million, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The details are contained in a letter dated 17 August 2026 from Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard to Conservative MP Mark Francois, deposited in the House of Commons in response to three parliamentary questions concerning the performance of the LETacCIS programme, the costs associated with Morpheus and the measures being taken to sustain the existing Bowman tactical communications system.
Pollard said the wider LETacCIS programme underwent an Infrastructure and Projects Authority-sponsored Gate 0 Review in February 2025, which resulted in a Delivery Confidence Assessment of RED. The subsequent review made several recommendations, including what the minister described as a strategic reset of the programme, after which the Army began work against those recommendations before a follow-up assessment was conducted in July 2025.
Pollard wrote: “I can confirm that in February 2025, the LETacCIS programme undertook a routine Infrastructure and Projects Authority sponsored Gate 0 Review which delivered a Delivery Confidence Assessment rating of RED. The subsequent report made several recommendations which included a strategic reset of the programme.”
He continued: “The Army immediately took action against the recommendations, and progress was later assessed in a follow up review in July 2025. Having demonstrated significant progress against all recommendations, the programme was reassessed as AMBER.”
The letter also provides a clearer figure for spending on Project Morpheus, which was intended to replace and modernise elements of the Army’s Bowman tactical communications architecture. Pollard confirmed that Morpheus was paused following the conclusion of the Evolve to Open Transition Partner contract in December 2023, by which point approximately £766 million had been spent on the project.
He said: “The MORPHEUS project paused on conclusion of the MORPHEUS Evolve to Open Transition Partner contract in December 2023. At that point, spend to date on the project was c.£766 million.” Pollard added that commercial sensitivities prevented the Ministry of Defence from providing a more detailed breakdown of expenditure across development, industry partnerships, external advice and sustainment activities.
The minister stressed that Morpheus formed only one part of the wider LETacCIS programme and said the Army had continued pursuing its underlying objectives since the end of the Evolve to Open contract. Rather than proceeding through the original Morpheus structure, tactical communications updates are now being delivered through what Pollard described as an iterative and incremental approach under the revised Land Domain C4 sub-portfolio.
The document also addresses the position of Bowman, which remains in operational use while the Army develops its replacement arrangements. Pollard said the Ministry of Defence had continued to meet operational requirements despite delays to Morpheus, with the Bowman Combat Infrastructure and Platform project being used to make incremental changes addressing known obsolescence and security issues.
Pollard wrote: “Despite the delays experienced by Project MORPHEUS, the Ministry of Defence has continued to meet all operational requirements. Through the BOWMAN ComBAT Infrastructure and Platform (BCIP) project, iterative and incremental updates continue to be undertaken to address known obsolescence and security requirements.”
He added: “These updates will ensure BOWMAN remains a capable and credible system until replaced. There are currently no plans to extend BOWMAN’s out of service date.”

Painting conservator: Soviet‑era artists had to paint with whatever materials they could get
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Painting conservator: Soviet‑era artists had to paint with whatever materials they could get
Polina Richter, a painting conservator at Kumu art museum who is researching Soviet‑era oil‑painting materials for her master's thesis, says that the scarcity of supplies in that period forced artists to invent creative solutions.
Richter is studying in the master's program in heritage protection and conservation at the Estonian Academy of Arts and is currently writing her thesis. Her research focuses on the materials used in Soviet‑era oil paintings — specifically the peculiarities of material use at the time and how artists obtained what they needed.
Richter said artists working during the Soviet period mainly got their materials from the Artists' Union shop. Quantities were limited, and artists were often allocated a fixed amount of specific paints. "Many came up with quite interesting solutions because of the lack of materials," she said.
She has not heard of artists making their own pigments when supplies ran out. "But certainly someone may have gone that far," she added.
Dentist tools in the conservator's toolbox
Richter's work at Kumu centers on preparing paintings for exhibitions. Many works have already been conserved, but some were restored decades ago and need to be reassessed before being shown again.
"Unfortunately, time does its work, so they need a bit of touching up again for the exhibition," she said.
Richter compares painting conservation to treating a patient. First, the conservator must determine the artwork's history and current problems, then choose the appropriate methods to address them.
Kumu's painting department has four staff members. The museum also has departments for paper, sculpture and frames. Workload varies throughout the year — autumn and spring are busier because more exhibitions are prepared then.
Before an exhibition, conservators assess which works need preparation and whether there is enough time to restore them all. The job also involves working closely with curators, storage staff and other museum employees.
Removing old varnish not always a necessity
A conservator's toolbox includes chemicals, primers and paints. "One of the most interesting things conservators use are actually dentist tools — something you wouldn't expect, but they're great for picking and doing fine detail work," she said.
Every intervention must be carefully considered. For example, removing old varnish is a decision conservators discuss thoroughly.
"Varnish is generally part of the painting. Since varnish yellows over time and undergoes various changes, you have to look very carefully at whether it should be removed at all," Richter explained.
If the materials of a work are not well known, tests are done before starting. Samples may be examined under a microscope or sent to a lab if needed.
Unexpected situations can arise during conservation. "These are usually accidental and human. They don't happen often, but the team tries to find solutions. And since we're conservators, we have to fix them ourselves," she said.
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Argo Ideon
Source: ERR interview by Bert Järvet and Margus Kamlat

Russian soldier sentenced to 10 years in prison for taking woman hostage in Kupiansk
A Russian prisoner of war has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for taking a local woman hostage and threatening to kill her and another woman during Russia's renewed offensive on the town of Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast in September 2025.
Source: Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office; Ukrainska Pravda sources
Quote: "Ten years of imprisonment – that is the sentence handed down by the court following the public prosecution brought by the Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office against a 54-year-old Russian serviceman. He was found guilty of ill-treatment of the civilian population, as well as another violation of the laws and customs of war (Article 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)."
Details: According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, the serviceman is Russian national Aleksandr Erzin, 54.
The Prosecutor's Office said that at the time of Russia's renewed attempt to capture Kupiansk, Erzin was a rifleman with the 121st Motorised Rifle Regiment of the 68th Motorised Rifle Division of the Russian Armed Forces' 6th Army.
The investigation established that the Russian soldier entered a local police station building and set up a firing position on the third floor.
After seeing two local women in the street, the serviceman forced one of them to come upstairs at gunpoint. He initially questioned the woman about her personal details and why she was in the vicinity of the police station, then ordered the other woman to bring him food, threatening to kill the hostage.
While the Russian soldier held one woman under armed guard, the other went home to get food and brought it to the police station.
The serviceman then questioned the women again, learned their addresses, and ordered them to bring him more food in a week's time. He threatened to come to their homes and kill them if they refused.
On the appointed day, the women returned to the police station with some food, but by then the Russian soldier had been captured by Ukrainian troops.
Background: Russian serviceman Sergei Karpilovich is standing trial in person in Ukraine on charges of raping a Ukrainian woman while she was living under Russian occupation.

How Taiwan Became Singapore’s Largest Trading Partner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

In 2025, Taiwan overtook China as Singapore’s largest merchandise trading partner for the first time. According to Singapore’s Ministry of Trade and Industry, bilateral trade reached approximately S$170.3 billion (US$134 billion), ahead of Singapore’s trade with China (S$162.9 billion) and Malaysia (S$145.0 billion). One year earlier, Taiwan had ranked fourth.
Singapore values Taiwan as a node in a diversified economic portfolio, but official diplomacy remains limited within the One China framework and Singapore has no incentive to revisit it.
The AI Boom
Much of the bilateral trade between Singapore and Taiwan involves the semiconductor industry. Both Taiwan and Singapore have heavily invested in their AI industries to take advantage of the global AI boom. Taiwan’s semiconductor industry accounts for over 60 percent of global foundry revenue and more than 90 percent of leading-edge chip manufacturing, while Singapore has built out its AI ecosystem to include public research, public service adoption, and diffusion into commerce and industry.
In 2025, roughly 80 percent of Taiwan’s exports to Singapore were semiconductors and related products, while about 60 percent of Singapore’s exports to Taiwan consisted of semiconductor equipment and intermediate goods. The surge in trade runs both ways. Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports to Taiwan last year grew 37.4 percent – the strongest performance among its major trading partners.
As both economies occupy different stages in the AI supply chain, they have formed a highly complementary and closely linked cooperative network in Asia’s AI industry chain. Taiwan fabricates the overwhelming share of the world’s leading-edge logic chips through TSMC and its foundry ecosystem. Meanwhile, Singapore supplies equipment, materials, assembly, advanced packaging, and test capacity, and operates as the regional logistics and headquarters hub through which chips and inputs circulate.
Both parties have also implemented national AI strategies that will end up strengthening this complementarity. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong recently established a National AI Council alongside a series of national AI missions in advanced manufacturing, financial services, connectivity, and healthcare. Singapore also unveiled the world’s first governance framework for agentic AI at the World Economic Forum in January 2026, positioning itself as a standards-setter in AI.
Concurrently, Taiwan has developed a Ten AI Initiatives Promotion Plan, an interagency effort that channels funding into silicon photonics, quantum technology, and AI robotics while building the infrastructure, talent, and capital to make Taiwan a “smart technology island.” Each set of measures raises domestic demand for end-use AI and embeds it in existing business models, feeding a cycle of rising demand and supply across both economies.
However, trade would never have scaled this quickly if the foundation hadn’t been laid years in advance. Under the agreement between Singapore and the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu on Economic Partnership (ASTEP), signed in November 2013, Singapore eliminated tariffs on all Taiwanese imports, while Taiwan phased out duties on nearly all Singaporean goods, including electronics, machinery, and chemicals. ASTEP also streamlined customs and rules of origin for electronics, protected covered investments against forced technology transfer and local-content requirements, and enabled digitally supplied services without requiring a local office.
Meanwhile, Taiwan’s New Southbound Strategy, implemented under former President Tsai Ing-wen’s administration, leveraged Singapore as a regional platform for Taiwanese investment and technology to expand into ASEAN and South Asian markets.
Capital Flows
In addition to technological partnership, two-way financial flows between Taiwan and Singapore have shown significant increase. Taiwan’s economy grew 8.7 percent in 2025, its fastest rate in 15 years, and the Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index (TAIEX) more than doubled to a total market capitalization of US$4.4 trillion. The combined wealth of Taiwan’s 50 richest individuals rose 56 percent in a single year to a record US$308 billion, up from US$197 billion. KPMG Taiwan and E.Sun Bank project Taiwan’s high-net-worth population at 124,000 in 2026, holding combined assets of NT$46.1 trillion (US$1.47 trillion).
Much of that capital is being invested abroad. Hong Kong, once the default for Taiwanese wealth, has lost its appeal as Beijing has tightened political control. Now Singapore is taking Hong Kong’s place in Taiwanese investment portfolios. More than 80 percent of Taiwanese offshore assets were once concentrated in Hong Kong, but today 60-70 percent are managed in Singapore, amounting to roughly US$326 billion. Singapore’s combination of political stability, low tax rate, mature private banking systems, and accessible residency pathways has made it the preferred alternative.
In addition, Singapore ranked as the largest foreign investor in Taiwan from January to July in 2026 with US$8.66 billion, accounting for 62.2 percent of inward Foreign Direct Investment during the period.
Taiwan and Singapore’s Strategic Outlook
While this unprecedented rise in trade owes in part to favorable economic tailwinds, it also reflects how both governments are managing national security and vulnerability in a region increasingly organized around geopolitical and technological competition.
For Singapore, the relationship fits into its broader strategy of economic diversification, even as it rejects the idea of taking sides. Singapore has consistently resisted pressure to frame its choices as being either pro-American or pro-Chinese. Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan described the objective as remaining “relevant” and “useful” to multiple partners, maintaining Singapore’s “strategic choice” and “strategic autonomy.”
Deeper economic ties with Taiwan can therefore be understood within that framework. Singapore wants to participate in the AI economy through relationships that span Taiwan, China, the United States, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia rather than depending on a single technology bloc. Taiwan’s value to Singapore is that it serves as another high-value economic partner, particularly in a sector that will shape future economic and military power.
Increased trade with Taiwan, however, doesn’t mean that Singapore is tilting away from Beijing. China is still Singapore’s second-largest merchandise trading partner, and the two maintain extensive political ties. Moreover, Beijing has generally tolerated Singapore’s substantive unofficial ties with Taiwan when they remain consistent with Singapore’s One China policy, only objecting when interactions appear to carry greater political symbolism.
For Taiwan, maintaining key economic relationships remains important in preserving its relevance to the world. Under President Lai Ching-te’s administration, “active diplomacy” and economic “indispensability” are two pillars of an emerging Taiwanese grand strategy. By embedding Taiwan more deeply in its partners’ technology ecosystems, Taipei gives foreign governments and firms a material stake in its continued autonomy and cross-strait stability.
Singapore therefore matters not simply as a buyer of high-end Taiwanese products, but as a regional financial, logistics, and manufacturing hub through which Taiwanese firms can extend their reach and remain central to Asia’s AI economy.
Nonetheless, Taiwan should not expect the diplomatic status quo to change. Singapore maintains firm support for the One China policy at the highest level. In October 2025, following a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Wong’s office stated that Singapore “has a clear and consistent ‘One China’ policy and is opposed to Taiwan independence.” In January 2026, Senior Minister (and former prime minister) Lee Hsien Loong restated the same formula at the Regional Outlook Forum, saying that Singapore upholds the One China Policy and is “against Taiwan independence” and “against unilateral changes to the status quo.”
Showing the complexity of the relationship, even while trade booms, Taiwan and Singapore’s security relationship has been eroding. Project Starlight is a military training program established in 1975 under an agreement between Lee Kuan Yew and Chiang Ching-kuo that permitted Singaporean troops to train annually in Taiwan. This has historically been an open secret that both parties have kept low profile to avoid Beijing’s protest. However, since the Terrex seizure incident in 2016, in which Hong Kong customs impounded Singaporean infantry carrier vehicles that were to transit to Taiwan, the scale of the training has dropped to roughly 3,000 people.
When Taiwanese media publicized details of Starlight exercises in Pingtung in May 2026, Nikkei Asia reported that the disclosure may itself have been a signal timed ahead of the meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents to convey wariness about any China-U.S. bargain struck over Taiwan’s head. Therefore, Singapore-Taiwan security cooperation now reads more as a bargaining chip than as a commitment, and could be a strain to Singapore-Taiwan ties writ large.
Singapore has traditionally been a trusted party to both Taiwan and China because it has deep commercial and cultural ties with both parties, and because it has never formally endorsed Taiwan’s sovereign status, which is a non-negotiable for Beijing. Singapore has used that position to cultivate the role of a trusted intermediary. It hosted the 1993 Wang-Koo talks, the first semi-official cross-strait negotiations, and the 2015 Ma-Xi meeting, the first encounter between leaders on the two sides of the Taiwan Strait since 1949.
Singapore’s neutrality provides a third-party venue for cross-strait contacts, which raises Singapore’s international reputation as an honest broker. But this neutrality will face increasing pressure as cross-strait relations worsen.
The Singapore-Taiwan relationship is primarily economic and financial; Singapore cannot, and will not, become a defender of Taiwan’s international status. Despite that limitation, Taiwan’s rise to the top of Singapore’s trade ledger is real and durable. Taipei should continue concentrating on the areas where returns are tangible: semiconductor supply chain integration, trade, capital markets, and talent flows. It should not, however, treat Singapore as a latent diplomatic partner or a candidate for public statements of support.

Stop the War's Lindsey German: Israel more isolated than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:29:29 UTC
22:29:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Stop the War's Lindsey German: Israel more isolated than ever since 1948
There is no organisation in Britain more popular and opposed to US plans in the Middle East and its wars around the world than the Stop the War Coalition. Even before Israel, with Western support, began its war of extermination against Palestinians in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Al-Aqsa Flood, the coalition considered Palestine its most important cause.
The New Arab met with Lindsey German, British activist and the coalition's coordinator, at its headquarters in far-north London.
The region is like a "powder keg", German warned, as conditions "can be kept under control for a period, but not forever".
In her view, the main driving factor are two wars: the Israeli war against the Palestinians with Western support and the Israeli-American war against Iran Moreover, Israel's war of extermination in Gaza pushed campaigns in defence of Palestine to the top of the coalition's priorities.
According to German, one of the coalition's achievements was "linking the Palestinian cause to the broader context of Western and Israeli policies in the Middle East" and what she describes as "American and British imperialism", whose plans Palestinians in Gaza disrupted.
German believes that "Trump has all kinds of plans for what he will do with Gaza and the Middle East", but they have not materialised, as he "tried to force Palestinians to go somewhere, but they do not want that".
Because of this resilience, German believes Palestinians "remain a huge challenge" to the ambitions of Trump and Israel.
Greater Israel threatens Arab regimes
German highlighted how Israeli officials at various levels speak of the "Greater Israel" project, which Trump supports and his ambassador to Tel Aviv, Mike Huckabee, promotes, and seeks to seize land from Arab countries neighbouring Palestine and beyond.
She opined that no decisive practical position has been issued by the governments of the Arab countries threatened by the project because they "have strategic relations with the United States and Britain through arms deals and economic interests", which "limits their ability to adopt independent positions towards Israel".
Nevertheless, she considered that the project and all of Trump's plans for Gaza "have led to a clash with the local regimes there, because they take part of this country or that country and force Palestinians to leave their land".
German argued that Israel's plans "pose a threat to the Arab regimes themselves", requiring "political and economic action" to curb Israel's expansion by "imposing an international boycott on it because of what it is committing" in terms of crimes.
Like others who reject Israel's crimes and the complicity of the West, including Britain, German frequently drew comparisons between Israel and Russia, noting that if another country had done what Israel has done, "we would have seen a broad international reaction, as happened with Russia after the invasion of Ukraine".
Why, then, do Arab countries not take such a position towards Israel? Lindsey German answered that "this position does not come from the rulers of the Middle East because many of them have very close relations with Donald Trump and with Britain, France and the old imperial powers, and this keeps them within this Western political framework of double standards."
She compared the issue of Palestine and the position of Arab rulers towards it with the problem of Britain's National Health Service, as she believed that "everyone (in the Arab countries) supports Palestine, but we do not see government action that can actually help the Palestinians, or we see very little action".
"When looking at Palestinians in Jordan, Lebanon or anywhere else, we find that they are treated extremely badly in the camps and are considered second-class citizens. This has been the situation for 50 years, and it seems to me that this is one of the reasons why people do not rise, whether because of the Palestinian cause or because of local issues related to living conditions and wages," she added.
German said that these living conditions are somewhat similar to what is happening in Britain, but the British have not remained silent.
In her view, the reason is that "opposing the government there is much harder than it is here", and this "largely explains why there have not been more movements (for Palestine or against domestic injustices) in the Middle East".
What has America done to us?
She stressed that the Israeli-American aggression against Iran as an additional factor reinforcing the failure of Israel and America. In her view, Iran "has proved that any resistance to the United States actually has an echo and receives a degree of support" in the Middle East.
Although she sees it as extremely difficult to predict accurately what will happen, she expects that the "result (of the war) will undoubtedly be great disruption and instability".
The Stop the War Coalition coordinator cites the case of the Abraham Accords (normalisation with Israel) as another example of the impact of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and the war on Iran in thwarting US efforts to impose Israel's presence and close the chapter on the Palestinian cause.
However, she stressed that "there is no doubt that Iran has stopped this now" because "the efforts for the Abraham Accords have effectively died" and she "does not see any possibility of reviving them".
She reiterated that credit for this outcome goes to Iran's resistance to the aggressive war, which "made it impossible" for normalisation to continue.
"If you were in government in any of these countries, the UAE or anywhere else, I should think about what we are actually getting from the Americans," she said.
Nevertheless, she quickly added, the prominent anti-war campaigner continues and "what is happening is that America launched a war on Iran with Israel, so what was the consequence? America could not, despite its enormous air power superiority, indeed its superiority in all military aspects, defeat Iran".
Fascists and the far right
Israel's position in the world after its crimes in the Palestinian territories strengthens Iran's position and weakens the chances of reviving the project to get rid of the Palestinians, German argued.
It is a state, according to her, that "has now become more isolated than at any time since its founding; its popularity has declined, and its isolation has increased", even in the United States, which has historically been Israel's strongest supporter. "This support is declining significantly, even among Jews, particularly young people".
Israel's position is no better in Britain.
Previously, according to the picture German described, the country enjoyed particular sympathy among leftists who saw it as a somewhat left-wing socialist state because of the agricultural cooperative communities (kibbutzim) and as a homeland for Jews.
"I had Jewish friends who saw it as the place they wanted to be", and "most of us tended towards Israel when the 1967 war broke out, because we saw it as a small country, and because we realised the scale of the terrible suffering that Jews had gone through, we asked: Why are people attacking them again?" she recalled.
This situation has now changed, German added, because "apart from very hardline Zionists and far-right currents–including fascists and the far right in this country (Britain)–very few people really want to defend Israel".
Among the questions now being raised more insistently than ever, particularly after the Israeli-American aggression against Iran on the pretext of preventing it from acquiring a nuclear weapon, is, according to the coalition coordinator, "Why the focus on Iran? Israel already possesses nuclear weapons, while Iran is still far from possessing such weapons".
British government waging disinformation campaign
When Andy Burnham took over as head of the British government, he announced a commitment to his predecessor Keir Starmer's policy towards the illegal war, allowing the US military to use bases inside and outside Britain to launch attacks that it considers "defensive" against Iranian territory.
"This (use) is part of the war and not self-defence, and there is no need to think about whether it is right or wrong. The bases are being used to launch offensive operations" inside Iran, German stressed.
She said that the British government's promotion of the claim that the use of the bases is "defensive" is merely part of a "disinformation campaign promoting the idea that the British rejected Trump's request" to participate in the war.
But German further said that they "did not actually reject it. They allowed Trump to use RAF Fairford, which is the only base in Europe capable of accommodating and operating the large long-range B-1, B-2 and B-52 bombers".
She pointed out that "it is also clear that they (the British and Americans) cooperate in areas such as intelligence sharing and the like", which indicates that this reflects "some of what is happening behind the scenes".
An unexpected change
The Stop the War Coalition was established in 2001 to prevent the Iraq War and was the main driving force behind the million-strong demonstrations that filled the streets of London.
However, the coalition and many anti-war activists were unable to prevent the invasion, and Tony Blair, the former Labour prime minister, took Britain into it alongside America.
Even with that defeat, the coalition did not tire over the following 25 years of organising protests against wars, particularly Israel's war of extermination against the Palestinians and the Israeli-American aggression against Iran.
German believes that without the anti-war demonstrations, Britain and America would have repeated the Iraq experience.
She said the coalition "succeeded in changing the British public's view of wars", and therefore "Britain has no longer been able since the invasion of Iraq to repeat the model of direct military occupation". Later interventions in Libya and Syria "took different forms as a result of growing popular opposition".
As for Palestine, Lindsey German credited the popular pressure exerted by the coalition and others with "pushing the Labour Party to modify some of its positions towards Palestine". Here she is referring to Burnham's widely known video about Gaza and his admission that Labour was wrong in how it initially dealt with the war in the territory, as well as his indication that he intended to take a "balanced" position on what is happening in the region.
However, she acknowledged that this will not bring about a fundamental change in the rhetoric or policy pursued by the British government, as it "will continue to arm Israel and maintain diplomatic relations with it".
Despite the growing pressure, she expected that the "Burnham government will continue to avoid talking about genocide because it does not favour using this term".
She predicted "more attempts to acknowledge that Israel has committed some bad practices, without any real change in fundamental policy, given that Britain, ultimately, has very close relations with Israel".
Lindsey German: Real madness in Britain
The Stop the War Coalition is among the pro-Palestinian organisations most affected by the conduct of Britain's ruling establishment towards the ongoing protests against Israel's extermination campaign.
Its secretary-general, Alex Kenny, is awaiting a criminal trial on charges related to an alleged breach of the conditions for protesting in support of Palestine.
His deputy, Chris Nineham, is also awaiting a hearing of his appeal, alongside Ben Jamal, director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, against a previous ruling that convicted him on the same charge.
This is "ridiculous in every sense of the word", according to German, who attributes the ruling establishment's position to "how frightened they are" by the impact of the protests.
She added another piece of evidence of this fear, saying, "the unprecedented massive level of arrests related to Palestine over the past 25 years".
"We now have political prisoners," German said, bitterly. The tone became more bitter when asked her about the Palestine Action movement and its members detained pending investigations or those who were tried for allegedly committing criminal acts but were sentenced by the judge, contrary to the law, under provisions set out in terrorism laws under which they had not been tried.
"I look at all those people who are being arrested. Many of them are retired from the technology sector, doctors and lawyers with prestigious standing, and people who have never committed a crime in their lives. They are all being treated as criminals simply for supporting the Palestinian cause," she remarked, describing all this as "madness in every sense of the word."
She warned that criminalising protests could push some activists to adopt more escalatory methods such as "direct action" to stop the extermination, and that history will not forget.
"Be sure that this will be considered in the years ahead, and people will say that it was a complete miscarriage of justice," she said.
The coalition's priority now remains to continue building a broad mass movement that includes trade unions and various sections of society, because the major demonstrations, in her assessment, were the main factor in raising public awareness of the Palestinian cause and pushing the Labour Party to review some of its positions.

Nepal avalanche, flash flood kill 22, leave hundreds missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

At least 98 people were killed and hundreds of others went missing in Nepal Wednesday when an avalanche triggered massive flash floods.
The prime minister's office in Nepal reported at least 95 dead. China's state broadcaster CCTV said a mudslide in the Tibet region's Gyirong County near the border killed at least three and left 265 missing. Drone footage showed roads destroyed and buildings buried. State news agency Xinhua reported significant casualties.
The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, destroying several villages, roads and hydropower projects, officials said.
"We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts," said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government.
Dozens of multistoried buildings, trucks, and vans were buried under vast quantities of mud in the district of Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected areas.
Officials warned residents in several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani rivers.
Officials in Nepal said 403 people, including 341 foreign nationals, were reported missing. Sunil Sharma, a tourism board spokesperson, said 133 were from India on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. Also missing were 47 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 24 from Canada, he said.
At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking in the Gosaikunda Lake area in Rasuwa, coinciding with the local festival of Janai Purnima on Friday, Sharma added. Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press at least 28 police officials were missing.
South Korean government officials said their citizens working on building a hydropower plant in Nepal were among those reported missing.
Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry also said its embassy in Kathmandu has received reports from travel agencies that they had lost contact with 11 Malaysians believed to be in the Rasuwa district, which was hit hard by the floods.
Meanwhile, Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Authorities didn't announce any numbers of dead or injured.
Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered authorities to step up the efforts for people missing after the mudslide, state news agency Xinhua reported. Xi also called for residents at risk to be evacuated from any area on the Chinese side.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah and offered help. "India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely coordinating on rescue and relief efforts,” Modi said in a social media post.
The same regions affected by Wednesday's disaster saw flash floods similar to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighboring Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged at the time.
Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood.
The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said.
"The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in fourteen months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.
"In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation,” he added.
The Himalayan region, which spans Nepal and several nearby countries, including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because it is warming faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research shows that extreme weather events, including heat waves and rains, and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region.
Researchers in Kathmandu found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000 primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.

Lithuanians buys up generators and essentials after storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:27:15 UTC
22:27:15 KST

After a weekend storm left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity in Lithuania as well, traders have reported a sharp increase in demand for generators and other emergency goods.
Some traders said that sales of generators had increased by as much as 30 times, and buyers were also snapping up chargers (power banks), portable gas stoves, flashlights and batteries. A similar peak in demand was observed only in 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At that time, Lithuanians bought generators both for themselves and to send to Ukraine.
Some Lithuanians have traveled a hundred kilometers or more to buy a generator. Tads from the Roķiškis district spent three days without electricity, and he only managed to find the generator he needed in Panevėžys. Lyubov went from Vilnius to Anykščiai district to get a generator. She said it was bad, and there was nowhere to even charge her phone. The local government had set up a point where residents could charge their phones, but it was complicated.
After the storm, generators became the most sought-after item. Sellers said that buyers were looking for devices of all possible sizes, and prices ranged from a few hundred euros. The price increased with the generator’s capacity.
Laurynas Nakas, head of the technical products department at Specagra, said that
people were not even particularly interested in the price, they were asking what was in stock
and what could be obtained quickly. He added that prices had not been raised – the company had what it had on offer. There were still a few units left, but they were reserved and waiting for buyers to come and pick them up.
Farmers were also among those looking for powerful generators. Nakas pointed out that cows need to be fed and watered. Most farmers who have called and asked for powerful generators have said they cannot water their cows because the water pumps are not working.
Generators can still be found in major cities, but retailers said that stocks are running out quickly. Kristina Petrulevičiūtė, communications manager for retailer Hermitage, said that stocks in Utena, Jonava and Vilnius have sold out. There are still a few units left in Klaipėda. A two-year trial of generators was reportedly sold over the weekend.
Buyers are also looking for other essential items for emergencies. Liubovė Aleksandra Zaiceva, communications manager for the Baltics at Senukai, said that people are making sure they have first aid kits, flashlights and other small items. Camping stoves are also being bought, and some products, such as large camping stoves, are already sold out.

Zelensky's Chief of Staff Budanov features in tapes linked to latest corruption case, media say
Key takeaways:
- President Volodymyr Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov is allegedly mentioned by his former deputy Iryna Mudra in the tapes
- In at least one conversation, Budanov's voice was allegedly recorded
- Timur Mindich, a top Zelensky associate, allegedly delivered cash to Budanov to pay a suspect's bail with laundered money
- Mindich also allegedly asked Budanov to take over Sense Bank's cash flows
- Sense Bank's management was allegedly prepared to take orders from Budanov
- Budanov allegedly told Mudra not to fight corruption but to control it
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the President’s Office, features in audio tapes recorded by investigators as part of the latest large-scale corruption case, the media outlet Hromadske reported on Aug. 26, citing court materials.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from the President’s Office and will publish its response once it is received.
The tapes were released as part of a major corruption investigation against President Volodymyr Zelensky’s former Deputy Chief of Staff Iryna Mudra and other suspects. Last week they were charged by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) with corporate raiding and money laundering.
The latest case is linked to last year’s probe into state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky’s tenure. The Mudra case also comes on the heels of corruption charges against Zelensky’s former Chief of Staff Andriy Yermak in May.
At a court hearing on Aug. 25, a lawyer for Sense Bank CEO Oleksiy Stupak, one of the suspects in the latest case, publicly cited NABU tapes referring to “Kyrylo Oleksiyovich" — a person whose first name and patronymic coincide with Budanov’s. He did not specify his last name.
“Listen, Kyrylo Oleksiyovich called and asked what’s going on with Sense Bank,” Mudra said, according to the tapes cited by the lawyer.
Meanwhile, transcripts included in the prosecutors' motions in the case explicitly state that Budanov took part in the conversations, Hromadske reported.
In the alleged transcripts, Budanov thanked ex-lawmaker Maksym Mykytas, a suspect in the case, for his work.
“I’m with Kyrylo Oleksiyovich,” Mudra told Mykytas. “I put it on speaker.”
“Thank you, hello,” Budanov allegedly replied. “Thanks a lot.”
According to the alleged transcripts, on June 9 Mudra and Myktytas discussed a request by Timur Mindich, a suspect in the Energoatom case and a close Zelensky associate, to take over Sense Bank's cash flows.
“Mindich approached Kyrylo," Mudra allegedly said in an apparent reference to Kyrylo Budanov. "To take control of it... Wait, there are some serious money flows there... There’s no one to take them over right now. Do you understand? And once Gera (an apparent reference to ex-Justice and Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko) gets out, he’ll get his hands on those flows again. So we need to bargain for something for ourselves before that happens.”
According to the alleged transcripts, Mudra said that Sense Bank’s management was prepared to follow instructions from Kyrylo — an apparent reference to Budanov.
“They’re ready to do anything," she allegedly said. "I mean, wherever Kyrylo tells them to bring (the money), they’ll take it... They’ll do whatever he says.”
Mudra and Mykytas are are accused of laundering Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) and transferring the funds through Sense Bank to post bail for Halushchenko.
Halushchenko was charged in February in the Energoatom case.
On June 17, Mykytas allegedly said that Mindich had personally delivered cash for Halushchenko's bail to “Kyrylo Oleksiyovych" — another apparent reference to Budanov.
“And if we pull this off smoothly now, you have no idea..." Mykytas said. "I mean Kyrylo Oleksiiovych... He’s doing Mindich a huge favor right now. And he brought the money, by the way. Mindich personally delivered it to him.”
Mudra also allegedly said that “Timur” called “Kyrylo” and said: “Listen, Kyrylo, please take over Sense Bank.”
“You can’t trust the bank to these crooks, and there are cash flows going through it,” she allegedly said, citing Timur. “Serious cash flows, he says... ‘Take the bank under your control,’ he says... You see how quickly Mindich changed tack. He had his hands on all the cash flows.”
According to the prosecutors' motions, Mykytas and Mudra also discussed measures to avoid detection on Feb. 9, 2026, according to the alleged transcripts published by Hromadske.
During the conversation, Mudra told Mykytas that she had been invited to a gathering that court chiefs were expected to attend. But she decided not to go because she did not want to be seen with judges at a restaurant by the NABU.
“They invited me,” Mudra allegedly said. “Well, I’m not going. It wouldn’t be right. I mean, I’m telling you, if Budanov finds out... Especially since they meet at restaurants that are definitely on the NABU’s radar, you know?”
“Well, Budanov said not to meet at restaurants,” Mykytas said.
Mudra also said in the alleged transcripts that she had told Budanov she wants "to do the right things."
"I think fighting corruption is a very good thing, and if we manage to ratify this convention now and become a party to it, that will be something you and I can take credit for," she allegedly said.
Budanov then allegedly asked her, as cited by Mudra in the transcripts: "Do you really want to fight corruption?"
"Well, I don’t want my country to become mired in corruption," Mudra allegedly replied.
"Look, that’s the wrong approach," Budanov allegedly said. "Corruption needs to be systematized and controlled."
Mudra also allegedly told Mykytas in their conversations that she regularly received unofficial payments of $20,000–$30,000 from "Kyrylo" — yet another apparent reference to Budanov.
The media outlet Ukrainska Pravda also reported on Aug. 20, citing its sources, that Budanov’s name is mentioned in the text of the charges against Mudra.
On the tapes officially published by the NABU, Mudra repeatedly refers to her “boss." Mudra has two bosses — Zelensky and Budanov.
Apart from Mudra, Mykytas, and Stupak, lawmaker Vadym Stolar and Viktor Dubovyk, head of the legal policy department at the President's Office, were also charged as part of the case last week. Stolar has fled abroad.
Stolar, Mudra and Myktytas are also accused of illegally seizing real estate by hacking the corporate register, forging documents, and bribing judges and law enforcement agencies.
