Beyond Ayodhya and the fish row: Why Nishad vote matters in UP's 2027 battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:04:27 UTC
22:04:27 KST

Beyond Ayodhya and the fish row: Why Nishad vote matters in Uttar Pradesh 2027 battle
Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 26, 2026, 18:54 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
The Nishad community finds itself at the centre of the fish row in Ayodhya ahead of 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls.
At a time when many Hindu devotees traditionally give up non-vegetarian food during 'Sawan', fish has acquired an unlikely political importance in Uttar Pradesh.The row began earlier this month with Uttar Pradesh minister and Nishad Party chief Sanjay Nishad's remark that fish cooked without garlic and onion could be considered vegetarian. It escalated on August 23, when a video purportedly showing fish being prepared at a Nishad community event in Ayodhya, attended by UP Congress president Ajay Rai, surfaced on social media.But behind the sparring over what was - or was not - on Rai's plate lies a larger electoral calculation. The Nishad vote has shifted political loyalties before, and with the BJP seeking to retain its non-Yadav OBC coalition and the opposition trying to prise open that support, the community could once again become an important factor in the 2027 contest.
The 'fish on your plate' row
The controversy began earlier this month when Sanjay Nishad said at a programme: "Bina lahsun-pyaz ki bani machhli shakahari hai."The remark came during Sawan, a month when many Hindu devotees observe dietary restrictions, and quickly attracted attention because of the community he represents. Nishads have historically depended on rivers and water bodies for fishing, fish-rearing, boating and related livelihoods, making food and fishing practices part of a broader social and economic identity.
Then came Ayodhya.On August 23, UP Congress president Ajay Rai travelled to Tarun, around 30 km from Ayodhya, after visiting Hanumangarhi, reciting the Hanuman Chalisa and offering prayers at the Ram temple. He attended a programme organised by members of the Nishad community. A video showing fish being prepared at the venue subsequently surfaced.
Sanjay Nishad said fish preparation mattered.
The timing and location gave the BJP an opening.BJP state president Pankaj Chaudhary described the alleged fish feast as "highly condemnable and unforgivable", while Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath accused Rai of "duplicity" for visiting a temple and then attending a fish feast during Sawan."You saw the conduct of the Congress state president yesterday. He goes to Hanumangarhi for darshan and, after coming out, enjoys a fish feast and then shouts 'Ram-Ram'," Adityanath said.Rai denied eating fish and challenged the CM to produce evidence. "If he can produce any pictures, I will be ready to resign immediately," he said.Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera defended the hosts, saying they belonged to the Nishad community and had their own traditions of eating and drinking.Later, cabinet minister Om Prakash Rajbhar entered the controversy, backing Nishad's earlier claim and asking Congress to clarify whether the fish allegedly served at the event had been cooked with garlic and onion."Sanjay Nishad machhli ke mahir hain, unhe zyada jaankari hai, hum thode kam hain," Rajbhar said.The political argument, however, goes well beyond the menu at one event. The larger story is the political importance of the community that hosted it.
Ajay Rai dared CM Yogi Adityanath to provide evidence.
Nishads — the 'jal kisans'
The Nishads are a cluster of riverine communities whose traditional livelihoods have been closely tied to rivers, ponds and other water bodies. Community organisations have increasingly used the term 'jal kisan', or water farmers, to describe this relationship.Fishing, fish-rearing, boating and the sale of fish have historically been central to these communities' economic lives. Questions over access to water bodies, fishing rights, sand mining and regulation of traditional occupations therefore have a direct political resonance.The term Nishad is also used as an umbrella for several communities and sub-castes, including Mallah, Kewat, Bind, Kashyap, Dhimar, Batham, Kahar, Manjhi and Turaha. Not all of these communities necessarily identify themselves as Nishad in the same way.
Organiser of the event defended the decision to keep fish in the menu.
In Uttar Pradesh, Nishads are classified among the Other Backward Classes (OBCs).Political estimates put the core Nishad population at around 4.5-5 per cent of the state's electorate. Estimates that include a wider set of related riverine communities put their combined share considerably higher.There is no recent official caste census providing a definitive figure, but the community's electoral importance comes less from its statewide percentage than from its concentration.Nishad voters have a significant presence across the Ganga-Yamuna belt and eastern Uttar Pradesh, including Gorakhpur, Varanasi, Azamgarh, Ballia, Mau, Ghazipur, Mirzapur, Bhadohi, Jaunpur and Prayagraj, besides parts of Sultanpur and Fatehpur.The community is considered electorally influential in more than 160 Assembly constituencies, with around 80 seats often identified as having a particularly substantial Nishad presence.That geographical concentration explains why a community accounting for a relatively small share of the state's electorate can command such political attention.
Estimated data based on reports.
Nishadraj and Ekalavya: The epic roots of identity
The Nishad political identity is also deeply connected to stories from the Hindu epics.In the Ramayana, Nishadraj Guha, the boatman-king, is described as an ally of Ram during his exile. Guha receives Ram, Sita and Lakshman and helps them cross the Ganga.
The 51-foot-high statue of Lord Ram and Nishadraj at Shringverpur Dham, 40 km from Prayagraj.
For the Nishad community, the story has long been invoked as a marker of their place within the Ram narrative — not as an identity created by contemporary politics, but as an older cultural association that acquired renewed political meaning during the Ram Janmabhoomi movement.The community also invokes Ekalavya from the Mahabharata, who is traditionally identified as belonging to the Nishad community. His story - of a skilled archer seeking to learn from Dronacharya and ultimately giving his thumb as guru dakshina - has come to represent a different strand of Nishad memory: talent, exclusion and the struggle for recognition.The two figures capture contrasting elements of the community's epic imagination: Nishadraj represents proximity to and loyalty towards Ram, while Ekalavya represents ability denied recognition.These narratives have subsequently been woven into the community's assertion of a distinct historical and social identity.
The Ram Janmabhoomi movement
Sections of the community found their cultural resonance in the Ram Janmabhoomi movement.As the campaign for a Ram temple in Ayodhya gathered momentum in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Nishad organisations and leaders participated in the wider mobilisation. The story of Nishadraj Guha gave the movement an immediate cultural connection for sections of the community, while the broader call for 'Ram Rajya' resonated with those who saw the temple campaign as a civilisational and cultural cause.The political landscape changed sharply after BJP leader LK Advani's Ram Rath Yatra in 1990, which transformed the temple issue into a mass political movement. The demolition of the Babri Masjid on December 6, 1992, further entrenched Ayodhya as a defining issue in BJP politics.
Source: Centre for Study of Developing Societies Lokniti.
As the BJP expanded its support among non-Yadav OBC communities, sections of the Nishad community also moved towards the party.But that support did not become a permanent political contract.
From support to sense of being left behind
Among sections of Nishad political opinion, a recurring grievance emerged: the community had supported the Ram movement but did not receive a commensurate political return.The complaint has, at various points, extended to BJP leaders associated with the Ram movement, including Advani and former UP CM Kalyan Singh, with Nishad voices arguing that their support for the Ram cause did not translate into adequate representation or resolution of longstanding demands regarding representation and farming on the riverside.In the coming years, the same community that participated in the Ram movement subsequently moved towards the Samajwadi Party, created its own political organisation and entered into an alliance with the BJP.That fluidity became particularly visible in the 1990s.
Phoolan Devi and politics of representation
Before the emergence of the Nishad Party, the strongest political association for sections of the community came through the social-justice politics of the Samajwadi Party.Phoolan Devi became the most recognisable symbol of that phase.A Mallah woman from Uttar Pradesh, Phoolan Devi contested the Mirzapur Lok Sabha seat on an SP ticket in 1996 and won. She retained the seat in 1999.
SP has given key post to Phoolan Devi's sister ahead of 2027 polls.
Her rise gave the community an unusually prominent political figure and turned caste identity into a language of representation.Her political legacy continues to be invoked in Uttar Pradesh.
Nishad Party enters equation
The next major shift came in 2016, when Sanjay Nishad founded the Nirbal Indian Shoshit Hamara Aam Dal, popularly known as the Nishad Party.The party sought to consolidate riverine communities and give political expression to demands involving reservation, representation, fishing rights and livelihoods.Its first major electoral breakthrough came in an unlikely place.In the March 2018 Gorakhpur Lok Sabha bypoll, Praveen Nishad, Sanjay Nishad's son, contested as an SP-backed candidate and defeated the BJP.The result was politically significant because Gorakhpur had been Yogi Adityanath's parliamentary stronghold for five consecutive terms.The defeat demonstrated that the BJP's support among non-Yadav OBC communities could be disrupted when Nishad mobilisation combined with the SP's wider social coalition.But the equation soon changed again.Before the 2019 Lok Sabha election, the Nishad Party moved into the BJP-led NDA. Praveen Nishad joined the BJP and contested the Sant Kabir Nagar Lok Sabha seat on a BJP ticket, winning the election.The BJP-Nishad Party alliance became an important part of the BJP's strategy to consolidate non-Yadav OBC support in eastern Uttar Pradesh.
2019 and 2022: Alliance and the unfinished bargain
The BJP and Nishad Party continued their alliance into the 2022 Uttar Pradesh assembly election.The BJP won 255 seats, while the Nishad Party won six. The NDA retained power with 273 seats in the 403-member assembly.For the BJP, the alliance helped reinforce its eastern Uttar Pradesh coalition.For Sanjay Nishad, however, being part of the government brought a different problem: once an ally enters government, its demands are increasingly judged against what it can actually secure from that government.The biggest unresolved issue remained the demand for Scheduled Caste status for sections of the Nishad community.Sanjay Nishad has repeatedly pressed the BJP government on the demand.On August 18, 2026, just months before the 2027 elections, he escalated the issue again, saying he was prepared to give up his ministerial position if necessary.His friction with the BJP had also become visible after the 2024 Lok Sabha election, when he blamed BJP leaders for his son Praveen Nishad's defeat in Sant Kabir Nagar.Praveen, who contested the seat on a BJP ticket, lost to the Samajwadi Party's Laxmikant Pappu Nishad.The result was another reminder that a BJP-Nishad Party alliance does not necessarily translate into a uniform Nishad vote.
SP and Congress try to prise open BJP's base
That fluidity is what the opposition is trying to exploit ahead of 2027.In March 2026, it appointed Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti as chairperson of the Uttar Pradesh Backward Classes Commission. The move came alongside the BJP's continuing alliance with the Nishad Party.The SP responded by appointing Phoolan Devi's sister, 67-year-old Rukmini Devi, as president of the party's Uttar Pradesh women's wing. The appointment was seen as part of Akhilesh Yadav's PDA — Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak — outreach ahead of the 2027 election.Rukmini Devi subsequently attacked Sanjay Nishad, questioning what he had delivered for the community while being part of the government.The appointments show that the competition for the Nishad vote is not merely about alliances. It is a contest over who represents the community's political memory.Congress, on the other hand, has a more difficult task because its organisational presence among Nishads is weaker.Its August outreach in Tarun was therefore significant. Ajay Rai's visit to the Nishad community programme was an attempt to establish a direct connection with the community.The party's subsequent defence of the event, that the hosts were Nishads with their own food traditions, also allowed Congress to frame the controversy around community identity and traditional livelihoods rather than solely religious conduct.For the SP and Congress, the broader argument is that the Nishad vote is not synonymous with the Nishad Party.
The VIP factor
The Vikassheel Insaan Party (VIP), led by Bihar-based Nishad leader Mukesh Sahani, adds another layer to this contest.VIP entered Uttar Pradesh politics in the 2022 assembly election, seeking support among Nishads and other Extremely Backward Classes, particularly in Purvanchal.The party did not emerge as a major electoral force, but its campaign showed how smaller caste-based parties can complicate a close contest.VIP contested more than 100 seats, primarily in eastern Uttar Pradesh, and said its candidates polled more votes than Congress candidates in 15 constituencies, including Bairia, Bansdih, Phephna, Alapur, Jalalpur, Ghanghata, Balha, Shahganj and Kerakat.Its relationship with the BJP has been politically fluid rather than a straightforward alliance in Uttar Pradesh.Sahani has been a vocal critic of the BJP at various points. However, in neighbouring Bihar where the Nishads remain relevant across the seats in the Ganga area, his political trajectory has repeatedly shifted. VIP contested as part of the opposition Mahagathbandhan in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, switched to the NDA for the 2020 Bihar assembly election (winning 4 seats and entering the cabinet), but was dropped from the NDA in 2022 after contesting against the BJP in UP. In last year's Bihar polls, his party failed to secure any seat.However, in upcoming polls in UP, a few thousand votes in its favour can alter the results in close constituencies.
The 2027 question
The fish controversy may fade, but the political question it has exposed is unlikely to disappear.The BJP has the advantage of a long association with the Ram movement, an established organisational network and an alliance with the Nishad Party.
The SP is seeking to revive the community's social-justice connection through Phoolan Devi's political legacy and the PDA framework.Congress is attempting to build a direct relationship with Nishad voters, while smaller parties such as VIP can potentially fragment the vote.For the Nishads themselves, however, the choice is unlikely to be framed around a single issue.Their political history has moved from the epic memory of Nishadraj and Ekalavya, to participation in the Ram Janmabhoomi movement, to the social-justice politics associated with Phoolan Devi, to the rise of the Nishad Party, its alliance with the BJP and subsequent friction over representation and reservation.The lesson from that history is clear: the Nishad vote has never been permanently owned by one party.In 2027, the contest will be over whether Ram and the BJP's organisational alliance can outweigh demands for reservation, representation and livelihoods - and whether the opposition can convert those demands into votes.

Landmark Bolivia same-sex marriage could pave way for more couples, activists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:04:00 UTC
22:04:00 KST

Landmark Bolivia same-sex marriage could pave way for more couples, activists say
LA PAZ, Aug 26 - The marriage of a same-sex couple in Bolivia this month could prompt other couples to seek the same recognition, activists say, potentially opening a new chapter in a years-long push for LGBT rights in the socially conservative Andean nation.
Fabiana Justiniano and Scarlett Rocha applied to marry in October 2022. After nearly four years of legal proceedings and two constitutional appeals, they won a ruling in March 2026 clearing the way for their wedding — Bolivia's first legally recognized same-sex marriage.
"We had many doubts, a lot of uncertainty ... because the process was so long and during the process there were so many barriers, so many limitations, even on the day of the wedding," Rocha said.
For Justiniano, the union brought a different kind of relief. "For me, marriage means peace," she said, recalling their first night home as a married couple, when she realized everything they had built now belonged "only and exclusively to us."
Nonetheless, the Bolivian court's ruling applies only to their specific case. Same-sex marriage is not yet available nationwide through Bolivia's administrative rules, and future access will hinge on further Constitutional Court rulings.
Mateo Rodrigo, a lawyer with Equal Bolivia who represented the couple, said the ruling has already triggered interest from others.
"Since Fabiana and Scarlett's wedding we have already received quite a few requests, around five to 10 couples have approached us," he said, though many remain hesitant given the nearly four-year fight the couple endured.
Same-sex civil unions similarly moved into legal territory after a landmark case in 2020, when David Aruquipa and Guido Montaño won a two-year legal battle.
It took until 2023 for further court rulings to make the registration of same-sex civil unions broadly available.
Since then, Bolivia has recognized 148 same sex-civil unions, said Paola Tapia, who oversees the vulnerable populations unit at Bolivia's Ombudsman's Office. She added that unions still carry fewer practical protections than marriage.
"With marriage, we're opening many more doors. With civil unions, we opened a few," said Montaño. "The situation now is much better for people who can choose between marriage and a civil union."
Cuba in 2022 became the latest country in Latin America to legalize gay marriage and adoption, but little has changed in the region since.
Same-sex marriage remains illegal or unrecognized across much of Central America, Paraguay, Peru, Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname and parts of the Caribbean. REUTERS

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals number of naval drones Russia will receive in 2026
Russia's navy is expected to receive more than 150 uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) in 2026, while the government's procurement order could increase to as many as 230 units.
Source: data provided by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: DIU identified several priorities for Russia's naval drone programme:
- developing versatile USVs using Russian-made components;
- integrating secure communications and artificial intelligence technologies into USVs;
- increasing the boats' operational range.
"Overall, USV production in Russia is complicated by a shortage of electronic components caused by sanctions. Moscow is finding it increasingly difficult to import and develop communications systems that are resistant to electronic warfare," DIU said.

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border?

Scientists may have found a shortcut to calorie restriction’s anti-aging benefits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:00:53 UTC
22:00:53 KST

Scientists may have found a shortcut to calorie restriction’s anti-aging benefits
- Date:
- August 26, 2026
- Source:
- Yale School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Moderate calorie restriction lowered an immune protein called C3 that appears to help drive chronic inflammation as the body ages. Blocking the same protein reduced age related inflammation in mice, raising the possibility that future treatments could mimic some benefits of calorie restriction without severe dieting.
- Share:
Reducing calorie intake has extended lifespan in animals including mice, rhesus monkeys, and fruit flies. In some studies, the animals also remained healthier for longer. But severe calorie restriction can come with serious costs. Mice placed on a diet with 40% fewer calories, for instance, become more vulnerable to infections, reproduce less successfully, and show impaired growth.
That has left scientists with a difficult question: Could humans gain some of the longevity benefits of calorie restriction without experiencing those harmful effects? A new study, published in Nature Aging, points to a possible answer involving an immune protein called complement component 3 (C3).
Yale researchers have previously shown that people who followed moderate calorie restriction, cutting calorie intake by 14% for two years, developed stronger immune defenses without experiencing problems related to growth or reproduction.
"This concept demonstrates that aging is actually malleable and a process that can be targeted," says senior author Vishwa Deep Dixit, PhD, Waldemar Von Zedtwitz Professor of Pathology, professor of immunobiology and of comparative medicine, and director of the Yale Center for Research on Aging (Y-Age) at Yale School of Medicine.
Calorie Restriction Lowers an Inflammation-Linked Protein
For the new study, Dixit and his colleagues at YSM examined plasma samples from 42 people who participated in a National Institutes of Health-funded two-year study called the Comprehensive Assessment of Long-Term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy or CALERIE.
"It's the only trial of its kind that has been done with such rigor and control and demonstrates relevance to human physiology," Dixit says. During the trial, participants reduced their calorie intake by 11 to 14% without feeling deprived.
The researchers measured more than 7,000 proteins across plasma samples collected over time. One stood out: complement component 3 (C3), an immune protein whose levels fell significantly after calorie restriction.
C3 drew particular attention because earlier research has suggested that activation of the complement system, a network of proteins that helps defend the body against pathogens, may contribute to chronic inflammation. That persistent inflammation is considered a major feature of aging and many age-associated diseases.
"But the causal effects of C3 in aging and chronic inflammation have not been identified. So, we were very excited to find that in our study," says Hee-Hoon Kim, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the paper.
Fat Tissue Emerges as a Key Source of C3
By comparing protein levels before and after two years of calorie restriction, the team found that white adipose tissue, the main form of fat tissue in mammals, appeared to be the primary tissue affected by the dietary change.
The researchers then tested the pattern in animals. As they had seen in human plasma, C3 expression rose with age in mice. Additional biochemical testing showed that visceral white adipose tissue was a major source of the age-related increase in C3.
"We were not expecting that because these proteins are mainly synthesized in the liver," says Manish Mishra, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the study.
Single-cell RNA sequencing allowed the researchers to narrow the source further. They found that C3 was being produced by age-associated macrophages, essential white blood cells located within adipose tissue.
"This whole process was unknown in the beginning," Mishra says. "Just to narrow it down to the subtypes of macrophages responsible for this complement protein production was very challenging."
Macrophages are among the immune system's first responders and are best known for engulfing pathogens. They also play an important role in maintaining normal tissue function, Dixit adds.
Could the Benefits Be Independent of Weight Loss?
The next question was whether reducing C3 could provide benefits even without weight loss.
The researchers initially thought that losing adipose tissue might itself reduce C3 production and contribute to healthier aging. Most participants in the study lost about 18 pounds after two years of moderate calorie restriction.
However, when the researchers compared changes in body mass index with changes in complement protein levels, they found no relationship between the amount of weight lost and the decline in those proteins.
"This suggests that calorie restriction has a beneficial effect that is unique to adipose tissues and is likely independent of weight loss," Kim says.
That raised the possibility that some of the biological benefits of calorie restriction might be reproduced without requiring people to lose weight.
Blocking C3 Reduces Inflammation in Mice
To test that idea, the researchers used a drug to inhibit C3 activation in mice, mimicking one of the effects of calorie restriction. The animals developed less age-related inflammation.
According to Dixit, the result illustrates how biological systems that are useful earlier in life can become harmful later. This concept, known as antagonistic pleiotropy, was proposed by biologist Peter Medawar in 1952 as an explanation for aspects of aging.
Growth hormone offers one example. It is essential during early development, but later in life it may also contribute to cancer.
C3 and similar proteins evolved to protect the body against infection. But because humans now live far longer than their ancestors, some of those same protective mechanisms may eventually begin contributing to disease. Dixit says reducing excessive C3 activity could potentially help extend health span.
Researchers Explore Existing Drugs as an Aging Target
The team is now studying whether FDA-approved inhibitor drugs could be used to suppress C3 production and potentially slow aspects of aging in humans.
The goal is not to eliminate the complement system entirely, because it remains essential for fighting infections.
"The idea is not to remove complement systems that are required for us to fight infections," Dixit says. "Instead, the goal is to restore the balance."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Yale School of Medicine. Original written by Kristel Tjandra. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Manish Mishra, Hee-Hoon Kim, Yun-Hee Youm, Elsie Gonzalez-Hurtado, Konstantin Zaitsev, Tamara Dlugos, Irina Shchukina, Christy Gliniak, Eric Ravussin, Subhasis Mohanty, Albert C. Shaw, Philipp E. Scherer, Maxim N. Artyomov, Vishwa Deep Dixit. Exoproteome of calorie-restricted humans identifies complement deactivation as an immunometabolic checkpoint reducing inflammaging. Nature Aging, 2026; 6 (5): 1064 DOI: 10.1038/s43587-026-01107-0

People are more willing to help strangers they perceive as agreeable or conscientious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:00:31 UTC
22:00:31 KST

People may be more willing to help strangers who seem agreeable and conscientious, partly because these traits make the person more likeable, according to research published in Evolutionary Psychological Science.
Cooperation requires people to decide whether another person is worth helping even when they know very little about them. Because we cannot directly observe how a stranger will behave in the future, these decisions often depend on limited social cues. Previous research suggests that personality traits can provide this kind of information by signalling relatively stable patterns of behavior.
For example, agreeableness, which is associated with trust, empathy, and concern for others, has consistently been linked with cooperation and helping, making it a potentially useful cue when evaluating a possible social partner. Conscientiousness may offer a different kind of information. Rather than primarily signalling warmth or cooperative motivation, it can suggest reliability, self-control, and consistency, qualities that may make someone seem like a dependable partner.
Ryo Oda examined whether people use these personality characteristics when deciding whom to help, and whether a person’s own personality changes how strongly they respond to the same traits in others. The study focused especially on agreeableness and conscientiousness, while also examining openness and extraversion, and tested whether patterns that look like a preference for similar people might instead reflect greater responsiveness to socially desirable traits.
Oda first created 40 short personality profiles in Japanese representing different levels of openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, and agreeableness. For each trait, five profiles were designed to represent relatively high levels and five relatively low levels. A separate preliminary sample of 61 Japanese adults rated these profiles to confirm that the intended personality differences were successfully conveyed.
Personality ratings were based on selected items from the short form of the Japanese Big Five Scale, and the high- and low-trait profiles were successfully distinguished for all four personality dimensions.
The main study included 120 Japanese adults (60 women and 60 men). Participants were evenly distributed across the 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, and 50-59 age groups. Each participant viewed all 40 personality profiles in randomized order.
For every target, participants rated how willing they would be to help in four situations: financial trouble, lying on a railway crossing as a train approached, struggling with heavy luggage, and wanting someone to listen to them. These ratings were averaged into a helping score. Participants also rated how much they liked each target using ratings of liking and friendliness.
All helping and liking items were rated on 9-point scales ranging from 1, “not at all,” to 9, “extremely.” Participants then completed the short form of the Japanese Big Five Scale to assess their own personality traits.
Agreeableness and conscientiousness stood out as the traits most relevant to helping decisions. Targets described as more conscientious received higher willingness-to-help ratings, and this relationship was particularly strong among participants who were themselves more conscientious.
Similarly, more agreeable targets received higher helping ratings, while more agreeable participants were also generally more willing to help. Agreeable participants were especially responsive to agreeableness in the people they evaluated. By contrast, openness and extraversion did not significantly predict helping intentions.
The same broad pattern appeared when participants rated how much they liked each target. More conscientious and more agreeable targets were evaluated more positively, particularly by participants who were themselves higher on the corresponding trait. However, additional analyses suggested that this was not simply a matter of people preferring others whose personalities matched their own. Instead, people higher in agreeableness or conscientiousness appeared especially responsive to those desirable traits in others.
Exploratory mediation analyses further showed that liking statistically accounted for the interactions between participant and target personality in predicting helping: once liking was taken into account, the previously significant interactions for agreeableness and conscientiousness were no longer significant. This suggests that these personality cues may influence helping largely by shaping how positively people evaluate a potential social partner.
Of note is that the study measured hypothetical willingness to help rather than actual helping or partner-choice behavior, so it cannot establish whether the same patterns occur when people must incur real costs. The sample also consisted entirely of Japanese adults, meaning that the importance of agreeableness and conscientiousness as social cues may differ across cultures.
Overall, the findings suggest that agreeableness and conscientiousness can serve as meaningful social signals that shape how people evaluate potential interaction partners and, in turn, whom they are willing to help.
The research “Personality Traits as Social Cues in Helping Decisions: The Roles of Agreeableness and Conscientiousness” was authored by Ryo Oda.

33 RAF Air Cadet squadrons still without permanent sites
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:00:20 BST
22:00:20 KST

Thirty-three RAF Air Cadet squadrons are still waiting for temporary parading locations after hundreds of buildings were found to have electrical compliance problems, according to a newly deposited Ministry of Defence letter.
Thirty-three RAF Air Cadet squadrons remain affected by the temporary closure of buildings following the discovery of electrical compliance problems across hundreds of sites, although the Ministry of Defence says the organisation’s planned summer activity has not been disrupted, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The figures are contained in a letter dated 7 August from Minister for Veterans and People Calvin Bailey to Conservative MP Mims Davies, deposited in the House of Commons following a parliamentary question about the number of RAF Air Cadet units whose headquarters remained temporarily closed. Bailey said the MOD was treating “headquarters” as RAF Air Cadet squadron buildings which had been shut because of electrical non-compliance identified from January 2026 onwards.
According to the letter, 370 non-compliant sites had been identified by 5 August. Remedial work had progressed sufficiently for 287 permanent buildings to reopen, while alternative parading spaces had been secured for 44 squadrons whose normal facilities could not yet be used.
Bailey wrote: “RAFACs are committed to providing safe and high-quality spaces for all its members and adult volunteers. As of 5 August 2026, of the 370 non-compliant sites identified, remedial work has been delivered at pace to ensure the re-opening of 287 permanent buildings, and alternative parading spaces have been secured for 44 Squadrons.”
He added: “RAFAC organisation continues to source temporary parading locations for the remaining 33 affected Squadrons. This is a priority for the organisation to ensure business as usual cadet activity can be delivered. The planned summer programme of activity is not affected.”
The figures indicate that the majority of the affected permanent buildings have returned to use, while a further group of squadrons is continuing activity from alternative accommodation. The MOD’s letter does not explain whether the figures for reopened buildings, alternative spaces and the 33 remaining squadrons overlap in any way, so they should not be treated as a simple breakdown of all 370 non-compliant sites.
The closures followed electrical compliance problems identified across RAF Air Cadet accommodation, requiring buildings to be taken out of use while inspections and remedial work were carried out. The response has involved both bringing permanent headquarters back into service and finding temporary locations from which squadrons can continue meeting where repairs have not yet been completed.
The Royal Air Force Air Cadets operates through a large network of local squadrons and other units across the UK, with permanent buildings used for training, administration and regular parade nights. Losing access to a squadron headquarters can therefore affect routine activities even where flying, camps and centrally organised events continue elsewhere.

Channel 5 drama to examine how Nicola Sturgeon’s estranged husband stole SNP funds

Channel 5 is reuniting with the producers of Power: the Downfall of Huw Edwards for a drama about how Nicola Sturgeon’s estranged husband embezzled £400,000 from the Scottish National party and the impact it had on her reputation.
To Nicola, Love Peter will examine the couple’s relationship over the 12-year period that Peter Murrell diverted funds from the SNP while he was the chief executive to spend on items including a £124,550 motorhome and more than £2,600 on a pair of luxury salt and pepper grinders.
Murrell was arrested in 2023, and Sturgeon subsequently discovered that the man who helped build her career and shared her life with had deceived and betrayed her.
After it emerged he had embezzled money to buy items such as a Jaguar SUV, Montblanc pens and luxury watches by falsifying invoices and using secret codes, he was jailed this summer for five years and three months.
Murrell’s ability to take the funds is understood to have been obscured at the time by the SNP’s heavy spending between 2010 and 2022. His conviction earlier this year left Sturgeon, once a hugely popular Scottish first minister, with her hard-earned political reputation in tatters. She revealed recently she had not spoken to him since he was imprisoned.
Channel 5 said To Nicola, Love Peter will lift “the lid on this extraordinary story and how it contributed to the downfall of one of the biggest political figures of a generation”.
The broadcaster and streamer’s chief content officer, Ben Frow, said: “This is an epic tale of Shakespearean proportions. An extraordinary tale of power, envy, deception and greed. It’s both a high-stakes political melodrama and bizarre domestic drama that has dominated headlines and gossip columns.
“We will be pulling together the events and characters involved to create a compelling revealing drama … as well as answering that very important question – why would anyone pay £2,000 for a pair of salt and pepper grinders?”
Making the announcement at the Edinburgh TV Festival, Frow said a casting huntwas under way to play Sturgeon and joked that the Duchess of Sussex could be a candidate, which was illustrated with a mocked up photo on the screen behind him of how she might look playing the former Scottish leader, along with other potential contenders such as Zendaya and Nicole Kidman.
Last week it emerged that, with Meghan returning to the UK with her family, there had been talks for her to make her acting return in Netflix show The Gentlemen. It was reportedly subsequently withdrawn but led to speculation about potential future roles in British programmes.
To Nicola, Love Peter continues a trend by Channel 5 to dramatise the stories of high-profile individuals such as Edwards and Kate McCann.
The new feature-length drama is being made by Wonderhood Studios, which made Power: the Downfall of Huw Edwards, starring Martin Clunes.
Wonderhood’s executive chair, David Abraham, said of To Nicola, Love Peter: “This project reflects our growing ambition to develop quality dramas about contemporary stories that resonate with broad audiences.”

Could the delay to China’s moon mission ease pressure on Nasa?
Postponement of ‘especially ambitious’ Chang’e-7 no surprise to space specialists, but the US agency will not be celebrating
Chinese space authorities said only that the mission did not “meet the launch requirements” and, by Monday evening, the rocket had been rolled back to its assembly building.
Space security strategist John Sheldon, a co-founder of the London-based consultancy AstroAnalytica, said space professionals in the US would certainly not be celebrating the delay.
“The same variables that caused the Chang’e-7 postponement can just as easily happen – and have happened – to US lunar missions.”
However, politically it could ease some pressure on Nasa, Sheldon said. A later Chang’e-7 launch pushed back the prospect of another successful Chinese moon landing, avoiding – for now – some of the “media and political angst” that could generate in Washington.

PeopleFinders’ New Website Runs Background Checks on Your Dates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

We’ve all been there. You meet someone new on a dating app, start to envision a life together, only to wonder: Is the person actually who they say they are?
It’s an experience that has led many singles, sometimes out of concern or just genuine curiosity, to prescreen dates by tracing their digital footprint: scanning social media posts, browsing their LinkedIn profile for clues.
The platform Stud or Dud—not to be confused with stud’s use as a slang term for a masculine-presenting Black lesbian—wants to introduce even more transparency into that part of the dating process. According to its website, the platform uses “public records, publicly available information, and other permitted sources” to create a profile of your potential match. It launched today in the US and was created by the company behind PeopleFinders.com, the online data broker service that collects public records from multiple sources and makes them searchable to help clients locate individuals or run background reports.
Intended to help daters make informed decisions about the people in their life, like identifying possible warning signs, Stud or Dud aggregates courthouse documents, bankruptcy filings, tax liens, pre-foreclosure data, phone directories, social media posts, and more to create a snapshot of your potential suitor’s personal life. All daters need is the person’s name or phone number to run a search. The aggregated data is presented in a single report, where it is divided into four categories: finances, property or assets owned, employment history, and criminal background. Each report comes with an AI-generated overview.
The tool will also earmark what it determines to be red or green flags about the person. Criminal records—a DUI or time spent in prison, for example—signal a red flag, but PeopleFinders CEO Amber Higgins encourages users not to pass judgement even if the site does.
“We give enough information for the user to determine, is that really a red flag for them or not? And that all kind of speaks to your lifestyle expectations.” In this sense, the reports lean prescriptive since the company suggests what safety details to consider, calling attention to things like how many times you’ve been evicted or if your name is on a sex offender registry. There is also an AI assistant (“the dating detective”) users can chat with when they want more tips for first dates or general advice.
According to the company, one of the biggest historical use cases of PeopleFinders.com has been for online dating safety.
“Modern dating has changed dramatically, and the tools people have used to establish trust haven’t kept pace,” Higgins says. “People are meeting across dating apps, social media, DMs. They have very little context of who's actually on the other side.”
While some might consider that the whole point of dating—the early talking stages, however awkward, are all about navigating the unknown when getting to know someone—Higgins adds that the site, which requires a subscription, was built to provide additional context on a potential match. She recommends that people use it as a “sidekick” to the apps. “This is meant to confirm your trust about a dating profile.”
Even as online vetting is a crucial safety measure and fully part of the modern dating process—daters in San Francisco, for example, lost more than $40 million to romance scams in 2025, according to the FBI—there also seem to be legitimate opportunities for bad actors to exploit the information gathered from the site. The platform assumes that the person doing the searching is the one at risk, but that may not always be the case.
“Obviously, there are a lot of problems with a site like this, starting with its potential use by stalkers,” says Eva Galperin, director of cybersecurity for digital privacy nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation. After running her own tests with different names and numbers, she adds that, “the site did not seem to be good at the very thing it is claiming to do well: flag potentially dangerous partners.”
The data broker industry that powers people-search websites is largely unregulated, since the US lacks comprehensive digital privacy laws. In addition to normalizing surveillance, these people-search sites have the potential to cause real harm; search results can contain false or outdated information that, if taken at face value by the institution running the search, can lead to people not being able to secure housing, a job, or public benefits.
Also, a report from Stud or Dud could be entirely clean and tell you nothing about whether someone poses a genuine threat. Sexual violence is one of the most underreported crimes in the US, with only a fraction of assaults being reported to the police or making it to the courts.
Higgins tells WIRED that any tool involving personal information has to be designed to be used responsibly, but no report can guarantee that someone is safe. “We provide the signals, clues, but ultimately it does not eliminate the need to take your normal precautions,” she says. She believes women will be the strongest early adopters, given that they carry more of a personal safety burden when meeting a new acquaintance.
Only 48 percent of US adults think online dating is safe, and women are more likely than men to say dating apps are dangerous, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey, with six in 10 Americans saying companies should require background checks before users can create a dating profile.
“Policing potential dates is intertwined with calls for surveillance,” says Christoper Dietzel, an assistant professor at Concordia University, who coauthored a 2026 study analyzing 30 dating apps’ safety materials, including eHarmony, Scruff, Bumble, and Grindr. “Dating apps already tell users to Google their matches, reverse-image search their photos, and look up their phone numbers. Seeking goes as far as telling users that personal research is not creeping.”
Wanting information about a date is a human reflex; people do this all the time by asking friends for input or advice. Likewise, Facebook groups like “Are We Dating the Same Guy?” have been dependable resources for women navigating dishonest men online. And while screening potential matches has become an integral part of the dating process, Dietzel has concerns about the data being collected. According to the site, people aren’t notified about what documents are being shared, nor do they have a way of knowing whether the data on them is accurate.
When asked about the accuracy rate, Higgins says, “I don't necessarily have a percentage, but we make our best case to provide the most accurate information available. Public records can be inaccurate. Sometimes there are mistakes.”
Because of the privacy laws the company must comply with, people can request that their information be deleted off the site; doing so does not require you to sign up.
When Higgins searched my name during the demo, I feared what might pop up. Suddenly, I felt exposed. The information already exists in disparate corners of the internet, but here, for the first time, I wondered how its AI would define me. What assumptions would it make?
“Low-key vibes with a hint of wanderlust,” the summary began, which correctly identified my age and the city I live in. “No criminal or financial drama in sight. The subject seems to have moved around a bit, but hey, who doesn't love a little adventure?” When it showed that I had no property records on file—sadly, I still rent—it mentioned how “this isn’t automatically a dealbreaker,” as if my worth was tied to material possessions. There were no red flags, and though insights are helpful in providing a semblance of context, data can never color the full picture of a person.

US provides equipment and training to protect Polish border from migratory pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:58:57 UTC
21:58:57 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

The United States has donated $2.1 million worth of equipment for border protection, including drones and thermal imaging cameras, to Poland under an agreement signed on Tuesday.
The Polish border guard says that the package is part of a wider US programme, worth an estimated €12 million, to support Poland and the Baltic states in response to the migration crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus on their borders.
Stronger border security strengthens our shared security.
Today in Warsaw, the United States and Poland marked the donation of more than $2 million in U.S.-funded equipment to the Polish Border Guard @Straz_Graniczna . The donation, funded by the State Department’s @StateINL and… pic.twitter.com/8Mh1eHLo0t
— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) August 25, 2026
“Stronger border security strengthens our shared security,” declared the US embassy in Warsaw, announcing the donation of equipment, which includes 45 drones and nine advanced thermal imaging cameras.
“This is just the next step in our security partnership,” they added. “Additional equipment, training, and expertise will follow.”
The Polish border guard also confirmed that the support includes training packages and bilateral study visits, as well as the delivery of 15 snowmobiles to Poland next year.
On Tuesday, it also hosted a delegation of senior figures from the US Border Patrol and US Customs and Border Protection for talks on “exchanging experiences, strengthening cooperation, and implementing advanced technologies in response to migratory pressures”.
Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging and assisting migrants – mainly from Africa and Asia – to attempt to irregularly cross into the European Union over its borders with Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. Tens of thousands of attempted crossings have been reported each year.
In response, Poland has strengthened physical and electronic barriers along the border with Belarus. It has also eased rules on the use of firearms by uniformed officers to protect the border, and has temporarily banned asylum applications by people who irregularly cross from Belarus.
As a result of such efforts, attempted illegal crossings are down 98% so far this year, while Poland also claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who do manage to cross.
The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%
Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026
After meeting with American officials on Tuesday, the Polish border guard said that the head of the US delegation, Jason E. Schneider, acting chief patrol agent for the US Border Patrol’s Rio Grande Valley sector, had praised Poland as a “model and benchmark” for dealing with migratory pressures.
It also noted that Stephanie Holmes, the deputy chief of mission at the US embassy, had noted Poland’s role “protecting the entire eastern flank of NATO and [acting] as a guarantor of transatlantic security”.
Belarus is a close ally of Russia, and the migration crisis engineered by Minsk on the EU and NATO’s eastern flank is seen as one element of the so-called “hybrid warfare” being waged by Moscow against the West.

The Polish border guard reported that, as well as donating equipment, the US has since 2024 been providing and funding “advanced tactical and technical training”, including “courses in border protection tactics”, for Polish officers.
Next month, they will provide training in operating the newly donated drones, which are being provided as part of a broader $12 million US programme to support Poland and the Baltic states in “direct response…to the situation on the Belarusian border”, said the Polish border guard.
In January this year, Polish officials also conducted study visits to El Paso and Detroit in the United States to “learn about methods used for counteracting illegal migration on the US borders with Mexico and Canada”. A further visit to the southern US border is scheduled for November.
Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland.
Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025
In 2024, the EU itself announced that it would allocate €170 million to help member states neighbouring Russia and Belarus “counter hybrid threats from the weaponisation of migration”, which it said was being used “as a political tool to destabilise EU society”. Poland was allocated the largest share of the fund, with €52 million.
Last year, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked Warsaw for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” being orchestrated by Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom she called a “predator”.

Probe deepens into death of former religious leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:57:13 UTC
21:57:13 KST

Prosecutors have opened a homicide investigation into the 2016 death of former Islamic group leader and ex-Transport Minister Arif Ahmet Denizolgun, after an expert report determined that his death was suspicious.
The chief prosecutor’s office in Istanbul’s Bakırköy district said on Aug. 26 that the investigation covers Alihan Kuriş, the current leader of the Süleymancılar religious group who has been jailed since Aug. 16, and other suspects named in the case.
The investigation follows the exhumation of Denizolgun’s grave at Istanbul’s Karacaahmet Cemetery on Aug. 19, ordered after his nephew and former lawmaker Fatih Süleyman Denizolgun filed a complaint over his uncle’s death.
An expert report dated Aug. 25 found indications of a suspicious death, prompting prosecutors to launch the new investigation.
The inquiry is examining not only members of the group’s leadership but also medical and forensic officials involved in the handling of Denizolgun’s death in 2016.
Denizolgun, a grandson of Süleyman Hilmi Tunahan, the founder of the religious movement, was elected to parliament from the Welfare Party in 1995 and served as transport minister from 1998 to 1999. He also chaired parliament’s NATO Commission.
He died in September 2016, after which Kuriş, another grandson of Tunahan, became the group’s leader.
Kuriş was arrested Aug. 16 in a separate investigation led by Ankara prosecutors into allegations including establishing and being a member of an organized crime group.
The Interior Ministry has said the investigation was based on financial and property movements linked to the group since Kuriş assumed its leadership.
Kuriş and other suspects face allegations including money laundering, aggravated fraud and violations of tax law. He has categorically denied the accusations, calling them baseless.

Lithuanian tourists among missing in Nepal following flash floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

A Nepalese tourism official said Wednesday tourists from Lithuania were among the missing foreign nationals following devastating flash floods in the country.
“Preliminary data from tourism and travel agencies show that 384 travellers are missing in the affected areas, including 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepalese citizens,” the Nepal Tourism Board said, adding that authorities were working to establish the whereabouts of the travellers.
Santos Panta, director of the Nepal Tourism Board, told the dpa news agency in Kathmandu on Wednesday that most of the missing foreign tourists were from India, but that travellers from several other countries, including the United States, Spain, Lithuania and Germany, were also unaccounted for.
The flooding hit an area where the popular Langtang Valley trekking route begins, as well as other areas visited by Hindu pilgrims.
A police spokesman said earlier that authorities did not yet know the full extent of the damage, but warned people living near the river to move to safer areas.
'We have no information' – MFA
Lithuania's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday it had no information about Lithuanian travellers missing in floods in northern Nepal, despite reports in Nepalese media suggesting some may be among the missing.
"The Embassy of the Republic of Lithuania in India is aware of the case, and the situation in the affected region is being monitored. At this time, we have no information regarding missing or injured citizens of the Republic of Lithuania," the ministry said on Wednesday.
The ministry said consular officials were prepared to provide all necessary assistance to Lithuanian citizens should such requests be received.
At least 19 people died on Wednesday during a major flood near the border with Tibet, while hundreds of tourists, including Lithuanian nationals, remained unreachable.

FACTBOX: What we know about FAZ journalist Martens’ international wanted status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

MOSCOW, August 26. /TASS/. Russia has put Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) correspondent Michael Martens on an international wanted list after a Russian court ordered his arrest in absentia over remarks targeting Russians, a source familiar with the case told TASS.
Authorities previously opened a criminal case against the journalist under an article on inciting hatred or hostility.
Martens asked what European countries could do to "help kill more Russians" at a press conference with Vladimir Zelensky and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic in Belgrade on August 8
TASS has compiled the key facts known so far.
International wanted list
- Moscow’s Basmanny District Court has ordered the arrest in absentia of Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) correspondent Michael Martens in a criminal case over his statements concerning the killing of Russians, a participant in the proceedings told TASS.
- Russian law enforcement authorities placed Martens on an international wanted list.
- Authorities charged him in absentia with inciting hatred or hostility over the statements, the source said.
Criminal case
- Russian authorities opened a criminal case against Martens over his comments about Russians, a source told TASS on August 15.
- Authorities opened the case under Part 2 of Article 282 of the Russian Criminal Code for inciting hatred or hostility, the source added.
- Martens could face up to six years in prison if convicted.
- The Russian Embassy in Germany asked the Berlin prosecutor’s office to assess Martens’ remarks under German law on August 18, the embassy said.
- Martens’ name appeared in the Russian Interior Ministry’s wanted database on August 20.
Incident
- Martens asked what European countries could do to "help kill more Russians" at a press conference with Vladimir Zelensky and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic in Belgrade on August 8.
- An online petition was launched following the incident, urging FAZ management to distance itself from Martens’ remarks and take disciplinary action, saying his comments damaged the reputation of the profession.
- The petition’s organizers said Martens had crossed the boundaries of journalistic impartiality.
FAZ reaction
- Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung expressed regret over its Balkan correspondent Martens’ "ambiguously worded" question about "Russian soldiers."
- The newspaper also said that calling for the deaths of as many Russian soldiers as possible "is not the editorial line" of the publication.
- Martens began receiving "threats" following the press conference, and FAZ said it would "take legal action" in response.
Foreign reaction
- Martens’ comments openly promote neo-Nazism, French war correspondent and International Reporters French-language editor-in-chief Christelle Neant told TASS.
- Martens’ Russophobic statements show that some Germans have failed to learn the lessons of the events on the Eastern Front during World War II, Serbian opposition New Democratic Party leader Milos Jovanovic told TASS.
- Serbian State Secretary at the Ministry of Information and Telecommunications Perko Matovic condemned Martens’ remarks, calling them an attempt to damage ties between Belgrade and Moscow.
- Former Serbian Deputy Prime Minister and Socialist Movement leader Aleksandar Vulin told TASS that the Serbian government should have expelled Martens over what he said.
- Co-chair of Berlin’s Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance branch and a member of the Berlin House of Representatives, Alexander King, said Martens’ conduct would have been unimaginable just a few years ago and reflected the German authorities’ broader policy of confrontation with Russia.
- German Foreign Ministry representative Martin Giese declined to comment, but accused Russia of allegedly "fearing independent and critical coverage of events."
- He also said the Foreign Ministry was closely monitoring developments and remained in close contact with Martens "about what may happen now."
Russian reaction
- Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Martens’ calls for Russians to be killed were unacceptable and criminal.
- Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman and United Russia Chairman Dmitry Medvedev expressed confidence that Martens would eventually face consequences.
- He noted that journalists who made such statements would once have simply been forced out of the profession.
- The Russian Embassy in Germany said Martens’ comments were repulsive and discredited him as a professional journalist, adding that Russia would consider legal mechanisms against him.
- Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev told TASS on August 20 that German authorities should distance themselves from Martens’ comments about "helping kill Russians" and condemn manifestations of hatred toward Russians.
- The Russian Embassy in Belgrade told TASS that Martens’ Russophobic remarks should receive a legal assessment from the competent authorities.
- The Russian Embassy in Washington said Martens’ controversial question at the Belgrade press conference reflected the German leadership’s dreams of a "Fourth Reich" and its cynical intention to wage war against Russia to the last Ukrainian.

Switzerland to introduce biometric identity cards from November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:56:45 UTC
21:56:45 KST

Switzerland to introduce biometric identity cards from November
From November 2, biometric identity cards will be issued by the relevant authorities in Switzerland and Swiss diplomatic missions abroad.
At its meeting on Wednesday, the Swiss government approved the necessary amendment to the ordinance.
According to a statement from the Federal Council, Switzerland’s executive body, the new biometric identity card will contain a chip, just like the existing biometric Swiss passport. As with the passport, the chip will store a facial image and two fingerprints. The amendment to the ordinance will come into force on November 1.
The Federal Council said the change will provide stronger protection against misuse of the new identity card. It will also help ensure that Swiss citizens can continue to travel freely within the European Union (EU). Since 2021, EU member states have issued only biometric identity cards for security reasons.
Two options in future
However, people who already hold a valid non-biometric identity card will still be able to travel freely within the EU until it expires, according to the information provided. The government recommends the biometric identity card for people renewing their identity card or applying for one for the first time, if they plan to travel within the EU.
Meanwhile, those who need the card only as proof of identity within Switzerland can still choose a non-biometric identity card. According to the Federal Council, this remains sufficient for that purpose.
According to the press release, the new biometric identity card will be available only from the relevant cantonal authorities and Swiss diplomatic missions abroad. By contrast, non-biometric identity cards will continue to be available from local authorities in some cantons, as they are now.
More
Swiss voters to decide – again – on introducing electronic ID
The Federal Council stressed that the new identity card with a chip should not be confused with the new electronic identity credential, known as the E-ID. Unlike the identity card, the E-ID is not a travel document. Instead, it is used to verify a person’s identity online.

New ecology trail to be organized on Solovki Islands

21:56:23 KST

ARKHANGELSK, August 26. /TASS/. Students of the Summer School on the Solovki Islands will develop an ecology trail to Cape Beluzhy on the Bolshoy Solovetsky Island, the School's Program Director, Director of the Intellectual Center at the Northern Arctic Federal University (NARFU) Svetlana Tyukina told TASS.
"We have organized the ecology workshop to make an ecology trail to Cape Beluzhy at the suggestion from the Solovki Museum-Reserve," she said. "Presently, we can see new approaches to organization of ecology trails. We will create this trail's passport, will specify the route, and will prepare information materials. Based on results of the field research, we will present proposals for landscaping in certain areas."
Cape Beluzhy is located on the western tip of the Bolshoy Solovetsky Island. This is one of the few places on the Earth where people can watch belugas from land. In other places, people have to get into the open sea to watch the animals. At low tide, belugas swim near Cape Beluzhy, and in shallow waters near the cape is their place for reproduction and upbringing of young animals. The Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of Oceanology has been observing the animals since 1994. Specialists have built a tower to conduct observations there.
The ecology trail project's implementation will play an important social and ecological role in the Solovki (Solovetsky) Archipelago's development, it will contribute to the organization of tourist flows, the development of ecology tourism and higher ecological culture of visiting tourists.
During the workshop session, students will collect materials on the Solovki Islands' natural ecosystems necessary for the development of an ecology trail; they will hold meetings with experts of the Solovki Museum-Reserve, the target audience representatives; will identify potential locations for infrastructure facilities; will design the ecology trail's signs and stands. "The young people will gain experience in design," the School's program director said. "The team will feature students of both environment and design from the University's Higher Engineering School. Students working in different areas will complement each other so that the work is done on a turnkey basis."
About the School
The Solovki School of Young Scientists is working on the Solovki Archipelago from August 23 to September 1. It is a field educational program for obtaining research and project experience in twelve areas. The students will focus on the Solovki Archipelago's studies, preservation and development of the natural, historical and cultural heritage. The School is organized by the Polyus Center for Young Researchers, and the Northern Arctic Federal University is a co-organizer. The project's partners are: the Solovki Museum-Reserve, the Solovki Maritime Museum, and the Foundation for the Preservation and Development of the Solovki Archipelago.

Netanyahu declares West Bank ‘our land’
Israel will continue building illegal settlements in the West Bank in preparation for a “major” wave of Jewish immigration, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. Israel’s most recent settlement expansion triggered rebukes from its Arab neighbors and Western partners.
“Today, many of our brothers and sisters around the world understand: This is our land and it will remain ours,” Netanyahu said in Jerusalem on Tuesday. “And when I say our land, every Jewish man and every Jewish woman, the door is open. We are waiting for you. We are preparing the door for major Aliyah (Jewish immigration to Israel).”
It is unclear whether the “major Aliyah” predicted by Netanyahu is actually coming. Israelis have emigrated in growing numbers since Hamas’ 2023 attack and the subsequent war on Gaza. More than 150,000 Israelis left the country from 2024 to 2025, according to a report by 972 magazine.
The Israeli prime minister spoke at an event organized by the Binyamin Regional Council, which governs 47 Jewish settlements in the West Bank. All of these settlements, which are located outside Israel’s 1967 borders, are considered illegal by the UN, and Israel’s transfer of population to them has been deemed a breach of the Geneva Convention by the International Criminal Court.
Although the Israeli state sometimes pre-authorizes the construction of settlements, they typically begin as outposts on Palestinian land, until they are retroactively legalized by the Israeli government. During his speech on Tuesday, Netanyahu boasted that his government has established and regularized “104 settlements and 160 farms and we continue to do more.”
“It isn’t easy, it’s never easy,” he continued. “The land of Israel is acquired through suffering. Sometimes also through smiles, sometimes also through arguments, but it is being acquired by us. We are not giving up, we have a vision, this is our land, and it will remain ours.”
Last week, Israel opened bidding for the construction of more than 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement project, located east of Jerusalem. Named after its designation on Israeli planning maps, the project will comprise more than 3,400 homes, and was green-lit by Netanyahu’s government last year.
The E1 plan will establish a land corridor between East Jerusalem and the existing settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, both of which are built on Palestinian land. It will also sever road links between the Palestinian cities of Ramallah and Bethlehem, located to the north and south of Jerusalem, respectively.
Eight Arab and Muslim states, including Mecca Pact members Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye, “categorically” rejected the plan, describing it as “a dangerous escalation.” The UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, European Commission, and 15 European states also condemned the project.
“The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank,” they said in a statement last Thursday. “At a time of grave instability in the West Bank with unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians, and serious restrictions on the Palestinian economy, this decision is even more concerning.”
Netanyahu has suggested for years that he intends to annex the entirety of the West Bank, describing the option as “on the table” even as he signed peace accords with Arab states in 2020. Netanyahu’s hardline coalition partners have been more explicit, with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urging the prime minister in June to “apply sovereignty here in Judea and Samaria [the West Bank] before the elections” in October.
