CCTV: China announced that President Xi Jinping will attend the 2026 SCO Summit. What message does China hope to convey?
Lin Jian: This year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO. Over the past 25 years, member states have upheld the Shanghai Spirit, worked in solidarity and coordination, and deepened all-round cooperation. The SCO has grown into a comprehensive regional cooperation organization that covers the biggest area and population with enormous development potential, successfully explored a new type of regional cooperation, and set an example of a new type of international relations.
Last year’s SCO Summit in Tianjin provided strategic planning on the development of the SCO for the next decade, and opened up a new stage of high-quality development of the organization. At this year’s summit in Bishkek, President Xi Jinping will have in-depth exchanges of views with participating leaders on deepening SCO cooperation in various fields under the new circumstances and major international and regional issues of our times. They will provide guidance for the SCO’s high-quality development and participation in the reform and development of the global governance system. China stands ready to work with various parties to build up consensus and write a new chapter of cooperation in Bishkek, and contribute to security, stability, development and revitalization of regional countries and the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.
CGTN: President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt. Could you share with us the arrangement? What’s China’s expectation on growing its ties with the two countries?
Lin Jian: China and Kyrgyzstan are good neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, good friends of mutual trust, and good partners with a common pursuit. Since the establishment of diplomatic relations 34 years ago, the two countries have been treating each other with good faith and sincerity, setting a stellar example of mutual support and mutual success among neighboring countries. In recent years, China-Kyrgyzstan relations have grown by leaps and bounds, with consolidating political mutual trust, fruitful outcomes in high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, numerous highlights of people-to-people exchanges, and close and effective coordination on international occasions. Last year, President Xi Jinping had three meetings with President Japarov, steering China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation into a golden period of rapid development. During the visit, President Xi Jinping will have an in-depth exchange of views on bilateral relations, cooperation in key areas, and international and regional situation with President Japarov in their talks, and attend various state events. China looks forward to working with Kyrgyzstan to take this visit as an opportunity to promote high-quality development of mutually beneficial cooperation on all fronts, add new dimensions to the China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future, and bring more benefits to the two peoples.
Egypt is the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with New China. In recent years, under the strategic guidance of President Xi Jinping and President El-Sisi, the two countries have deepened political mutual trust, achieved fruitful outcomes in cooperation across various fields, and engaged in increasingly frequent people-to-people exchanges and close and effective coordination on multilateral occasions. China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership has grown by leaps and bounds, and been at its best in history, setting a stellar example of solidarity, collaboration and mutual benefit among developing countries. This visit marks President Xi Jinping’s first state visit to Egypt in 10 years. As we are celebrating the 70th anniversary of the establishment of China-Egypt diplomatic relations, this visit carries great significance in building on the past achievements and charting the future. During the visit, President Xi Jinping will hold talks with President El-Sisi. They will have an in-depth exchange of views on China-Egypt relations and international and regional issues of mutual interest. Through the visit, China looks forward to working with Egypt to carry forward traditional friendship, render each other firm support, expand mutually beneficial cooperation, and bolster each other’s modernization, so that we can jointly draw a new chapter of China-Egypt relations and make positive contributions to peace and stability in the region and beyond.
Bloomberg: Following Scott Bessent’s public comments on the so-called “Economic D-Day” regarding sanctions on Iran and its trading partners, has there been any communication between the U.S. and the Chinese side on this matter? And if so, can you provide any additional details?
Lin Jian: I have no information to share at the moment.
Bloomberg: Chinese authorities are urging Chinese citizens in Eswatini to evacuate, and urging others not to visit the country, citing local security and scamming concerns. Can you elaborate a little bit on some of the thinking behind this advisory? Could you also tell me how many Chinese citizens roughly live in Eswatini?
Lin Jian: Eswatini is faced with a complex security situation with rampant telecom fraud and online gambling and extremely high safety risks. Issuing travel advisories is a common practice worldwide. Committed to a people-centered approach and diplomacy for the people, we will do everything necessary to safeguard the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens overseas.
Bloomberg: Would you be able to give me some examples of other similar travel advisories that China has issued, specifically regarding scamming and related risks? And also, China doesn’t have diplomatic relations with Eswatini. Is that a factor in this advisory or is it unrelated?
Lin Jian: We have issued similar advisories. For this one, I need to stress that given the extremely high safety risks and rampant telecom fraud and online gambling in Eswatini, the Chinese government, for the safety of Chinese nationals, issued the travel advisory after prudent evaluation.
Bloomberg: Going back a little bit to the SCO and also the trips to Egypt by President Xi Jinping. You mentioned that international and regional issues would be on the agendas in both Kyrgyzstan and Egypt. Specifically, can I ask you, how prominent do you think Iran will feature in the discussions? Is there anything a bit more specific you could share about what regional conflicts in particular will be dealt with as part of this trip?
Lin Jian: For more about the visits, we will release readouts in due course. Please stay tuned.
Bloomberg: We know that Canada has matched the tariffs that President Trump set, including 50 percent on items such as dairy and steel. Broadly speaking, is there some kind of opinion or perspective that you could share from the Chinese foreign ministry’s point of view in terms of the actions that Canada or perhaps other countries might take in response to Trump’s tariff war. Is there some advice, for example, or some comments that you can provide?
Lin Jian: China believes that economic and trade concerns should be addressed through dialogue and consultation on an equal footing.

Amnesty urges Saudi Arabia to release French-Egyptian national
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:52:36 UTC
20:52:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Amnesty renews call for Saudi Arabia to release French-Egyptian national facing torture
Amnesty International has renewed its calls for Saudi Arabia to free Dr Amr Abdelfattah, a French-Egyptian national detained in the kingdom for over two years, accusing Saudi authorities of torturing him and denying him any contact with his family.
Abdelfattah was arrested in June 2024 after reportedly completing the Hajj pilgrimage with an invalid visa permit, but was later tried before a specialised criminal court where he faced charges on what Amnesty has described as "expression-related offences".
The telecommunications engineer had travelled to Saudi Arabia with his wife for the first time to perform Hajj, but was detained on 16 June in Makkah before being transferred to the Dhahban Central Prison near Jeddah.
Earlier this month, Abdelfattah’s France-based lawyer raised concerns that he had been sentenced to prison for an unspecified number of years, with authorities failing to state how long his sentence would be or what his conviction was.
According to Amnesty, Abdelfattah has faced ill treatment, repeated torture, and had access to his lawyer denied. The rights group further added that he has been held incommunicado and has been denied contact with his family.
Calls for the release of the father-of-three have also grown among activists, particularly as Amnesty revealed that credible sources have reported seeing signs of physical violence on Abdelfattah’s body.
Abdelfattah’s lawyer told Amnesty that on 23 August 2024, interrogators threw him against a wall and threatened to kill him. Later that same year in December, six masked officers reportedly restrained and beat him, causing him to lose consciousness.
Another account states that on 11 March 2025, he was forced to run with his feet tied and was denied food for 24 hours.
Earlier this year, reports state he was beaten by other detainees, threatened and assaulted. In May, prison officers also beat him after he requested the transfer who he said posed a danger to other prisoners.
Health concerns
Abdelfattah’s family have raised the alarm over his health, noting that he has astigmatism and has not had access to his glasses since last year.
He has told his family that he has developed back pain while behind bars, which has now started affecting his legs and reduced control of his left hand.
Contact with his family has also been restricted, with only a 15-minute call with his wife permitted in September 2024.
However, reports state that prison authorities monitored the calls and interjected when he mentioned prison conditions and his legal case. His family have said that they are forced to speak Arabic so that conversations can be monitored.

Trump sends Saudi nuclear deal to Congress – media

Trump sends Saudi nuclear deal to Congress – media
US President Donald Trump has reportedly submitted a landmark nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia for congressional review and renewed demands that Riyadh normalize relations with Israel as part of the deal.
According to US media outlets, citing unnamed administration and congressional sources, the document was sent to Congress on Monday. The White House has yet to publicly confirm the move.
Lawmakers now have 90 session days to review the US-Saudi pact. If they attempt to block it, Trump is expected to use his veto powers to push it through. A two-thirds majority in both chambers would be required to overrule the president.
The agreement was originally signed last month and aims to allow American companies to play a major role in developing Saudi Arabia’s civilian nuclear energy program. The 30-year deal is expected to involve the construction of US-designed nuclear reactors in Saudi Arabia and could be worth tens of billions of dollars.
Riyadh says it wants nuclear power to meet the growing domestic energy demand, reduce the amount of oil consumed at home, and free up more crude for export.
However, the deal has raised concerns over nuclear proliferation. Unlike a similar US deal with the United Arab Emirates, the pact does not permanently bar the kingdom from reprocessing nuclear fuel or enrichment, which could potentially be used to make weapons.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman previously suggested that the kingdom could seek a nuclear weapon if Iran ever acquires one.
Trump has also tied the nuclear agreement to Saudi Arabia formally joining the Abraham Accords and establishing diplomatic relations with Israel. The condition was unexpectedly announced by Trump late last month after the agreement had already been negotiated and signed.
An administration official cited by Reuters on Wednesday said Trump’s position on the issue “has not changed.”
The Abraham Accords, brokered during Trump’s first term, established diplomatic relations between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority countries, including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Morocco.
The US has also pushed for Saudi-Israeli normalization, but the efforts have stalled since the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly said it will not normalize relations with Israel without an irreversible path toward the creation of a Palestinian state.

11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has labeled the Iranian leadership "savages" and claimed that a diplomatic deal with Tehran was impossible.
He also praised President Donald Trump’s renewed campaign of economic pressure.
Recounting a recent meeting with Trump, Netanyahu said they had discussed the possibility of diplomacy with the Islamic republic and added: "I doubt, however, that an agreement can be reached with that group there, with those savages."
"I tell you – an agreement cannot be reached," Netanyahu said late Tuesday at an event in Jerusalem for Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu has long opposed diplomacy with Iran, openly campaigning against a 2015 nuclear deal brokered by then U.S. president Barack Obama, but he has been publicly careful not to criticize Trump who has also sought a negotiated settlement.
Trump joined Netanyahu in a U.S.-Israeli joint attack on Iran in late February but agreed to a cease-fire in April in the face of widespread U.S. public opposition to the war, which had sent oil prices spiraling.
Trump Monday declared "economic D-Day" aimed at destroying Iran's economy, which has already endured years of sanctions, but he has shown reluctance to resume a full-scale war even as he grows frustrated that Tehran will not accept his demands.
Netanyahu, who is trailing in some polls ahead of Oct. 27 elections, voiced support for Trump's economic pressure campaign and took a degree of ownership, saying he told Trump of this "third option."
He praised the U.S. president for pursuing the economic path in "a very, very, very strong way."
Trump had chosen to target not just Iran itself but decided on "tightening the siege on those who assist this regime, this terrible dictatorship. This is very important," Netanyahu said.
The Israeli leader had pushed for years for a U.S. attack on Iran, whose Shiite cleric-run state supports armed groups like Hezbollah and Hamas, which led the devastating Oct. 7, 2023 incursion on Israel.
Netanyahu met Trump at the White House on July 28. In his remarks Tuesday, Netanyahu said that the two also discussed renewing military action against Iran.
"I told him: We are there, we will defend ourselves, and we will not allow Iran to attack us," Netanyahu said.
"And if, God forbid, they attack us, they will suffer a blow they never dreamed of – much stronger than anything they have suffered so far," he said.
The war has become even more personal for Netanyahu as he revealed Monday that Iran tried to kill one of his sons.
He did not give further details. The U.S. news channel Newsmax, quoting an anonymous U.S. law enforcement source, said the target was Yair Netanyahu, his 35-year-old son who has long lived in the Miami area and is known for his outspoken support for hawkish Israeli policies.
The younger Netanyahu abruptly returned to Israel, leaving his belongings behind, Newsmax said.
Israel in the opening salvo of the war on Feb. 28 ,killed Iran's then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with much of his family.
His son Mojtaba, one of Khamenei's six children, was named the new supreme leader a week later and has not been seen in public since.
In a message read out on his behalf on state TV, Mojtaba Khamenei said that in addition to his father, he had lost his wife, his sister, her child and his brother-in-law.

Taiwan to broaden tax incentives for small and micro businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:49:00 UTC
20:49:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet plans to submit a bill in September to expand tax incentives and support for small businesses, Deputy Economics Minister Ho Chin-tsang (何晉滄) said Wednesday.
CNA reported that the proposed bill for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses would broaden support under the existing Act for Development of Small and Medium Enterprises. It would cover businesses in shopping districts, markets, and night markets, as well as small shops that are not registered as companies.
Ho said the government would also review eligibility rules for equipment investment tax breaks. The goal is to lower the thresholds so more small businesses can qualify.
The bill would also expand incentives for hiring workers and raising salaries, Ho said. He said the government is considering widening the age range covered by hiring incentives and increasing tax deductions for businesses that raise wages.
Under current rules, small and medium-sized businesses receive incentives for hiring entry-level Taiwanese workers aged 24 or younger or 65 or older. Businesses can deduct twice the eligible salary expenses from taxable income, while qualifying wage increases receive a 175% deduction.
The government plans to spend NT$100 billion (US$3.14 billion) over eight years on measures to help businesses transform and grow. The funding would support research and development, credit guarantees, and efforts to reach new markets, per Economics Daily News.
The economics ministry said the country had about 1.72 million small and medium-sized businesses in 2025, accounting for 98.9% of all businesses. They employed about 9.19 million people, or around 80% of Taiwan's workforce, per UDN.
These businesses generated NT$3.2 trillion in exports and accounted for 79.3% of total business sales, according to the ministry. Ho said the proposed law would support equipment upgrades and business services in areas where small businesses are concentrated.
Ho said the economics ministry aims to submit the bill to the legislature for review in September. He said the ministry hopes lawmakers will support the proposal.
In Taiwan, a small or medium-sized business is generally defined as a registered business with paid-in capital of no more than NT$100 million or fewer than 200 regular employees. A micro business is one with fewer than five regular employees.

9 Taboos to avoid during Ghost Festival in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:48:45 UTC
20:48:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Ghost Festival is on Thursday, when people traditionally honor their ancestors and offer food and other items to wandering spirits.
The festival falls on the 15th day of the seventh month of the lunisolar calendar, halfway through Ghost Month. It is traditionally believed to be a time when wandering spirits return to the world of the living.
Offerings typically include rice wine, fruit, chicken, pork, fish, snacks, incense, and joss paper. Gold joss paper is traditionally burned for gods, while silver joss paper is burned for spirits, and some people choose fruits with leaves because they are associated with career and business prosperity.
Wandering spirits are often referred to as “Good Brothers” or “Good Sisters” rather than ghosts, as the terms are considered more respectful. Folk beliefs hold that generous offerings can help appease these spirits and bring peace and good fortune to a household, while failing to make offerings could invite bad luck.
Folk custom expert and the founding chair of the Taichung Numerology Education Association, Yang Teng-kei (楊登嵙), listed nine traditional taboos associated with the Ghost Festival, per CTWant.
1. Avoid getting married
Some Good Brothers are believed to have died before they could marry. Getting married on this day is traditionally considered likely to provoke their jealousy.
2. Avoid buying a new home
Traditionally, it is believed that one should keep a low profile during Ghost Festival, making major changes such as buying a home or moving less desirable.
3. Avoid elective surgery
Traditional beliefs hold that major physical changes, including surgery, could attract the attention of wandering spirits. Serious or emergency medical conditions, however, should be treated according to medical advice.
4. Avoid scheduled births
Some people avoid scheduling elective C-sections or inductions on this day out of concern that they could attract the jealousy of spirits. This does not apply to natural labor or medical emergencies.
5. Avoid opening a new business
Yang considers opening a business during the Ghost Festival an inauspicious beginning, as traditional beliefs associate the period with a higher risk of failure.
6. Avoid holding a funeral
Yang advises against holding a funeral on this day, but says that if one is necessary, the burning of joss paper should be postponed until after the seventh lunar month. This is traditionally based on the belief that wandering spirits could interfere with the proceedings.
7. Avoid buying a car
Many Taiwanese traditionally avoid buying cars during Ghost Month because they associate major purchases during this period with potential misfortune.
8. Avoid swimming in certain areas
Rather than avoiding swimming altogether, some traditions advise staying away from dangerous coastal areas and mountain streams during Ghost Month. This is based on the folk belief that water spirits seek people to replace them.
9. Avoid major milestones
Yang generally advises avoiding major activities or important undertakings during the Ghost Festival.

Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:47:00 UTC
20:47:00 KST

Zambia after the polls: A test for democracy
August 26, 2026
The Electoral Commission of Zambia has declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema winner of the August 13 presidential election.
His closest challenger, Brian Mundubile, received 38% of the vote, according to official results published last week. However, Mundubile has since announced on several occasions that he would be challenging that result, and that his National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) "shall not relent" in the face of any obstacle.
That challenge, however, comes as Zambia's courts have all remained closed since August 24 until further notice, with officials citing "security concerns."
The timing of this closure has raised questions about opposition voices having access to judicial election safeguards during this crucial stage of the post-election process, as random reports of irregularities continue to surface.
Election dispute continues to unfold
The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) has called for the urgent restoration of access to the courts and for alternative arrangements to be enacted for urgent cases.
LAZ President Arnold Kaluba said security measures must not undermine any access to justice or judicial independence.
"Such measures must be lawful, proportionate and implemented in a manner that preserves access to justice and respects the constitutional independence and autonomy of the judiciary," he stressed.
Meanwhile, the Human Rights Commission of Zambia has also expressed concern; its chairperson, Pamela Towela Sambo, warned that disruption to judicial operations could affect fundamental rights in the country, including access to a fair trial and legal remedies.
"[If] the right to a fair trial is delayed, there is increased risk of arbitrary detentions, while access to remedies is effectively blocked," she said.
'Irregular' submission of petition documents
However, the ongoing election dispute has taken a new turn: Zambia's Chief Justice Mumba Malila, acknowledged on August 25 that he had received documents described as a presidential election petition through his private email-address.
Malila described the method of submission as "highly irregular" —despite the current circumstances allowing no access to legal procedures. He said he nevertheless referred the documents to the Constitutional Court to determine whether this qualified as a petition having been formally filed.
The distinction here is important: The receipt of such documents does not confirm that a presidential election petition has been formally lodged per se.
The latest development comes as the courts remain closed, adding to questions about how election-related cases can be filed and processed.
Government continues to cite security concerns for court closure
Meanwhile, the presidency has rejected suggestions that the court closures were intended to prevent and intervene with any challenges to the election result.
Hichilema's chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the security measures were of a "intelligence-led and preventive" nature, adding that they involved several government institutions beyond courts, and that they were intended to protect officials, institutions and members of the public.
He also maintained that people with legitimate grievances remained free to pursue remedies provided by law.
But during the election itself, there had already been suspensions of voting at some ballot boxes amid reports of violence. Questions about the independence of the media had also surface in the run-up to the vote.
Concerns about access to justice and public confidence remain strong, especially against this backdrop; the Zambia Executive Director Maurice Nyambe of Transparency International said in this context the country needs stronger institutions for resolving political disputes.
"At this stage of the electoral process, Zambia does not need fewer avenues for resolving political disputes. It needs stronger, accessible, and trusted institutions through which those disputes can be peacefully resolved."
Political commentator and human rights activist Laura Miti meanwhile questioned the lack of a fuller public explanation for the closure, writing on Facebook that "if you are going to unprecedentedly close the courts, you owe the nation an explanation beyond a blanket — there is a security threat."
A test beyond the ballot box
Zambia has long been regarded as one of Southern Africa's more stable multiparty democracies with a reputation for political stability and peaceful transfers of power.
But the current dispute comes at a time when democratic institutions across the region keep facing growing scrutiny over contested elections and political transitions. Therefore, the handling of situation will likely be observed beyond Zambia and the southern African region.
For Zambians, the issue goes beyond the contest between Hichilema and Mundubile; it is about how political disagreements can be resolved peacefully through independent, accessible and trusted institutions.
That notion is perhaps best reflected on the streets of Lusaka; a citizen of the capital simply told DW: "We are anxious and afraid because we do not know the truth about what is happening."
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

Berlin wants to buy immunity for the first German genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:46:42 UTC
20:46:42 KST

The first German genocide the West chose to forget
The deep physical and structural wounds inflicted on the African continent by European colonialism will take generations to heal – if they ever heal at all. In today’s fast-moving geopolitical landscape, where crises like illegal migration, economic turbulence, and regional conflict dominate African headline news, the question of historical justice is often forced onto the back burner. Yet, through continental efforts, Africa refuses to let the issue recede into memory.
The landmark Algiers Declaration, adopted last December under the auspices of the African Union, marked a shift from moral grievance to a legal strategy, demanding the codification of colonial atrocities as crimes against humanity and establishing that justice requires binding legal reparations, not voluntary Western aid usually publicized as gifts.
This week, that continental demand for accountability finds its most vivid expression in Namibia. On August 23, the Herero and Nama people gathered in the historic town of Okahandja in central Namibia, just 70 kilometers north of the capital, Windhoek, for the annual Herero Day (Red Flag Day) commemorations. The event honors Chief Samuel Maharero, leader of the Herero resistance against German rule. After he died in exile in Botswana, his body was returned to Namibia and reburied in Okahandja in 1923.
The march through the ancestral burial grounds of the paramount chiefs stands as an active protest against modern colonial evasion – and a direct challenge to a European power attempting to settle a multi-century blood debt on its own convenient, unilateral terms.
To understand the full weight of this grievance, one must return to 1904, when Imperial German colonial forces unleashed a systematic campaign of destruction following an indigenous uprising against relentless land dispossession and colonial tyranny. In October 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued his notorious ‘Vernichtungsbefehl’ (extermination order), explicitly declaring: “Within the German borders, every Herero, with or without a gun... will be shot.”
Far from facing criminal prosecution, von Trotha was long celebrated as a hero at home – a street in Munich bore his name until public pressure finally forced the city council to rename it ‘Hererostrasse’ in 2006.
Under his command, German troops drove tens of thousands of Herero families into the hyper-arid Omaheke Desert in eastern Namibia, systematically poisoning and sealing off water wells to ensure death by thirst and starvation. Those who survived, along with the Nama people who rebelled shortly afterward, were swept into concentration camps (most notoriously at Shark Island) where they faced forced labor, lethal living conditions, and pseudoscientific racial experiments.
By the time the campaign ended in 1908, it had claimed an estimated 70,000 lives, systematically wiping out 80% of the Herero population and 50% of the Nama population in what historians and legal scholars recognize as the 20th century’s first genocide.
Yet, when confronting the modern reckoning for these atrocities, Imperial Germany’s successor state has constructed a masterclass in diplomatic and legal evasion. In May 2021, after six years of closed-door bilateral negotiations, Berlin and Windhoek initialed a joint declaration in which Germany acknowledged the atrocities as “genocide from today’s perspective” – a carefully calculated semantic formula designed specifically to avoid admitting legal liability under international law. Rather than offering legally binding reparations, Berlin committed €1.1 billion over 30 years earmarked for state-level development projects, framing the financial support strictly as a voluntary gesture of reconciliation.
The contrast with Germany’s handling of European historical crimes could not be more glaring. In the aftermath of World War II, Germany recognized direct legal liability for the Holocaust, paying tens of billions of euros in formal reparations directly to survivors and representative organizations – commitments that continue to this day. When dealing with African victims, however, Berlin invoked intertemporal legal loopholes, arguing that international law against genocide did not exist in 1904. By bypassing the Herero and Nama leaders to cut a state-to-state deal, Germany sought to buy immunity from future legal claims. This double standard is precisely why affected communities rejected the 2021 agreement.
Two years later, traditional leaders from the Ovaherero Traditional Authority (OTA) and the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), representing the direct descendants of the victims, launched a legal challenge in the Namibian High Court to invalidate the 2021 Joint Declaration. They argue that by excluding affected indigenous communities from negotiations, the Namibian government breached its duty to protect its citizens’ rights and heritage.
The resulting political impasse has paralyzed parliamentary ratification in Windhoek, while opposition lawmakers in Berlin increasingly view the agreement as a diplomatic liability. By challenging a deal struck over their heads, the Herero and Nama are establishing a critical precedent: Sovereign states cannot settle the blood debt of indigenous genocide without the direct inclusion and consent of the victim communities themselves.
This domestic legal battle has become the focal point of a broader international legal push. In August 2026, Amnesty International officially filed court papers in the Namibian High Court seeking to join the Herero and Nama litigation as ‘amicus curiae’. Amnesty’s legal intervention targets a fundamental principle: State-to-state development packages cannot override the recognized rights of indigenous communities under international law to seek direct, full reparations for genocide. Former European powers have long shielded themselves behind the principle of non-retroactivity, claiming that atrocities committed prior to the 1948 Genocide Convention fall outside modern judicial frameworks. However, joint efforts between the African Union and the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) are systematically dismantling this defense.
Germany’s refusal to accept legal liability in Namibia is thus exposed as a deliberate attempt to preserve a legal shield protecting ex-empires from reparatory claims.
As the African Union moves to codify colonial atrocities into international law, the ongoing High Court challenge in Windhoek serves as a test case for former colonial powers across the West. Until Berlin meets its obligations with the same legal and financial rigor applied to European historical crimes, the solemn gatherings in Okahandja will stand as an active front line in the global struggle against impunity.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday he had been informed about CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow but declined to discuss the substance of the meeting.
“We knew about the meeting,” Nausėda said. “I would not want to discuss its content because, first of all, that is a matter for the parties to the meeting.”
Lithuania had been informed by its partners that details about the meeting, including its purpose and content, would be shared with Vilnius promptly, Nausėda said.
“We were informed by our partners that information about this meeting, its objectives and content would be provided to us immediately – probably next week,” he said.

The CIA and White House have not commented on the purpose of the visit.
The Kremlin said Wednesday that Ratcliffe had “contacts” with Russian intelligence services during his visit to Moscow, without providing further details.
Nausėda said he believed the meeting was intended to help reduce geopolitical tensions in the region.
“This makes me feel positive,” he said.
The last CIA director to visit Moscow was William Burns, who travelled to the Russian capital in November 2021 and warned Russian officials against sending troops into Ukraine. Several months later, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Ukraine expects sanctions against Russian ballistics manufacturers in coming months – presidential commissioner
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
14:41:50 EEST
20:41:50 KST

Ukraine has provided partners with information on Russian ballistics manufacturers, as well as foreign technical and chemical components used by Russia to produce ballistic missiles, reported Commissioner of the President of Ukraine on Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
"And, accordingly, one of the first points of our plan (to counter ballistics – IF-U) is maximum synchronization. That is, in all jurisdictions of countries that adopt sanctions against Russia, all entities identified as manufacturers of Russian ballistic strike weapons must be sanctioned," Vlasiuk told journalists on Wednesday.
According to him, this involves more than 100 Russian enterprises involved in ballistics production.
"Accordingly, in September-October, we expect all Russian manufacturers of ballistic strike weapons to be added to the sanctions lists. We are talking about 100 plus enterprises," he said.
Separately, the presidential commissioner reported that Ukraine handed over information to partners regarding foreign technical components used by Russia in the production of ballistic missiles. According to him, among the countries where companies associated with supplying such components are registered are the US, Switzerland, China, France, Great Britain, Taiwan, Japan, and Germany.
Ukraine also provided partners with information regarding chemical components on whose import Russian ballistics production depends.
"We handed over substance files to our partners and expect decisions in the coming months. All these files are also being transferred. For each item, we disclosed in detail there how exactly this item is used for ballistics production," he noted.
According to him, Ukraine expects partners to introduce corresponding restrictions on the export of such components to Russia in the coming months.
At the same time, he emphasized that this year there were successful cases of blocking the export of foreign components to Russia thanks to US assistance.
The presidential commissioner reported that in the near future he may pay a visit to the US to promote a sanctions bill by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Vlasiuk also noted that Ukraine expects several intermediate sanctions packages from the European Union prior to the adoption of the 22nd package, which, according to him, is expected no earlier than the end of October.
"We would like them (the EU – IF-U) to adopt several intermediate packages before this large 22nd package. That is no earlier than the end of October. We would like them to adopt a small intermediate package as early as September, specifically aimed at countering ballistics sanctions packages. Then another package in October," he said.
According to Vlasiuk, the EU’s 22nd sanctions package should address, in particular, the Russian military-industrial complex and measures aimed at countering Russian ballistic capabilities.

Cambridge Pixel to showcase USV sensor software
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
12:40:18 BST
20:40:18 KST

UK firm Cambridge Pixel will showcase radar, tracking and sensor-processing software for uncrewed and autonomous surface vessels at SMM 2026 in Hamburg.
Cambridge Pixel will use the SMM 2026 maritime exhibition in Hamburg to showcase software designed to help developers integrate radar, cameras and other sensors aboard uncrewed and autonomous surface vessels, according to the company.
The Cambridge-based firm says its modular software can support both commercial and military USV and ASV projects, providing functions including radar processing, target tracking, obstacle detection, sensor fusion, camera control, recording and navigation support in GPS-denied environments. The company will exhibit the technology between 1 and 4 September as part of SMM 2026, which this year includes a dedicated Maritime Security & Defence Expo.
At the centre of the offering is Cambridge Pixel’s SPx Server V2, which provides radar video processing, proximity detection and tracking functions intended to support collision avoidance and autonomous navigation. A Detection Server configuration can provide plot extraction and proximity detection, while the Tracking Server adds multi-hypothesis target tracking to follow contacts in more complex environments.
Cambridge Pixel says obstacle and target information generated by the software can then be passed to an external autonomy or vessel-control system using established data formats including ASTERIX, NMEA-0183, TAK and SAPIENT. This allows the radar-processing layer to be integrated with a wider vessel architecture rather than requiring developers to adopt a complete proprietary control system.
The company is also promoting its ability to interface with existing maritime radars, saying its software has already been integrated with more than 80 different radar types. For developers of uncrewed craft, that can provide a route to using commercial or military radar hardware with custom autonomy, navigation and command software without having to develop the radar-processing layer from scratch.
The technology is intended to address several practical problems facing autonomous surface vessels, including navigation where satellite positioning is degraded or unavailable, maintaining awareness of nearby traffic and obstacles, and combining information from radar with cameras and other sensors. Cambridge Pixel says those functions can be provided through software components without requiring extensive bespoke hardware.
The company has worked with uncrewed and autonomous vessel developers for more than a decade and says its technology is already used by organisations in 65 countries. Customers and integration partners cited by Cambridge Pixel include BAE Systems, Hensoldt, L3Harris, Lockheed Martin, QinetiQ, Saab, Thales, the Royal Navy and the US Navy, although the announcement does not identify which specific systems or programmes use the USV-focused software being demonstrated at SMM.
The Hamburg event will also provide a wider defence backdrop for the company’s maritime autonomy work. SMM expects more than 2,200 exhibitors and almost 50,000 visitors from over 100 countries, while the new Maritime Security & Defence Expo will focus on areas including uncrewed systems, cyber security, maritime surveillance and protection of critical infrastructure.
For Cambridge Pixel, the emphasis is less on producing complete uncrewed vessels than on supplying the processing and integration layer that allows radar and other sensors to feed useful information into navigation and autonomy systems. That approach places the company within a wider market in which naval and commercial operators are seeking to add increasingly autonomous functions to existing and new surface platforms without replacing every component in the vessel’s sensor architecture.
The SMM demonstration will therefore centre on how established radar and sensor data can be processed, fused and distributed into external control systems, with Cambridge Pixel positioning its modular software as a means of reducing integration time for developers building both military and commercial autonomous maritime platforms.

Top US official to meet NATO allies over force review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:40:03 UTC
20:40:03 KST

US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby arrives to testify before the Senate Armed Services Committee at the Hart Senate Office Building in Washington, US. (AFP photo)
A senior U.S. defense official will brief NATO countries on Aug. 27 on Washington's review of its forces in Europe, officials said, in the face of fears over an American pullback from the continent.
U.S. Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby will meet ambassadors from NATO countries at the headquarters of the 32-country alliance in Brussels.
"The United States is consulting with allies as part of its force posture review," a NATO official said on Aug. 26.
Washington launched a six-month review in July as it presses European countries to take principal responsibility for the conventional defense of their continent.
The move was announced by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth amid U.S. anger at the response of European nations to the war with Iran, including restrictions on U.S. forces using their bases at the start of the conflict.
As part of the process the United States is quizzing countries over their defense spending and approach to American forces using bases, European diplomats said.
"We need to send a united European message on Aug. 27 to show how we are stepping up together as a whole," said one diplomat. "It is not a beauty contest."
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defense as it signals it wants to step back to focus on other challenges such as China.
The Pentagon has already told allies it is reducing the number of assets it makes available for NATO's defense plans.
Washington also said in May it would withdraw 5,000 troops from Germany, but Trump later said he was sending the same number to neighboring Poland.
European countries are massively ramping up military budgets, agreeing in 2025 to Trump's demand to devote five percent of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.

August 26, 2026, Chișinău – The NATO Political Committee held a working session in Chișinău, providing an opportunity to discuss key priorities in Moldova–NATO relations and prospects for further deepening cooperation with the North Atlantic Alliance. During the session, the delegation held talks with Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Foreign Affairs Mihai Popșoi and State Secretary Valeriu Mija.
The discussions focused on the priorities for cooperation between the Republic of Moldova and NATO, as well as ways to further advance political dialogue and practical cooperation.
In their remarks, the Moldovan and NATO official reiterated the importance of the partnership between the Republic of Moldova and NATO, which has played an important role in building resilient institutions and supporting the modernization of the national security and defence sector.
The exchange also covered the development of cooperation between the Republic of Moldova and the North Atlantic Alliance, with an emphasis on implementing the objectives of the Moldova–NATO Individual Partnership Programme (ITPP) for 2025–2028.
“Cooperation with NATO contributes to enhancing our country’s resilience and building stronger institutions capable of responding to current security challenges. The Republic of Moldova is interested in deepening political dialogue and practical cooperation with the Alliance, in full accordance with its constitutional status of neutrality,” underlined Deputy Prime Minister Mihai Popșoi.
State Secretary Valeriu Mija and Ms. Tanya Hartman, Chair of the NATO Political Committee, addressed the priorities of the Republic of Moldova–NATO cooperation agenda for 2026–2027.
The Moldovan side reaffirmed its interest in deepening its partnership with the Alliance, including by continuing efforts to modernize the national security and defence sector and enhancing the capacity of institutions to respond effectively to current security challenges.
The Chair of the NATO Political Committee welcomed the progress made in the Republic of Moldova–NATO partnership and commended the efforts of the authorities in Chișinău to strengthen the country’s resilience and modernize the security sector. Moldova’s contribution to international peacekeeping efforts was also recognized, including the participation of National Army contingents in the KFOR operation in Kosovo since 2014.
The Republic of Moldova has been cooperating with NATO under the Partnership for Peace Program since 1994. This cooperation focuses, in particular, on consolidating institutional resilience, reforming and modernizing the security and defence sector, professional development and training, cybersecurity, strategic communications, and contributing to international peacekeeping efforts, in full compliance with the Republic of Moldova’s constitutional neutrality.

17th Odesa International Film Festival kicks off in Kyiv: what will be shown this year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26

17th Odesa International Film Festival kicks off in Kyiv: what will be shown this year
Kyiv • UNN
The Odesa International Film Festival will take place in Kyiv from August 27 to September 4.
The 17th Odesa International Film Festival will start in Kyiv on August 27. Over nine days—from September 4—viewers will be shown premieres of the most anticipated national films and international festival hits. Industry professionals will be able to join discussions and master classes, UNN writes with a link to the press service of OIFF.
The festival’s main venues will be the Zhovten and Oscar cinemas. The festival program includes International and National Competition Programs, special screenings, and separate industry and educational events. OIFF traditionally combines Ukrainian cinema with international festival works and gives audiences the opportunity to see most of the films on the big screen before their theatrical release in Ukraine.
Ukrainian and international films
As part of the National Competition Program, OIFF will present 13 Ukrainian feature films. The films address the themes of war, its consequences, and the search for a future.
Participants include the documentaries "Because He Was of Cossack Stock" directed by Roman Krupach, "The Miner" directed by Mykola But, "Clouds Fly at Great Speed" directed by Roman Ostrovskyi, "Maidan Time Machine" directed by Volodymyr Tykhyi, and others. There are also the fiction films "For Victory!" directed by Valentyn Vasianovych, "Kira’s Dream" directed by Denys Kolesnikov, and "The Soloist" directed by Serhii Storozhev.
The International Competition Program includes feature films from Europe, North and South America. This year’s selection brings together films about women’s lives in different countries and historical circumstances.
Among the announced films are the Polish-Czech film "Brother" directed by Maciej Sobieszczański, the Bulgarian-Greek film "Dirty Money—White Nights" by directors Kristina Grozeva and Petar Valchanov, the American film "Hot" by Ramsey Bashur, and other works by international male and female directors.
OIFF will also present the "Gala Premieres" program separately. It includes films that reflect in different ways on the experience of war and the desire to change the future. They include the Ukrainian-Canadian film "Distance to Independence" directed by Dariia Sarycheva, the Ukrainian film "Dreamland? Land of Action!" by director Volodymyr Mula, the Ukrainian documentary "Photographs from the War" directed by Ivanka-Kate Yakovyna, and others.
The winners of the competition programs will be determined by international and national juries according to the categories, while the winner of the Grand Prix will be determined by the audience vote. The Grand Prix winner will receive the "Golden Duke" statuette and a cash prize of UAH 75,000.
OIFF Professional Program
An important part of the festival will be the Film Industry Office. It is a platform for professional communication, support, and development of Ukrainian film projects and the film industry as a whole, as well as for presenting the Ukrainian film industry to the international community.
Distributors, buyers, festival selectors, representatives of cinemas and specialized film companies, investors, film creators (actors, directors, screenwriters, cinematographers, production designers), and producers may participate.
The festival is held with the support of the State Film Agency of Ukraine and the Ukrainian Cultural Foundation. Partners include Work.ua, KSE, VETERANKA, "Children of Heroes," as well as the BRIGHT POINT Skalyha Foundation Charitable Foundation.

IMF chief says energy shock caused by closure of Strait of Hormuz not over yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:35:19 UTC
20:35:19 KST

LONDON, August 26. /TASS/. The global economy has weathered the energy shock caused by shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz better than feared, though the crisis is not yet over, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.
"Thus far, it (global economy - TASS) has weathered the energy shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz better than we feared, thanks to a combination of factors," she was quoted as saying by Reuters.
Among those factors Georgieva mentioned drawdowns of oil and gas reserves by many countries, increases non-Gulf energy supplies, lower energy demand, increased renewable energy capacity, and a return to coal power generation in some places. She also cited investments in the United States and other countries in projects related to artificial intelligence, which supports corporate turnover and consumer demand.
That said, Georgieva warned against complacency, noting that oil prices have remained elevated since mid-June, albeit well below the highs seen at the peak of the crisis in the spring. "The energy shock is not over. A renewed rise in oil prices could fuel inflation, forcing central banks to retain a restrictive policy stance with knock-on implications on debt service costs and on economic activity," she explained.

UN committee raises racial discrimination concerns over Israeli threats of Gaza-level destruction in Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:34:05 UTC
20:34:05 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) on Wednesday expressed alarm over statements by Israeli officials threatening to impose on Lebanon the "same level of destruction" as inflicted in Gaza and called for an end to rhetoric that dehumanizes the Lebanese population.
Acting under its Early Warning and Urgent Action Procedure, CERD stressed that the prohibition of racial discrimination cannot be suspended during armed conflict.
CERD said it was alarmed by civilian deaths, mass displacement, and widespread destruction resulting from Israeli military operations in Lebanon, including airstrikes, shelling, and the use of explosive weapons in densely populated areas.
The committee also cited a statement by the Israeli defense minister characterizing "the Shia inhabitants of 24 villages in southern Lebanon as enemies" while justifying the complete destruction of their homes.
It urged Israel to "cease the use of rhetoric that dehumanises the population of Lebanon" and refrain from rhetoric that "legitimises collective punishment or incites violence."
More than 4,300 people have reportedly been killed and at least 12,200 injured, according to the committee.
More than 1 million people were displaced in less than three weeks in March following displacement orders affecting at least 189 towns and villages, it added. More than 360,000 remained displaced at the end of July, including around 27,200 staying in collective shelters.
It expressed concern over reports that entire villages in southern Lebanon had been rendered uninhabitable, with homes and civilian infrastructure, including schools, health facilities, water and electricity infrastructure, places of worship, and agricultural land, destroyed by strikes and demolitions.
CERD also raised concerns over rockets fired by the Lebanese group Hezbollah into populated areas in Israel, which it said had caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure.
The committee called on Israel and all parties to the conflict to immediately cease attacks directed against, or indiscriminately affecting, civilians and civilian objects.
CERD also called on Israel to rescind blanket displacement and evacuation orders in Lebanon and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of displaced people.
It further called for unimpeded humanitarian access and urged states to refrain from transferring arms or military equipment where there is a clear risk they could be used to facilitate violations of international law.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday expressed condolences over the loss of lives in devastating floods in Nepal and offered India’s assistance for rescue and relief efforts.“Spoke to Prime Minister Balendra Shah and conveyed condolences on the loss of lives due to the floods in Nepal,” PM Modi wrote on X. “The people of India stand in solidarity with their sisters and brothers in Nepal at this difficult time.”

The floods swept through northern Nepal on Wednesday morning after the Bhote Koshi River surged, reportedly from the direction of Tibet. Timure in Rasuwa district and nearby Syafrubesi suffered extensive damage, with vehicles, goods and other property washed away.105 Indians among hundreds missing after deadly flash floodFloods battered Nepal on Wednesday after a sudden flash flood swept through Rasuwa district near the Tibet border, leaving at least eight people dead and hundreds missing, including 105 Indians.
The Bhote Koshi River surged through the Rasuwagadhi-Timure area at around 9am, affecting parts of Rasuwa as well as neighbouring Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Vehicles, bridges, goods and other infrastructure were washed away, while several hydropower projects were damaged.
According to a preliminary list compiled by the Nepal Tourism Board, 384 travellers, including 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepalis, were reported missing. The list includes 105 Indians and travellers from countries including Australia, the US, UK, Malaysia, the Netherlands and South Africa. Authorities said the figures were still being verified.Many of those missing are believed to be pilgrims travelling to Tibet for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. “Except for a few, we have not been able to establish contact with the pilgrims as of 3pm,” Bashu Kumar Adhikari of Touch Kailash Travels & Tours said, according to The Kathmandu Post.More than 25 people had been rescued by Wednesday afternoon. The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police launched search operations, using helicopters, drones and sniffer dogs.

Mortgage rates hit highest level in 3 weeks, weakening demand further
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:33:07 UTC
20:33:07 KST

Mortgage interest rates moved even higher last week, causing demand for loans to weaken yet again.
Total mortgage application volume dropped 1% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances of up to $832,750 increased last week to 6.78% from 6.77% the prior week, with points rising to 0.66 from 0.65, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. That is the highest level in three weeks.
Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly rate moves, fell 2% for the week. They were 17% lower than the same week one year ago, when rates were 9 basis points lower.
"Refinance applications decreased, particularly for FHA and VA loans, and the average loan size for refinances was at its lowest since June 2025," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release.
Applications for a home mortgage fell 0.3% for the week and were 5% lower than the same week a year ago.
Even though rates are higher than last year, fewer buyers are using all cash, according to a separate report from Realtor.com. Less competition in the overall market makes sellers more likely to accept buyers who need financing.
"Purchase activity was down over the week, driven by a 7 percent decrease in FHA applications. The purchase market has also slowed these past two months," Kan added.
Mortgage rates are lower this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily, with rates dropping Tuesday thanks to falling oil prices.
"News reports suggested progress in the peace process via Pakistani mediators. Oil prices dropped sharply in response, and bond yields followed the move. Bond yields correlate with mortgage rates," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily.

Outspoken influencer Andrew Tate claimed to have Estonian passport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26

20:33:00 KST

Outspoken influencer Andrew Tate claimed to have Estonian passport
Claims made by controversial influencer Andrew Tate, currently in custody in the US, to hold an Estonian passport have been shown to be false, Eesti Ekspress reported.
Tate made the claim on a 2022 podcast as part of a strategy to avoid any single country's control, but what he held at the time was e-residency, which does not confer citizenship.
Andrew Tate, 39, and his brother Tristan, 38, built a controversial social media empire and have been accused of human trafficking, rape and organised sexual exploitation in Romania and the UK. The brothers, who left Romania for Florida last year after a travel ban was lifted, deny all charges.
Tate's connection to Estonia dates back to 2018, when he became an e‑resident. In March 2023, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) invalidated his e‑resident digital ID card, "because supervisory proceedings found that his activities did not correspond to the purpose of e‑residency, which is to promote the development of Estonia's economy, science, education or culture."
The specific claim about Estonia came in a 2022 appearance on the Mars Mindset podcast, where Tate outlined a strategy of heightened visibility in as many systems as possible, with the aim of none of them being able to control him.
"The reason I kind of got this mindset is, for a while I really wanted to live off‑grid, I wanted to just be left alone, and I realized then in the modern world that's absolutely impossible – you can't be off‑grid if you want to live any kind of life worth living. So then I came up with the idea of, why don't I put myself on as many grids as possible. And the goal behind that is, that no one grid controls me, so for example, I have seven passports; I have 15 drivers' licenses. So let's say I'm driving my car and the police stop me. I'll just pull out a license from some random country. I'm in Romania, I'm driving a Slovakian‑plated car, I've got an American drivers' license, I've got an Estonian passport, and I'm speaking English. You think they're going to take my license over this? They're just going to look at me and go 'just slow down, bro, bye'. The paperwork's not worth it for them," Tate explained.
PPA spokesperson Martin Raid told Eesti Ekspress that Tate had certainly never held an Estonian passport, only an e‑residency card, which does not confer citizenship or physical residency and cannot be used as a travel document. Raid would not specify whether Tate had any activities in Estonia or what these might involve, citing data protection concerns.
Eesti Ekspress also reported in 2023 that Tate owned a string of online casinos in Eastern Europe and had claimed in interviews that he did business with a couple of "brothers, mafia guys" who owned "400 [gambling] locations from Estonia all the way down through Eastern Europe." It is not clear what if any business interests Tate might have had in Estonia. Tate holds dual U.S.‑U.K. citizenship.
U.S. legal research site Court Listener on August 10 issued documentation showing the U.S. government denying a bail request from Tate and his brother; the U.K. has issued an extradition request for both men and asked the U.S. to keep them in custody.
The brothers face 59 charges in the UK including rape and sex trafficking, and have been held in Florida since their arrest last month. British prosecutors are urging a US court to deny bail, arguing the brothers are a flight risk and would intimidate witnesses.
Tate has built his brand on misogyny, teaching that women are inferior and that men must dominate them — a message critics say has fueled the spread of toxic masculinity and the radicalization of young men. Among his supporters are figures reportedly close to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Healed and homeward: Russian soldiers discharged from Gomel hospital, head home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:33:00 UTC
20:33:00 KST

GOMEL, 26 August (BelTA) - Ten Russian military personnel have been discharged from a Gomel hospital after receiving medical care and are headed home, BelTA has learned.
 
On 24 August 10 individuals who had previously been detained in Belarus for violating migration and other legislation were handed over to Ukraine. In turn, Ukraine transferred to Belarus 10 Russian servicemen who had been held captive.
Before being sent home, the Russian citizens were taken to healthcare facilities in Gomel to receive the necessary assistance based on their health status.
Gomel City Clinical Hospital No. 3 emphasized that all 10 patients admitted to the inpatient ward received the required medical care. They underwent clinical, laboratory and instrumental tests, X-rays as indicated, and CT scans. When required, the patients were referred to doctors in therapeutic and surgical fields. The medical team emphasized that their primary commitment is to offer proper care to all patients, no matter what country they come from.
Before discharge - lunch. “Have a meal for the road! Bon appétit!” the ward staff wished the servicemen. “Will you come and sit with us!” the patients invited the staff member who had become almost like family to them.
The Russian patients, almost in unison, thanked the medical staff for their warmth, care, and attentiveness. “You can tell it’s genuine care,” they emphasized. In addition to the meals from the hospital menu, patients were also brought home-cooked food.
The servicemen thanked the Belarusian leader and the doctors for the care and consideration shown to them.
This morning is especially clear and joyful for Aleksei from Tyumen. The bright wards of Hospital No. 3 became a little haven of peace for him over the past few days. He keeps a soft toy in his hands, a gift from his 13-year-old daughter, Lesya. “I made her a promise to come back, to bring this Mickey back and hand it to her personally. In all sorts of situations, I kept it close to my heart, making sure it didn’t get lost. She’s waiting for me so much. I managed to call her and she said: ‘Daddy, I’m waiting for you so much, you're my hero.’ My Lesya Alekseyevna,” the man said clutching his charm.
Aleksei could not stop thanking Belarus and the head of state. “These days in the hospital flew by unnoticed. We were examined and had tests done. Belarusians are so warm-hearted. We lacked nothing. Everything was more than plentiful. Thank you to all of Belarus. I address the words of special gratitude to Aleksandr Grigoryevich [Lukashenko]. Once I’m demobilized, I’ll come back to Belarus with my wife and daughter for a holiday,” Aleksei shared his plans.
“Words can’t describe the emotions. I just want to get home as soon as possible and hug my family. I spent about a year in captivity. When they told us we were lucky and would soon be heading home, I couldn’t quite believe it,” Sergei from Penza shared his story before discharge. The serviceman had been wounded on a combat mission, and the time spent in captivity had also taken a toll on his health.
The man is counting the hours until he can see his family again. “Just imagine, for many months, my loved ones didn’t even know if I was alive,” he said.
Pavel from Saratov Oblast made no secret of his emotional state. “I’ve been waiting nearly two years to see my family again. Back home I have a daughter, a wife, my mother, and my father. He also took part in combat operations and is already home,” he said with emotion.
A few days ago, he was able to call his family and hear their voices. “We were received very well in Belarus. Everything was top-notch. The hospital gave us a full check-up. I’m feeling good,” the serviceman said. The thought of the upcoming reunion with his family is the best medicine of all. The soldier hopes to celebrate his daughter's 9th birthday surrounded by his loved ones.
Belarus firmly maintains a peaceful stance and continues its humanitarian mission. Incidentally, before discharge, Belarus provided the Russians with clothing.
Belarus has always stood for peace, emphasized Irina Kostevich, Chairwoman of the Standing Commission on Labor and Social Affairs of the House of Representatives. “Today was the final stage of the humanitarian operation that began on 24 August on the instruction of the Belarusian head of state. Ten Ukrainian citizens who had violated migration legislation were handed over to Ukraine. Meanwhile, ten citizens of the Russian Federation, prisoners of war, remained on Belarusian territory. Here they received the necessary medical care. They were supplied with fresh clothing and received nothing but warmth, attention, and genuine human kindness.That is so important, because at times they had lost hope of ever returning home. Here they felt the love and care of the Belarusian people. We heard words of gratitude from these men to Belarusians and, of course, to the medical staff who looked after them throughout these days,” she said, noting that the Russians underwent tests and received treatment in the hospital, and that they will continue rehabilitation back home.
“This is not the first humanitarian operation, and we hope it will not be the last. We are ready to continue along this humanitarian track. Belarusians are known for their human solidarity with others and their capacity for empathy. whether for Ukrainian or Russian citizens. The actions we are taking today in the name of humanity once again confirm that borders do not prevent us from jointly resolving very difficult and very important issues for people. We are glad that Belarus has the opportunity to help people and to contribute to solving such crucial matters,” Irina Kostevich emphasized.

Drone strike kills two in Russia, Wildberries warehouse ablaze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:32:37 UTC
20:32:37 KST

A woman walks past a residential building damaged in an air strike in the town of Izium, in the eastern Kharkiv, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Two people were killed when a drone crashed into a house in southwestern Russia, while an attack by Ukrainian drones on a warehouse belonging to the e-commerce giant Wildberries triggered a fire, Russian authorities said on Aug. 26.
Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, is regularly targeted by Kiev, which alleges the company supplies components to the Russian army.
A fire broke out at a Wildberries logistics center in Kotovsk, in the Tambov region, about 500 kilometers southeast of Moscow, overnight from Aug. 25 to Aug. 26 after Ukrainian drone strikes, regional governor Yevgeny Pervychov said on Telegram.
He said the fire covered an area of more than 100,000 square meters.
Videos posted on social media show the scale of the blaze, with flames and plumes of smoke rising into the sky. In addition to Wildberries, Ukrainian forces are now also targeting its competitor Ozon.
The logistics centers and warehouses of these companies, both compared to Amazon because of their dominance of e-commerce in Russia, are far less protected than military targets.
Ukrainian drone attacks have already caused damage amounting to billions of dollars, with several of these centers completely destroyed by fires.
The Russian Defense Ministry said air defense systems “intercepted and destroyed” a total of 426 Ukrainian drones during the night.
In the Lipetsk region, next to Tambov, a drone “crashed, causing a fire in a house,” governor Igor Artamonov reported.
“Unfortunately, two people died: A man and a 14-year-old child,” he said.
Four and a half years after the start of Russia’s large-scale offensive against Ukraine, strikes on both sides of the front have intensified in recent months, causing a growing number of civilian casualties.
Meanwhile, South Korea said on Aug. 26 that it had scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military aircraft entering its air defense zone, the second such incursion in weeks.
The relationship between the countries has worsened since South Korea joined Western sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and since Moscow built stronger ties with North Korea.
Seoul’s Defense Ministry said multiple Russian aircraft had entered and then left its air defense identification zone over the East Sea, also called the Sea of Japan.
“South Korea’s military detected the Russian aircraft before they entered the zone and deployed Air Force fighter jets to prepare for any contingency,” it said, without giving details.
The Russian aircraft did not violate South Korean airspace, it said.
An air defense identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area where countries require foreign aircraft to identify themselves for security purposes.
In late June, more than 10 Chinese and Russian military aircraft entered South Korea’s air defense zone.
