Swedish army takes delivery of new Archer 8×8 artillery systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:27:29 UTC
18:27:29 KST

- Sweden handed over its first new Archer 8x8 artillery systems to the army and the A 9 regiment on Tuesday at Villingsberg.
- FMV has a $500 million contract with BAE Systems Bofors for 48 Archer 8x8 systems, entering conscript training this fall.
Sweden’s armed forces received the first new Archer 8×8 artillery systems on Tuesday, handed over by the Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) to the army and then to the Bergslagen Artillery Regiment, A 9.
The ceremony took place at the Villingsberg firing range under clear skies. FMV has a contract with BAE Systems Bofors for 48 Archer 8×8 systems.
“The upgraded version of the Archer artillery system represents a major capability increase for the army and the artillery. Archer 8×8 will be important for strengthening artillery capability in southern Sweden and on Gotland. Modern warfare depends on indirect fire and requires long-range systems,” said Brigadier General Per Nilsson, acting chief of the army.
“When authorities and industry cooperate, the results are very good. We are not just building materiel systems together, we are building Swedish defense capability. Today’s handover is an important step for both the armed forces’ operational capability and the growth of Swedish artillery,” said Jonas Lotsne, head of army materiel at FMV.
Archer 8×8 will be introduced at A 9 this fall. The new version enters conscript training starting with the current training year, 2026 to 2027, and will become part of future war units.
“Archer 8×8 is being introduced at A 9 this fall. The new version enters conscript training as of this training year, 26-27, and will become part of upcoming war units,” said Colonel Henrik Rosdahl, commander of the Bergslagen Artillery Regiment A 9.
Archer 8×8 is a 155 mm artillery system integrated on an all-terrain 8×8 vehicle with a road speed of up to 90 km/h (56 mph). The system builds on experience from the Archer 6×6 and gives the armed forces greater operational and tactical mobility.
The vehicle can move into and out of firing position in about 20 seconds. That allows a crew to fire six rounds, leave the position and move 500 meters (550 yards) in under two minutes, while the crew stays inside the armored cab. Archer 8×8 has a range of more than 50 km (31 miles), depending on ammunition. It is built by BAE Systems Bofors in Karlskoga.
The 8×8 version replaces the Volvo A30D 6×6 chassis used on earlier Archer systems. FMV ordered the 48 systems in September 2023 in a contract worth about $500 million. BAE Systems Bofors then contracted Rheinmetall MAN Military Vehicles in March 2024 to supply 48 HX2 8×8 chassis for the order, a deal worth about €71 million. Deliveries of the chassis were scheduled to run from the third quarter of 2024 through the end of 2027.
FMV received the first Archer 8×8 unit for acceptance inspection in April 2026, ahead of Tuesday’s handover to the army.
The Archer 6×6, mounted on the Volvo chassis, remains in Swedish service but is being phased out on the divisional artillery role as the 8×8 systems arrive. In March 2025, the Swedish government authorized FMV to purchase 18 Archer systems with the intent of donating the Volvo-based fleet to Ukraine.
FMV has not disclosed how many Archer 8×8 systems have been delivered beyond the first unit, or a full timeline for equipping additional units after A 9.

Burak Bir
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
Millions of households in Britain will face their highest energy bills in three years this winter after the country’s energy regulator announced Wednesday a 4% increase in the energy price cap from October.
In a statement, Ofgem said that the gas and electricity price cap will rise 4% for the period from Oct. 1 to Dec. 31, 2026, due to higher wholesale gas prices linked to the Iran war.
“This increase reflects higher wholesale gas prices as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with volatile global gas markets remaining the dominant driver of price changes,” it said.
The energy regulator for Great Britain updates the energy price cap every three months to reflect changes in the underlying costs of supplying energy.
“The energy price cap protects around 22 million households on default tariffs by limiting the maximum rates and standing charges that energy suppliers can charge,” Ofgem said.
The new rate for about 22 million households is equivalent to £1,723 ($2,348) a year for a typical household’s gas and electricity use, compared with £1,663 ($2,266) for the July-September period.
“We know people are under huge amounts of pressure due to the cost of living, and I know that people are really worried about their energy bills, and we are absolutely alongside them and trying to do everything we can,” Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh told the BBC.
Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho, meanwhile, said the government had to “put cheap energy first.”
“Labour promised to cut energy bills by £300 ($408), but they have gone up by nearly £400 ($545) instead,” she was quoted as saying by the BBC.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Artificial intelligence company Anthropic is preparing for a potential stock market debut that could become the largest initial public offering in history, with the Claude-maker expected to tell investors that the market for its AI technology exceeds $30 trillion, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.
The figure represents a total addressable market — the theoretical annual revenue opportunity if a company captured all of its potential market — rather than a forecast of Anthropic's actual revenue. The estimate is based on the broad range of work that could potentially be performed using AI models, according to the report.
Anthropic could seek to raise as much as $100 billion and potentially be valued at about $2 trillion, according to the Journal. The company is reportedly considering a listing as early as September or October, although the size, valuation, and timing have not been finalized.
Anthropic has officially confirmed only that it confidentially submitted a draft registration statement to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1 for a proposed initial public offering (IPO). The company said the filing gives it the option to go public after SEC review and that the offering would depend on market conditions and other factors.
The potential offering comes after a rapid rise in Anthropic's valuation and revenue as demand for its Claude AI models and Claude Code software has surged. The company was valued at about $965 billion following a $65 billion funding round in May, while its quarterly revenue more than doubled to about $11.6 billion, according to the Journal.
If completed at the reported scale, Anthropic's IPO could surpass SpaceX's record $75 billion offering in June, which valued Elon Musk's space, satellite, and AI company at about $1.77 trillion. SpaceX's IPO broke the previous record held by Saudi oil giant Aramco, which raised about $26 billion in 2019.

In Michigan, racist attack ads against Abdul El-Sayed ramp up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:23:41 UTC
18:23:41 KST

Breadcrumb
In Michigan, racist attack ads by Republicans against Abdul El-Sayed ramp up
After a hard-fought Democratic Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed is facing an expected, though nevertheless unsettling, barrage of racist attack ads in his general midterm election campaign.
Over the past several weeks, as he prepares to face off against Republican nominee Mike Rogers in November, people across Michigan have seen campaign ads depicting El-Sayed as an "un-American" outsider. It is an old strategy, though it comes at a time when many people from marginalised communities are already seeing a spike in biased incidents and attacks.
"They're making him out to be a scary guy. It's obscene and frightening that this is happening in 2026," Hannah Fertig, co-director of Fighting for Michigan, a political action committee (PAC) focused specifically on electing El-Sayed, told The New Arab. She previously worked for his 2018 campaign for Michigan governor.
"The minute the primary stopped, the racist ads started. Most other politicians are not getting this treatment," she said.
"Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed, the most radical Senate candidate in America," says the voiceover in a TV ad issued by the National Republican Senatorial Committee.
"El-Sayed pledged support for the leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, a designated foreign terrorist group," the voice continues, referring to an article El-Sayed wrote in 2011 in support of Egyptian protesters who were demonstrating against then-president Hosni Mubarak. There is no evidence that El-Sayed has supported any extremist groups.
The ad goes on to highlight El-Sayed's ties to Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who focuses on progressive politics and is known for making controversial statements, which have become fodder for conservative attacks on Democrats.
"Abdul El-Sayed. Too radical. Too Dangerous. Wrong for Michigan," the attack ad concludes.
In the wake of the launch of these attack ads, El-Sayed's team issued a statement saying that while his opponents are focused on his ties to social media stars, he will be talking about the needs of people in Michigan.
"While politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare. Because that’s what Michiganders keep asking about. It’s why I keep fighting to get money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All," reads a statement from El-Sayed's campaign.
Rogers, El-Sayed's Republican opponent, has publicly stated that he does not want campaign support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), though it would still be possible for the lobby group to indirectly support him through other groups.
The smear campaign against El-Sayed, his full name is used, he is tied to the most controversial statements of his acquaintances, and he is characterised as dangerous. It is reminiscent of how former president Barack Obama, was attacked during his run for the White House.
Obama's opponents often referred to him by his full name of Barack Hussein Obama, he was tied to controversial statements by his reverend, and old photos were resurfaced of him wearing traditional African clothing.
Similar to Obama, El-Sayed has responded with a mix of humour, inclusivity and a focus on issues that concern everyday people. Like Obama, he has also run ads highlighting his mother's side of the family (in El-Sayed's case, his stepmother), whose roots in the US go back to the American Revolution.
Though it could be seen as unfortunate that El-Sayed might feel compelled to play into identity politics, it could also be seen as a strategy of inclusivity. He has not shunned his Middle Eastern roots, but instead has included his stepmother’s side of his family into his personal narrative, a blended family makeup many Americans can relate to.
Another strategy has been to embrace his own name. All of his rallies start out with the audience chanting his name, Abdul.
"I think it's a breakthrough campaign. He's Muslim, and he's proud of it. And he's proud of his step-grandparents," David Frank, a professor of rhetoric and political communication at the University of Oregon, told TNA. "El-Sayed is good at shifting the focus from himself to the system. There are people who aren't earning enough money to pay for food."
Though El-Sayed has been responding to the racist attack ads and social media commentary with a focus on the needs of Michiganders, the overall rhetoric has nevertheless had an impact on those with Middle Eastern backgrounds.
Since the primary at the beginning of August, Jake Lang, a far-right activist, who participated in the 6 January 2021 Capitol riot, has visited Michigan three times. During this time, Arab neighbourhoods were vandalised, local businesses closed, and some parents kept their children home from school fearing for their safety. Some people experienced death threats for calling out Lang's Islamophobic rhetoric, according to the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
"He came here with the sole intent to terrorise the Muslim community," Amy Doukoure, lead attorney with CAIR-Michigan, told TNA. "I don't know if it can be directly linked to Rogers' campaign, but it’s part of [US President Donald] Trump's Make America Great Again campaign."
"I think people need to rise above this divisive political rhetoric. It's not a new phenomenon. We need to call it like it is. Change happens when people take a moral stand and don’t shy away," she added.

Great Offensive ceremonies begin in western Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:20:57 UTC
18:20:57 KST

Thousands of citizens and military personnel marched with torches to Kocatepe in the western province of Afyonkarahisar late on Aug. 25 to mark the 104th anniversary of the Great Offensive.
Governor Naci Aktaş and military officials led the procession from a schoolyard in Şuhut district’s Çakırözü village following an official ceremony. The crowd retraced the exact historical route that modern Türkiye founder Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and his forces took 104 years ago before launching the decisive military operation.
Earlier in the day, attendees visited the Şuhut Atatürk House, which served as a temporary headquarters for the military leadership. Mounted gendarmerie units began their symbolic journey retracing the path taken by Turkish cavalry forces advancing from Afyonkarahisar to İzmir.
During the evening ceremonies, participants watched special video presentations detailing the offensive and the history of the Turkish Armed Forces. The Afyon Kocatepe University State Conservatory music group performed heroic folk songs reflecting the spirit of the era. A military unit reciting the commando oath drew heavy applause from the gathered crowd.
The victory week celebrations will continue through Aug. 30 with daily events across the province. The Aug. 26 program includes a wreath-laying ceremony at the Kocatepe Commander-in-Chief Mustafa Kemal Monument, followed by a bicycle tour and a visit to the Captain Agah Efendi Martyrdom memorial site.
The schedule for Aug. 27 features a Mevlit program, photography exhibitions, a public walk, liberation day celebrations at Republic Square and a concert by singer Kıraç. On Aug. 28, attendees will see a ceremony at the Anıtkaya Martyrdom and a performance by the Aegean Army Band.
Traditional sports games, a lantern procession and a show by the Afyonkarahisar Municipality City Theater are planned for Aug. 29. The week concludes on Aug. 30 with official ceremonies at Kocatepe Park and the Zafertepe monument in the neighboring province of Kütahya.
Meanwhile, the Youth and Sports Provincial Directorate organized multiple tournaments running from Aug. 13 to Aug. 26. Athletes competed in muay thai, cricket, badminton, karate, fencing, archery, table tennis and chess at city facilities.
The Great Offensive launched on Aug. 26, 1922, serving as the final military operation of Türkiye’s War of Independence against occupying allied forces following the Ottoman Empire’s defeat in World War I.
Turkish troops secured a critical victory at the Battle of Dumlupınar within five days, marking the turning point of the war. They eventually drove retreating Greek forces out of the country and captured the coastal city of İzmir on Sept. 9, 1922.

The Bulgarian village that fears becoming an Iranian target
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:20:33 UTC
18:20:33 KST

The Bulgarian village that fears becoming an Iranian target
Two US Air Force refuelling planes left Bulgaria after weeks of anxiety in the village of Bezmer, but while their departure has brought relief, tensions persist.
Bezmer, Bulgaria – The news landed on Saturday, bringing relief to nearby villagers: two United States Air Force (USAF) refuelling aircraft had left Bulgaria’s Bezmer airbase.
“The USAF air tankers took off yesterday and left Bulgaria,” the country’s defence minister, Dimitar Stoyanov, announced, as President Iliana Yotova declared: “For now, this mission is over.”
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2NATO ‘prepared’ to defend allies amid report of Iranian strike plans
- list 2 of 2Why Iran is threatening Europe’s ‘strategically important’ southeast
The US Air Force said the Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, intended to aid Washington’s war on Iran, had left to support “other operational requirements”.
The village had spent weeks worrying that the aircraft could make their area in southeastern Bulgaria a target for Iranian attacks.
Tehran had urged Bulgaria against allowing its territory to be used for the US and Israel’s military operation against Iran. Later, citing unnamed Iranian sources, the Financial Times reported that in the event of Washington’s escalation in Iran, Iranian forces had “assessed striking US assets in southeastern European countries such as Bulgaria” after Sofia had approved the use of its Bezmer airbase for US refuelling aircraft.
“I pray to God that our village won’t be attacked,” a woman working at a local grocery shop, who requested anonymity, told Al Jazeera days before the tankers left. “We are scared, but nothing depends on us.”
Although the planes are gone, geopolitical tensions – as well as fears in Bezmer of being drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran once again – persist.
This week, Stoyanov told reporters that Iran had carried out an effective hybrid operation, aided by Bulgarian politicians in the opposition.
“Unfortunately, this hybrid operation will continue,” he predicted in comments understood to have been directed at the opposition. Stoyanov did not elaborate further.
In Bezmer, a village of about 1,000 people that sits beside the base, Bulgarian military aircraft have long been part of the landscape. Many residents work at the base, according to Rosen Rusev, the mayor, and the sound of aircraft overhead is routine.
But in late July, the Bulgarian government proposed – and Parliament approved – the deployment of as many as eight US Air Force Stratotankers and up to 250 personnel.
Within two days, residents of Bezmer and nearby villages had collected more than 3,000 signatures against the deployment and held peaceful protests.
They did not want their village to become part of the war on Iran.
Rusev said a buzzy atmosphere took hold of Bezmer on Friday, when residents realised the tankers had left.
“Now they feel their voice is finally heard,” he told Al Jazeera. “It happened just as they wanted.”
The government had moved to reassure residents. Stoyanov said military intelligence had identified no threat to national security, the US aircraft or other facilities in Bulgaria. A United Kingdom assessment requested by the government had reportedly judged the risk as extremely low.
But reassurances did little to calm everyone.
With temperatures soaring to about 30 degrees Celsius (86F), two friends, Dinka Todorova, 67, and Ganka Vlaeva, 78, sat in plastic chairs in the shade.
Both have children who work at the airbase.
“We shiver day after day and pray that the war doesn’t come here,” Vlaeva said. “We are the first target, and many people will die.”
“And children, too,” Todorova added quietly. “For the ambitions of the greedy.”
Vlaeva said she was disappointed with the government and lawmakers, accusing them of ignoring the villagers’ petition.
“They don’t want to hear the voice of the people who elected them,” she said.
Not everyone in Bezmer shared that concern.
Ivan, a 33-year-old who sat beside the village church with his electric bicycle nearby, said that “groundless panic” was spread “recklessly”.
“There’s no danger for the village,” he concluded.
He is more worried about the possibility of interceptor missiles, or “something coming from Russia across the Black Sea”.
As residents protested, Antoniya Ivanova, whose father is a serviceman at the base, hung a white sheet over an aerial photograph of Bezmer. Animated films were projected onto it for children “to wind down the accumulated stress”, she explained.
“We’re the most innocent in this whole situation,” she said. “We didn’t want those aeroplanes near our homes.”
Children filled the playground as the afternoon cooled.
“Maybe there is a chance of attacks, but I think the media exaggerates,” said Tsonka Moskova, a mother in the village. “Whatever is meant to happen will happen. Those above us decide – the government. They are to blame.”
A low-flying AS532 Cougar helicopter passed overhead. Nobody looked up. The residents are accustomed to Bulgarian military aircraft.
Rusev, the fourth-term independent mayor, spent days trying to navigate between the villagers’ fears and officials. The protests were not an attempt to bring down the government, he said.
“We just wanted adequate information about the potential threats if the planes remained stationed here and what the guarantees for our safety were,” he said.
Social media made the situation harder, he added.
In Facebook groups, officials and experts struggled to compete with thousands of comments, many speculative and panic-inducing.
Military police also patrolled the village and the area around the airbase, adding to a sense of fear for some, and a sense of safety for others.
While Bulgaria is in the range of some Iranian missiles, some analysts argue that Iran is unlikely to have the capacity – or genuine will – for successful missile attacks against Bulgaria or elsewhere in continental Europe.
On Monday, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that the tankers had not made a single flight “south from the airport”, but had travelled to fellow NATO member nations for training and exercises.
But also on Monday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Tehran reserved the right to counter “any action regarded as supporting US and Israeli military aggression” against it.
“We have no issue with the Bulgarian people,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said. “It was previously announced – and reports have also confirmed – that several refuelling aircraft have left Bulgarian territory.
“As many Bulgarian citizens and politicians themselves have acknowledged, this action is contrary to international law and amounts to support for the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”
Back in the village, a woman said she was not afraid of Iran’s threats.
She did not want to be named or photographed for this article.
“I am definitely not scared. God is keeping us safe,” she told Al Jazeera. “I lie down and sleep in peace, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety,” she said, reciting a line from the Bible.

Poland to get four A330 MRTT tankers by 2030 under Spain deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:18:24 UTC
18:18:24 KST

- Spain's Council of Ministers approved up to €5.4 billion for a joint purchase of seven Airbus A330 MRTT tankers with Poland on Aug. 25.
- Poland is set to receive four of the aircraft by 2030 under the EU's SAFE loan program, with a final contract still to be signed.
Spain’s government has approved spending of up to €5.4 billion ($6.3 billion) to jointly purchase Airbus A330 MRTT tanker and transport aircraft with Poland, clearing the way for a final contract between the two countries.
Madrid’s Council of Ministers signed off on the framework agreement during a meeting on Aug. 25. The deal covers seven new A330 MRTT aircraft: three for Spain and four for Poland. The agreement runs through the SAFE mechanism, and the aircraft will be assembled in Getafe, Madrid.
Poland’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, announced the Spanish approval on social media Wednesday. He said the next step is signing the final contract and that Poland expects to receive four aircraft by 2030.
The framework agreement will last seven years from the date of formalization, according to the readout from the Spanish Council of Ministers. The number of aircraft covered by the Spanish spending approval was not specified in that readout, though Spanish media reported the total split as three units for Spain and four for Poland.
The purchase runs through the European Union’s Security Action for Europe program, known as SAFE, which provides low-cost loans to member states for defense procurement. Poland’s defense budget is set to draw around €43.7 billion ($49.9 billion) in SAFE loans, the largest allocation among EU member states, with funds required to be disbursed by the end of 2030.
Poland has been negotiating the acquisition with Spain since the spring. Kosiniak-Kamysz said the two countries signed a memorandum on May 29 committing to move forward with the purchase together. He and Spanish Defense Minister Margarita Robles discussed the program during an official visit to Madrid on June 22 and 23, when the Polish delegation toured the Airbus conversion line in Getafe.
Poland initially examined buying two A330 MRTTs on its own. The arrangement with Spain allows Warsaw to increase its order to four aircraft by sharing Madrid’s production and delivery slots.
The A330 MRTT is a militarized version of the Airbus A330 airliner, fitted for aerial refueling and for carrying cargo, passengers or wounded personnel. Poland’s aircraft are expected to be based on the newer A330neo airframe.
Kosiniak-Kamysz has tied the acquisition directly to Poland’s F-35 fleet. He said tanker aircraft would let Poland’s F-35s “operate further, longer, and with greater effectiveness.”
Poland currently has no dedicated aerial refueling aircraft. The Polish Air Force’s only heavy transport aircraft are six C-130 Hercules, and Warsaw has depended on allied tankers to extend the range of its fighter fleet.
Poland was a founding member of NATO’s Multinational Multi-Role Tanker Transport Fleet, a pooled fleet of A330 MRTTs. Warsaw withdrew from that program at the turn of 2015 and 2016, leaving it without access to shared tanker capacity since. The NATO fleet has since grown to 12 aircraft operated by member states including Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Luxembourg, Norway, the Netherlands, Sweden and Denmark, with Finland expected to join.
The Spanish Air Force flies three modified former Iberia A330-200s, currently equipped only with a hose and drogue refueling system, though they can be fitted with a boom later if required.
Poland’s tanker effort has been pursued for years under a national requirement known as the Karkonosze program. That program dates to around 2008, was postponed around 2010, and has since gone through repeated attempts at a multinational solution. Early requirements under Karkonosze called for both boom and hose-and-drogue refueling and the ability to carry cargo, passengers and wounded personnel, criteria the A330 MRTT meets.

Erdoğan says Türkiye is shaping history through peaceful policies

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on Aug. 26 said that Türkiye is helping shape a new regional order, vowing that no “provocations or traps” would derail the country’s course.
“Everyone, friend or foe, should know and understand this: History is being rewritten in our region. Türkiye is directing history with its conscientious, principled, and peaceful policies. No one can stop this anymore,” Erdoğan said at commemorations in the eastern province of Muş marking the anniversary of the Battle of Manzikert.
Erdoğan attended the annual commemorations with Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli, his key political ally. The president had chaired a cabinet meeting the previous day in the nearby district of Ahlat, close to the historic battlefield where Seljuk forces defeated the Byzantine army on Aug. 26, 1071.
“Those who think they can stop the blessed march of Türkiye and the Turkish nation through provocations and traps are doomed to disappointment,” Erdoğan said. “We will neither deviate from the path we know to be right nor take different paths because of someone’s provocations.”
The president has attended the annual Ahlat commemorations in each of the past two years, accompanied by senior government officials. A speech he delivered in Ahlat in 2024 was widely viewed as signaling the beginning of the latest government effort to end the decades-long conflict with the PKK.
“We have no other option in this geography than to be strong, united, and together,” he said, adding that Türkiye must remain strong not only to protect its own rights and interests but also for “millions of brothers” looking to the country.
He said efforts spanning defense, diplomacy, education, transportation, the economy, and health were aimed at building a prosperous and effective Türkiye.
The remarks came as the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” initiative moved into a new phase. Parliament overwhelmingly approved Aug. 10, a law establishing a legal framework for the initiative, with 467 lawmakers voting in favor.
The process began in late 2024 after Bahçeli called for a new effort to resolve the issue. It reached a major turning point in February 2025, when jailed PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan called on the terror group to end its armed campaign and dissolve.
PKK subsequently announced in June 2025 that it would disarm and disband, followed by a symbolic weapon-burning ceremony by members in northern Iraq a month later.
Erdoğan said his government’s broader goals were to “build the Century of Türkiye, establish a terror-free Türkiye and a terror-free region, and turn the surrounding region into a place of peace and prosperity.”
Türkiye regards the PKK as a terrorist organization, as do the United States and the European Union.
The Manzikert commemoration comes during “Victory Week,” when Türkiye also marks the start of the 1922 Great Offensive against occupying forces and celebrates Victory Day on Aug. 30.

Tarun Tejpal’s Conviction and India’s Discussions About the ‘Perfect Rape Victim’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

She wore the wrong clothes. She was out at the wrong hours. She went to the wrong place. She is always in the wrong company. She was drunk. She invited it.
There have been plenty of ways to dismiss a rape or sexual harassment survivor by simply blaming them. This is so commonplace that, in 2021, a district court in the western Indian state of Goa acquitted a prominent magazine editor, holding that the accuser did not look traumatized in the CCTV footage captured moments after the incident.
Recently, a high court overturned the verdict, specifically dismissing the approach of scrutinizing how the survivor behaved.
The high-profile case involves Tarun Tejpal, who was the editor of the investigative news magazine Tehelka. A female junior colleague accused him of rape in 2013. In the August 2026 judgement, the Bombay High Court sentenced Tejpal to 10 years’ imprisonment.
The high court’s reliance on evidence rather than survivor behavior has been strongly welcomed by gender rights and civil rights activists and a section of journalists. “I believe the High Court judgment is important not just because of the individual involved, but because it reinforces a larger principle,” wrote political commentator Sujit Nair.
Even in 2002, Indian laws allowed men accused of rape to show that the survivor was of generally immoral character. Section 155(4) of the Indian Evidence Act stated that “when a man is prosecuted for rape or an attempt to ravish, it may be shown that the prosecutrix was of generally immoral character.”
Way back in 1980, the Indian Law Commission had recommended that in a case of rape or attempted rape, any evidence or cross-examination related to the past immoral character of the survivor “should be prohibited except as regards sexual relations with the accused.” The commission held it was necessary to “exclude the possibility of evidence of general immoral character being tendered.”
While Section 155(4) was finally deleted in 2003, the government did not impose the explicit prohibition in such questioning as suggested by the commission. This loophole was subsequently exploited, journalist and author Manoj Mitta wrote in a recent article. “The prohibition only on the questions about her character proved insufficient to save her from interrogation about her sex life,” Mitta wrote.
The loophole was finally blocked when India rewrote its anti-rape law in the aftermath of the 2012 gang-rape of a medical student in a moving bus in the national capital of New Delhi. The new law also expanded the definition of rape — covering penetration of the vagina, anus, urethra, or mouth by any object or any part of the body, not just the penis.
The Tarun Tejpal case was the first high-profile case filed soon after the new law came into effect. And yet, during the trial, the survivor faced the same harrowing questions about her behavior after the alleged incident.
The lower court judgement showed it relied on the survivor’s behavior, which it thought did not match that of a raped woman. The survivor’s conduct “neither demonstrates any kind of normative behavior on her own part that a prosecutrix of sexual assault on consecutive two nights might plausibly show, nor does it demonstrate any such behavior on the part of the accused,” said the 2021 judgement.
While hearing the appeal against the judgement, a Bombay High Court judge had even commented that the lower court judgement “seems like a manual for rape victims,” criticizing how much space it devoted to prescribing appropriate survivor behavior.
After the recent verdict, the survivor broke her silence for the first time in 13 years. In a Substack essay, she wrote that she knew only the truth of her body, “frozen with fear, sexually assaulted by a man nearly twice my age, a man responsible for my livelihood, a man who my father knew and trusted, whose family I was close to.”
She explicitly mentioned how the “good victim vs bad victim” battle exhausted her: “My past became a way to deny, and worse, justify my assault: My relationships, my financial precarity, my loneliness, my clumsiness as a 20-something woman figuring her way as a young adult in a new city with new friends. Even my professionalism became a cudgel in the hands of male rage.”
But it’s not only “male rage” that she speaks about. She also mentions how she faced questions on her motivation in accusing a “supposed ‘liberal’ ‘hero’ of rape.”
This is where the second aspect of the Tejpal controversy comes up — the role of the liberal media and the liberal intelligentsia in handling cases where one of their own is involved.
The incident took place inside a hotel elevator in 2013 during an event organized by the magazine in Goa. Tejpal had initially written to the survivor, saying, “I apologize unconditionally for the shameful lapse of judgement that led me to attempt a sexual liaison with you on two occasions…. despite your clear reluctance.” However, later he called himself a victim of a political conspiracy.
Tejpal had become a big name in Indian journalism. A sting operation he led in 2001 had severely hurt the Bharatiya Janata Party government under then-Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. He had earned accolades like “powerful and pioneering,” “one of Asia’s 50 most powerful communicators,” among “50 leaders at the forefront of change in Asia,” and India’s “most feted journalist.”
In 2013, when the controversy broke out, Goa was under the BJP, the party which bore the brunt of Tehelka’s 2001 sting operation. Therefore, Tejpal alleged a political vendetta behind the allegations.
During the subsequent months, several liberals voiced support for Tejpal. Tehelka managing editor Shoma Choudhury was accused of trying to shield Tejpal. In 2014, the news magazine Outlook carried a cover story in which journalist and best-selling author Manu Joseph wrote a highly controversial piece dissecting the behavior of the survivor from CCTV footage he managed to access. The piece, which was highly sympathetic toward Tejpal, quoted him as saying: “She may not have intended to but what she has done is that she has delivered me to the right wing. That’s what she has done.”
In the words of journalist Ranjona Banerji, “Tragically, as in so many cases, the bulk of the old media ganged up against young women journalists for daring to have a voice.”
Even after the recent high court conviction, documentary filmmaker Anand Patwardhan, a prominent face in India’s left-liberal intelligentsia circuit, expressed his suspicion that the high court verdict was possibly a way of pleasing India’s ruling party, the BJP.
“Tejpal preying on young colleagues is reprehensible,” Patwardhan commented on a social media post, adding, “Was it rape?” He then said the CCTV footage of Tejpal and the survivor “entering the lift as well as exiting from it on the upper floor, talking normally” leads him to conclude that no violent incident happened in the lift itself.
When a leading left-liberal voice invests in investigating survivor body language, it does not speak well of those who hold their likes in high esteem.
In her essay, Banerji had asked, “Is rape therefore tolerable if the assaulter is a liberal?” Perhaps this is a question that the high priests of accountability and public-spirited journalism need to ask themselves more deeply. The time has arrived — no matter how the Supreme Court deals with Tejpal’s appeal against the Bombay High Court judgment.

The previous day, officials had reported flooding along Provincial Highway 17 in Linbian Township, with the road expected to reopen after drainage work.
Transportation has also been affected. While major highways and most public transportation services continued operating, the eastern section of the Central Cross-Island Highway remains temporarily suspended because of a landslide, with workers hoping to open the road by Wednesday evening.
Maritime transportation was disrupted, with two international cross-strait routes involving eight sailings and six domestic routes involving 45 sailings suspended on Tuesday. Travelers were advised to check the latest sailing information before departure, per CNA.
Prolonged rainfall has pushed water levels at reservoirs across Taiwan higher. The central government has been closely monitoring major reservoirs and drainage systems as the weather system affecting southern Taiwan gradually weakens.
The Central Weather Administration lifted its heavy-rain advisory at 8:20 a.m. Wednesday as rainfall conditions eased in southern Taiwan. However, a heavy rain advisory remains in effect for central mountainous areas.
Typhoon Saudel is also expected to pass north of Taiwan, with a sea warning expected early Thursday and related effects through Friday evening. Authorities urged local governments to remain on alert and prepare for the approaching typhoon while continuing flood recovery operations.

Meanwhile, across the border in Nepal, authorities said flash floods killed at least nine people and washed away villages while damaging roads, bridges and power projects.
The areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, were severely affected, officials said, while urging those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River to seek higher ground.
"We have reports of villages and infrastructure project sites being washed away," district administrator Narendra Pariyar told Reuters.
"There could be heavy casualties or loss of property," he added. 
"But I cannot say for sure now."
The reason for the inundation was not immediately clear but a deadly flash flood on the same river last year was eventually traced to the draining of a glacier lake.
Nepal's water resources ministry said hydroelectric projects were among the infrastructure damaged by the floods, along with roads and bridges.
Electricity supply in the area has been disrupted as a result of such damage, the government added.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said rescue and relief teams, as well as police and the military had been dispatched to help in the aid effort.
Last year's flood in the Bhote Koshi killed nine people, with 24 missing, and washed away a "Friendship Bridge" linking Nepal and China to disrupt trade and transport for months. (Xinhua and agencies)

There are also plans to enable dual launches.

The developers successfully defended their preliminary design and received positive feedback from industry institutions. Next year, they plan to prepare a complete set of design documentation, followed by preparations for mass production.
The NK-3 liquid-fuel rocket engine, with a thrust of 4.5 metric tons, is being developed under an agreement between the UEC and the Voskhod Venture Fund, while the direct customer for the Voronezh launch vehicle is the Russian private aerospace startup 3D Research and Development.

Brazil vote offers opposing politics, similar fiscal outcomes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:09:07 UTC
18:09:07 KST

Brazil vote offers opposing politics, similar fiscal outcomes
NEW YORK/SAO PAULO, Aug 26 - Brazil’s October election offers voters yet another stark left-versus-right choice, but investors see less difference on the fiscal front with debt likely to keep rising under either candidate.
Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of far-right firebrand and former President Jair Bolsonaro, has painted a picture of a troubled economy as he aims to unseat leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whom polls show holding a narrow lead.
Analysts are pricing a Lula victory followed by an adjustment that only slows the pace of debt accumulation, but markets are skeptical that either candidate could make a credible start on significantly changing the trajectory of debt.
Stabilizing Brazil’s debt by 2031 would require a fiscal effort of at least 2.5 percentage points of gross domestic product, or roughly 350 billion reais ($68 billion) according to Roberto Secemski, the New York-based chief Brazil economist at Barclays.
But any fiscal tightening is made exceptionally difficult by Brazil’s rigid budget and fragmented Congress. Voters will also elect all 513 lower-house lawmakers and 54 of 81 senators, making the legislative result part of the president’s ability to deliver.
“It seems unlikely that either candidate would be able to engineer a full fiscal effort” of that size, Secemski said, adding that it makes the opening measures sought by the winner an important marker, because they must be large enough to convince investors more will follow.
Brazil’s nominal deficit averaged 8.6% of GDP from 2023 through 2025 and widened to 9.99% in the 12 months through June, central bank data show.
Gross government debt reached 81.9% of GDP, up 3.3 percentage points in the first half. A central bank survey shows market economists expect primary deficits through 2029, contrary to government targets.
The 2026 budget classifies 92% of primary spending as mandatory, leaving discretionary expenditure at roughly 2% of GDP. A lasting adjustment would have to reach pensions, payrolls, social benefits and spending indexation.
“There are virtually no ‘low hanging fruits’ in the fiscal effort to be pursued ahead,” Secemski said.
TS Lombard argues Lula would pursue spending reforms after the election, even as mandatory outlays leave progressively less room for other cuts. Under its reform scenario, however, debt peaks at 94.7% of GDP in 2034.
It models a faster adjustment under Bolsonaro, including a proposed debt-linked spending rule, but still sees debt peaking at 90% in 2032.
It also noted that Bolsonaro dropped earlier proposals to loosen the automatic indexation of government spending after encountering political opposition.
“Maybe he’d have a greater willingness,” said Marcelo Kalim, CEO of Brazilian digital bank C6, when asked whether Bolsonaro would adjust more. “But I think you only know once someone actually has the pen in hand.”
REAL STRENGTH
The real, up 5.8% this year versus the dollar and nearly 20% stronger since the end of 2024, shows why investors can expect limited fiscal progress and still remain invested in Brazil.
A 14% benchmark policy rate, against annual inflation of 4.44%, combines with a weak dollar, strong external accounts and favorable terms of trade to further support the currency.
Median forecasts in the central bank’s weekly survey of economists see the benchmark rate at 13.75% by year end and 12% in 2027, preserving much of the differential that fuels carry trades.
Morgan Stanley said the real’s unusually high carry could absorb more election pressure than in previous cycles, shifting some of the repricing into domestic interest rates.
The support has narrowed, however. Non-residents pulled $4.2 billion from Brazilian equity and debt portfolios between March and June after adding $18.8 billion in January and February, IIF estimates show.
Richard Hall, EM portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price, said hedge funds and local investors have also reduced their exposure, leaving less fuel for a sudden unwind than several months ago.
High interest rates have deeply impacted the economy, with spikes in corporate bankruptcies and families' indebtedness. But the next president may have little sway over the real's performance.
Hall said that, while carry gives Brazil a buffer, an external shock combined with pressure on indebted households and weaker companies could trigger a sharper slowdown, currency depreciation and even higher rates.
Pramol Dhawan, head of emerging-market portfolio management at PIMCO, said those economic constraints would matter more than the winner’s ideology.
Without restored fiscal credibility, he said, Brazil would lack the conditions for a sustainable decline in interest rates, deepening the pressure on growth and debt.
“The only question," he added, "is whether that adjustment happens proactively or is ultimately imposed by market forces.” REUTERS

One asteroid strike may explain two mysteries of Mars’ moon Deimos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:05:48 UTC
18:05:48 KST

One asteroid strike may explain two mysteries of Mars’ moon Deimos
- Date:
- August 26, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bern
- Summary:
- A single asteroid impact may explain two of Deimos’s most puzzling features: its huge southern depression and unusually smooth, dusty surface. Simulations suggest a roughly 320-meter asteroid struck the Martian moon at an angle, throwing debris around the entire world without breaking it apart. New observations from ESA’s Hera spacecraft support the scenario and indicate that Deimos is surprisingly porous and fragile.
- Share:
An international team led by the University of Bern has found evidence that a single asteroid collision may have dramatically reshaped Deimos, the smaller of Mars' two moons. By combining detailed computer simulations with recent images from ESA's Hera spacecraft, the researchers concluded that one impact could account for both the moon's large southern depression and its unusually smooth, dusty surface.
The research is the first scientific study to incorporate observations collected during Hera's flyby of Deimos. The findings could also help guide future missions, including the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission.
The Mystery of Deimos' Smooth Surface
Deimos is the smaller and more distant of Mars' two moons. It has a roughly oval shape and a prominent depression near its south pole. Its surface also looks strikingly different from that of Phobos, Mars' other moon.
While Phobos is heavily marked by craters, Deimos appears smoother because much of its surface is covered by loose dust and rocky debris known as regolith. Spacecraft have photographed the moon with increasing detail over several decades, but scientists have not been certain what created either the southern depression or the widespread layer of debris.
A new study led by Dr. Sabina Raducan investigated whether the two features could share the same origin. The international collaboration included researchers from the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, the University of Arizona, and the University of Tokyo, among other institutions.
Raducan worked in the Division of Space Research and Planetary Sciences (WP) at the Physics Institute at the University of Bern until October 2025. She is now Science Program Manager at the International Space Science Institute and a Senior Fellow at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel.
Using high-resolution simulations produced with the "Bern Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH)" code, the team found that the distinctive depression near the south pole was most likely produced by a single asteroid impact that was powerful but not strong enough to destroy Deimos. According to the simulations, the same collision could also have generated the regolith that now blankets much of the moon.
The research, published in Nature Astronomy, is the first scientific publication to use observations gathered when ESA's Hera spacecraft flew past Deimos. Hera is currently traveling toward its main destination, the asteroid moon Dimorphos.
Simulating a Massive Asteroid Collision
To reconstruct what may have happened, the scientists used the Bern SPH code, which has been developed at the University of Bern over roughly two decades. The software is designed to model collisions involving asteroids, comets, and planets.
In the simulations, colliding objects are represented by millions of individual particles. Researchers can adjust factors such as gravity, density, and material strength to see how different types of impacts unfold.
The University of Bern has extensive expertise in numerical impact modeling. The same approach was previously used to simulate NASA's DART spacecraft crashing into Dimorphos.
"The code runs on a high-performance computing cluster here at the University of Bern and is one of the few codes capable of performing this type of simulation," explains study leader Sabina Raducan, who is also co-chair of the Hera Impact Physics Working Group for ESA's Hera mission.
The researchers tested many possible scenarios, changing the impactor's size, speed, and impact angle while also varying assumptions about the internal structure of Deimos.
"We carried out about a hundred simulations -- each one took about a week."
They then compared the results with observational data collected by ESA's space probe.
Hera's main mission is to closely examine what happened when NASA's DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos. Those observations are intended to help researchers evaluate the deflection of asteroids as a potential method to defend Earth against asteroid impacts.
In March 2025, Hera passed Mars and used the planet's gravity to alter its trajectory toward Dimorphos. The maneuver also gave the spacecraft a rare chance to observe Deimos from close range.
One Impact Could Explain Two Major Features
The simulations favored a specific collision scenario. According to the researchers, an asteroid about 320 meters across striking Deimos at an angle of 45 degrees could have produced the size and shape of the depression now visible near the moon's south pole.
The same impact could also explain why regolith is spread across the entire moon. Enormous quantities of material would have been thrown outward during the collision and redistributed across Deimos, burying many older surface features. In some locations, the deposited material may exceed 200 meters in depth.
"Our simulation thus shows that a single impact was sufficient to decisively shape the current landscape of Deimos," explains co-author Martin Jutzi from the Division of Space Research and Planetary Sciences (WP) at the University of Bern, who also serves as co-chair of the Hera Impact Physics Working Group.
"The impact was violent enough to redistribute material globally, but not so strong that it would have shattered the moon."
Comparing the simulations with spacecraft observations also revealed clues about the physical makeup of Deimos. Its uppermost layers appear to be exceptionally weak, while the moon's interior seems highly porous. That porous structure would have absorbed and weakened some of the energy from the collision, helping Deimos survive the impact.
"In terms of its physical properties, Deimos more closely resembles the so-called rubble-pile asteroids than our Earth's Moon," says Raducan. "But that doesn't necessarily mean that Deimos is actually an asteroid. It could also have formed from material ejected during impacts on Mars."
What Future Missions Could Discover
Other explanations for Deimos' southern depression and smooth surface are still possible. However, the new impact scenario provides a single mechanism capable of explaining both features and makes specific predictions that future spacecraft can test.
One important opportunity will come from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), which is preparing the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission for launch in 2026. MMX is designed to study both Martian moons in detail and return samples from Phobos to Earth.
"Our study provides important, concrete predictions for this Japanese MMX mission, such as the thickness and distribution of the regolith layer and the mechanical properties of Deimos's material," explains Raducan.
"This gives MMX a clearer picture of what its instruments -- and ultimately the sample collection -- can expect."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Bern. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. D. Raducan, H. F. Agrusa, E. Asphaug, C. M. Ernst, M. Jutzi, P. Michel, M. Popescu, S. Sugita. Deimos’s shape and geology explained by a subcatastrophic impact. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02956-w

====================================================================================================

Shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of heart attack and stroke, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:00:39 UTC
18:00:39 KST

The current shingles vaccine appears to significantly lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to scientists who say it could help prevent thousands of deaths each year.
The research, based on records of 70,000 people in the US, found that those who had received Shingrix had a 12% lower risk of a cardiovascular diagnosis in the following three and a half years. If confirmed, this benefit would be comparable to taking a daily blood pressure-lowering medication, the scientists said.
Dr Maxime Taquet, a clinical lecturer at the University of Oxford, who led the study, said: “If confirmed in clinical trials, vaccinating older adults against shingles could prevent hundreds of thousands of coronary heart diseases, strokes and cases of heart failure worldwide, making it one of the most impactful interventions we could offer to protect both the brain and the heart in later life. The effect might be enormous.”
Shingles is a painful and serious condition caused by reactivation of the chickenpox virus, which remains dormant in the body after an earlier infection. It can cause a rash and nerve pain that may persist for months or years after the rash clears, a complication known as post-herpetic neuralgia.
The first vaccine against shingles, Zostavax, was made available in 2006 and was based on a weakened version of the chickenpox virus. This was succeeded by a more effective vaccine, Shingrix, which uses newer vaccine technology and which in the UK is being made available incrementally to people aged 65-79 in a phased rollout.
Several previous studies have suggested that vaccinated people may have a lower risk of cardiovascular disease. However, these studies compared vaccinated and unvaccinated people, leaving the results open to distortion. The new study got around this by comparing the incidence of cardiovascular disease in people who were vaccinated before and after the rapid switch from Zostavax to Shingrix in the US in 2017.
The researchers tracked health records of 70,000 adults aged 60 and over for seven years after vaccination, which involved an initial dose and a booster. Shingrix was associated with a 12% reduction in cardiovascular events – including heart attacks, heart failure and stroke – in the first three and a half years after vaccination. By the end of the follow-up, the vaccine was associated with a 4% lower risk of cardiovascular diseases, according to the study in Nature Medicine.
While this represents a small change in absolute risk, the overall impact could be substantial given that heart disease and stroke are leading causes of death. “If confirmed in a [randomised controlled trial], the effect of Shingrix would be equivalent to antihypertensives,” Taquet said.
Several trials are under way that could provide more definitive evidence. The scientists are also investigating why the vaccine may help to protect cardiovascular health. One possibility is that shingles may increase the risk of heart and vascular diseases, and so the more effective vaccine reduces this risk. Alternatively, the vaccine could be having broader effects on the immune system that suppress inflammatory proteins.
Dr Hugo Pedder, a research fellow in statistical modelling at the University of Bristol who was not involved in the research, said: “A randomised trial would be the best way to confidently answer whether recombinant vaccines do provide the benefits seen here versus live vaccines, but until such a trial is done this study provides some of the best-quality observational evidence supporting an effect of recombinant v live vaccines for cardiovascular outcomes.”

====================================================================================================

Moringa lattes and tigernut kebabs: the Ghanaians ‘taking back the power’ of their food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
09:00:39 UTC
18:00:39 KST

After three years at catering school in Accra, Abiro Wisdom was certain of one thing – he did not want to go into catering. At least not the route that he might be expected to take. His course had prepared students for working in international hotels, focusing on French, Italian and Mexican cuisine. The nutritious, homegrown food that Wisdom had eaten while growing up in Bolgatanga, northern Ghana, did not feature at all.
“I didn’t see myself there,” he says of the big chain hotels. “I felt I wouldn’t be myself working there – I wouldn’t be able to talk about the food from where I come from.”
Wisdom instead joined the Ghana Food Movement (GFM), which was founded in 2019 – the year he graduated – and quickly became a champion for Indigenous foods. He says: “We’re a community of food lovers, of believers in the potential of Ghanaian food.”
Ghana imports at least half of its food and is heavily influenced by foreign cuisine and ingredients, but Wisdom believes northern Ghana, the country’s agricultural heartland with its huge variety of nutritious and climate-resilient crops and vegetables, could be the secret to the country’s broken food system.
The GFM was initially a network of volunteers interested in food systems – chefs, farmers, entrepreneurs and experts in food security. In the early days they met in cafes and set up events in whatever space they could find to deliver three-course meals highlighting a single crop and the diverse ways it can be used.
“[Traditionally] we make tigernut milk, but you can make so many different things, for example tigernut burgers and tigernut kebabs,” says Aimee Wallin, the group’s Malian-Swedish co-managing director. “We want people to taste what we are about, not just talk about what we are about.”
The group has been registered as a non-profit organisation for the past five years and now has its own kitchen where it brainstorms new recipes, many of them thought up by Wisdom. It runs monthly pop-ups and dine-and-dance nights, as well as panel discussions and recipe testing events for chefs and local businesses. Wisdom says: “We might brainstorm ideas around a single food, such as moringa leaves, to show how it’s possible to sell – and make a profit from – dishes and drinks using Indigenous ingredients.”
The GFM has started working with schools, helping children appreciate local ingredients.
Wisdom hopes this multi-pronged approach will help instil more national pride in Ghanaian food. “My goal is that we have a generation of chefs who believe in Ghanaian food and its own identity,” he says.
“I’ve come to understand how food contributes to politics, to the economy, how it contributes to self-identity. [Now I can] trace the impact of food on our society, on our land, to the sea, to the farmer, down to how the food gets to the market, then to our plates. As chefs, we have to be able to tell the story of the food.”
This month the group won a Champions of Change title in the 50 Best Restaurants Awards in recognition of the transformational work it is doing.
Foreign, colonial influence has played a heavy role on African food systems, when ruling powers dictated land should be used for cash crops for export, such as cocoa or peanuts, at the expense of food for local consumption.
At the same time, they put more value on imported ingredients such as rice, disrupting the sustainability of countries’ food systems. The impact has continued to modern times, making African countries heavily reliant on imports and vulnerable to price shocks when wars or other crises disrupt shipping.
But, as Wisdom discovered at university, there is also a lingering cultural influence, with western food still taught in culinary institutes and sought after in restaurants.
“The narrative has always been that our practices are wrong and the west’s practices are right. It’s just super-stupid. Why would you do that when you can just grow your own food?” says Wallin.
“Part of the postcolonial agenda is for us to still have to depend on other countries. If it’s not to buy their products, to buy their vegetables, then at least we need to buy their seeds and their pesticides and their fertilisers,” says Wallin, who points out that many of the local ingredients they champion do not need extra agricultural inputs because they are adapted to the local environment.
“The one who feeds us will control us and that’s how it is today. So, if we want to control ourselves, we also need to feed ourselves. It’s power. Taking back the power of our foods and using it to our advantage.”
For younger Ghanaians there is a new international pull towards heavily advertised trends and social media fads such as matcha lattes, bubble tea and smash burgers.
Wallin says that also offers a culinary opportunity – to earn the interest of young people, by offering alternatives, replacing matcha with moringa lattes or making shawarma out of tigernut instead of meat.
Both Wallin and Wisdom believe that their movement has the urgent task of saving Ghana’s food heritage before knowledge is lost.
“If we want to talk about what our future food system should look like,” says Wallin, “we need to talk to our grandmas, to our grandpas, to the farmers out in the communities because they sit on that knowledge. If we don’t talk to them now, it’s going to be too late. So it’s really now or never.”

ryo yamada’s sea-level installation prediction rises at edinburgh art festival 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26

ryo yamada’s in vitro / zero metre above sea level
Presented as part of the Edinburgh Art Festival 2026 at Summerhall Arts, Japanese artist Ryo Yamada designed and self-built In Vitro / Zero Metre Above Sea level as a site-specific architectural installation. Initiated in 2025 as part of his ongoing Zero Metre Above Sea Level series, this iteration confronts Scotland’s projected sea-level rise resulting from global climate change. Situated approximately 79-meters above sea level, this installation uses physical space to map time, translating complex environmental projections into a profound spatial experience.
the windows encourage visitors to look out and imagine the passage of 20,000 years in the future
vitro gallery floods open during edinburgh art festival 2026
Set within the grand, window-lined in Vitro Gallery, the structure spans nearly eight meters wide and stands 3.8-meters high – roughly twice the size of its previous enclosed iteration. The upper ceiling of the installation represents a projected future sea level roughly 20,000 years into the future at this specific location. Lined with large windows, the gallery invites shifting natural light and shadows to continuously transform the visual atmosphere of the space throughout the day. Visitors are encouraged to look through the installation toward the historic Edinburgh landscape outside, framing a dialogue between human history, historical architecture, and deep geological time.
Yamada designed and hand-assembled the entire monolithic framework over a rigorous preparation process, utilizing delicate pine timber strips measuring just 21 x 21-mm. Although the web of slender wooden elements appears fragile, its precise connections provide remarkable structural stability. Stretched non-woven fabric catches and diffuses light throughout the frame, evoking the ethereal, ephemeral presence of rising ocean waters. Through meticulous materiality and scale, Yamada’s installation invites quiet contemplation on humanity’s place within the Earth’s climate trajectory.

Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao bets on takeaway, new brands, lower-tier reach for growth
Takeaway emerges as Haidilao’s fastest-growing segment as it diversifies its formats, expands into lower-tier markets despite a soft economy
China’s largest hotpot chain Haidilao International Holding has seen takeaway emerge as its fastest-growing segment, with demand for single-serving meals like rice-bowl sets surging, amid positive revenue and profit growth in the first half.
Takeaway revenue for the Hong Kong-listed group reached 2.05 billion yuan (US$305 million) in the first six months, surging 121.2 per cent year on year. The segment accounted for 9.2 per cent of total revenue, up from 4.5 per cent a year earlier, according to its interim results released on Tuesday evening.
“China’s restaurant industry is highly fragmented – chains hold roughly 20 per cent of the market versus around 40 per cent globally. That means a well-run chain like Haidilao can still gain share even in a soft macro environment,” said Ivan Su, director of equity research at Morningstar.
Over the six-month period, the group posted total revenue of 22.34 billion yuan, up 7.9 per cent year on year. Net profit rose 0.5 per cent to 1.77 billion yuan. The Haidilao brand’s dine-in customers spent an average of 97 yuan, little changed from a year earlier.

France to ease strict rules on iconic cheeses as heat dries pastures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

France to ease strict rules on iconic cheeses as heat dries pastures
France is temporarily relaxing strict production rules for several iconic cheeses as drought and record heat leave pastures severely depleted. Producers of abondance, beaufort and comté can now use more imported fodder and grain to feed their cows, while other traditional cheeses will also receive temporary exemptions.
Widespread drought and record-breaking heatwaves have forced France to relax some of its famously strict rules on cheese production, with authorities announcing Wednesday special measures for abondance, beaufort and comte.
France's vast array of local cheeses are a source of national pride and authorities go to great lengths to protect traditional production methods and ensure authenticity.
To earn a coveted "appellation d'origine protegee" (Protected Designation of Origin) label -- and the right to give their cheese a particular protected name -- producers must follow rigid rules on where their animals graze and what they eat.
But the summer's drought, which affected 95 percent of mainland France in July, has left normally rich pastures dry and bare.
Watch moreHoly cow: Paris Agriculture Fair moo-ves forward without the bovine
In response, the government has said producers of abondance, beaufort and comte, hard cheeses made from the raw milk of cows grazing in the Alps and Jura mountains, can supplement the animals' diet with more fodder and grain brought in from elsewhere.
Growth on permanent grasslands as of August 10 is a third less than the 1989-2018 average, according to the Agriculture Ministry's statistical service.
The fodder situation is "highly degraded" in almost all regions, the ministry said earlier this month.
Watch moreClimate-change driven heatwave brings uncertainty to French farmers
The National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO), the government agency that administers and enforces rules of origin, says it will also grant temporary relief for several other cheeses including reblochon, cantal, bleu d'Auvergne, and fourme d'Ambert.
Europe's record-breaking summer heat has caused thousands of excess deaths, set wildfires blazing and seen major rivers drop to record lows.
In France, farmers are bracing for their smallest corn crop since 1980, and winegrowers are reporting some of the earliest harvests on record.
Scientists say human-caused climate change has intensified the drought, with extreme heat rather than low rainfall driving the dry conditions.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The southwestern Japanese city of Fukuoka experienced another day of sweltering heat Wednesday, as heatstroke nationwide last month left at least 79 people dead.
The mercury in Hakata Ward in Fukuoka reached 40.4C (104.7F), marking a record 10th consecutive day of extreme heat, Kyodo News reported.
A wide area of Japan experienced scorching temperatures driven by high pressure, with Fukuoka also affected by hot, moist air flowing from a nearby typhoon into the region.
Average summer temperatures across Japan have continued to rise, prompting authorities to categorize days when temperatures reach 40C (104F) or higher as “kokushobi,” or “cruelly hot days.”
The persistent heat wave has taken a heavy toll on public health, with more than 41,000 people hospitalized nationwide for heatstroke in July alone, resulting in at least 79 confirmed deaths, according to Japan’s Fire and Disaster Management Agency.
“Among those taken to hospitals, 24,769 were aged 65 or older, accounting for more than 60% of the total. Seventy-nine people were confirmed dead,” Jiji Press reported Tuesday.
The extreme heat follows severe weather earlier this month, when torrential rains and flash floods battered eastern Japan.
Early this month, heavy downpours inundated Chiba prefecture, east of the capital Tokyo, triggering urban flooding that submerged residential areas and killed at least 13 people.

US immigration agents arrested more than 49,500 people in July
The number of arrests in July showed a rise of roughly 15 percent over June’s count.
United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 49,571 people in July, the highest in a month since President Donald Trump took office for his second term, according to the latest figures available.
The figures for July showed a rise of roughly 15 percent over June’s count and about 70 percent above February’s total, according to government data provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles and analysed by The Associated Press news agency.

The month before Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, monthly arrests were slightly more than 8,000, a figure largely made up of immigrants transferred from city or state jails and prisons and turned over to ICE to remove from the country.
In his first year back in office, the monthly numbers started climbing as officials eased limits on where and whom agents could target. By December, monthly arrests had surpassed 40,000.
In the aftermath of two fatal shootings in Minnesota in January that led to protests and an uproar from Democratic lawmakers, arrests began to fall in February. After remaining stagnant for months, the numbers surged in June and then again in July.
Nearly 20,000 of the July arrests happened in Texas and Florida. Both states have taken part in cooperation deals with ICE known as 287(g) agreements that enable local law enforcement to essentially operate as additional arms for immigration enforcement.
The expanding arrest campaign comes after a hiring drive, with ICE bringing on roughly 12,000 additional officers and agents last year.

At least 47 people were killed, more than 50 others kidnapped, and another 22 people injured in a gang raid near Haiti’s capital of Port-au-Prince, the United Nations has said, prompting anger over violence amid repeated deadly attacks.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday condemned the attack in the town of Kenscoff, which took place on the evening of August 23.

Jean Massillon, Kenscoff’s mayor, said armed men “sowed chaos” as they set homes on fire and killed residents. He said gang members targeted a church and homes, including that of Jean William Pape, a leading public health expert.

The hillside community of Kenscoff, in a strategic position overlooking routes into the capital, has suffered a dozen attacks by armed gangs since last year, forcing thousands to flee their homes.
Powerful gangs under a broad alliance have for years cemented their influence over Haiti’s capital and expanded to nearby regions, despite attempts by foreign nations to reinforce the country’s outgunned police.

Asia-Pacific Community: Chinese-built rehab center restores hope to Mongolia's disabled children
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
16:54:31 CST
17:54:31 KST

A staff member designs supportive devices for child patients at a rehabilitation and development center for children with disabilities in Ulan Bator, Mongolia, July 1, 2026. On the western outskirts of Ulan Bator, beside the gentle Tuul River, stands a whimsical building striped with bright multicolored panels. This is Mongolia's largest, best-equipped rehabilitation and development center for children with disabilities, a humanitarian landmark funded and constructed by the Chinese government.(Xinhua/Yao Qilin)
ULAN BATOR, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- On the western outskirts of Ulan Bator, beside the gentle Tuul River, stands a whimsical building striped with bright multicolored panels. This is Mongolia's largest, best-equipped rehabilitation and development center for children with disabilities, a humanitarian landmark funded and constructed by the Chinese government.
Since opening its doors in May 2019, the facility has delivered rehabilitation, education and psychological counseling to more than 70,000 disabled Mongolian children, evolving into a warm sanctuary that restores hope to countless struggling families.
Spanning roughly two hectares with a construction area of nearly 15,000 square meters, the center houses 250 inpatient beds and brims with thoughtful, child-centered design touches.
Playfully painted walls, yurt-style lounge nooks for rest, spacious sunlit lobbies and animal-shaped outdoor installations soften the stark clinical feel typical of medical institutions. Children from across Mongolia receive one-stop care here, including physical rehabilitation, autism intervention, speech and language therapy and professional psychological counseling.
Amarjargal Myangaa, the center's director and a former neurologist, has visited small children's rehabilitation facilities in many countries. She spoke candidly about how rare it is to find a comprehensive rehabilitation complex of this scale.
"Few integrated pediatric rehabilitation facilities of this size exist worldwide," Amarjargal said. "We are deeply grateful that China fully recognized Mongolia's massive unmet demand for children's rehabilitation and built this fully functional center for us."
Day after day, cross-border kindness and professional expertise unfold inside its therapy rooms, healing young bodies and minds little by little.
In the art therapy studio, veteran art therapist Erdenesuren pulls out drawings by a seven-year-old girl with cerebral palsy. Over just one week, the child's work transformed from faint, abstract lines to vivid, fully realized scenes bursting with rich color -- tangible proof of her growing expressive ability. A dedicated exhibition space in the main hall showcases a rotating selection of the children's artwork each month.
In the speech and social therapy room, language instructor Solongo uses picture flashcards to lead training sessions; many nonverbal children say their first words within these walls.
Advanced hardware and sustained technical support from China have rewritten the fates of many ordinary Mongolian families.
Oyuntsetseg sits in the inpatient ward with her grandson, who is attending his 23rd round of rehabilitation therapy. When the boy first arrived in early 2020 with cerebral palsy, he could only move with a wheelchair. After consistent training, he now walks independently.
China's backing has never ended after construction wrapped up; ongoing multi-layered support continues to fuel the center's development.
Last year, the Chinese Embassy in Mongolia donated a set of medical and teaching equipment and inaugurated an on-site clinical skills training room. China Railway No. 4 Engineering Group Co., Ltd., the project's general contractor, has regularly donated supplies and equipment to the facility for years.
In addition, Chinese authorities have also organized two training exchanges for the center's medical staff at a major public children's hospital in central China's Hunan Province, with Erdenesuren and Solongo among those who took part and gained valuable professional experience.
"Investment in people is the most valuable investment of all, and personnel exchanges are our most precious form of cooperation," Amarjargal said.
In April, Amarjargal led a delegation to pay a field visit to the Inner Mongolia rehabilitation center for disabled children, where she was deeply impressed by China's intelligent rehabilitation gear. One system in particular captured her attention -- an AI motion analysis platform that captures children's body movements via multiple cameras and automatically generates personalized rehabilitation training regimens.
"Every year, we look forward to new exchange programs," Amarjargal said. "We hope to visit and study in China more often, and we also welcome teams of Chinese specialists to Mongolia to share expertise with us." ■
