Kindergartens in Ukraine: Are There Enough Places in the New Academic Year?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
10:17:04 EEST
16:17:04 KST

Kindergartens in Ukraine: Are There Enough Places in the New Academic Year?
Kyiv • UNN
There are 11,622 kindergartens operating in Ukraine, but places and waiting lists are determined by local communities. A total of 9,270 institutions have shelters, and the state has allocated UAH 1 billion.
Recent years have significantly changed Ukraine’s preschool education system. Parents preparing to send their child to kindergarten in the new academic year are facing realities that practically did not exist before the start of the full-scale war. When choosing an institution, the ability to stay safely in the kindergarten during air raids, the availability of a shelter, and the format in which the institution can actually operate are becoming increasingly important.
At the same time, the situation can differ dramatically across different regions and even neighboring communities. In one district, groups may be overcrowded and parents may have to wait for enrollment, while in another, places remain available. Some kindergartens operate in person, some combine in-person and remote formats, while others cannot accept children on their premises at all due to security restrictions.
What is the situation with kindergartens in Ukraine on the eve of the new academic year, are there enough places in the capital and the regions, and what should parents prepare for - details in the UNN report.
Details
To determine the current state of affairs in the preschool education system, UNN journalists sent an inquiry to the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine. In response, the ministry provided data on the number of institutions, their operating formats, and the provision of safe spaces. At the same time, the Ministry of Education and Science emphasized that information about specific available places, waiting lists, and the actual occupancy of groups is formed primarily at the local level.
How many kindergartens will operate in Ukraine from September 2026
According to operational data from local state executive authorities, as of June 2026, 11,622 preschool education institutions are operating in Ukraine.
Of these:
-  9,301 operate in person; 
-  1,111 - in a mixed format; 
-  1,210 - remotely. 
In other words, 80% of the institutions included in the Ministry of Education and Science’s statistics are already operating in person. At the same time, approximately one in five kindergartens depends either fully or partially on the remote organization of the educational process.
The Ministry of Education and Science also separately emphasizes that the figures cited do not cover the entire academic year.
The figures indicated are operational and may change depending on the security situation, decisions by founders, and the specifics of organizing the educational process in particular institutions
The number of kindergartens that will operate in person in the autumn may change even over the course of several weeks. If the security situation deteriorates, an institution may change its operating format, while after a shelter is equipped, it may, on the contrary, gain the opportunity to return children to in-person education. Therefore, parents who have already chosen a particular kindergarten should additionally clarify the institution’s operating schedule, the procedure to follow during an air raid, and the location of the shelter before attendance begins.
Are there enough places for preschoolers in kindergartens in Kyiv and the regions
There is no single figure that could show how many available places remain in kindergartens across Ukraine before the start of the 2026/2027 academic year.
The Ministry of Education and Science explained to UNN that the ministry does not maintain a centralized record of available places in every institution across the country.
Information on the number of available places in preschool education institutions, the number of children requiring enrollment, the order in which they are enrolled, and the actual occupancy of groups is compiled and recorded by the founders of preschool education institutions and local self-government bodies
Because of this, the total number of places in the system does not yet indicate how easy it will be for a particular family to enroll a child in a kindergarten near home. Demand is distributed unevenly: the residential district, the child’s age, the number of groups for the relevant age, the availability of a shelter, and the institution’s ability to actually accept preschoolers all matter.
An important nuance also concerns enrollment itself. The Law of Ukraine "On Preschool Education" establishes the order of admission to municipal institutions. Priority is given, in particular, to a child's residence within the service area of the relevant kindergarten; within this category, the law identifies specific groups of children that have priority. Therefore, the fact that enrollment applications are in the electronic system does not in itself mean that they all have the same position in the queue.
What is happening with places in Kyiv's kindergartens
In Kyiv, it became easier for parents in August 2026 to assess their chances of enrollment. The city's Services Portal introduced the option of viewing the queue for municipal kindergartens. The registry now shows how many applications have been submitted to a particular institution, which groups the children are seeking admission to, and how many vacancies remain in those groups.
In addition, the system shows the child's position not only in the overall queue but also in the relevant age group — nursery, younger, middle, or older. This is important because groups are formed by age, and a large total number of applications to a kindergarten does not necessarily mean the same level of competition in the group the child is to join. For parents, this makes it possible to compare several institutions before enrollment and, if the situation at one kindergarten is critical, consider an alternative.
Kindergarten queues: where the most people are applying and where kindergartens are not full
The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine has no nationwide ranking of cities or regions by the length of kindergarten queues. The ministry notes that it is not authorized to determine the number of available places, queues, or occupancy levels at every preschool education institution in all territorial communities of Ukraine.
Therefore, it is impossible to compile an accurate list of regions with the longest queues based on the Ministry of Education and Science's data. It is likewise incorrect to claim that a particular region generally has a surplus of places: within a single region, the situation in a large regional center and in a small community may be the opposite. Information about children awaiting enrollment, available places, and the actual occupancy of groups is maintained at the local level.
For parents, this means that the most reliable approach remains checking several sources: the community's electronic system, information from the specific kindergarten, and data from the local education authority. If there are no places at the preferred institution, it is worth checking neighboring kindergartens. In the preschool education system, the absence of a place at one particular institution does not automatically mean that the child will be unable to attend kindergarten at all.
Shelters in kindergartens: how many institutions can provide a safe space
One of the key factors determining whether a kindergarten can operate fully in person during martial law is the availability of an accessible shelter where preschoolers and educators can evacuate during an air raid alert.
According to the Ministry of Education and Science, as of June 2026, 9,270 preschool education institutions have shelters. This is almost 80% of the total number of institutions that, according to operational data, are operating in Ukraine.
According to the ministry, this includes, in particular:
-  703 civil protection protective structures; 
-  65 shelters in dual-purpose structures; 
-  6,114 simplest shelters; 
-  2,550 facilities belonging to other business entities; 
-  109 equipped protected spaces. 
At the same time, these figures cannot simply be added together. The Ministry of Education and Science explains that some categories may overlap, meaning that one institution may be counted under more than one characteristic.
The figures provided are operational and may change depending on the construction of new protective structures, changes in the security situation, and decisions by the founders
The problem of safe facilities remains systemic. In the state program for adapting preschools to civil protection requirements, approved at the end of 2025, the government separately acknowledged that a significant proportion of the existing facilities require conversion, while some of the already equipped basic shelters do not fully take into account the age-related needs of preschoolers and accessibility requirements. That is why work on shelters is continuing in 2026 as well.
How much the state will spend on shelters in preschools
A separate state subvention of UAH 1 billion was allocated for equipping shelters in preschool education institutions in 2026.
Preschools with at least 100 children, special preschools, as well as the only preschool education institutions in communities where creating a shelter would make it possible to provide in-person or blended learning, among others, were eligible for funding.
According to information provided by the Ministry of Education and Science to UNN, the authorized commission received and processed 60 project applications from regional and the Kyiv City state military administrations. Following the review, 18 sites — future shelters — were approved. Their construction and equipment are to be financed through the subvention.
Therefore, the "map" of preschools capable of operating in person is not final at present. Once the construction and equipment of the new shelters are completed, individual institutions that are currently limited in their ability to admit children may receive additional places and accept more preschoolers.
What parents should pay attention to when choosing a preschool with a shelter
The mere presence of a shelter in a preschool does not yet give parents a complete picture. Before enrolling a child, it is advisable to find out where it is located, how much time children need to get there, and whether it is designed for all the children and employees who are simultaneously present at the institution.
This is especially important for the youngest groups. Evacuating nursery-age children is fundamentally different from evacuating schoolchildren, so the actual algorithm of staff actions during an air raid alert and the time required for this are important.
In addition, the shelter may not be located directly in the preschool building, but in premises belonging to another business entity. That is why the Ministry of Education and Science’s statistics separately list thousands of such facilities.
Opening preschools in the new academic year: what parents should expect
The Ministry of Education and Science is not compiling a single nationwide list of new preschools that are to open by the end of 2026. The reason is the same: the development of the preschool education network largely falls within the competence of the founders.
Decisions on establishing preschool education institutions, resuming their operations, creating additional places, and developing the network are made by the founders in accordance with the law and taking into account the needs of the respective territories
New places for preschoolers in a particular community may appear either because a new building has been constructed for a preschool , or because local authorities may resume the operation of an institution that was previously not functioning, create additional groups, or reorganize the existing network.
Therefore, parents and guardians of preschoolers should monitor information about the opening of new preschools or groups on the websites of local councils, military administrations, and education authorities.
Closing preschools: what will change for parents
In response to UNN’s request, the Ministry of Education and Science explained that it likewise does not make centralized decisions on the closure or reorganization of municipal preschools. Under the Law of Ukraine "On Preschool Education," the decision to establish, reorganize, reprofile, or liquidate an institution is made by its founder. Therefore, there is no nationwide list of preschools that will cease operations in the 2026/2027 academic year.
The reasons for changes in the network may vary — from the security situation and the inability to use a building to demographic changes or the reorganization of institutions at the community level.
For families, the most important thing is not to wait until the start of the school year if information emerges about the possible closure of the chosen preschool. In such a case, they should immediately clarify with the founder what option will be offered to the children and whether places are available in other institutions in the community.
What parents of preschoolers should ultimately know before September
It would be incorrect to speak of a general shortage or, conversely, an excess of places in Ukraine's kindergartens on the eve of the 2026/2027 academic year. The Ministry of Education and Science does not maintain centralized statistics on waiting lists and available places, while the actual situation is determined at the level of each individual community and specific institution.
At the same time, most kindergartens currently operating have already organized the educational process in person. Of the 11,600 institutions, more than 9,300 accept children directly on their premises.
The main limitation on further expanding in-person education remains safety. A total of 9,270 institutions have been provided with protective facilities, and in 2026 the state is separately funding the construction and installation of new shelters.
Therefore, before the new academic year, the most practical thing for parents is to check three things at once: whether there is a place in the required age group, in what format the kindergarten actually operates, and which shelter the institution uses.
A reminder
Earlier, UNN explained how to enroll a child in kindergarten in 2026, how the waiting list works, which documents are required for enrollment, and who is eligible for benefits.

"I was so nervous I chewed through a pencil while my men were crossing the open ground": Ukraine's six-month advance on the Oleksandrivka front
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
10:15:00 EEST
16:15:00 KST

"I was so nervous I chewed through a pencil while my men were crossing the open ground": Ukraine's six-month advance on the Oleksandrivka front
Dedicated to the reconnaissance troops who cleared wooded areas on the Oleksandrivka front
In late April, some servicemen from the 80th Air Assault Brigade who had spent the previous two years fighting in Sumy Oblast let slip to Ukrainska Pravda that they were being redeployed to a new "secret" front.
At the time, several possible locations were being discussed in military and press circles: Kupiansk, Lyman, and Stepnohirsk in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
A few days later, UP learned that the "secret" front was in fact the Oleksandrivka front – where Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts meet.
It would be hard to describe this front as "high-profile" or even particularly well-known: it is not centred on a major city such as Pokrovsk or Kramatorsk, and it has also been closed to journalists for the past few months. Yet it played a significant role in the context of Russia's spring-summer offensive campaign this year – an offensive that ultimately failed to materialise – as we will explain below.
In late April, fresh forces, including paratroopers, were being deployed for the defence forces' second offensive operation on this front. The first operation, on the Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole fronts, had taken place at the beginning of the year and enabled the Ukrainian military to breach the Russian defensive line and liberate eight settlements.
The second operation started in early May and was kept secret for a long time. Some said this was because the defence forces had not fully accomplished their mission, others that the operation was still underway and it was therefore worth waiting before announcing it.
A sergeant in the Air Assault Forces whom UP met in Pavlohrad a week before this article was published joked that the Air Assault Forces command would announce the offensive "when we've fallen back to the positions we started from".
What he meant was that the longer the operation went on, the harder it became for his brigade to sustain its pace.
The sergeant summed up the operation: "The overall plan and concept worked, but our forces aren't limitless, and after a month of active fighting, we started to have problems with personnel. Another factor working against us was extensive Russian infiltration: they were wandering around chaotically [remember this part of the quote, as we'll come back to it in the third section – ed.] in areas in our rear."
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy unexpectedly decided to announce the results of both offensive operations on 12 August. In a video he released about the Ukrainian military's work, newly appointed Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi briefs him on the results, with Air Assault Forces Commander Oleh Apostol, who commanded the operation itself, sitting next to him.
The key statistics cited by Drapatyi were as follows: between January and August, the defence forces liberated 26 villages across three oblasts, retaking 745 sq km of territory. That's almost equivalent to the area of Kyiv.
Even allowing for the possibility that the figure may be overstated and doesn't distinguish between territory that was "fully liberated" and territory that was "cleared of infiltrating Russian troops", the scale of the offensive is impressive. Most of UP's sources among company and battalion commanders regard the offensive as a success.
The concept, stages, participants and details of the defence forces' Oleksandrivka offensive have so far remained largely in the shadows.
To remedy that, UP spoke to former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and around a dozen commanders and soldiers from four air assault and assault units that took part in the operation.
The operation at a glance
Name: Defence forces offensive on the Oleksandrivka front.
Time and place: January-August 2026 (still ongoing), at the junction of Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
Initiated by: Oleksandr Syrskyi, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine from 2024 to 2026.
Commander of the offensive grouping: Air Assault Forces Commander Oleh Apostol.
Main Ukrainian forces: Air Assault Brigades (95th, 82nd, 80th, 79th and 78th) and assault regiments (425th Skelia Regiment and 1st Separate Assault Regiment).
Likely objective: Disrupt the Russian offensive towards Orikhiv and thereby protect the city of Zaporizhzhia; drive Russian forces out of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
Tactics: mechanised assaults and infiltration.
Result: The Russian offensive towards Orikhiv did not take place. Almost all of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast has been liberated from Russian forces, with the exception of the village of Dachne. Ukraine regained control of 26 villages across three oblasts.
The defence forces' Oleksandrivka offensive was intended to draw Russian troops away from Huliaipole and protect Orikhiv and Zaporizhzhia
Since early 2026, journalists had been closely following the defence forces' offensive actions on the Huliaipole and Oleksandrivka fronts without fully understanding what they were intended to achieve.
The emergency effort to save Huliaipole, the offensive towards Dobropillia-Solodke, the 95th Brigade's initial strike on the Oleksandrivka front and the deployment of fresh forces in May did not appear to form a single, coherent picture.
So UP put the question about the purpose of the Oleksandrivka operation to the man who initiated it – former commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. It was the defence forces' final offensive operation launched under his command.
In written responses provided to UP, Syrskyi said that in the second half of 2025, he and the General Staff officers working in the combat zone had identified the Russians' plan.
Russian forces intended to advance not only on the Pokrovsk front, but also on the Huliaipole front.
"The enemy's plan was to breach our defences along the Huliaipole-Dobropillia line and subsequently create a threat of encirclement for the Ukrainian grouping near Orikhiv," Syrskyi wrote.
"To thwart these plans, inflict maximum losses on the enemy and at the same time straighten the front line, an offensive operation was planned on the Oleksandrivka front, involving a grouping of Air Assault Forces and assault units supported by units and formations from other branches of the Armed Forces."
Servicemen of various ranks told UP they believe the defence forces could not attack Russian troops on the Huliaipole front head-on because of the high concentration of Russian forces there.
The decision was therefore made to draw some of those forces away to the neighbouring Oleksandrivka front.
Sudden and genuinely secret strikes seem to have been a strong point both for the previous commander-in-chief and for the paratroopers in general.
In response to follow-up questions, Syrskyi said: "This strike [on the Oleksandrivka front] went into the rear of the advancing troops and forced the enemy to redeploy forces from the main axis [towards Orikhiv]. They were even forced to pull some units of the 90th Division back from near Pokrovsk. The objective was to destroy the enemy's assault grouping."
The "Oleksandrivka offensive" actually consisted of two separate operations with a short break between them. The first was centred around Huliaipole, the second around the Komar-Velyka Novosilka area
The first Ukrainian offensive operation began in early 2026, north of Huliaipole, which the Russians had already captured.
The paratroopers and assault troops advanced in two directions – north-west and north-east of the town. It is now clear that the Ukrainian defence forces were attempting to squeeze the Russians from two sides. Both heavy equipment and small infantry groups were used for this.
The Ukrainian defenders advanced 9-11 km into Russian positions as a result.
"It was an infantry operation where everything depended on the soldiers' training," Anton Derliuk, Commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 95th Air Assault Brigade, told UP several months ago.
However, the maximum objective was not achieved.
According to information available to UP, at least one part of the plan envisaged the defence forces advancing another 10+ km deeper and reaching the Russian rear from the direction of the village of Uspenivka.
"We didn't have enough forces for that," one senior participant in the operation told UP.
Although the maximum objective was not achieved, the Ukrainian offensive grouping (as Dmytro "Perun" Filatov, Commander of the 1st Separate Assault Regiment, noted in an interview with UP) blocked the Russians' ability to advance, we now know, towards Orikhiv. It also narrowed the area under Russian control.
The first offensive operation also created the conditions for the next one – the recapture of part of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast that had been seized by the Russians in 2025.
The second offensive operation began on 5 May along an extremely wide stretch of the front line – over 50 km, roughly from Nove Zaporizhzhia in Zaporizhzhia Oblast to Filiia in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. Its aim was to push the Russians as far as possible out of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, most likely towards Komar and Velyka Novosilka.
Velyka Novosilka is a fairly large settlement and a strategically important logistics hub, and its fall 18 months earlier had opened the gateway for the Russians to two neighbouring oblasts at once – Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia.
For the second offensive operation on the Oleksandrivka front, reinforcements arrived from the 78th, 79th and 80th Air Assault Brigades.
A company commander from one of these brigades told UP: "The 95th had slightly run out of steam during the first offensive – they'd taken on a huge amount of work. After that, they needed reinforcements."
Several months later, the same commander would mention this in a conversation with UP, this time talking about his own unit: "The Hospis [medics from the Hospitallers medical battalion] came to us today, but I don't know what they're going to do or who they're going to evacuate. There's no infantry left [this mostly refers to soldiers that were wounded]."
So when the second offensive operation began, Apostol was commanding a large part of the strongest brigades from the 7th and 8th Air Assault Corps. According to UP's information, the 95th Brigade also came under his direct command.
One battalion commander who spoke to UP described Apostol as a competent and understanding commander. Soldiers could always call him and ask for help. He treated even "non-organic" assault units – those that were not directly part of his own formation – reasonably and fairly.
However, it is worth noting that not all assault troops accept the "authority" of the paratroopers. Some believe they can achieve better results if they operate more autonomously.
As usual, the defence forces' casualty rate in the operation has not been disclosed. Some of UP's sources claimed that it was "abnormally low". At least two units operating different types of unmanned systems that UP spoke to did not have a single person killed during the two offensive operations.
Some of our other sources, however, hinted that while the number of deaths was relatively small, the number of soldiers reported missing or AWOL was significant.
During the second offensive operation, the defence forces regained control of more than ten villages stretching along the edges of the three oblasts – Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk. Practically the entire territory of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast was cleared of Russian troops. The operation is still ongoing.
The map produced by DeepState, a Ukrainian group of military analysts, clearly shows how the operation created a huge "protected zone" in front of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. If the defence forces can hold it, it will protect Dnipropetrovsk Oblast from a ground war for some time.
It won't, however, protect it from guided aerial bomb strikes, unfortunately. This is an area where the Russians make particularly intensive use of them. As a result, settlements that are 30-50 km away from the line of contact – which might otherwise seem almost like the rear – are now impossible to live in.
The defence forces' advantages in this offensive were the element of surprise and the infantry's training. Their disadvantages were false information about the actual depth of the Russian advance, difficult terrain, and Russia's numerical superiority in terms of UAVs
In the previous two sections, we mainly presented the views of the military commanders who initiated both offensive operations and were responsible for carrying them out at the highest level. Now we'll look at how the operations were seen by the lower-level commanders and soldiers who directly put the plan into practice with their own feet, rifles and drones.
The first two or three weeks of both offensive operations were "extremely successful". In the initial stages, the Russians (a) didn't yet realise that the defence forces had launched a major offensive, and (b) were afraid to report it to their superiors.
"They saw these servicemen running around wearing the paratroopers' 'mohnatky' [a camouflage covering worn over the head] and spent two days arguing about whose 'mohnatky' they were," one paratrooper company commander told UP, laughing.
"It was only when we reached Myrne [10 km inside the Russian positions] that they realised something was going on. Up until then, they'd been sitting there without any communications or food," his fellow soldier added.
"The early days of the operation were not difficult. We found positions quickly, we could even drive to them, unload the equipment and get to work," explained Maksym Maslivets, commander of a UAV platoon in the Boryviter unmanned systems battalion of the 95th Brigade.
But the main reason why the Russians didn't understand what was happening was down to a tactic the Ukrainian forces were applying – infiltration.
The defence forces literally mirrored the enemy's modus operandi. Instead of carrying out frontal assaults, they quickly and imperceptibly seeped through the Russians' positions in small groups. This was aided by the good training of the Ukrainian paratroopers and assault troops.
"We had to advance as deep as possible without being noticed, bypass the wooded areas held by the enemy, establish a line, cut them off, and then capture those who remained on our side of the line," the paratrooper company commander we mentioned earlier explained.
When using these tactics, a large part of the work falls to traditional reconnaissance troops. They are the ones who later go in to mop up those same wooded areas where Russians cut off from their own remain in the Ukrainian rear, still posing a danger.
Sometimes these Russian forces can be taken out by explosives dropped from bomber drones (still a specific advantage of the Ukrainian military); sometimes they have to be cleared out by hand.
Clearing out enemy troops by hand is one of the most difficult and dangerous tasks in the current war. In the Air Assault Forces, this task is typically carried out by an elite brigade-level reconnaissance unit.
"Everyone ran through the wooded areas – and that was right, because that was how it was supposed to be, but then we had to sweep it all. All that fell on the reconnaissance troops," the commander of one reconnaissance unit told UP. "And we lost a lot of people doing that. Our greatest losses were in these small-arms engagements and from drones. As soon as the enemy detected us, they'd rain everything down on that position. One of our groups was hit by 12 Molniya drones within half an hour."
One of our sources for this article asked UP to mention, in the context of the Oleksandrivka operation, one of his brothers-in-arms, Junior Sergeant Volodymyr Shyshoholik. As part of a reconnaissance group of the 80th Air Assault Brigade, he cleared the wooded areas "that everyone had run through". He was killed with a weapon in his hands, aged 27.
In both the first and the second operation, Russian UAVs kicked in a few weeks into the operation. Rubicon, one of Russia's most effective units, was speedily redeployed to the Oleksandrivka front.
"Within three weeks the enemy realised that something wasn't right here, and both the Russian armies standing opposite us brought in their reserves," explained Andrii Serhiienko, commander of a strike UAV company in the Boryviter unmanned systems battalion of the 95th Brigade.
Service members told UP the Ukrainians had the edge in terms of the quality of the drone crews' work, but the Russians had it in terms of the number of drones.
After the second Ukrainian offensive operation began, the Russians set about intensively mining roads and planting ambush drones at junctions where vehicles would usually slow down.
To counter this, Ukrainian units had to form separate crews that would regularly fly over the roads, monitor them for ambush drones, and drop explosives on them.
Maksym Maslivets, the platoon commander from the 95th Brigade we mentioned before, told UP: "Mid-spring, Rubicon effectively cut off all our logistics routes. My vehicle was attacked by between 30 and 50 drones when it got stuck. And the challenges were compounded by the fact that there was a lot of rain that spring, which turned the field roads we used into mud. Everything got bogged down. There were times when nothing could get through – not Humvees, nor pickups, nor even Urals. And as soon as the enemy spotted that, they'd fire everything at it.
What helped us was that a few weeks into stage two of the operation, we were supplied with better drones that could fly 25-30 km rather than 10-15. This enabled us to reach the enemy further away and to work from a safer place."
Regarding the particular challenges of this offensive, our sources singled out three key aspects.
1. Lies from their own side about the actual depth of the Russians' penetration. Unfortunately, at the start of the second offensive operation Ukrainian troops were faced with the fact that the real line of contact was not the same as the one plotted on the map.
Russian troops had infiltrated 2-10 km deeper than they had been told. So before the main offensive operation started, Ukrainian forces had to finish mopping up their own rear or, worse still, find out that there were Russians in their rear after advancing. This is the "chaotic infiltration" by the Russians that we mentioned in the introduction to this article in the words of the paratrooper sergeant.
One participant in the operation told UP: "As soon as we came in, we were told: 'Everything's fine here, go forward, towards Maliivka.' We take the analysis, we look at where the enemy was last detected, and it was in the Velykomykhailivka Forest [a couple of kilometres into the Ukrainian forces' rear – UP], beyond the crossing – the enemy had crossed the river and was sitting there!"
UP is aware of a similar situation in at least three areas:
- the settlement of Andriivka-Klevtsove (formerly named Iskra) in Donetsk Oblast, which the 80th Brigade passed through. There was up to a platoon of Russians in Iskra;
- Kolomiitsi and Oleksiivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, which the 95th passed through. There were also Russian drone pilots in Oleksiivka;
- the forest east of Velykomykhailivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, which the Skelia regiment passed through.
2. In some sectors of the offensive, practically all the wooded areas had been cut down or mined, forcing the Ukrainian troops to advance across open terrain for long stretches at enormous risk.
One of UP's sources described his unit's offensive zone as one where "nobody was intending to advance". It was only suitable for static defence.
One commander who took part in the operation told UP: "I was so nervous I chewed through a pencil while my men were crossing the open ground. All the wooded areas had been either mined or cut down for a kill zone. Nobody was intending to advance there, I don't know why they [the Ukrainian units that had previously been holding the sector] did it. It f**ked things up for us so badly. Zaits [commander of the 20th Corps – UP], who arrived when the offensive was already underway, wouldn't have allowed that – he's a very sensible guy."
Incidentally, three of UP's sources in the defence forces said that Sviatoslav Zaits, the commander of the 20th Corps, who comes from the Air Assault Forces, is being considered as a candidate for Commander of the Ground Forces. His place in the 20th Corps may be taken by the current commander of the 141st Brigade and former commander of the 59th Brigade, the young Lieutenant Colonel Bohdan Shevchuk.
3. The advance was complicated by a long logistics chain (more than 10-20 km) and by the rivers that cut across the Oleksandrivka sector in several places at once (particularly the Vovcha River).
Some of the servicemen UP spoke with were convinced that the command had not taken the brigades' logistical capabilities into account – some lacked unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), while others faced such intense enemy activity that bringing anything up to their position was practically impossible.
"In our case, for instance, neither quad bikes nor the armoured vehicles that delivered supplies could drive the distance required. We went on our own two feet, and on UGVs when we had them. The logistics were tough," the paratrooper sergeant told UP.
"My infantry used to walk 20 km, and that was only to the line of contact. And after that you still have to conduct assaults, to work," another battalion commander added.
The servicemen assigned a separate role in this operation to logistics and transport across the river. To cross the water bodies, temporary crossings were set up where possible, and boats were used. In one of the videos passed to UP, two paratroopers can be clearly seen crossing the river, to the sound of explosions, on an inflatable boat with their equipment and moving on further to clear the wooded areas.
There were also those who swam across the river, with dry clothes then dropped to them by drone.
"The crossings, the pontoons, would be destroyed within half an hour of being set up – it wasn't worth it," one of the commanders told UP. "I didn't want to send my men there. So ours swam across. It was wet, but we dropped clothes for them from drones straight afterwards. We tried to look after our people."
***
The operation on the Oleksandrivka front is ongoing. However, the key surges have probably already been made. The Russian offensive on Orikhiv has been thwarted (for now), Dnipropetrovsk Oblast is practically free of Russians, and for the paratroopers and assault troops, new tasks and sectors await.
Olha Kyrylenko, UP

Boeing wins $163 million order for B-52 bomb rack kits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:12:48 UTC
16:12:48 KST

- Boeing received a delivery order worth up to $162,966,689 to build Bomb Rack Modernization System kits for the B-52 bomber.
- The sole-source order supports the B-52 Radar Modernization Program and work will be performed in San Antonio through December 2028.
Boeing has been awarded a delivery order worth up to $163 million to build and deliver Bomb Rack Modernization System kits for the B-52 bomber, the Department of War announced. The order supports the broader B-52 Radar Modernization Program and was issued under an existing indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract that dates to 2019.
Work will be performed at Boeing’s facility in San Antonio, Texas, and is expected to be completed by December 20, 2028. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is managing the order, designated FA8628-26-F-B002. About $35 million in fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds were obligated at the time of award, which the Air Force listed as August 21. The action was a sole-source acquisition, and the order combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-reimbursement and firm-fixed-price elements.
The Bomb Rack Modernization System kits are tied to the same radar upgrade program that centers on installing the AN/APQ-188 active electronically scanned array radar across the B-52H fleet, replacing the aircraft’s Cold War-era mechanically scanned radar. Boeing has said the new radar and associated systems are meant to improve situational awareness, speed up target identification, and enhance aircrew survivability in contested environments. The radar system relies on new mission computers and cockpit displays, including two 8-by-20-inch touchscreens and fighter-style hand controllers for radar operation, along with upgraded liquid cooling to handle the new hardware’s power demands.
Boeing’s San Antonio site, at Port San Antonio, houses one of the largest military aircraft maintenance and modernization complexes in the world, including a hangar capable of holding up to 15 wide-body aircraft at once. The facility has handled ground integration and initial system checks for the B-52 radar program, and Boeing delivered the first B-52 fitted with the new APQ-188 radar to the Air Force’s 412th Test Wing at Edwards Air Force Base in December 2025 for flight testing.
“The new radar will significantly increase B-52 mission effectiveness by improving situational awareness, speeding target prosecution and enhancing aircrew survivability in contested environments,” said Troy Dawson, vice president of Boeing Bombers.
Boeing has continued to add B-52 modernization work at both its San Antonio and Oklahoma City sites over the past year. In December 2025, the Air Force awarded Boeing a $2.04 billion task order to begin hands-on integration and structural modification work on two B-52 aircraft under the separate Commercial Engine Replacement Program, which will fit the bombers with new Rolls-Royce F130 engines. That engine work spans sites in Oklahoma City, San Antonio, Seattle and Indianapolis, with completion scheduled for May 2033.
The radar program itself has faced delays and rising costs in recent years, with flight testing pushed back from fiscal 2024 to fiscal 2026 and the Air Force reviewing program requirements to manage expenses. Data collected during ongoing test flights is expected to inform later phases of the program and the eventual retrofit of all 76 operational B-52 aircraft with the new radar and associated hardware.

Asia-Pacific Community: How modern Chinese builders continue Zheng He's legacy in Indonesia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:12:24 CST
16:12:24 KST

by Xinhua writer Zhang Yisheng
SEMARANG, Indonesia, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Semarang, a major port on Indonesia's Java island, traces its rich history back to the 15th century, when Chinese navigator Zheng He made multiple stops here during his historic maritime voyages.
Historical records show that Zheng's "treasure ships" brought not only thriving trade but also lasting bonds between the two peoples. Local tradition even holds that the city was named in honor of Zheng, with the iconic Sam Poo Kong temple standing today as a timeless testament to his legacy.
Heading north from downtown Semarang, engines roared amidst waves of stifling heat. At the construction site of Indonesia's first dike-highway, Yue Zhenhong, project manager of toll road development of Semarang-Demak 1B built by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), navigated the main access route in a hard hat and blue work uniform.
Behind him, bulldozers and road rollers operated in shifts, while over a thousand dump trucks transported materials around the clock, creating a bustling scene filled with the blare of horns.
"We are working 24-hour non-stop shifts to try to complete the basic earthmoving construction before the rainy season arrives," said the 35-year-old, wiping sweat from his forehead.
Both Semarang and Demak are situated on the northern coast of Central Java province. For years, traffic congestion along the existing national highway connecting the two places has been severe. The Indonesian government hopes to ease traffic pressure and solve a long-lasting problem of tidal flooding along the coast through this project.
According to Yue, the project integrates transportation and flood control functions. Once completed, travel time between the two cities will be drastically reduced from 60 minutes during peak traffic to just 10 minutes, significantly lowering logistics costs and injecting fresh momentum into local economic growth.
However, turning the vision into reality requires overcoming formidable challenges. Deep layers of soft mud reaching depths of 30 meters beneath the seabed along the route made construction akin to "building a house on tofu." Enhancing the bearing capacity of the soft foundation while controlling construction stability and post-construction subsidence presented a tough nut to crack for the project team.
"Tailored to local geological conditions and resource availability, we creatively implemented a foundation treatment solution for very soft ground: bamboo piles and mats plus vertical and horizontal drain boards with surcharge preloading," Yue explained.
He noted that the strength of this solution lies in tapping into the local abundance of bamboo. By replacing high-carbon materials like steel and cement with bamboo, the project significantly cuts carbon emissions across its entire life cycle.
For more than 20 years of doing business in Indonesia, the CRBC has built a string of landmark projects across the archipelago country. Those projects have not only accumulated rich expertise for constructing the dike-highway but also cultivated a pool of local engineering talent.
Muhammad Rizky Pradana, a 26-year-old engineer who joined the company a year and a half ago, has developed a profound appreciation for the rigor of Chinese engineering standards.
Rizky admitted that he initially felt considerable pressure facing the project's stringent quality management requirements. However, under the hands-on guidance of his Chinese colleagues, he quickly mastered the know-how.
"The project's strict control over quality has enabled me to learn many new professional skills and management methods. Being able to grow on such a platform makes me feel truly fulfilled," he said.
For 37-year-old Mochamad Zumar Habibi, this year marks his 10th year working with the CRBC, an example of the company's long-term commitment to nurturing local staff.
Habibi said the efficiency and dedication of the Chinese enterprise have continuously inspired him. Working in the CRBC has improved his family's livelihood, making his parents and wife immensely proud of his job. "I hope to stay with the CRBC all the way until retirement."
For local residents, Chinese builders have brought not only technology and skills but also a strong sense of social responsibility.
"In the past, severe sea erosion damaged homes, roads, and fish ponds. Every time high tide came, seawater nearly 1 meter deep poured in, paralyzing the roads," recalled Kumaidi, a local village official, noting that tidal flooding had haunted his village for ages.
Upon learning of the situation, the CRBC project team extended a helping hand by elevating nearly 5 kilometers of surrounding rural roads by about 1 meter, greatly enhancing their flood-prevention capacity.
Kumaidi remarked with gratitude that travel conditions in the village have improved immensely, and residents no longer frequently suffer from being stranded by floods. Furthermore, the team installed streetlights along key sections, illuminating roads that were once pitch-black at night.
"Just like Zheng He's fleet when it arrived here centuries ago," Kumaidi said, "the Chinese builders today have also come bearing friendship and win-win cooperation." ■

Study finds sugar tax could boost Australians' oral health
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:12:16 CST
16:12:16 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Millions of cases of tooth decay could be prevented if Australia introduced a 20 percent tax on sugar, according to new research from Australia's Griffith University.
The study estimated that such a tax could prevent 3.7 million cases of tooth decay, 191,000 cases of gum disease and 115,000 cases of complete tooth loss, Professor Lennert Veerman from Griffith's School of Medicine and Dentistry said in a statement released Wednesday.
A 20 percent tax would also generate approximately 500,000 health-adjusted life years for Australia's 2019 population over their lifetime, through improvements in dental health and reductions in weight-related illness, according to the findings published in BMJ Public Health.
Oral diseases affect about 3.5 billion people globally, while nearly 32 percent of Australian adults have untreated tooth decay, the study noted.
The research found that males would experience the most health benefits from a sugar tax, as they consume more sugary drinks and have higher baseline levels of some oral diseases. ■

Across China: Chinese-developed cell therapy shows promise for severe heart failure
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:12:12 CST
16:12:12 KST

NANJING, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have recently developed a novel cardiac cell therapy that helps repair damaged myocardium and improve heart function in patients with severe heart failure.
The therapy, pioneered by Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital in east China's Jiangsu Province, uses lab-cultivated cardiomyocytes to replace necrotic heart tissue, enabling both vascular recanalization and myocardial regeneration.
"Bypass surgery can unblock vessels, but it cannot regrow dead myocardium," Professor Wang Dongjin, who led the research, told Xinhua. The new therapy, he added, is designed to solve this problem. "We wanted to inject new cardiomyocytes directly into the heart to replace dead muscle and restore function. It's like the old Chinese saying: you eat what you lack."
Long-term follow-up results of the clinical study were published on Aug. 19 in Nature Medicine.
Twelve-month follow-up data showed that 90 percent of the patients who received the cell therapy recovered to New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class II, reporting significant relief from shortness of breath and chest tightness during daily activities. In the bypass-only control group, this figure was 60 percent.
Patients in the cell therapy group also posted an average gain of 168.8 meters in the six-minute walk test, nearly double the control group's improvement. Cardiac pumping function diverged further: stroke volume increased in the treatment group but declined in the control group.
"For the first time, we have proven the therapy is safe," Wang said. Over the follow-up period, no patient developed tumors or sustained malignant arrhythmias. "We also confirmed that the transplanted cells beat in sync with the patient's own heart rhythm. That's a critical global validation."
The cell product used in the trial, HiCM-188, is an off-the-shelf therapy that can be produced and stored in standardized batches, bypassing the lengthy customization required for patient-specific cell products -- a critical advantage given that heart transplants are out of reach for most end-stage patients due to a chronic shortage of donors.
"Instead of patients waiting for cells, we want cells waiting for patients," Wang said. "That could fundamentally ease the donor shortage."
Industry experts said that despite the limited sample size, the rigorous randomized controlled design offers strong proof of concept, placing China's cardiac regenerative medicine among the global frontrunners.
With larger trials ahead, this homegrown therapy has the potential to reshape the treatment paradigm for severe heart failure and benefit a vast number of patients, according to the experts. ■

U.S. State Department pauses immigrant visa applications worldwide: FT
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:11:52 CST
16:11:52 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has paused immigrant visa applications worldwide to conduct "in-depth training" for consular officers amid its ongoing immigration crackdown, the Financial Times reported Tuesday, citing a State Department spokesperson.
As Washington seeks to screen out individuals "deemed likely to need U.S. assistance," immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at U.S. embassies and consulates have been notified by email that their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would receive future notice of a new date and time, the report said.
The visa pause came just a few days after the Trump administration faced legal setbacks last week.
A federal judge on Friday struck down the administration's ban on visa applications for citizens of 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, whom it deemed likely to seek public benefits in the United States.
Since Trump returned to the White House, his administration has tightened immigration policies, cracking down on undocumented immigrants and increasing scrutiny of U.S. visa holders.
On Aug. 10, the State Department announced that it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since January 2025, when Trump began his second term.
On Monday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed a fee of 103,265 U.S. dollars for H-1B cap-subject petitions, marking the agency's latest move to restrict the visa program on new grounds. This came after previous efforts to charge 100,000 dollars for the visa were struck down by the courts.

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Rising penetration highlights vitality, innovative strength of China's NEV industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
15:11:38 CST
16:11:38 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Nearly two in every three passenger cars sold at retail in China are now new energy vehicles (NEVs), a share that signals both the vitality of China's NEV market and the industry's capacity to turn new technologies into reliable products at scale.
Industry association data showed that NEVs accounted for 65.1 percent of passenger-car retail sales in July, up 11.6 percentage points from a year earlier and marking the fourth consecutive month above 60 percent.
For August, passenger-car retail sales are estimated at 1.58 million units, including about 1.04 million NEVs, which would put the penetration rate at 65.8 percent, 10.6 percentage points higher than a year earlier.
LOWER COSTS, BETTER USER EXPERIENCE
Lower costs, technology upgrades and changing consumer preferences have helped lift NEVs' share of passenger-car sales, industry insiders said.
As battery material prices have normalized and new processes such as integrated die-casting and battery-chassis integration have been adopted at scale, manufacturing costs have continued to fall, allowing some NEVs to match or undercut comparable gasoline-powered vehicles, said Jiang Tianci, head of an automobile dealers association in Anhui Province in east China.
At an NEV store in Chongqing, southwest China, where sales rose more than 10 percent month on month to exceed 220 units in May, the manager said buyers were shifting their attention from power specifications to intelligent features.
In the Haizhu District of Guangzhou in south China, a customer visiting an NEV showroom tried voice controls, a large in-car display and driver-assistance features, and praised the experience.
Charging access has also improved, with the number of EV charging points reaching 23.68 million by the end of July, up 41.9 percent year on year, according to the National Energy Administration.
Higher gasoline prices have further strengthened the operating-cost advantage of NEVs, with retail gasoline prices still up a net 1,345 yuan (roughly 198 U.S. dollars) per tonne from the start of the year, even after a mid-August reduction, according to calculations based on data from the National Development and Reform Commission.
A Chongqing resident surnamed Wang recently replaced his gasoline-powered car with an EV, saying that the switch had cut his monthly commuting costs from more than 1,200 yuan for gasoline to less than 200 yuan for electricity, saving him around 12,000 yuan a year.
FROM MARKET SCALE TO FASTER ITERATION
The growing presence of NEVs in China's passenger-car market is supported by an industrial ecosystem capable of moving new technologies quickly from development to production.
China's automotive and EV sectors have expanded on an unprecedented scale and at unprecedented speed over the past decade, Shalini Palmer, corporate vice president of automotive business at Analog Devices, said at the Global New Energy Vehicle Cooperation and Development Forum in east China's Shanghai last week.
China now has one of the world's most dynamic and robust automotive ecosystems, a result Palmer attributed to sustained investment, rigorous engineering discipline and a pace of execution that exceeded industry expectations.
China's automotive competitiveness is rooted in a virtuous cycle between technological progress and industrial development, said Jiang Yaoping, former vice minister of commerce, at the forum.
The industrial scale underpinning that cycle is visible in the Yangtze River Delta, which accounts for approximately 40 percent of China's NEV output and has formed a "four-hour industrial circle" in which all the components needed for an NEV can be sourced within a four-hour drive.
Jiang said the country's complete industrial system and vast market provide a testing ground for new technologies, with frequent user feedback and diverse use cases allowing such technologies to be refined quickly through large-scale application.
The pace of iteration is evident in product development, with Chinese automakers shortening development cycles from three to five years to around 18 months in recent years, according to Zhang Lin, chief representative and general manager of the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA) China.
Battery development shows the same pattern, with CATL launching its first Shenxing superfast-charging battery in 2023, a second-generation version in 2025, and a third-generation version this April. The company said the latest version can charge from 10 percent to 80 percent in three minutes and 44 seconds and retain more than 90 percent of its capacity after 1,000 full charging cycles.
RAPID ITERATION TO RELIABLE DELIVERY
Kevin Li, president of Magna China, described China as one of the world's most dynamic auto markets, where competition is producing a steady stream of new models and a faster pace of iteration.
He cited Magna's work with Chery to bring its DHD Duo dedicated hybrid drive system into series production on the JETOUR G700 after an 18-month development cycle, as an example of balancing development speed with reliability.
Before the prototype design was finalized, engineers identified hundreds of potential risks, while accumulated development data and capabilities in simulation, testing and verification helped avoid repeated design changes and additional rounds of testing during the first two prototype stages, Li said.
At the industry level, draft amendments to three recommended national standards, released for public comment in July, proposed setting a minimum reliability-test mileage of 30,000 km for electric, hybrid and fuel-cell vehicles.
A mandatory national standard on EV battery safety that took effect on July 1 includes seven cell-level tests and 17 battery-pack or system tests, covering risks including high temperatures, collisions, short circuits and overcharging.
Under the standard, batteries must not catch fire or explode in thermal propagation tests, and the same requirement applies to an external short-circuit test conducted after 300 fast-charging cycles.
Li said the auto industry had no shortage of good ideas, but the real challenge was turning them into products that could be delivered at scale while meeting requirements for regulatory compliance, quality, cost, efficiency and reliability. Doing so, he added, requires strong engineering and manufacturing capabilities, resilient supply chains and disciplined operations. ■

UN and ICRC called for restrictions on autonomous weapons
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
10:11:04 EEST
16:11:04 KST

UN and ICRC called for restrictions on autonomous weapons
Kyiv • UNN
Guterres and Spoljaric called on states to begin negotiations on legally binding restrictions on autonomous weapons. They warned of risks to civilians.
States must immediately begin developing legally binding rules governing the use of autonomous weapons systems, including drones. As reported by the UN, this joint appeal was issued by UN Secretary-General António Guterres and Mirjana Spoljaric, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), reports UNN.
Details
According to them, the world is rapidly approaching a dangerous threshold beyond which a machine will be able to independently select a person as a target—and this is an "ethically unacceptable situation."
Guterres and Spoljaric recalled that three years ago they had already called on countries to establish prohibitions and restrictions on such systems. Since then, technology has been developing so rapidly that the gap between weapons' capabilities and existing legal norms has only widened. The use of advanced autonomous systems on the battlefield increases risks to civilians and infrastructure, exacerbating human suffering in armed conflicts, the appeal states.
In the view of the appeal's authors, further development of autonomous weapons will lead to escalation and a weakening of human control over the use of force. The race toward increasingly autonomous systems is already under way, and, as noted, even the engineers creating these technologies are expressing concern. "If even the creators of this technology are calling for its limitation, states cannot afford to remain on the sidelines," the appeal emphasizes.
Guterres and Spoljaric believe that this year must be a turning point. Significant progress has already been made in the UN General Assembly and in the Group of Governmental Experts of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in understanding what human control should be exercised and what measures are necessary to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law. Now, in their view, political will must be demonstrated: the time has come to move from discussions to action.
The heads of the UN and the ICRC called on states to begin negotiations on adopting a legally binding treaty with clearly defined restrictions and prohibitions. Delay, they warn, will lead to even greater loss of human life.
Particular attention in the appeal is devoted to the upcoming Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which will take place in November. Guterres and Spoljaric hope that states will be able to adopt a decision to launch negotiations on a legally binding document.
"The painstaking work carried out over the past three years provides an ideal foundation for such negotiations," the appeal states.
Guterres and Spoljaric emphasize that continuing to develop weapons that make warfare easier undermines collective efforts to create a safer world. Innovation, they say, must serve humanity rather than threaten it.

Aldi and Colruyt recall courgettes due to excessive levels of heptachlor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:10:42 UTC
16:10:42 KST

Following Aldi, supermarket chain Colruyt is now also recalling courgettes because they contain excessive levels of heptachlor, an insecticide. Anyone who has bought the courgettes is asked not to eat them and to return them to the store. “As this is a slight exceedance of the limit, there is little cause for concern,” explains toxicologist Jan Tytgat.
At Aldi, the affected courgettes, known as zucchini in Australia and the US, were sold in packs of two. They can be identified by the batch number 100320823962. The courgettes were sold there from 10 to 22 August.
At Colruyt, the issue concerns loose courgettes, with item number 29707. These were sold from 10 to 24 August. Aldi and Colruyt have since removed the affected courgettes from their shelves.
Both supermarkets are asking customers who bought the courgettes not to eat them. Anyone who returns them to the shop will be refunded, even without the original packaging or receipt.
What is heptachlor?
Heptachlor is a pesticide that was formerly used in agriculture to control insects and termites. Its use has been banned in the European Union since 1978, but traces of the substance continue to turn up in crops to this day as a result of its past use.
Excessive exposure to heptachlor (epoxide) can damage the liver and may cause cancer.
“We measured 0.011 milligrams of heptachlor per kilogram of courgettes, whilst the limit is 0.010 milligrams per kilogram,” explains Hélène Bonte of the Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain (FASFC). She adds that the courgettes were most likely contaminated due to historical soil pollution with heptachlor.
“Minimal health risks”
“As this is only a slight exceedance of the limit, people need not be overly concerned,” explains toxicologist Jan Tytgat. “However, it is wise not to eat the contaminated courgettes and simply to return them to the shop.”
“But there are few health risks for those who did eat them. Unless you ate more than two courgettes in quick succession, but even then you won’t develop symptoms straight away. For example, if you made a spaghetti sauce with a courgette in it, you can still eat it without any problem. That remains below the standard of 0.007 milligrams that an adult weighing 70 kilograms is allowed to consume per day.”

Tracker reveals details of Russia’s secretive satellite launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:05:43 UTC
16:05:43 KST

- A Soyuz-2.1b rocket launched a classified Russian military satellite from Plesetsk on August 24, reaching an orbit consistent with GLONASS navigation satellites.
- Astronomer Jonathan McDowell said the satellite likely carries the designation Kosmos-2619, though Russia has not officially confirmed its identity.
The classified satellite Russia launched from Plesetsk Cosmodrome on August 24 has reached an orbit consistent with a GLONASS navigation satellite, astronomer and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell reported.
The U.S. Space Force cataloged two objects from the launch in an orbit measuring 19,045 by 19,150 kilometers with an inclination of 64.8 degrees, McDowell said.
“Space Force has cataloged two objects from yesterday’s Soyuz launch, in a 19045 x 19150 km x 64.8 deg orbit, consistent with analyst’s expectations that this was a GLONASS navigation satellite mission,” McDowell wrote on X.
The launch took place at 2:40 a.m. UTC on August 24 using a Soyuz-2.1b rocket with a Fregat upper stage, lifting off from Site 43/3 at Plesetsk in northern Russia. Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed only that the flight carried a defense ministry satellite into orbit, without naming the payload. McDowell said the satellite is likely to carry the designation Kosmos-2619.
Russia has stopped publicly announcing designations for its military satellites in recent years, leaving outside trackers to identify payloads based on orbital parameters and launch patterns. The orbit McDowell described matches the medium Earth orbit used by GLONASS satellites, Russia’s satellite navigation system comparable to the U.S. GPS and European Galileo constellations.
Some tracking sites had listed the mission in advance as the likely launch of a Glonass-K1 satellite, the 19th in that series, based on notice-to-airmen filings pointing to a possible August launch window. Glonass-K1 satellites weigh about 935 kilograms (2,062 pounds), operate unpressurized, and are designed for a 10-year service life, improving on earlier GLONASS generations in accuracy and power consumption.
Confirmation of the payload’s identity is based on orbital analysis rather than official Russian disclosure. RussianSpaceWeb, which tracks Russian space launches, noted that Russia’s pattern of navigation warnings and debris impact zone closures in the weeks before the launch was consistent with prior GLONASS missions from Plesetsk, though the outlet stopped short of confirming the payload without direct orbital data.
Russia has continued modernizing its GLONASS constellation with Glonass-K and Glonass-K2 satellites, the newest generations in the system. Russian space officials have said they plan to begin launching a separate cluster of high-orbital GLONASS-V satellites in 2026 and 2027, intended to improve navigation accuracy over Russian territory by as much as a factor of four once the cluster becomes fully operational around 2030.
The payload’s exact identity remains based on orbital analysis by independent trackers rather than official Russian disclosure.
Russia’s satellite launches from Plesetsk this year have had mixed results. Two satellites from the second Rassvet batch, a 16-spacecraft cluster of Bureau 1440 broadband satellites launched July 19 from the same cosmodrome, are heading toward reentry after never performing orbit-raising maneuvers

At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
07:05:43 UTC
16:05:43 KST

At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals.
The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.
A statement by the hospital administration confirmed that 14 newborn babies in the intensive care unit (ICU) died in the fire.
Dr Aneeza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson, told the Dawn newspaper that 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that one baby was saved by a doctor.
Women who had just given birth had to run down several flights of stairs and climb out of windows and down ladders to escape.
The health minister, Mustafa Kamal, said many of the babies were in incubators or on oxygen, and that the oxygen canisters made the fire worse.
Investigators said the fire was started by a faulty air conditioning unit, which exploded inside the nursery where newborn infants under intensive care were sleeping.
Among the witnesses was Sardar Atti ur Rehman, 38, whose wife had given birth to a girl at the hospital the previous day. He had been sleeping at the hospital and rushed into the maternity ward as the fire was spreading, desperately looking for his wife and child.
He described scenes of panic as thick smoke filled the ward. “I could not see my family including my newborn baby in the room but kept searching,” he said. “My heart was heavy.” He later discovered they had both escaped the fire alive.
He said he saw a woman laid out on a stretcher and helped to drag her out of the ward, but other women refused to leave as they cried out for their babies.
“I saw a mother who was crying and screaming for her child who was admitted inside the ICU,” he said. “I tried to enter the ICU but failed as the smoke was too thick. I could not see anything and I was facing issues to breathe. I begged her that you need to save yourself and we will look for the child later.”
Rehman said there were few staff on the ward at the time of the fire and that the families were left to fend for themselves.
One father at the scene, whose newborn son was among the dead, claimed that there had been a lock on the door of the nursery and that no staff had been present to unlock it. The windows of the nursery were smashed by rescuers as they tried to reach the babies.
Sohail Ashraf, the Islamabad chief commissioner, said the emergency call was made just before 7am and rescue and police teams quickly reached the scene.
The hospital administration said: “The fire was immediately brought under control and the children were immediately shifted to the intensive care unit.”
Alamzaib Khan, 26, was also among those who tried to run into the ward as it burned. His wife had given birth to a baby girl two days ago and she was still in the hospital recovering from a C-section, while his baby had already been taken home.
“I was sleeping on the pavement when I heard people screaming and wailing,” he said. “I ran towards the ICU and children’s ward and I saw my wife while climbing down a ladder.”
After checking on his wife, he tried to help with the rescue of others. “The moment I approached the children’s ward, I couldn’t see anything because the smoke was so thick,” he said. “I tried to go inside but it was not possible.”
“People were crying, screaming and asking for help. Women from the operation room had to run for their lives,” he said. “Women were in pain themselves but crying and begging everyone to help them to rescue their children. It’s hard to describe this terrible moment.”
The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation into the incident, which was one of the deadliest hospital fires in years.
“Such a situation involving children is irreparable,” Sharif said. “Those responsible should be identified, and the strictest action should be taken.”
Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, expressed condolences to the families of the newborn babies. In a statement, he said the loss of lives was heartbreaking.
Fires in large buildings such as factories and shopping centres are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and lax enforcement of building codes.

Ukraine has been hitting Wildberries facilities since mid-July and broadened its strategy in recent days to include the retailer's main rival, Ozon.
More than 20 Wildberries and Ozon warehouses have been attacked with at least 1.9 million square metres of warehouse space severely damaged by fire, according to Reuters analysis of satellite imagery.
The pair dominate one of the fastest-growing parts of the Russian economy, which is otherwise close to stagnation after 4-1/2 years of war in Ukraine.
In neighbouring Lipetsk region, a man and a 14-year-old were killed in a fire lit by a falling drone, while a woman was killed in a drone attack in Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, local authorities said on Telegram.
Both Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly denied targeting civilians since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. REUTERS

NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Wednesday reiterated its plan to hold a march in Delhi on September 5, saying three of the four demands that led it to call off its protest on July 25 were still pending.In a post on X, the party said it had withdrawn the protest a month ago after receiving assurances that all four demands would be met.It said the pending demands were compensation for the families of students, withdrawal of FIRs and no action against student protesters, and an apology from the Rapid Action Force (RAF) and Delhi Police.
“Everything will be remembered” the party said in its post, while referring to its archive titled “Black Monday Record”, which it said documents the crackdown on protesters, including the use of lathis, tear gas and pellet guns and alleged assaults by unbadged personnel.
CJP also said the archive records 11 unanswered questions that it has raised as part of its demand for accountability.“With each passing day, these questions become harder to ignore and the demand for answers grows stronger,” the party said.
CJP plans India Gate to Police HQ march on September 5

Türkiye’s state-owned Halkbank secured an additional $1.1 billion from international markets following the dismissal of a criminal case against the lender in the United States, the bank said on Aug. 25.
In a statement to Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform (KAP), Halkbank said the conclusion of the case in its favor had improved its access to overseas funding.
