It was Dolly Parton's proudest legacy. Now an Australian town must keep it alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
06:06:58 UTC
15:06:58 KST

In Brief
- Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has delivered more than two million books across Australia.
- But those in regional areas say more financial help is needed to keep the initiative alive.
In the regional NSW city of Tamworth, more than 3,000 children are reading more books because of Dolly Parton — a mark of Australia's connection to the legendary country singer, actor and philanthropist that runs deeper than one might initially think.
Parton died on Wednesday morning at 80. Tributes have poured in from around the world, but in Tamworth, the loss is more personal.
The city, dubbed the country music capital of Australia, holds an official sister-city bond with Parton's adopted hometown of Nashville and hosted Parton herself on her last Australian tour in 2014.
"It's an incredible nod to us that she would come here when most stars are looking for the big 70,000-seater auditoriums, whereas ours is 5,000 seats," Cheryl Brown, from the Tamworth Country Music Festival, told SBS News.
"So for her to come here, she certainly validated us as the country music capital and that saw us being an important part of country music here in Australia."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But it's her gift of the Imagination Library program, one of Parton's most personal philanthropic projects, that has really transformed Tamworth.
Founded in 1995 as a tribute to her illiterate father, Dolly Parton's Imagination Library is a free book-gifting program — now running across the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Ireland, and Australia — that mails new, age-appropriate books to children from birth until they turn five, completely free of charge.
It has gifted more than 300 million books to children since it started 31 years ago. In Australia, more than two million of those books have been delivered to 151,000 children across 480 communities since its launch here in 2013.
Dolly's 'gold star' pupil
In Tamworth, where the program has run since 2019, its ambassador Lisa Rennie says it has fundamentally changed how children relate to reading and literacy.
"Children from birth to the age of five are eligible to receive the books, which are chosen by qualified speech pathologists and early literacy teachers," Rennie told SBS News.
"There are currently about 3,500 children on average on the program in the Tamworth region."
Since 2019, more than 98 per cent of children born in Tamworth have been enrolled.
"We've been classed the gold star program," Rennie said.
Families sign up at no cost, ensuring accessibility for those experiencing disadvantage — books are posted to each home each month, and caregivers are also given reading guidance sheets to help foster lifelong reading in families.
About 70 per cent of those books are by Australian authors and 10 per cent by First Nations authors.
Research from United Way Australia, which delivers the program in Australia, found children involved in the program in Tamworth were being read to more often, for longer, and had more books in the home than the average Australian child.
They were also significantly more likely to demonstrate emerging literacy skills, with Rennie expecting that, as graduates of the program enter primary school, they will show an increased level of literacy reflected in NAPLAN results in the region.
"Children in our region are being read to more often, for longer, and if they're on the program for the full five years, they're receiving a whole library of 60 books that they can cherish," she said.
"There's more people visiting our local libraries, which is fantastic, which is purely as a result of this program," she adds.
United Way CEO Dr Lyndsey McKee says Parton started the program as a response to her own upbringing in a family that experienced poverty.
"Her father was illiterate and she was one of 12, so she didn't have access to opportunities that many children have," McKee told SBS News. "With that lived experience, she really wanted to bring storytelling to the world."
"It's a huge legacy beyond her singing ... she's such an incredible philanthropist."
Keeping the legacy going
In lieu of flowers, Parton's family has asked for donations to be made to the Imagination Library.
It's a request that carries extra weight in Australia: the Imagination Library is the only program of its kind in the country, and it could sit in a precarious financial position, particularly amid Parton's death.
The program operates through a shared funding model with The Dollywood Foundation, Parton's charity organisation, and United Way Australia.
But the costs of running the program are left to the community.
"United Way send the books out, but we arrange the funding here locally with fundraisers and sponsorships from local businesses, council, local clubs, and even individuals reach out to give the gift of literacy," Rennie explained.
In July, US singer-songwriter Taylor Swift and her husband Travis Kelce donated US$2 million ($2.78 million) to the Imagination Library as part of a wider round of wedding-week giving — but that kind of support doesn't necessarily flow through to the grassroots costs faced by groups like Tamworth's.
Those costs add up. Each book delivered costs $9 per child per month.
In somewhere like Tamworth, that equates to just under $400,000 a year required to keep every eligible child enrolled.
McKee said there's an "absolute need" for Parton's program in Australia.
"Twenty per cent of children are starting school developmentally vulnerable. One in three children in the recent NAPLAN results were not meeting the reading benchmark."
"The evidence says this program works.
"We want to use this important moment to actually do more and bring this program to more children and communities in the years ahead."
Brown says Dolly will "be on the streets of Tamworth forever" as a result of the program.
"It's a wonderful gift that Dolly has given to us here in Tamworth, and we will certainly endeavour to carry that on forever," she said.
Rennie says it's even more important that donations continue to flow through the program following Parton's death.
"The Tamworth region will be forever grateful for Dolly Parton introducing this program to Australia," she said.
"But I think now more than ever, this program needs to continue because it'll be in her legacy.
"We need the financial support to ensure that it does continue."

Britons face highest price cap in three years as energy bills rise 4% from October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
06:04:34 UTC
15:04:34 KST

Millions of British households will face the highest energy charges in three years this winter after months of rising market prices pushed up the government’s price cap for the second time in three months.
Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap, after climbing 13% at the start of July to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the war on Iran.
The regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, said the new cap for about 22m households was equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical household’s gas and electricity use, up from £1,663 for the July to September period.
The cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to the energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872.
Andy Burnham said rising energy bills were “difficult for people and I recognise that”. Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the prime minister said: “It’s why, within days of taking office, I announced that we would remove VAT off electricity bills … We’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term.”
The government faces growing pressure to tackle the UK’s energy costs, which are some of the highest in the developed world, after its pre-election promise in 2024 to cut energy bills by £300 a year by 2030.
Clare Moriarty, the chief executive of Citizens Advice, said the rising price cap was “another sign of the relentless erosion of living standards across the country: energy bills are simply too high, prices leapfrog incomes, and debt levels continue to grow.”
From October, the typical household using a standard tariff will pay £350 a year more than in 2024 under the price cap. About a third of households buy their energy via fixed-rate deals, which will not be affected.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said bills were being driven up by the Iran war and the government would “keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills”.
Energy market prices are the largest single cost within energy bills. They will represent £812 of the average energy bill under the price cap from October – 78% higher than before the Ukraine crisis began in early 2022.
However, the cost of upgrading Great Britain’s energy networks is rising too and will make up £417 of the annual household bill from October – an 85% rise over the same period.
Fahnbulleh told LBC radio that upgrading the UK’s energy infrastructure was “not a choice” because if the government failed to invest, no one “would forgive us”. She said: “We absolutely need to do that.”
The increase in energy costs has reignited calls for the government to help vulnerable households. There have been repeated calls for it to fund extra measures by raising the windfall taxes on profits made by energy companies and by introducing a windfall tax on banks.
“It’s plain common sense,” said Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary. “Banks are raking it in … they can well afford to pay more tax to ease the pressure on working people.”
The regulator calculated the average annual bill of £1,723 based on the estimated energy use of a typical household. Since July it has assumed lower annual energy use than in previous years because the high cost of energy has forced many people to use less gas and electricity. Under the previous calculations, the price cap would have climbed to £1,940.69 from October.
More than a third of households have begun turning down the temperature on their washing machine and radiators in empty rooms since 2023, according to research commissioned by the End Fuel Poverty Coalition.
Meanwhile, about a fifth of households have begun going to bed early during colder weather in order to keep warm, or are heating only one room to save energy, the survey found.
From October, the unit rate for electricity will rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.32p, while gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.97p. However, the actual household bill will depend on how much each consumes.
Gas standing charges, which are paid daily whether you use energy or not, will rise from 29.04p to 29.68p, while the daily standing charge for electricity will fall from 57.19p to 54.83p because of the government’s VAT cut for electricity bills.
The increased unit rates and other costs will take combined energy charges to their highest level since July 2023.

Top official says Iran, Oman have agreed new temporary route in Hormuz

Iran, Oman agree on new temporary route in Hormuz
Kazem Gharibabadi says Iran and Oman had agreed the route’s entry would run through Iranian territorial waters, with part of the exit also passing through them.
A top Iranian official says Iran and Oman have agreed on a new temporary route for shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, but insisted that the waterway will not reopen until the United States fulfils its commitments under an interim peace deal signed in June.
The remarks by Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, came on Tuesday, after Iran and Oman’s top diplomats held talks in Tehran to finalise the details of a phased framework for managing the strait.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Sanctions or missiles? How Gulf will view Trump’s new Iran approach
- list 2 of 2Iran, Oman discuss temporary shipping lane through Strait of Hormuz
Iran and Oman, both coastal nations on the strait, have been in on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic waterway, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the US-Israel war on Tehran began in February.
Most shipping in the strait has been shut down since then.
Gharibabadi, speaking on state television, said Iran and Oman had agreed the new route’s entry “would be through our territorial waters, and part of the exit route would also be through our territorial waters”.
The transit corridor would be seven miles (11.3km) wide, he said.
“The agreed-upon transit route with Oman is a temporary route,” he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, in Tehran to discuss the temporary navigation corridor as well as a project to clear mines from the strait, according to a joint statement.
Albusaidi said on X he hoped the countries would “soon announce” the corridor, adding that “future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course.”
Technical talks are planned to develop a long-term arrangement, including mechanisms for information sharing and navigational and security services, according to the statement.
Mines in Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz became a flashpoint after Tehran responded to the US-Israel war by closing the waterway. It then announced a new shipping route through its territorial waters, bypassing the internationally recognised Traffic Separation Scheme adopted by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in 1968. Tehran said that route had been mined.
Then in June, when Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to end the war, Oman and the IMO announced a new transit corridor in the Strait of Hormuz – backed by the US – that hugged the Omani coast.
Iran said the so-called southern route violated the MoU and launched attacks on ships using the corridor, resulting in the collapse of the interim deal.
Diplomatic efforts towards a broader peace deal have since stalled, and passage through the strait remains dangerous. An oil tanker was disabled by an unidentified projectile on Tuesday near Oman’s Ash Shishah, close to the strait’s entrance, the United Kingdom’s maritime trade watchdog said.
Gharibabadi, in his comments on Tuesday, said Iran would not consider the strait open despite the agreement with Oman.
He also dismissed a claim by US President Donald Trump that all mines had been cleared from the strait’s international waters, saying it was “only aimed at calming the markets”. He warned that US mine-detection vessels would become “very good targets” if they entered the area.
Gharibabadi insisted the US must fulfil its commitments under the MoU – including sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian assets – if it wants a return to the diplomatic track.
He also urged countries to resist US pressure over sanctions on Iran.
Trump had announced last week the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Iran, and threatened sanctions against any country that does business with it.
“We are urging countries not to succumb to American pressure regarding the sanctions that Washington wants to impose on us,” Gharibabadi said, adding that Washington was “mistaken about its ability to enforce its sanctions against our neighbours”.
He said an earlier US sanctions campaign under Trump had failed to achieve its goals and predicted new measures would meet the same fate.
“The new American sanctions are doomed to failure, and we have our own methods to counter them,” he added.

Kremlin stated that the CIA director visited Moscow for contacts between security services
Kyiv • UNN
CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. The purpose of the trip was contacts between the security services.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow for contacts between security services, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, The Washington Post writes, citing UNN.
Details
According to the publication, citing people familiar with the matter, CIA Director John Ratcliffe was in Moscow on Tuesday in a rare visit by the head of a U.S. intelligence agency, amid the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.
U.S. officials did not announce Ratcliffe's trip, but publicly available flight-tracking data recorded a U.S. government transport aircraft traveling from Joint Base Andrews on the outskirts of Washington to Russia's capital. The aircraft departed Moscow approximately eight and a half hours later, according to Flightradar24 tracking data.
Spokespeople for the CIA, the Pentagon, and the U.S. Air Force declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
It was not immediately clear what the purpose of the trip was or whether any other senior U.S. officials were part of the delegation.
Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow coincided with a tense period in relations between the United States and Russia. Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes against each other's territory, and there is no end to the war in sight, the publication writes. Some analysts warn that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin may resort to escalation through a military "probe" against the Baltic countries or other NATO members, which could lead to a new crisis.
As the publication notes, "the two superpowers are on opposite sides of the conflict involving Iran. Iran is Moscow's most important ally in the Middle East, and Russia has provided Tehran with intelligence on the location of U.S. military assets in the region." On Monday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced a major campaign of sanctions and diplomatic pressure aimed at strangling Iran's economy.
The Kremlin remained silent about the visit. Asked about the purpose of Ratcliffe's visit, spokesman Dmitry Peskov told The Post that it involved "contacts between security services" and declined to provide any additional details.
Earlier on Tuesday, he said that the Kremlin had no information about a U.S. military aircraft that had arrived at Moscow's Vnukovo International Airport. Russia did not plan to meet with representatives of the U.S. administration this week, he said.
CBS News had previously reported on Ratcliffe's visit to Russia.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe departed for Moscow aboard a C-1725.08.26, 17:25 • 5316 views
The last known visit by a CIA director to Moscow took place in November 2021, when William J. Burns, who headed the agency under President Joe Biden, warned Putin and his top aides not to attack Ukraine and clearly explained what the consequences would be. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion within a few weeks.
The U.S. aircraft that arrived in Moscow, a C-17A Globemaster III, is a heavy transport aircraft operated by the U.S. Department of Defense. The aircraft is particularly valuable for confidential diplomatic visits, allowing leaders to bring a specialized complement of vehicles, electronic equipment, and support personnel, the publication writes.
A second U.S. Air Force aircraft, a C-40B, also departed from Joint Base Andrews and landed in Riga several hours after the C-17A arrived in the country.
Publicly available flight-tracking data do not show the C-40B on a subsequent flight to Moscow. The aircraft is a modified business jet used to transport senior government officials.
A video shared on social media Tuesday and geolocated by The Washington Post showed a motorcade, some of whose vehicles had red diplomatic license plates, traveling east along Novy Arbat in central Moscow near a building belonging to Russia's armed forces.
The C-17A departed Moscow shortly after 5:30 p.m. local time and landed in Riga a little more than an hour later, according to Flightradar24 data.

Walking on the edge: a three-day hike along Cumbria’s rugged, overlooked coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
06:00:35 UTC
15:00:35 KST

What’s the edgiest region in the UK? I don’t mean in the sense of sketchy or fashionable, but where on the map of these four nations feels most at the margins of everywhere else? For my money, the north Cumbrian coast is a strong contender. Hemmed in by the Lake District fells on one side and the Solway Firth and Irish Sea on the other, this strip of towns and villages, farms and nature reserves, clinging to the low-lying littoral, has been battling nature, weather, geology and geography throughout its history.
Coastal erosion is part of the challenge. Like the railway navvies before them, the planners and builders of the England Coast Path (ECP) have done sterling work at plotting a viable footpath and shoring it up. But there are and always will be sections that are compromised and even impassable. I chose a section that would take three days, walking southwards, and my final destination, St Bees, was only reachable via a diversion. It’s all part of the adventure, and we’re lucky to have the ECP as a national trail, as it means issues and obstacles on the English coast will usually be promptly addressed.
I began my walk at Maryport, a natural choice as it’s where the Cumbrian Coast Line, travelling south from Carlisle, meets the seashore. I resisted the urge to jump off the train and set off walking, instead taking time to look around. I’m glad I did. It’s a lovely place, in a ramshackle way, and quite fascinating. The Romans, who called it Alauna, built a fort here; the Senhouse museum boasts Britain’s largest collection of Roman altars and inscriptions found at a single site.
An LS Lowry trail takes in places he painted. I followed it from the church beside the quay, up the steep town steps, and along some of the streets he worked into his compositions. Information panels celebrated less well-known, similarly gifted local painters: Sheila Fell, from nearby Aspatria, and Percy Kelly, born in Workington, known for his thick lines and dark landscapes, who played for Workington AFC under Bill Shanklyand, in later life, became Roberta Penelope.
Out on the coast path, I took in my first views of Dumfriesshire to the north. There were few walkers on the empty strand. At Flimby, the “path” was just a line of kelp on a pebble beach, bordered by flowering sea kale. Clouds of cabbage white and small blue butterflies sprang up as I walked. West Cumbria is the only area where the latter can be found in northern England. An unfamiliar call and a flutter of white wings sent me to my birder app. It was a pair of sandwich terns – an “amber” status bird on the RSPB website.
There were patches of heather and rosehip, occasional dunes and a few birds. Swallows picked off flies. Herring gulls shouted. Black-headed gulls planed. Carrot-beaked oyster catchers fluted their alarm calls. On my left, above the marram grass, I could see industrial plants and old workers’ terraces. The Cumbria coast is more Morrissey lyric than Countryfile fantasy. Boulders have been arrayed to protect against storms. Two teenage girls bronzed (or pinked) themselves on rocks in the midday sun.
Workington welcomed me, after seven miles. I’d been here before, for a “Where tourists seldom tread” feature for this newspaper, but it felt new arriving on foot and from the shore. Workington looks as its name sounds. Decades of industry have made the people steely and friendly. I spent the night above town at the Hunday Manor hotel, which has superb views over the coast and back to the fells.
The next day’s walk to Whitehaven was the longest at about 12 miles. The opening stretch, back down into Workington, was a pleasant surprise. From above town, I’d noted fuel silos, warehouses and industrial estates, but around the harbour the land was all grassy knolls. I could see Scafell Pike rising up to the south-east, and Scotland shimmering to the north. In the distance were cliffs and a wide inlet – my destination, Whitehaven.
I undertook this walk during the the UK’s fifth heatwave, one of the driest, warmest periods in living memory in these parts. As the mercury rose, I climbed up on to the clifftops, pausing at the Howe, a hill originally created from industrial slag, to gulp down water and look up at a 3-metre steel and wood crucifix put up by a local man in memory of his wife. From here, there was a messy section with scant waymarking, but I eventually came to Harrington, a bonny little suburban village, with kite flyers on the bluff and smart little terraces marching up the side streets. I ate lunch and watched trains come and go; they’re regular enough that you can always cut short a walk and hop on one.
Up on the cliffs again, I passed a large windfarm, and approached the village of Parton on a bridleway that sliced through sheep fields. The air was filled with the hairy seeds of thorns, bursting in the heat.
A path beneath dramatic sandstone cliffs guided me into Whitehaven. One of northern England’s loveliest towns, it has all the amenities a tired walker needs. But while it caters to visitors, it hasn’t sold its entire soul to tourism – which is the case with some Lakeland towns.
Whitehaven used to be an industrial powerhouse, shipping tobacco, coal, ceramics, iron ore, limestone and textiles, and it was the fifth most active British port involved in the transatlantic slave trade. The older streets are lined with crumbling mansions. Victorian-era lighthouses and a chimney known as the Candlestick are unmissable landmarks; between these are ghostly traces of tenements, coastal batteries and long-silenced engine houses. Silting and larger ships led to the town being eclipsed by the deepwater ports of Liverpool and Glasgow. Shipbuilding moved to Belfast. Nostalgia, grit, grandeur and decay all mingle in Whitehaven’s collective maritime memory.
I swotted up on Whitehaven’s layered history at The Beacon, one of the UK’s finest and most rejuvenating town museums. Underneath the museum, the Howling Wolf Bakery and cafe serves delicious cakes, toasties and coffee. There are great restaurants all over town – I can recommend The Peddler, in the former bus station, and Zest on the waterside – and every kind of pub, chippy and cafe.
The Edge hotel, which opened last October, will bolster Whitehaven’s ambitions to compete with the Lake District. It was created as a base for coastal activities; the harbour commission, which owns the property, is committed to supporting walkers, cyclists, musicians and community groups. There are 16 ensuite rooms looking out over the marina – an attractive mix of historic quays and jetties (known as tongues), and modern add-ons. The Edge’s irregular polyhedral shape is striking and yet apt. Rust-coloured, it looks post-industrial but also like a storm barrier. Its air-source underfloor heating and solar panels are in keeping with a region famed for renewable energy.
An alternative route was in place for the final leg, with erosion on the footpath forcing me inland. But I was too elated to be bothered by a minor diversion. My coast walk (23 miles direct, but considerably more with walks around towns and hikes to/from the Workington hotel) culminated at St Bees Head with views of spectacular coves, secret beaches and sheer cliffs.
Where the ECP crossed paths with the recently inaugurated Coast to Coast National Trail, I met a few walkers, Aussies rather than Brits, all heading inland for Ennerdale and Helvellyn, there to encounter crowds and join queues. My only company was fulmars, cormorants, herring gulls, ravens and kestrels. When I came across a little colony of kittiwakes nesting on tiny ledges, I decided it was time to sit down too, and soak up the gentle sea breezes and the wide, all-encompassing silence.
The trip was supported by Cumbria Tourism, Avanti, Northern and Stagecoach buses. Stagecoach has DayRider and 3-day Explorer passes. Doubles at The Edge from £117 B&B and at Hunday Manor Country House hotel from £125 B&B.

Text description provided by the architects. In Bramois, on the outskirts of the city of Sion, this two-family home project challenges the typology of dual-unit housing that is currently widespread in low-density development zones. It contrasts the typology of the standardized, cubic block with an "open" structural system. By using a dense core to free up the periphery, the project explores two antithetical yet complementary ways of connecting to the ground: immersion and overhang.

Amid heatwaves in Europe, at least 35,000 additional deaths recorded

Amid heatwaves in Europe, at least 35,000 additional deaths recorded
Kyiv • UNN
This summer, heat claimed at least 35,000 lives in Europe. The highest number of deaths was recorded in Germany, France and Spain.
At least 35,000 more people than normally expected died in Europe this summer during four record-breaking heatwaves in a row, according to incomplete data obtained from almost half of the continent, The Guardian reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to preliminary data, excess mortality in just the three largest EU countries — Germany, France and Spain — has already exceeded 25,000, and experts say the death toll will rise significantly after the overall data for August are compiled.
Successive heatwaves in Western Europe have broken historical temperature records at hundreds of weather stations since May, while France recorded the hottest day averaged across the country in the entire history of observations.
Records were broken for three consecutive days in Germany at the end of June, when temperatures exceeded 40°C at 46 stations, while Spain experienced sustained highs above 42°C. Scientists say that human-caused global warming is making such extreme events more frequent and intense.
The highest number of deaths has been recorded in Germany, where approximately 14,000 heat-related deaths from 6 April to 9 August were reported at the end of last week. The health agency of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI) reported that 9,600 people died in just one week, from 22 to 28 June.
Systematically collected excess-mortality data across the EU, available since 2008, show that the only other summer week when a higher level of additional deaths was recorded was July 2022, when Covid-19 was still active.
This summer was the worst on record in Germany for the number of heat-related deaths since records began. The previous high in the EU's most populous country was 8,900 in 2018. According to the RKI, the number of heat-related deaths during a typical summer is often below 2,000.
Data from the Carlos III Health Institute's mortality-monitoring system indicate that 4947 deaths in Spain can be attributed to heat from May through this week, making 2026 Spain's worst year on record for heat-related deaths, surpassing the 4520 deaths recorded in 2022.
A final determination of the cause of death can take weeks or even months, and many countries have not yet released data even for the beginning of August. Karl Lauterbach, Germany's former health minister, said last week that the data published so far would probably prove to be underestimates.
In France, where more than 500 weather stations recorded temperatures above 40°C and, at one point, 98% of the country was under a heat alert, the national health agency said last week that the number of excess deaths "from all causes" from the end of May to 22 July was 7300. August data were not yet available, and the initial figures were based on electronic death certificates, which account for only 80% of total mortality, the statement said.
In Italy, modelling shows that 2700 more people than usual died between 22 and 28 June alone, while epidemiologists said that the total number of heat-related deaths in the country would probably be between 5000 and 8000 by the time they were officially registered.
Other European countries that have already reported excess deaths include the United Kingdom, where the health agency said in July that its modelling showed that the heatwaves in May and June had caused 2877 heat-related deaths in England.
Belgium said its preliminary data showed that mortality rose by 39% between 18 and 29 June, equivalent to 1222 additional deaths, while the Netherlands said that at least 900 more people than usual died between 22 June and 5 July.
According to rapid modeling cited by the European Commission, 1,070 more people than usual died in Poland during the heatwave at the end of June, while data from the Swiss health authority indicate 220 cases of excess mortality linked to the heat during the same week.
Preliminary data from Luxembourg, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria and Denmark indicate approximately 40 cases of excess mortality in each of these countries. Agence France-Presse calculated that temperatures exceeded 40°C this summer in areas where more than 80 million Europeans live.
The World Health Organization said in May that heat-related mortality in the European region had increased by more than 30% over the past 20 years and was highly likely to rise significantly as a result of the climate crisis and an aging population.

More than 50 children die in diphtheria outbreak in northwestern Nigeria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:50:32 UTC
14:50:32 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
More than 50 children have died from a diphtheria outbreak in Rano Local Government Area of Nigeria’s northwestern Kano state, a state lawmaker said Tuesday, urging authorities to step up efforts to contain the disease.
 
Ibrahim Malami, who represents Rano Constituency in the Kano State House of Assembly, raised the alarm during a motion of urgent public importance, saying the outbreak had severely affected communities in Rurum Ward, including Rurum A, Rurum B and Sabuwar Kaura.
He said the local government’s medical department had launched emergency measures, while his office had provided medicines to support the response.
 
Malami called on Kano Gov. Abba Kabir Yusuf and state health authorities to deploy additional medical personnel, medicines and other emergency assistance to the affected communities.
 
“We want to inform the Governor and the Commissioner for Health to send further emergency aid to the region because the disease has spread heavily in that area,” Malami said. 
 
Another lawmaker, Usman Abubakar Tasiu, representing Kiru Constituency, warned that the outbreak had spread beyond Rano, with cases also reported in Kwanar Dangora, Garin Dangora and Yelwa communities in neighboring Kiru Local Government Area.
 
The state Assembly subsequently adopted a resolution urging immediate government intervention and tasked its health committee with coordinating with the state Health Ministry to ensure emergency measures are implemented in the affected areas.
 
Diphtheria is a highly contagious bacterial infection that can cause severe illness and death, particularly among unvaccinated children. Nigeria’s Centre for Disease Control and Prevention advises parents to ensure children receive the recommended three doses of the pentavalent vaccine, which protects against diphtheria, at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of age.
Nigeria has faced recurring diphtheria outbreaks in recent years, with Kano among the states hardest hit. The World Health Organization said Kano accounted for the majority of suspected cases during a major nationwide outbreak in 2023.
The latest deaths underscore ongoing challenges in vaccination coverage, disease surveillance and access to timely treatment as Nigerian authorities work to contain diphtheria outbreaks.

The antisemitism royal commission hearings are over. What happens now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:45:05 UTC
14:45:05 KST

In brief
- Commissioner Virginia Bell will now analyse evidence and submissions before writing her final report.
- Her recommendations could shape Australia's response to antisemitism and social cohesion.
After more than 340 witnesses were called to give evidence across 62 days, the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion hearings have concluded.
The inquiry was established in response to the Bondi Beach terror attack, in which 15 people were killed during a Hanukkah celebration last December. It was tasked with investigating the circumstances of the attack, the impact of antisemitism on Jewish Australians and how social cohesion can be promoted.
The ninth and final block of hearings concluded on Wednesday, after examining how social cohesion could be understood, measured and promoted.
What happens next?
The inquiry will now turn to preparation of a final report, authored by commissioner Virginia Bell, who will summarise submissions, analyse evidence, establish facts and make recommendations.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
As with the interim report released in April, some material may remain confidential because of national security concerns or to avoid prejudicing criminal proceedings.
The sole surviving alleged gunman, Naveed Akram, has been charged with terror and murder offences, in a case that is separate from the commission. He has yet to enter a plea.
The commission does not determine criminal guilt or impose criminal penalties. It can, however, refer matters to law enforcement or prosecuting authorities.
Its recommendations will be considered by governments, which will decide whether and how to implement them.
Bell was due to submit her final report by 14 December — the one-year anniversary of the shooting — but she has requested a four-day deadline extension.
That request was in response to concern from Australia's Jewish community that the report coming out on the day of the anniversary of the attack would be a distraction from memorials.
How has the Jewish community responded?
Leaders of Australia's Jewish community expressed gratitude for those who gave evidence at the commission, often at a personal cost.
The commission heard directly from roughly 14,000 community members through evidence submitted in person and in writing, Bell said.
Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief Peter Werheim said the community had put its heart and soul into the commission.
"Hundreds of people have told the truth about their everyday experience of antisemitism, and thousands more have provided detailed accounts through written submissions. We thank everyone who has made a contribution. The commissioner has a great deal of evidence to weigh, and we trust her to do that carefully."

Berk Kutay Gokmen
26 August 2026•Update: 26 August 2026
The death toll from a catastrophic magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia has risen to 331, according to an updated report released Tuesday by the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).
The agency said 240 people remain missing, while 4,449 have been injured and 364 people have been rescued alive. In total, 406,273 people from 188,034 families have been officially registered as affected across 494 municipalities in 16 of Colombia's 32 departments.
The earthquake, which struck at 7.34 am local time (1234GMT) on Aug. 10, was the most powerful seismic event to hit Colombia this century. Its epicenter was located near San Jose del Palmar in the Pacific department of Choco at an intermediate depth of roughly 110 kilometers (68 miles).
The disaster has caused extensive damage to homes and public infrastructure across western Colombia. According to figures provided by the UNGRD on Tuesday, 33,275 homes have been completely destroyed, while 185,889 others have sustained damage.
Health, education and essential services have also been severely affected. The UNGRD reported damage to 376 health centers, 3,819 educational facilities and 4,337 community facilities.
Transport and water infrastructure have suffered significant disruption, with 440 roads, 74 vehicle bridges, 17 pedestrian bridges, five airports and 119 water-supply systems affected.
The earthquake has also taken a toll on animals, with 2,149 affected and 2,949 rescued, according to the latest assessment.
The UNGRD said the figures remain preliminary and are being consolidated by local authorities and operational agencies as emergency response and damage assessments continue.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) —The Ministry of Agriculture has launched a lottery offering 30,000 NT$300 (US$9.40) pet vouchers and 100 health-care packages worth up to NT$3,000 each to encourage owners to register their dogs and cats, per UDN.
The ministry announced the Pet Login program on Tuesday at a press conference, calling on owners to complete pet registration and ensure their animal and owner information is up to date. Taiwan has approximately 1.46 million domestic dogs and 1.74 million domestic cats, according to the ministry's latest nationwide survey.
Under the Animal Protection Act, dogs and cats must be registered and implanted with microchips by the time they are 4 months old. Owners who fail to comply can be fined between NT$3,000 and NT$15,000.
Pet registration has been mandatory for dogs for decades, while cats were added to the list of animals requiring registration, with enforcement starting Jan. 1. The ministry said dog microchipping has increased steadily, rising from 61.84% in 2021 to 75.47% in 2025. The rate for domestic cats rose from 49.83% in 2023 to 63.75% in 2025.
Department of Animal Welfare Director Chiang Wen-chuan (江文全) said many owners regard their dogs and cats as companions and family members. Registration provides identification information that can improve the chances of recovering lost animals while helping authorities implement measures such as vaccinations and sterilization. Chiang added that source management is the key to controlling stray dog and cat populations, per UDN.
Under the lottery rules, owners of registered dogs or cats can participate from Sept. 1 to Sept. 30 by logging onto the website, confirming their pet and personal information, and completing the online lottery registration. Each owner can enter only one dog or cat, and each animal can be entered only once.
The ministry will conduct the lottery through a livestream on its YouTube channel on Oct. 2. Physical vouchers are scheduled to be sent by registered mail by the end of October.
The pet vouchers can be used at participating stores to purchase pet-related food and supplies. The ministry said its program includes nine pet-related businesses and 14 agricultural and fisheries associations, with a total of 436 participating outlets as of its announcement Tuesday. The vouchers cannot be exchanged for cash or change and must be used by Dec. 10.
The 100 healthcare package winners can take their dogs or cats to licensed public or private veterinary clinics for health checks and medical services. After treatment, winners can submit receipts and related documents to apply for reimbursement of eligible expenses, up to NT$3,000, by Dec. 10.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) inspected flood-control efforts in Pingtung County on Tuesday, backing a proposed NT$13.6 billion (US$427 million) project to reduce flooding along a section of Provincial Highway 1.
Cho visited the Dahu Drainage Improvement Project in Linluo Township, where the Pingtung County Government has proposed a sixth-phase expansion to improve drainage along the highway and nearby areas. Cho was accompanied by Pingtung County Magistrate Chou Chun-mi (周春米) and Legislators Hsu Fu-kuei (徐富癸) and Su Ching-chuan (蘇清泉), per CNA.

The county government has therefore proposed the sixth phase of the Dahu Drainage Improvement Project. Pingtung County asked the central government to support the project.
Cho said the government has moved on from a previous eight-year, NT$80 billion flood-control program to a four-year, NT$100 billion program for improving county- and city-managed rivers and drainage systems at the source. He said the expanded investment is necessary as Taiwan faces increasingly frequent extreme weather events.
For Pingtung, the central government plans to invest NT$83.9 billion over four years in the management of county- and city-controlled rivers and drainage systems. Combined with the NT$13.6 billion Dahu project, the planned investment totals NT$97.5 billion, per CNA.
Cho called on relevant government agencies to work with Pingtung to complete the Dahu project as a comprehensive system rather than through fragmented improvements. The premier also said Pingtung has proposed approximately NT$2.99 billion in smaller emergency flood-control projects.
Of that amount, NT$1.6 billion has already been approved, while the remaining projects are expected to undergo expedited review. Cho said he hoped the projects would produce more visible results by 2027.
Pingtung County Magistrate Chou said the heavy rain in June and the continued downpours in August had presented significant challenges for Pingtung. She said the proposed drainage improvements would strengthen the county's ability to cope with extreme weather.
She thanked the premier for supporting the projects and called for faster reviews of six proposed emergency works. With central government support, she said, Pingtung would be better prepared to withstand extreme weather.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Lead frame maker Chang Wah Technology Co. is seeing demand improve across its major markets.
Second-quarter net profit reached NT$656 million (US$20.6 million), up 543% from the same period a year earlier. It was the company’s strongest quarterly result since the fourth quarter of 2022, according to CTEE and MoneyDJ.
Lead frames are metal structures used in semiconductor packaging to support chips and connect them to external circuits. Chang Wah has raised prices three times this year as orders recover across its major product lines and end markets, according to Pocket Securities.
Consumer electronics, industrial control, and automotive applications accounted for 46%, 28%, and 24% of revenue, respectively. Industrial control recorded the fastest growth, supported by higher shipments of products used in AI data centers, robotics, and low-Earth-orbit satellites.
The company has also seen stronger orders for lead frames used in quad flat no-lead (QFN) packages. QFN is a compact semiconductor package that allows chips to connect to circuit boards while helping dissipate heat. The package is increasingly used in power management, AI servers, and industrial applications, according to Gugu Fund.
Meanwhile, higher copper and precious-metal prices have driven up lead-frame prices. The rising power requirements of AI servers are also prompting data centers to upgrade their power systems, boosting demand for high-end lead frames.
Customers have also started placing more orders after reducing excess inventories. Chang Wah said inventory days at its major lead-frame buyers fell for five consecutive quarters to 199 days as of late July, suggesting that stock levels were gradually returning to normal.
Looking ahead, the company expects its operations to continue improving in the third quarter. It is also expanding production capacity in Taiwan, China, and Malaysia to prepare for longer-term growth.
Chang Wah’s new plant in Weihai, China, is scheduled to begin equipment installation and sample production in the first quarter of 2027. Its planned Malaysian facility is expected to reach structural completion in the fourth quarter of 2027.

Swiss to vote on whether to tighten neutrality, end peacetime cooperation with NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
05:38:58 UTC
14:38:58 KST

Swiss to vote on whether to tighten neutrality, end peacetime cooperation with NATO
ZURICH, Aug 26 - Swiss voters will decide in a referendum next month whether to approve a more restrictive form of neutrality that would block their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
Posters featuring doves of peace and asking voters to reject war have appeared across the Alpine nation in a campaign that has won the backing of the Kremlin but has raised fears that it could isolate Switzerland from its European neighbours.
Opinion surveys suggest voters will reject the proposal, with one recent poll showing 62% against to 36% in favour, but with campaigners for change outspending supporters of the status quo, the gap could narrow, said pollster Fabio Wasserfallen.
Swiss neutrality, internationally recognised since 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, kept Switzerland out of both world wars.
But this status is under threat after Switzerland imposed sanctions on Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, said Christoph Blocher, a veteran politician and backer of the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) which supports the campaign.
"Switzerland has not had a war for 200 years because it has remained permanently armed and neutral," Blocher told Reuters in an interview.
CAMPAIGNERS SAY SWISS NEUTRALITY IS BEING ERODED
The terms of Swiss neutrality are not explicitly spelled out in the constitution. Its scope is defined by the 1907 Hague Convention, which says neutral countries must not allow military use of their territory and be impartial between belligerents.
Blocher, who has led successful campaigns against closer ties with the European Union, said neutrality was being undermined, with Russia now seeing Switzerland as a party to the conflict because of the sanctions.
"A third world war may not be that far away, and then it will matter whether we are credibly neutral or not," he said.
Russia's foreign ministry has weighed into the debate, with spokeswoman Maria Zakharova criticising Switzerland in a social media post for aligning its sanctions with those of the EU.
"In legal terms, 'flexible neutrality' means no neutrality at all," said Zakharova, who is herself under Swiss sanctions.
The campaign wants the constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defence alliance, unless attacked, and that it refrain from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations.
OPPONENTS OF PROPOSAL SAY NO CHANGE IS NEEDED
The Swiss government and most political parties apart from the SVP oppose the proposal, with Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis saying it would harm national security and prevent it from training with NATO.
"We'd only be able to issue verbal condemnations but take no concrete action, that would certainly cause a major problem with our neighbours," Cassis told a press conference.
The government's legal experts said there was no need to change what they call a successful formula, which recently has seen Switzerland ban overflights by U.S. military aircraft during the Iran conflict.
"Neutrality is clearly defined and understood around the world," said Franz Perrez, head of international law at the foreign ministry. "Implementing these measures would not make Switzerland more neutral."
Laurent Goetschel, a political scientist at Basel University, said the campaign's posters saying "No to war, yes to neutrality" could sound attractive to voters who may not fully understand how neutrality was applied.
"Neutrality is not a dogma," he added. "It makes sense for Switzerland to be neutral, but the way it handles it should be up to the discretion of the government and not fixed in the constitution."
The referendum will take place on September 27. REUTERS

China Focus: China's cotton know-how takes root in Central Asia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:39 CST
14:30:39 KST

URUMQI, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Several hundred kilometers from Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan, cotton plants in a 1,000-mu (about 66.67 hectares) demonstration field are approaching one meter in height, each bearing 8 to 10 bolls.
For Song Meizhen, chief scientist of a high-quality cotton research team at the Institute of Western Agriculture under the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, the crop is developing as expected.
"Given the current growth and field management, the field is well on track to exceed the target of 550 kilograms of seed cotton per mu this year," Song said.
This high-standard cotton seed breeding demonstration field is jointly operated by Xinjiang Huaxing Investment Group and the institute. From surveying the land and selecting varieties before spring planting to designing cultivation methods and setting technical standards for sowing and field management, Chinese researchers have been involved throughout the process.
They have also provided regular video guidance and remote technical support.
The project combines high-quality cotton varieties with a range of techniques already widely used in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, including drip irrigation under plastic film, denser planting designed to improve light use, and mechanized harvesting.
Song said the cooperation endeavor is aimed at introducing a package of Chinese cotton-growing technologies and management practices to Uzbekistan.
Xinjiang is China's largest cotton-producing region. In 2025, it produced 6.17 million tonnes of cotton, accounting for 92.8 percent of the national total. The region's cotton sector is already among the world's most mechanized, with an overall mechanization rate for cultivation and harvesting surpassing 97 percent.
At a smart cotton field jointly developed by the Xinjiang Changji National Agricultural High-tech Industry Demonstration Zone and the institute, weather stations and soil-moisture sensors collect field data around the clock, helping growers manage irrigation, fertilizer and other field operations more precisely.
According to the institute, the system can save more than 10 percent of water and nearly 20 percent of fertilizer per mu while increasing yields by over 10 percent.
Similarities in climate, water and soil conditions between Xinjiang and Central Asian countries have laid the groundwork for cross-border adoption of improved cotton varieties, cultivation techniques and agricultural machinery.
Shadman Namazov, an academician of the Uzbek Academy of Sciences who has visited the Changji demonstration zone several times, said Chinese cotton-growing techniques have brought improvements in planting density, water use, yields and quality compared with traditional local practices.
He cited precision irrigation and fertilizer use, mechanized operations and modern field management, saying these technologies were scientifically grounded and could be replicated on a wider scale.
Namazov added that the use of Chinese techniques in Uzbekistan has helped raise cotton yields while reducing production costs, contributing to higher incomes for local growers.
These cooperation efforts are also translating into stronger demand for Chinese cotton seeds and agricultural machinery in Central Asia.
Hilltide, a Xinjiang-based seed industry company, sells cotton seeds and provides related technical services in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan. Company executive Lu Yang said its cotton seed exports to Central Asia rose from 800 tonnes during the sales season from late 2024 to early 2025 to 1,500 tonnes during the season from late 2025 to early 2026.
Lu revealed that the company's cotton seeds have maintained a market share of more than 70 percent in its Central Asian markets, attributing the growth to high-yield, stress-resistant varieties and technical services provided in addition to the seeds.
Chinese cotton pickers are gaining ground in Central Asia as well.
The Xinjiang branch of China Railway Construction Heavy Industry Co., Ltd. dispatched a batch of new four-row box-type cotton pickers to Central Asia in early July. The company said its cotton pickers have been developed to suit planting patterns and harvesting conditions in Central Asia, and orders from the region account for more than 70 percent of its production capacity this year.
At Xinjiang Boshiran Intelligent Agricultural Machinery Co., Ltd., Vice President Feng Guang said Chinese high-end cotton pickers can match leading international products in harvesting efficiency while costing about half as much as comparable European and U.S. machines.
Feng said a high level of domestically produced components, shorter delivery times and more timely after-sales service have also helped Chinese machines meet demand in Central Asian markets. The company has seen a sharp increase in overseas orders since last year, he added.
Alongside business exchanges, research cooperation has also deepened. Since 2023, Chinese institutions have worked with agricultural research institutes across all five Central Asian countries on joint research and technical training in cotton breeding, high-yield cultivation and water-saving irrigation, while promoting standardized technical guidelines in English and Russian.
The Uzbek demonstration field is one place where the results of this cooperation can be seen in the crop itself. Across Central Asia, Chinese cotton expertise is increasingly arriving not as a single product, but as a combination of seeds, farming techniques and machinery. ■

Across China: "China can set an example": U.S. delegation seeks lessons on aging, healthcare reform
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:36 CST
14:30:36 KST

Members of the exchange program "Harvard Healthcare China Trek 2026" pose for photos while visiting Peking University in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 19, 2026. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- China can set an example for the world in confronting demographic change, a U.S. public health scholar said, as a 25-member American delegation tours the country to learn from its healthcare reform, biotech innovation and artificial intelligence application.
David Crumpacker, assistant professor at Texas A&M University and a master of public health graduate from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, stressed the importance of learning from Chinese experience, such as primary care infrastructure, and efforts to manage the intersection of economic development with population health.
"These are insights that are not fully reflected in global health literature. We want to understand those insights from the people who generate them," he said.
The delegation, comprising scholars, medical professionals and students from Harvard University and other leading U.S. institutions, has been in China since Aug. 16.
They have visited the National Healthcare Security Administration and a national artificial intelligence medical pilot base in Beijing, as well as hospitals in Shanghai. They are also scheduled to tour health companies in Shenzhen, a global tech hub in southern Guangdong Province, and the Boao Lecheng International Medical Tourism Pilot Zone -- the country's sole medical special zone -- in Hainan Province.
China is racing to upgrade its healthcare system to meet the needs of an aging society. With more than 300 million people aged 60 and above, it has the largest elderly population of any country in the world.
By the end of 2025, the national basic medical insurance program covered 1.331 billion people, with the participation rate remaining stable at over 95 percent.
"Over one billion people means over one billion patients," said Jennifer Miles-Thomas, vice chair of integration and innovation at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago.
She said China and the United States are "very aligned" in the goal of delivering the highest quality care, but the U.S. faces challenges with expensive healthcare and incomplete insurance coverage. "I'm here to observe and to receive information and ideas about what we can do better," she said.
The exchange program, "Harvard Healthcare China Trek 2026," is hosted by the China Center for International People-to-People Exchange under the Ministry of Education, with support from Peking University Health Science Center and Fudan University Shanghai Medical College. It is part of a broader initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China over five years for study, research and dialogue.
During a visit to the BioPark in Beijing, Khaoula Belahsen, a 28-year-old master's student at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and an AI researcher at Harvard Medical School, was impressed by the scale and speed of the pharmaceutical and biotechnology hub. First announced in October 2025, the BioPark has drawn nearly 5,000 medical and healthcare companies, including global leaders Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Bayer, AstraZeneca and Medtronic.
"I've always dreamed of coming to China. The country has so much history, but also so much progress economically and scientifically," Belahsen said.
Morgan Moncada, 35, a Harvard graduate and founder of an AI digital health company, said strong incentives exist for medical companies to engage with the Chinese market, citing lower costs and vast reach. "China is open to collaboration, and that is really exciting," he said.
China is pushing artificial intelligence deeper into healthcare, with a roadmap to bring AI-assisted diagnosis to all primary-care clinics by 2030. Major hospitals are already using AI for imaging analysis and treatment planning.
Noting that his company uses AI agents to help people manage chronic diseases such as sleep apnea and diabetes, Moncada expressed his hope to introduce the technology they're building in the U.S. to China and adapt it for the Chinese population.
"I think something that we're really interested in is how we can contribute to China's healthcare system and how we can learn from China's healthcare system to improve healthcare in the United States and other countries around the globe," Moncada added.
In the Boao Lecheng pilot zone, patients can access innovative drugs and medical devices not yet approved on the mainland -- a policy that has benefited nearly 280,000 people and spared many costly overseas medical trips. The zone also uses real-world patient data to accelerate regulatory approvals, helping more products reach the wider Chinese market faster.
"We're very interested in seeing how this special zone actually helps, and how all those incredible medical technologies take effect," said Ze'ev Drukker, a 26-year-old bioengineering graduate from Tufts University who is applying for a master's program at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
As the delegation explores China's healthcare landscape, they are also building bridges of understanding between the younger generation of U.S. and Chinese health professionals, paving the way for joint efforts to advance global public health.
"What I like about healthcare is that it's something shared between all people, and across all countries. We all face the same challenges, and all want to integrate innovation to save people's lives and reduce burdens," Belahsen said. "It's really inspiring to come to China and see what innovation looks like here." ■

Syria's Kurdish-led group announces dissolution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
13:30:34 CST
14:30:34 KST

Mazloum Abdi, commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), speaks at a press conference at the People's Palace in Damascus, Syria, Aug. 25, 2026. Abdi announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria.
Abdi also announced the dissolution of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration and affiliated military and civilian formations, following their full integration into state institutions. (Xinhua)
DAMASCUS, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Mazloum Abdi, commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), announced Tuesday the dissolution of the force following the completion of its integration into Syrian state institutions, ending a decade-long chapter in which the U.S.-backed group controlled large parts of northern and northeastern Syria.
"Today, we announce the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces, and we responsibly announce its dissolution as a military force," Abdi said at a press conference at the People's Palace in Damascus, according to Syria's state-run Al-Ikhbariya TV.
Abdi also announced the dissolution of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration and affiliated military and civilian formations, following their full integration into state institutions.
He described the move as the beginning of a new chapter focused on peace, stability and rebuilding Syria after years of conflict.
The transition should mark a genuine shift "from the battlefields to the fields of construction," said Abdi, calling for the building of a unified country encompassing Syria's different communities.
He also raised the issue of Kurdish cultural and linguistic rights, saying he had sought an open position from Syrian interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa regarding the right to education in one's mother tongue.
Tuesday's announcement caps months of difficult negotiations and intermittent military confrontation between Damascus and the SDF over the future of northeastern Syria and the shape of the country's post-war state.
The two sides initially agreed in early 2025 to integrate the SDF and the Kurdish-led administration's civilian institutions into the Syrian state. Implementation, however, became bogged down amid disagreements over the structure of the integration, military command arrangements and the degree of autonomy Kurdish authorities would retain.
Tensions subsequently escalated, including clashes in Kurdish-held neighborhoods of Aleppo, before developing into a broader military confrontation in January this year.
Government forces advanced into SDF-held territory in northern and eastern Syria, substantially reducing the territory controlled by the Kurdish-led force.
On Jan. 18, Damascus and the SDF reached a ceasefire and integration agreement providing for an immediate halt to fighting, the withdrawal of SDF formations to areas east of the Euphrates River and the transfer of administrative and military authority in Raqqa and Deir al-Zour provinces to the central government.
A more comprehensive agreement followed later that month, setting out the phased integration of the SDF's military and administrative structures.
The arrangements included the deployment of Interior Ministry security forces in Hasakah and Qamishli and the incorporation of SDF fighters into formations operating within the Syrian military structure.
Implementation continued over the following months. Damascus assumed control over key state institutions and facilities in the northeast, including Qamishli airport and major oil fields, while government security forces entered Hasakah and Qamishli.
Yet disagreements persisted over the SDF's ultimate status, particularly whether it could retain a distinct command structure within the Syrian military. As recently as early August, dissolution remained a key issue under negotiation between Abdi and al-Sharaa.
Abdi announced on Aug. 20 that the integration of the Kurdish administration's military, security and civilian institutions into the Syrian state had been completed, paving the way for Tuesday's formal dissolution.
Tuesday's announcement also came one day after Washington formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had lasted since 1979.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the decision was part of Washington's effort to give Syria a path toward prosperity.
Washington also revoked the designation of Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a former al-Qaida-linked rebel group that played a dominant role in the formation of Syria's new government, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.
Since its formation in 2015, the SDF had been backed primarily by the United States and served as Washington's main local partner in the fight against Islamic State militants.
But following the fall of the former Syrian government in December 2024, Washington increasingly supported efforts to bring Syria's institutions and armed groups under a unified state framework while building closer ties with the new authorities in Damascus. ■

ISLAMABAD, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- At least 14 infants were killed when a fire broke out in the gynecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences here on Wednesday, police sources said.
The fire broke out at around 6:40 a.m. local time (0140 GMT) in the gynecology ward area on the third floor of the hospital, where children were present, the sources told Xinhua on condition of anonymity.
The hospital administration launched rescue operations, while fire brigade personnel, ambulances and police rushed to the scene. Several children were reportedly rescued from the ward.
The sources said that initially nine children died on the spot, while the others later succumbed to their injuries after being shifted to the children's ward.
Rescue operations were still underway, while police were ascertaining the cause of the fire and exact details regarding the casualties. ■

BISHKEK, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Board of the National Bank of Kyrgyzstan has decided to keep its key interest rate unchanged at 12 percent, the bank's press service said on Tuesday.
Since the beginning of 2026, consumer prices have risen by 7.3 percent, while annual inflation has reached 11.7 percent. Rising fuel and lubricant prices, as well as higher food prices amid volatility in global food markets, have been among the main drivers of inflation.
At the same time, economic activity remains strong, with real GDP growing 11.1 percent in January-July 2026. Growth has been supported by high investment activity, particularly in construction, as well as increased domestic consumption.
The National Bank said persistent external inflationary risks require maintaining tight monetary conditions. Keeping the key rate at its current level will help contain secondary inflationary effects and create conditions for a sustainable decline in inflation over the medium term. ■

City Tower One is a 358-meter-tall (1,175 ft.) tower in Dubai designed by Pelli Clarke & Partners. The 93-story mixed-use skyscraper completed construction and launched for leasing in June 2026. The building is located in the Trade Centre First neighborhood, on a site connecting Sheikh Zayed Road to Al Badaa Road along Eleventh Street, and includes 608 residential units across from Hazel Wong's Emirates Towers and Killa Design's Museum of the Future. The building's presence in Dubai's skyline and everyday urban life was recently captured by local photographer Ahmad Alnaji, founder of SARAB Art Production and a contributor to the visual identity of landmark buildings across the region, including projects by architecture practices such as Foster + Partners, UNStudio and Killa Design.
Pelli Clarke & Partners' City Tower One comprises a mix of residential units ranging from studios to four-bedroom penthouses and duplexes, together with office and retail space. With nearly half of all residential units being three-bedroom homes, the tower has low-density floors, with eight to nine homes per floor. Indoor amenities include a gym, a movement studio, a residents' multi-purpose lounge and children's play areas. A dedicated residential amenity deck, linked to the main tower by a skybridge above a nine-story parking structure, provides additional indoor and outdoor shared facilities. Outdoor amenities include an infinity pool, a tennis court, landscaped lounge areas, children's play areas, and a specialty café.
Particularly noticeable in the photographs, the tower's champagne hue shimmers in the desert sun. A grand-scale, expansive and light-filled entrance space is defined by mashrabiya-inspired aluminum screens that dapple and modulate light. A rooftop amenity deck, designed by the firm as "an oasis for leisure and wellness," sits atop the parking structure. The deck stretches wide, offering views of the Gulf and the Burj Khalifa, alongside a full-service fitness facility, a yoga studio, a residential lounge, and a pool and recreation area for children. The photographs place these design elements within the context of everyday urban life, presenting the tower as an integral part of Dubai's skyline and a recognizable landmark at all hours.

- European nations are preparing new sanctions and military aid for Ukraine, but Russia continues covert efforts to destabilise the West and weaken support for Kyiv.

BRUSSELS – Russia is expanding its campaign of hybrid attacks against countries that supply weapons and money to Kyiv and has caught Europe without a plan to respond.
From cyberattacks to armed drones and mysterious cases of arson, tensions are rising across the continent as the war in Ukraine is set to enter its fifth winter.
Poland said in August that it thwarted an attempted assassination of a US citizen originally from Ukraine that was ordered by Russia, while Estonia accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone maker.
Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Aug 25 that those responsible for hybrid attacks “will pay the price” after an explosive-laden drone was discovered at an airport in Leipzig near a Ukrainian cargo plane, raising speculation that Moscow was involved in an attempted strike.
European officials have been anticipating for months that Russia may escalate its aggressive campaign against the continent.
But the bloc has yet to change its fundamentally defensive posture, according to people familiar with how the institutions gauge outside threats, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
That has likely encouraged Moscow to probe how far it can go in trying to intimidate and wear down Western allies as it remains locked in a war of attrition with Ukraine.
“NATO, European and national responses have largely been reactive and defensive,” said Agnia Grigas, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council in Vilnius.
“They have focused on detecting and countering individual provocations, but have not built a record of effective deterrence by consistently dissuading Moscow from continuing or escalating them.”
That lack of preparedness comes as Europe has taken on the primary role in supporting Ukraine, with the US shifting away from the continent.
While NATO’s mutual defence clause commits member states to help one another in case of an attack, Russia’s alleged actions have so far fallen short of what would become a trigger for such a response.
Moscow has increasingly relied on recruitment via social media to carry out arson or other sabotage attacks after large-scale expulsions of its diplomats following the invasion of Ukraine.
Two Ukrainian nationals were handed prison sentences in Britain in June after a jury found them guilty of conspiring to commit arson attacks on a car and property linked to then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
The prosecution said during the trial that one of the perpetrators was recruited online by a Russian-speaking Telegram user.
Lithuanian prosecutor-general Nida Grunskiene said last week that the drone attack in Germany has “links” to an ongoing investigation into an attempt to detonate a parcel on a DHL cargo plane in 2024.
Lithuania has charged five in the attempted sabotage, allegedly hired by Russia’s military intelligence.
While Germany has not singled out Russia as being behind the armed drone or the recent discovery of a cache of weapons on the outskirts of Berlin, a slew of investigative media reports have pointed the finger at Moscow.
It also added to fresh warnings that Europe’s biggest economy must grapple with the new dimensions of asymmetrical risks.
There are indications that Russian intelligence and security services are looking at hybrid warfare operations against the Baltic states and Poland, an intelligence official told Bloomberg earlier in August.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said Moscow is weighing a potential false flag operation using captured Ukrainian drones to strike critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.
“Russia’s ongoing hybrid warfare in Europe is a highly coordinated, sub-threshold campaign aimed at destabilising Western political systems, fracturing NATO and EU unity, and eroding support for Ukraine,” said Alex Kokcharov, geoeconomics analyst at Bloomberg Economics in London.
“To achieve these goals, the Kremlin maintains plausible deniability by exploiting anonymity and utilising proxies to obfuscate direct state attribution.”
Some European Union members have called on the bloc to respond by adopting the sanctions that have been blocked, including seizing assets, a ban on transporting Russian liquefied natural gas and restricting visas, according to people familiar with the matter.
The EU is preparing another package of sanctions on hundreds of individuals and entities, which it aims to adopt in the fall, they said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
But as previous such measures have failed to restrain Moscow, it is unlikely they will do now.
“Russia is willing to use kinetic means because until now, they have been unsuccessful in discouraging support for Ukraine,” said Marek Kohv, head of the security and resilience programme at the Tallinn-based International Centre for Defence and Security.
“It is directly connected to how Russia is doing on the front line.”
NATO members have pledged US$80 billion (S$101.5 billion) in military aid to Ukraine for 2026 and “at least the equivalent levels” in 2027 at the alliance’s July summit in Ankara.
The money is overwhelmingly coming from Europe.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham handed over cruise missile blueprints to Kyiv in a visit on Aug 24.
He also compared Ukraine’s fight with Britain’s resistance to the Nazis in World War II, drawing a response from Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
He accused Britain of “methodically and regularly adding fuel to the fire” and “methodically and regularly plotting to prevent any progress in the peace process” in his remarks to reporters on Aug 24.
Russia has also warned that Britain would face “consequences for which it will have to answer” after reports that Kyiv used drones made by British companies to carry out strikes inside Russian territory.
In August, the Estonian authorities said they were investigating Russian involvement in a fire at Milrem Robotics, a drone manufacturer that supplies Ukraine.
A Latvian charity for Ukraine said its warehouse was the subject of an arson attack in July.
“Russia is clearly seeking to escalate the situation – not through direct military escalation, but perhaps by influencing Western countries, particularly those supporting Ukraine,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in Helsinki on Aug 24. “But it is not working. South Korea said on Wednesday it had scrambled fighter jets in response to Russian military aircraft entering its air defence zone, the second such incursion in weeks.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area where countries require foreign aircraft to identify themselves for security purposes.
