Lok Sabha Speaker seeks response from 20 rebel TMC MPs on disqualification petitions
Edited by: Karan Manral / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 26, 2026, 12:52 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Rebel TMC MPs with Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla in June
NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has issued notices to 20 rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs who are now affiliated with the little-known Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), seeking their responses within seven days to disqualification petitions filed by the TMC.The disqualification petitions are currently pending before Birla.This comes after Solicitor General of India Tushar Mehta on Tuesday informed the Supreme Court that the Speaker had already issued notices to the 20 MPs on the disqualification petitions filed by the TMC under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.
Mehta made the submission before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant while appearing for the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Secretary General of the House. The bench was hearing a plea filed by senior TMC leader Abhishek Banerjee, challenging the delay in deciding the petitions seeking the disqualification of the rebels.Responding to the submission, the bench said, "It is not a question of issuing notices, it is a question of concluding the proceedings within a time frame."During the hearing, the bench indicated that it was inclined to issue notices to the respondents on Abhishek Banerjee’s writ petition.
Mehta, however, submitted that there was no need to issue notices to the Speaker or his office, stating that he would appear on behalf of Birla.The TMC has accused the 20 MPs of “abandoning” the party and subsequently joining the NCPI. Abhishek Banerjee has contended that their conduct attracts disqualification under the anti-defection provisions of the Constitution.
The petition names the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Secretary General of the House as the principal respondents and also impleads the MPs whose disqualification is being sought.
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

US authority allocates almost $40 million for drone purchases to combat crime in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:31:27 UTC
13:31:27 KST

WASHINGTON, August 26. /TASS/. So far this year, the US Department of State has channeled almost $40 million to purchase unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to combat crime in Ukraine, according to documents released on the US public procurement portal, seen by TASS.
In February, the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement (INL) at the US Department of State allocated some $32 million to Ukraine’s Stream Techno for drone and UAV ground control station purchases under two contracts, the data showed. In August, the sum was raised to $39.9 million.
According to data released on the State Department’s data, the authority works with foreign governments, law enforcement agencies and the private sector to combat "narco-terrorism, drug trafficking, transnational organized crime, and other criminal threats at the source."

At least 14 babies killed in Pakistan hospital nursery fire
Only one infant rescued from the neonatal facility where the fire broke out, in Pakistan’s capital.
At least 14 newborn children have been killed in a fire that broke out in the nursery of a government-run hospital in Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said, as he ordered an investigation.
The fire broke out on Wednesday on the third floor of the Mother and Child Centre at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital, according to media reports.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can Pakistani army chief make Iran’s military leaders restart US talks?
- list 2 of 3Sanctions or missiles? How Gulf will view Trump’s new Iran approach
- list 3 of 3Pakistan says significant progress made in talks on Iran-US war
Local broadcaster Geo TV, quoting hospital sources, put the death toll at 15.
It said the blaze, which began shortly before 7am local time (02:00 GMT), has now been extinguished. Only one infant was rescued, it added.
In a statement on X, Sharif offered his “deepest condolences to the bereaved families” and directed authorities to conduct “an immediate investigation”.
He promised that those responsible would face the “strictest action”.
Geo TV cited rescue sources as saying that the fire was likely caused by a short circuit in a malfunctioning air conditioning unit.
Building fires are common in Pakistan, where safety regulations and building codes are routinely ignored or poorly enforced. In January, at least 65 people died when a massive fire swept through a crowded shopping complex in the southern port city of Karachi.
Wednesday’s blaze is one of the deadliest hospital fires in Pakistan’s history. While the government provides subsidised medical treatment through public hospitals, the state sector remains severely underfunded, mismanaged and overcrowded.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said that Tokyo would continue to support the International Criminal Court amid pressure from the United States. Bloomberg reported this, UNN writes.
Details
As the ICC’s largest financial donor, we must protect this important institution
According to the Japanese prime minister, Tokyo repeatedly urged Washington not to impose sanctions against Akane, but the United States ignored these appeals. Japan also plans to continue supporting the ICC president and, if necessary, may raise this issue with the American side.

In 2024, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and earlier for Russia’s dictator Vladimir Putin. The United States and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, on the basis of which the court operates.

Was PoK's Skardu airbase next after Sargodha? Ex-CDS Chauhan reveals why India switched targets

Was PoK's Skardu airbase next after Sargodha? Ex-CDS Chauhan reveals why India switched targets
Edited by: Abhishek Mishra / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 26, 2026, 12:25 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Skardu military base, PoK (AP file photo)
NEW DELHI: Did India plan to strike Pakistan-occupied Kashmir’s Skardu airbase after targeting Sargodha? Former chief of defence staff General Anil Chauhan has revealed that Indian forces had cleared Skardu in Gilgit-Baltistan as a possible target during Operation Sindoor but had to change plans because of “bad weather”.Chauhan, who was heading the military when Operation Sindoor was carried out, made the remarks while speaking at the Vivekananda International Foundation on Operation Sindoor and its aftermath.Recalling the counterterror operation, former CDS Chauhan said, "Once the Pakistanis had picked up the phone and said they wanted to talk at about 10 AM. The Air Chief asked me whether he should strike Sargodha, I said, Go ahead... I said, could you please identify two more targets, so one of the targets he identified was Skardu."
"We gave a yes, but after some time, the weather was bad over it and they had to change over to Bholari," he added.
What Ex-CDS Chauhan said about Kirana Hills
Chauhan also clarified that Indian forces “did not target” Pakistan’s Kirana Hills, an area reportedly linked to a nuclear facility.He backed Air Marshal AK Bharti, who was the then Director General of Air Operations (DGAO) of the Air Force.
Bharti had said on May 12 last year, “We have not hit Kirana hills, whatever is there.”Bharti was responding to questions about reports and social media claims that Indian forces had targeted Kirana Hills during Operation Sindoor.Chauhan said, “There was a small episode about what Air Marshal Bharti was asked, the Kirana Hills episode. I think I'll clarify this. On occasions, it's been asked whether Kirana Hills were hit; that is where their (Pakistan's) nuclear facilities are.”He said Bharti had “rightly clarified that we did not target Kirana Hills”.Chauhan explained that Indian forces had sent several loitering munitions towards Sargodha before the strikes. Kirana Hills is around 10 km north of Sargodha.“I can, maybe give a kind of an explanation... Before those strikes, we had sent in a lot of loitering munitions to Sargodha, and Kirana Hills is about 10 km north of Sargodha. So the loitering munition is looking for radars which are in and around Sargodha, and it has a time span, which means it will loiter for about two hours, and once it does not find a target, it comes down and hits somewhere,” the former CDS said.
He added, “It must have come and hit one of those hills. So that could be one of the reasons as to what people asked... Because Pakistani media also showed some images in which there was smoke coming out from Kirana Hills.”India launched Operation Sindoor in May 2025, targeting nine major terror infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) following Pakistan-sponsored Pahalgam terror attack on April 22.The counterterror strikes killed more than 100 terrorists. During the military confrontation, Indian forces also struck Pakistan's Sargodha airbase.Chauhan also underlined that Operation Sindoor is “still ongoing”.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

Ukrainian Embassy calls on US orchestra to cancel performance by pro-Kremlin violinist
The embassy stated this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
The "Forces of Nature" concerts featuring the Russian performer are scheduled for November 6–7 at Maryland Hall.
"The decision to invite Mr. Repin raises serious concerns given his documented involvement in Russian state-sponsored and state-linked cultural initiatives," the embassy said in its post.
The diplomatic mission recalled that Repin performed at a concert organized by a Kremlin foundation to honor Russia's "great defenders."
It also noted that since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Repin's Arts Development Foundation has received significant funding from the so-called Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives of the Russian Federation.
The embassy noted that a number of cultural institutions have already reconsidered their cooperation with Repin. These include the Mannheim Philharmonic Orchestra in Germany, the Hungarian National Philharmonic Orchestra, and the Palm Beach Symphony Orchestra in Florida, which canceled the Russian violinist's performance in March.
"We hope the Annapolis Symphony Orchestra will give these concerns careful consideration and reaffirm the solidarity with Ukraine it demonstrated in 2022, when it withdrew Mr. Repin from its program and replaced his performance with a musical tribute to Ukraine," the embassy emphasized.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Repin's performance in Budapest was canceled following efforts by the Embassy of Ukraine in Hungary.

US conservative gay rights group says it is ending advocacy for transgender causes
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 - Log Cabin Republicans, a conservative gay rights group, said it is ending advocacy and support for transgender causes, with the decision coming at a time when Republican President Donald Trump's administration has acted to limit transgender rights.
• Ross Hemminger, the conservative gay rights group's board president, said in an online essay that the board of directors has voted for its advocacy to "concentrate specifically on issues of sexual orientation and conservative values — in other words, we are an LGB advocacy organization."
• Hemminger, who said Log Cabin Republicans first embraced transgender rights issues in 2015, wrote that the transgender movement now pushes a "radical gender ideology."
• Trump has cast the gender identity of transgender people as a lie, issued a series of executive actions targeting their rights and stated in a directive that the U.S. government will recognize only two sexes: male and female.
• He has also launched probes against educational institutions and threatened to cut their federal funding over transgender policies.
• Some rights groups have condemned moves by Trump and governors in Republican-led states, saying such actions in recent years have created an unsafe climate for the transgender community. REUTERS

'They had gone towards Sargodha': Ex-Navy officer backs former CDS Anil Chauhan on Kirana Hills remarks

'They had gone towards Sargodha': Ex-Navy officer backs former CDS Anil Chauhan on Kirana Hills remarks
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 26, 2026, 09:41 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
File photo: Former CDS Anil Chauhan
NEW DELHI: Former director of naval operations and intelligence commodore Ranjit Rai (Retd.) on Tuesday said former Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General Anil Chauhan's remarks on Pakistan's Kirana Hills indicated that Operation Sindoor was a "total success", particularly highlighting India's use of loitering munitions during the 87-hour military operation.Speaking to news agency ANI, Rai was reacting to Chauhan's remarks that an Indian loitering munition deployed to search for radars in and around Sargodha in Pakistan "must have" hit an area in the Kirana Hills after failing to locate its intended target.
"He made it absolutely clear that it was a total success (Operation Sindoor)," Rai told ANI. He said Chauhan had made it clear that during the 87-hour operation, loitering munitions were deployed and operated around Sargodha.Rai also pointed to the significance of Kirana Hills, located around 10 kilometres north of Sargodha."He disclosed that during the operation, loitering munitions, which are drones, were used. They were loitering 10 miles from Sargodha; they had gone towards Sargodha, but 10 miles from Sargodha is the Khirana Hills. Pakistan has carried out some critical nuclear tests at the Khirana Hills. Underground in Kirana, they have got some nuclear facility.
I mean, this is a revolution, telling the world about Operation Sindoor," he said.
Chauhan, speaking at the Vivekananda Centre in New Delhi on Tuesday, said India had sent loitering munitions towards Sargodha to search for radars in and around the area. He explained that the weapons had a flight time of around two hours and, if they failed to locate a target during that period, would eventually come down and hit an area."I think I'll clarify this...at occasions, it's been asked whether Kirana Hills were hit or not, which is where their (Pakistan's) nuclear facilities are... Before those strikes, we had sent in a lot of loitering munitions at Sargodha and Kirana Hills is about 10 kilometres north of Sargodha. So the loitering ammunition is looking for radars which are in and around Sargodha, and it has a lifetime, which means it will loiter for about two hours and once it does not find a target, it comes down and hits somewhere," Chauhan said.
"It must have come and hit one of those hills. So that could be one of the reasons as to what people asked, because Pakistani media also showed some kind of images in which there was smoke coming out from Kirana Hills," he added.
What Chauhan said about Kirana Hills
Chauhan's remarks clarified that Kirana Hills was not deliberately selected as a target during Operation Sindoor. Rather, according to his account, a loitering munition searching for radars around Sargodha may have struck one of the hills after failing to find its intended target.The comments also put his remarks in the context of an earlier statement by Air Marshal AK Bharti, who was director general of air operations during Operation Sindoor.On May 12, 2025, Bharti had rejected speculation that Indian forces had deliberately targeted Kirana Hills."Thank you for telling us that Kirana Hills houses some nuclear installations. We did not know about it. We have not hit Kirana Hills. I did not brief in my briefing yesterday," Bharti had said.Chauhan similarly referred to the earlier statement and explained that the possible impact on Kirana Hills was linked to the operation of loitering munitions sent towards Sargodha.Operation Sindoor was launched by India following the Pahalgam terror attack in which 26 people were killed.
The Indian Armed Forces targeted terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). As Pakistan sought to escalate the conflict, India also struck Pakistani airbases before Pakistan sought a ceasefire.Chauhan also said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had given the military "complete freedom of action" before Operation Sindoor and told the armed forces to decide the timing of the operation while ensuring there was no scope for failure.The ex-CDS had said the Prime Minister told the military to act at its own time, ensure there was no reason for failure, maintain evidence of the actions taken and exercise "complete freedom of action."

Butchers report chicken meat sales drop amid bird flu anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26

13:10:37 KST

Butchers report chicken meat sales drop amid public anxiety about bird flu
A Perth butcher says he has seen a decline in his otherwise stable chicken sales in recent weeks which he attributed to unfounded public anxiety about the threat of bird flu.
As parts of Australia grapple with H5 bird flu with the wash-up of dozens of infected migratory seabirds, Tom Randolph said his Mt Hawthorn business had seen chicken sales plunge.
"Chicken has been one of the most reliable and stable product lines that we have," he said.
"Over the last five or six weeks, we've seen the sales drop by about 20 to 25 per cent."
Another two butchers in Perth told the ABC they were experiencing a similar trend, including John Nazary who runs the Wattle Grove Butcher.
Mr Nazary said his chicken sales have plummeted by about 60 per cent in the past three weeks.
"In the last two weeks I threw a couple of boxes [out], maybe two, four boxes," he said.
"I used to order every day, every second day, but the last two, three weeks, no."
Is bird flu a threat to WA?
Western Australia reported the first confirmed Australian cases of the deadly H5N1 bird flu strain detected in a migratory seabird in June.
On Sunday, WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti, said it had been over a month since bird flu was detected in the state.
"We've been working closely with wildlife rescue organisations, supporting them to be at the front line helping Western Australians detect and report," Ms Saffioti said.
Food Standards Australia New Zealand stated in July it was safe to continue eating cooked chicken and eggs, adding there is "no evidence of bird flu infection in Australian poultry or the wider agriculture industry".
"Avian influenza is not known to transmit to humans via food, and it is safe to eat properly cooked chicken meat and eggs," the statement said.
"Proper storage and preparation remain important in reducing risks, and good personal hygiene must be practised when handling raw poultry and eggs."
Surging interest in backyard chickens
WA Poultry Association president Reece Jerrett said the livestock sector was experiencing the opposite to butchers, with breeders reporting a surge in interest from people wanting to keep chickens in their backyards.
"We're assuming that's because people are expecting a bit of an impending egg shortage, if H5N1 gets into the commercial sector," Mr Jerrett said.
He said similar spikes had been witnessed during the COVID-19 pandemic and more recently, when NSW, VIC and the ACT were hit by the H7 variant of bird flu in 2024 — 2025.
On farms across Australia, the poultry industry had to cull about 2 million chickens in a bid to eliminate the H7 variant.
Almost a year after the H7 variant was eradicated, the industry is only just recovering from Australia's largest outbreak, which led to egg shortages for almost a year.
The Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry have warned the public of the high mortality rate in poultry and Mr Jerrett said he was concerned more people were purchasing chickens for their backyard.
"Chickens are livestock; we should be practising livestock biosecurity," he said.
"There is that really important factor of running poultry is that you need a good set up to look after those birds adequately.
"They're not just a set and forget pet."
Loading...
Mr Jerrett explained chickens required a lot of care including ensuring they have clean water, good food, constant clean bedding and a draught-free home that is fully enclosed from wildlife.
What next?
In a statement, the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions said it continued to monitor WA's situation through a vaccination trial for vulnerable species.
Authorities have recorded 318 positive events of H5 bird flu in wildlife.
It came as Australia's first case of bird flu in a mammal was confirmed following testing of a long-nosed fur seal found in South Australia.
The seal was found at Beachport, 300 kilometres south of Adelaide.
Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the detection was concerning but not unexpected, particularly in marine mammals.

RTHK editor gets 160 hours of community service for upskirt video
Chong Tak-yin, 57, pleaded guilty to unlawful recording of intimate parts after police found an upskirt video on his phone
A Hong Kong court has ordered a civil servant at public broadcaster RTHK to complete 160 hours of community service after he admitted taking upskirt footage of a woman in public.
Chong Tak-yin, an assistant chief assignment editor in RTHK’s Chinese news and current affairs division, was sentenced on Wednesday at West Kowloon Court after pleading guilty to one count of unlawful recording or observation of intimate parts.
The 57-year-old told arresting officers the offence was “a momentary lapse of judgment” driven by sexual impulse when he filmed the woman in a skirt in Mong Kok on November 14 last year.
According to court documents, patrolling officers spotted him suspiciously following the woman. A stop and search found a video on his phone showing the woman’s lower body.
At an earlier hearing, defence counsel Joe Chan Wai-yin said Chong was married with two sons and earned about HK$90,000 (US$11,480) a month as the family’s sole breadwinner.

NEW DELHI: India has called on the international community to work collectively to safeguard critical sea lanes and maritime infrastructure, saying secure and predictable shipping routes are essential to ensure the uninterrupted movement of food, fertilisers, fuel and other vital commodities amid conflicts and growing disruptions to global supply chains.Speaking at a UN Security Council high-level open debate on Tuesday on the theme ‘Food Under Fire: The Security Council's Role in Mitigating Global and Local Food Crises’, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said regional conflicts were increasingly producing consequences far beyond the immediate theatres of hostilities.“Secure and predictable maritime trade routes are indispensable for the uninterrupted movement of food, fertilisers, fuel and other essential commodities," Parvathaneni said, underscoring the need to preserve the safety and freedom of navigation for commercial shipping in accordance with international law.The call comes as conflicts and attacks on key maritime routes continue to threaten global food and energy supplies. UN secretary general Antonio Guterres told the Council that the Strait of Hormuz carries around a fifth of global oil supplies and a third of global fertiliser trade.“Restrictions and closures have driven up commodity prices and made availability plummet. And attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea are further threatening supply chains for food and other commodities,” Guterres said.
Parvathaneni warned that disruptions to commercial shipping during conflicts could have cascading effects well beyond the affected region, with food-importing developing countries and humanitarian operations bearing a disproportionate burden.“The international community must therefore work collectively to safeguard critical sea lanes and maritime infrastructure, while ensuring that legitimate commercial trade and humanitarian shipments are able to proceed without undue impediment,” he said.India said the immediate priority for the Security Council should be to reduce the humanitarian consequences of conflicts by facilitating safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access, supporting de-confliction arrangements where appropriate and ensuring that Council measures, including sanctions regimes, do not inadvertently obstruct humanitarian assistance or legitimate food and agricultural trade.Parvathaneni also called for timely assessments of disruptions to critical supply chains covering food, fertiliser, fuel and humanitarian logistics, drawing on the expertise of the food and agriculture organisation, the World Food Programme and other relevant agencies.“Such assessments must remain objective, evidence-based and free from politicisation,” he said.The envoy said food insecurity was fundamentally a consequence of conflict, political instability and underdevelopment, rather than their root cause. He called for greater cooperation among member states, international financial institutions, regional organisations and development partners to strengthen domestic agricultural production, diversify supply chains and improve storage and logistics infrastructure.“Predictable and affordable access to fertilisers, quality seeds, technology and concessional finance remains indispensable, particularly for developing countries. Open, transparent and rules-based trade in food and agricultural inputs also remains critical to global food security,” he said.India also cautioned against “over-reliance " on any single model of production, arguing that such dependence could leave food systems vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions, economic coercion and weaponisation.
“We must encourage small and marginal farmers to enhance their productivity and contribute to ensuring food security in developing countries of the Global South. We must also encourage climate-resilient crops such as millets rather than limit conceptions of food security to the biggest staple, grain crops such as rice, wheat and corn,” Parvathaneni said.Guterres said 2025 saw the highest number of armed conflicts since World War II alongside some of the highest levels of global acute hunger on record, with at least 266 million people facing acute food insecurity.
He described the simultaneous confirmation of famine in Sudan and Gaza in 2025 as a “shameful milestone”, adding that conflict and violence were the primary drivers of hunger in 12 of the 13 hunger hotspots of greatest concern identified in the UN’s latest Hunger Hotspots report.

Call to ban marmot hunting in France as campaigners say they are ‘killed for fun’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:35 UTC
13:00:35 KST

Animal rights campaigners are gearing up for protests and petitions aimed at persuading the French government to ban the hunting of Alpine marmots.
Open season on the rodents, members of the squirrel and groundhog family, begins in September, a few weeks before they go into a long winter hibernation.
Although the marmot is not a threatened species in France, its numbers are reportedly declining as a result of the climate emergency. Campaigners say they are opposed to them being hunted for fun.
Pauline di Nicolantonio, the president of the Association for Justice for Savoie Animals (AJAS), which has launched protests against marmot hunting for the last two years, said: “The question is a moral one.
“When you tell people that hunting marmots is allowed in France, they are shocked. The marmot is extremely popular and symbolic in the Savoie where we are based and elsewhere in the Alps. You only have to go into any tourist office to see it’s the main logo or emblem.”
Plant-eating marmots are spread across mountainous areas of Europe and North America. Most live in family groups organised by one dominant couple; when threatened they emit a high-pitched signal. In late summer and into autumn their bodies swell to up to 8kg as they stock up on food for a five- to six-month hibernation.
There are 15 marmot species in the world and as wild game they were traditionally hunted for their meat, fat and fur. Today, hunting is allowed in certain states in the US and Canada, and in France, Switzerland and Austria but banned in Italy and Germany. An average of 1,000 marmots are shot in France each year.
For generations of French children the marmot has been celebrated as the subject of folk tales and poems – one by Goethe set to music by Beethoven – the mascot of Alpine ski resorts and the sympathetic star of a popular television advert for a well-known brand of milk chocolate.
In fact, the rodents’ cuddly reputation belies a bloodier reality; much of its waking life is spent in a vicious battle for dominance and territory that often involves killing its parents or children.
Christophe Bonenfant, a scientist at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at the University of Lyon, studies marmots in the Grande Sassière alpine nature reserve. Evidence of the climate crisis in Europe is most evident in the Alps where rock faces are fissuring and glaciers shrinking at an unprecedented rate.
Bonenfant and his colleague Rébecca Garcia have noticed the marmots’ domestic and territorial battles becoming increasingly brutal as the climate emergency destroys the animal’s “social stability”.
They have also noted that while the animals are not listed as endangered, females are producing fewer marmot pups and a combination of the cycle of violence and smaller litters is leading to a steady drop in populations.
“What we are seeing is the breaking up of social groups, which are lasting less long, and more rapid changes of dominant animals in those groups,” Bonenfant said.
“As a herbivore the marmot is quite low down the food chain but its importance is as food for carnivores like eagles and foxes and from time to time badgers. It also makes galleried tunnels that contribute to the aeration of the soil. It’s not classified as a nuisance species.”
He said of hunting: “It’s not a species that raises questions about conservation, so the root of the question is the morality of hunting animals, not just in France but everywhere, and why people enjoy killing animals for fun.”
There are strict hunting regulations set by individual local authorities limiting the number of marmots that can be killed and the season dates, but AJAS wants a national ban similar to that introduced in Italy in 1992.
French farmers claim the animals are a nuisance making holes in their fields causing damage to machinery. The National Hunters Federation says hunting marmots is “strictly supervised and regulated” and the open season lasts at most a month. “There is no justification for banning marmot hunting: the species is not threatened, there are no plans to classify it as a protected species and their numbers are on the rise.”
Di Nicolantonio said: “We know they are affected by the climate crisis and the data is worrying. Hunters often commission scientific reports to say there are lots of marmots around to justify killing them.
“Hunting them is cruel, absurd and unpopular but isn’t banned because it’s considered a tradition. In the past, we might have eaten marmots but now shooting them is simply recreational.”

In Poland, compassion for Ukrainians has turned to contempt. The consequences could be dramatic | Mateusz Mazzini
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:35 UTC
13:00:35 KST

One of the unintended consequences of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine was that it gave Poland a rare slice of geopolitical stardom. When Russian tanks started their ultimately unsuccessful cavalcade towards the Ukrainian capital, ordinary Poles rushed to help millions of people fleeing the looming conflict. As Polish people opened their doors to civilians running from Russian bombs, even the then ruling populist Law and Justice party had to follow suit.
It seemed that Poland and Ukraine were bound for an iron-clad alliance, unprecedented in their shared history. Poland advocated for the Ukrainian cause in the west, with some success. Ukrainian leaders, in turn, praised Poles for their generosity and the government in Warsaw for contributing weapons and money to the war effort. Given that recent history between the two countries had been marked by accusations of second world war-era genocide, border shifts and postwar displacements of millions of people, it was a remarkable change.
But it has not lasted. According to a an opinion poll by CBOS, Poland’s largest polling institution last month, 52% of Poles now oppose their country accepting Ukrainian refugees. A steadily growing number are becoming weary of supporting Kyiv, with many rightwingers arguing that weapons transfers have depleted Poland’s own capacity to defend against a potential Russian incursion.
Memory politics has unhelpfully reared its head after Volodymyr Zelenskyy named a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a branch of which massacred about 100,000 Poles in 1943. The Polish right responded in kind, and the president, Karol Nawrocki, revoked Zelenskyy’s Order of the White Eagle, the highest state honour available to non-Poles. Both sides refused to back down, returning further honours and pretty much freezing mutual relations.
This is all great fodder for the Russian propaganda that runs amok on Polish social media. Misinformation about Ukrainian “welfare queens” claiming benefits at the expense of hard-working local people is fuelling tensions that, increasingly, turn to violence. A particularly vicious incident took place on 26 July, when a young Ukrainian couple was attacked outside a grocery store in Wrocław. The suspected attackers allegedly shouted, “go away to war”. Headlines trickle out almost daily about Ukrainian citizens being verbally abused or physically attacked in Polish streets.
Personal spats between leaders, historical disputes, Russian influence – these are some of the many reasons why the honeymoon is over. But another dimension of this deteriorating relationship keeps being overlooked. In dealing with the urgent fallout of the conflict, neither country had done enough to understand each other beyond the war. That failure is now coming back to haunt them.
To put it bluntly, Poland had failed to fully realise that Ukrainians were not just helpless victims of Vladimir Putin, but actual people with agency. As soon as they could, many Ukrainian refugees moved out of their hosts’ living rooms and rented or bought apartments. They set up businesses, many of which are now flourishing, and created a robust community, often engaging in direct competition with local people. They refused to behave as grateful or passive recipients of Polish charity. This is an understandable, indeed desirable progression, but as a result, compassion ceased to be the currency of the relationship between Poles and Ukrainians. For Poland, a country nearly entirely ethnically homogenous since its postwar years, such a change became difficult, if not impossible, to handle.
But Ukraine is of course, a country like any other, with a large economy and national interests beyond its resistance to Putin’s war of aggression. It has evolved from passive recipient of western aid in the aftermath of the full-scale invasion in 2022, to a global exporter of new military technology and knowhow. Accustomed to direct talks with US and western European leaders, Ukranians do not need an “advocate”, certainly not in Warsaw. Zelenskyy can run his own show.
What emerges, therefore, is contempt in place of cooperation, and hate in place of hope. The initial enthusiasm was bound eventually to disappear, and both governments should have prepared for that. Instead, they allowed a vacuum to be filled by Russian misinformation aimed at pulling the two countries further apart, thus weakening Europe’s support for Ukraine. Such an outcome could and should have been avoided, especially by Donald Tusk’s liberal governing coalition.
It failed to recognise Ukraine’s growing ambitions and continued to feed the myth that Warsaw was destined to play a Promethean role in Kyiv’s future. It did not prepare its own people for accepting refugees as fully fledged members of society. And it fostered the delusion that it was Poland that, somehow, had a decisive vote on whether Ukraine enters democratic Europe.
Poland’s shortsightedness is a cautionary tale. Whatever happens in the next few years, it seems certain that Ukraine will be drawn closer to Europe, and Ukrainians closer to the European economies. They will become business competitors to the French and Germans, just as they have been to the Poles. Ukrainian leaders will come to Brussels, Paris and Berlin, asking not for free bullets and money, but for an equal voice, arguing that their defence of the continent against Russian barbarism has earned them a seat at the table.
None of this should come as a surprise: Ukrainians are more than victims, and Ukraine is more than a country at war. Poland’s failure to take this into account has already had dramatic consequences. The rest of Europe still has time to prepare for that obvious reality.
- 
  Mateusz Mazzini is a Warsaw-based journalist writing on global affairs for Poland’s Gazeta Wyborcza and Polityka

Man on trial for Daphne Caruana Galizia murder claims he was framed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:34 UTC
13:00:34 KST

A businessman on trial for the murder of the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia has spoken about the charges for the first time in court since his arrest seven years ago, telling the jury he was framed by police and had nothing to do with the killing.
During four days of questioning by defence and the prosecution lawyers, Yorgen Fenech, 44, accused the most senior adviser to Malta’s prime minister of giving the go-ahead for the murder.
Fenech’s defence lawyers have repeatedly sought to identify Keith Schembri, Malta’s most powerful unelected official in the years leading up to the killing in October 2017, as the mastermind and instigator.
Fenech repeated those claims as he began giving testimony on Friday after unexpectedly waiving his right under Maltese law to refuse to give evidence at his own trial.
Fenech claimed that Schembri, who was chief of staff to the then prime minister Joseph Muscat, repeatedly leaked sensitive details to him, including advance warnings of raids and arrests.
During a court session on Saturday, the judge asked Fenech: “Do you know who the real mastermind is?” Fenech replied: “Keith Schembri.”
Police have told the jury that Schembri was never a suspect. He was called as a witness during the trial and has denied any involvement in the murder. The prosecution’s case rests on the testimony of the self-confessed middleman Melvin Theuma, a taxi driver who alleges Fenech gave him €150,000 (£128,000) to hire the three men convicted of planting the fatal car bomb.
In his testimony, Fenech spoke of his drug addiction and his close ties to senior police leaders and politicians, including WhatsApp messages he shared with Schembri and Muscat.
He began his testimony by describing a close friendship with Schembri. He said they had played football as children and reconnected as adults. Fenech said he had come to rely on Schembri, a successful businessman with interests in printing and packaging, and spoke to him most days.
Fenech claimed the idea of killing Caruana Galizia was raised during a barbecue at his family ranch. She had written about Schembri having a brain tumour before he had told his family about his condition.
“Keith was very emotional,” Fenech said. “He felt very strongly about it. We had to tell him to calm down … It wasn’t the first time he spoke about it, he was almost fixated with Daphne … He kept a file with all her articles.”
Fenech claimed Theuma, who also attended the barbecue, wound Schembri up further, saying of Caruana Galizia: “She’ll reap what she sows.”
“Then I was in the kitchen and Melvin came up to me and said ‘we can easily get rid of her’,” Fenech said. “It seemed a bit over the top, so I played it down and offered him a drink. I went outside for a smoke and Melvin and Keith continued chatting.”
Fenech claimed Theuma raised the subject again two weeks later. “Melvin was driving me to the airport. As soon as I got into the car, he told me that he had spoken to some people who told him there was already an active plan to murder Daphne Caruana Galizia.
“He said: ‘I’ve spoken to them, they’re already working on it and want €120,000.’ I was shocked, I told him I’d get back to him. At first I wasn’t going to tell Keith, but it kept playing in my mind and then I decided to tell him. He said ‘go ahead, go ahead, go ahead’.
“For Keith it was pure revenge, because he’d say she crossed a line by writing about personal matters.”
Fenech’s testimony painted a picture of a fixer gone rogue, with Theuma pressing ahead on his own initiative.
After the murder, Fenech claimed, Schembri began using him to relay messages to Theuma. One message was intended to warn the hitmen of their impending arrest.
“When I told Melvin, he brushed it off at first,” Fenech said. “He said it was normal for police to arrest people and then release them without charges 48 hours later. I relayed that back to Keith. He told me that the police had proof – a bomb code and some proof of phones being used. That one of the killers had topped up the bomb phone’s credit.
“I went back to Melvin and told him that, and that the arrest date was set for 4 December.”
Two brothers, George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their associate Vincent Muscat were arrested on 4 December 2017. They have all been convicted of the murder, with Muscat confessing his involvement in return for a shorter sentence.
Fenech claimed Schembri also warned him of Theuma’s arrest in 2019.
Under questioning by the prosecution, Fenech also said Schembri had shared a screenshot of a confidential report by Europol, which was helping the Maltese police, listing potential suspects.
The prosecution has relied in part on a series of recordings made by Theuma of his conversations with Fenech after the killing, in which they discussed the crime and leaks about the police inquiry.
Fenech said those recordings had been used to extract money from him. He claimed: “Melvin used recorded calls as blackmail … Keith got to know and panicked.”
He said he had handed over €400,000 to Theuma to pass on to the Degiorgio brothers to help pay their legal costs. He claimed the stress had destroyed his family life and his relationship with his wife.
“It drove me to drug addiction,” he said. “I spent my life being against drugs, seeing my brother abusing drugs. And I ended up taking drugs myself.”
He claimed investigators had helped to cover up Schembri’s role. “I felt betrayed,” Fenech said. “You combined Melvin Theuma’s lie and a cover-up of Keith Schembri to frame me.”
Challenging Fenech’s version of events, the prosecution lawyer Godwin Cini asked: “Would I be correct in saying you were the one with the power, not Melvin Theuma?”
The judge, Edwina Grima, later asked: “Why did Melvin Theuma feel he had power?” Fenech replied: “He knows who the real mastermind is.”
The judge then asked Fenech if he knew who the real mastermind was. He replied: “Keith Schembri.” Asked how he knew, he said: “I knew because Melvin Theuma would mention it and Keith Schembri intimated it.”
Ending his cross-examination, Cini said to Fenech: “Who are you trying to fool? Your fingerprints are all over this.”
Fenech is pleading not guilty to complicity in Caruana Galizia’s murder.
The trial continues.

Mood-boosting benefits of birdsong drowned out by traffic noise, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:34 UTC
13:00:34 KST

Hearing the trill or whistle of a bird while going about daily life is well known to boost people’s mood. But a new study suggests the psychological benefits of hearing birdsong are being threatened by traffic noise.
Researchers found that even low levels of traffic noise negatively affected the benefits to wellbeing that could otherwise be derived from listening to natural sounds.
Bird song has previously been associated with psychological benefits, including stress reduction and positive mood changes, while noise from traffic has been linked to both stress and annoyance.
“Bird sounds tend to be one of the elements of nature soundscapes that people perceive as being most relaxing, most pleasant, beneficial for them psychologically,” said Dr Eleanor Ratcliffe, associate professor in environmental psychology at the University of Surrey, and co-author of the study published in People and Nature.
The study involved more than 1,500 participants who listened to nine simulated soundscapes consisting of both birdsong and traffic noise and were asked questions about how they made them feel.
“We set up the study with the interest of looking at these differences in the objective properties of the soundscape, these levels of acoustic complexity that relate to different levels of biodiversity,” Ratcliffe said. “And our hypothesis was that these would lead to different effects on wellbeing and restoration and stress recovery.”
However, listening to birdsong was found to have a psychological benefit, irrespective of its acoustic characteristics. “It shows us that we should support and protect nature for the sake of nature, regardless of whether or not humans have some increased utility benefit from it,” said Ratcliffe.
In comparison, the presence of traffic noise negatively affected the psychological benefits of nature’s sounds. Analysis of complementary heart rate measurements on a group of participants showed significantly lower variability for those listening to soundscapes including traffic noise, indicating a greater physiological stress response.
The negative effect was found to be more evident when the acoustic characteristics of soundscapes were at high levels, something which may be attributed to overstimulation.
Researchers also analysed how differently aged participants responded. Younger participants reported higher feelings of wellbeing than their older peers, something suggested to result from their better hearing and enhanced acoustic experience.
Interestingly, the researchers found that greater feelings of wellbeing were recorded when participants perceived greater diversity in the types of birds they were listening to. This increased for participants who claimed greater knowledge of birds, suggesting perceptions of bird species richness may boost the benefits.
The work has design implications, the researchers said. “With urban planning now including more green spaces it is important that steps are taken so that people enjoy such areas to their fullest,” said Ratcliffe.
Suggested measures to minimise traffic noise include reducing speed limits and increasing the density of ground-level vegetation around parks. The study also has implications at an individual level. “Listening to birds is quite an accessible way to engage with nature. So, I think it’s something that people can do without a lot of effort,” she added.

‘A mockery’: how offshore tax havens are thwarting the UK’s transparency push

13:00:34 KST

Since Britain’s offshore secrecy jurisdictions caved in to pressure from Westminster to embrace corporate transparency, finding out who owns a company in one of these island havens is, in theory at least, a piece of cake.
Take the Cayman Islands.
All you have to do is show that you have a “legitimate interest” in the data by proving that you are a researcher, journalist, member of a civil society group or a business person considering a transaction with the subject of your inquiry.
Next, you must explain how the information will be used for “preventing, detecting, investigating, combating or prosecution money laundering or its predicate offences or terrorist financing”.
There is a fee of at least $75 (£55) for each application. Until recently, this could only be done via the tricky method of an international wire transfer, although card payments are now available.
Now, fill out a lengthy form outlining exactly what information you’re after, cross your fingers and wait.
It isn’t exactly Companies House (for all its faults).
Even when the form has been submitted, the subject of the inquiry can apply for a three-year “protection from disclosure” (at a cost of $1,000) to stop the information being sent on, on the basis that corporate transparency could expose them to harm.
These applications are refused more often than not, a Cayman Islands spokesperson said, but justifications for exemption appear to be drawn quite widely.
Reasons could include revealing any connections to “activity such as testing products on animals, which might lead to them being targeted by activists”, according to guidelines written by the Cayman Islands government. This is not an uncommon precaution. It is also available in the UK for a fee of £100.
Transparency campaigners believe aspects of the system in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) are even worse.
There, officials will inform the subject of any inquiry – perhaps a powerful oligarch or a narco-trafficker – of the name of any organisation asking the inconvenient questions, though not the names of individuals.
Don’t expect a quick outcome either.
“Three months ago we asked whether a sanctioned Russian oligarch still owns a company holding millions worth of UK property,” said Steve Goodrich, the head of research and investigations at the anti-corruption campaign group Transparency International. “We still haven’t had a reply.”
Margaret Hodge, the veteran anti-corruption campaigner, said that the sclerotic and unpredictable nature of these corporate registries “makes a mockery of their purpose”.
Legitimate interest access registers of beneficial ownership (or Liarbos for fans of ironic acronyms) have come about after a seven-year campaign by the UK government to bring overseas territories – and crown dependencies such as Jersey and Guernsey – to heel.
The campaign has gathered steam amid mounting real-world examples of how Britain’s offshore havens had been used to launder money, avoid taxes or otherwise flout laws or other norms, such as the financial rules governing football.
Cayman Islands entities played a central role in the 1MDB scandal, one of the largest corruption cases in history.
The Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich secretly funded Chelsea FC with cash funnelled through companies in the BVI, a Guardian investigation revealed last year.
The BVI was the single most-used jurisdiction in the now infamous Pandora papers leak.
By earlier this year, after several missed deadlines, all of the overseas territories had responded to the drive to introduce Liarbos.
But, according to Stephen Abbott Pugh, of the transparency group Open Ownership, the registers are “too costly, too complicated and [it] takes too long to access this crucial information.
“So it remains locked away in most cases out of the reach of users with a legitimate interest in accessing it.”
A spokesperson for the Caymans said only 25 applications for information had been received in 19 months, citing this as evidence of lack of demand, rather than difficulty in accessing the system.
The spokesperson rejected criticism that the register was hard to use or costly and defended the islands’ reputation.
“In spite of the public perception created by Hollywood fiction, misguided NGOs, and the politicians whom they have influence over, no credible evidence has ever been presented that Cayman has a problem with illicit finance,” they said.
The new registers, according to the UK government’s own rhetoric, are only supposed to be an “interim step” towards fully public corporate registers accessible to all.
Dispute over the pace of progress towards greater transparency has fuelled simmering tension between London and offshore outposts.
Last year, Hodge – the government’s “anti-corruption champion” – was dispatched to the BVI on what was officially called a fact-finding mission but looked more like a shot across the bows.
Criticism of the BVI by two other leading anti-corruption voices in Westminster – Phil Brickell MP and Joe Powell MP – led to one BVI media outlet printing a cartoon of the duo.
Wearing thick boots, they were depicted kicking lumps out of Riley Right – a cartoon parakeet in a suit who serves as the islands’ corporate transparency mascot.
“The only way to shine a light on the dirty money flowing through British overseas territories like the BVI is to have full transparency over who owns the companies registered there,” said Powell.
“It’s completely unacceptable that following the money is still so hard, and it is a flagrant breach of their agreement with the British government.”
Brickell said the “eyes of the world” will be on the UK government when it hosts a summit on countering illicit finance this December.
“Failure to get our own house in order by then would be an acute embarrassment,” he said.
Hodge isn’t backing off either.
Earlier this year, she indicated that Westminster could force crown dependencies to improve transparency. Guernsey’s top politician responded by bemoaning “outdated prejudices” about the island.
Hodge fears that crown dependencies are now “hiding” behind a prolonged EU row over how corporate registers in the 27-nation bloc should look.
She doesn’t want to wait to see how that process plays out.
“With a new government in place under Andy Burnham, I would hope we will be able to review our approach and be effective,” she said.
Spokespeople for the Cayman Islands and the BVI rejected the suggestion that public access to corporate ownership registers were an accepted international standard and pointed out that tax and criminal authorities already had full access.
A BVI spokesperson said: “We are proud of our legitimate interest access (LIA) regime which has significantly strengthened the accuracy, security, and accessibility of beneficial ownership data.
“The regime offers greater transparency alongside appropriate protections for individual privacy, while remaining aligned with international standards, including the EU’s sixth anti-money laundering directive.”

Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:33 UTC
13:00:33 KST

Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leaving Iran increasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions?
It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon.
One analysis written by Hamid Paktinat, the founder of the Forum of Economic Activists, suggests the construction of alternative pipelines and export routes by Iran’s Gulf neighbours will halve the strait’s strategic value within three years.
Those who worry about wasting assets inevitably set store by the separate visits this week to Tehran of Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, and Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir. These two men are critical to renegotiating the terms for the reopening of the strait and the revival of the discarded memorandum of understanding agreed by the US and Iran in June.
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have both recently made unusually blunt comments about the need to end the war – and the economic consequence of continuing it. Ghalibaf said that regardless of how much military power Iran possessed, “if people are hungry” and there was no economic growth, the country could not endure. Security, he argued, could not be sustained without a functioning economy. He added that, as someone with a military background, “we know the value of peace better than those who talk about peace”.
Pezeshkian was even more blunt: “The war must end at some point,” he said. His argument was that Iran should end the conflict now, while Tehran still believes it is negotiating from a position of strength, rather than wait until its position weakens.
The Iranian central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, also recently went on TV to warn about the economic pressures. “We are facing four or five major challenges simultaneously, including maximum sanctions, blockade, cutting off oil exports, and a budget imbalance, each of which puts pressure on the economy,” he said. “One of the neighbouring countries told me that if one-fifth of what happened in your country happened in our country, we would not be able to govern the country.”
What is driving these remarks is the pressure on ordinary people in Iran, and an acceptance that the strait cannot become a permanent security doctrine in itself.
Hamid Asefi, a Tehran-based journalist specialising in geo-economics, is one of many warning that if Hormuz is to be played as Iran’s final card every time a crisis arises, this card will gradually lose its value. “A threat that is constantly repeated turns from ‘deterrence’ into a political habit; and a political habit, if not accompanied by concrete achievements, sooner or later leads to an inflation of threats,” he said.
The main question is no longer: can Iran close the strait, he wrote, but if Iran closes Hormuz to the world, does it open the door to power for itself or lock part of its power behind that door?
“This is the Hormuz paradox. In international politics, a lever that is constantly flaunted can become its own enemy because it forces others to plan to reduce their vulnerability […] the main question of Iranian policy in Hormuz must change from: ‘How can we make the passage difficult?’ to ‘How can we make the passage so safe and stable that everyone needs Iran to maintain this order?’”
That does not imply the lever is valueless. Far from it.
According to data compiled by the ship tracker Kpler, only 112 oil and gas tankers went through the strait between 1 and 19 August. Almost 79% used unconfirmed routes, 19% used Iran’s preferred northern route and 2% used the Omani route. In reality many of the ships that used the unknown routes probably turned off their transponders and used US protection along the Oman route.
It also appears that aided by the US government, Saudi, Emirati, Qatari and Kuwaiti oil companies have chartered a small group of oil tankers to take cargo through the southern route to the Gulf of Oman, where they then offload the oil to waiting tankers owned by their customers. Much of the risk is therefore transferred from shipping companies and oil customers to the more highly motivated state oil producers and to the US government. Iran has drawn up a blacklist of about 48 ships that it will try to ban or fine.
But the US government is probably exaggerating the impact of these workarounds. Chris Wright, the US secretary of energy, claimed on 18 August the US navy had assisted in the transfer of more than 15m barrels of oil and other products. He also claimed the average daily transfer of oil through the strait was now more than 8m barrels, but even this figure is less than half the prewar average and is anyway seen as inflated. Most ship data trackers estimate the daily figure at closer to 6m barrels a day.
Arsenio Dominguez, the secretary general of the International Maritime Organization, furthermore dismissed Donald Trump’s outlandish claim that the US navy had all but opened the strait, telling Bloomberg: “Given the very small number of ships that transit the strait of Hormuz, it is clear that this strait is, in practice, not open.” The US president has countered that all mines in the strait have been removed, leaving Iranian drone and naval attacks as the chief threat.
 But the fact that before the war the strait accounted for 20% of oil and oil-related products is serving as a catalyst for the restructuring of the global energy infrastructure. Countries in the Gulf are rapidly building a network of alternative pipelines, with the aim of protecting more than half of their prewar exports from the impact of Hormuz by the end of this decade.
Paktinat has looked through the region at the capacity, length and cost of pipelines being prepared in six countries over the next one to four years. He concluded Saudi Arabia’s reliance on the strait of Hormuz would decrease from 70% to 15%. The UAE’s reliance would decrease from 50% to 15%, and Iraq’s dependence would fall from 100% to 30%.
Kuwait and Qatar’s reliance would decrease from 100% to less than half. Bahrain’s reliance would fall from 100% to 15%, he assessed. Finally, Oman’s reliance would change from 0% to becoming a major coastal oil transfer hub for the entire region.
 Overall, he says, the strategic value of the strait of Hormuz will be halved within three years and almost lost within six years with the implementation of these projects. The narrow horseshoe waterway will remain, but its strategic importance – the centre of Iranian gravity – will have evaporated. 
 In the meantime, the US will try to turn Trump’s premature boast that the Iranian economy has completely collapsed into reality. It will try once again to block the vital arteries of the Iranian government across five key sectors: gold, cryptocurrency, technology, shipping and aviation.
Success is by no means guaranteed, as Trump must know from the failure to defeat Iran in his first term. But slowly chipping away at Iran’s economic resilience until the strait finally becomes an irrelevance may be Trump’s only remaining option.

Ming dynasty work shows how Chinese understood the world in the 1600s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:05 UTC
13:00:05 KST

Ming dynasty work shows how Chinese understood the world in the 1600s
Scholar Zhang Huang set out to document heaven, Earth and humanity in vast compendium described as a ‘visual summary of Chinese culture’
The result was an encyclopaedia spanning 127 volumes known as the Tushu Bian, or Compendium of Illustrations and Texts.
The work – published in 1613 – was compiled by Neo-Confucian scholar Zhang Huang and drew on more than 200 printed sources across several decades to document the concepts of heaven, Earth and humanity.
“His goal was to gather all the illustrations and texts an educated person needed to understand the world,” information designer Paul Kahn, who analysed the encyclopaedia, wrote in his book Mapping Knowledge Across Time: Seven Books That Visualised the World.
“The result was too costly to print during his lifetime. It was eventually carved on woodblocks and printed after his death,” Kahn wrote.
Kahn compared the Tushu Bian with six other books that described the world from the perspective of Euro-Mediterranean culture.

An Architecture of Attention: Inside Syn Architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

As Saudi Arabia's cities expand through increasingly ambitious cultural projects, Syn Architects has spent much of its practice looking at what predates that transformation. The practice's participation in the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale grew out of years spent documenting Najdi architecture, disappearing urban fabric, local materials and inherited forms of knowledge. For Syn, heritage becomes useful when it can be documented, tested and brought back into use.
This approach can be traced back to Shamalat Cultural Center, a 615-square-metre intervention on the outskirts of Diriyah. Originally an old mud house acquired and converted into a cultural hub by Saudi artist Maha Malluh, the project was developed through two distinct phases: restoration and addition. Parts of the earthen structure were retained, while a new volume was inserted within the footprint of the former yard and organised around remnants of the original adobe fence. Riyadh stone forms a deliberately contemporary backdrop to the textured mud walls. What matters at Shamalat is what the two phases allow the building to accommodate. The restored structure and new addition accommodate galleries, an artist residency, a darkroom and workshops, allowing the building to remain useful rather than becoming a static historical object.

Three Russian agents sentenced to 15 years for directing enemy attacks in Donetsk region
According to Ukrinform, the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) press center reported this.
One of those convicted was an employee of a repair facility serving Ukraine's Defense Forces who had been recruited by Russia. The SSU detained him in April 2025 in the Kramatorsk area.
The investigation established that the suspect came to the attention of Russian intelligence officers through his brother, who lives in Russia and works for the FSB.
During his shifts at the defense facility, the traitor recorded the locations of repair workshops used to restore heavy armored vehicles belonging to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The agent attempted to send photographs along with the coordinates of the buildings to his Russian handler through an anonymous chat on a messaging app.
Another convicted individual was an agent of Russian military intelligence who was detained by SSU counterintelligence officers near Pokrovsk in March this year.
"The enemy's task was carried out by an unemployed man from Dobropillia, who came to the attention of the Russians through anti-Ukrainian comments in Telegram channel chats," the SSU reported.
Investigators established that the suspect directed 1.5-ton guided aerial bombs at fortified areas and artillery positions of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, which are keeping Russian army assault groups under fire control in the Pokrovsk area.
A third individual, a resident of Kostiantynivka recruited by the FSB, was also sentenced to prison. SSU military counterintelligence exposed him in August 2025.
The suspect contacted Russian intelligence officers through pro-Kremlin Telegram channels and offered them his assistance.
According to case materials, the traitor directed Russian guided aerial bombs and FPV drones at civilian infrastructure in the frontline city. He also tracked the positions of Ukrainian military tactical UAV units carrying out combat missions in the Kramatorsk area.
"SSU officers exposed the Russian agents in advance and secured the positions of Ukrainian defenders in Donetsk region within the area of enemy intelligence activity," the agency emphasized.
Based on SSU materials, the court found all three guilty under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
As Ukrinform previously reported, SSU counterintelligence in Rivne region detained an FSB agent who had been directing Russian strikes against the western region and was preparing to physically eliminate members of Ukraine's Defense Forces.

The number of deaths rose 2.0 percent to 27,794 in June compared to the same month of last year.
Affected by still-low births and high deaths, the natural population decline stood at 4,683 in the month. ■

The weighted average rate for new bank loans dipped 0.04 percentage points from a month earlier to an annualized rate of 4.27 percent in July, shifting downward from an increase of 0.12 percentage points in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The rate for banks' new corporate loans declined 0.07 percentage points to 4.20 percent in July on a monthly basis.
The lending rate for large companies ticked up 0.01 percentage point to 4.18 percent, driven by a growth in short-term market interest rates, while the rate for small and medium enterprises tumbled 0.16 percentage points to 4.22 percent.
Amid rising inflationary pressure, the BOK raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent in July, turning toward monetary tightening in about three and a half years since January 2023.
The rate for fresh bank loans to households surged 0.14 percentage points over the month to 4.64 percent in July.
Mortgage loan rate for households swelled 0.12 percentage points to 4.48 percent, and credit loan rate soared 0.25 percentage points to 5.97 percent.
The weighted average rate for new bank deposits was up 0.13 percentage points over the month to an annualized 3.21 percent in July. ■

Feature: First Russian-born panda "Katyusha" celebrates 3rd birthday in Moscow
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:53:21 CST
12:53:21 KST

by Xinhua writer Vladislava Chugueva
MOSCOW, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Even in August, months after the Chinese New Year, Moscow Zoo takes on a distinctly Chinese air.
Scarlet lanterns, an iconic symbol of joy and festivity in Chinese culture, sway above a tea-ceremony stall, while visitors pose in colorful costumes and gather around images of "Katyusha," the first giant panda born in Russia. The festive scene is all in celebration of the little celebrity's third birthday.
On Monday, the zoo marked her birthday with the start of a thematic "panda week," bringing together zoo staff, visitors and guests, including Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui and Svetlana Akulova, the zoo's general director.
"After all these years, we see that 'Katyusha' was born and has thrived. This is a fine fruit of our friendship, bringing our peoples closer," said Zhang, pledging continued support for the Moscow Zoo and expressed hope for more fruitful outcomes.
The cub's parents, "Ru Yi" and "Ding Ding," arrived in Moscow in April 2019 as part of a China-Russia panda conservation collaboration. On Aug. 24, 2023, "Ding Ding" gave birth to her first cub, making "Katyusha" the first giant panda born in Russia. The cub's name was chosen via a public vote that drew over 380,000 Russian participants.
Akulova extended her heartfelt gratitude to the Chinese people and her zoo's Chinese co-operating partners, thanking them for their unwavering trust and for the invaluable opportunity to join a conservation program dedicated to protecting this rare and captivating species.
"'Katyusha' turns three today. It may sound young, yet it represents a major milestone. Tremendous efforts have been made by our keepers and staff, as well as through our diplomatic cooperation," Akulova added.
On her birthday, "Katyusha" was the center of attention. A large portrait of the panda hangs near her enclosure against a traditional Chinese-style backdrop, while visitors nearby use tufting techniques to create a carpet featuring her likeness.
For young visitor Lida Yermolaeva, the celebration means more than just pandas. "When we talk about things that are simple, warm and positive, I believe they have a very positive effect and only serve to strengthen our bonds," she told Xinhua.
As zookeepers brought out a bespoke birthday cake decorated with flowers, parents lifted their children into the air for a better view of the young panda enjoying her special treat.
Among the visitors was Irina, a middle-aged woman who had traveled from another city to visit Moscow Zoo. She told Xinhua that pandas inspire people to embrace kindness and peaceful coexistence. "They are so fluffy, soft and gentle. It is simply wonderful," she said with a smile.
The celebration reached another high point when a traditional Chinese lion dance began in front of the enclosure. As the performers, dressed in colorful lion costumes, blinked and bounded through a series of acrobatic routines, visitors gathered around to take group photos.
Once the cake was gone, "Katyusha" returned to her usual routine, sitting quietly beneath the roof of her enclosure and munching on bamboo. Around her, visitors lingered, watching and smiling. It was a small birthday celebration, but one that offered a simple reminder of how a panda can bring people closer. ■

Inflation slows again in July but heightens risk of interest rate hike by RBA
In short:
Headline inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in the year to July, making it lower than before the Iran War in February.
However, the RBA's preferred measure of inflation did not budge, staying at 3.6 per cent for the third straight month.
What's next?
Economists say the figures have increased the risk of a rate hike by the RBA at its September meeting.
Economists have warned that another interest rate hike by Australia's central bank is a "live" possibility this year, despite inflation cooling again.
Figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed the annual headline inflation rate rose to 3.5 per cent last month, down from 3.8 per cent for the year to June.
Housing was the largest contributor to the Consumer Price Index in July, which increased by 5 per cent due to rising costs associated with new dwellings.
Food inflation also increased by 3.2 per cent in the year to July, driven mostly by higher prices for dining out and takeaway meals, while annual inflation for transport rose 1.6 per cent.
"On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 7.5 per cent in July after falling for three months in a row," said the ABS's head of price statistics Rachel McCririck.
"This was driven by higher world oil prices and the partial unwinding of the federal government's fuel excise relief measures in July."
The headline rate of 3.5 per cent in July was slightly higher than the 3.3 per cent figure predicted by many economists, but the annual rate is now lower than it was before the start of the Iran war in February.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers welcomed the "moderation" in annual inflation, but said he expected the data to fluctuate further in the coming months.
"It does mean that inflation is substantially lower than the budget forecast, but we're under no illusions because we know that people are still under pressure," he said.
"Fuel was a big driver of inflation in July and the fuel excise relief comes off in August, so we expect that to play out in next month's figures.
"Inflation will bounce around a bit as it gets further down to the Reserve Bank's target range."
The underlying inflation or "trimmed mean" figure preferred by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which strips out volatile items like fuel, remained unchanged at 3.6 per cent.
But the monthly trimmed mean figure increased to 0.5 per cent, leading economists to warn the figures could warrant a further interest rate hike from the RBA.
"If you annualise that number, we get 3.6 [to] 3.8 per cent, so that's just way too far from the RBA's target [between 2.5 to 3 per cent]," said AMP economist My Bui.
"And even on the annual numbers, it has been 3.6 per cent three months in a row, contrary to people's hope that it has been softening somewhat.
"This inflation seems not to move at all. It is still stuck around that really high range."
Increased risk of rate hike
Prior to the release of the July inflation data almost 83 per cent of economists polled by Reuters expected the RBA to keep interest rates on hold at its next meeting in late September.
But Ms Bui said it was likely the RBA would be concerned by the figures and would consider lifting rates at a future meeting.
"I think the RBA would be quite worried. Yesterday we got the minutes from their latest meeting and they actually admitted to us that they think the risk to inflation is on the upside," she said.
"They should be quite worried … because the ABS said a lot of the drivers of inflation were concentrated in the sticky services area.
"We do think that there is a very high chance of another rate hike coming for Australia before the end of the year."
David Bassanese, the chief economist at Betashares, said the figures meant the RBA's September meeting was "live".
"Today's higher-than-expected underlying inflation result is an unfortunate kick in the guts for an already ailing economy as it increases the risk of yet another Reserve Bank interest rate increase at next month's policy meeting," he said.
"The only question now is whether today's result is bad enough to force the RBA's hand as early as next month, or whether it would be prepared to wait for the following monthly inflation report on 30 September — which would be one day after its September policy meeting.
"At this stage I still anticipate the RBA will hold fire. There are still important GDP and employment results to come in the next few weeks.
"That said, the risk of an RBA rate hike next month is now at least 30 to 40 per cent and mortgage holders are in for a nervous wait."
However, not all economists believe the data warrants an increase to the cash rate in the coming months.
Callam Pickering, APAC economist at Indeed, said while Australia clearly had an inflation problem, he did not think the RBA would raise rates this year.
"Demand exceeds supply and productivity growth is absolutely dreadful — that's not typically a recipe for low and stable inflation," he said.
"We no longer anticipate another rate hike this year. However, the RBA still appears to be hawkish.
"On balance, the next move is still more likely to be up than down, particularly if productivity growth doesn't improve."
The RBA will announce its next interest rate decision on September 29.

“I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction over cancelling a private event,” Mamdani, the first Muslim and Indian American mayor of New York City, said when asked if the event should be cancelled.
