Chinese envoy calls for cessation of hostilities to ensure food production
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
11:00:23 CST
12:00:23 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Tuesday called for greater efforts to end hostilities and create a secure environment for food production.
Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations, made the remarks at a Security Council open debate on the council's role in mitigating global and local food crises.
"Raging conflicts displace people, destroy farmland and disrupt food production, and are an important driver of humanitarian crises and hunger," said Fu.
"The Security Council bears the primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. It should make promoting political solutions to conflicts a priority, actively engage in mediation and good offices, encourage the parties to resolve their differences through dialogue, and work for an early and lasting ceasefire to create the basic conditions for restoring agricultural production," he said.
International humanitarian law is a fundamental baseline that must be respected, Fu said, stressing that hunger must never be used as a weapon of war.
Parties to conflict should always put the protection of life first, protect agricultural infrastructure, avoid disrupting agricultural activities, and ensure the unimpeded delivery of humanitarian assistance, including food aid, he said.
In the context of economic globalization, food production and supply are closely linked to the international situation, particularly the global logistics and transportation system. In the face of intensifying geopolitical rivalry and regional conflicts, the international community should ensure the safe and unobstructed operation of land and sea trade routes and the normal flow of essential goods such as food and fertilizer, Fu said.
China welcomes the UN initiative to establish a time-bound mechanism for the Strait of Hormuz and supports a greater role for the United Nations, he said.
At the same time, all parties should further uphold open and transparent market policies, deepen international cooperation on food supply, and promote the rational allocation of food resources globally, he said.
Food security governance is a global issue that requires coordinated action and a collective response from all countries. It cannot be dictated by a handful of countries or interest groups, Fu said.
All parties should firmly support the United Nations in playing a central role, while the representation and voice of emerging market economies and developing countries in international organizations dealing with food-related issues should be effectively enhanced, he said.
"We should uphold the principles of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, promote a more equitable, reasonable, inclusive and effective global food security governance system, and safeguard the common interests of all countries," Fu said.
As the world's largest grain producer, China feeds more than 1.4 billion people with less than 9 percent of the world's arable land. Through its own efforts, China has achieved basic self-sufficiency in grain supply and absolute security of staple food, Fu said.
"This is not only a great achievement in China's development, but also a major contribution to safeguarding global food security," he said.
China has always been committed to strengthening international cooperation, helping improve global food security and contributing to global poverty reduction, Fu said.
China stands ready to continue upholding the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, work with all parties, and make greater contributions to the complete eradication of global hunger and to world peace, security, development and prosperity, he added. ■

Writing the rulebook? China to steer world’s first solid-state battery standards
As next-gen EV tech accelerates, the global standard agency’s nod could allow Beijing to export its domestic testing benchmarks worldwide
A Chinese-proposed international standard for automotive solid-state batteries has been approved as a new work item by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) – marking the first of its kind for the advanced power systems and the nation’s latest effort to shape rules in emerging industries.
Led by China, with input from technical experts in France, Japan, South Korea and other countries, the proposal outlined application guidelines, items and conditions for testing rechargeable lithium-ion solid-state batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs), according to an official statement by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR).
The governmental agency said the framework would draw on domestic research and development benchmarks to standardise testing specifications for solid-state batteries, which are widely viewed as the next frontier for EV power systems.
Announced by the SAMR last week, the China-led proposal comes amid intensifying global competition in advanced technologies, as major economies increasingly leverage standard-setting to secure long-term industrial influence.
“When Chinese products go to an overseas market, they will more easily meet the requirements – there will be few major changes in parameters, production processes and so on,” said a veteran Chinese researcher on international standardisation, who spoke on condition of anonymity. This would place China in the position of setting benchmarks that others followed, she noted.

NMC orders monthly reporting of student suicides by medical colleges

NMC orders monthly reporting of student suicides by medical colleges
Anuja Jaiswal / TNN / Updated: Aug 26, 2026, 10:54 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
For each suicide or unnatural death, colleges have to report the student's course/year, date and place of occurrence, police intimation, FIR status, institutional inquiry and corrective measures.
NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has directed medical colleges to maintain updated records of student suicides and unnatural deaths and submit a certified Action Taken Report (ATR) every month, following Supreme Court directions on student mental health and safety. It has also asked institutions to fill vacant faculty and key administrative posts within four months.The commission has marked the compliance exercise “MOST URGENT” and asked institutions to accord it top priority.The move comes amid a rise in student suicides. On this issue, Dr Om Prakash, Professor of Psychiatry and Head, Department of Geriatric Mental Health, sharing NCRB data, said 14,488 student deaths by suicide were recorded in 2024, up 4.3% from 13,892 in 2023. The number rose from 8,068 in 2014 to 14,488 in 2024, an increase of around 80% over the decade. More than 1.15 lakh student deaths by suicide were recorded during 2015-24.For each suicide or unnatural death, colleges have to report the student's course/year, date and place of occurrence, police intimation, FIR status, institutional inquiry and corrective measures.The NMC has also sought department-wise details of sanctioned, filled and vacant faculty posts, non-teaching vacancies and key administrative positions, including dean/director, medical superintendent, registrar, wardens and counsellors.
Colleges have been given four months to fill vacant faculty and key administrative posts, with special recruitment drives for reserved posts. The compliance format also requires 24x7 access to qualified medical assistance on campus or within 1 km.
The IHBAS presentation highlights the role of faculty as “gatekeepers”, who can often notice changes in attendance, academic performance, withdrawal or behaviour. Faculty are advised to recognise warning signs, approach distressed students, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, facilitate referral and follow up, without taking on the role of therapists.It also cautions against attributing suicide to a single trigger such as examination failure, relationship problems or social media. Academic pressure, fear of failure, bullying, ragging or harassment, discrimination, social isolation and financial difficulties are among the factors identified as contributing to vulnerability.The NMC said information submitted by institutions will be consolidated to monitor compliance with the Supreme Court's directions and submitted to the Ministry of Education as required.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

“There is still a big hole in my heart,” Nordone told supporters at a rally, “but I know he’s looking down right now very proud of everyone in this room.”

In June, Graham won the Republican primary race to compete for his fifth term as Senator, but after his death the following month, a special primary election was called for Aug. 11. While Nordone, who was appointed by South Carolina’s Governor to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term, earned the highest share of the vote on Aug. 11, she fell short of the majority she needed to win the race, triggering the runoff. Nordone earned nearly 33% of the vote on Aug. 11, while her opponent, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, came in second, with nearly 25%, sending both candidates to the runoff race.

He added that he asked Nordone to run for a full term, saying, “I hope Darline does this, in that there would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina.”
Although Nordone was a strong supporter of her brother’s political career over the years, she had never before held elected office. Her lack of political experience was the subject of scrutiny during her campaign, particularly after a debate against Norman leading up to Tuesday’s runoff. When asked during the debate if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S., Nordone replied: “I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security, so.”
Her opponents were quick to criticize her for the remark. Nikki Haley, Trump’s former U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. who endorsed Norman in the race, shared a clip of Nordone’s response to the debate question on X, saying, “Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not. This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate.”
Nordone responded to the backlash in an interview on Fox News.
“I tripped up on one question last night,” she said. “But you know, I’ve said many times, I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician. You know, I was just honest, and I think that’s kind of a foreign concept.”

The talks also covered the Middle East, Africa, and other global hotspots, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. Moscow and the Vatican also found common ground on protecting traditional values and discussed emerging issues such as AI.
Here are the key takeaways from Lavrov’s remarks following the meeting:
Ukraine conflict
Moscow praised the Vatican’s “balanced position” on the Ukraine conflict and briefed Gallagher on Russia’s approach to ending the hostilities by addressing the “root causes.”
President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia was forced to launch the military operation in Ukraine to protect civilians in the largely Russian-speaking Donbass. Moscow has also long described Kiev’s deepening military cooperation with NATO as a major threat to Russian national security.
Lavrov also praised the Vatican’s involvement in humanitarian efforts linked to the conflict, including work to reunite children separated from their families.
‘Blatant cruelty’
Lavrov noted the “blatant cruelty” of Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilians. He accused Kiev of striking civilian targets “on a daily basis,” including facilities where children are present.
Lavrov said another wave of Ukrainian strikes on several southern Russian regions early Monday killed three minors and injured six others at a childcare center in Krasnodar.
“We will [also] never forget and will seek justice for [Ukrainian leader Vladimir] Zelensky’s bloody terror attack in Starobelsk,” Lavrov said, referring to a drone strike in May on a college dormitory in the Donbass city. The attack killed 21 people, most of them teenage girls.
Russian language crackdown
Lavrov accused Kiev of waging an unprecedented campaign against the Russian language and Russian culture.
Ukraine is the only country to have outright banned Russian, he stated, arguing that no other state has gone as far in targeting Russian speakers.
“We discussed how Ukraine treats the Russian language, Russian education, Russian media, and Russian culture in general,” Lavrov said. He expressed hope that Vatican diplomats would raise the issue directly with Kiev.
Plight of Ukrainian Orthodox Church
Gallagher was also given a copy of its latest report on Kiev’s persecution of the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church. The report details “unlawful actions” against the church, the clergy, and parishioners and has already been submitted to the UN and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Lavrov said.
The Ukrainian authorities are “legislatively pursuing the destruction of the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church,” he warned, urging the Vatican to take a closer look at the issue.
Zelensky’s government has targeted the Ukrainian Orthodox Church for several years, accusing it of maintaining ties with Moscow despite the church declaring independence from the Russian Orthodox Church in 2022.
The crackdown has included monastery raids, property seizures, and dozens of criminal cases against clergy on collaboration charges. Kiev also supports the rival Orthodox Church of Ukraine, which the Russian Orthodox Church considers schismatic.
Moscow-Vatican ties
Despite deep geopolitical divisions elsewhere, Russia and the Vatican have managed to keep their relationship “trustworthy, friendly and pragmatic,” Lavrov said.
He praised the Holy See for favoring diplomacy and peaceful solutions and said Moscow remains ready to work closely with the Vatican on humanitarian issues.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the two sides discussed defending traditional spiritual and moral values, family reunification, prisoner exchanges, and the protection of Christian communities around the world.

SpaceX to build $100 billion rocket launch facility in southern Louisiana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:36:40 UTC
11:36:40 KST

SpaceX to build $100 billion rocket launch facility in southern Louisiana
SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday for a $100 billion rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, its largest yet, aimed at supporting Starship and AI satellite missions. The 125,000-acre Starbase Louisiana site on Pecan Island could eventually handle thousands of Starship launches annually, the company said.
SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build its largest rocket launch complex yet in southern Louisiana, a $100 billion effort to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company's Starship and AI satellite launch ambitions.
The 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site on Pecan Island, which SpaceX named Starbase Louisiana, is an expansion of the company's Starship launch operations beyond South Texas and those planned for Florida as its next-generation rocket remains in late-stage development.
The company's second Starbase campus will eventually launch thousands of Starship flights a year, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said, reiterating its goals for an ambitious cadence contingent on solving steep engineering challenges and regulatory hurdles.
Construction will begin next year with the first Starship launch in 2029, SpaceX said.
Shotwell detailed the plans near the proposed site in Louisiana's Vermilion Parish at an event with Governor Jeff Landry and other senior state officials.
Read moreAstrophysicist Jonathan McDowell explains why we need an international space traffic control agency
The "self-sustaining" spaceport envisioned by SpaceX will include its own methane production for propellant, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities to transport Starships from Texas, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport, Shotwell said.
The marshland site is more than eight times the size of Manhattan. Shotwell said "very large portions" of the land will remain natural wetlands with no infrastructure, while an animated SpaceX video showed the area dotted with several launch pads surrounded by greenery.
The site had been at the center of a decade-long lawsuit against ExxonMobil brought by local parishes alleging the oil major's coastal drilling and canal dredging contributed to the state's wetland loss. The state reached an agreement with Exxon to settle the lawsuit in June, prompting its dismissal the following month, a court order shows.
That cleared the way for SpaceX's launch plans for the 18-mile (29-km) coastal strip, which the company had beendiscussing with the state since February, Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois said.
SpaceX has significantly expanded its southern US footprint in recent years, having built Colossus AI data centers in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas. It is planning a chip plant in central Texas.
"This project means more than just steel, technology, and capital," Landry said. "It represents jobs for our families. It represents momentum for our communities, and it represents protection for our coast."
SpaceX said the Louisiana site will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region. The governor's office said those jobs are expected to pay an average salary of $92,600, or 192% higher than the average wage in Vermilion Parish.
Read moreSchool-bus-sized chunk of SpaceX rocket believed to have crashed into the Moon
Second Starbase
The launch site, which will be SpaceX's fourth in the US appears to replicate at a larger scale its widening footprint in South Texas, site of its first Starbase rocket campus. However, the Louisiana site will not have rocket production facilities.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk sees Starship as central to the company's goals of expanding its Starlink constellation and eventually deploying up to 1 million AI data-processing satellites in orbit. The rocket also plays a key role in NASA's Artemis moon program.
Pecan Island is situated in a geographically convenient location for Musk's satellite ambitions. It allows a rocket to launch south over the Gulf waters and into a sun-synchronous orbit that offers plenty of sunlight for solar-powered AI satellites.
Starbase Texas is Starship's only active launch site as the rocket remains in development, while SpaceX builds two Starship pads in Florida next to its flagship Falcon 9 launch pads. The company also has Falcon 9 launch facilities at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
As SpaceX developed Boca Chica, Texas, into the company town of Starbase with support from local government officials, it has faced resistance from residents concerned about water, environmental and noise pollution and pressure to sell their land.
Shotwell highlighted environmental plans and outlined efforts to restore Pecan Island's receding marshlands and coastline, which act as a natural buffer to protect inland areas from flooding during heavy rainfall.
Pecan Island is a protected hub for dozens of migratory bird species seasonally traveling throughout the Western Hemisphere.
At Starbase Texas, Starship launches have blasted shorebirds and their nests with gravel and debris, according to environmental groups.
"The birds might fly away during a launch, but I guarantee they come back," Shotwell said, prompting applause from state officials. "As soon as the rocket's gone, the birds come back. It's not like months later."
She said SpaceX will help fund environmental "protection, restoration, and stewardship" while the launch site is constructed.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Search expert details exhumation of Polish Army soldiers in Lviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:32:00 UTC

Search expert details exhumation of Polish Army soldiers in Lviv
Liubomyr Horbach, head of the Pamiat Society for the Search for War Victims, told Ukrinform.
According to him, the Ukrainian side is represented by a team from the Pamiat Society, while the Polish team includes specialists from Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance and Wroclaw Medical University. The Ukrainian and Polish teams include search experts, archaeologists and anthropologists. About 30 specialists will work at the site in total.
“Based on search operations conducted in 2010 and 2019, 110–120 individual graves of Polish Army soldiers were discovered at the cemetery. They were killed in battles against German military units that had encircled Lviv from the west and south in September 1939. The graves include Poles, Ukrainians and representatives of other nationalities who served in or were mobilized into the Polish Army,” Horbach said.
The graves are arranged in three rows. The area where the Ukrainian and Polish specialists will work measures 40 by 12 meters. Some of the graves have been flooded by groundwater, which will have to be pumped out. The teams initially plan to excavate five graves per day.
“We will work manually because using machinery would be impractical in this case. Once the remains are uncovered and recovered, anthropologists will examine them. In particular, they will collect samples for DNA testing. The soldiers buried here are officially listed as missing. Work is underway in Poland to locate their relatives and obtain their DNA so that we can establish the identities of the soldiers buried here. Items found in the graves may also help with identification, including military identification tags, if they have survived,” Horbach said.
According to him, the exhumed remains will be reburied at a cemetery in Mostyska, where the remains of about 200 Polish soldiers were reburied in 2015–2016 and again in 2025.
As reported, the exhumation of the remains of Polish Army soldiers has begun at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv. The exhumation research is being carried out in accordance with agreements reached through the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on National Remembrance.

Three takeaways from Tuesday's South Carolina Republican Senate primary
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 - South Carolina Republicans on Tuesday nominated Darline Graham to run in November's general election for her late brother's U.S. Senate seat, as she defeated Representative Ralph Norman in a primary runoff.
Here are some takeaways from the result:
TRUMP ENDORSEMENT PAID OFF
President Donald Trump didn't just endorse Graham – sharing a stage with her in South Carolina on Friday, he declared that he too was "on the ballot."
A day before the primary runoff, he appeared to hedge his bets: For "a few" of the candidates he endorsed it was "almost impossible for them to win," he posted on Truth Social, but he felt "obligated" to back them. He did not specify which candidates he was referring to, though the post came amid concerns about the viability of Graham's campaign.
By late Tuesday, however, it was clear she had pulled it off. While Norman performed well in his home base of Greenville, Graham outperformed him in much of the rest of the state – including a resounding win in the area surrounding Myrtle Beach, where Trump campaigned with her last week.
It was a much-needed win for Trump, facing mounting public concerns over inflation, the conflict with Iran and an escalating trade war with Canada.
Only 33% of Americans approve of his performance, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, but Tuesday's result shows he still has singular influence among Republican voters.
The president's ability to boost turnout among his party faithful will be a key factor in determining whether Republicans are able to retain control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in November's midterm elections.
MAGA INC. MEGA MONEY
A political action committee, MAGA INC., established to support Trump, spent $827,711 to bolster Graham's campaign, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission.
While Trump has given his vocal endorsement to Republicans in races across the country, his PAC has rarely contributed to their campaigns.
It appears to have paid off for Trump, and could embolden MAGA INC. to keep the money flowing to the president's favored candidates in key races going forward.
GRAHAM AN UNLIKELY REBEL IN THE SENATE
The late Senator Lindsey Graham became a close ally of Trump's after a rocky start in 2016 when, as a candidate in the Republican presidential primaries, he referred to Trump as a "bigot" and "complete idiot."
He would go on to become a frequent golfing companion of the president and one of his most loyal supporters in Congress.
Darline Graham so far has followed in her brother's footsteps, and would appear to be another ally in the making for Trump. It is still unclear, however, whether Republicans will be able to hold onto their slim Senate majority next year.
Whether they do or not, Graham is looking like she could be in the mold of many first-term senators who have held to another tradition, keeping their heads down during their maiden year and following their leadership's desires. REUTERS

Taiwan wholesale revenue hits record NT$1.76 trillion in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:21:46 UTC
11:21:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's wholesale revenue reached a record NT$1.7573 trillion (US$55.16 billion) in July, surging 56.4% from a year earlier, according to a Ministry of Economic Affairs press release on Tuesday.
The July total was the highest monthly wholesale revenue on record and marked the 18th consecutive month of year-on-year growth. Demand for AI, high-performance computing, and cloud services drove shipments across related supply chains.
Wholesale revenue for the first seven months rose to NT$10.7905 trillion, up 36.2% from the same period last year and a record for the first seven months. At the current pace, wholesale revenue could surpass the annual record set in 2025 as early as September, according to MOEA Department of Statistics Deputy Director-General Chen Yu-fang (陳玉芳).
Retail revenue also reached a record for July, totaling NT$418.3 billion, up 7.7% year on year. Revenue for the first seven months reached NT$2.881 trillion, up 4.6% from the same period last year and a record for the January-July period.
The automotive and motorized two-wheel vehicle sector grew 12.6% year on year, while department stores rose 9.6% and information and communications technology and home appliance retailers increased 12.5%. Hypermarkets and convenience stores also posted gains of 10.3% and 4.2%, respectively.
Chen said the automotive and motorized two-wheel vehicle market benefited from summer promotional campaigns and the introduction of new models, contributing to growth for a second consecutive month. However, she cautioned that major purchases typically slow during Ghost Month, which falls in August this year.
Food services revenue reached NT$88.7 billion in July, up 2.5% from a year earlier and the highest July figure on record. Revenue for the first seven months totaled NT$642.2 billion, up 3.9% year on year and also a record for the period.
Restaurant revenue increased 0.8%, while beverage shops posted a 9.7% increase as summer vacation boosted dining out and group meals. Catering and group meal contracting services rose 7.7%, supported by continued cross-border travel and increased demand for in-flight catering.
Chen said the number of days affected by typhoons in July was greater than expected, weighing on retail and food-service revenue growth. While supermarkets and hypermarkets benefited from increased demand for supplies ahead of storms, some businesses were hurt by typhoon-related closures and cancellations.
Regarding the impact of the Central Union Oil food-safety incident on July retail and food-service sales, Chen said the availability of substitute products meant the overall impact was not significant. The ministry attributed the weaker-than-expected growth primarily to typhoons.
Looking ahead, the ministry expects retail sales in August to benefit from Father's Day and Chinese Valentine's Day promotions, while food services are expected to receive support from summer travel, dining out, festive gatherings, and demand for cold beverages amid high temperatures.

Productivity Commission slams political attacks on integrity after GST report
In short:
WA Premier Roger Cook called the Productivity Commission "east coast clowns" over its interim findings on GST, with a senior federal minister casting doubt over the report's validity.
The interim report recommended changing the current GST arrangements, saying they were a "costly mistake" and the only state better off was WA.
What's next?
Angela Jackson told the ABC the commission welcomed debate ahead of their final report, which she stressed would not be influenced by politics.
The Productivity Commission says the WA premier "crossed a line" with his criticisms of the body's interim report on GST, adding that political commentary from federal government ministers undermines the commission's integrity.
The report, released earlier this month, was tasked with looking at GST distribution reforms put in place in 2018. It described those arrangements as a "costly mistake" that had forced Australian taxpayers to foot the bill of almost $23 billion, and the only state better off was WA.
WA Premier Roger Cook lashed the report authors as "east coast clowns" and described the commission's proposals for change as "dodgy, deceitful, and quite frankly dumb".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese labelled the findings as an "economic rationalist" position, while Resources Minister Madeleine King sympathised with the WA premier's comments and cast doubt on the report's methodology.
Within days of the interim report's release, Mr Albanese stood with Mr Cook in Perth, pledging not to unwind any deal for WA while he was prime minister.
Productivity commissioner and economist Angela Jackson, who co-authored the report, said the body welcomed public debate, but the WA premier's remarks went too far.
"Our view is that a line was crossed in terms of the nature of those comments," she told ABC Radio National.
"To undermine and, I guess, attack our integrity, I think, is an additional bridge too far.
"We want to call this out as being unacceptable as a result. But that said, in doing that, we welcome ongoing dialogue with Western Australia."
Mr Albanese this week distanced his party from the commission's report, pointing out the previous Morrison government commissioned it.
"This report was commissioned by the Morrison government, not us," he said.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who wrote the terms of reference for the report, said today the Productivity Commission is "full of really good people ... publicly-spirited people".
"I want them to know just how much I value their work," he said.
"I don't consider what the PM said to be inappropriate, but I think some of the other commentary around it has been unfortunate," Mr Chalmers said.
"I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them."
Commission says it is 'above politics'
Dr Jackson said the prime minister's comments were "disappointing" but added that most economists would take being described as "economic rationalists" as a "badge of honour".
She said the findings were part of an interim report and were subject to consultation and change.
The productivity commission was independent and would not be swayed by politicians' views, she added.
"We often refine our recommendations. We may well change our recommendations in some instances, depending on the feedback we receive," she said.
"It's important for us to indicate that that process will not be influenced by the prime minister's comments,"
"We are above politics."
Dr Jackson's comments come after her co-author, Alex Robson, told The Australian Financial Review (AFR) he was disappointed by senior Labor member's comments, which he called inappropriate.
"I totally reject those comments and the language used. It doesn't advance the policy debate at all," he told the AFR.
Other government ministers have declined to condemn Mr Cook's remarks.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres today told the ABC his "east coast clowns" comment was "colourful language" but insisted Labor welcomed debate and MPs did not have a "glass jaw".
Ms King, who hails from WA, said Mr Cook's comments were "fair enough", although she would not use that language herself.
"I don't actually quite agree that it [the Productivity Commission] has gone through it as methodically as it might have," she told ABC's Radio National on Tuesday.
"I respect the work of the commissioners. And I also note there are no Western Australians on the Productivity Commission."
The Productivity Commission is the independent research and advisory body for the Australian government, undertaking research in areas like housing supply, childcare subsidies and hospital funding and carrying out ongoing work on Closing the Gap.

The trade war came too soon for Mark Carney’s middle powers alliance
The Canadian prime minister called for pro-trade democracies to resist great-power coercion together. Seven months later, he is largely fighting Trump alone.
At the start of the year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called on the world’s middle powers to band together against Donald Trump. But a new trade war with the U.S. came before they were ready.
Seven months after Carney called in a landmark speech in Davos on fellow democracies and supporters of free trade to join together and resist economic coercion, they have largely left him to do battle with Trump alone.
The U.S. president’s 50 percent tariffs imposed on $20 billion in Canadian goods last week should be a wake-up call to Ottawa’s allies, said one Canadian official with knowledge of the trade talks.

Other countries have tried to appease Trump, the official said. But Canada, which has the most to lose since it’s so economically and geographically intertwined with the U.S., has “put out our chest.”
After Carney walked away from a deal that in his view threatened Canada’s sovereignty, he vowed to fight back. Advertisement
Gondor calls for aid
For more than a year, the EU, Canada, the United Kingdom and other economies have talked up plans to deepen ties between the EU and an Asia-Pacific trade bloc called the CPTPP — which includes Canada, Australia, Japan and the U.K. — to counter Trump’s trade coercion.
Since Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea at a summit of EU leaders in June 2025, progress on bringing the EU and the 12-nation CPTPP together has been glacial.
“The mechanisms for responding collectively to economic coercion are still at an early stage,” said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft — a new Canadian foreign policy think tank.
Ursula von der Leyen speaks at a press conference in Brussels on March 18, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/Getty Images
“I would describe the progress as meaningful, but incomplete: the political alignment is increasingly there; the institutions and instruments now need to catch up,” Nadjibulla said. “There needs to be much greater coordination among Canada, Europe and democratic partners in Asia on economic security.”
The European Union, the U.K. and allies like Japan are now keeping their heads down as they digest the lessons from Carney’s lonely stand against Trump.
Advertisement
Bernd Lange, the chair of the EU Parliament’s trade committee, was quick to express solidarity with Canada. But the European Commission, EU leaders and the U.K. have avoided taking sides publicly. Behind the scenes, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke with Carney on Monday.
When asked if the EU would stand by Canada’s side following Trump’s tariff threats, deputy chief spokesperson Arianna Podestà said on Tuesday that “the U.S. and Canada are both important trade partners for the European Union, and we of course continue to work closely with both, aiming to maintain stability and predictability in transatlantic as well as in global trade.”
“We are opposed to tariffs as they are taxes which end up being paid by importers and consumers,” she added.
Since Trump’s return to the White House, EU institutions and governments have been determined to keep him onside and avoid escalation. That approach resulted in a trade truce that was seen as one-sided until the European Parliament pushed hard to strengthen its guardrails following Trump’s threats at the start of this year to take over Greenland, a Danish territory.
“The Europeans will push back to defend their own interests when they have to, but they are also trying to accommodate Trump because they still need America,” said Tom Wright, a foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution who was a senior director at the National Security Council during the Biden administration. “Europe is politically close to Canada, but coordinating a collective pushback against Washington would feel like a significant escalation.”
The U.K. isn’t likely to join a collective pushback against Trump, either.
Advertisement
Both the U.S. and Canada are “among the very top trade and investment partners for the U.K.,” said William Bain, head of trade policy at the British Chambers of Commerce, noting “there are no winners from the escalation of this trade dispute.”
British firms, Bain said, “value” the Economic Prosperity Deal struck with the Trump administration last year, which halved the White House’s steel tariffs and lowered automotive tariffs. The BCC also wants to see the U.K.-U.S. Technology Prosperity Deal “implemented in full through continuing negotiations between both governments,” Bain added, after parts of the pact were frozen last year.
Trump’s threats to levy further tariffs on the U.K. over its Digital Services Tax have also prompted Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government to say it’s “open to discussing U.S. concerns” about the revenues it collects from U.S. tech firms.
Andy Burnham engages with local community members in Stevenage, England, on Aug. 12, 2026. | Ben Montgomery/Getty Images
The world as it is
The latest clash with Washington has led Carney to step up his outreach toward the EU.
“This fall we will begin intense discussions with the European Union, the world’s second-largest economy, to build a much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership,” Carney said on Monday. “We can build such unparalleled access, because we can be trusted.”
Brussels has a lot riding on Carney’s gambit. Like the EU a year ago, Canada balked at U.S. requests it saw as encroaching on its sovereignty. In Canada’s case, they relate to Canada’s French-language and cultural protections — enshrined in its constitution — and demands that would have compromised Ottawa’s ability to strike trade deals with other partners.
Advertisement
Washington has similarly been pushing Brussels to cut back its green and tech rulebooks, doubling down on those demands over the summer. The EU executive insists its rulebooks aren’t up for negotiation. If Carney prevails, that could help Brussels hold the line.
Canada is also confronting a weaker Trump than Brussels did a year ago. His original tariffs have since been struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court, while the November midterm elections could further weaken his hand.
“There was also a political calculation from Canada that trying to reach a deal now was not a good idea and that it was actually better to stay firm, with the expectation that after the midterms, if anything, the United States administration may be in a weaker position,” said Ignacio García Bercero, the European Commission’s former top official on U.S. trade.
An EU-Canada summit is due to take place at the end of October, when the two sides will look to cement their partnership.
London and Ottawa are also working toward striking a new strategic partnership this year that would deepen trade ties.
“We are continuing to deepen these ties through the CPTPP and the Economic and Trade Working Group,” a U.K. government spokesperson said of Britain’s economic relations with Canada.
Advertisement
But diversifying away from the world’s biggest economy and building a coalition capable of resisting U.S. pressure could still take years, particularly while potential allies remain wary of confronting Trump.
“The middle powers tend to be the ones most committed to the multilateral trading system. But let’s be frank: Without the U.S. and China, it’s gonna have a hollow ring to it. For the moment, we have to be patient,” said Keith Rockwell, a former WTO spokesperson who is now a senior research fellow at the Hinrich Foundation.
Camille Gijs and Kathryn Carlson reported from Brussels, Graham Lanktree reported from London, and Stefanie Bolzen from Washington. Additional reporting by Nick Taylor-Vaisey in Ottawa.

Transgender former CIA officer Curlee opens up, over a year after leaving agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:15:00 UTC

Transgender former CIA officer Curlee opens up, over a year after leaving agency
WASHINGTON – When US President Donald Trump returned to power in 2025, Julia Curlee, a long-time Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analyst and transgender woman, opted to continue serving as a senior official at the White House despite right-wing attacks on trans issues.
But after a far-right influencer publicised her transgender identity online, the White House immediately dismissed her.
“They needed me. They asked me to stay” when Trump succeeded Joe Biden in the presidency, Curlee told AFP in an interview, over a year after she was fired.
“But the moment (my gender identity) became public and a political problem with their supporters, that’s when they got rid of me.”
Curlee, who has since resigned from the CIA after 20 years of service, recently shared her experience in a first-person essay published by The Atlantic magazine.
In her view, she was the victim of hypocrisy by Trump’s Republican Party.
Trump himself promised to end “transgender madness”, after campaigning on an agenda that included banning trans people from competing in sports, serving in the military and using bathrooms different from their birth sex.
“To live up to the hatred that they say they have, they had to fire me,” Curlee said.
‘It wasn’t ever an issue’
Now in her mid-40s, Curlee in 2013 became the first CIA officer to transition while working at the agency.
In 2017, during Trump’s first term, she successfully made it onto the National Security Council (NSC), the White House’s top advisory body on issues of national security, the military and foreign policy.
For a year, she gave daily intelligence briefings to then vice-president Mike Pence, a staunch conservative with a history of opposing LGBTQ rights.
Despite her close proximity to Pence as a trans woman, Curlee noted that his views did not impact her work.
“He never made it a problem. Everyone in his staff knew that I was transgender, but it wasn’t ever an issue,” she said.
It made her think working under a second Trump administration would be possible, she added. “Obviously, I was wrong.”
‘Humiliating’ return to CIA
Although Curlee decided to continue working for the White House after Trump won re-election in 2024 following an openly anti-trans political campaign, she lived with constant fear of being fired.
Three days after Trump’s return to office, many NSC staff were let go, but she was asked to stay.
“It was just being a handful of people, and it was complete chaos,” Curlee recalled of those initial months.
For about 10 weeks Curlee continued her White House work, despite administration officials’ public attacks against the transgender community.
“Senior staff at the new Trump administration, they all treated me very well,” she told AFP.
But on a Saturday afternoon that March, while eating barbecue with family, she got a call from her new boss. “‘You’ve been fired, but I can’t tell – I don’t know why,’” she remembered him saying.
Earlier that day, prominent far-right influencer Laura Loomer posted on X: “SCOOP: A transgender, Biden holdover who hates President Trump is still working in the NSC intel office.”
In response to an AFP inquiry on Curlee’s dismissal, a White House spokesperson said: “Anyone who writes a 3,000-word op-ed bragging about themselves while attacking the President clearly doesn’t belong in public service,” referring to The Atlantic essay.
Pence spoke warmly of Curlee on Aug 23.
“My wife and I believe in treating others the way that we’d like to be treated, with decency and respect,” Pence, a devout Christian, told CNN. “And I was heartened to hear Julia reflect that that was the experience that took place in our office.”
Curlee returned to the CIA for less than a year, finding going back to her old employer “impossible” for several reasons.
“I would spend my days walking across the CIA compound to the... unisex or family bathroom, which I could use, and it was humiliating having to do that,” she described.
Now a fellow at Lawfare, a nonprofit publication covering national security, Curlee said she hoped her story broke the transgender “caricature” fuelled by the American right to convince voters to back “an extremist agenda based on fear”. AFP

Five ways the US-Iran conflict is shifting - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:11:57 UTC
11:11:57 KST

The confrontation between the United States and Iran has entered a new phase. The war that dominated headlines earlier this year is increasingly giving way to a broader contest involving economic pressure, maritime security, diplomacy, and power. This conflict has accelerated trends across the world, ushering in a new world order.
The Trump administration has made it clear that it believes the next stage of the campaign will rely less on airstrikes and more on isolating Iran economically while maintaining military deterrence. Tehran, meanwhile, seeks to mobilize its remaining friends and demonstrate that it still retains leverage.
Here are five ways the US-Iran conflict is changing:
One: The Strait of Hormuz may be shifting from a battlefield to a shipping corridor
One of the clearest signs of the transition came today, when President Donald Trump announced that the US Navy had successfully cleared naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz. “All mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The message concerned far more than just mines. It demonstrates Washington’s intent to guarantee freedom of navigation despite Iran’s many attempts to disrupt maritime traffic. Trump also warned that Iran had been informed that any vessel attempting to lay additional mines would be “immediately and systematically destroyed.” The US has backed freedom of navigation as a policy going back to the Woodrow Wilson administration more than 100 years ago.
Currently, the US’s objective appears to be removing Iran’s leverage while reassuring global energy markets that international shipping can continue.
Two: Economic pressure has become Washington’s primary weapon
The Trump administration has signaled that economic pressure is the centerpiece of the US’s strategy.
US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent announced the launch of Operation Economic Outcast. He described it as an unprecedented campaign to financially isolate Iran.
“In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions,” Bessent said. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe.”
The Treasury Department indicates that it has mapped Iran’s financial networks, oil smuggling operations, sanctions evasion mechanisms, and funding channels linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The US’s goal is to sever what it describes as every remaining economic lifeline supporting the regime.
Unlike previous sanctions campaigns, this initiative appears designed as an open-ended global effort rather than a series of individual sanctions packages. Washington is also framing the campaign as a choice for third-world countries: align with the United States or risk becoming economically isolated alongside Iran. It remains to be seen if this will work.
Three: China is beginning to express its concern about the conflict as it inches its way into the region
The new American strategy immediately highlighted another reality: the growing importance of China. China criticized the new sanctions, warning that they would “only further intensify tensions” and arguing that its legitimate cooperation with Iran should not be disrupted. Chinese officials once again opposed what they described as unilateral American sanctions.
China has a 25-year economic deal with Iran. Notably, China benefits from the US being tied up in its fight against Iran.
Iranian officials have similarly emphasized that China remains one of Tehran’s most important partners. Iran’s Economy Minister, Seyed Ali Madanizadeh, argued that both China and Russia have shown no indication that they intend to fully comply with Washington’s new campaign.
This reflects a broader geopolitical competition. For years, Iran has looked eastward as relations with Western countries deteriorated. China has purchased Iranian oil, invested in infrastructure, and expanded political ties. Russia has likewise deepened military and strategic cooperation with Tehran. Iran expects more from China, but China has shown itself to be pragmatically cautious thus far.
As a result, the US-Iran confrontation is becoming inseparable from wider competition among major powers as the world order shifts to accommodate. The effectiveness of Operation Economic Outcast may depend not only on American enforcement, but also on whether China and Russia decide to reduce their engagement with Iran.
Four: Iran is responding to economic pressure
Iran’s response illustrates that Tehran increasingly views economic pressure as another form of warfare. Madanizadeh described the new sanctions as an “economic terrorist attack” and warned that Washington should “expect an attack” in response. “We know how to play the game too,” he said during an interview broadcast on Iranian state television.
Although the precise meaning of these comments remains unclear, Iranian leaders have sought to respond to economic pressure through so-called asymmetric means. Previous periods of sanctions have coincided with responses that included cyberattacks, threats by Iranian-backed proxy groups, maritime attacks, and efforts to disrupt regional energy infrastructure. Washington’s successes against Iranian mines imply that Iran can no longer control the tempo of war.
Five: Regional diplomacy is continuing despite war. Diplomacy has not yet evaporated
On August 25, Oman and Iran issued a joint statement following consultations between Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. They posted on social media platform X/Twitter about their new initiative.
The discussions focused on restoring safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz while respecting sovereignty. Both governments said they discussed a phased framework that could provide a practical basis for moving forward after the recent conflict.
Oman has long played a key role in regional diplomacy. The Sultanate has maintained relations with both Washington and Tehran, and has frequently served as a discreet channel for negotiations. Previous US-Iran nuclear talks also benefited from Omani mediation. This has led to US threats against Oman.
Iran is seeking to demonstrate its resilience while preserving diplomatic options through partners such as Oman. Regional states are attempting to prevent another escalation that could once again threaten global energy markets. Oman’s outreach comes after Pakistani officials visited Tehran.

sweeping bamboo roof to shape rammed-earth community center in senegal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:10:27 UTC
11:10:27 KST

a familiar typology grows to the scale of a village
A broad bamboo roof dips toward the ground around the winning proposal for the 2026 Kaira Looro Architecture Competition, tracing a loose semicircle around an open gathering space. Designed by Greece-based Afroditi Ioannidou and Vladimir Gligorovski of K-Studio, the community center takes its starting point from the traditional impluvium houses of Senegal’s Casamance region, where domestic life is organized inward around a central courtyard that gathers people, light, and rainwater. Here, that arrangement expands from the scale of the home to the scale of the village, all within a structure of rammed-earth.
The proposal has been awarded first prize in this year’s competition, organized by humanitarian nonprofit Balouo Salo around the design of a community center for rural southern Senegal. The brief asked young architects and students to imagine a place for education and collective life that could eventually be constructed by local communities themselves, using accessible techniques and natural materials without heavy machinery or specialist labor. The first-prize design is now set to move beyond the competition drawings, with construction of the winning project included as part of the award.
first prize | image by Afroditi Ioannidou, Vladimir Gligorovski
one roof gathers the community beneath it
Architects Ioannidou and Gligorovski organize the competition-winning center along an elongated, gently twisting arc. A library and study area sit alongside a larger community space, workshop and service areas, while each opens toward the graveled clearing at the center. The effect is somewhere between courtyard and amphitheater: people can occupy the rooms independently during the day, then turn toward the middle for larger meetings, performances or village events.
Much of the project’s character comes from the roof above. Its two pitches rise unevenly along the arc before dropping low toward either end, creating deeper shade where people can gather outside the enclosed rooms. The gap around the raised ridge lets hot air escape while drawing cooler air from below, allowing the center to rely on passive ventilation. Beneath the outer metal cladding, a layer of thatch adds insulation, while paired bamboo columns and beams form the primary structure.
first prize | image by Afroditi Ioannidou, Vladimir Gligorovski
simple construction methods
The architects developed that system around construction methods that could remain relatively simple on site. Locally harvested bamboo is joined with rope and galvanized wire, while independent rammed-earth volumes are formed from laterite soil found in the region. Small diamond-shaped openings perforate sections of these walls, bringing air and filtered daylight through the heavier earthen enclosures. Bamboo shutters can open the rooms almost entirely, allowing the covered spaces to expand into one larger pavilion when the community needs them.
Rain is treated with similar economy. Water falling across the large roof is directed toward handwashing stations, while the gravel at the center allows water to infiltrate into the ground during Casamance’s rainy season. The familiar inward-looking logic of the impluvium house therefore carries through the project in several ways: the center gathers people beneath its roof while gathering water through the same form.
first prize | image by Afroditi Ioannidou, Vladimir Gligorovski
the second- and third-prize winners
Kaira Looro’s brief placed those practical decisions at the center of the competition. The proposed building is intended for a rural region where villages average around 1,500 inhabitants and infrastructure remains limited, so the center is expected to accommodate everyday learning and meetings alongside workshops and larger community activities. Its construction is conceived as a participatory process as well, giving residents a role in assembling and later maintaining the building.
The jury awarded second prize to Marta Kuczynska and Jakub Czak of Poland, whose rectangular proposal wraps flexible rooms and handwoven pivoting panels around a shaded communal area. Third prize went to a Colombian team — Karol Eliana Cuellar Narváez, Jhuliana Giraldo, Juan Sebastian Piedrahita, Juan Santiago Uribe and Oscar Valencia — for a partially excavated crescent of rammed earth that uses the ground itself to temper the interior climate.
Across the three schemes, shade and self-construction emerge repeatedly as architectural tools, though the first-prize proposal makes its clearest move by enlarging a local domestic type into a piece of shared village infrastructure.
second prize | image by Marta Kuczynska, Jakub Czak
third prize | image by Karol Eliana Cuellar Narváez, Jhuliana Giraldo, Juan Sebastian Piedrahita, Juan Santiago Uribe, Oscar Valencia

Iran war drives US farmers into worst crisis in 40 years – FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:10:27 UTC
11:10:27 KST

Iran war drives US farmers into worst crisis in 40 years – FT
US grain farmers have been plunged into their worst financial crisis in four decades as the war with Iran drives up diesel and fertilizer costs, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. The latest price shock compounds years of weak crop prices and falling incomes.
The mounting pressure follows the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, which prompted Tehran to largely block commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route that previously served about a fifth of the world’s energy supplies. The resulting surge in energy costs is hitting the US heartland ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
Farmers across the Corn Belt have been particularly hard hit by soaring diesel and crop nutrient prices since the military campaign began, the FT reported. Nebraska Farmers Union president John Hansen described the downturn as the sector’s worst since the 1980s.
”Inputs are way out of whack,” Nebraska corn and soybean farmer Matt Bailey told the newspaper. He said a phosphorus-rich fertilizer used at planting now costs more than $900 per ton, compared with about $470 a decade ago.
Diesel prices have also surged after the conflict disrupted energy markets and sharply reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The nationwide average has climbed to about $5.45 per gallon from $3.81 before the war, according to US Energy Information Administration data.
”The [Iran] war has made so much uncertainty for us as farmers,” Pam Johnson, a former president of the National Corn Growers Association, told the FT. “It’s projected that farmers aren’t going to make any money for the next two years.”
The latest shock comes after several difficult years for major US crops. American Farm Bureau Federation economists estimate that growers of nine principal crops will lose about $31 billion in 2026 without federal assistance, with losses expected to reach $32 billion next year. Corn producers are projected to lose $131 per acre this year and $167 in 2027, while soybean losses are forecast at $80 and $138 respectively.
Farmers also blamed Washington’s trade disputes for weakening overseas demand, particularly for US soybeans in China. The Trump administration asked Congress in June for another $11 billion in assistance for the sector after billions of dollars in earlier payments.
Drought and unusually hot weather have compounded the pressure, damaging crops across parts of the Corn Belt, including Nebraska. Corn prices have risen as traders cut estimates for this year’s harvest, while soybeans and wheat have also rallied, fueling concerns that higher commodity costs could add to inflation already running above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.

From military alliance to economic partnership: How Trump is redefining U.S.-South Korea ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
02:06:21 UTC
11:06:21 KST

President Donald Trump's move last week to scale back annual military drills with South Korea came as Seoul finalizes hundreds of billions of dollars in investment commitments to Washington.
Trump's frustration over U.S. military spending overseas and stalled implementation of Korea's investments signal a shift in the allies' relationship from one based on security to economics, experts said.
Doubts now remain about whether investments will ensure U.S. commitments to Korea's security, as many in Seoul and Washington hoped, said Darcie Draudt‑Véjares, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. She was referring to the $350 billion Korea promised to invest in the U.S. in exchange for lower "reciprocal" tariffs last year.
"Looked at a different way, we could see a shift from a relationship centered around a military alliance to one centered around integrated industrial ecosystems," Draudt‑Véjares said. That puts "economics rather than security as the basis of the U.S.-South Korea partnership."
Trump on Aug. 16 said that he had instructed the Pentagon to cut military drills because they were "costly" and send "inappropriate and hostile" signals to North Korea.
The post was made around the time Korean Trade Minister Kim Jung-kwan arrived in Washington, D.C., to discuss the investment commitments and tariffs with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The order partly stemmed from Korea's slow pace of deploying the investments, compared to Japan, Politico reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
Trump had canceled the annual exercises in 2018 as well after his historic meeting with Kim Jong Un in Singapore. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, which traces its roots to 1954, involved around 18,000 Korean troops and an undisclosed number of American soldiers this year.
U.S. Commerce Department and the Korean Trade Ministry did not respond to CNBC's requests for comments.
Investments for security?
It would be a mistake for allies to think that increased defense spending or economic ties will buy U.S. military commitment, said Jennifer Kavanagh, senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities.
Semiconductor trade or cooperation on shipbuilding can continue, separate from the U.S. military presence in Asia, she said.
"The terms of exchange might change, but a smaller military footprint and narrower set of commitments in Asia would also free U.S. economic resources for investment at home and abroad," she said.
The two economies have deepened ties, particularly as Korean chip giants have become central to the global AI boom, with Nvidia as their most important client.
Korean businesses are benefiting from Trump's push for reindustrialization aimed at getting ahead in the competition with China.
Korean companies, for their part, have significantly increased investments across semiconductors, electric vehicles, and shipbuilding in the U.S. For example, Korean chip giant SK Hynix is building a $4 billion advanced packaging plant in Indiana and allocating $10 billion to invest in new product lines and back its U.S. business.
Read more
But not all experts are convinced that scaling back the U.S. military footprint in Asia serves American interests.
Trump's decision to cut the annual drills "further exacerbates allies' concerns of the unreliability of the U.S. as a security and economic partner," said Bruce Klingner, a former senior Central Intelligence Agency officer in the Koreas.
He added that Trump is seeking to direct American voters' attention away from the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections in November.
The shortened military exercises do not seem to have mollified North Korea. It launched more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea Thursday, the South Korean Defense Ministry said.
Richard Haass, president emeritus of the Council on Foreign Relations, said on "Squawk Box" last week that Trump's decision weakens the U.S.' credibility and leverage concerning North Korea.
The greater danger is that South Korea could pursue nuclear weapons to protect itself, and it would be "incomparably worse because it would ultimately bring in China and potentially Japan," he said. "It's a fiasco."

RIJEKA, Croatia, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Mexican twins Mia Cueva Lobato and Lia Cueva Lobato won the girls' synchronized 3m springboard title, while Russia's Matvei Pomoshnikov triumphed in the boys' Group A 1m springboard at the 2026 World Aquatics Junior Diving Championships here on Tuesday.

Mia said her focus in synchronized diving was simply to "trust the training."
Also on Tuesday, Pomoshnikov topped the podium after collecting two silvers and one bronze earlier in the championships.
Germany's Finn Awe held the lead after the preliminary scores were carried into the final, but a mistake in the fourth round opened the door for Pomoshnikov, who moved ahead and sealed victory with a competition-high 76.80 points on his final dive. He finished with 333.90 points.
Awe took silver, while Canada's Arnaud Corbeil claimed bronze.
The boys' Group B 3m springboard and girls' Group B platform will take place on Wednesday. ■

Feature: In China's Tianshan Mountains, horse jams tell a story of change
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-26
10:05:03 CST
11:05:03 KST

by Xinhua writers Yi Yangang and Zhang Yunlong
URUMQI, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- In the height of summer, China's most popular tourist sites are known for their gridlock. Deep in the Tianshan Mountains, in a Kazakh village called Qiongkushitai, the jam is made of horses, not cars, as growing numbers of tourists line up to ride into the mountains.
Ars, 24, in a checked shirt, felt hat and a pair of sneakers, sat in the saddle among the riders in the line one recent morning, his horse occasionally stopping to nibble on nearby leaves and grass as the queue moved along. He didn't seem to mind the delay.
"We're short of horses when tourist numbers peak," he said, laughing.
Guiding tourists on horseback along the northern stretch of the Wusun Ancient Trail, a historic route connecting the northern and southern sides of the Tianshan Mountains, used for centuries by traders and herders, is now Ars's job. It wasn't really his plan.
He grew up here. As a child, he played in the spruce forest along the river valley and grazed his family's herd there.
"Back then, the forest was just a forest, and the stream was just a stream," he said. Today, he said, both draw tourists eager to photograph them.
Qiongkushitai -- the name means "great platform" in Kazakh -- sits in the mountains in Tekes County, in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. For generations, it was a waypoint for herders moving between seasonal pastures, and the northern gateway to the Wusun Ancient Trail. Today it draws hikers, photographers and tourists from around the country.
The village's growing popularity has come amid a broader surge of interest in travel to Xinjiang in recent years. Demand to visit the region's grasslands, mountains and pastoral landscapes received an additional boost after the popularity of "To the Wonder," a 2024 TV drama adapted from writer Li Juan's essay collection "My Altay." The drama drew widespread attention to northern Xinjiang's scenery and slower-paced way of life.
There's no admission fee and no wall around the village. Visitors encounter not only forest, pasture and streams but also the daily life of the herding families who still live there, some of them in log cabins built from spruce and pine, joined without nails. Some have stood for nearly a century.
In recent years, some residents have begun folding traditional skills such as baking naan bread, felting wool, and making dairy products into the visitor experience, giving tourists a closer look at herding life rather than just its scenery.
Local tourism officials in Tekes County said the village had received close to 600,000 visitors this year as of early August.
Ars's family has herded livestock on a few hundred mu (one mu equals about 667 square meters) of contracted pastureland for generations. But when it came time for him to choose a path, he went to college first, enrolling at Shihezi University in 2019 -- the same year Qiongkushitai, already designated a Chinese historical and cultural village, was named among the country's first batch of key rural tourism villages.
After graduating, he chose not to stay in the city. Instead, he returned home, becoming one of more than 20 college graduates who came back to the village in recent years to work or start businesses, according to local officials.
With his family, he renovated eight aging houses and began renting them to a tourism company to run as homestays. This decision now brings in more than 100,000 yuan (about 14,700 U.S. dollars) a year, according to Ars.
Village officials said Qiongkushitai now has 167 registered homestays, up from a handful of rooms once offered informally to hikers passing through. What began as a bed and a meal has, in many cases, grown into an immersion in local customs, they said.
The village's horses have also found new value.
After local cooperatives were formed to coordinate bookings, Ars's family began entrusting its horses to one of them, earning a share of the proceeds based on how often they are hired out. According to Li Sheng, a local official involved in tourism development, two such cooperatives now manage 523 horses. Together, he said, they generated 4.5 million yuan in tourism revenue last year and are on track to exceed 5 million yuan this year.
Ars and a growing number of young people have returned to the village and are now creating new opportunities.
Some have opened homestays. Others run coffee shops, camping sites, or businesses built around Kazakh cultural traditions. They know the horses and the spruce forest, but they have also seen life beyond the mountains. Some residents say they have brought new ways of thinking about the local economy back with them.
Even so, the season is short. Road conditions and the mountain climate limit the tourist season to roughly five months. By mid-October, the weather turns colder and visitors thin out.
Ars, like many in the village, will head back to the county seat for the winter, where he has already bought an apartment. He plans to marry his girlfriend, who works there, next spring.
Winters in northern Xinjiang are long, and snow settles over the forest and the old trail.
When the grass turns green again, Ars said that he expects to be back in the saddle, riding once more through the forest he grew up in -- ready for another crowded summer. ■

SEOUL, Aug. 26 (Xinhua) -- Sentiment for South Korean businesses over the economic situation improved for a second straight month thanks to an earnings recovery in service sectors, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The composite business sentiment index (CBSI) in all industries increased 1.1 points from a month earlier to 99.6 in August, after rising 0.8 points in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea.
